article_title: Pathway to Academic Success
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021). Pathway to Academic Success Project: Intervention Report | English Learners Topic Area. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Cognitive strategies toolkit for reading and writing instruction
description: The intervention's core instructional pattern is a cognitive strategies toolkit that teachers demonstrate to students through "direct instruction, modeling, and guided practice." "The cognitive strategies include goal setting, tapping prior knowledge, asking questions, making predictions, articulating and revising understanding of text, and evaluating writing." Teachers are trained to apply the strategies to literary response, analysis of informational nonfiction, synthesis of multiple texts, and development of clear, coherent, focused essays, and to use a student writing assessment to tailor instruction.
requirements: Teachers need professional development in the toolkit and in instructional strategies for demonstrating the strategies, plus classroom materials such as posters, readings, and sentence starters
constraints: The approach was studied with English learners at intermediate English proficiency in secondary general education ELA classrooms
target_learning_goals: Analytical reading, interpretive reading, and text-based analytical writing
examples: Teachers receive model lessons based on culturally relevant texts and materials helping students apply cognitive strategies to revise a pretest writing assessment into a finished essay.
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2021). Pathway to Academic Success Project: Intervention Report | English Learners Topic Area. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/724

article_title: Fast ForWord® (English Language Learners)
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2006). WWC Intervention Report: Fast ForWord Language. http://www.scilearn.com
title: Continuously adaptive task difficulty targeting about 80% item success
description: In Fast ForWord Language, "The difﬁculty of each task is continuously adapted so that students would get about 80% of the items correct." Each of the seven exercises begins with basic skills and builds up to more complex skills, so learners work within an individually calibrated difficulty band maintained by continuous adaptation. This pattern keeps success rates near a target level while skills progress from simple to complex across the exercise sequence.
requirements: Computer-based exercises that can adjust item difficulty continuously during use
constraints: The 80% success target is stated as the design goal of this specific program's tasks
target_learning_goals: English language proficiency
reading skill
cognitive skills including memory, attention, processing, and sequencing
examples: Fast ForWord Language's seven game-like exercises each begin with basic skills and build up to more complex skills with continuously adapted difficulty
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. (2006). WWC Intervention Report: Fast ForWord Language. http://www.scilearn.com
grain_size: task/exercise level within a computer-based instructional program

article_title: Corrective Reading — Elementary
citation: Corrective Reading. (2021). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/
title: Deliver Corrective Reading in small groups with sessions 4-5 days per week for optimal achievement gains
description: The article states the program "is most effective when taught in small groups" and that "Sessions should occur 4-5 days per week for optimal achievement gains". Delivery can occur inside or outside the regular classroom, and instructors may teach multiple groups across the school day.
requirements: Instructors may include general classroom teachers, special education teachers, intervention specialists, and paraprofessionals
constraints: The frequency recommendation reflects the article's stated conditions for optimal achievement gains, not a tested comparison in the summary
target_learners: Upper-elementary struggling readers in small intervention groups
target_learning_goals: Reading achievement gains
examples: Lesson delivery can occur within the regular classroom or outside of the regular classroom (pull-out).
key_sources: Corrective Reading. (2021). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/

article_title: Core-Plus Mathematics
citation: Core-Plus Mathematics. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Core-Plus Mathematics, High School Math. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.wmich.edu/cpmp
title: Core-Plus multi-day lesson cycle: launch, small-group investigation, Checkpoint discussion, and independent task
description: Core-Plus units are organized around multi-day lessons cycling through instructional activities: a full-class launch of a problem situation with the teacher as "director and moderator"; small-group investigation in which students gather data, look for patterns, construct models, and make and verify conjectures with the teacher as facilitator; a whole-class Checkpoint discussion with the teacher as moderator; and an individual task with the teacher as "an intellectual coach". Materials promote collaborative small-group investigations followed by teacher-led whole-class summarizing that leads to analysis, abstraction, and further application.
requirements: Classroom configurations supporting small-group work in class and individual work outside class, with teacher roles shifting across director, facilitator, moderator, and coach
constraints: The cycle is described for the first edition of the curriculum reviewed by the WWC
target_learning_goals: Mathematical thinking, problem solving, and conceptual understanding through investigation of problem situations
examples: Lessons begin with a full-class discussion of a problem situation, then shift to investigating focused problems by gathering data, looking for patterns, constructing models and meanings, and making and verifying conjectures
key_sources: Core-Plus Mathematics. (2010). WWC Intervention Report: Core-Plus Mathematics, High School Math. What Works Clearinghouse, U.S. Department of Education. http://www.wmich.edu/cpmp

article_title: OnYourMark
citation: OnYourMark. (2023). OnYourMark program description and evaluation summary. https://www.onyourmark.education
title: Pair students with a consistent tutor at a small student-tutor ratio to build positive tutoring relationships
description: The program builds positive tutor-student relationships by keeping the student-tutor ratio small and "pairing students with a consistent tutor for the duration of the program". Relationship-building is treated as part of effective delivery, alongside content knowledge, in tutors' ongoing professional development.
requirements: Tutors receive initial training and ongoing professional development focused on content knowledge, building relationships, and effective delivery of the intervention
target_learning_goals: foundational early literacy skills supported through positive tutor-student relationships
examples: Students were paired with a consistent tutor for the duration of the program in 1:1 or 2:1 sessions embedded into the school day.
key_sources: OnYourMark. (2023). OnYourMark program description and evaluation summary. https://www.onyourmark.education

article_title: BookNook
citation: BookNook: Evidence Rating Strong. (2023). https://www.booknook.org
title: Keep the same tutor and small student group together so the tutor can learn each student's strengths and skill gaps
description: BookNook assigns students so that "students meet with the same tutor and small group of students to build relationships and to facilitate the tutor to develop an understanding of each student's strengths and skill gaps." The principle is that tutor-student consistency and small grouping serve relationship-building and diagnostic knowledge, which the program treats as integral to tutoring effectiveness.
requirements: A tutoring roster that keeps each student with the same tutor and the same small group across sessions
constraints: The page asserts this design rationale without reporting a separate test of the consistency mechanism itself
target_learning_goals: Reading skills addressed through tutor knowledge of individual strengths and skill gaps
examples: BookNook's model pairs each small group with one tutor across the program's 12-week, multi-session schedule.
key_sources: BookNook: Evidence Rating Strong. (2023). https://www.booknook.org

article_title: Core-Plus Mathematics Project
citation: Core-Plus Mathematics evidence review. (2019). https://www.coreplusmath.org
title: Provide teachers multi-day professional development before and during Core-Plus implementation
description: The review specifies professional development as an implementation requirement for Core-Plus Mathematics: ideally a 5-day summer workshop prior to implementation and at least 2 PD days during the first year. In the qualifying studies, teachers received up to a total of two weeks of professional development before school opening and periodically during the school year to develop understanding of the curriculum organization, content progressions, and associated instructional and assessment strategies.
requirements: Ideally a 5-day summer workshop prior to implementation and at least 2 PD days during the first year
target_learners: High school mathematics teachers implementing Core-Plus Mathematics
target_learning_goals: Understanding of the curriculum organization, content progressions, and associated instructional and assessment strategies
examples: Teachers in the qualifying studies received up to a total of two weeks of professional development before school opening and periodically during the school year
key_sources: Core-Plus Mathematics evidence review. (2019). https://www.coreplusmath.org

article_title: Connect Science
citation: Connect Science program description and evidence rating summary. (2022). https://www.connectscience.org
title: Adopt Connect Science without additional staffing, using existing classroom teachers trained through its professional development
description: The program is designed to be delivered by regular classroom teachers rather than added personnel: the article states "No additional staffing requirements." Implementation instead depends on teacher preparation through the staged professional development sequence and provision of a manual, science materials kit, and trade books, making adoption a matter of teacher training and materials rather than new hires.
requirements: Teachers complete the professional development sequence and receive the lesson manual and materials kit
constraints: Teachers will need computers to access the web for videos, resources etc.
target_learning_goals: science achievement through NGSS-aligned, service-learning instruction
examples: In the cluster randomized evaluation, treatment classroom teachers delivered the lessons after summer professional development, with no additional staff reported.
key_sources: Connect Science program description and evidence rating summary. (2022). https://evidenceforessa.org/program/connect-science/

article_title: Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use
citation: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use
title: Correctly interpret data findings to improve policy and practice
description: The brief's third key recommendation is to "Correctly interpret findings to improve policy and practice." It notes that many districts do not know how to interpret findings, positioning interpretation as a distinct capacity from data collection or question formulation. Correct interpretation is presented as the step that connects analysis to actual improvements in policy and instruction.
requirements: Districts need the capacity to interpret analysis findings, not just generate them
target_learning_goals: interpreting data findings to improve policy and instructional practice
examples: The brief suggests ways districts can overcome challenges associated with this recommendation
key_sources: Cassie Pickens Jewell, Libby Makowsky, Kristin Hallgren. (2014). Districts and Data: Developing Capacity for Effective Data Use. Issue Brief. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/districts-and-data-developing-capacity-for-effective-data-use

article_title: A Road Map for Building Evidence that Drives Learning and Improvement
citation: Kate Place, Kara Conroy, Gregory Chojnacki. (2023). A Road Map for Building Evidence that Drives Learning and Improvement. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Engage the community in focus as collaborators throughout all phases of research and design
description: Evidence-based innovation should begin by identifying a need, problem, or challenge together with the community whose goals should drive design. The publication states that "The M&E approach engages this community as collaborators throughout all phases of research and design," making sustained partnership a core feature rather than a one-time consultation.
requirements: Identify the need, problem, or challenge in partnership with the community in focus before design begins
target_learners: Communities in focus whose goals drive solution design, such as schools and districts
target_learning_goals: Ensuring solution design and evidence building align with community goals
examples: The M&E approach was applied in the evaluation of middle years math teaching and learning solutions prepared for the Gates Foundation
key_sources: Kate Place, Kara Conroy, Gregory Chojnacki. (2023). A Road Map for Building Evidence that Drives Learning and Improvement. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/a-road-map-for-building-evidence-that-drives-learning-and-improvement

article_title: Implementing Covid-19 Routine Testing in K-12 Schools: Lessons and Recommendations from Pilot Sites
citation: Divya Vohra, Patricia Rowan, John Hotchkiss, Kenneth Lim, Aimee Lansdale, So O'Neil. (2021). Implementing Covid-19 Routine Testing in K-12 Schools: Lessons and Recommendations from Pilot Sites. Mathematica Research & Evaluation.
title: Build community engagement and stakeholder buy-in, supported by effective communication and simplified informed consent, to sustain school testing programs
description: The report's implementation lessons hold that testing programs succeed when schools invest in community engagement and buy-in from key stakeholders. It states that "Community engagement and buy-in from key stakeholders are critical to the success of a testing program," and that "Effective communication and simplified informed consent processes can a long way in building trust in testing programs and boosting participation rates." Schools should therefore pair testing logistics with trust-building communication and streamlined consent.
requirements: Community engagement and buy-in from key stakeholders
Effective communication with the school community
Simplified informed consent processes
target_learners: K-12 students, teachers, and staff in schools implementing routine Covid-19 testing
target_learning_goals: Maintaining safe, trusted in-person school environments so learning can continue
examples: Pilot sites in the Rockefeller Foundation's K–12 Testing Protocol Demonstration Project implemented routine Covid-19 testing in 335 locations between September 2020 and June 2021, and Mathematica drew on their experiences to identify lessons about acceptability, feasibility, and effectiveness.
key_sources: Divya Vohra, Patricia Rowan, John Hotchkiss, Kenneth Lim, Aimee Lansdale, So O'Neil. (2021). Implementing Covid-19 Routine Testing in K-12 Schools: Lessons and Recommendations from Pilot Sites. Mathematica Research & Evaluation. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/implementing-covid-19-routine-testing-in-k-12-schools-lessons-and-recommendations-from-pilot-sites

article_title: Instructional Practices and Student Math Achievement Correlations from a Study of Math Curricula (Issue Brief)
citation: Douglas H. Clements, Roberto Agodini, Barbara Harris. (2013). Instructional Practices and Student Math Achievement: Correlations from a Study of Math Curricula (Issue Brief). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Use correlational evidence on instructional practices to generate specific hypotheses for future experimental study
description: The brief positions correlational evidence on instructional practices as a hypothesis-generating step: additional relationships observed in large studies "can suggest specific hypotheses for the future study of such instructional practices". Those future studies, in turn, are expected to produce research evidence that could inform teacher professional development and the writing of instructional materials. The principle treats correlation-based findings as inputs to a research pipeline rather than as directly actionable causal conclusions.
requirements: Correlational studies large enough to detect relationships between specific instructional practices and achievement
constraints: The brief states the results reveal relationships "largely consistent with earlier research, but not in every case", so hypotheses require further study before informing practice
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement in early elementary grades
examples: The brief reports its correlational findings explicitly as evidence that can suggest hypotheses for future study of instructional practices.
key_sources: Douglas H. Clements, Roberto Agodini, Barbara Harris. (2013). Instructional Practices and Student Math Achievement: Correlations from a Study of Math Curricula (Issue Brief). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/

article_title: Measurement Models for Behavioral Frequencies: A Comparison Between Numerically and Vaguely Quantified Reports
citation: Jamie Lynn Marincic. (2012). Measurement Models for Behavioral Frequencies: A Comparison Between Numerically and Vaguely Quantified Reports. Working Paper 10. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Choose behavioral frequency report formats with awareness that quantification format shapes measurement structure and findings
description: Survey designers collecting behavioral frequency information should treat the choice between "numerically or vaguely quantified frequency reports" as a measurement decision, not a cosmetic one. The working paper shows the two formats yield measurement models with different structure, so the format chosen "directly influences substantive findings." Format selection should therefore be justified against the intended analyses.
requirements: Researchers must anticipate the measurement model they intend to build before selecting a frequency report format.
constraints: Support comes from one experiment embedded in the 2006 National Survey of Student Engagement; the available text prints no effect sizes.
target_learners: Postsecondary students surveyed about engagement behaviors
target_learning_goals: Valid measurement of behavioral frequencies in survey-based educational research
examples: The article compared measurement models built from the two report formats using data from an experiment embedded in the 2006 National Survey of Student Engagement.
key_sources: Jamie Lynn Marincic. (2012). Measurement Models for Behavioral Frequencies: A Comparison Between Numerically and Vaguely Quantified Reports. Working Paper 10. Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/measurement-models-for-behavioral-frequencies-a-comparison-between-numerically-and-vaguely-quantified-reports

article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Assess for Early Evidence of Success (Phase 3)
citation: Ruggiero, R., Manley, M., Knechtel, V., Place, K., & Shoji, M. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Assess for Early Evidence of Success (Phase 3). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/
title: Build and evaluate learning solutions in collaboration with stakeholders from a priority community
description: The M&E Checklist frames evidence building as a collaborative activity: it "guides users through an evidence-building process to design, refine, and test a solution in collaboration with stakeholders from a priority community." Stakeholder collaboration is positioned as integral across all phases, from design through validation, rather than as an add-on at evaluation time.
requirements: Identification of a priority community and engagement of its stakeholders in each evidence-building phase
target_learning_goals: solutions associated with improved outcomes for priority-community students
examples: The checklist's stated purpose names stakeholder collaboration as part of designing, refining, and testing the solution
key_sources: Ruggiero, R., Manley, M., Knechtel, V., Place, K., & Shoji, M. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Checklist: Assess for Early Evidence of Success (Phase 3). Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/measurement-and-evaluation-checklist-assess-for-early-evidence-of-success-phase-3

article_title: Measurement and Evaluation Plan Template
citation: Kate Place, Gregory Chojnacki, Virginia Knechtel, Andy Gothro, Megan Shoji, Lindsay Fox. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Plan Template. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Co-develop the M&E plan with the implementing organization, research partner, and priority communities
description: The authors recommend that "the implementing organization and research partner work together to co-develop the M&E plan, in partnership with representatives from the priority communities." Co-development is presented as the way plans should be produced, ensuring community involvement in both solution design and evaluation design rather than plans written by one party alone.
requirements: Participation of the implementing organization, a research partner, and representatives from the priority communities
target_learners: organizations and funders commissioning evaluations of learning solutions
target_learning_goals: community-involved evaluation planning
examples: The template includes a component documenting how priority communities were and will be involved in the design of the solution and the evaluation
key_sources: Kate Place, Gregory Chojnacki, Virginia Knechtel, Andy Gothro, Megan Shoji, Lindsay Fox. (2023). Measurement and Evaluation Plan Template. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/measurement-and-evaluation-plan-template

article_title: Roadmap for Effective School-Based Practices to Support Expectant and Parenting Youth: Lessons from the New Heights Program in Washington, DC
citation: Subuhi Asheer, Susan Zief, Ruth Neild. (2020). Roadmap for Effective School-Based Practices to Support Expectant and Parenting Youth: Lessons from the New Heights Program in Washington, DC. Maternal and Child Health Journal, vol. 24. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Program elements and practices used together improved academic outcomes for New Heights participants
description: The study's central pattern is that it was the program elements and practices "when used together" that improved academic outcomes for New Heights participants, rather than any single component in isolation. The page frames this combination as defining "a possible roadmap for service providers interested in replicating the program's success". The pattern concerns a coordinated system of school-based supports for expectant and parenting students.
requirements: Elements and practices must be implemented together as a well-defined system of supports
constraints: Pattern is drawn from one school-based program in Washington, DC
target_learning_goals: improved academic outcomes
examples: The study explored the New Heights program's elements and practices and how their combined use related to improved academic outcomes for participants.
key_sources: Subuhi Asheer, Susan Zief, Ruth Neild. (2020). Roadmap for Effective School-Based Practices to Support Expectant and Parenting Youth: Lessons from the New Heights Program in Washington, DC. Maternal and Child Health Journal, vol. 24. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/roadmap-for-effective-school-based-practices-to-support-expectant-and-parenting-youth-lessons

article_title: Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief)
citation: Various authors. (2013). Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-a-coherent-plan-for-effectively-using-data
title: Develop a coherent plan for effectively using data before or alongside building data systems
description: The brief's central recommendation is that education agencies should develop a coherent plan for using data effectively, treating data use as something that requires deliberate planning rather than assuming data alone drives improvement. The brief states it "focuses on developing a coherent plan for effectively using data", positioning planning as one of three companion topics alongside developing a data system and supporting its effective use.
requirements: A coherent plan must be developed deliberately by the education system seeking effective data use
target_learning_goals: using data to inform decisions that improve classroom instruction, school performance, and student achievement
examples: The brief is one of a series; the other two briefs address considerations for developing or enhancing a data system and supporting the effective use of a data system.
key_sources: Various authors. (2013). Developing a Coherent Plan for Effectively Using Data (In Focus Brief). Princeton, NJ: Mathematica Policy Research. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/developing-a-coherent-plan-for-effectively-using-data

article_title: What Are Error Rates for Classifying Teacher and School Performance Using Value-Added Models?
citation: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2013). What Are Error Rates for Classifying Teacher and School Performance Using Value-Added Models? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 38, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications
title: Policymakers must carefully consider likely system error rates when using value-added estimates for high-stakes educator decisions
description: This principle holds that before using value-added estimates to make high-stakes decisions about educators, decision-makers should account for the likely error rates of the measurement system. The article's results show nontrivial misclassification rates, and it concludes that "policymakers must carefully consider likely system error rates when using value-added estimates to make high-stakes decisions regarding educators." The principle operationalizes the article's error-rate findings as a design consideration for educator evaluation systems.
requirements: A value-added measurement system whose likely error rates can be estimated from the amount of data available, such as one versus three years of test score gain data.
constraints: The stated error rates apply to measuring teacher and school performance in the upper elementary grades using student test score gain data.
target_learners: Upper elementary grade students whose teachers and schools are evaluated
target_learning_goals: Accurate classification of teacher and school performance for accountability decisions
examples: The article derives error rates of about 25 percent with three years of data and 35 percent with one year of data for comparing a teacher to the average, and 10 percent and 20 percent for overall false positives and false negatives.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2013). What Are Error Rates for Classifying Teacher and School Performance Using Value-Added Models? Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, vol. 38, no. 2. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/what-are-error-rates-for-classifying-teacher-and-school-performance-using-value-added-models

article_title: Error Rates in Measuring Teacher and School Performance Based on Student Test Score Gains
citation: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2010). Error Rates in Measuring Teacher and School Performance Based on Student Test Score Gains. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/
title: Policymakers should carefully consider likely system error rates before using value-added estimates for high-stakes educator decisions
description: The report recommends that performance measurement systems based on value-added estimates account for their statistical error before being used for high-stakes decisions about educators. Because simulations show error rates of roughly 25 to 35 percent for teacher comparisons under typical data conditions, the authors conclude that "policymakers must carefully consider likely system error rates when using value-added estimates to make high-stakes decisions regarding educators."
requirements: Performance measurement systems should be designed and evaluated using hypothesis-testing error rate calculations, as the report does with its OLS and Empirical Bayes error rate formulas.
constraints: Findings apply to value-added models applied to student test score gain data in the upper elementary grades; error rates depend on the number of years of data available.
target_learners: Upper elementary grade students whose teachers and schools are evaluated
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement of teacher and school performance for accountability decisions
examples: The report develops error rate formulas based on OLS and Empirical Bayes estimators and applies them in simulations of realistic performance measurement system schemes.
key_sources: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley S. Chiang. (2010). Error Rates in Measuring Teacher and School Performance Based on Student Test Score Gains. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/

article_title: A Participatory Approach to Designing a Student-Facing Dashboard for Online and Distance Education
citation: Herodotou, C., Shrestha, S., Comfort, C., Andrews, H., Mulholland, P., Bayer, V., Maguire, C., Lee, J. & Fernandez, M. (2025). A Participatory Approach to Designing a Student-Facing Dashboard for Online and Distance Education. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(2). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8481
title: Select dashboard features through a combination of student-reported usefulness, frequency of agreement, and data feasibility
description: This principle holds that participatory dashboard design should decide which features to include by weighing three factors together rather than frequency alone: what students explain as useful, how many students agree, and whether the data can actually be retrieved. The authors used it because their small, self-selected sample made frequency-based decisions invalid. It operationalizes student voice in learning analytics design.
requirements: Student explanations of usefulness collected alongside frequency counts
Access to institutional data sources to judge feasibility
constraints: With a small, self-selected sample, frequency alone cannot validly determine feature inclusion
target_learners: online and distance learning undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: study progress awareness
study planning
self-regulation
examples: The team included assignment scores, credits passed, tutorials attended, forecasts, and contact features, and excluded extensions, credits failed, and comparison data, citing usefulness, agreement, and feasibility in Table 5.
key_sources: Herodotou, C., Shrestha, S., Comfort, C., Andrews, H., Mulholland, P., Bayer, V., Maguire, C., Lee, J. & Fernandez, M. (2025). A Participatory Approach to Designing a Student-Facing Dashboard for Online and Distance Education. Journal of Learning Analytics, 12(2). https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2025.8481

article_title: "Double-Dose" Algebra as an Alternative Strategy to Remediation
citation: Takako Nomi and Elaine M. Allensworth. (2008). “Double-dose” Algebra as an Alternative Strategy to Remediation: Effects on Students’ Academic Outcomes. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Chicago. http://www.informaworld.com/smpp/content~db=all?content=10.1080/19345740802676739
title: Combine regression discontinuity with interrupted time series (and instrumental variables) to estimate policy effects when the policy affects both targeted and non-targeted students
description: When a threshold-based policy changes conditions for non-targeted students too, a standard regression discontinuity cannot estimate the policy effect, only the enrollment effect. The authors show that "combining the two designs—a regression discontinuity and a time series design we address limitations that are usually inherent in each": the discontinuity provides a within-cohort check while cohort comparisons reveal effects on non-targeted students and on students far from the cutoff, with instrumental variables addressing imperfect compliance.
requirements: Pre-policy cohorts for the time-series comparison
A sharply defined eligibility cutoff as an instrument
Attention to SUTVA violations when treatment status of other students affects outcomes
constraints: Estimates are local average treatment effects among compliers and are specific to a policy year with a given level of policy compliance
target_learners: District- and system-level policy evaluators studying ninth-grade course interventions
target_learning_goals: Causal estimation of remediation-policy effects on achievement, grades, and course failure
examples: The study used the 50th-percentile cutoff as an instrument in a within-cohort IV analysis and policy year as an instrument in a cross-cohort IV analysis, estimating effects separately for each post-policy cohort
key_sources: Takako Nomi and Elaine M. Allensworth. (2008). “Double-dose” Algebra as an Alternative Strategy to Remediation: Effects on Students’ Academic Outcomes. Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Chicago. http://www.informaworld.com/smpp/content~db=all?content=10.1080/19345740802676739

article_title: CCSR's 2007 Survey Reports for Chicago Public Schools
citation: Luppescu, Stuart, Hart, Holly, Rosenkranz, Todd, Montgomery, Nicholas, Sporte, Susan, and Sebring, Penny Bender. (2007). Consortium on Chicago School Research 2007 Individual School Survey Report. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/ISR
title: Color-coded percentile-band display for comparing a school to other schools
description: The report translates each school's measure scores into a five-band color scheme so educators can see at a glance how their school compares to other CPS schools: "Red: one standard deviation or more below average (16th perc entile or lower)" through "Green: one standard deviation above average (84th percenti le or higher)". Sub-categories and the Five Fundamentals square use the same coding, and trend displays add a star position within a gray box showing the middle two-thirds of schools.
requirements: Comparison distributions from the school system and demographically similar schools, identified using test scores, enrollment, mobility, racial composition, and neighborhood characteristics
constraints: The report cautions there is unavoidable imprecision in locating the star, so small differences between a school and the system should not be over-read
target_learners: school leadership teams, teachers, and local school councils
target_learning_goals: interpreting survey-based school climate and instruction data for improvement planning
examples: Sample Elementary's Instructional Leadership is displayed as Far Above Average while Learning Climate and Instruction are Average
key_sources: Luppescu, Stuart, Hart, Holly, Rosenkranz, Todd, Montgomery, Nicholas, Sporte, Susan, and Sebring, Penny Bender. (2007). Consortium on Chicago School Research 2007 Individual School Survey Report. http://ccsr.uchicago.edu/ISR

article_title: Declining High School Enrollment
citation: Elaine M. Allensworth & Shazia Rafiullah Miller. (2002). Declining High School Enrollment: An Exploration of Causes. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Consider a district policy's long-term effects on downstream schools before adopting it
description: The report argues that elementary-school policies reverberate through high schools in ways that should be anticipated. It shows the eighth-grade promotion gate reduced high school enrollment through retention, APC placement, faster progression, and changed special education concentrations, concluding that "before the system adopts a policy to prompt change in the elementary schools, it should be considered in light of its possible long-term effects on high schools."
requirements: District-level administrative data linking student progression across school levels, so downstream effects can be traced
constraints: The report could not isolate the promotion gate's effects from simultaneous policy changes such as new magnet schools and course-taking requirements
target_learners: high school students in urban districts
target_learning_goals: system-level policy design that anticipates cross-level consequences for student progression and school composition
examples: The 1996 CPS promotion gate shrank ninth-grade cohorts and reduced grade repetition, depressing enrollment by 11.5 percent by 1999-00 while graduation rates held steady.
key_sources: Elaine M. Allensworth & Shazia Rafiullah Miller. (2002). Declining High School Enrollment: An Exploration of Causes. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/declining-high-school-enrollment-exploration-causes

article_title: Improving Chicago's Schools
citation: Luppescu, S., Hart, H., Nagaoka, J., Easton, J. Q., & Sweeney, R. E. (2001). Pablo Neruda High School: Improving Chicago's Schools, 2001 Survey Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Enhance teachers' knowledge and skills through coherent, sustained professional development as the leading school improvement initiative
description: The report holds that enhancing teachers' knowledge and skills is arguably the single most important initiative schools can undertake to improve student learning. It warns that in many schools professional development is happenstance, left to individual choice and not organized or supported by any coherent and sustained school improvement plan. Schools should therefore assess whether learning opportunities are in place so new instructional initiatives have a greater likelihood of being implemented well.
requirements: Professional development must be organized and supported by a coherent and sustained school improvement plan rather than left to individual choice
constraints: The report notes uncoordinated professional development is a negative measure on which low levels are more desirable
target_learning_goals: Improved instructional practice to enhance student learning
examples: The report provides measures of Access to New Ideas, Quality Professional Development, and Uncoordinated Professional Development so schools can assess whether learning opportunities are in place before improvement initiatives
key_sources: Luppescu, S., Hart, H., Nagaoka, J., Easton, J. Q., & Sweeney, R. E. (2001). Pablo Neruda High School: Improving Chicago's Schools, 2001 Survey Report. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/improving-chicagos-schools-pablo-neruda-high-school

article_title: School Instructional Program Coherence
citation: Newmann, F. M., Smith, B., Allensworth, E., & Bryk, A. S. (2001). School Instructional Program Coherence: Benefits and Challenges. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Schoolwide coherence through a common literacy framework with sustained coaching support
description: Chelsea Elementary achieved strong instructional program coherence by implementing a schoolwide literacy framework based on Reading Recovery, with sustained investment in training and school-based literacy coordinators who coached teachers daily. At the time of the visit, 60 percent of teachers had taken a six-month intensive training course, and three full-time literacy coordinators visited classrooms regularly to observe, demonstrate, coach, and co-teach. An external partner staff person described it as "an 'in-your-face' approach."
requirements: Sustained investment in school-based coaching staff
All teachers, regardless of grade or assignment, working with the same framework
Leadership that persuades reluctant teachers to adopt the framework
constraints: The coherent vision of language arts instruction did not carry over into math, social studies, or science at Chelsea
target_learners: Elementary school students from working poor families in urban schools
target_learning_goals: Literacy development across all grades through common instructional practices and assessment
examples: Chelsea hired three full-time school-based literacy coordinators who offered after-school workshops, searched for materials, and visited classrooms regularly to observe, demonstrate, coach, and co-teach
key_sources: Newmann, F. M., Smith, B., Allensworth, E., & Bryk, A. S. (2001). School Instructional Program Coherence: Benefits and Challenges. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED

article_title: Parent Advisory Councils
citation: Building Better Parent Councils: A Research Brief. (2024). National Center for Families Learning. https://www.familieslearning.org
title: Shift from top-down leadership to collaborative family engagement to empower parent councils
description: The brief urges school leaders to move away from hierarchical control of family engagement. It states that "Principals, school administrators, and family-facing practitioners should shift from a top-down leadership model to a collaborative approach that empowers families across different domains of school operations," including parent advisory councils. Professional development on consensus-building and shared decision-making is offered as the supporting mechanism for leaders.
requirements: Professional development on consensus-building and shared decision-making for school leaders
target_learning_goals: shared decision-making
consensus-building
empowering families in school operations
examples: The brief recommends training school leaders in consensus-building so they can support parent councils more effectively across domains such as parent advisory councils.
key_sources: Building Better Parent Councils: A Research Brief. (2024). National Center for Families Learning. https://www.familieslearning.org

article_title: Achievement and growth norms for English MAP Reading Fluency Foundational Skills
citation: Wei He, NWEA Psychometric Solutions. (2022). Achievement and Growth Norms for English MAP Reading Fluency Foundational Skills. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org
title: Combine normative information with other evidence rather than relying on norms alone for placement and major instructional decisions
description: The report cautions that users "should exercise caution about the limited generalizability of the inferences" supported by the 2018-2019 norming data, and that placement or instructional decisions relying solely on normative performance "are likely to be less accurate". It recommends that normative information be combined with other evidence about student performance or growth when making placement or other major instructional decisions.
requirements: Access to additional evidence about student performance or growth beyond the norm-referenced score
constraints: The limitation stems from the norms being based on a single pre-pandemic (2018-2019) administration with limited generalizability
target_learners: Students in Grades K-3 whose scores are interpreted with these norms
target_learning_goals: Accurate placement and instructional decision-making in early reading
examples: The report states NWEA will continue monitoring student achievement as schools recover from pandemic-related learning loss and will update the norms as more appropriate data become available
key_sources: Wei He, NWEA Psychometric Solutions. (2022). Achievement and Growth Norms for English MAP Reading Fluency Foundational Skills. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/achievement-and-growth-norms-for-english-map-reading-fluency-foundational-skills/

article_title: Do response styles affect estimates of growth on social-emotional constructs? Evidence from four years of longitudinal survey scores
citation: James Soland, Megan Kuhfeld. (2020). Do response styles affect estimates of growth on social-emotional constructs? Evidence from four years of longitudinal survey scores. Multivariate Behavioral Research. https://www.tandfonline.com
title: When estimating growth from Likert survey scores, compare scoring models that do and do not account for response styles
description: Because response styles can affect growth parameter estimates, the article's approach is to score longitudinal surveys using IRT models that do and do not account for response styles, then compare the growth-model results. The authors "conducted empirical and simulation analyses in which we scored surveys using item response theory (IRT) models that do and do not account for response styles." This dual-scoring comparison serves as a sensitivity check for growth inferences.
requirements: Longitudinal survey data on the construct of interest
Access to IRT scoring models both with and without response-style parameters
constraints: Effects vary by psychological construct, response style, and IRT model used, so results of the comparison are not uniform
target_learners: K-12 students assessed on social-emotional constructs
target_learning_goals: Valid estimation of growth on survey-measured constructs
examples: The study scored four years of survey data under both model types and compared slope estimates in growth models
key_sources: James Soland, Megan Kuhfeld. (2020). Do response styles affect estimates of growth on social-emotional constructs? Evidence from four years of longitudinal survey scores. Multivariate Behavioral Research. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/do-response-styles-affect-estimates-of-growth-on-social-emotional-constructs-evidence-from-four-years-of-longitudinal-survey-scores-journal/

article_title: The phantom collapse of student achievement in New York
citation: John Cronin, Nate Jensen. (2014). The phantom collapse of student achievement in New York. Phi Delta Kappan 96(2), 60-66. https://www.nwea.org
title: States should closely coordinate new assessment data with existing data when switching measuring instruments
description: This principle holds that when a state adopts a different measuring instrument, the new results must be interpreted against, and coordinated with, the existing data stream so that changes in scores are not mistaken for changes in achievement. The article draws this as an explicit lesson from New York's Common Core release: "states need to closely coordinate new data with existing data when they switch to different measuring instruments." It is used to explain why the new exam results were misread as a collapse in achievement.
requirements: Existing achievement data from the prior instrument must be available for comparison when new exam results are released
constraints: The article states this need specifically for states switching to different measuring instruments, such as the move to Common Core exams
target_learners: K-12 students in states adopting new assessments
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of achievement trends across assessment transitions
examples: New York released the first results of exams under the Common Core State Standards, and the results were misread as dramatic declines in achievement
key_sources: John Cronin, Nate Jensen. (2014). The phantom collapse of student achievement in New York. Phi Delta Kappan 96(2), 60-66. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-phantom-collapse-of-student-achievement-in-new-york/

article_title: Interview Protocol for Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses
citation: Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses: Interview Protocol. (2025). Digital Promise / Achieving the Dream. https://digitalpromise.org/
title: Interview coverage spanning five question domains from platform experience to belonging
description: The protocol organizes its questions into recurring domains: general platform and structure, courseware-specific features, course content, student learning behaviors, and student perceptions and sense of belonging, closing with overall impressions and 0-10 ratings. Each domain pairs experience questions with follow-ups, such as asking what impacts a student's decision whether or not to review topics suggested by Readiness Checks, and ending with recommendation and instructor ratings from 0 to 10.
requirements: Questions from each domain should be asked within one interview session
Follow-up branches are scripted for supportive, neutral, and negative student responses
target_learning_goals: Capture holistic student experience including usability, content inclusivity, learning behaviors, and belonging
examples: Domain-specific prompts cover Introduce Yourself module, Lumen Community, Readiness Checks, Apply it Exercises, Self-Checks, Worked Example Videos, and Instructor Messages
key_sources: Voices of Undergraduate Students Taking Introductory Statistics Courses: Interview Protocol. (2025). Digital Promise / Achieving the Dream. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/05ccd902-1e80-4c94-9cd9-f706a98d0cc0

article_title: Transforming Teachers’ Knowledge for Teaching Mathematics with Technologies through Online Knowledge-Building Communities
citation: Niess, M. L., & Roschelle, J. (2018). Transforming Teachers' Knowledge for Teaching Mathematics with Technologies through Online Knowledge-Building Communities. Proceedings of the 40th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education, Greenville, SC. https://www.pmena.org/proceedings/
title: Combine practical classroom teaching experiences with knowledge-building discourse and extensive critical reflection to transform teachers' TPACK
description: The article's concluding design recommendation for teacher educators is that transforming teachers' TPACK requires practical experiences combined with community discourse and critical reflection. As printed, the work "identified the importance of combining practical experiences with opportunities for the teachers to engage in discourse through the knowledge-building communities of learners and extensive critical reflection on teaching in their classrooms." This combination lets teachers rethink, unlearn and relearn content and pedagogical strategies in light of technologies' affordances.
requirements: Access to teachers' own classrooms for practical implementation
Knowledge-building communities of learners for discourse
Extensive critical reflection on classroom teaching
constraints: The discussion notes a knowledge-building community is aspirational and would go beyond the results reported here, which emphasized individualized problems of practice
target_learning_goals: transforming TPACK toward student-centered, technology-integrated instruction
examples: In SED 594 teachers designed and taught a five-day technology-integrated unit while weekly discussing reform-based strategies online, gathering two instruction videos, student products, and multiple critical reflections
key_sources: Niess, M. L., & Roschelle, J. (2018). Transforming Teachers' Knowledge for Teaching Mathematics with Technologies through Online Knowledge-Building Communities. Proceedings of the 40th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education, Greenville, SC. https://www.pmena.org/proceedings/

article_title: Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms
citation: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210
title: Collaborate with the DLP team to align planned experimental comparisons with platform capabilities and constraints
description: The report's third consideration is that researchers should hold ongoing conversations with the platform team, since interventions must fit existing content and structure. Researchers "may need to refine their interventions/planned comparisons based on DLP capabilities and other limitations," and must learn what content can be created or modified. Higher-customization studies may require active recruitment or additional consent processes rather than drawing on the full user base.
requirements: Frequent collaboration between researcher and DLP team, especially during initial planning stages
constraints: Some platform content components cannot be modified or manipulated; studies with high customization may require the researcher to actively recruit participants
target_learners: Education researchers designing experimental comparisons within DLPs
target_learning_goals: Designing experimental contrasts that are feasible within platform constraints
examples: Researchers need to understand limits on the type of content that can be created or modified for experimental designs and the reasons for those limitations
key_sources: Schellinger, A., Zacamy, J., Roschelle, J., Closser, A., & Zepeda, C. D. (2024, April). Considerations for Conducting Research in Digital Learning Platforms. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/210

article_title: A Guide to the Adult Learning Ed-Tech Market
citation: Amber Laxton, Mike Berlin, Patti Constantakis, Ph.D. (2017). Accelerating Change: A Guide to the Adult Learning Ed-Tech Market. Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Contextualize instruction by integrating reading, math, and digital literacy into industry-specific training for workforce segments
description: The guide identifies contextualized instruction as the most critical value driver for employers and workforce channels, so that employees gain skills directly related to their industry and professional goals. It states that integrating reading, math, and digital literacy into industry-specific training is proving to be quite effective, citing examples such as airline mechanic courses that teach literacy and math through real job problems and home healthcare workers taking mobile ESL classes to communicate with doctors. Entrepreneurs serving this segment should ensure content is contextualized to a work environment or learners' daily lives.
requirements: Content must map to the specific industry and professional goals of the employing organizations
constraints: The guide's support is practitioner testimony and program examples rather than controlled evidence of effectiveness
target_learners: adult learners in employer and workforce training programs
target_learning_goals: job-related basic skills: literacy, math, digital literacy, and ESL in work contexts
career advancement and middle-skill role readiness
examples: Savannah Technical College offers airline mechanic training integrating literacy and math where those skills solve real problems on the job; Cell-Ed delivers mobile ESL to Los Angeles home healthcare workers
key_sources: Amber Laxton, Mike Berlin, Patti Constantakis, Ph.D. (2017). Accelerating Change: A Guide to the Adult Learning Ed-Tech Market. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/36eceee2-6442-4c5c-8fa1-7b9e7eab4533

article_title: An Ethical and Equitable Vision of AI in Education: Learning Across 28 Exploratory Projects
citation: Noakes, S., Shell, A., Murillo, A., Van Nostrand, P., Ruiz, P., Cornick, S., and Karim, S. (2024, October). An Ethical and Equitable Vision of AI in Education: Learning Across 28 Exploratory Projects. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/232
title: Center educators' and students' voices throughout the AI research and development process through co-design and collaboration
description: This principle holds that successful, equitable AI-enabled educational tools require deliberate collaboration with end users. The report states it is crucial to establish meaningful relationships with educators and students, "ensuring their voices are central throughout the research and development (R&D) process," so developers gain insight into authentic needs and priorities. Cohort projects such as EdLight's family co-design and KIPP Chicago's teacher co-design exemplify this approach, using sandbox environments and small-scale testing to gather feedback and iterate.
requirements: Meaningful relationships with educators and students established early in R&D
Sandbox environments for safe exploration and small-scale testing to gather feedback
target_learning_goals: Development of equitable AI-enabled educational tools that address authentic classroom needs
examples: EdLight co-designed a platform with families based on surveys, focus groups, and empathy interviews
KIPP Chicago developed AI-powered tools through the co-design efforts of its teachers
key_sources: Noakes, S., Shell, A., Murillo, A., Van Nostrand, P., Ruiz, P., Cornick, S., and Karim, S. (2024, October). An Ethical and Equitable Vision of AI in Education: Learning Across 28 Exploratory Projects. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/232

article_title: A New Narrative: How Unlocking the Power of R&D Through Inclusive Innovation Can Transform Education
citation: Smith, K., & Young, V. M. (2024). A New Narrative: How Unlocking the Power of R&D Through Inclusive Innovation Can Transform Education. Digital Promise, Center for Inclusive Innovation. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Collective Ownership requires side-by-side collaboration and intentional power distribution with communities
description: Collective Ownership recognizes that "creating effective education solutions requires side-by-side collaboration with the students, parents, families, and communities that education is meant to serve." It requires people with traditional power to embody humility that enables intentional distribution of power across the entire team, creating conditions that invite team members to lead, contribute, and take risks. The article's four R&D principles include committing to a shared understanding of collective leadership, developing a shared vision, creating a plan to co-lead implementation, and establishing shared approaches to support and sustain solutions. Superintendents must be listeners and learners with the capacity to sit back and let others lead.
requirements: District leaders must cede traditional hierarchical power and adopt listening and learning postures
Teams must establish mutually agreed-upon processes, decision-making structures, and continuous improvement cycles
target_learners: students, families, and communities historically excluded from education decision-making
target_learning_goals: equitable solution design
community ownership of education innovation
shared leadership capacity
examples: Three Pennsylvania districts (Avonworth, Hampton Township, South Fayette) supported teachers of color to design and lead Teaching is My Favorite Color, with superintendents explicitly stepping back to let teachers lead
key_sources: Smith, K., & Young, V. M. (2024). A New Narrative: How Unlocking the Power of R&D Through Inclusive Innovation Can Transform Education. Digital Promise, Center for Inclusive Innovation. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/73f2e0fa-dca8-4cd0-a8da-eb18b59453c4

article_title: Emerging Technology Adoption Framework: For PK-12 Education
citation: Ruiz, P., Richard, E., Chillmon, C., Shah, Z., Kurth, A., Fekete, A., Glazer, K., Pattenhouse, M., Fusco, J., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Lin, L., Arriola, S., Lockett, D., Crawford-Meyer, V., Karim, S., Hampton, S., & Beckford, B. (2022). Emerging technology adoption framework: For PK-12 education. [Educator CIRCLS white paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/161
title: Include the whole education community in technology evaluation and adoption decisions
description: The framework's core principle is that educational leaders, technology specialists, teachers, students, and families should all participate in evaluating and adopting emerging technologies. It was "created with education community members to help ensure that educational leaders, technology specialists, teachers, students, and families are all part of the evaluation and adoption process." Questions are addressed to each stakeholder group, and some questions can be asked of multiple members of the community.
requirements: Questions listed under the procurement decision makers and district leaders section can usually also be asked of educators
target_learning_goals: equitable, community-informed technology procurement and implementation
examples: The framework gathers feedback from researchers, policy experts, the edtech community, educators, and families
key_sources: Ruiz, P., Richard, E., Chillmon, C., Shah, Z., Kurth, A., Fekete, A., Glazer, K., Pattenhouse, M., Fusco, J., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Lin, L., Arriola, S., Lockett, D., Crawford-Meyer, V., Karim, S., Hampton, S., & Beckford, B. (2022). Emerging technology adoption framework: For PK-12 education. [Educator CIRCLS white paper]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/161

article_title: Nico & Nor Family Flyer
citation: Early Science with Nico and Nor. (2022). WGBH Educational Foundation. https://www.wgbh.org
title: Collaborative co-design process across five partner roles for early science curriculum development
description: The program was developed through a collaborative process in which five partner groups each contributed: children and families co-designed activities "helping identify everyday experiences and meaningful contexts in which science, math, and engineering could be promoted authentically"; researchers documented learning goals and facilitated research activities; curricula developers and media designers leveraged families' and educators' insights to create resources and digital tools; and teachers shared classroom needs to inform activity design. The process is summarized as "Building collaborative relationships, Centering children & families (asset-based approach), Co-designing, pilot testing and refining, Evaluating implementation & outcomes, Disseminating lessons and resources broadly."
requirements: Sustained collaboration among families, teachers, researchers, curricula developers and media designers
Iterative cycles of co-design, pilot testing and refinement
target_learning_goals: early science, math and engineering learning grounded in everyday family experiences
examples: Families tested the activities and projects in their homes, and their insights informed iterations of the curricular resources and digital tools.
key_sources: Early Science with Nico and Nor. (2022). WGBH Educational Foundation. https://www.wgbh.org

article_title: Automated Essay Scoring in Middle School Writing: Understanding Key Predictors of Students’ Growth and Comparing Artificial Intelligence- and Teacher-Generated Scores and Feedback
citation: Greene Nolan, H. L., & Vang, M. C. (2023). Automated essay scoring in middle school writing: Understanding key predictors of students' growth and comparing artificial intelligence- and teacher-generated scores and feedback. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/187
title: Use human and automated essay scoring in complementary ways that draw on the strengths of each
description: The report recommends pairing AES/AWE tools with teacher scoring rather than substituting one for the other. It argues that "human and automated essay scoring should ideally be used in complementary ways that draw on the strengths of each"—the AI's time savings, class-level data, and immediate feedback on one hand, and the teacher's holistic judgment and attention to students' humanity on the other. It further urges designers to factor teachers' knowledge, priorities, and understanding of students into AES design, and cautions current users about potential differences and biases in AI scoring.
requirements: Teachers remain involved in scoring and giving feedback alongside the tool, particularly for struggling writers
constraints: Current AES tools read and provide feedback line by line and cannot grasp essays holistically, detect voice, or judge whether ideas connect
target_learners: Middle school writing students, especially struggling writers
target_learning_goals: Argumentative writing quality and revision
examples: Topeka teachers who saw the score comparisons pivoted to teaching students how such systems work and how to judge whether AES feedback makes sense before addressing it
key_sources: Greene Nolan, H. L., & Vang, M. C. (2023). Automated essay scoring in middle school writing: Understanding key predictors of students' growth and comparing artificial intelligence- and teacher-generated scores and feedback. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/187

article_title: Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology
citation: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274
title: Co-design emerging technology tools with educators and learners as context experts
description: The report recommends that development teams partner with educators and learners throughout development, since developers cannot fully understand all contextual nuances of use. Co-design is defined as 'a process to collaboratively and iteratively design a solution that meets the authentic needs of the intended users in their contexts.' The process moves from clarifying roles through discovery of pain points, ideation, prototyping, and iterative refinement before broader deployment.
requirements: Partners should represent the diversity of lived experiences across intended user demographics; power dynamics should be shifted to elevate each voice, with fair compensation and formal acknowledgment
constraints: The report notes educators often have to retrofit what developers produce when they are left out of conversations
target_learners: educators and learners as intended users across classroom contexts
target_learning_goals: tools that authentically reflect user needs, goals, and intended use cases
examples: GIANT Remix co-designed with students, educators, and families through online bootcamps, in-person workshops, community stations, and school programs; Research-Practice-Industry Partnerships are offered as one approach
key_sources: Mills, K., Noakes, S., Pattenhouse, M., Shell, A., & Vollavanh, A. (2025). Powerful Learning with Emerging Technology. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/274

article_title: Evidence for ESSA: Number Rockets
citation: Number Rockets. (2020). Number Rockets: first-grade math tutoring program description. Tutoring provided through AIR. https://www.air.org
title: Build struggling students' conceptual understanding by sequencing tutoring from concrete tasks toward abstract tasks and procedures
description: The Number Rockets curriculum orders instruction along a concreteness fading sequence: it is "intended to build students' conceptual understanding by starting with concrete tasks and moving toward abstract tasks and procedures, including math facts." This principle recommends that small-group tutoring for struggling math students begin with manipulable, concrete activity before transitioning to abstract procedures.
requirements: A scripted curriculum that supplies the concrete-to-abstract task sequence
Tutors trained to deliver the sequence as designed
constraints: Evaluated as a Tier 2 supplement for first graders below the 38th percentile in math
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of number and operations, math facts
examples: Number Rockets sessions move from concrete tasks to abstract tasks and procedures, including math facts, across 63 days of 40-minute sessions
key_sources: Number Rockets. (2020). Number Rockets: first-grade math tutoring program description. Tutoring provided through AIR. https://www.air.org

article_title: Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom
citation: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Draw on relationships with professional colleagues and students' families for continued guidance and support
description: Social relationships and collaborative opportunities play a critical role in supporting teachers managing disruptive behavior. The guide recommends that teachers treat "parents, school personnel, and behavioral experts as allies who can provide new insights, strategies, and support" when addressing individual students' behavior problems, collaborating with other teachers, building partnerships with school, district, and community behavior experts, and encouraging families to participate as active partners in teaching and reinforcing appropriate behavior. This recommendation carries a moderate evidence rating.
requirements: Collaborate with other teachers for continued guidance and support
Build collaborative partnerships with school, district, and community behavior experts when problems warrant help from outside the classroom
Encourage parents and other family members to participate as active partners
constraints: When behavior problems warrant behavioral or mental health professionals, teachers are encouraged to ensure services address classroom behavior issues directly
target_learners: Elementary students whose behavior problems warrant support beyond the classroom teacher
target_learning_goals: Reducing individual students' problem behavior through coordinated school and home support
examples: The overview notes schools with strong, trusting staff relationships are more likely to have teachers willing to engage in new practices and consequently help produce gains in student outcomes, citing Bryk and Schneider (2002).
key_sources: Epstein, M., Atkins, M., Cullinan, D., Kutash, K., and Weaver, R. (2008). Reducing Behavior Problems in the Elementary School Classroom: A Practice Guide (NCEE #2008-012). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/4

article_title: Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools
citation: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Maintain a consistent focus on improving instruction throughout the turnaround
description: Turnaround schools should use data to set goals for instructional improvement, make changes that immediately and directly affect instruction, and continually reassess student learning and instructional practices to refocus goals. The guide reports that "All schools in the case studies focused on improving teaching and student learning by analyzing student assessment and classroom data" and by regularly monitoring progress and adjusting strategies.
requirements: Examine school-level, classroom-level, and student-level data; establish priority instructional areas; provide targeted professional development; and conduct a collaborative curriculum review aligned with state standards
constraints: In one case study of 10 schools, 8 realized they did not have access to sufficient data on student achievement to guide decision-making
target_learners: students in chronically low-performing K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: improving teaching quality and student achievement in targeted subject areas
examples: Schools disaggregated performance data by grade level and learning objectives to identify students needing help on specific skills; principals spent as much as 40 percent of their time in classrooms observing teaching
key_sources: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/7

article_title: Southwest English Learner Literacy (SWELL) Partnership
citation: Southwest English Learner Literacy (SWELL) Partnership. (2023). https://ies.ed.gov/nrel/southwest
title: Two-enhancement design: refined teacher collaboration plus CLRI role-play
description: The Write to Succeed program is refined through "two enhancements for refined teacher collaboration and culturally and linguistically relevant instruction (CLRI) role-play." Role-play is used as the practice format for embedding CLRI in instruction, and teacher collaboration practices are a measured short-term teacher outcome in the logic model.
requirements: Coaches trained to support the enhanced program components
target_learners: New Mexico teachers participating in Write to Succeed

article_title: Strategic Instruction Model (SIM)
citation: Strategic Instruction Model (SIM). (2024). University of Kansas Center for Research on Learning. https://sim.ku.edu
title: Content Literacy Continuum: tiered schoolwide literacy structure combining whole-class routines with targeted intensive instruction
description: The Content Literacy Continuum (CLC) organizes schoolwide literacy efforts into tiers: whole class/whole school instruction through CLC routines applied across classes by content and support teachers, and a targeted tier (Xtreme Reading, Learning Strategies Curriculum, Fusion) providing further support and intensive instruction to struggling readers. School schedules accommodating an additional daily reading period for targeted students

reading comprehension
decoding

Time and resources for collaborative planning of team teaching

Faculty professional development for staff coordinating and collaborating around delivery of student supports

citation: Angela Johnson, Megan Kuhfeld, Greg King. (2021). Measuring middle school achievement trajectories for college readiness. Educational Policy. https://doi.org/10.1177/08959048211006833

Student-level and school-level demographic data to model trajectory predictors

target_learning_goals: Staying on track toward college readiness benchmarks in math and reading

article_title: From High School to the Future
citation: Roderick, M., Holsapple, M., Clark, K., & Kelley-Kemple, T. (2018). From High School to the Future: Delivering on the Dream of College Graduation. description: The report organizes college choice through the concept of college match: "match schools are colleges where, on average, students who are admitted have comparable qualifications to the student," contrasted with reach schools (a stretch) and safety schools (near-certain admission). Undermatch means attending a less selective college than qualifications allow. This framework underpins the report's simulations of match and avoidance strategies and its finding that match benefits rise with student qualifications.

target_learning_goals: Making college choices that translate high school preparation into the highest chance of earning a college degree

article_title: Potholes on the Road to College
citation: Roderick, M., Coca, V., & Nagaoka, J. (2011). Potholes on the Road to College: High School Effects in Shaping Urban Students' Participation in College Application, Four-year College Enrollment, and College Match. Sociology of Education, 84(3), 178-211. https://doi.org/10.1177/0038040711411280
title: College-going climate framework: two mechanisms by which high schools shape college enrollment
description: The article proposes that urban high schools shape college enrollment among low-income students through two mechanisms: (1) ensuring that seniors who aspire to a four-year degree take the steps to apply to and enroll in a four-year college, and (2) influencing whether students enroll in colleges with selectivity levels at or above the kinds of colleges they are qualified to attend (college match). This framework distinguishes between enrollment steps (planning, applying, acceptance, enrollment) and the quality of college choice (match/undermatch). It draws on Schneider's (2007) conceptualization that effective practice is embedded in school climate and shared norms rather than isolated counseling activities.
requirements: High schools must develop organizational norms and structures that guide students through the college application process
constraints: The association between climate measures and outcomes may reflect student composition effects as well as educator behavior, since the authors note only 58 high schools at level 2 and high correlations among school-level variables constrain independent estimation
target_learning_goals: College aspiration follow-through
Effective college search and application
Enrollment in matched four-year colleges
examples: Applied to 2005 CPS graduates using SEQ, CCSR surveys, NSC tracking, and administrative records to measure both sequential steps and college match outcomes
