article_title: Passing Through Science
citation: Montgomery, N., & Allensworth, E. M., with Correa, M. (2010). Passing Through Science: The Effects of Raising Graduation Requirements in Science on Course-Taking and Academic Achievement in Chicago. Consortium on Chicago School Research at the University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/passing-through-science
title: Raising course requirements alone is insufficient to improve learning; policy must also address student engagement and the quality of classroom instruction
description: The report's central policy conclusion is that mandating course exposure changes transcripts but not learning: "Course content matters only when students are engaged in learning that content and are earning strong grades." In Chicago, most post-policy graduates earned Cs or lower in the new required science courses, suggesting minimal engagement and learning. The authors therefore argue that "policy solutions need to go beyond adding course requirements to address student engagement and the quality of classroom instruction in advanced science courses."
requirements: Schools must develop classroom instruction capable of advancing science learning in the required advanced courses, not merely schedule them.
constraints: The report grounds this in one policy, in one district, at one moment in time, in a setting where many students dropped out before benefiting from the requirements.
target_learners: All high school students subject to college-preparatory graduation requirements, including those with weak prior science preparation
target_learning_goals: Science content knowledge and college-preparatory science course completion
examples: CPS required three college-preparatory science courses beginning with 1997 ninth-graders; course completion more than doubled among graduates while most earned Cs or lower and college outcomes did not improve.

Passing Through Science: The Effects of Raising Graduation Requirements in Science on Course-Taking and Academic Achievement in Chicago. article_title: College Preparatory Curriculum for All
citation: Allensworth, E., Nomi, T., Montgomery, N., & Lee, V. E. (2009). College Preparatory Curriculum for All: Academic Consequences of Requiring Algebra and English I for Ninth Graders in Chicago. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 31(4), 367-391. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373709343471
title: Conceptual model of how curricular policy influences student outcomes through changes in the school's instructional program
description: The article proposes a conceptual model in which policy effects on academic outcomes must flow through changes in the school's instructional program: courses, content, and pedagogy. As the authors state, "any policy effects on students' academic outcomes must flow through changes in the instructional program of the school: the courses, content, and pedagogy that students receive." Enrollment combined with student response shapes ninth-grade learning, which in turn shapes later outcomes such as graduation and college enrollment. The model guided the study's three research questions distinguishing enrollment effects from total policy effects.
requirements: Schools' instructional programs must adjust to the policy as expected, and students must respond with better freshman-year performance, for beneficial effects to occur
constraints: Some schools may have difficulty enacting substantial changes in their instructional programs in ways that benefit students, and students who would otherwise take remedial classes may not respond as expected
target_learners: First-time ninth graders in urban public high schools
target_learning_goals: Ninth-grade academic performance in algebra and English, later high school achievement, graduation, and college enrollment
examples: The study traced the Chicago policy's effects through course enrollment changes, ninth-grade performance, and long-term outcomes including graduation and college enrollment

citation: Iwatani, E., Tackett, T., Tackett, K., Arnett, N., & May, P. (2021). Leveraging Community Cultural Wealth to Support K-8 CT Education in Kentucky Appalachia. IEEE. https://ieeexplore.ieee.org
title: Community cultural wealth framework: assets marginalized communities possess, in aspirational, familial, navigational, resistant, social and linguistic forms
description: The article introduces community cultural wealth as "the often underappreciated strengths and assets that marginalized communities tend to possess," drawing on Yosso's 2005 critical race theory discussion. The framework holds that this wealth takes multiple forms, including aspirational capital and familial capital, alongside navigational, resistant, social and linguistic capital. The panel uses it as the organizing lens for connecting K-8 CS/CT education in Kentucky Appalachia to local strengths.

article_title: Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models
citation: Soland, J., Thum, Y.M., & King, G. (2019). Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models: Evidence and implications from a longitudinal study. (The Collaborative for Student Growth at NWEA Working Paper). https://www.nwea.org
title: Compound Polynomial (CP) growth model for jointly estimating within-year and between-year growth
description: The CP model is a multilevel growth model whose design matrix combines a within-year (fall-to-spring) matrix with a between-year (spring-to-spring) polynomial matrix, so that both kinds of growth are estimated in one model. The authors use it "to simultaneously estimate fall-to-spring (within-year) and spring-to-spring (between-year) growth over five years using a single model," producing conditional Z-scores via contrast matrices that allow school effectiveness comparisons across timespans on a consistent sample. The preferred specification treats all coefficients as random except the within-year quadratic, which is fixed at the school level.
requirements: Requires vertically scaled test scores on a common scale (here the RIT scale) administered fall and spring so within- and between-year growth are comparable
A consistent sample of students across timespans, handled here via conditional multivariate distribution Z-scores
constraints: Excludes schools serving fewer than 10 students at a test administration as potentially anomalous
The cohort is not intact: students need at least one valid test score to remain in the sample
target_learning_goals: Estimating school contributions to student academic growth in math and reading
examples: Applied to a Southern-state cohort taking MAP Growth in fall and spring of grades 2–6, estimating school effects for 570 schools
key_sources: Soland, J., Thum, Y.M., & King, G. (2019). Reconciling long-term education policy goals with short-term school accountability models: Evidence and implications from a longitudinal study. article_title: A path to completion? The impacts of statewide articulation agreements on enrollment and attainment
citation: Greg King. (2019). A path to completion? The impacts of statewide articulation agreements on enrollment and attainment. NWEA Research white paper. https://www.nwea.org
title: College-completion crisis framing of US post-secondary policy
description: The paper frames US post-secondary policy around a completion problem: the crisis arises not solely from too few students enrolling but from enrolled students not finishing. It argues states increasingly depend on a highly skilled and educated workforce, and it cites the estimate that "over 31 million students over the last 20 years have enrolled in but not completed post-secondary education." This framing motivates policies, such as articulation agreements, that aim to reduce students leaving school prior to earning a degree.
requirements: States' workforce needs and enrollment-without-completion data as the problem definition
constraints: Framing applies to US public post-secondary education as described in the paper
target_learners: US post-secondary students, particularly those who enroll but do not complete
target_learning_goals: degree completion
reducing attrition before degree completion
examples: The paper's introduction positions articulation agreements as a state response to enrollment followed by non-completion.

article_title: The Role of Micro-Credentials in Lifelong Learning and Development: Empowering Learners, Empowering Organizations
citation: Galindo, M., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., Franklin, K., Luna, C. (2024, August). The Role of Micro-Credentials in Lifelong Learning and Development: Empowering Learners, Empowering Organizations. Digital Promise. https://doi org/10 51388/20 500 12265/225
title: Competency-based micro-credentials as a credential type distinct from macro-credentials and learning programs
description: The eBook defines micro-credentials as a type of digital credential that verifies competency in a specific skill or set of skills, contrasted with macro-credentials such as degrees and certificates. Digital Promise specifies that micro-credentials are "competency-based, research-backed, personalized, on-demand, and shareable" and use badging technology to issue verifiable certifications. Crucially, the article states micro-credentials "are not learning or training programs like courses or MOOCs" and are not completion-based or time-based; they certify skills regardless of how they were acquired, through formal or informal learning, work, and life experiences.
requirements: Assessment requires the learner to implement the new skills in a workplace setting and show evidence of this implementation, judged against rubric criteria by the issuing organization
constraints: The definition varies depending on who uses the term and in what context; in this eBook micro-credentials represent the ability to apply learning rather than the learning program itself
target_learning_goals: Verification of competency in a specific skill or set of skills
Reskilling and upskilling recognition
examples: An educator earns the Integrating Computational Thinking into Curriculum micro-credential by demonstrating how they support students using computational thinking

The Role of Micro-Credentials in Lifelong Learning and Development: Empowering Learners, Empowering Organizations. article_title: Computational Thinking for a Computational World
citation: Digital Promise. (2017). Computational Thinking for a Computational World. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Three-competency framework distinguishing coding, computer science, and computational thinking
description: The paper organizes its argument around distinctions among three linked competencies: "Coding is the practice of developing a set of instructions that a computer can understand and execute"; computer science is the study of computers and algorithmic processes including their societal impact; and computational thinking is Wing's "a way of solving problems, designing systems, and understanding human behavior that draws on concepts fundamental to computer science." It concludes coding is a technical skill, computer science an academic discipline, and computational thinking a problem-solving process applicable to any discipline. The framework underpins the paper's recommendation to integrate computational thinking across K-12 subjects without replacing computer science efforts.
requirements: Computational thinking should be recognized as valuable in its own right and simultaneously linked to coding and computer science
constraints: The paper notes current literature often fails to recognize the distinctions between computer science and computational thinking
target_learning_goals: computational thinking
problem solving across disciplines
examples: The paper diagrams the three competencies as a mutually linked triangle and reviews Wing (2006) and Bundy (2007) as sources for computational thinking's broad applicability
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2017). Computational Thinking for a Computational World. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/a84a9ab5-6541-417f-ba96-4a66715e7732

article_title: Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career
citation: Luna, C., & Weisgrau, J. (2025, March). Exponential Change Brings Exponential Choice: Navigating Life, Learning, and Career. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/244
title: Competency-based micro-credentials as verifiable recognition of specific skills
description: Micro-credentials are described as digital credentials that let individuals gain recognition for specific skills, such as coding in Python or marketing design, providing tangible proof of capabilities not reflected in traditional transcripts. When issued as verifiable credentials such as Open Badges, they align closely with competency- and skills-based models and let learners build a personalized, stackable set of qualifications. Digital Promise hosts a platform that issues hundreds of competency-based Open Badges.
requirements: Verifiable credential formats such as Open Badges
assessment artifacts acceptable for demonstrating the skill
constraints: There is yet no consensus on what artifacts are acceptable to know a skill has been demonstrated and who should be assessing them
target_learning_goals: recognition of specific demonstrated skills
customized learning pathways
examples: Companies including Meta, PwC India, Salesforce, and SAP have launched micro-credentials for over 25 digital job roles, attracting nearly 7 million all-time enrollments globally, per the World Economic Forum

article_title: Every Learner Everywhere and Lighthouse Institutions: First-Year Experiences
citation: Digital Promise. (2020). Every Learner Everywhere and Lighthouse Institutions: First-Year Experiences. https://www.everylearnereverywhere.org/
title: Multidimensional view of scaling educational innovations (Coburn)
description: The report adopts Cynthia Coburn's (2003) argument that scale in education cannot be measured by head counts or product purchases because innovations have multiple components present to varying degrees. Her conceptualization includes "depth (change in underlying pedagogical beliefs and practices), sustainability, and a shift in ownership" as well as spread measured as penetration within each educational unit. The report uses this framing to justify assessing institutional capacity rather than counting adoptions.
requirements: Assessment of scale must attend to depth, sustainability, ownership shift, and penetration within units, not just counts of participating units
target_learners: higher education institutions implementing innovations at scale
target_learning_goals: institutional capacity for improving teaching and learning
examples: The report applies this framing to judge that lighthouse changes involved only a minority of faculty and that sustainability after the grant was uncertain

article_title: Engaging English Learners with Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics
citation: Haiwen Chu, Brent Jackson. (2024). Engaging English Learners With Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Three general approaches to reasoning about equivalence: convergent, relational, and transformational
description: Adapted from Cook and colleagues (2022), this framework describes three approaches students use to reason that two objects are equivalent. In the convergent approach, "Two objects are equivalent if they are related to a third object"; in the relational approach, objects are equivalent if they serve the same purpose or share characteristics; in the transformational approach, one object can be transformed into another via a sequence of allowable moves. The brief applies the framework across K-12 content and RAMPUP activities.
requirements: Educators are told they do not need to share the categories with students or require students to classify their reasoning; the framework serves teachers listening to student thinking
constraints: The brief notes the transformational approach was not applicable in the Perspective Plane context, so the framework does not apply uniformly across all mathematical contexts
target_learners: K-12 students, including students designated as English Learners
target_learning_goals: reasoning about mathematical equivalence across domains (arithmetic, algebra, geometry, statistics)
examples: In the Mean as Point of Balance activity, students employed a mix of transformational, relational, and convergent approaches to whether two dot plots share the same point of balance
key_sources: Haiwen Chu, Brent Jackson. (2024). Engaging English Learners With Equivalence as a Crosscutting Concept in Mathematics. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED671702

article_title: Compass Care at Valor Collegiate Academies: Attendance Program Spotlight
citation: Zimiles, J., Nakamoto, J., & Boal, A. (2025). Compass Care at Valor Collegiate Academies: Attendance program spotlight. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Compass Care: a six-phase, family-centered wraparound program model for chronic absenteeism
description: Compass Care is a wraparound support model in which a dedicated Compass Care Team staff member works with chronically absent students and their caregivers over a 10-week cycle. The article describes it as "a family-centered wraparound program that leverages strengths-based practices to address the barriers that prevent students from attending and succeeding in school." The model serves 10 to 15 families per cycle and is consistently composed of six phases—referral, onboarding, engagement, action, transition, and sustainability—while remaining adaptable to school context.
requirements: A staff member from the Compass Care Team assigned to each school, implementing three to four cycles per school year
Families must consent to enrollment after outreach offering the program as support
constraints: The program can be adapted to align with the unique school context, but the six phases are constant
Piloted at a charter network of two middle schools and one high school; generalization evidence pending
target_learners: Students experiencing chronic absenteeism (missing at least 10 percent of school days)
target_learning_goals: School attendance
Academic achievement
Student social and emotional well-being
Caregiver capacity to support students
examples: At Valor Collegiate Academies, Compass Care staff reviewed chronic-absence lists, solicited school-staff input, and enrolled families through outreach by email and phone
key_sources: Zimiles, J., Nakamoto, J., & Boal, A. (2025). Compass Care at Valor Collegiate Academies: Attendance program spotlight. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED677597

article_title: Compass Care at Valor Collegiate Academies: Attendance Program Spotlight
citation: Zimiles, J., Nakamoto, J., & Boal, A. (2025). Compass Care at Valor Collegiate Academies: Attendance program spotlight. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Six-phase program cycle from referral through post-program sustainability
description: The article specifies a reusable program structure: although adaptable to school context, "Compass Care is consistently composed of six phases: referral, onboarding, engagement, action, transition, and sustainability." Referral identifies students missing at least 10 percent of school days; engagement builds rapport through nonjudgmental communication; action involves weekly student meetings and biweekly caregiver meetings with SMART goals; transition celebrates completion; sustainability adds check-ins for three months after the cycle ends.
requirements: Staff trained in the development of SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound) goals
A 10-week cycle during the school year with periodic follow-up in the subsequent three months
constraints: Some students are reenrolled in an additional cycle when challenges to attendance continue
target_learners: Chronically absent students and their caregivers in K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: Attendance improvement
Goal attainment across attendance, grades, homework, behavior, and mental health
examples: Staff complete activities such as creating safety plans and providing transportation support like metro cards or carpooling information

title: Colorado Educational Stability Grant Program (HB 18-1306)

The legislation "appropriated approximately $2.8 million in its first year," with roughly $800,000 per year awarded in competitive grants in the first 2 years and recent appropriations increasing to about $1.04 million in FY 2024–25. It supports strategies to improve attendance, grade-level promotion, and graduation while reducing disciplinary incidents and dropout, and requires coordination with local and state agencies.
requirements: Requires coordination with local and state agencies
Ongoing program subject to annual appropriations
constraints: Originally focused on youth in foster care, later broadened to include youth experiencing homelessness and youth classified as migrant

Attendance
Grade-level promotion
Graduation and completion
Reduced disciplinary incidents and dropout

article_title: From Rural Districts to Statewide Pathways: A Blueprint for Scaling Cybersecurity Workforce Development Through Regional Collaboration
citation: Babineau, K., Aso, C., Ganoo, K., Jacobs, B., Lenderman, K., Shah, Z., Smith, K., & Young, V. M. (2025). From Rural Districts to Statewide Pathways: A Blueprint for Scaling Cybersecurity Workforce Development Through Regional Collaboration. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/263

description: Collaborative Innovation is Digital Promise's research and development model underpinning its regional pathways work: "a structured process where those most directly impacted by educational challenges lead, shape, and benefit from the solutions". As an R&D model, it engages communities and schools in the co-research and co-design of innovative approaches, centering the voices of students, families, educators, and community members alongside researchers and solution developers. The report claims the resulting solutions are more effective, relevant, and responsive, particularly for rural learners and historically underserved communities, and it grounded the co-design of district cybersecurity pathways in the national initiative.

constraints: The report presents this as a guiding framework and rationale rather than a tested comparison; effectiveness claims are the authors' interpretation

article_title: Strengthening Policies and Practices for the Initial Classification of English Learners: Insights from a National Working Session
citation: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org

Common guidance should include a clear statement of purpose, a flowchart and checklist of the classification process, a screening timeframe, allowed instruments with scoring guidelines, evidence standards for detecting and correcting misclassifications, and required qualifications and training.

article_title: Thought Leadership Forum Brief: Formative Assessment and Agency as Drivers of Instructional Transformation
citation: Center on School Turnaround at WestEd. (2018). Thought Leadership Forum brief: Formative assessment and agency as drivers of instructional transformation. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://centeronschoolturnaround.org
title: Coburn's four dimensions of scale for scaling instructional change
description: The brief describes ADE's statewide formative assessment implementation plan as organized around Coburn's (2003) four dimensions of scale: depth ("deepening understanding of formative assessment to generate a change in teachers' beliefs, norms of social interaction, and pedagogical principles"), spread (more teachers, schools, districts, plus policies reflecting changed practice), shifts in ownership (from SEA/LEA or outside provider to teachers and students), and sustainability (institutionalizing the changes). The framework treats scale as more than numbers, encompassing deep and lasting change.

examples: ADE designed its statewide formative assessment implementation plan using the four dimensions, reporting accomplishments along each: shared definitions, policy changes, increased participation, committed staff, more professional learning, and a statewide community of practice

article_title: Getting Better at Getting More Equitable: Opportunities and Barriers for Using Continuous Improvement to Advance Educational Equity
citation: Valdez, A., Takahashi, S., Krausen, K., Bowman, A., & Gurrola, E. (2020). Getting better at getting more equitable: Opportunities and barriers for using continuous improvement to advance educational equity. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Continuous improvement as an umbrella term for disciplined system-improvement methodologies
description: The report frames continuous improvement as "an umbrella term to capture a range of disciplined system-improvement methodologies, including improvement science, networked improvement communities, Lean, Six Sigma, and Design-Based Implementation Research." These methodologies empirically test changes to a system by improving the interactions of people, processes, materials, and norms, and centrally include the voices of those at the front lines of the system and those who use it. The report applies this framework to examine how California education leaders use such approaches to advance educational equity.
requirements: A data infrastructure that provides feedback tied to organizational outcomes, shared improvement methodology, and leadership practices that build and sustain a continuous-improvement culture
constraints: The report notes current continuous improvement efforts in California are insufficient on their own to address persistent inequities without an intentional equity commitment
target_learners: K-12 students in California education systems, particularly students of color and other underserved student groups
target_learning_goals: Reducing disparities in learning experiences and outcomes through disciplined system improvement
examples: California's statewide system of support uses continuous improvement principles and methods, with county offices of education providing differentiated assistance such as needs assessments and root-cause analyses
key_sources: Valdez, A., Takahashi, S., Krausen, K., Bowman, A., & Gurrola, E. (2020). Getting better at getting more equitable: Opportunities and barriers for using continuous improvement to advance educational equity. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED606089

article_title: Reimagining Excellence: A Blueprint for Integrating Social and Emotional Well-Being and Academic Excellence in Schools
citation: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://selcenter.wested.org
title: Use a collaborative, data-driven cycle of inquiry with students and families as co-constructors
description: The blueprint "promotes a data-driven cycle of inquiry" intended as a collaborative process of ongoing self-reflection in which educators, leaders, students, and school communities question and adapt traditional methods based on input from, and co-construction with, students, families, and community stakeholders. Valuing student and family agency means co-creating services and supports with them rather than delivering services and supports to them. Issues identified during implementation should be seen not as deficits, but as fertile ground for growth.
requirements: Include representatives from all stakeholder groups, including students and families, to interpret and analyze data used to inform the decision-making process
Establish procedures to collect reliable and valid data multiple times per year to inform program planning, monitoring, and improvement
constraints: The blueprint acknowledges that embracing continuous improvement means taking risks and inevitably needing to deal with failures, since at least some well-planned interventions will not work out
target_learners: All students, with families and community stakeholders as co-constructors of the program
target_learning_goals: Continuous improvement of integrated equity, well-being, and academic outcomes
examples: The leadership dimension directs teams to allow stakeholders, including students and families, to co-design, co-lead, and co-refine the program with multiple ways to engage in evaluation and improvement
key_sources: Reimagining Excellence: A blueprint for integrating social and emotional well-being and academic excellence in schools. (2021). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED613077

article_title: Serving the Whole Person: An Alignment and Coherence Guide for Local Education Agencies
citation: Walrond, N. (2021). Serving the whole person: An alignment and coherence guide for local education agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/whole-person-alignment-and-coherence-guide-for-local-education-agencies
title: Conditions for equitable learning and development framework: personal, school, and system conditions
description: The guide organizes the conditions needed for equitable learning and development into three categories drawn from ecological models of development. As the guide states, "the conditions for equitable learning and development can be organized into three categories": personal conditions (health and well-being of students and adults), school conditions (climate, culture, safety, connectedness, belonging, and responsive relationships), and system conditions (policies, funding, and cross-agency collaboration beyond the school's direct control). The framework anchors Chapter 4's activity, in which teams rate each initiative's impact on the three condition types.
requirements: District teams must map each whole-person initiative against the personal, school, and system conditions to use the framework as intended in Chapter 4
constraints: System conditions are described as beyond the direct control of the school, so school-level teams depend on SEA and cross-agency collaboration for that category
target_learning_goals: equitable academic, social, and emotional learning and development
examples: In Chapter 4, a hypothetical district rates initiatives such as a family connection initiative and culturally responsive teaching professional learning on a 0-3 Likert scale for their impact on personal, school, and system conditions

article_title: Redefining Approaches for Engaging English Learners with Mathematical Ideas
citation: Chu, H., Tran, T., & Hamburger, L. (2022). Redefining approaches for engaging English Learners with mathematical ideas. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/
title: Concept images and example spaces as the basis for an ongoing process of defining
description: The brief draws on Vinner's notion of concept images—the working examples and illustrative instances learners use to make meaning—and on Watson and Mason's example spaces, proposing that students explore different example spaces from which they can later articulate concise descriptions of key properties. Through an ongoing process of defining, students develop what Molina terms "simple but deep" definitions or working definitions that are just enough to offer access to ideas for deeper exploration.
requirements: Students need opportunities to explore examples, including borderline cases, before verbal descriptions of essential properties are formalized.
target_learners: secondary English Learners in mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: generating and refining working definitions of mathematical concepts
connecting informal uses of terms to formal definitions
examples: Students may explore the arithmetic mean as a point of balance and later connect this idea to the standard algorithm for calculating the mean, a procedure the brief says is often conflated with the definition.

article_title: Reimagining School Safety: A Guide for Schools and Communities
citation: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Codesign school safety with those kept farthest from institutional power as equal collaborators
description: Because human systems are designed by humans and are inherently not neutral, the guide argues that safety is typically defined by people operating at a satellite level and implemented top-down. Equitable design requires "zooming in" to the voices and experiences of those on the margins: "Centering those who are kept farthest from institutional power means more than just inviting them to offer their feedback or to be part of the conversation; instead, they should be codesigners, equally participating as collaborators in the process of reimagining school safety." It also requires "zooming out" to examine the larger systems and structures that cause harm.
requirements: Those kept farthest from institutional power must participate as equal codesigners and collaborators, not only as feedback providers.
constraints: The guide states that without zooming out to institutional structures, policies only address harm at individual or interpersonal levels, so the harm is likely to happen again.
target_learning_goals: equitable school safety policy design
shared power and agency in design processes
examples: The guide suggests using the Relationship Mapping Strategy to identify which students have at least one positive connection to at least one adult, and profiles Forest Park Middle School staff codesigning school climate with students.
key_sources: Trout, L., Pate, C., Wu, K., & McKenna, J. (2022). Reimagining school safety: A guide for schools and communities. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED628885

article_title: Navigating the Landscape of Data Literacy: It IS Complex
citation: Mandinach, E. B., & Gummer, E. S. (2012). Navigating the Landscape of Data Literacy: It IS Complex. White paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED535250
title: Cognitive framework of data literacy as declarative, schematic, procedural, and strategic knowledge
description: The paper applies a cognitive framework from science education research to characterize the facets of data literacy. It states that "The cognitive framework identifies declarative, schematic, procedural, and strategic knowledge components that need to be addressed to ensure effective use of data by educators." Declarative knowledge is knowing that (language and terminology of data use), schematic is knowing why (purposes of data sources), procedural is knowing how (how data are organized and analyzed), and strategic is knowing when, where, and how to apply data literacy. The paper also identifies a volitional component of reflective, improvement-seeking educators that was neither expected nor found in the text analyses.
requirements: All four knowledge components need to be addressed to ensure effective use of data by educators
constraints: The volitional component was not identified in the text analyses and was not expected by the authors
target_learning_goals: using data effectively to inform educational practice
examples: Participants' pre-meeting definitions were cognitively analyzed using this framework to discern the knowledge and skills they saw as components of data literacy
key_sources: Mandinach, E. B., & Gummer, E. S. (2012). Navigating the Landscape of Data Literacy: It IS Complex. White paper. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED582807

article_title: Building an Early Learning System That Works: Next Steps for California
citation: Melnick, H., Meloy, B., Gardner, M., Wechsler, M., & Maier, A. (2018). Building an early learning system that works: Next steps for California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/early-learning-ca
title: Promising county-level coordination practices: centralized eligibility lists, streamlined multi-agency collaboration, and pooled QRIS resources
description: Across its county case studies, the report identifies a recurring pattern of local practices that partially offset state-level fragmentation. San Mateo and San Luis Obispo counties "coordinate resources and have streamlined processes for families and providers"; San Francisco and Sacramento counties "maintain centralized waiting lists for ECE programs to efficiently link eligible families with available slots"; and seven Northern California counties "have pooled resources to develop a more comprehensive QRIS and offer stronger incentives and training than any county could offer on its own." These practices emerge where local agencies fund coordination themselves despite lacking state support.
requirements: Local funding sources to sustain coordination activities the state no longer funds, such as centralized eligibility lists
constraints: State and federal administrative structures still create the underlying tangle; local administrators "struggle to undo the administrative tangle created by the state and federal governments"
target_learners: Families and children birth to age 5 navigating county ECE systems in California
target_learning_goals: Access to subsidized early care and education and connection to programs matching family needs
examples: Sacramento's Child Action Inc. maintains a voluntary countywide centralized eligibility list using its own assessment process
San Francisco is piloting Child Care Connections, a centralized list designed to match slots with family preferences
Seven Northern California counties pool resources for a shared, more comprehensive QRIS

article_title: Community Schools as an Effective School Improvement Strategy: A Review of the Evidence
citation: Maier, A., Daniel, J., Oakes, J., & Lam, L. (2017). Community schools as an effective school improvement strategy: A review of the evidence. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/community-schools-effective-school-improvement-report
title: The four-pillar framework of community schools
description: The report organizes the community schools approach around four common features, or pillars: integrated student supports, expanded learning time and opportunities, family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership and practice. The review states that although community schools vary by local context, four features—or pillars—appear in most community schools and support the conditions for teaching and learning found in high-quality schools. The framework structures the report's evidence review: each pillar is reviewed in its own chapter, and the pillars are mapped onto characteristics of high-quality schools (Table 3, Figure 1) and onto addressing out-of-school barriers to learning.
requirements: A comprehensive approach bringing all pillars together requires changes to existing structures, practices, and partnerships at school sites
constraints: Community schools vary in the programs they offer and the ways they operate, depending on their local context; successful community schools do not all look alike
target_learners: children and adults served by community schools
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
attendance and engagement
social-emotional and physical well-being
closing opportunity and achievement gaps
examples: The report's Table 3 maps the four pillars onto characteristics of high-quality schools, and Figure 1 illustrates what the four pillars look like in action

article_title: Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity through the Every Student Succeeds Act
citation: Cook-Harvey, C.M., Darling-Hammond, L., Lam, L., Mercer, C., & Roc, M. (2016). Equity and ESSA: Leveraging Educational Opportunity Through the Every Student Succeeds Act. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/equity-essa
title: CORE districts' multiple-measures accountability system spanning academic and social-emotional domains
description: The California Office to Reform Education (CORE) districts, a network of 10 districts that secured an ESEA flexibility waiver in 2013, use a multiple measures accountability system with two domains: Academic Achievement, including growth and achievement on state English Language Arts and math tests, graduation rates, and an 8th grade on-track-to-graduate rate; and Social/Emotional and School Culture and Climate, including "measures of social-emotional skills; suspension/expulsion rates; chronic absenteeism; culture/climate surveys from students, staff, and parents; and English learner redesignation rates." students at risk of disengaging from school

social-emotional skills
positive school climate

article_title: Community Schools the New Mexico Way
citation: Oakes, J., & Espinoza, D. (2020). Community schools the New Mexico way. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/improving-education-new-mexico-way
title: Community schools framework: four pillars for a whole-child, whole-school, whole-community approach
description: The report describes community schools as an approach in which schools partner with local communities to provide high-quality teaching plus additional resources and supports that mitigate barriers poverty erects. It is explicitly "an approach to schooling based on evidence-based principles, rather than a 'program'" and is built on "four pillars—integrated health and social supports, expanded learning time and opportunities, strong family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership and practice" that meet community needs and use community assets. Together the pillars provide more than wraparound services, using a whole child, whole school, whole community redesign of schools.

constraints: The report notes New Mexico's community schools vary considerably in the extent and quality of their implementation and, as a consequence, in their achievements

Practices include de-escalation, conflict resolution through dialogue and reparation of harm, attention to signs of trauma, healing-oriented practices such as mindfulness and counseling, and instruction that builds on students' cultures and identities while reducing bias.

article_title: Developing Effective Principals: What Kind of Learning Matters?
citation: Darling-Hammond, L., Wechsler, M. E., Levin, S., Leung-Gagné, M., & Tozer, S. (2022). Developing effective principals: What kind of learning matters? [Report]. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/641.201

proactive recruitment
cohort or network structures
applied learning including extended internships with mentors
curriculum focused on instruction, organization, people, and change

organizational development
change management

The report describes them as associated with reduced absenteeism, improved academic outcomes, and more positive school climates, and notes statewide initiatives in California, Maryland, New Mexico, New York, and Vermont.

school engagement

title: Community Integrated Data System for coordinating student supports

article_title: Oakland International High School: A Thriving Community School for Oakland's Newcomer Students
citation: Charlie Thompson. (2023). Oakland International High School: A Thriving Community School for Oakland's Newcomer Students. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org
title: Language-embedded, project-based college-preparatory curriculum integrating content and language objectives
description: At Oakland International, all students learn English language skills alongside academic content within college-preparatory courses, using a project-based curriculum centered on students' lives and cultures. Teachers pair a content objective (the "bricks") with a language objective (the "mortar") in every subject, group students heterogeneously across grades and language backgrounds, and end units with performance-based assessments. article_title: Striving for Relationship-Centered Schools: Insights from a Community-Based Transformation Campaign
citation: Hernández, L. H., & Rivero, E. (2023). Striving for relationship-centered schools: Insights from a community-based transformation campaign. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/621.856
title: Community organizing cycle as a model for school transformation
description: The report describes the community organizing cycle as the change model embodied by the RCS campaign. It explains that this cycle "seeks to build collaborative power in relationship-centered and incremental ways and to elevate the voices of often marginalized groups in change efforts." Key dimensions include a focus on relationship-building, deliberate efforts to ensure diverse actors can share experiences and concerns to identify actionable issues, and leadership development through educational campaigns and training sessions that expand reach and build alliances. This model positions youth, educators, and leaders as co-drivers of equity-oriented continuous improvement rather than recipients of top-down reform.

constraints: Because the approach is modeled after the community organizing cycle, relationship-centered transformation manifests differently in local settings

Understanding of systemic racism and education inequity
examples: CFJ chapter or after-school meetings serve as a forum for leadership development, engaging students in discussions of critical issues and opportunities to hone interpersonal and leadership competencies

article_title: Teacher Residencies: State and Federal Policy to Support Comprehensive Teacher Preparation
citation: Saunders, R., Fitz, J., DiNapoli, M. A., Jr., & Kini, T. (2024). Teacher residencies: State and federal policy to support comprehensive teacher preparation. Learning Policy Institute & EdPrepLab. https://doi.org/10.54300/358.825
title: Common elements of high-quality teacher residencies
description: Research on graduate-level residency programs with demonstrated strong outcomes identifies a set of common design elements that distinguish residencies from traditional and most alternative preparation pathways. Well-designed residencies "consist of strong partnerships between local education agencies and teacher preparation programs," require a full year of residency alongside an accomplished mentor teacher who is the teacher of record, tightly integrate coursework with classroom practice, place cohorts in teaching schools, offer post-residency mentoring, recruit diverse candidates for district needs, and provide financial support in exchange for a multiyear teaching commitment.

a full year of residency working alongside an accomplished mentor teacher who is the teacher of record
coursework tightly integrated with classroom practice
financial support for residents, often in exchange for a multiyear district teaching commitment
constraints: These features reflect evidence collected from graduate-level teacher residency programs; newer undergraduate and no-service-requirement variations have yet to be studied, per the report.
target_learners: postbaccalaureate and undergraduate teacher candidates preparing for PK–12 teaching
target_learning_goals: comprehensive clinical teacher preparation
teacher effectiveness and retention in high-need districts and subject areas
examples: State policies in the 12 states studied reflect most or all of these features, and the federal Teacher Quality Partnership grant program incorporates them.

article_title: Educating for Equity: Alder Graduate School's Teacher Residency
citation: Yun, C., Fitz, J., Nakajima, T., & Mauerman, C. (2025). Educating for equity: Alder Graduate School's teacher residency. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/812.965
title: Yearlong coteaching residency with gradual release into full instructional responsibility
description: Alder's clinical model places residents 4 days per week in selected school sites as coteachers with mentor teachers, using a coteaching and gradual release model. Residents teach at least one component of the school day from the first day of school, share all lesson plans with mentors before leading instruction, complete monthly "takeover days" in fall, and move to full takeover weeks in spring. Gradual release documents for each month suggest activities, responsibilities, and foci for residents, mentors, and clinical directors, and mentors and residents may customize the model.

target_learning_goals: Development of instructional practice, professional identity, and full classroom leadership readiness
examples: Takeover days served the dual function of freeing mentors' time to attend Mentor Seminar while scaffolding residents' readiness for full spring takeover weeks

citation: Swain, W., Leung-Gagné, M., Maier, A., & Rubinstein, C. (2025). Community schools impact on student outcomes: Evidence from California. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/541.498
title: Community schools four-pillar whole-child framework
description: The report describes community schools as an evidence-based strategy in which students, families, educators, and community partners organize in- and out-of-school resources, aiming to "improve learning conditions and support the well-being of students, families, and communities through four core pillars of integrated student supports, expanded learning opportunities, collaborative leadership, and family engagement." California's state-approved CCSPP framework extends this into four areas (pillars, key conditions for learning, cornerstone commitments, proven practices) broken into 16 features that grantees align to. The framework functions as a design anchor for transformative systems change rather than isolated service expansion.
requirements: Grantees are expected to align their work and reporting with the framework's four areas and 16 features to ensure a comprehensive whole-child approach
constraints: Specific programs and services vary by local context; the approach depends on local adaptation rather than a fixed model
target_learners: Pre-K through high school students in high-need California schools
target_learning_goals: Improved attendance and engagement
Academic growth in math and English language arts
Reduced exclusionary discipline
Student social and emotional development
examples: The CCSPP implementation grants funded community school coordinators, asset mapping, advisory councils, and integrated supports aligned to the framework across 2,493 school sites
key_sources: Swain, W., Leung-Gagné, M., Maier, A., & Rubinstein, C. (2025). Community schools impact on student outcomes: Evidence from California. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/541.498

article_title: Community Schools: An Evidence-Based Strategy for Equitable School Improvement
citation: Oakes, J., Maier, A., & Daniel, J. (2017). Community Schools: An Evidence-Based Strategy for Equitable School Improvement. Boulder, CO: National Education Policy Center. http://nepc.colorado.edu/publication/equitable-community-schools
title: Community schools framework: four pillars creating conditions where all children learn
description: The brief describes community schools as a place-based strategy in which "schools partner with community agencies and local government to provide an integrated focus on academics, health and social services, youth and community development, and community engagement." Four pillars appear in most community schools: integrated student supports, expanded learning time and opportunities, family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership and practices. The pillars emerged from a comprehensive review of community schools research, are often organized by a full-time community schools coordinator, and align with evidence-based features of good schools.
requirements: A full-time community schools coordinator typically organizes the pillars and conducts needs assessments, partners with agencies, and tracks program data
constraints: Community schools vary in the programs they offer and the way they operate, depending on local context, needs, assets, and school system capacities
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement
Attendance and behavior
Social, emotional, and physical development
examples: The Tulsa Area Community Schools Initiative used a holistic community schools model including all four pillars, offering comprehensive services and community voice in governance

article_title: Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges
citation: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center
title: Completion pathways as integrated institutional designs for student progress
description: Completion pathways are the central design concept of the guide: "integrated sets of institutional policies, practices, and programs that are intentionally designed to maximize students' progress at each point of their community college experience, from the time students first consider attending the community college to their attainment of a credential." The guide positions developing strong completion pathways as a key attribute of a high-performing college and the chief means of raising completion while containing costs, maintaining open access, and ensuring quality. It stresses that pathways require systemic and structural change across all instructional programming and student support services, not isolated best practices at a single stage.
requirements: Colleges must revisit and be prepared to redesign all aspects of their education endeavor, with faculty, staff, and administrators working across organizational silos
constraints: The guide states there is no single model for developing effective completion pathways across colleges
target_learners: community college students, especially low-income students
target_learning_goals: increased credential completion rates
examples: The guide's eight design principles and the loss and momentum framework operationalize what a completion pathway must address
key_sources: Nodine, T., Venezia, A., and Bracco, K. (2011). Changing Course: A Guide to Increasing Student Completion in Community Colleges. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://knowledgecenter.completionbydesign.org/knowledge-center

article_title: Promising Models for Preparing a Diverse, High-Quality Early Childhood Workforce
citation: Gardner, M., Melnick, H., Meloy, B., & Barajas, J. (2019). Promising models for preparing a diverse, high-quality early childhood workforce. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/preparing-diverse-high-quality-early-childhood-workforce
title: Six common features of promising early educator preparation models
description: Across three case studies targeting different workforce segments, the report identifies shared design features: "Local early educator pipelines and pathways," relationship-building among students, instructors, and staff; "Opportunities for clinical practice in feedback-rich environments"; multifaceted student supports; well-supported and diverse staffs of instructors, advisors, and coaches; and community partnerships and funding to strengthen preparation. The report suggests these features may be developed locally and supported at the state level.
requirements: Dedicated staff who understand their local context, plus partnerships and funding that provide financial supports, student teaching opportunities, and classroom space
constraints: The features were observed in three California case study programs and New Jersey's state-level example; the report presents them as promising rather than proven at scale
target_learners: Diverse current and future early educators of children birth to age 5
target_learning_goals: Effective early childhood teaching practice, credential and degree attainment, and persistence through preparation
examples: All three case study programs create cohorts of students who take coursework and advance through their preparation together.

article_title: The College Promise Guidebook for California and Beyond
citation: Rauner, Lundquist, & Smith. (2019). The College Promise Guidebook for California and Beyond. WestEd. https://californiacollegepromise.wested.org/guidebookresources/
title: College Promise as a comprehensive place-based access and completion model combining financial assistance, student support services, early messaging, and cross-sector collaboration
description: The Guidebook frames College Promise as more than financial aid: "A strong program also provides students and their families with targeted student support services and early messaging about program benefits and requirements." Programs are collaborative, engaging education institutions, nonprofits, local government, and philanthropy, and increasingly serve part-time students, GED completers, and incumbent workers alongside recent high school graduates attending full time. More than 300 programs across 44 states are reported nationwide. The model aligns with California's Vision for Success goals of increasing completion and transfer and reducing equity gaps.
requirements: Collaboration across education segments and community sectors
Financial support combined with targeted student support services
constraints: The majority of programs target recent high school graduates attending full time, though eligibility is broadening

target_learning_goals: postsecondary access, persistence, certificate and degree completion, and transfer
examples: California's AB19 allocated $46 million in the 2018–2019 state budget, allowing schools to cover one year of tuition fees for first-time, full-time community college students

article_title: State Strategies for Investing in Community Schools
citation: Maier, A., & Rivera-Rodriguez, A. (2023). State strategies for investing in community schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/612.402
title: The four-pillar framework of community schools: integrated student supports, expanded learning time, family and community engagement, and collaborative leadership
description: The report organizes community schools implementation around four evidence-based pillars, or features: "(1) integrated student supports, (2) expanded learning time, (3) family and community engagement, and (4) collaborative leadership." State grant programs use these pillars to structure allowable uses of funds—New Mexico implementation grants, Vermont grants, and Georgia's certification process all fund activities mapped to the pillars. The framework functions as the report's organizing account of what a community school is and does, alongside practices grounded in the science of learning and development such as trauma-informed supports.
requirements: Implementation requires organizing in- and out-of-school resources, supports, and opportunities across educators, families, community members, and students as partners.
constraints: The report notes the strategy "takes time and resources to put into place" and, when implemented well, is associated with improved student outcomes.
target_learners: K-12 students in high-need schools and districts
target_learning_goals: Student attendance, academic achievement, high school graduation, and healthy development
examples: New Mexico implementation grant funds support a full-time community school coordinator with flexibility for expenditures supporting the four pillars; Georgia's Whole Child Model pairs the pillars with five whole child tenets (healthy, safe, engaged, supported, challenged).

article_title: Survey Development for Assessing Student Computing Career Intentions. Technical Report
citation: Kao, Y., Murphy, D., Hubbard Cheuoua, A., Kannan, P., Tsan, J., Jennings, K. E., Smith, H., Emanuel, S., & Miller, E. R. (2023). Survey development for assessing student computing career intentions: Technical report. WestEd. https://wested.org
title: Computing career intentions survey instrument (32-item full version and 12-item short form)
description: A brief, culturally sensitive survey measuring computing career intentions, developed by WestEd with Google and validated through cognitive interviews, a small-scale field test, and a large-scale field test. The full version has 32 computing-related items across seven constructs, administered as 5-point Likert items in matrix questions. A reduced 12-item version was selected for embedding in longer program evaluation surveys, with items chosen for content, readability, factor loadings, DIF categories, and classical statistics.

constraints: Some items showed ceiling effects, making them less than ideal for measuring changes over time; several demographic comparison groups fell below the recommended minimum group size of 200 for DIF analysis

target_learning_goals: assessing coding self-efficacy, interest, career intention, practical and social support, and sense of belonging in computing
examples: Participants responded between August 22, 2022, and October 24, 2022, spending an average of 5.5 minutes to complete it

article_title: Coaching at Scale: A Strategy for Strengthening the Early Learning Workforce
citation: Schachner, A., Yun, C., Melnick, H., & Barajas, J. (2024). Coaching at scale: A strategy for strengthening the early learning workforce. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/984.909
title: Coaching as a collaborative expert-practitioner relationship distinct from technical assistance, mentoring, and supervision
description: The report defines coaching as a distinct professional learning mechanism: "there is general agreement in the field that coaching involves a collaborative relationship between an expert and a practitioner with the aim of developing specific knowledge and skills through the use of planning, observation, action (e.g., modeling), feedback, and reflection." The report distinguishes coaching from technical assistance (which may not involve a collaborative relationship and can address noninstructional topics), from mentoring (typically between colleagues in similar roles), and from supervision (which evaluates job performance). In its purest form, coaching is distinct from supervisory and compliance functions.
requirements: A collaborative relationship between an expert coach and a practitioner aimed at developing specific knowledge and skills
constraints: Coaching is distinct from supervisory and compliance functions in its purest form, though some supervisors may act as coaches
target_learners: Early childhood educators and program leaders
target_learning_goals: Development of specific instructional knowledge and skills
examples: Coaching recipients are typically lead classroom educators, but coaches may also work with teaching teams including assistants and aides, and with program leaders on leadership knowledge and skills.

article_title: New Mexico Community Schools: Improving Student Opportunities and Outcomes
citation: Germain, E., Maier, A., & Espinoza, D. (2025). New Mexico community schools: Improving student opportunities and outcomes. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/new-mexico-community-schools-outcomes-brief
title: Community schools as a whole-child strategy partnering with local organizations and families
description: The brief defines community schools, quoting the New Mexico PED, as "a whole child, comprehensive strategy to transform schools into places where educators, local community members, families, and students work together to strengthen conditions for student learning and healthy development." Schools achieve this by partnering with local organizations and families to organize in- and out-of-school resources such as health services, meals, and after-school programming. The strategy is positioned as an equity-centered, evidence-based approach to school transformation.

target_learners: K-12 students, particularly in under-resourced communities
target_learning_goals: Conditions for student learning and healthy development
examples: Los Padillas, Peñasco, and Roswell sites organized health clinics, food distributions, after-school programming, and family engagement structures under the strategy.

article_title: Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems: What Is the Role of Performance Assessments?
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2025). Instructionally relevant assessment systems: What is the role of performance assessments? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/411.469
title: Constants-and-knobs framework for designing performance assessments by purpose
description: The report frames performance assessment design as governed by constants and knobs. Constants are the non-negotiables true of all high-quality performance assessments: designed for targeted high expectations, open-ended and generative, equitable and accessible to all, requiring authentic sense-making, and including clear evaluation criteria. Knobs are variable features turned based on philosophy, priority, purpose, and goals, including student choice/agency, connection to student identities, disciplinary sophistication, transfer, creativity, collaboration, integration across domains, student reflection, range of evidence, and coverage. No single task attends equally to all knobs; a series of tasks over time can reveal a complete picture of student learning.
requirements: Constants must be present for performance assessments to be trustworthy measures of student learning
constraints: No single performance task will measure all knobs equally; a given assessment may foreground some knobs and background others
target_learning_goals: authentic sense-making
demonstration of knowledge, skills, and abilities
examples: A student portfolio and defense may suit graduation readiness decisions but be less useful as a stand-alone curriculum-embedded task for assessing progress at a point in time
key_sources: Badrinarayan, A. (2025). Instructionally relevant assessment systems: What is the role of performance assessments? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/411.469

article_title: Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems: What Is the Role of Performance Assessments?
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2025). Instructionally relevant assessment systems: What is the role of performance assessments? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/411.469
title: Common tasks and rubrics with calibrated scoring for system-level performance assessment
description: Large-scale systems using performance assessments rely on common tasks or sets of calibrated tasks designed for common rubrics that can be reliably used and scored across classrooms and contexts. Systems may give all students the same task, one of a set of equated tasks, curriculum-embedded tasks, or options for equated assessments connected to the statewide summative. Reliable scoring depends on clear, evidence-based rubrics and trustworthy, calibrated ratings among scorers, often using expert-vetted student work benchmarks to anchor training and calibration.
requirements: Clear, evidence-based rubrics field-tested and validated on a wide range of student work; rater training building shared conceptual understanding and consistent rubric application
constraints: Locally developed tasks lacking these features should not be used within large-scale systems
target_learners: K-12 students in state, district, and national assessment programs
target_learning_goals: comparable and trustworthy measurement of student performance
examples: AP, IB, and NAEP develop rubrics from content-specific research on learning, expert responses, task-based student work, and cognitive labs; some systems use trained local teachers with a central audit of a representative sample of scored work
key_sources: Badrinarayan, A. (2025). Instructionally relevant assessment systems: What is the role of performance assessments? Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/411.469

article_title: Community Schools in Rural California: Leveraging Shared Resources in West Kern County
citation: Hernández, L., & Germain, E. (2026). Community schools in rural California: Leveraging shared resources in West Kern County. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/643.620
title: Coherent cross-district professional development system for community school personnel

The report states "these capacity-building opportunities coalesced to create a coherent professional development system, which is a critical systems-level support for high-quality community school implementation." target_learning_goals: Professional capacity for family engagement, service connection, and community school implementation

article_title: Teacher Residencies in Texas: Supporting Successful Implementation
citation: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., Ralph, K., Snyder, J., Bland, J. A., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Teacher residencies in Texas: Supporting successful implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/630.675
title: Contextualized preparation model of teacher residencies
description: The Texas Education Agency framed the TCLAS residency model as "contextualized preparation": teachers are prepared within the district where they will work, learning from district context and culture, engaged in daily practice-based learning in district classrooms, coached daily by a high-quality mentor teacher, and building relationships within the school community during preparation. The report describes this as a departure from licensure systems premised on teachers being equally ready to work at any school in the state.
requirements: District–EPP partnership with shared ownership over preparation, support, and success of the resident
constraints: Preparation is shaped to the needs and goals of the specific partner district rather than transferable statewide

examples: TEA launch materials asked district leaders to imagine incoming teachers prepared in the district prior to day 1, with daily coaching from a high-quality mentor teacher

article_title: Community Schools in Lynwood Unified: Building Capacity for Districtwide Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934
title: Clearly define the community school coordinator's skills, responsibilities, and position classification before hiring to support selection and onboarding
description: Because the community school coordinator is a role that previously did not exist in most schools, the report recommends defining its skills, disposition, and classification up front. The report states that "Clearly defining the skills, responsibilities, disposition, and position classification for the community school coordinator helped ensure the right people were hired and enabled a smooth onboarding process." Lynwood sought people with commitment to community, familiarity with existing resources, and relationship-building ability, and designated the position as classified management so coordinators could lead on campus without being diverted into certificated duties.
requirements: District vision for the coordinator role; a job description emphasizing relationship-building, assets and needs assessment, and governance committee development; collaboration with principals and unions
constraints: Classification choice (classified management) was made on the recommendation of the Los Angeles County Office of Education and may not transfer to districts with different labor contexts
target_learners: New community school coordinators and the students and families they serve
target_learning_goals: Effective coordination of integrated student supports and community school implementation
examples: Lynwood listed the coordinator position as classified management, onboarded coordinators by meeting with every campus entity to set expectations, and clarified collaboration points with community liaisons.
key_sources: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934

article_title: Community Schools in Lynwood Unified: Building Capacity for Districtwide Implementation
citation: Germain, E., Klevan, S., & Espinoza, D. (2026). Community schools in Lynwood Unified: Building capacity for districtwide implementation. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/947.934
title: Community schools as a whole child transformation strategy anchored by a cross-boundary coordinator role
description: The report frames community schools as an evidence-based school transformation strategy that unites students, families, educators, and community partners to improve learning and well-being through a whole child approach. Its central organizing concept is the coordinator: "a school-based staff member not traditionally found in schools, who is charged with organizing access to a range of public and private resources tailored to student and family needs and weaving them into the fabric and daily operations of the school." Coordinators act as cross-boundary leaders and connectors between schools, community partners, and families, and require targeted capacity building because the role is new and distinct from typical school positions.

article_title: AgentSchool: An LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Simulation for Education
citation: Yulei Ye, Wenhao Li, Zhong Wen, Yunshu Huang, Yichen Hu, Zifan Wei, Yige Wang, Xinyu Xie, Haoxuan Yang, Yanjun Huang, Ruijia Li, Hong Qian, Yu Song, Bo Jiang, Bingdong Li, Lijun Li, Bo Zhang, Pinlong Cai, Xingcheng Xu, Shuangye Chen, Xia Hu, Liang He, Aimin Zhou, Jingjing Qu, Jing Shao, Xiangfeng Wang. (2026). AgentSchool: An LLM-Powered Multi-Agent Simulation for Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30144
title: Cognitively growable student agents with weighted knowledge graphs, thinking-workflow pools, and explicit misconceptions
description: Student agents are stateful learners rather than fixed personas. The paper states that "AgentSchool implements these components as a dialogue memory repository, a weighted subject knowledge graph, and a weighted thinking workflow pool," plus explicit misconception objects with persistence scores and stable learner attributes. Mastery updates follow a bounded transition formula combining instructional exposure quality, learner uptake, decay, and scaffolded support, so weakness can be localized to a node or subgraph and misconceptions persist until challenged.

Observable performance treated as evidence for inferring internal state, not as the state itself
constraints: The mastery update formula is an explicit update interface, not a claim that learning reduces to a single number

target_learning_goals: Concept mastery
misconception repair
thinking-workflow development
examples: A misconception is stored as a competing edge or false proposition with a persistence value, letting teacher agents target high-persistence misconceptions through conflict, analogy, demonstration, or guided questioning

article_title: Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does
citation: Hou, X., Weng, Y., Yeh, C. H., Lee, D. L., Zheng, L., Li, F., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22993
title: The contingency dimension: separating the load a system carries from the demand it places on the learner
description: The paper defines a design axis on which tutor designs sit: "We call the line those positions lie on thecontingency dimension, and contingent tutoring is movement along it during a task." Structuring changes how much load the system carries; problematizing changes how much demand the learner faces. Existing LLM tutors fix one position at design time; contingent tutoring moves along the dimension during a task, escalating after failure and fading after success. The theory has three parts: direction (the contingent shift rule), unit (decision points), and warrant (what justifies fading).
requirements: A signal the tutor can read from the learner's writing to decide when support rises and falls
constraints: Positions of prior systems on the dimension are illustrative; the warrant part was tested only on a text-channel tutor with authored decision points
target_learners: adult novice programmers using AI tutors
target_learning_goals: regulatory work such as deciding, articulating and judging before help arrives
examples: Table 1 places prior LLM systems and the three study tutors on the dimension as five properties: withholds, structures, gates, escalates, fades
key_sources: Hou, X., Weng, Y., Yeh, C. H., Lee, D. L., Zheng, L., Li, F., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22993

article_title: Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does
citation: Hou, X., Weng, Y., Yeh, C. H., Lee, D. L., Zheng, L., Li, F., Wang, W., & Liu, Y. (2026). Adaptive Scaffolding Needs Contingency: An AI Tutor That Escalates and Fades on What the Learner Does. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22993
title: CoMeT: a browser-based contingent AI programming tutor with a support ladder over authored decision points
description: CoMeT is "a browser-based environment in which a learner works through a short programming task beside a chat tutor", with a sketchpad and code editor. Tasks run three gated phases (Planning with the editor locked, Monitoring, Evaluating), and correctness is decided by authored test cases, never by the model. Tutor C escalates one rung at a time through three asks (Socratic question, specific hint, contrasting case), concedes a point after R = 3 rounds, and returns to the first rung on take-up; coverage is decided by authored patterns rather than holistic model judgement.
requirements: Decision points must be authored per task and phase, with coverage patterns and scaffold wording, so the difference between tutors is auditable
constraints: All three tutors ran on the same model backbone (Claude Haiku 4.5); take-up where patterns do not settle it falls to a one-word model judgement and a length threshold that errs on the learner's side
target_learners: adult learners with no prior programming threshold through over five years of Python experience
target_learning_goals: settling the decisions a program turns on before code is written
monitoring and evaluating one's own solution

description: The article argues that threshold-based accountability frameworks oversimplify institutional performance because institutions just below a cutoff are treated identically to those far below it, masking meaningful incremental differences.
