citation: Veronica Pimenova, Chris Lee, Baramee Bhakdibhumi, Simon Chu, and Andrew Begel. (2026). Leveling the Playing Field: Temporal Video Segmentation for Individuals with ADHD in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.24612
title: Cognitive load framing of instructional video barriers for learners with ADHD
description: The article organizes its intervention around Cognitive Load Theory's three load types and working memory constraints. It states that "CLT emphasizes that reducing extraneous cognitive load while optimizing intrinsic and germane loads should enhance comprehension," and draws on the phonological loop account to explain why ADHD learners may lose verbal instructions before acting on them. Segmentation with pauses is presented as reducing extraneous load and supporting dual-channel integration in line with Mayer's segmenting principle.
requirements: Instructional content that can be decomposed into complete semantic units aligned with logical learning activities
constraints: Benefits are predicted to be largest for learners with low prior knowledge or limited working memory capacity, per the expertise reversal effect the article cites

managing extraneous cognitive load during video instruction
examples: The study applied the segmenting principle by injecting 4-second system-defined pauses after logical actions in Scratch instructional videos

article_title: Agreement Is Not Quality: Blind Expert Verification of Human and LLM Qualitative Coding When Human Consensus Is Not Ground Truth
citation: Liu, A., Esbenshade, L., Xiao, M., Tian, V., Zhang, Z., He, K., & Sun, M. (2026). Agreement Is Not Quality: Blind Expert Verification of Human and LLM Qualitative Coding When Human Consensus Is Not Ground Truth. Preprint, no identifier printed in text.
title: Code-level division-of-labor framework for allocating qualitative coding between human coders and LLMs
description: A two-dimensional classification that triangulates how often human and LLM coders converge (human-LLM Jaccard) with which source an independent blind expert prefers when they diverge (endorsement on contested applications). The article states the division of labor "cannot be determined from agreement alone; it requires a two-dimensional classification considering both how often sources converge and which source an expert prefers when they diverge". Applied to the 72-code instrument it yields four categories with full code lists in the article’s Appendix B: Automatable (6 codes), LLM-assisted (16 codes), LLM-preferred (12 codes), and Human required (15 codes).
requirements: Model evaluation on the target instrument should precede deployment, since the gap between the best and worst model is far larger than the gap between the best model and the best human coder.
The division of labor should be set at the code level using the two-dimensional assessment; the article states blanket decisions in either direction are suboptimal.
Confidence-based triage should be used only after testing that high-confidence annotations are in fact endorsed more often than low-confidence ones for the chosen model.
constraints: Findings rest on a single codebook and a single dataset, so the specific codes identified as automatable or human-required may not generalize to other domains, data structures, or coding approaches.
The aggregate finding of no human-LLM preference is conditional on the mix of five verified models selected under a fixed verification budget.
target_learners: Researchers designing large-scale qualitative coding pipelines
Education researchers evaluating LLM-assisted annotation of educator or learner data
target_learning_goals: Valid, reliably evaluated qualitative coding of educational data at scale
Appropriate delegation of coding work between human coders and LLM systems
examples: Automatable codes combine Jaccard above 0.40 with comparable or higher LLM endorsement; four codes meet both criteria fully (Grading, Special Education (IEP), Entire Lesson Planning, Unit Planning) and two are automatable with light human review.
LLM-assisted codes show moderate agreement (Jaccard 0.20 to 0.40) with adequate LLM endorsement, where the confidence lift averages 40 percentage points.

LLM-preferred codes such as Inquiry and Deep Questions and Research and Source Analysis show low agreement but consistent verifier endorsement of LLM application, so replacing human coding there would improve rather than degrade quality.
key_sources: Liu, A., Esbenshade, L., Xiao, M., Tian, V., Zhang, Z., He, K., & Sun, M. (2026). Agreement Is Not Quality: Blind Expert Verification of Human and LLM Qualitative Coding When Human Consensus Is Not Ground Truth. Preprint, no identifier printed in text. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28890

article_title: Enacting Constructive Conflicts with AI Agents to Enhance Reconsideration among Novice Interaction Designers
citation: Howard Ziyu Han, Nikolas Martelaro. (2026). Enacting Constructive Conflicts with AI Agents to Enhance Reconsideration among Novice Interaction Designers. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04166
title: Constructive conflict grounded in agonistic pluralism as a design-learning framework
description: The article grounds its agent in agonistic pluralism, which "reframes collective decision-making as “grounded in productive conflict,” where competing values are continuously contested rather than reconciled." Building on this, adversarial design creates "spaces of confrontation" to challenge assumptions, positioning constructive conflict as a means to reveal hidden assumptions and negotiate design implications. The framework treats stakeholder disagreement as productive rather than something to be resolved, and the authors operationalize it as sustained, steerable pushback rather than one-shot critique.
requirements: Approaches that help designers actively engage with stakeholder tensions, since simply inviting tensions into the room does not automatically translate into better design outcomes and can fall into tokenism
constraints: In participatory design practice there is often a push toward harmony and consensus, which can inadvertently silence important disagreements
target_learners: Novice designers working on multi-stakeholder design problems
target_learning_goals: Surfacing hidden assumptions and stakeholder tensions rather than resolving differences prematurely
examples: The Stepwise Guidance condition translated the framework into written prompts mirroring the agent's system prompts

Generative AI is described as most valuable when it preserves student agency and requires students to explain, verify, and extend their own reasoning.

title: Make direct correction of bot responses, not abstract prompt writing, the primary authoring unit for teacher-facing AI tutor tools

The article argues this "transforms an abstract engineering task into a familiar pedagogical one," leveraging teachers' deep experience giving corrective feedback on student work. PromptDecipher implements this by making "the modification directly on the simulated tutoring chat — not the prompt — the primary unit of authoring."

article_title: The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices
citation: Eimler, S.C., Erle, L., Flood, D., Haiman, A., Häckert, L., Helgert, A., McGinness, L., Yapici, B. (2026). The Environmental Cost of LLMs in AIED: Reporting and Practices. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.11215
title: CodeCarbon: open-source Python package for estimating carbon emissions of local AI workloads
description: CodeCarbon is an open-source, lightweight Python package that measures the power draw of local hardware and estimates carbon intensity using assumptions about the local electricity grid. It queries hardware interfaces to measure instantaneous wattage over the duration of a computational process; when low-level measurements are unavailable it assumes the hardware uses 50% of its Thermal Design Power, falling back to global constants such as 85W for a CPU. The article proposes it be used to report total CO2 estimates with AIED publications.
requirements: Access to local hardware interfaces for power measurement, or hardware detectable via internally stored TDP lookup tables
constraints: Dynamic tracking of hardware usually underestimates total energy consumption by approximately 20% because software tracking cannot profile power supply unit inefficiencies, cooling systems, or peripheral devices
It effectively defaults to a PUE-equivalent of 1.0, so local measurements may not represent the footprint of models deployed in local production environments
target_learners: AIED researchers publishing educational AI systems
target_learning_goals: Transparent reporting of the environmental cost of educational AI research
examples: The article suggests stating a total CO2 estimate after the abstract but before the introduction of a paper, e.g., reporting carbon intensity per minute of tutoring for a tutoring system or per question graded for an automated grading system

citation: Olaoye DD, Owolabi HO and Olaoye OT (2026). Automated software scoring of senior school certificate examination mathematical items in economics using a contextual similarity model. Front. Educ. 11:1669504. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1669504
title: Contextual similarity scoring model for automated essay grading
description: The article's scoring framework matches a student's response to an examiner-supplied model answer using semantic contextual search similarity, returning a similarity index of 0–1 that is multiplied by the item's allotted marks. Its matching phase "combines the similarity algorithm (answer matching), which are Generic Words (GW), Longest Common Subsequence (LCS), and Semantic Distance (SD)", weighted by each algorithm's strength. The model begins with tokenization or normalization of the two strings and considers all possible ways examinees could phrase responses, so it awards scores without manual training on many model answers.

Student responses collected in a web-based environment

article_title: BEAGLE: Behavior-Enforced Agent for Grounded Learner Emulation
citation: Hanchen David Wang, Clayton Cohn, Zifan Xu, Siyuan Guo, Gautam Biswas, Meiyi Ma. (2026). BEAGLE: Behavior-Enforced Agent for Grounded Learner Emulation. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13280
title: Competency bias and the multi-dimensional fidelity problem for LLM student simulation
description: The article names competency bias as "the inherent tendency of preference-tuned models to produce correct solutions even when prompted to simulate novice students", and frames simulating learners as a multi-dimensional fidelity problem with behavioral, epistemic, and perceptual components. Behavioral infidelity is the linear construction trap avoiding iterative trial-and-error; epistemic infidelity is the curse of incompetence, where LLMs act as masked experts who diagnose errors before execution; perceptual infidelity is RLHF-flattened output diversity. BEAGLE is designed explicitly against these three objectives.
requirements: Authentic student behavior is treated as emerging from SRL processes (cognition, metacognition, motivation/affect) rather than outcome quality, so fidelity objectives must be defined over process distributions, not correctness
constraints: The framework targets open-ended problem-solving trajectories in coding-embedded domains; porting requires a knowledge component taxonomy and action schema
target_learners: novice learners in open-ended programming and physics problem-solving environments
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning behaviors including planning, enacting, monitoring, and reflecting during problem solving
examples: Fig. 1 contrast: real students debug persistently (D→D: 28%) while LLM-generated students dominate continuous construction transitions and bypass debugging

article_title: Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction
citation: Li Li, Yu Cao. (2025). Awareness of Technological Isomorphism: Integrating AI into Elementary Mathematics Teaching on Data and Prediction, A Case Study of the Compound Line Graph.
title: Compound Line Graph lesson (Jiangsu Education Edition, Grade 5) integrating AI prediction comparison into mathematics instruction
description: A Stage 2 lesson built on the textbook's vacuum-flask temperature dataset, in which "The lesson was organized into three instructional segments: Mathematical Inquiry (15 minutes), AI Prediction Comparison (8 minutes), and Reflection on Prediction Failures (5 minutes)." Students construct compound line graphs, estimate when the stainless steel flask reaches 70°C (around the 130-minute point, dropping about 6°C per 30 minutes), compare their estimates with an AI prediction, and then reflect on a prediction failure caused by an opened lid. Mathematical literacy objectives are core; AI cognitive objectives are extended.

Introduction after students have mastered data extraction and trend analysis using single-line graphs

description: CogTax classifies bash commands covered in a course by two integrated dimensions: "cognitive complexity (C)" and "operational impact (O)". Integration follows L = max(C,O), so a command's level is set by whichever dimension is higher, ensuring instructors and students must address both conceptual mastery and operational awareness.

article_title: Chat Debugging: An Exploratory Study of Human-AI Collaboration to Debug Analog Circuits
citation: John Hu and Andrew J. Ash. (2026). Chat Debugging: An Exploratory Study of Human-AI Collaboration to Debug Analog Circuits. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02955
title: Cognitive task analysis of troubleshooting identifies human pain points that human-LLM collaboration is positioned to address
description: The paper builds on cognitive task analysis models that frame debugging as multi-step processes, including Katz's model of understanding the system, testing, locating errors, and repairing errors, and Johnson's model of problem space construction and reduction. It identifies three human pain points: limited hypothesis generation, lack of experience, and working memory overflow during problem space reduction. LLMs are positioned to supply experience recall, hypothesis generation, reasoning, and planning, while humans contribute hands-on measurements. The article states that "a case library that stores relevant past experiences as advice for the learner" is one of Jonassen's three essential components.
requirements: The framework presupposes structured functional or topological system representations for effective selective search of the problem space
constraints: The article notes early cognitive models omitted experience, which Jonassen's architecture was proposed to capture
target_learners: undergraduate electrical and computer engineering students
target_learning_goals: analog circuit debugging and troubleshooting skill
examples: The study maps observed student-LLM chat logs onto these pain points, using the models to interpret where LLMs compensate for novice deficits

article_title: Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks
citation: Paul A. Jewsbury and Steven W. Nydick and Manqian Liao and Siyuan (Marco) Chen. (2026). Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13590v1
title: Consensus calibration: a divide-and-conquer Bayesian procedure that reconstructs the pooled posterior of an evolving IRT item bank from independently calibrated periods
description: Consensus calibration treats recalibration as a divide-and-conquer Bayesian computation: each time period is calibrated independently and the period posteriors are combined without revisiting earlier data. The procedure works in two layers — per-draw robust characteristic-curve linking to a common metric, then precision-weighted aggregation in which the prior contributed by each period is removed and a single consensus prior is reinstated. The article states that "The correction targets the posterior dispersion, not only its location", and that an update's cost scales with the new data rather than the full history.
requirements: Disjoint examinee samples across periods so period likelihoods are conditionally independent
Simple structure: each item loads on a single latent dimension
Aggregate anchor invariance across periods
Gaussian summaries of each period's item posterior, prior contribution, and population-coefficient posterior
constraints: Cross-period conditional independence requires disjoint examinee samples, since substantial overlap would count some responses more than once
The factors combined are plug-in Gaussian summaries of each period's hierarchical posterior, an approximation whose validity was assessed empirically in the benchmark comparison
The aggregation targets each item's marginal posterior; the joint dependence across items induced by shared hyperparameters and common linking constants is not reconstructed
target_learners: language-assessment examinees (e.g., Duolingo English Test test takers)
target_learning_goals: accurate item calibration and test scoring in continuously evolving assessment item banks
examples: Applied to four consecutive quarterly calibration periods of the Duolingo English Test, each with tens of thousands of items and hundreds of thousands of examinees, and compared against a pooled single-run benchmark
key_sources: Paul A. Jewsbury and Steven W. Nydick and Manqian Liao and Siyuan (Marco) Chen. (2026). Bayesian Consensus Calibration of Continuously Evolving IRT Item Banks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13590

citation: Cohn, C., Ashwin T S, Mohammed, N., & Biswas, G. (2026). CoTAL: Human-in-the-Loop Prompt Engineering for Generalizable Formative Assessment Scoring and Feedback. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02323
title: CoTAL: a three-phase framework unifying Evidence-Centered Design, human-in-the-loop prompt engineering, chain-of-thought prompting, and active learning for formative assessment scoring
description: CoTAL is an LLM-based approach to formative assessment scoring defined as an approach "that(1)leveragesEvidence-CenteredDesign(ECD)toalignassessments andrubrics with curriculum goals, (2) applieshuman-in-the-loopprompt engineering to automate responsescoring,and(3)incorporateschain-of-thought(CoT)promptingandteacherandstudent feedback to iteratively refine questions, rubrics, and LLM prompts." Phase I is human-driven assessment and rubric development; Phase II co-develops and optimizes prompts via response scoring with inter-rater reliability, prompt development with few-shot CoT exemplars, and active learning against a validation set; Phase III deploys the refined prompt in classrooms and uses teacher and student critique to refine questions, rubrics, and prompts.
requirements: Human consensus scoring with Cohen's κ reaching at least 0.70 before prompt development, with disagreement 'sticking points' documented and used as few-shot exemplars
Few-shot examples balanced across subscores, including at least one positive and one negative instance per subscore (multi-label) or one instance per score (multi-class)
constraints: The authors found the LLM tended to overfit when few-shot instances were numerous or CoT chains too granular, so they insert only a single instance during active learning
Token limitations in GPT-4's context window prohibited active learning in the Debugging Task
target_learners: K-12 STEM+C students (sixth-grade, ages 11-12 in the study)
target_learning_goals: Formative assessment of cross-domain science, computing, and engineering understanding, including conservation of matter, computational modeling, and fair-test engineering reasoning
examples: Teachers and researchers applied ECD to develop the SPICE curriculum's Rules, Debugging, and Engineering formative assessments; prompt patterns used included persona, context manager, template, and meta language creation patterns.

title: CogMath-948 dataset of eighth-grade math interactions with cognitive state annotations
description: CogMath-948 is a dataset the authors constructed from real educational scenarios because suitable open datasets were lacking for fine-grained cognitive evolution research. It "covers real learning data from 1,245 eighth-grade students over six months", with four dimensions per interaction: question and response information, reflective explanations of reasoning or error causes, ICAP-based cognitive engagement labels, and fine-grained misconception classifications for incorrect answers. It serves as the evaluation corpus for all CogEvolution comparisons and ablations.

article_title: CogEvolution: A Human-like Generative Educational Agent to Simulate Student's Cognitive Evolution
citation: Wei Zhang, Yihang Cheng, Zhirong Ye & Kezhen Huang. (2026). CogEvolution: A Human-like Generative Educational Agent to Simulate Student's Cognitive Evolution. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14786v1
title: CogEvolution framework: ICAP perception, IRT-based memory retrieval, and evolutionary cognitive state update
description: CogEvolution is a generative educational agent architecture that shifts from static personas to dynamic cognitive flow. It "consists of three highly coupled components": a Cognitive Adapter for depth perception mapping interaction features to a probability distribution over the four ICAP levels; an IRT-Driven Memory Retrieval Module that scores hybrid semantic and structural (item-characteristic-curve) similarity to decide whether to reuse an old schema or trigger confusion and exploration; and an Evolutionary Cognitive State Update Mechanism using a mutation-selection-update cycle in which LLM-generated cognitive hypotheses are fitness-evaluated under a ZPD constraint and integrated with a step size set by the ICAP-based cognitive evolution rate. The update magnitude depends on cognitive engagement depth: passive participation yields minor mutations while constructive participation allows significant structural restructuring.
requirements: Perceived cognitive conflict (input not fully explained by the current knowledge structure) to trigger mutation
A ZPD-formalized search radius constraining hypothesis fitness, penalizing excessive leaps or stagnation
A memory bank of interaction quadruples and a structural-similarity threshold for schema reuse
constraints: Evaluated on eighth-grade mathematics practice data (CogMath-948); the article's claims are about simulated student cognitive evolution in that setting
target_learning_goals: modeling knowledge internalization, transfer, and cognitive state transitions during practice
examples: The agent outputs behavioral decisions, mastery confidence probabilities for AUC/RMSE evaluation, and an alignment check marking low-confidence steps when the semantic alignment coefficient falls below the threshold

article_title: Catching The Correct Answer Trap: Characterising AI Tutor Blind Spots When Analysing Student Reasoning
citation: Moiz Imran and Sahan Bulathwela. (2026). Catching TheCorrectAnswerTrap: Characterising AI Tutor Blind Spots When Analysing Student Reasoning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23925
title: The correct answer trap and coincidental correctness paths as an account of AI reasoning-assessment failure
description: The correct answer trap (CAT) is the paper's named failure mode in AI misconception detection: models under-detect misconceptions when students reach a correct answer via flawed reasoning, because "if a model treats correctness as evidence of understanding, systematic under-detection of misconceptions will prevail". The paper explains item-level vulnerability through a "coincidental correctness path", a form of what Kapur calls "unproductive success", where common flawed procedures happen to produce the correct output for the specific values chosen. The account draws on assessment design theory, including Barton's principle that a diagnostic question should not be answerable correctly while a key misconception is held, and the procedural/conceptual knowledge distinction of Hiebert and Lefevre.
requirements: Detection systems must evaluate student reasoning explanations, not only final answers, for the trap to be assessed at all
constraints: Characterised within mathematics education on the Eedi dataset; whether the trap extends systematically to other domains and populations remains an open question per the authors
target_learners: school mathematics students on the Eedi tutoring platform
target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis of student misconceptions in mathematics reasoning
examples: Integer subtraction (−8)−(−5), where the flawed rule 'subtract then make negative' yields the correct answer but fails on (−5)−(−8)

article_title: Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models
citation: Fang, L., Zhang, Y., Park, J., Wang, Z., Ma, P., Zhai, X. (2026). Confidence-Aware Automated Assessment of Student-Drawn Scientific Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20264
title: Confidence-aware selective automated scoring framework
description: The framework adapts a pretrained ViT with LoRA and derives a response-level confidence score from the stability of predictions under semantic-preserving test-time perturbations (crops, rotations). The article states that "automated scoring systems must decide not only what score to assign, but also whether that score can be trusted." A Top-η test-time selection step retains only the most decisive perturbed views before aggregating the final prediction and confidence. Varying the threshold τ controls the trade-off between automated coverage and scoring risk.
requirements: A pretrained ViT backbone adapted via LoRA, M semantic-preserving test-time perturbations per response, and a confidence threshold τ
constraints: Expert-provided scores were the reference, so systematic tendencies in human scoring may be reflected in model performance
Data from middle school classrooms in one region of the United States
target_learning_goals: rubric-based proficiency levels (Beginning, Developing, Proficient) on NGSS-aligned scientific modeling tasks
examples: The framework was evaluated on six NGSS-aligned middle school drawing items with K=3 proficiency levels, using M=20 perturbations and η=0.75.

citation: Alonso-Carracedo, M., Fernandez-Boullon, R., Celard, P., Rodríguez-Martínez, F. J., & Otero-Cerdeira, L. (2026). CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00140
title: CogTax: a four-level cognitive taxonomy integrating cognitive complexity and operational impact via a maximum rule
description: CogTax is a four-level cognitive taxonomy for command-line computing education that integrates two dimensions: cognitive complexity C, derived from Bloom's Revised Taxonomy, and operational impact O, the degree to which commands modify system state and the reversibility of those modifications. The article states that "The taxonomy explicitly considers whether actions are observational (read-only, zero risk), reversible (modifiable, low risk), structural (altering logical organization, moderate risk), or administrative (system-wide impact, high complexity)." The taxonomy level is the maximum of the two dimensions, ensuring both conceptual understanding and operational awareness are addressed. It was developed and validated in a second-year undergraduate Linux system administration course.
requirements: Commands must be classifiable along both a cognitive-complexity dimension and an operational-impact dimension; the framework targets command-line domains such as Linux/bash system administration
constraints: Developed and validated in the context of a second-year undergraduate Linux system administration course; the reviewed literature identifies no prior taxonomy jointly modelling the two dimensions for command-based domains
target_learners: second-year undergraduate Computer Engineering students in an Operating Systems course
target_learning_goals: command-line and system administration competence spanning read-only inspection through advanced system management

citation: Alonso-Carracedo, M., Fernandez-Boullon, R., Celard, P., Rodríguez-Martínez, F. J., & Otero-Cerdeira, L. (2026). CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00140
title: 585-command expert-annotated Linux/bash dataset with balanced four-level representation
description: A dataset of Linux/bash commands annotated with CogTax levels by domain experts, combining commands from authentic student assessments with synthetically generated commands. The article states: "The complete dataset consists of 585 Linux/bash commands organized into two partitions: a held-out test partition of 117 commands and a training partition of 468 commands." The training partition was deliberately balanced across levels: L1 (143 commands, 24.4%), L2 (151 commands, 25.8%), L3 (144 commands, 24.6%), and L4 (147 commands, 25.1%). Expert annotators discussed ambiguous cases and established consensus classification rules applied uniformly across the dataset.
requirements: Expert annotation by computer science professors with systems programming instruction experience; consensus rules for ambiguous cases
constraints: The balanced distribution contrasts with naturally skewed educational distributions where introductory-level commands predominate
target_learning_goals: evaluation of automatic taxonomy-level classification of commands
key_sources: Alonso-Carracedo, M., Fernandez-Boullon, R., Celard, P., Rodríguez-Martínez, F. J., & Otero-Cerdeira, L. (2026). CogTax: A Four-Level Cognitive Taxonomy for Command-Line Computing Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.00140

article_title: Commenting with Copilot: A Taxonomy and Multi-Year Analysis of Student Code-Generation Specifications
citation: Nasser Giacaman, Valerio Terragni, Paul Denny, and Viraj Kumar. 2026. Commenting with Copilot: A Taxonomy and Multi-Year Analysis of Student Code-Generation Specifications. Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference (SIGCSE Virtual 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3795867.3830978
title: Three-dimensional taxonomy for classifying student comments as AI code-generation specifications
description: The article introduces a multidimensional taxonomy characterizing each student comment by three dimensions: comment type (What/How/Why, adapted from prior work on comment purpose), code expression level (Strict-Code, Code-Like, Natural-Language), and code construct (13 Java-based categories such as Conditional-Return, Loop-Iteration, Multi-Step-Block). It states: "We coded each extracted student comment on three dimensions: comment type, code expression level, and code construct, assigning one label per dimension." The taxonomy treats comments not as documentation but as "student-written specifications for Copilot" that steer an LLM.
requirements: Comments must be extractable from student submissions and assignable one label per dimension; comments with no meaningful directive are ignored
constraints: Developed for a constrained comment-based Copilot workflow in Java tasks, not open dialogue prompting
target_learning_goals: expressing intended program behavior as natural-language specifications for AI code generation
examples: Applied via GPT-5.4-family LLM classification pipelines to 52,172 comment instances from 1,161 students, with human-LLM agreement of 92.5% (κ = 0.781) for Comment Type
key_sources: Nasser Giacaman, Valerio Terragni, Paul Denny, and Viraj Kumar. 2026. Commenting with Copilot: A Taxonomy and Multi-Year Analysis of Student Code-Generation Specifications. Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference (SIGCSE Virtual 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3795867.3830978

Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference (SIGCSE Virtual 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3795867.3830978
title: Four-year Copilot comment-specification dataset from an undergraduate OOP course
description: A dataset spanning four yearly offerings (2023 to 2026) of a Copilot activity in a second-year Java OOP course, reconstructed from CodeRunner submission logs into anonymized per-student folders preserving each attempt's comments, generated code, and test results. "The dataset included 1,161 students and 10,257 recorded submission attempts." Across all attempts 136,424 comment instances were extracted, reduced to 52,172 for content analysis; 3,458 of 3,483 submissions (99.3%) reached a fully passing solution.
requirements: Submission logs capturing the full iterative state of each attempt, including comments and test results
constraints: One course, one institution, one activity design; students reproduced short Java classes from screenshots rather than solving open-ended problems
target_learning_goals: specifying intended behavior in comments to guide AI code generation
examples: Test-suite adequacy assessed with JaCoCo coverage and PIT mutation score, e.g. SimpleMath 100% line, 100% branch, 82% mutation

article_title: What Does the Credential Still Certify? Cognitive Stewardship for AI-Mediated Education
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). What Does the Credential Still Certify? Cognitive Stewardship for AI-Mediated Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19988
title: Cognitive stewardship framework for AI-mediated assessment
description: Cognitive stewardship is "the institutional practice of governing how cognitive work is divided between humans and AI while preserving understanding, verification, responsibility, access, and contestability." It aligns four elements: the learning claim being certified, the delegation boundary specifying what AI may do, the evidence standard showing what observable work remains, and the safeguards protecting privacy, accessibility, proportionality, equity, and appeal. A policy is under-specified when any element is missing. The framework treats validity as a warrant structure and is applied to institutional policy revision, not to individual competency checklists.
requirements: A policy must state the learning claim, delegation boundary, evidence standard, and safeguards; any missing element makes it under-specified
constraints: The framework is a normative lens; the audit applying it is a diagnostic application, not a framework-neutral test of institutional quality
target_learning_goals: credential validity of certified human capacities under AI-mediated assessment
examples: A first-year writing course redesign distributes evidence across diagnostic work, a source map, an AI-feedback workshop, the final essay, and a revision memo; a programming course splits claims between AI-limited tracing tasks and AI-permitted projects with explanation and defense of choices
key_sources: Kai Yao. (2026). What Does the Credential Still Certify? Cognitive Stewardship for AI-Mediated Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19988

article_title: ConnectED: A Curriculum-Aligned AI System for Vietnamese Instructional Lesson Planning and Student Learning
citation: Thang Doan Viet, Anh Nguyen Hoang, Tinh Luong Son, Anh Hoang Thi Ngoc, Huyen Giang Thi Thu, Tai Le Quy. (2026). ConnectED: A Curriculum-Aligned AI System for Vietnamese Instructional Lesson Planning and Student Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28647
title: ConnectED web application with student-facing Playground interactive learning environment
description: ConnectED is a web application that supports curriculum-aligned lesson creation and real-time classroom use, delivering lesson artifacts to students through an interactive environment called Playground. After a teacher approves a lesson, students engage via quizzes, review slides, and flashcards while VietEduQwen provides step-by-step hints and emotionally supportive feedback; the system "collects structured learning signals that teachers can use to guide lesson refinement". The frontend is React/TypeScript with a FastAPI backend, Celery workers, Redis, and MongoDB. Implementation details: teacher-in-the-loop review at every step, lesson repository for reuse, and class-level learning analytics.
requirements: Teacher approval of lesson artifacts before student delivery
All AI-suggested lesson refinements remain teacher-reviewable
constraints: The evaluation did not include a controlled learning outcome study, so causal claims about student learning are not made
target_learners: Vietnamese secondary school teachers and students in grades 6-12
target_learning_goals: Guided interactive learning, emotional support, and teacher-directed lesson refinement from student learning signals
examples: Teachers generate lesson plans with slides, interactive virtual experiments, and STEM videos with synchronized narration; students interact in Playground while the system analyzes feedback at individual and class levels
key_sources: Thang Doan Viet, Anh Nguyen Hoang, Tinh Luong Son, Anh Hoang Thi Ngoc, Huyen Giang Thi Thu, Tai Le Quy. (2026). ConnectED: A Curriculum-Aligned AI System for Vietnamese Instructional Lesson Planning and Student Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28647

article_title: The Tragedy of the Cognitive Commons: How AI Could Disrupt the Regeneration of Professional Expertise
citation: Lovett, N. (2026). The tragedy of the cognitive commons: How AI could disrupt the regeneration of professional expertise. Human Resource Development Review. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/15344843261470602
title: The Cognitive Commons framework
description: The Cognitive Commons is defined as "the collective pool of deep human expertise within a profession that functions as a shared resource whose regeneration can no longer be taken for granted." It exhibits three commons characteristics: collective dependence (a free-rider problem where organizations benefit from a talent pool they avoid paying to develop), non-excludability, and degradability through overexploitation of the regeneration mechanism. Degradation manifests through generational employment patterns rather than visible scarcity, so apparent stock stability can mask regeneration failure. An integrative six-node causal chain (Figure 1) and construct definitions (Table 1) formalize how entry-level position elimination and augmentation-without-internalization erode Internalized Mastery, degrading validation and raising latent systemic risk.
requirements: Applies only when AI substitutes for developmental cognitive labor, the pathways are hard to replicate outside organizational work, and the three commons characteristics co-occur
constraints: Excludes professions facing wholesale disintermediation; assumes AI still requires human oversight; assumes a Western model of professional formation through organizational entry-level employment and credentialing
target_learning_goals: Development of deep, validation-capable professional expertise
Sustained regeneration of profession-wide expert capacity
examples: The paper applies the framework to software engineering, financial analysis, and legal research as higher-vulnerability occupations, with medicine and engineering facing slower dynamics due to regulatory intensity and safety criticality.
key_sources: Lovett, N. (2026). The tragedy of the cognitive commons: How AI could disrupt the regeneration of professional expertise. Human Resource Development Review. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/15344843261470602

article_title: CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities
citation: Arthur Nijdam, Paul Stankovski Wagner, Sara Ramezanian. (2026). CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05910
title: CourseGraph: an LLM-plus-sBERT-plus-Random-Forest pipeline for detecting overlap between university courses
description: CourseGraph is a four-step methodology for automatically assessing whether an external course overlaps with courses in a home curriculum. As the authors describe, "CourseGraph first extracts information such as course titles, descriptions, and learning outcomes from a course's webpage using a Large Language Model (LLM) and a tailored prompt." The extracted fields are embedded with sBERT, cosine similarities are computed between course pairs, and size-independent features (max, min, mean similarity, and fractions above 0.5, 0.6, 0.7) feed a 15-dimensional feature vector into a Random Forest classifier that outputs an overlap/no-overlap decision. Embedding each course component separately supports explainability of which components drive an overlap prediction.
requirements: Course webpages must publicly provide course title, description, prerequisites, learning outcomes, and level for extraction
constraints: The methodology assumes that all course information is publicly available and can be compared between institutions
target_learners: university students in mobility programs such as Erasmus+
target_learning_goals: identifying overlapping educational content when selecting external courses toward a degree
examples: Trained on the TU/e CS overlap matrix (60 positive pairs augmented with 180 negative pairs) and validated on 24 LU Erasmus+ decisions
key_sources: Arthur Nijdam, Paul Stankovski Wagner, Sara Ramezanian. (2026). CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05910

article_title: CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities
citation: Arthur Nijdam, Paul Stankovski Wagner, Sara Ramezanian. (2026). CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05910
title: Two annotated datasets: the TU/e CS overlap matrix and the LU Erasmus+ decision set
description: The evaluation rests on two datasets. The TU/e CS dataset derives from the university's examination-committee-approved 'overlap matrix' for the 180 ECTS Computer Science BSc program; "After processing, this resulted in 60 unique overlapping course pairs," augmented with 180 negative pairs for training. The LU Erasmus+ dataset contains approximately 25 exchange courses (24 decisions after cleaning) taken by C-program students between 2018 and 2020, approved or partially approved by the former program director, spread over 5 students' programs and 3 universities, released on an anonymized GitHub repository.
requirements: Course webpages scraped and standardized to JSON with title, description, prerequisites, learning outcomes, and level extracted by DeepSeek-V3
constraints: The LU Erasmus+ dataset is too small to support meaningful computation of metrics, so it is analyzed qualitatively
target_learners: Computer Science students in exchange programs
target_learning_goals: automated course-overlap assessment for curriculum alignment
examples: The TU/e dataset supplies labeled positive and negative course pairs used to train the Random Forest classifier
key_sources: Arthur Nijdam, Paul Stankovski Wagner, Sara Ramezanian. (2026). CourseGraph: Finding overlaps and differences in Computer Science courses across universities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05910

article_title: ChatGPT Solves All Tested Qiskit Homework Assignments
citation: Alexei Kaltchenko and Gurnivaj Tiwana. (2026). ChatGPT Solves All Tested Qiskit Homework Assignments. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19707
title: Do not interpret a correct personalized, execution-oriented take-home artifact as evidence of independent understanding; directly assess conceptual understanding instead
description: The article argues that correctness of a take-home artifact, even a personalized and execution-oriented one, is insufficient evidence of independent understanding, since all tested artifacts were produced by direct ChatGPT outsourcing. Instructors should distinguish AI-supported production from verified understanding and directly assess whether students can explain and adapt the result. The authors state their tested measures were recommendations derived from the observed failure mode, not experimentally compared in this study.
requirements: Assessment must specify which claim each artifact supports: execution occurred, a circuit is semantically correct, or the student understands and can transfer the concept
constraints: The recommended measures were not experimentally compared in this study
target_learning_goals: independent conceptual understanding of quantum circuits and algorithms beyond artifact production
examples: The study found that seeded personalization, non-palindromic data, reversed measurement maps, custom oracle masks, hidden references, JSON output, circuit metrics, reflections, and optional hardware did not prevent direct ChatGPT completion
key_sources: Alexei Kaltchenko and Gurnivaj Tiwana. (2026). ChatGPT Solves All Tested Qiskit Homework Assignments. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19707

article_title: CogEvol: Towards Efficient and Reliable Learning Environment Generation
citation: CogEvol Team, CogEvol Inc. & Tsinghua University. (2026). CogEvol: Towards Efficient and Reliable Learning Environment Generation. arXiv:2608.30968v2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30968
title: CogEvol-4B open-weight model release with GGUF build and MAIC-UI editing harness
description: CogEvol-4B is the open release of the CogEvol family, a 4B-parameter model post-trained from Qwen3.5-4B for Learning Environment Generation in both modalities. It is released "under the Apache 2.0 license" with full-precision weights, a Q4 K M GGUF build for on-device use, and a deployment guide with the MAIC-UI editing harness; the 27B production model is served via a low-cost API. On the internal suites it scores 61.7 on HTML-500 and 75.1 on slide-std.
requirements: Deployment uses the provided MAIC-UI editing harness and deployment guide; HTML scores in the paper come from the single fixed hardened-reward scorer configuration.
constraints: The evaluation suites and judge prompts are maintained internally and not released, so external models are scored only by API submission through the identical harness.
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education learners served by AI-generated courseware
target_learning_goals: Generation of renderer-valid presentation slides and executable interactive HTML courseware across six educational sub-types
examples: The report lists the Hugging Face weight releases and the GitHub deployment guide with the MAIC-UI editing harness; CogEvol-27B has served OpenMAIC production traffic since 2026-08.
key_sources: CogEvol Team, CogEvol Inc. & Tsinghua University. (2026). CogEvol: Towards Efficient and Reliable Learning Environment Generation. arXiv:2608.30968v2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30968

article_title: Testing Our Foundations: Citation Trends, Errors, and Emerging Hallucinations in the Computing Education Literature
citation: Paul Denny, Gweneth Barbre, Musa Blake, Yan Cathy Hua, Juho Leinonen, Andrew Luxton-Reilly, James Prather, and Brent N. Reeves. (2027). Testing Our Foundations: Citation Trends, Errors, and Emerging Hallucinations in the Computing Education Literature. SIGCSE-TS 2027. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16574
title: Conservative taxonomy and definition for classifying hallucinated and erroneous references
description: The article defines a "hallucinated" reference narrowly as one containing "verifiably fabricated bibliographic information", treating incomplete references as non-hallucinations when present information is correct and the work is identifiable. It adapts Li et al.'s citation hallucination taxonomy with letter codes: S (ACM metadata mismatch), H (author-field error), R (valid bibliographic variant), W (working group and task force reports), M (other typos), and A (alternative substitutions for et al.). This taxonomy structures the manual coding of 828 SET A records and provides a starting point for automated checking systems.
requirements: Classification requires inspection of the raw reference, matched metadata, ACM DOI page, source PDF, and where useful external bibliographic records
constraints: The definition is deliberately conservative; incomplete but identifiable references are not hallucinations
Source PDFs must be checked before labelling a case as potentially hallucinated, since apparent errors may reflect ACM metadata discrepancies
target_learning_goals: understanding reference integrity and citation verification in scholarly writing
examples: Two coders classified 828 SET A records using the adapted taxonomy, finding S (229) most common, then H (225) and R (188)
key_sources: Paul Denny, Gweneth Barbre, Musa Blake, Yan Cathy Hua, Juho Leinonen, Andrew Luxton-Reilly, James Prather, and Brent N. Reeves. (2027). Testing Our Foundations: Citation Trends, Errors, and Emerging Hallucinations in the Computing Education Literature. SIGCSE-TS 2027. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.16574

article_title: CoLearn: An Agentic Tutor that Learns its Learner in a Human-AI Co-Learning Loop
citation: Kailai He, Zhihao Wu, Linhai Zhang, Runcong Zhao, Yulan He, Jiazheng Li. (2026). CoLearn: An Agentic Tutor that Learns its Learner in a Human–AI Co-Learning Loop. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21154
title: Human–AI co-learning loop: persistent learner-state memory, adaptive question generation, and a transparent evidence view
description: CoLearn operationalises the ideal tutor as a loop in which the learner practises while the agent refines a persistent memory of the learner's mastery and misconceptions. It has "three components: (i) a persistent learner-state memory that updates per-topic mastery with a soft-evidence variant of Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, where a large language model acts as a continuous observation function", (ii) adaptive question generation targeting the weakest topic and recurring misconceptions, and (iii) an evidence view making personalisation visible and testable. Co-learning here is deliberately modest: the question strategy stays fixed while only the agent's memory adapts.
requirements: A persistent per-(learner, subject) memory record so evidence accumulates across sessions rather than per-session logs
An LLM grader emitting continuous mastery_evidence and evidence_strength values in [0,1] as the observation function
constraints: The strategy guideline is a fixed text consulted on every generation; automatic revision from accumulated outcomes is planned but not yet implemented
A rising mastery estimate is evidence that the agent's belief has changed, not proof that the learner has mastered the skill
target_learners: secondary-school science learners (evaluated on Biology and Chemistry curricula)
target_learning_goals: topic-level mastery diagnosis
misconception identification and remediation through targeted practice
examples: In a worked live round, a clearly wrong GCSE Biology answer lowered mastery 0.56→0.23 via competence-gated BKT, stored three misconceptions, and the adaptive engine re-targeted that skill next turn
key_sources: Kailai He, Zhihao Wu, Linhai Zhang, Runcong Zhao, Yulan He, Jiazheng Li. (2026). CoLearn: An Agentic Tutor that Learns its Learner in a Human–AI Co-Learning Loop. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21154

article_title: CoLearn: An Agentic Tutor that Learns its Learner in a Human-AI Co-Learning Loop
citation: Kailai He, Zhihao Wu, Linhai Zhang, Runcong Zhao, Yulan He, Jiazheng Li. (2026). CoLearn: An Agentic Tutor that Learns its Learner in a Human–AI Co-Learning Loop. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21154
title: CoLearn deployable containerised web system (Vite/React SPA, FastAPI backend, provider-selectable LLM)
description: CoLearn is a container-deployed web application whose frontend is a Vite + React + TypeScript single-page app and whose backend is FastAPI with an async MongoDB store, JWT/bcrypt authentication, and SSE streaming for live generation and grading. The LLM backend is provider-selectable (AWS Bedrock with Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the live default; an OpenAI-compatible path is also supported). "The whole stack starts with one command via Docker Compose", and the backend ships with a test suite covering BKT, grading, generation, streaming, RBAC, and the A/B analytics.
requirements: A provider-selectable LLM backend; the live default is AWS Bedrock with Claude Sonnet 4.5
constraints: Accounts are admin-provisioned with no public signup, learner data is stored locally in the single-node deployment, and the system can run fully offline with a deterministic LLM for privacy-sensitive settings
target_learners: secondary-school science learners practising Biology and Chemistry
target_learning_goals: diagnostic practice with adaptive question generation and misconception feedback
examples: The demo workflow spans learner and administrator views: session configuration, adaptive questions with answer-linked annotations, live mastery bars, blind A/B analytics, and agent convergence diagnostics
key_sources: Kailai He, Zhihao Wu, Linhai Zhang, Runcong Zhao, Yulan He, Jiazheng Li. (2026). CoLearn: An Agentic Tutor that Learns its Learner in a Human–AI Co-Learning Loop. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21154

article_title: CoLearn: An Agentic Tutor that Learns its Learner in a Human-AI Co-Learning Loop
citation: Kailai He, Zhihao Wu, Linhai Zhang, Runcong Zhao, Yulan He, Jiazheng Li. (2026). CoLearn: An Agentic Tutor that Learns its Learner in a Human–AI Co-Learning Loop. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21154
title: Make an adaptive tutor's personalisation visible and testable through live mastery visualisation and built-in blind A/B comparison
description: CoLearn renders the agent's evolving belief in real time so "personalisation is something the user can see rather than take on trust", and includes a blind A/B interface presenting personalised and non-personalised questions in randomised, unlabelled positions. Results aggregate into an analytics dashboard reporting the preference rate, a 95% confidence interval, and a two-sided sign test against the 0.5 chance rate, making the adaptation inspectable and empirically testable by anyone.
requirements: A progress dashboard (branch-graph timeline, concept-mastery radar, mastery-over-time trajectory) exposing how estimates and misconception summaries change
An A/B tool that hides provenance server-side and stores picks with hidden provenance for later analysis
constraints: A/B items are not written back into the learner-state memory, and the A/B study measures perceived relevance rather than learning outcomes
target_learners: learners using adaptive tutoring systems, plus administrators and researchers evaluating them
target_learning_goals: transparency of learner-state estimation and question targeting
examples: The built-in A/B tool randomised slot order and hid provenance server-side, and the 18-rater study reported preference rates with 95% CIs and sign tests

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Driven Physics Assignments using Context Prompts
citation: Miguel Rodriguez and Peter Wulff. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Driven Physics Assignments using Context Prompts. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22578
title: Context prompts: instructor-designed prompts defining role, task, and boundaries of a Gen AI interaction
description: The article's central framework is the context prompt: instructor-designed prompts that establish guidelines for generative AI to follow during student interactions. The authors write that through a context prompt, instructors establish guidelines for Gen AI to follow that can guide students in exploration and reflection activities, and that it is important to provide Gen AI specific guidelines in order to scaffold it to stay on target. The prompt is prioritized at the start of the chat and maintained across the conversation.
requirements: The context prompt must contain key elements of prompt engineering so that the outputs remain constrained and on-target
constraints: Gen AI models are not equal, and the choice of platform matters
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of physics topics through AI-guided dialogue
examples: An exploration context prompt instructs the AI to act as a learning guide taking a Socratic approach, break down every step, and suggest resources when appropriate
key_sources: Miguel Rodriguez and Peter Wulff. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Driven Physics Assignments using Context Prompts. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22578

article_title: Culturally-Aware AI for Cross-Boundary Community Learning: Undergraduate Innovation at the Intersection of Computation
citation: Jiaojiao Zhao, Weisheng Zhang, Jiawen Cai, Haibin Gao, and Luyao Zhang. (2026). Culturally-Aware AI for Cross-Boundary Community Learning: Undergraduate Innovation at the Intersection of Computation and Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09041
title: Collaborative framework for culturally aware AIED across education, technology, and culture dimensions
description: The article contributes a "collaborative framework for culturally aware AIED" organizing the field around three dimensions—education (students become co-producers), technology (AI augments while "people validate"), and culture (community insight guides meaning)—supported by participatory elicitation of cultural knowledge, bilingual representation, and stakeholder validation. It bridges social work's Community-Based Learning methodologies with computational science, treating students as knowledge producers whose final projects are released as open-source software to widen participation in underrepresented Asia-Pacific contexts.

Community partner review of AI outputs as a validation mechanism
constraints: As a single-site pilot, the authors state generalizability requires multi-site validation
Without a pre/post intercultural-sensitivity measure, activities are opportunities for development rather than evidence of stage progression
target_learners: Undergraduate students in interdisciplinary computation and design programs
target_learning_goals: Culturally aware AI development
Community-engaged design for cultural heritage preservation and sustainable development

article_title: Curriculum as Code: An AI-Assisted Architecture for Instructional Design in STEM Education
citation: Henrique Mohallem Paiva. (2026). Curriculum as Code: An AI-Assisted Architecture for Instructional Design in STEM Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07364
title: Mitigate LLM hallucinations in material generation by drastic context pruning and segmented, section-by-section generation rather than single-prompt deck generation
description: The architecture keeps only a condensed three-paragraph context summary carried forward, plans structure without code, and generates LaTeX and Python section by section in an iterative loop. The article reports that "attempting to generate a full slide deck in a single prompt inevitably leads to token exhaustion and hallucinations", while feeding the model only isolated sections alongside a condensed summary kept attention focused and yielded accurate code outputs. Restricting the human-AI interface to plain text, Markdown, and source code further avoids formatting glitches.
requirements: A Phase 1 condensed text summary as the only context carried into code generation, a structural skeleton produced before any code, and an automated secondary review agent plus human-in-the-loop validation
constraints: Generative models may show behavioral drift after provider updates, occasionally requiring minor prompt recalibrations; minor syntactic anomalies such as mismatched brackets still occur
target_learners: Instructors and instructional designers producing STEM materials
target_learning_goals: Production of mathematically accurate, visually consistent instructional materials
examples: Phase 1 deliberately carries forward only the concise text artifact to prevent context window overflow; Phase 5 iteratively generates one section at a time until the structural plan is implemented
key_sources: Henrique Mohallem Paiva. (2026). Curriculum as Code: An AI-Assisted Architecture for Instructional Design in STEM Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07364

article_title: Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education
citation: Andy Gray, Jake Hobbs. (2026). Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21600
title: Course-specific RAG as an intermediary layer between independent study and formal academic support
description: The article proposes that course-specific RAG systems occupy an intermediary space between independent study and formal academic support: rather than replacing educators, they offer "private,immediate,andcourse‐specificguidance" as a low-friction first point of support before students engage lecturers or tutors. The account holds that help-seeking barriers extend beyond availability of services to confidence, anxiety, fear of judgement, and perceptions of whether questions are appropriate, so an accessible private channel can lower the threshold for initiating help-seeking while preserving the pedagogical role of educators. This framing informed both Beacon's design objectives and the study's evaluation questions on trust, learning support, and help-seeking.
requirements: Responses must be grounded in approved teaching materials and remain aligned with module learning outcomes, so guidance is educationally appropriate rather than unrestricted.
constraints: The article states course-specific AI is not a substitute for effective teaching or student support services, and the findings come from a single institution's computing modules.
target_learners: higher education students reluctant to seek help through conventional channels due to anxiety, low confidence, or fear of judgement
target_learning_goals: initiating help-seeking
accessing academically appropriate guidance
building confidence before engaging formal academic support
examples: Beacon was positioned as an accessible first point of support when students encountered difficulties outside scheduled teaching, complementing rather than replacing lecturers and tutorials.
key_sources: Andy Gray, Jake Hobbs. (2026). Reducing Barriers to Academic Support: Evaluating a Course-Specific RAG System for Addressing Help-Seeking Disparities in Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21600

article_title: Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education
citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: Cognition Intelligence: transforming learner behaviours into interpretable cognition structures for expert-level reasoning
description: The article introduces Cognition Intelligence as a new paradigm for AI-driven educational interpretation, defined as "the transformation of learner behaviours into interpretable cognition structures that support expert-level reasoning, adaptive intervention, and educational decision-making." It shifts the analytical object from observable behaviour to expert-informed cognition structures. The article states it "does not replace behavioural analytics; rather, it extends and reorganises behavioural analytics within a cognition-centred framework," with behavioural data as the first interpretive layer.
requirements: AI Tutors, reporting systems, and cognition-aware dashboards that collectively transform behavioural traces into higher-level cognition structures
constraints: Behavioural data remains necessary but becomes only the first layer in a larger interpretive process
target_learning_goals: expert-like interpretation of learner development, misconceptions, and adaptive pedagogical decision-making
examples: The article contrasts a conventional pipeline (behaviours to statistics to visualisation) with a cognition-centred pipeline in which AI Tutor analysis produces cognition structures before dashboard aggregation
key_sources: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263

article_title: Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education
citation: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263
title: Five cognition structures as analytical objects: identity cognition, interpretation, cognitive tension, value recognition, and misunderstanding
description: The article enumerates five higher-order cognition structures that form "the core analytical objects of the ECD": identity cognition (how learners position themselves within a domain), interpretation (how learners construct meaning across situations), cognitive tension (conceptual conflicts and uncertainty marking cognitive transition), value recognition (negotiation of priorities and ethical judgments), and misunderstanding analysed as "structured cognitive divergence" rather than incorrect performance. These structures aim to represent learner development at a deeper interpretive level than behavioural outputs.
requirements: Dashboards must model these structures through AI Tutor interpretation rather than direct behavioural measurement
constraints: The article states these representations are not intended to fully capture learner cognition
target_learners: learners whose interpretive development is analysed in AI-native systems
target_learning_goals: interpreting conceptual understanding, identity formation, value negotiation, and cognitive transition
examples: Repeated hesitation around a concept may indicate unresolved cognitive tension; frequent revisions may suggest interpretive instability
key_sources: Yuan, A. (2026). Expert Cognition Dashboard: From Learning Analytics to Cognition Intelligence in AI-Driven Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.17263

article_title: Gen-AI-tecture: using generative AI to support architectural students in design tasks
citation: Kapsalis, T. (2026). Gen-AI-tecture: using generative AI to support architectural students in design tasks. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1598-6426
title: The GenAI workflow as a constructionist microworld and socio-constructivist cognitive mediator in studio education
description: The authors interpret their findings through constructionist and socio-constructivist lenses: "the bespoke, locally run GenAI workﬂow functions as a constructionist “microworld” for architectural ideation rather than as a mere image generator", echoing Papert's objects-to-think-with. They further read the AI as "a “more knowledgeable other” that suggested plausible yet negotiable alternatives", prompting students to articulate constraints and values, and as a connectivist interaction agent within students' personal learning environments. Learning is evidenced by cycles of making, inspecting and remaking, with the human-in-the-loop configuration preserving learner agency.
requirements: Outputs must be interrogated rather than accepted uncritically for the scaffold/ZPD effect to hold, per the article's reading
constraints: Interpretation drawn from a small, single-institution focus-group study with self-report data; the article notes instances where AI outputs risked narrowing exploration were identified and problematised in group discussion
target_learners: Undergraduate architecture students in studio-based education
target_learning_goals: Design reasoning and metacognitive talk about design moves
Critical management of human-AI learning networks
examples: Students described AI-edited images as provocations that opened up unforeseen options, especially when switching between masking modes
key_sources: Kapsalis, T. (2026). Gen-AI-tecture: using generative AI to support architectural students in design tasks. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1598-6426

article_title: Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education
citation: Nicholas Micallef, Olga Petrovska. (2026). Structuring Transparency: Developing Domain-Specific Generative AI Declaration Frameworks in Higher Education. International Symposium on Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of Higher Education Symposium (AITHE). https://www.swansea.ac.uk/staff/nicholas.micallef
title: Coding-focused GenAI declaration structure with five activity categories
description: A parallel declaration structure for coding assessments reflecting typical phases of software development and code-based learning, with five activity categories: Planning & Design, Code Generation, Code Improvement, Understanding & Learning, and Documentation & Reporting. As in the writing structure, students indicate whether GenAI was used and to what extent, with a short description and example prompts. The structure lets students and instructors "distinguish between GenAI as a learning aid (e.g., understanding error messages) and GenAI as an authoring tool (e.g., generating core solution code)".
requirements: Students complete per-category use, extent, and description fields; institutional guidance on tool scope is recommended by the authors
constraints: Derived from a computing-education taxonomy; relies on accurate self-reporting in a context where students may misattribute GenAI contributions
target_learners: Computer Science students in programming-based assessments, from novices learning Python syntax to degree apprentices debugging legacy codebases
target_learning_goals: Transparent disclosure of GenAI use in coding tasks
Distinguishing GenAI as learning aid versus authoring tool
examples: Code Improvement covers debugging errors, refactoring, optimising performance, and requesting code review-style feedback; Understanding & Learning covers explaining error messages and learning syntax or design patterns

article_title: Adoption-Ready Project-Based Learning for Computing Education: The FORAP Framework and a Multi-Scale Project Portfolio
citation: Suleiman, A. D., DeWaters, J., Shepherd, D. C., Korkmaz, T., Hussain, F., Liu, Y., & Hou, D. (2026). Adoption-Ready Project-Based Learning for Computing Education: The FORAP Framework and a Multi-Scale Project Portfolio. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11129
title: Provide coordinated instructor and student support packages as essential to PjBL project success
description: The article concludes that both instructor support and student support proved essential to project success. Instructor packages (project overview, instructor notes, sample solutions, reference courses) reduce adoption workload, while student packages (installation guidelines, laboratory exercises, task scaffolding, resources) address recurring technical barriers such as installation, prerequisite gaps, and task difficulties. This principle motivated revisions strengthening documentation, setup guidance, troubleshooting resources, and TA support recommendations.
requirements: Coordinated instructor, student, and assessment packages built around aligned learning objectives
Support materials kept current as tools and platforms change
constraints: Even with support packages, effective implementation depended heavily on instructor preparation, TA readiness, class size, and platform or environment constraints
target_learners: instructors adopting PjBL in computing courses
target_learning_goals: sustained student progress and engagement during open-ended project work
examples: Instructors valued documentation, videos, laboratory exercises, and timely help from knowledgeable graduate assistants or TAs, which helped students bridge content gaps and helped faculty adapt projects

article_title: Generative artificial intelligence and the transformation of medical education: a scoping review
citation: Zhao J, Yang K, Gao H and Jiang G (2026). Generative artificial intelligence and the transformation of medical education: a scoping review. Front. Educ. 11:1907589. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1907589
title: Conditional effectiveness of GenAI learning activities: benefit depends on bounded tasks, grounding, active engagement, iterative feedback, and faculty oversight
description: The review's central interpretive account is that GenAI's educational value is conditional rather than uniform: "GenAI was neither uniformly superior nor uniformly harmful. Its effects depended on the instructional system in which it was embedded." Across illustrative studies, positive findings tended to co-occur with bounded tasks, curated grounding, active engagement, feedback requiring comparison or revision, and faculty oversight, while null or unfavorable cases involved replaced stronger resources, disrupted team cognition, or unreliable content.
requirements: Task bounded with curated content or structured case grounding
Learners engage actively and feedback requires comparison or revision
Faculty retain oversight of factual and pedagogical quality
constraints: These conditions are hypothesis-generating rather than a tested moderator analysis
The review did not test grounding as a quantitative moderator
target_learners: entry-to-practice medical students, preclinical through clerkship
target_learning_goals: history taking, communication, clinical reasoning, diagnostic performance, and selected knowledge outcomes
examples: The review contrasts controlled simulation gains with trauma-pilot teamwork disruption and fabricated-syndrome self-study as illustrations of the conditional pattern
key_sources: Zhao J, Yang K, Gao H and Jiang G (2026). Generative artificial intelligence and the transformation of medical education: a scoping review. Front. Educ. 11:1907589. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1907589

article_title: Under surveillance: Mapping remote proctoring practices in the assessment of nursing students — a scoping review
citation: Harerimana A, Mtshali N, Mchunu G. (2026). Under surveillance: mapping remote proctoring practices in the assessment of nursing students— a scoping review. International Journal for Educational Integrity. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00229-7
title: Implement context-sensitive, ethically grounded proctoring policies supported by integrity-by-design assessment approaches
description: The review recommends that nursing programs adopt proctoring policies tailored to local context and ethics, rather than assuming a single universally effective approach. It states "Nursing programs must implement context-sensitive, ethically grounded proctoring policies, supported by integrity-by-design assessment approaches that prioritize authentic learning, student well-being, and equity." This follows from its finding that success is highly context-dependent and that proctoring can impose performance penalties, exacerbate inequalities, and normalize intrusive surveillance.
requirements: Balancing exam security with student well-being, fairness, and equitable access to digital tools
constraints: Only six empirical studies met the inclusion criteria, limiting the breadth and generalizability of the findings; most studies relied on self-reported perceptions
target_learners: nursing students in online and hybrid assessment programs
target_learning_goals: academic integrity in online assessment while prioritizing authentic learning, student well-being, and equity
examples: The review recommends future longitudinal, multi-site, and theory-informed designs and more studies from low- and middle-income settings to guide equitable, context-sensitive assessment strategies
