article_title: A meta-analysis of the effect of generative AI on productivity and learning in programming
citation: Maier, S., Gunzenhäuser, M., Schweisthal, J., Schneider, M., & Feuerriegel, S. (2026). A meta-analysis of the effect of generative AI on productivity and learning in programming. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04779
title: Cognitive offloading: reliance on GenAI can allow students to bypass core learning processes, reducing active engagement and impairing fundamental programming skill development.
description: Cognitive offloading, as described in this article, is the phenomenon whereby reliance on GenAI tools allows students to bypass core learning processes such as trial-and-error learning, debugging, and iterative refinement when they delegate core tasks to GenAI. The article states this "may reduce active engagement with problem solving, which, in turn, can lead to shallow understanding and ultimately impair the development of fundamental programming skills." As an explanatory framework, it accounts for the meta-analytic finding that GenAI assistance shows no significant pooled learning benefit: students may complete tasks without internalizing underlying reasoning, producing tool-dependent capabilities that fail to persist without AI support.
requirements: Students must have access to GenAI tools during learning phases for offloading to occur.
The framework presupposes that foundational programming skills require active engagement with problem-solving processes.
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretive framework consistent with prior research in other educational domains, not as a mechanism directly tested within the meta-analysis itself.
The article notes that capabilities developed during AI-assisted coding may prove tool-dependent, failing to persist without AI support.
target_learners: Computer science students at university and pre-university levels
target_learning_goals: Development of fundamental programming skills
Internalizing core concepts through debugging and iterative refinement
examples: The article cites this phenomenon to explain why learning effects emerged only when GenAI was permitted during assessment: students perform better with tools available, but gains may reflect tool-dependent augmentation rather than durable learning.
The article warns that reliance on GenAI tools may backfire when students are required to explain, adapt, or debug AI-generated code.
key_sources: Maier, S., Gunzenhäuser, M., Schweisthal, J., Schneider, M., & Feuerriegel, S. (2026). A meta-analysis of the effect of generative AI on productivity and learning in programming. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.04779

article_title: Faster Completion, Less Learning: Generative AI Reduced Study Time on Math Problems and the Knowledge They Build
citation: Rismanchian, S., Uzun, H., Matayoshi, J., Cosyn, E., & Kurd-Misto, E. (2026). Faster Completion, Less Learning: Generative AI Reduced Study Time on Math Problems and the Knowledge They Build. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21629
title: Cognitive surrender versus cognitive offloading as the explanatory framework for AI-related learning loss
description: The article adopts Shaw & Nave's distinction between cognitive offloading and cognitive surrender. Offloading is "the strategic outsourcing of a narrow task (e.g., a calculator for arithmetic)" while the user retains the structure of reasoning; surrender is "the adoption of an AI-generated output as one's own answer with minimal scrutiny", relinquishing cognitive control of problem-solving. The authors use this framework to explain why earlier tools produced efficiency gains without retention decline, whereas generative AI produces the selective, supervision-sensitive, age-graded behavioral signature and retention loss they document.
requirements: Interpreting the behavioral pattern as surrender requires that the decline be selective to AI-transcribable formats, supervision-sensitive, and age-graded, as the article states
constraints: The article notes the boundary between AI-susceptible and AI-resistant problem formats is a moving target as multimodal and agentic AI capabilities advance
target_learning_goals: Durable retention of mathematics knowledge
examples: The article contrasts a student using a calculator, who still constructs the solution strategy, with a student who copies a word problem into a chatbot and pastes the returned solution
key_sources: Rismanchian, S., Uzun, H., Matayoshi, J., Cosyn, E., & Kurd-Misto, E. (2026). Faster Completion, Less Learning: Generative AI Reduced Study Time on Math Problems and the Knowledge They Build. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21629

article_title: From tool to scaffold: Structured human–AI collaboration and its effects on academic writing and digital critical thinking
citation: Alshehri OAO, Lamouchi A, Abdellatif MS, Al-Dosari MNA, Mekheimer M and Nemt-allah MA (2026). From tool to scaffold: structured human–AI collaboration and its effects on academic writing and digital critical thinking among Saudi EFL learners. Front. Psychol. 17:1830103. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1830103
title: Conditional mediational framework: AI as scaffold for writing and digital critical thinking only under critical, verificatory, responsibility-oriented interaction
description: The article synthesizes constructivist and sociocultural accounts of mediated learning with process-writing and self-regulation models. Generative AI is conceptualized as a mediational means operating within the learner's zone of proximal development, able to propose outlines, model genre conventions, and surface alternatives. Its central claim is explicitly conditional: "AI applications can act as mediational tools supporting both writing development and digital critical thinking only when instruction structures human–AI interaction to be critical, verificatory, and responsibility-oriented." Learning benefits therefore depend on how learners interact with mediation—questioning, comparing drafts, rejecting or adapting suggestions—rather than on tool access alone.
requirements: Instruction must structure human–AI interaction to be critical, verificatory, and responsibility-oriented
Learners must engage with AI outputs by questioning, comparing drafts, rejecting or adapting suggestions, and justifying compositional choices
constraints: When used without instructional scaffolding as a shortcut to finished text, AI can undermine independent composing, weaken engagement with primary sources, blur authorial boundaries, and introduce integrity risks
target_learners: EFL university students in AI-rich writing environments
target_learning_goals: Writing development
Digital critical thinking and AI literacy
Self-regulated, ethically grounded authorship
examples: The study's intervention operationalized the framework through verification routines, hallucination-detection instruction, and structured ethical self-regulation coupled with ideation and revision support
key_sources: Alshehri OAO, Lamouchi A, Abdellatif MS, Al-Dosari MNA, Mekheimer M and Nemt-allah MA (2026). From tool to scaffold: structured human–AI collaboration and its effects on academic writing and digital critical thinking among Saudi EFL learners. Front. Psychol. 17:1830103. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1830103

article_title: Reimagining mathematics education through intelligent tutoring: evidence, opportunities, and implementation challenges
citation: Ogunsakin IB, Ayanwale MA, Falebita OS and Felemu OJ (2026) Reimagining mathematics education through intelligent tutoring: evidence, opportunities, and implementation challenges. Front. Educ. 11:1943906. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1943906
title: Connectivism as the underpinning theoretical lens for AI-supported mathematics learning
description: The review adopts connectivism, which "conceptualises learning as the formation, navigation, evaluation, and maintenance of connections within distributed knowledge networks". ITSs and adaptive platforms function as technological nodes within learners' knowledge networks, collecting interaction evidence, estimating performance, recommending resources, and providing feedback. Teachers remain central nodes who contextualise content, evaluate AI recommendations, and connect digital activities to curricular objectives. The framework rejects the assumption that AI can independently direct mathematics learning.
requirements: Learning is understood as interaction across human and technological knowledge networks, requiring learners and teachers able to judge the accuracy and relevance of networked information.
constraints: The review notes connectivism does not fully explain how an intelligent system modifies instruction in response to learner performance, so adaptive instruction is added as a complementary mechanism.
target_learners: mathematics learners across educational levels using AI-supported tutoring environments
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding, problem-solving, and use of networked mathematical resources
examples: The review uses connectivism to interpret a learner attempting a problem, receiving an adaptive prompt, examining an alternative representation, revising strategy, and applying revised understanding to a more demanding task.
key_sources: Ogunsakin IB, Ayanwale MA, Falebita OS and Felemu OJ (2026) Reimagining mathematics education through intelligent tutoring: evidence, opportunities, and implementation challenges. Front. Educ. 11:1943906. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1943906

article_title: Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning
citation: Qusay H. Mahmoud. (2026). Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning. Preprint, September 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29473
title: Comprehension debt: deferred learning and maintenance cost when AI-assisted production outpaces the ability to explain, test, modify, and justify software
description: Comprehension debt, building on Ahmad's socio-cognitive account of GenAI-assisted student projects, is defined in this review as "thedeferred learning, maintenance, and accountability cost incurred when AI-assisted artifact production outpaces the learner's or team's ability to explain, test, modify, and justify the artifact". Individual indicators include inability to explain control or data flow, poor defect localization, and inadequate test-oracle design; team indicators include uneven ownership and undocumented provenance. Conventional activities—delayed change requests, walkthroughs, independent tests, live debugging—can be repurposed as debt probes comparing what was produced with what can later be demonstrated. Frequency of AI use is a poor proxy: heavy use with active verification can carry low debt.
requirements: Assessment must compare what was produced with what can later be explained, tested, modified, and justified, using measures such as explanation quality, tracing accuracy, and independently designed tests
constraints: The construct remains a research agenda rather than a validated scalar metric
It is not identical to technical debt, academic misconduct, ordinary forgetting, or low code quality
target_learning_goals: retained code comprehension
independent verification and maintenance capability
accountability for AI-assisted artifacts
examples: Ahmad's underlying study drew on 621 reflective diaries from 207 students, identifying black-box acceptance, context mismatch, dependency-induced atrophy, verification bypass, and AI as a comprehension scaffold
key_sources: Qusay H. Mahmoud. (2026). Judgment-Centred Software Engineering Education: A Post-Hype Review and Framework for AI-Augmented Learning. Preprint, September 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29473

article_title: Analysing AI utilisation in education through learner question types: A constructivist approach
citation: Lee, H., Atif, A., & Kang, K. (2026). Analysing AI utilisation in education through learner question types: A constructivist approach. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 79–96. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10657
title: Constructivist three-role taxonomy of learner-generated questions: knowledge transmitter, facilitator and co-learner
description: The article organises learner-generated questions through a constructivist framework drawing on Piaget and Vygotsky's theories, in which student inquiries are categorised into three roles: "knowledge transmitter, facilitator and co-learner". This taxonomy serves as the class scheme that the NLP models are trained and evaluated against, linking question type to inquiry depth and to personalised learning and adaptive feedback in educational settings.
requirements: Learner-generated questions must be collected and expert labelled into the three roles before models can be trained on the taxonomy.
constraints: The article notes models struggle to distinguish the higher-order facilitator and co-learner categories, limiting automated use of those classes.
target_learners: higher education students in information technology courses
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking through learner questioning
personalised learning and adaptive feedback
examples: Student inquiries from 11 students across 12 information technology courses were categorised into the three roles and used as classification targets.
key_sources: Lee, H., Atif, A., & Kang, K. (2026). Analysing AI utilisation in education through learner question types: A constructivist approach. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 79–96. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10657

article_title: What Students Ask Matters: LLM Interaction Depth, Task Quality, and Immediate Recall in Higher Education
citation: Vangelis Tsiligkiris. (2026). What students ask matters: LLM interaction depth, task quality, and immediate recall in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00617-6
title: Dissociation between performance quality and short-term recall in LLM-supported study
description: The article's central explanatory account: the same interaction signal — explanation-seeking depth — relates positively to applied task quality but not to immediate recall, indicating "a dissociation between performance quality and short-term recall in LLM-supported study". It aligns this with cognitive-psychology evidence that elaboration improves comprehension while retrieval practice consolidates retention, and with cognitive off-loading and "illusion of competence" accounts: fluent on-demand explanations may limit effortful retrieval and encoding when the learning sequence lacks explicit retrieval demands.
requirements: Interpretation rests on a lexical depth proxy rather than verified cognitive engagement, as the article itself states
constraints: Single-group design, small sample (n = 22), immediate testing only, and keyword-based depth proxies, as the article lists
target_learners: higher education students using LLMs in study sessions
target_learning_goals: applied task quality
knowledge recall and retention
examples: The study modelled task quality and recall side by side against the same interaction traces, finding depth predicted one but not the other
key_sources: Vangelis Tsiligkiris. (2026). What students ask matters: LLM interaction depth, task quality, and immediate recall in higher education. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00617-6

article_title: Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction
citation: Chenguang Wang, Ming Li, Xinyue Zeng, Zhuochun Li, Hong Jiao, Tianyi Zhou, Dawei Zhou. (2026). Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28186
title: Cognitive episodes: an eight-way taxonomy of functional problem-solving states grounded in Schoenfeld's Episode Theory
description: Cognitive episodes organize LLM reasoning traces into temporally ordered functional problem-solving states. The framework builds on Schoenfeld's Episode Theory, which "models the problem-solving process as a temporally ordered sequence of functional episodes", comprising Read, Analyze, Plan, Implement, Explore, Verify, and Monitor, plus an added Answer episode capturing final answer commitment. In this article the taxonomy supplies a cognitively grounded vocabulary for characterizing how problem-solving burden is distributed across stages of long reasoning traces, enabling interpretable difficulty prediction.
requirements: Reasoning-oriented LLMs that produce explicit reasoning traces, segmented into sentences and labeled with episode tags by a trained classifier
constraints: The article states model-generated reasoning traces are proxy evidence, not direct observations of human cognition
target_learners: Assessment items for college admissions, English reading comprehension, and medical licensure populations
target_learning_goals: Predicting and interpreting human item difficulty in educational assessment
examples: Sentence-level episode profiling of traces from QwQ-32B and Qwen3-32B, labeled with a RoBERTa classifier trained on ThinkARM annotations
key_sources: Chenguang Wang, Ming Li, Xinyue Zeng, Zhuochun Li, Hong Jiao, Tianyi Zhou, Dawei Zhou. (2026). Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.28186

article_title: Aligning LLM-Simulated and Human Examinees for Psychometric Calibration: A Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling Approach
citation: Wenjie Zhou, Yunting Liu, Renjiao Tang, & Mark Wilson. (2026). Aligning LLM-Simulated and Human Examinees for Psychometric Calibration: A Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling Approach. https://osf.io/p6fam/
title: Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling (CDP): a six-step zero-shot framework for simulating examinees with binary attribute-mastery profiles
description: CDP is a zero-shot framework that draws on cognitive diagnostic models "to represent each simulated examinee as a binary attribute-mastery profile and prompts an LLM to generate item responses consistent with that profile." It proceeds in six steps: construct decomposition into binary attributes, mastery-pattern formation over 2^K patterns, natural-language rendering of mastered and unmastered skills, simulated pool assembly under an uninformative (uniform) or informative (population-prevalence) sampling distribution, response generation, and standard psychometric analysis. It applies the generative logic of assessment design traditions in the opposite direction: it generates examinees rather than items.
requirements: An attribute-level description of the test (attribute decomposition and Q-matrix) produced by content analysis or existing assessment-design artifacts
constraints: The informative variant requires an information source about the target population, such as a prior CDM fit, expert judgment, or published statistics
Alignment achieved is psychometric rather than cognitive: matching parameters does not imply human-like solution processes
target_learners: Simulated examinees representing school populations such as middle-school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: Psychometric item calibration and cognitive diagnostic assessment design for constructs decomposable into binary attributes
examples: Applied to the Tatsuoka fraction-subtraction dataset with five attributes and 15 items, evaluating eight LLM configurations under no-profile, uninformative, and informative conditions
key_sources: Wenjie Zhou, Yunting Liu, Renjiao Tang, & Mark Wilson. (2026). Aligning LLM-Simulated and Human Examinees for Psychometric Calibration: A Cognitive Diagnostic Profiling Approach. https://osf.io/p6fam/

article_title: Rethinking LLM-Judged Helpfulness as a Pedagogy Signal: A Pre-Registered Audit Across Tutor Models
citation: Shuyi Fan, Boyuan Deng, Mengyu Xu, Jiale Liu, Hongyang Zhang, Qiaoxin Yang, Chongyang Gao. (2026). Rethinking LLM-Judged Helpfulness as a Pedagogy Signal: A Pre-Registered Audit Across Tutor Models. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28128
title: Controlled tutor-audit testbed: ConvTutor, PedTutor, and cold baseline over identical frozen weights with a weak simulated student
description: A within-base testbed in which two tutoring policies are instantiated from identical frozen model weights so that only the policy layer differs. ConvTutor is a minimal one-call helpful tutor whose answer-giving is emergent; PedTutor is a four-node routed policy with a learner-state tracker and three responders (problem decomposer, answer-deferral gate, hint cascade). All conditions face one deliberately weak simulated student, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, with "about11% unaided accuracy", making tutoring load-bearing, plus a no-tutor cold baseline and a frozen 19-problem mixture/weighted-average instrument.
requirements: A weak simulated student so that tutoring is load-bearing and a process contrast is measurable
Frozen judge, rubrics, metric definitions, and outcome-interpretation table fixed before confirmatory data collection
constraints: The serving vendor co-varies with the tutor base and Gemini's provider enforces a minimum reasoning setting, so no base is a pure base-model swap
Results describe one simulated learner on one algebra domain and do not license claims about human learners
target_learning_goals: Translating word problems into mixture or weighted-average balance equations
examples: Ten replicates per condition per base gave 90 confirmatory sessions; each session ran six tutored training problems followed by immediate, interference, delayed, and transfer probes answered unassisted
key_sources: Shuyi Fan, Boyuan Deng, Mengyu Xu, Jiale Liu, Hongyang Zhang, Qiaoxin Yang, Chongyang Gao. (2026). Rethinking LLM-Judged Helpfulness as a Pedagogy Signal: A Pre-Registered Audit Across Tutor Models. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28128

article_title: Is It Ethical for Teachers to Use AI for Student Feedback?
citation: Luo, J. (Jess), & Eaton, S. (2026). Is It Ethical for Teachers to Use AI for Student Feedback?. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(3). https://doi.org/10.53761/887m5346
title: Contextual-complexity framework for judging the ethics of teacher AI feedback use
description: The article proposes that ethical evaluation of teachers' AI feedback use requires "a more nuanced understanding of what it means for teachers to use AI for feedback" rather than a blanket judgment. The framework turns on contextual factors the authors name: "the purposes of assessment, the features of student assignments, and the types of feedback automated by AI." It functions as an organizing account for the study's eight ethical areas, situating each within the specific assessment context in which AI feedback is deployed.
requirements: Ethical judgments must be made with reference to the specific assessment purpose, assignment features, and feedback types involved rather than applied generically.
target_learning_goals: ethical use of AI in assessment and feedback practices
examples: The study grounds the framework in university policy reviews, social media posts, and interviews with university teachers and students.
key_sources: Luo, J. (Jess), & Eaton, S. (2026). Is It Ethical for Teachers to Use AI for Student Feedback?. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(3). https://doi.org/10.53761/887m5346

article_title: Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement
citation: April Joy Miles, Paige Haber-Curran, Khalid Arar. (2026). Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement. Open Praxis, 18(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1191
title: Build classroom norms for LLM use collaboratively with students rather than imposing compliance rules
description: The article recommends that instructors empower students by building classroom norms for LLM use together, opening dialogue about appropriate usage and limitations so students take ownership of ethical practices. When norm-setting is treated as a teaching moment rather than a compliance exercise, students develop a working understanding of authorship as something they actively construct and protect, and shared norms position ethical AI engagement as a collective responsibility.
requirements: Discussions can be linked directly to institutional academic integrity policies
constraints: Recommended on conceptual grounds drawing on an ethics of care, not empirically tested here
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
ethical AI engagement
ownership of authorship norms
examples: Students can develop and assess classroom AI use policies or collaboratively develop guidelines for permitted AI in group work
key_sources: April Joy Miles, Paige Haber-Curran, Khalid Arar. (2026). Prompts to Practice: A Pedagogical Framework for Human-Centered AI Engagement. Open Praxis, 18(3), 481–494. https://doi.org/10.55982/openpraxis.18.3.1191

article_title: Control vs. Agency: Exploring the History of AI in Education
citation: Mishra, P., Henriksen, D., Woo, L. J., & Oster, N. (2025). Control vs. Agency: Exploring the History of AI in Education. TechTrends. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11528-025-01064-2
title: Control versus autonomy as an enduring organizing tension in the history of AI in education
description: The article organizes the history of AI in education around an enduring struggle between control and autonomy in learning. It frames this tension through a comparative analysis of two contrasting AI-driven educational models: John Anderson's structured cognitive tutoring systems and Seymour Papert's constructionist approach emphasizing creative agency. The framework is used to interpret how current GenAI debates continue this historical pattern rather than representing a wholly new situation.
requirements: Understanding current GenAI debates requires situating them within the historical evolution of AI in education, including early conceptual and terminological choices
constraints: The framework is developed through historical and comparative analysis rather than experimental testing
target_learners: educators and educational designers integrating AI technologies
target_learning_goals: understanding the historical and philosophical tensions shaping AI-supported learning environments
examples: The article traces the historical evolution of AI in education and compares Anderson's cognitive tutoring systems with Papert's constructionist approach as two poles of the control-autonomy tension
key_sources: Mishra, P., Henriksen, D., Woo, L. J., & Oster, N. (2025). Control vs. Agency: Exploring the History of AI in Education. TechTrends. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11528-025-01064-2

article_title: Cognitive Agent Compilation for Explicit Problem Solver Modeling
citation: Hyeongdon Moon, Carolyn Rosé, and John Stamper. (2026). Cognitive Agent Compilation for Explicit Problem Solver Modeling. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07040
title: Cognitive Agent Compilation: a failure-driven loop compiling Teacher LLM knowledge into an explicit Knowledge Base
description: CAC is a pipeline that converts a strong model's problem-solving capability into a target agent operating over an explicit knowledge representation. It separates knowledge representation, problem-solving policy, and verification/update rules through a four-step failure-driven cycle: solve, analyze failure, update the Knowledge Base, and retry. The authors state the goal is 'not merely compression, but explicitness', so behavior is attributable to a declared knowledge state rather than latent weights.
requirements: The Teacher LLM must be able to predict behavioral shifts from adding or removing knowledge elements and correct the agent solely by modifying the Knowledge Base
constraints: The authors treat CAC not as a validated cognitive replica but as a bounded and inspectable problem-solving model; design goals are not validated against student traces
target_learners: students in intelligent tutoring system settings
target_learning_goals: problem-solving knowledge represented as explicit knowledge components and misconceptions
examples: A prototype compiled with an SLM Cognitive Agent and a gemma-3-27b-it Teacher LLM over the OLI_Biology dataset
key_sources: Hyeongdon Moon, Carolyn Rosé, and John Stamper. (2026). Cognitive Agent Compilation for Explicit Problem Solver Modeling. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07040

article_title: MindCopilot: Towards Formalizing and Evaluating Granular Human-LLM Co-Writing
citation: Youqing Fang, Yinhao Tang, Yanan Sun, Jiangning Liu, Ziyi Wang, Xun Zhao, Bin Liu, Weiming Zhang, Kuikun Liu, Wenwei Zhang, Kai Chen. (2026). MindCopilot: Towards Formalizing and Evaluating Granular Human-LLM Co-Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23535
title: Co-Writing Fidelity Suite (HAR and KED metrics)
description: A set of interaction-aware evaluation metrics for human-AI co-writing. The article states: "we introduce the Co-Writing Fidelity Suite, a set of interaction-aware metrics designed to evaluate human-AI collaboration along two complementary dimensions: alignment and interaction friction." Hierarchical Acceptance Rate models acceptance as a structured multi-stage decision, while Knowledge-aware Editing Distance weights edit operations by cognitive cost, so that semantic rewrites and factual corrections cost more than surface edits. The suite is validated against expert annotation, editing-duration logs, simulation, and a user study.
requirements: KED evaluation requires writing logs recording human revisions to AI-generated suggestions together with timestamps, using editing duration as a behavioral proxy for cognitive effort.
constraints: The metrics are designed for suggestion-based proactive completion; the authors state that how HAR and KED generalize to tool-augmented or multi-agent co-writing settings remains a promising future direction.
target_learners: adult writers using LLM writing assistants
target_learning_goals: evaluating user-assistant alignment and cognitive editing effort in co-writing systems
examples: HAR was evaluated on 1.2K expert-annotated instances with a checklist-style protocol; KED was evaluated using writing logs from the CoAuthor dataset.
key_sources: Youqing Fang, Yinhao Tang, Yanan Sun, Jiangning Liu, Ziyi Wang, Xun Zhao, Bin Liu, Weiming Zhang, Kuikun Liu, Wenwei Zhang, Kai Chen. (2026). MindCopilot: Towards Formalizing and Evaluating Granular Human-LLM Co-Writing. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.23535

article_title: Designing Against Deskilling: Metacognitive Feedback Reduces Cognitive Offloading to LLM Assistants
citation: Sebastian Maier, Kai Schwabe, Manuel Schneider, and Stefan Feuerriegel. (2026). Designing Against Deskilling: Metacognitive Feedback Reduces Cognitive Offloading to LLM Assistants. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20143
title: Cognitive offloading paradigm extended to LLM-assisted learning, distinguishing answer offloading from instrumental help
description: The article extends the cognitive offloading paradigm to LLM-assisted learning by focusing on users' decisions about how much of a task to solve themselves versus hand over to the assistant. It defines cognitive offloading as "using actions or external tools to change a task's processing requirements and reduce cognitive demand" and coins "answer offloading" for requesting the complete solution, which removes the effortful processing on which durable learning depends, in contrast to instrumental help such as asking how to approach a problem, which leaves practice intact. The amount of help requested is treated as an offloading decision shaped by effort, incentives, confidence, and metacognitive monitoring.
requirements: The assistant must leave the offloading decision to the learner; in the study the LLM provided guidance by default and complete answers only on explicit request, so offloading reflected an active, deliberate choice.
constraints: The article notes offloading is not harmful per se; whether reduced cognitive effort helps or harms skill development depends on what is offloaded relative to the skill being developed.
target_learners: Adult online participants practicing fraction arithmetic (aged 18-80)
target_learning_goals: Fraction arithmetic procedure skill; regulating how much cognitive work to delegate to an LLM assistant
examples: In the study, requesting the complete answer reduced the reward to 1 point while any number of guidance requests preserved the full 10 points, operationalizing the distinction between answer offloading and guided help.
key_sources: Sebastian Maier, Kai Schwabe, Manuel Schneider, and Stefan Feuerriegel. (2026). Designing Against Deskilling: Metacognitive Feedback Reduces Cognitive Offloading to LLM Assistants. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20143

article_title: The nature of science in the age of generative artificial intelligence: Epistemic authority and materiality
citation: Muminova, Z. O., Mamatkulov, D. M., Turokulova, R. I., Rakhmonova, N. T., Shavqiyev, O. S. O., & Zoirova, S. U. (2026). The nature of science in the age of generative artificial intelligence: Epistemic authority, materiality, and a synergetic response. EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education, 22(10), em2943. https://doi.org/10.29333/ejmste/19481
title: Synergetic coupled-system model of the science classroom with verification norm, requirement, and materiality
description: The article proposes a coupled-system model in which the student, the generative model, and scientific practice interact as coupled subsystems. As the abstract states, "the classroom verification norm is the order parameter, the teacher-set verification requirement the control parameter, and materiality the boundary condition." The requirement is exogenous and adjustable in graded steps, while the norm emerges from mutually observable verification acts and then constrains individual behavior through the slaving principle, outlasting the requirement that seeded it.
requirements: Materiality in the form of laboratory work, observation, and data collection must keep the classroom system open to reality, treated as structurally necessary
constraints: Synergetic is used as a structured analogy with rules of correspondence; no claim is made that classroom dynamics conform to the equations of laser physics
target_learning_goals: developing a classroom norm of verifying model output against independent sources
examples: The mechanism runs in a loop of four steps: a requirement prompts verification acts, the acts become visible and are taken up by peers, perceived practice shifts, and the perceived practice then regulates individual acts
key_sources: Muminova, Z. O., Mamatkulov, D. M., Turokulova, R. I., Rakhmonova, N. T., Shavqiyev, O. S. O., & Zoirova, S. U. (2026). The nature of science in the age of generative artificial intelligence: Epistemic authority, materiality, and a synergetic response. article_title: Beyond Task Completion: A Theoretical Integration and Framework for Guiding Students' ChatGPT Use for Learning
citation: Øby, E. (2026). Beyond Task Completion: A Theoretical Integration and Framework for Guiding Students’ ChatGPT Use for Learning. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. https://doi.org/10.53761/5apqd333
title: Cognitive load theory perspective on students' reliance on generative AI during complex academic tasks
description: The article uses cognitive load theory as one of its two foundational lenses, treating cognitive demands as a mechanism shaping students' decisions about AI reliance. The abstract states that "cognitive demands, motivational orientations, perceived competence, and perceived task value may shape students’ decisions about when and how to rely on generative AI tools during academic work". Within the framework, cognitive load considerations help explain when AI support may aid or bypass essential cognitive processes.
requirements: Integration with goal orientation theory and the mediating constructs to form the full framework
constraints: Applied conceptually to generative AI use; no empirical measurement of load is reported
target_learning_goals: Managing cognitive demands during complex academic tasks
key_sources: Øby, E. (2026). Beyond Task Completion: A Theoretical Integration and Framework for Guiding Students’ ChatGPT Use for Learning. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice. https://doi.org/10.53761/5apqd333

article_title: Comparative analysis of peer group and AI-generated feedback in peer assessment: Insights into feedback quality and student perceptions in higher education
citation: Li, X., Zhang, Y., & Liu, T. (2026). Comparative analysis of peer group and AI-generated feedback in peer assessment: Insights into feedback quality and student perceptions in higher education. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(4), 129–146. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.11467
title: Combine peer group feedback with AI-generated feedback so contextualised human insights are integrated with structured, objective AI support
description: The article recommends combining human and AI feedback in peer assessment, arguing this "can enhance formative assessment by integrating contextualised human insights with structured and objective AI support". It positions the two sources as complementary rather than substitutable, grounded in its finding that each source showed distinct perceived strengths.
requirements: AI-generated feedback used alongside, not instead of, peer group feedback
constraints: AI feedback should be "used as a supplementary tool rather than a standalone assessor, with ongoing human oversight"
target_learning_goals: improving quality of peer assessment feedback
formative assessment and revision
examples: In the study, 13 undergraduate peer groups received both peer group and ChatGPT-4o feedback across two assessment stages in a smart learning environment design course.

article_title: How Human-Centered Is AI-Aided Learning in Education?
citation: Katia Tödt, Corinne Büching, and Bastian Granas. (2026). Digital Education and Innovation: Objectives and Conceptual Classification of the Volume. In Digital Education and Innovation. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-26816-7_1
title: Transfer of research knowledge into educational practice requires cooperative, recontextualising processes rather than one-way dissemination
description: The chapter argues, citing a position paper of the German state institutes, that research transfer fails when treated as one-way dissemination. It states that 'transfer is not a one-sided, mechanistic process' but demands communicative, cooperative processes and recontextualisation for each field of action, and that scientific institutions alone cannot achieve it. Co-constructive, design-oriented research approaches are presented as a response.
requirements: Cooperation between the key players in the field of education, accounting for differences between practical, political, administrative, and scientific action
constraints: The chapter notes research knowledge is criticised as insufficiently considered in practice, while administrators and policy actors assess its applicability pessimistically
target_learning_goals: evidence-informed improvement of educational practice, administration and policy
examples: The chapter names research-based learning, inquiry-based learning and action research as forms of close exchange between research, learning and practice

article_title: On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware–Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor
citation: Sidney Shapiro and Joshua Lindemann. (2026). On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware–Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02510
title: CourseChat: an on-premises multi-course RAG tutor with course-isolated collections, twin serving nodes, and prebuilt quiz banks
description: CourseChat is an on-premises retrieval-augmented generation tutor for undergraduate business courses, deployed behind a campus web gateway and intended for Moodle-embedded use. As the abstract states, "Six isolated course offerings—each keyed by its own course reference number (CRN)—share twin edge AI hosts running a FastAPI service, a local vector database, and a local large language model (LLM) served by Ollama." It offers grounded conversation with citations and module-scoped practice quizzes, keeping textbooks and student dialogue on institutional infrastructure.
requirements: Isolation is enforced by separate course ids, separate on-disk trees, separate Qdrant collections, and ?course= routing
constraints: The authors state the results do not establish learning gains; faculty ratings, peak-load capacity, and complete public-gateway acceptance remain separate evaluation needs
target_learning_goals: engaging with assigned course material
independent problem attempts with hints and feedback
checking explanations against course sources
examples: Six offerings (Courses 1–6) share one application binary while remaining isolated at the data and routing layers; production runs llama3.1:8b on both nodes
key_sources: Sidney Shapiro and Joshua Lindemann. (2026). On-Premises Multi-Course RAG Tutoring for Business Education: Hardware–Software Trade-offs in a Campus AI Tutor. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02510

article_title: Teacher Involvement in Developing Sustainable Education Materials for AI Integration in Green Energy Education
citation: Riandi Riandi, Ismail Ismail, Ida Kaniawati, Wahyu Sopandi, Diana Ayu Rostikawati, Defrizal Hamka & Suhendar Suhendar. (2026). Teacher involvement in developing sustainable education materials for AI integration in green energy education. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-34422-4
title: Integrated conceptual model of AI integration in green energy education combining Constructivism, TAM, and TPACK
description: The article proposes a conceptual model integrating three theoretical frameworks to explain teachers' ability to integrate AI into green energy education. It states: "Figure 2 presents a revised conceptual model that integrates three main theoretical frameworks: Constructivism, Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK)." Constructivism frames ESD material development as reflective, collaborative practice; TAM contributes AI knowledge and attitudes as cognitive and affective readiness; TPACK is represented by a Perceived TPACK construct capturing self-assessed ability to integrate technology, pedagogy, and content. Five constructs are theorised to influence AI Integration Ability directly.
requirements: Measurement of the five constructs (AI knowledge, attitudes toward AI, use of AI in green education, ESD material development, ability to use AI) via validated questionnaire indicators
constraints: The model was tested as an exploratory baseline assessment in which participants received no specific AI training before the survey
target_learners: in-service teachers in professional development programs
target_learning_goals: integrating AI into sustainability-oriented (green energy) teaching practices
examples: The model was tested with PLS-SEM on survey data from 122 in-service teachers using five dichotomous-item constructs

article_title: Scaffolding critical engagement with GenAI: Transforming ethnic minority preparatory students' collaborative discourse
citation: Deliang Wang and Cunling Bian. (2026). Scaffolding Critical Engagement with GenAI: Transforming Ethnic Minority Preparatory Students’ Collaborative Discourse in Prompt Engineering Tasks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28630
title: Instructor modeling with contrasting cases to disrupt uncritical reliance on GenAI
description: A lesson-level design pattern in which the instructor presents two simulated collaboration transcripts — a negative example of passive copying and superficial agreement, and a positive example of critical discussion and iterative inquiry — so students can identify and emulate productive collaborative behaviours. The article reports that "The instructor presented two simulated collaboration transcripts: a negative example illustrating passive copying and superficial agreement, and a positive example demonstrating critical discussion and iterative inquiry." Students did not experience this merely as technical training but as a deliberate challenge to their initial blind trust in algorithmic outputs.
requirements: Simulated transcripts must contrast high- and low-quality collaboration so students can recognize their own passive practices as detrimental
target_learning_goals: critical collaborative norms with GenAI
recognition of passive acceptance practices
examples: The Week 3 intervention paired the contrasting-case modeling with a subsequent authentic co-creation task using DeepSeek
key_sources: Deliang Wang and Cunling Bian. (2026). Scaffolding Critical Engagement with GenAI: Transforming Ethnic Minority Preparatory Students’ Collaborative Discourse in Prompt Engineering Tasks. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28630

article_title: Faithful Where It Can Be Checked: Auditing a Reflection Agent Against Its System Prompt in a Randomized Trial
citation: Subigya K. Nepal, Serena Soh, Noah Vinoya, SoHyun Park, Mahnaz Roshanaei, and Gabriella Harari. 2027. Faithful Where It Can Be Checked: Auditing a Reflection Agent Against Its System Prompt in a Randomized Trial. In Proceedings of CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '27). ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19635
title: Countable versus dispositional prompt rules, audited from deployment transcripts
description: The paper's organizing framework splits system-prompt instructions into two kinds. Countable rules "set targets that anyone can check from the output, such as the two-sentence cap on replies", while dispositional rules "describe how the agent should behave or its manner, such as not being overly agreeable". Instruction-following benchmarks only test the first kind, leaving manner rules unmeasured; the paper supplies the missing scoring mechanism through human coders and validated LLM annotators applied to a deployment's own transcripts, treating an unaudited agent as an unverified treatment in the health-intervention sense.
requirements: Complete conversation logs from the deployment, a randomized comparison so outcomes can be interpreted, and ideally the same model running more than one prompt so failures can be traced to the model or the wording
constraints: Differences in agent behavior between the two studies are descriptive only, because the sample and the prompt changed together between studies
target_learners: emerging adults in career reflection programs
target_learning_goals: career exploration and commitment-making
reflective self-insight
examples: The audit coded all 17,930 trial turns for nine agent moves and participant commitment language, validated annotators field by field against two human coders, and compared behavior rates against each prompt's own written rules

article_title: Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices
citation: Strydom, S. (2026). Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.11
title: Human-GAI engagement patterns vary across disciplinary, socio-technical and institutional contexts
description: The article conceptualises human-GAI paradigms as "enacted patterns of engagement that emerge across different disciplinary, socio-technical and institutional contexts". This means engagement with generative AI is not a stable individual attribute but a pattern that takes shape within a specific discipline's knowledge practices, an institution's socio-technical arrangements, and its governance environment. Designers of learning and policy should therefore expect and plan for context-dependent variation in how staff and students engage with GAI.
requirements: Analysis of engagement must attend to the disciplinary, socio-technical and institutional context in which it occurs
constraints: The framework is offered as an exploratory heuristic requiring empirical validation
target_learning_goals: context-sensitive design of AI-supported learning activities and policies
examples: The article examines each of the seven paradigms against the five epistemological dimensions as patterns emerging across contexts
key_sources: Strydom, S. (2026). Framing human-AI dynamics: An epistemological perspective on generative AI practices. Journal of Applied Learning and Teaching, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.37074/jalt.2026.9.2.11

article_title: How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops -- A Taxonomy
citation: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966v1
title: A hierarchical taxonomy of novice difficulties with selection and iteration in code reading
description: The article introduces a fine-grained taxonomy categorizing novice programmers' difficulties with reading control flow constructs. Its top dimension is the control structure involved (selection or iteration), with lower levels grouping difficulties by what students do not understand and then by how they struggle. The authors state it categorizes "difficulties specifically related to reading and understanding the control flow constructs selection and iteration". It is intended to harmonize research results, classify errors unambiguously, and hint at undiscovered difficulties.
requirements: It is scoped to conceptual-knowledge difficulties in reading code, excluding syntactic, lexical, and writing-only difficulties
constraints: It covers imperative languages such as C, C++, Python and Java and block-based languages like Scratch; the authors note they do not claim to have incorporated every paper on control-structure difficulties yet
target_learners: novice programmers in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: understanding of control flow, conditional statements, and loops
examples: Categories with literature references retain the source's wording; categories without references are newly created or newly found difficulties from the authors' own research
key_sources: Dimitri Eckert and Christian Kautz. (2026). How Students (Mis)understand Conditionals and Loops – A Taxonomy. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.26966

article_title: Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence
citation: Amrita Ganguly, Sai Sharanya Garika, Aditya Johri. (2026). Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Uncovering+Students%27+Mental+Models+of+Generative+Artificial+Intelligence%22
title: Concept map elicitation with holistic scoring and hierarchical clustering for studying GenAI mental models
description: The article's methodology combines concept map collection, holistic scoring, and hierarchical clustering to externalize mental models. Maps from a technology ethics course assignment were scored by two researchers on comprehensiveness, organization, and correctness on a 1-to-3 scale with pluses and minuses, mapped to a nine-point scale and four levels; 64 of 86 enrolled students' maps were retained after exclusions. Components were coded with a 16-code inductive codebook and clustered, with merge height indicating dissimilarity. The authors offer this as an initial elicitation step to be validated with interviews or think-aloud studies.
requirements: Students with basic familiarity with concept maps; two independent raters with discussion to resolve scoring disagreements
constraints: Six maps excluded as Level 1 for being difficult to read or lacking meaningful connections; two unstructured maps retained for rich examples; 29 level-identification disagreements resolved by discussion
target_learning_goals: eliciting and diagnosing students' conceptual understanding of generative AI
examples: Maps were scored on a nine-point scale and categorized into four levels, with Level 1 maps lacking meaningful concepts or connections
key_sources: Amrita Ganguly, Sai Sharanya Garika, Aditya Johri. (2026). Uncovering Students' Mental Models of Generative Artificial Intelligence. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Uncovering+Students%27+Mental+Models+of+Generative+Artificial+Intelligence%22

article_title: When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals?
citation: Zhengxu Li, Junling Wang, and April Yi Wang. (2026). When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals? arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10672
title: Control timing as a design dimension for AI-assisted visual authoring: pre-, mid-, and post-generation control
description: The article introduces "control timing" as a key design dimension in AI-assisted visual authoring, operationalized through three interaction paradigms that differ in when teachers intervene relative to AI output. Pre-generation control means users "specify intent solely through natural language prompts before generation"; mid-generation control means users "inspect and confirm an explicit layout structure before the system completes generation"; post-generation control means users "directly modify AI-generated visuals after generation through object-level edits". The framework holds task content constant and varies only the timing of human control.
requirements: The paradigms require a multi-stage generation pipeline with distinct points (intent specification, intermediate planning, localized refinement) at which control can be exercised.
constraints: The article instantiates and evaluates the three paradigms only for primary mathematics word problems in a single-session study.
target_learning_goals: creating pedagogically correct instructional visuals for arithmetic word problems
examples: A web-based prototype implemented all three paradigms for the same math word problems, using GPT-5 for text understanding and GPT-image-1.5 for image generation, with Math2Visual powering the post-gen pipeline.
key_sources: Zhengxu Li, Junling Wang, and April Yi Wang. (2026). When Should Teachers Control AI Generation for Mathematics Visuals? arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10672

article_title: From Experimentation to Integration: Embedding GenAI in Business Higher Education through the Lens of Constructive
citation: Zhou, X., Chai, Q., Chilukuri, B., & Quach, J. J. Y. (2026). From Experimentation to Integration: Embedding GenAI in Business Higher Education through the Lens of Constructive Alignment. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(2). https://doi.org/10.53761/pc04tp05
title: Extension of Biggs' constructive alignment for embedding GenAI in existing curricula
description: The article extends Biggs' theory of constructive alignment into the GenAI era, using it as the lens for curriculum integration of generative AI in business higher education. Its theoretical contribution is "demonstrating how GenAI can be embedded into existing pedagogical strategies without requiring full curriculum redesign". On this account, GenAI tools are aligned with intended learning outcomes and existing teaching and assessment strategies, so adoption proceeds by integration into the aligned system rather than by rebuilding the curriculum around the technology.
requirements: GenAI use must be aligned with strategic learning outcomes for adoption to be coherent and sustainable
constraints: The extension is demonstrated in business higher education contexts at one UK university during first-year implementation
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate business higher education students
target_learning_goals: meaningful integration of GenAI tools into business curricula aligned with learning outcomes
examples: The study analysed 17 cases of GenAI adoption at a UK Russell Group university through this lens during the first year of implementation.
key_sources: Zhou, X., Chai, Q., Chilukuri, B., & Quach, J. J. Y. (2026). From Experimentation to Integration: Embedding GenAI in Business Higher Education through the Lens of Constructive Alignment. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice, 23(2). https://doi.org/10.53761/pc04tp05

article_title: \"Is this a trap?\": Student teachers' perceptions and adoption of GenAI in assessments in three teacher education courses
citation: Zou, T. X. P., Hounsell, D., Huijser, H., & Tse, R. T. L. (2026). “Is this a trap?”: Student teachers’ perceptions and adoption of GenAI in assessments in three teacher education courses. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 1–17. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10549
title: Maintain consistent GenAI assessment policies and communicate them clearly to students
description: The study concludes that GenAI assessment policy should be consistent and communicated effectively. It states that "This study shows the importance of consistent assessment policies and effective communication", and that "Effective communication with students about what GenAI usage is or is not allowed in assessment is critical to avoid misunderstanding." The principle directs instructors to state explicitly what GenAI use is permitted in each assessment so students are not left guessing.
requirements: Instructors must specify what GenAI usage is or is not allowed in each assessment and convey this clearly to students.
target_learners: teacher education students in higher education
target_learning_goals: authentic demonstration of learning in non-exam assessments without unwanted GenAI reliance
examples: The three teacher education courses embedded GenAI use in assessment with declarations of GenAI use in submitted assignments, and the study derived the communication recommendation from students' reported misunderstandings and concerns.
key_sources: Zou, T. X. P., Hounsell, D., Huijser, H., & Tse, R. T. L. (2026). “Is this a trap?”: Student teachers’ perceptions and adoption of GenAI in assessments in three teacher education courses. Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 42(1), 1–17. https://doi.org/10.14742/ajet.10549

article_title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task
citation: Nataliya Kosmyna, Eugene Hauptmann, Ye Tong Yuan, Jessica Situ, Xian-Hao Liao, Ashly Vivian Beresnitzky, Iris Braunstein, Pattie Maes. (2009). Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task. Preprint, under review. https://www.brainonllm.com/
title: Cognitive debt: accumulated cognitive cost of relying on an AI assistant for essay writing
description: The article's organizing account is that using an LLM for essay writing accrues a "Cognitive Debt" — a cumulative cost carried across sessions, visible as reduced neural connectivity, impaired quoting and memory, and low ownership even after the tool is removed. It frames this via cognitive offloading concerns, arguing that reduced immediate cognitive load may come at the price of diminished engagement in deep analytical processes during learning tasks.
requirements: The account is grounded in a four-session longitudinal design with EEG, NLP, and interview measures, including the session-4 crossover reassignment of participants.
constraints: The authors present the study as a preliminary guide to understanding cognitive and practical impacts of AI on learning environments, not a definitive account.
target_learners: adult essay writers (participants writing SAT-style essays)
target_learning_goals: essay writing
memory and recall of one's own writing
critical engagement with produced text
examples: Session 4 crossover: LLM-to-Brain participants wrote without tools and showed weaker connectivity; Brain-to-LLM participants showed a connectivity spike across bands.
key_sources: Nataliya Kosmyna, Eugene Hauptmann, Ye Tong Yuan, Jessica Situ, Xian-Hao Liao, Ashly Vivian Beresnitzky, Iris Braunstein, Pattie Maes. (2009). Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task. Preprint, under review. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08872

article_title: The Effects of Agent Type and Feedback Style on Self-Directed Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study
citation: Han Xue, Cao Jing, Wang Zi, Luo Heng. (2026). The Effects of Agent Type and Feedback Style on Self-Directed Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071069
title: Customized vs. general-purpose LLM-based educational agents on the Coze platform
description: The study built four AI agents on the Coze platform, all on the same LLM (Kimi-32K) with identical interfaces and dialogue parameters. "Customized agents used two specialized knowledge bases alongside prompts: the “Instructional Design Textbook,” covering key design principles, and the “Instructional Design Evaluation Rubric,” with a seven-dimensional evaluation framework." Customized agents followed a predefined workflow ordering the seven dimensions with entry and termination conditions, while general-purpose agents relied only on prompts, with progression determined by the model's context. Feedback style (Socratic questioning vs. directive correction) was operationalized within each agent type.
requirements: Domain-specific knowledge bases and a structured evaluation rubric for the customized configuration
Anchoring of feedback to the student's submission to avoid generalized advice
constraints: All agents shared one underlying model and platform, so differences reflect configuration rather than base-model architecture
target_learners: Postgraduate students completing instructional design tasks
target_learning_goals: Improving instructional design drafts through AI feedback
examples: Socratic prompts such as “Have you considered …?” versus directive feedback that directly pointed out deficiencies and gave improvement directions
key_sources: Han Xue, Cao Jing, Wang Zi, Luo Heng. (2026). The Effects of Agent Type and Feedback Style on Self-Directed Learning: A Mixed-Methods Study. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071069

article_title: Guidelines for Designing AI Technologies to Support Adult Learning
citation: Jennifer M. Reddig, Glen R. Smith Jr., Sanaz Ahmadzadeh Siyahrood, Wesley G. Morris, Yoojin Bae, Kaitlyn Crutcher, John Kos, Rahul K. Dass, Jinho Kim, Momin Naushad Siddiqui, Daniel Weitekamp, Ploy Thajchayapong, Sandeep Kakar, Alex Endert, Scott Crossley, Min Kyu Kim, Chris Dede, Ashok Goel, and Christopher J. MacLellan. 2026. Guidelines for Designing AI Technologies to Support Adult Learning. In Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS '26), Singapore, Singapore. ACM, New York, NY, USA. https://doi.org/10.1145/3800645.3813102
title: Community of Inquiry framework: meaningful online education arises from the interaction of teaching, social, and cognitive presence
description: The Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework, introduced by Garrison et al. and adopted by AI-ALOE as a core design framework, holds that "a meaningful educational experience occurs through the interaction of teaching presence, social presence, and cognitive presence". Cognitive presence is the learner's internal engagement; social presence is group collaboration and authentic self-projection; teaching presence is the organizational structure, design, and facilitation of the environment. The article uses CoI to label each of its 19 design guidelines by the presence(s) they support, noting the presences are interconnected and that G1 (data practices) sits outside the framework.
requirements: Adult and online learning environments require intentional design and support for the three presences, since adult learners often engage in distributed, asynchronous contexts
constraints: Guideline G1 (data practices) was not assigned a Community of Inquiry component because aligning with it would not increase student cognitive, social, or teaching presence
target_learners: Adult learners in online and hybrid education
target_learning_goals: Meaningful educational experience through cognitive, social, and teaching presence
examples: The AI-ALOE technologies were designed to support different elements and combinations of CoI elements, and Figure 3 organizes the 19 guidelines across the three overlapping CoI dimensions
key_sources: Jennifer M. Reddig, Glen R. Smith Jr., Sanaz Ahmadzadeh Siyahrood, Wesley G. Morris, Yoojin Bae, Kaitlyn Crutcher, John Kos, Rahul K. Dass, Jinho Kim, Momin Naushad Siddiqui, Daniel Weitekamp, Ploy Thajchayapong, Sandeep Kakar, Alex Endert, Scott Crossley, Min Kyu Kim, Chris Dede, Ashok Goel, and Christopher J. MacLellan. 2026. Guidelines for Designing AI Technologies to Support Adult Learning. In Designing Interactive Systems Conference (DIS '26), Singapore, Singapore.
