article_title: Beyond Positive or Negative: Latent Profiles of University Students’ AI Attitude and Their Career-Development Correlates
citation: Song Hongfeng, Hu Anqi, Li Xueyan. (2026). Beyond Positive or Negative: Latent Profiles of University Students’ AI Attitude and Their Career-Development Correlates. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16091460
title: Configurational, bivalent framework of AI attitudes as within-person combinations of capability appraisal, threat, and AI creative self-efficacy
description: The study adapts Park et al.'s (2024) AAAW multidimensional framework to university students, treating AI attitudes as configurations rather than a single favorable-unfavorable continuum. Six indicators capture "evaluations of AI capability, perceived use-related and career-related threat, and AI creative self-efficacy." Building on the evaluative-space model and cognitive appraisal theory, favorable and unfavorable reactions can coexist within individuals, so a person-centered latent profile approach reveals evaluative complexity that an overall attitude score would obscure.
requirements: Person-centered analysis (latent profile analysis) over multiple object-anchored attitude indicators rather than a single composite score
constraints: Framework was developed for workplace settings and adapted to university students; AI creative self-efficacy replaces personal utility as a contextually adapted, non-equivalent indicator
target_learners: first-year university students preparing for AI-affected careers
target_learning_goals: career preparation and adaptive readiness in response to AI-driven change
examples: Four empirically derived profiles: Positive Empowerment, Anxious Acceptance, Low-Perception Detached, and High-Perception High-Vigilance
key_sources: Song Hongfeng, Hu Anqi, Li Xueyan. (2026). Beyond Positive or Negative: Latent Profiles of University Students’ AI Attitude and Their Career-Development Correlates. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16091460

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health
citation: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393
title: Continuum hypothesis of caring relationships ordering entities by descending responsiveness
description: The paper proposes that 'All entities that trigger a sense of connectedness in individuals form a spectrum ordered by descending responsiveness.' Humans with full moral subjectivity occupy one end, animals with limited subjectivity and nonverbal responses the middle, and nature and artifacts without subjective consciousness the other end. AI occupies an exclusive zone: it can simulate empathy, attention, and acceptance with response intensity approximating human interaction, yet its feedback stems from algorithmic optimization rather than genuine subjective care. Differences across the spectrum lie in the authenticity, symmetry, and subjectivity of mutual feedback, not in whether connection exists.
requirements: The spectrum is defined by each entity's responsiveness and co-constructive capacity rather than by whether the entity is human.
target_learning_goals: understanding human-AI relational bonds
examples: The article cites human-pet bond research showing individuals form stable caring connections with animals even without symmetric linguistic communication.
key_sources: Fu Jinbin & Zhao Fang. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Connectedness: Theoretical Reconstruction of Connectedness and Its Impacts on Adolescent Mental Health. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081393

article_title: A Feasibility and Implementation Integrity Study of the Community Builder (CoBi): An AI-based Collaboration Support System in K-12 Classrooms
citation: Breideband, T., Bush, J. B., Reitman, J. G., Rose, S., Weatherley, J., Penuel, W. R., & D'Mello, S. (2025). A Feasibility and Implementation Integrity Study of the Community Builder (CoBi): An AI-based Collaboration Support System in K-12 Classrooms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00509-2
title: CoBi: an AI-based classroom-wide collaboration support system with privacy-preserving visualizations
description: CoBi is a classroom-wide AI system that "uses speech recognition and language understanding to create non-evaluative and privacy-preserving visualizations of uplifting small group student discourse." Audio is captured with omnidirectional table-top microphones, streamed in 10-s chunks, transcribed with Whisper ASR, and classified by discourse classifiers to detect when students enact community agreements. Feedback is always aggregated at the classroom level; student- or group-level feedback is not available, a design constraint to protect privacy and build trust.
requirements: Commodity equipment including omnidirectional microphones and Chromebooks; a scalable cloud-based speech processing pipeline; embedding in the Sensor Immersion curriculum unit
constraints: Visualizations are aggregated at classroom level only; only three CA categories were currently representable in noticings; system operates under low-bandwidth conditions
target_learners: middle school students in K-12 classrooms
target_learning_goals: collaboration skills and community agreement enactment
examples: Deployed in two classroom studies with 61 students across six middle school classrooms in the Western US
key_sources: Breideband, T., Bush, J. B., Reitman, J. G., Rose, S., Weatherley, J., Penuel, W. R., & D'Mello, S. (2025). A Feasibility and Implementation Integrity Study of the Community Builder (CoBi): An AI-based Collaboration Support System in K-12 Classrooms. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00509-2

article_title: Designing for Reach: Seven Levers and the Student Alone with AI
citation: Halani, A. (2026). Designing for Reach: Seven Levers and the Student Alone with AI. Tang Institute at Phillips Academy. https://www.tanginstitute.andover.edu
title: Coordinate multiple lever settings rather than adjusting one lever alone
description: Because a single lever's reach depends on the settings of the others, the paper recommends coordinated adjustment: telling students process matters (Frame) has smaller reach than making the product less valuable (Structure), and warning students (Frame) has smaller reach than designing a task the pitfall does not work on (Material). The paper notes "It is certainly possible, and perhaps even likely, that combining the adjustment of both settings is more powerful than simply adjusting one (Jang et al., 2010)."
requirements: Teachers must identify which lever settings send conflicting messages before adjusting
constraints: The paper states this combining claim as possible and likely, citing Jang et al. (2010), not as established for these levers
target_learning_goals: making design messages consistent in unsupervised moments
examples: The paper contrasts telling students the process matters with making the product be considered less valuable under Structure
key_sources: Halani, A. (2026). Designing for Reach: Seven Levers and the Student Alone with AI. Tang Institute at Phillips Academy. https://doi.org/10.35542/osf.io/t4cd2_v1

article_title: Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols
citation: Li Shijin & Liu Junjian. (2026). Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081365
title: Combine interaction traces with brief learner-authored checkpoints for formative visibility, treating channels as complementary
description: Because verbalized monitoring and enacted control leave different observable traces, the article recommends that, where feasible and ethically appropriate, "educators could combine low-burden interaction traces with brief learner-authored checkpoints to improve formative visibility, not to enable surveillance, automated proficiency scoring, or validation of one source against the other." The absence of evidence in one channel should not be taken as evidence the process did not occur: logs can preserve revisions without rationales, while speech can preserve evaluations never enacted.
requirements: Formative interpretation should rely on temporally linked participant-level sequences rather than pooled label prevalence, using a coding scheme validated for the task, population, and GenAI system
constraints: The authors warn against surveillance use, automated proficiency scoring, and treating either channel as a criterion measure
target_learning_goals: making monitoring–control coordination visible for formative feedback
examples: When a revision appears in the log without an articulated rationale, an instructor might invite the learner to explain the basis for the change; when a discrepancy is verbalized without action, the learner might be prompted to decide whether adaptation is warranted
key_sources: Li Shijin & Liu Junjian. (2026). Mapping the Distribution and Depth of Metacognitive Processes in Generative AI-Assisted Learning: Evidence from Interaction Logs and Concurrent Think-Aloud Protocols. Behavioral Sciences. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16081365

article_title: Community-Based AI Learning: Redistributing Artificial Intelligence's Epistemic Authority in Education
citation: Santiago Ojeda-Ramirez, Symone Gyles and Kylie Peppler. 2026. Community-Based AI Learning: Redistributing Artificial Intelligence's Epistemic Authority in Education. In Proceedings of 2026 Conference for Research on Equitable and Sustained Participation in Engineering, Computing, and Technology (RESPECT 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3796496.3811760
title: Community-based AI learning: a framework anchoring AI education in community epistemologies
description: The paper defines community-based AI learning as "an approach to learning with and about AI that anchors epistemic activity in locally meaningful concerns, redistributes authority across heterogeneous forms of expertise, and orients AI engagement toward collective sense-making and action in relation to lived conditions." Drawing on community-based science education and constructionism, it positions learners and communities as legitimate knowers alongside AI systems, treating local experience as the evaluative standard for AI outputs rather than a cultural enrichment resource.
requirements: Learning must be anchored in locally meaningful community concerns rather than abstract or universally transferable AI knowledge
constraints: The paper is a perspective piece; the framework is theorized, not empirically tested in this article
target_learners: K-12 and higher education learners engaging with generative AI
target_learning_goals: Critical AI literacy
Epistemic judgment about when to trust, interrogate, or reject AI
examples: The paper sketches a unit in which students design something real for their community—a restaurant concept, a neighborhood tool, a local cultural archive—using AI as a design resource while community practitioners serve as co-evaluative judges.
key_sources: Santiago Ojeda-Ramirez, Symone Gyles and Kylie Peppler. 2026. Community-Based AI Learning: Redistributing Artificial Intelligence's Epistemic Authority in Education. In Proceedings of 2026 Conference for Research on Equitable and Sustained Participation in Engineering, Computing, and Technology (RESPECT 2026). https://doi.org/10.1145/3796496.3811760

article_title: Situated AI ethics: a cultural-historical and ecological framework for education
citation: Juliana Elisa Raffaghelli, Henriikka Vartiainen, Matt Bower, Martina Ronci, Chris Shelton, Kathryn MacCallum, Jihyun Lee, Mary Webb, Yousra Cthouki, David Smith. (2026). Situated AI Ethics: A Cultural-Historical and Ecological Framework for Education. Computers and Education Open. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100368
title: Comparative table mapping national AI-ethics approaches onto the ecological model
description: The article developed 'a comparative table mapping the different ecological levels—Self, Classroom/Group, State, Cultural Norms, and Global—within K-12 education across a selection of countries'. Seven countries (Australia, Finland, England, France, Italy, New Zealand, South Korea) were mapped by author-experts with 10 to 30 years of experience, drawing on grey literature such as mass media articles, policy documents, case studies, institutional websites, and research publications collected between June and September 2025 and validated by country experts.
requirements: Country experts actively engaged in research, teaching, and policy-making in the represented context
constraints: The article notes the table 'serves as a heuristic device' and that the underlying model is demonstrated rather than validated
target_learning_goals: understanding situated variation in AI-ethics decision-making across national contexts
examples: Two researchers reviewed the contributed sources for alignment and coherence, and each author revised a final country report presented in Annex 1
key_sources: Juliana Elisa Raffaghelli, Henriikka Vartiainen, Matt Bower, Martina Ronci, Chris Shelton, Kathryn MacCallum, Jihyun Lee, Mary Webb, Yousra Cthouki, David Smith. (2026). Situated AI Ethics: A Cultural-Historical and Ecological Framework for Education. Computers and Education Open. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeo.2026.100368

article_title: Reinforcement Learning in Education: A Systematic Literature Review
citation: Anna Riedmann, Philipp Schaper, Birgit Lugrin. (2025). Reinforcement Learning in Education: A Systematic Literature Review. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00494-6
title: Two-axis taxonomy of RL-based adaptation in education: content-related versus guidance-related
description: The review organizes RL-based educational applications by the kind of action the RL agent takes, distinguishing two main categories. The content-related category covers instructional sequencing (also called reinforcement scheduling) of learning activities to create personalized learning plans, including selecting content and adjusting pace or difficulty. The guidance-related category covers pedagogical strategies: "selecting the type of activity or hint to provide in response to a given learning task or problem", including hint generation, personalized feedback, and tutorial planning. This extends Doroudi et al.'s instructional-sequencing focus to a more holistic scope.
requirements: Studies must implement a single-agent RL algorithm whose actions are either instructional activities or problem-solving steps to be classifiable in this taxonomy
constraints: Student modeling, learning-content generation, bandit-based A/B testing, and multi-agent systems are explicitly excluded from the taxonomy's scope
target_learners: learners across preschool, school, higher education, and adult education contexts as covered by the reviewed studies
target_learning_goals: adaptive and personalized learning through content sequencing and pedagogical guidance
examples: The review classified 53 included papers as content-based and 36 as guidance-related using this taxonomy
key_sources: Anna Riedmann, Philipp Schaper, Birgit Lugrin. (2025). Reinforcement Learning in Education: A Systematic Literature Review. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00494-6

article_title: Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach
citation: Adeeb Obaid Alsuhaymi and Fouad Ahmed Atallah. (2026). Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach. Sustainability 2026, 18, 1257. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18031257
title: Conditional model of AI and sustainable education: AI supports sustainable education only under five governance conditions
description: The article synthesizes its four analytical results into a conditional explanatory model stating that AI supports sustainable education only when five conditions hold: sustainability is not substituted by efficiency metrics, datafication is governed by public-oriented and ethical accountability, normative friction constrains instrumental adoption, equity is treated as a governance responsibility, and epistemic integrity is actively protected. The article states: "AI supports sustainable education only when (i) sustainability is not substituted by efficiency metrics, (ii) datafication is governed by public-oriented and ethical accountability, (iii) normative friction constrains instrumental adoption, (iv) equity is treated as a governance responsibility, (v) epistemic integrity is actively protected". It positions the model as moving beyond the generic claim that AI has benefits and risks by specifying mechanisms, boundary conditions, and governance pathways.
requirements: Explicit educational purposes, ethical constraints, equity-oriented governance, and protection of epistemic integrity must subordinate AI adoption
constraints: The model is derived from qualitative value-critical analysis of literature, not from empirical evaluation of specific AI applications
target_learners: learners in AI-mediated educational systems across higher education and value-based educational contexts
target_learning_goals: long-term intellectual, ethical, and social flourishing; educational purpose, equity, epistemic integrity, and governance of AI-mediated learning
examples: Table 2 summarizes each analytical result with its core mechanism, risk under weak governance, and boundary condition for sustainable education
key_sources: Adeeb Obaid Alsuhaymi and Fouad Ahmed Atallah. (2026). Sustainable Education in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Digitalization: A Value-Critical Approach. Sustainability 2026, 18, 1257. https://doi.org/10.3390/su18031257

article_title: Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership
citation: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957
title: Integrated framework linking cognitive ownership, mutual evaluation, and outcome-aligned verification for assessing AI-assisted work
description: The article develops a conceptual framework connecting cognitive ownership, mutual evaluation, and selected verification performances so that institutions can make bounded claims about learner capability. It distinguishes product quality, capability demonstrated during assessment, and learning established through change and retention. The framework's contribution is integrative: it specifies relationships among existing ideas within an assessment design and explains how competing evidence should affect decisions. As the author states, these components "support bounded claims about learner capability while preserving legitimate opportunities for AI-assisted work."
requirements: The assessor must explicitly state the claim to be supported and the assistance conditions under which performance is interpreted
constraints: The framework is proposed rather than empirically validated; no validated instrument, established threshold, or demonstrated treatment effect is presented
It concerns capability demonstrated within specified tasks and conditions, and is not a psychological ownership scale, a test of legal authorship, or an instrument for identifying misconduct
target_learners: higher education students in tasks involving analysis, interpretation, design, or professional judgment
target_learning_goals: individual analytical capability under specified assistance conditions
effective collaboration with AI while remaining accountable for consequential decisions
examples: A worked hypothetical graduate leadership-development course illustrates task design, scoring weights, verification with live generative assistance excluded, a transfer variation, and responses to conflicting evidence
key_sources: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957

article_title: Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership
citation: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957
title: Cognitive ownership defined as demonstrated capacity to understand, evaluate, adapt, and accept responsibility for consequential reasoning under stated assistance conditions
description: Cognitive ownership is defined as a task-specific, conditional construct: the learner's demonstrated capacity to understand, evaluate, adapt, and accept responsibility for consequential reasoning represented in assessed work. It is an inference supported by performances, not a directly observed mental state. The article distinguishes product quality, provenance, demonstrated capability, and learning, noting that an AI-use declaration addresses provenance only. The author writes that ownership "names an inference supported by performances" and that the interpretation "should be no broader than the sampled performances justify."
requirements: Assessment must explicitly state the conditions of assistance under which ownership performances are elicited
constraints: The construct is task-specific: competence in judging one task does not establish ownership of different reasoning in another
Competent performance with permitted resources should not be reported as unaided competence unless the assessment supports that interpretation
target_learners: higher education students, particularly adults in applied professional programs
target_learning_goals: accountability for consequential reasoning in assessed work
examples: A student who can explain a choice, identify an error, and adapt the reasoning to a new case provides stronger support for the ownership inference than a student who merely states the work is understood
key_sources: William J. Rothwell. (2026). Assessing Learning When AI Can Produce the Product: An Integrated Framework for Cognitive Ownership and Mutual Evaluation. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-4503-1957

article_title: A mixed-methods analysis of AI scaffolding patterns and student inquiry profiles in a middle-school agriculture-STEM classroom
citation: Kilinc, S., Aldemir, T., Misiejuk, K., Kaliisa, R., Sabanwar, V., Bicer, A., Song, D., & Yalvac, B. (2026). A mixed-methods analysis of AI scaffolding patterns and student inquiry profiles in a middle-school agriculture-STEM classroom. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 11, 100683. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100683
title: Cognitive apprenticeship as a design and analytic framework for AI-delivered scaffolding
description: The article uses cognitive apprenticeship (Collins et al., 1991) both to configure the Aspen chatbot's pedagogical support and to code its responses for analysis. The framework treats six strategies as coordinated rather than isolated moves: "modeling makes expert reasoning visible, coaching provides tailored feedback and guidance as students attempt the task, and scaffolding supplies temporary structured support," while articulation, reflection, and exploration move students toward cognitive and metacognitive control. The pedagogical meaning of any single move depends on how it connects to others in interaction, which motivated Epistemic Network Analysis of AI-student exchanges.
requirements: Support strategies must operate as coordinated forms of connected support rather than isolated moves
constraints: Applying the framework to AI-delivered scaffolding is a relatively new context, allowing examination of where its strategies succeed or break down when enacted by an LLM agent
target_learners: middle school students in STEM inquiry
target_learning_goals: formulating and revising scientific research questions and hypotheses
examples: Aspen was configured to model expert-like reasoning, coach with targeted feedback, scaffold tasks into steps, prompt articulation, support reflection, and encourage exploration across the inquiry cycle
key_sources: Kilinc, S., Aldemir, T., Misiejuk, K., Kaliisa, R., Sabanwar, V., Bicer, A., Song, D., & Yalvac, B. (2026). A mixed-methods analysis of AI scaffolding patterns and student inquiry profiles in a middle-school agriculture-STEM classroom. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 11, 100683. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100683

article_title: A mixed-methods analysis of AI scaffolding patterns and student inquiry profiles in a middle-school agriculture-STEM classroom
citation: Kilinc, S., Aldemir, T., Misiejuk, K., Kaliisa, R., Sabanwar, V., Bicer, A., Song, D., & Yalvac, B. (2026). A mixed-methods analysis of AI scaffolding patterns and student inquiry profiles in a middle-school agriculture-STEM classroom. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 11, 100683. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100683
title: Design AI inquiry support to facilitate a complete pedagogical cycle connecting guidance, modeling, and metacognitive reflection, not models alone
description: Based on the contrast between the Struggling profile's fragmented support pattern and the Most Improved profile's integrated pattern, the article concludes that effective AI support in this context "may depend not only on providing models but also on facilitating a complete pedagogical cycle that connects guidance, modeling, and metacognitive reflection." This principle treats cognitive apprenticeship strategies as coordinated moves whose value lies in their local connections, so chatbot designs should pair modeled examples with diagnostic coaching and reflection prompts that invite evaluation rather than uncritical acceptance.
requirements: AI responses coded and connected across modeling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, and exploration rather than isolated answer provision
constraints: The finding is specific to this rural middle-school agriculture-STEM context and a two-week RQ/hypothesis revision activity; the article hedges that effective support "may depend" on the full cycle
target_learners: middle school students revising inquiry artifacts with AI support
target_learning_goals: criterion-aligned revision of research questions and hypotheses
examples: Aspen paired modeled stronger RQ examples with coaching that diagnosed drafts and reflection prompts asking students to compare revisions against evidence and criteria

article_title: A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI
citation: Inie, N., Kristensen, A. M., Misfeldt, M., & Dalsgaard, P. (2026). A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522
title: Cognitive-psychological account: critical thinking as goal-directed skill involving cognitive skills and strategies, related to fluid intelligence and executive functioning
description: In the cognitive-psychological tradition, "critical thinking is a type of thinking that is goal-directed and involves using cognitive skills and strategies that increase the likelihood of a desirable outcome (Halpern, 2013)". The review links the construct conceptually to fluid intelligence and executive functions, particularly cognitive flexibility, and stresses that it is a trainable skill requiring time and practice. Assessment in this tradition typically uses psychometric multiple-choice tests of skills and dispositions, plus newer performance-based assessments.
requirements: Assessment typically uses validated instruments or controlled laboratory-based studies with a limited number of factors
constraints: Quantitative tests rarely encourage elaborate reflections and multiple solutions to a problem otherwise associated with critical thinking
target_learners: Adults and students whose critical thinking skills and dispositions are assessed or trained
target_learning_goals: Purposeful, reflective judgment; argument analysis; reasoning; problem solving
examples: Standardized tests named in the review include the California Critical Thinking Skills Test with 34 multiple-choice items and the Halpern Critical Thinking Assessment with 25 everyday scenarios
key_sources: Inie, N., Kristensen, A. M., Misfeldt, M., & Dalsgaard, P. (2026). A Critical Review of Critical Thinking in HCI Research About AI. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1080/10447318.2026.2722522

article_title: Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning
citation: Tatyana Ivanova. (2026). Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning. Mathematics 2026, 14, 808. https://doi.org/10.3390/math14050808
title: Combine ontologies with sequencing rules, learning analytics, and machine learning for effective personalized learning
description: The article argues that ontologies alone are insufficient for personalized learning because they are mostly static or slowly evolving and have limited handling of uncertainty, while personalization needs dynamic adaptation based on real-time learner behavior. It therefore recommends combining ontologies with teaching strategies expressed as sequencing rules, learning analytics to infer and predict learner needs, and machine learning techniques for extracting and storing implicit knowledge. The article states: "For effective personalized learning, ontologies should be combined with: teaching strategies, expressed effectively by sequencing rules; learning analytics (to infer and predict learner needs); machine learning techniques for extracting and storing implicit knowledge."
requirements: A shared, machine-understandable model of tutoring knowledge, pedagogy, interface, and learners expressed via ontologies, complemented by LA and ML components
constraints: Ontologies are mostly static or slowly evolving and have limited handling of uncertainty, per the article
target_learners: learners in intelligent educational systems and intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: personalized content recommendation, adaptive sequencing, difficulty adjustment, prediction of learning outcomes
examples: The proposed architecture stores procedural knowledge as rules and implicit knowledge via learning analytics or machine learning alongside mapped ontologies
key_sources: Tatyana Ivanova. (2026). Ontology-Based Layered Hybrid AI-Driven Knowledge Model for Personalized E-Learning. Mathematics 2026, 14, 808. https://doi.org/10.3390/math14050808

article_title: Retrieval Practice Consistently Benefits Student Learning: a Systematic Review of Applied Research in Schools and Classrooms
citation: I. Elaine Allen and Jeff Seaman with Russell Poulin and Terri Taylor Straut. (2016). Online Report Card - Tracking Online Education in the United States. Babson Survey Research Group. https://onlinelearningconsortium.org
title: Course-mode taxonomy by proportion of content delivered online (traditional, web-facilitated, blended/hybrid, online)
description: The report defines a four-category classification of higher education courses by the proportion of content delivered online, used consistently across its thirteen annual surveys and presented to respondents at the start of the survey. An "online course is defined as one in which at least 80% of the course content is delivered online," face-to-face covers 0-29% (traditional and web-facilitated), and blended/hybrid covers 30-80% with typically reduced face-to-face meetings. It contrasts these with IPEDS's separate distance education definition.
requirements: Respondents must be presented these definitions at the beginning of the survey and in individual questions, as the report states it does
constraints: IPEDS uses a different definition for distance education than the survey's course-mode categories
target_learning_goals: Characterizing online, blended, and face-to-face course delivery modes for institutional reporting and policy analysis
examples: The report's prototypical classification table assigns 1-29% of content online to web-facilitated courses and 30-79% to blended/hybrid courses
key_sources: I. Elaine Allen and Jeff Seaman with Russell Poulin and Terri Taylor Straut. (2016). Online Report Card - Tracking Online Education in the United States. Babson Survey Research Group. https://onlinelearningconsortium.org

article_title: Synthesizing Results From Empirical Research on Computer-Based Scaffolding in STEM Education: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Belland, B. R., Walker, A. E., Kim, N. J., & Lefler, M. (2017). Synthesizing Results From Empirical Research on Computer-Based Scaffolding in STEM Education: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 87(2), 309-344. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654316670999
title: Framework of computer-based scaffolding design characteristics and moderators
description: The article organizes computer-based scaffolding research along several coded dimensions: context of use (problem-based, case-based, design-based, project-based, inquiry-based, modeling/visualization, problem solving), scaffolding change (none, fading, adding, fading/adding), scaffolding logic (none, performance adapted, self-selected, fixed), scaffolding scope (generic or context-specific), and scaffolding intervention type, where "conceptual scaffolding suggests things to consider when addressing the problem" while strategic, metacognitive, and motivation scaffolding boot strategies, self-evaluation, and motivational variables respectively. This framework guided coding of all 333 outcomes and the meta-analysis's moderator questions.
requirements: Studies must employ scaffolding as defined by Wood et al. (1976) while learners engage ill-structured STEM problems, with a control condition and sufficient information to calculate effect sizes
constraints: The synthesis covers studies published between January 1, 1993, and December 31, 2014, measuring cognitive outcomes only; motivational and metacognitive outcomes were excluded by scope
target_learners: primary through adult learners in STEM education
target_learning_goals: cognitive outcomes including deep content knowledge, problem-solving and argumentation ability
examples: The SE-Coach adjusted both frequency and nature of scaffolding via a probabilistic model of student understanding; Chang et al. (2001) let students self-select hints through feedback and hint buttons
key_sources: Belland, B. R., Walker, A. E., Kim, N. J., & Lefler, M. (2017). Synthesizing Results From Empirical Research on Computer-Based Scaffolding in STEM Education: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 87(2), 309-344. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654316670999

article_title: Concreteness Fading in Mathematics and Science Instruction: a Systematic Review
citation: Fyfe, E. R., McNeil, N. M., Son, J. Y., & Goldstone, R. L. (2014). Concreteness Fading in Mathematics and Science Instruction: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9249-3
title: Concreteness fading: a framework combining concrete and abstract instructional materials
description: Concreteness fading is an instructional framework in which learners begin with concrete materials and then move explicitly and gradually to more abstract representations. The article positions it as an approach that moves beyond the dichotomy of treating concrete and abstract materials independently, arguing that "concreteness fading provides advantages that go beyond the sum of the benefits of concrete and abstract materials." It is proposed for mathematics and science instruction.
requirements: Instruction must begin with concrete materials and then explicitly and gradually fade to the more abstract, per the article's recommendation
constraints: The framework is proposed for domains such as mathematics and science instruction
target_learning_goals: Interpreting abstract symbols
Grounding abstract thinking in perceptual and physical experience
Transfer of generalizable properties

article_title: Expertise Reversal Effect and Its Implications for Learner-Tailored Instruction
citation: Kalyuga, S. (2007). Expertise Reversal Effect and Its Implications for Learner-Tailored Instruction. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 509–539. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9054-3
title: Cognitive load theory provides the prediction and explanation of the expertise reversal effect
description: The review organizes the expertise reversal effect within cognitive load theory, the framework in which interactions between prior knowledge and instructional effectiveness have been investigated. The article states the findings have "cognitive load theory-based prediction and explanation", meaning the theory predicts which techniques suit which expertise levels and explains reversals in terms of changing load as knowledge develops. It serves here as the explanatory account the review uses to interpret the reviewed empirical patterns.
requirements: Instructional techniques whose effectiveness varies with learner expertise, so that prior knowledge level can be treated as a moderating variable
target_learners: Learners across levels of prior knowledge or expertise in a domain
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of domain knowledge and skills under techniques matched to expertise level
examples: The review interprets recent empirical findings on the expertise reversal effect through this cognitive load account.
key_sources: Kalyuga, S. (2007). Expertise Reversal Effect and Its Implications for Learner-Tailored Instruction. Educational Psychology Review, 19, 509–539. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9054-3

article_title: Why Minimal Guidance During Instruction Does Not Work: An Analysis of the Failure of Constructivist, Discovery, Problem-Based, Experiential, and Inquiry-Based Teaching
citation: Kirschner, P; Sweller, John; Clark, Robert. (2006). Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work: An analysis of the failure of constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential, and inquiry-based teaching. Journal Article. http://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/50516
title: Human cognitive architecture, expert-novice differences, and cognitive load as the explanatory framework for the superiority of guided instruction
description: The article explains the superiority of guided instruction in terms of human cognitive architecture, expert-novice differences, and cognitive load. It argues that unguided or minimally guided approaches "ignore both the structures that constitute human cognitive architecture" and the accumulated empirical evidence. The framework treats the learner's cognitive architecture as the reason external guidance is needed during skill acquisition, with prior knowledge eventually supplying internal guidance.
requirements: Instructional approaches must take account of the structures that constitute human cognitive architecture, which the article says minimally guided approaches ignore.
constraints: The advantage of guidance recedes when learners have sufficiently high prior knowledge to provide internal guidance.
target_learners: Novice learners in constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential, and inquiry-based instructional settings
target_learning_goals: Effective and efficient acquisition of knowledge and skills through guided instruction
key_sources: Kirschner, P; Sweller, John; Clark, Robert. (2006). Why minimal guidance during instruction does not work: An analysis of the failure of constructivist, discovery, problem-based, experiential, and inquiry-based teaching. Journal Article. http://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/50516

article_title: Applying the science of learning: Evidence-based principles for the design of multimedia instruction.
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2008). Applying the Science of Learning: Evidence-Based Principles for the Design of Multimedia Instruction. American Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0012841
title: Cognitive theory of multimedia learning: dual channels, limited capacity, and active processing
description: The article presents the cognitive theory of multimedia learning as a framework explaining how people learn from words and pictures. It rests on three assumptions: dual channels, limited capacity, and active processing, with selecting, organizing, and integrating as core processes moving information from sensory memory through working memory to long-term memory. The article states that "The most relevant elements in a science of learning are (a) dual channels—the idea that humans possess separate channels for processing visual and verbal material; (b) limited capacity—the idea that each channel can process only a small amount of material at any one time." The 10 design principles are described as theoretically grounded in this theory.
requirements: Instructional design decisions should be judged against research-based theories of how people learn
constraints: The theory assumes each channel can process only a small amount of material at any one time
target_learners: learners in multimedia instructional settings, from school students to employees in training
target_learning_goals: deep learning and transfer of multimedia lesson content
examples: Figure 2 depicts the theory: words and pictures enter sensory memory, are selected into verbal and pictorial channels of working memory, organized into models, and integrated with prior knowledge in long-term memory
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2008). Applying the Science of Learning: Evidence-Based Principles for the Design of Multimedia Instruction. American Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066x.63.8.760

article_title: Multimedia Design for Learning: An Overview of Reviews With Meta-Meta-Analysis
citation: Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Harris, N. R., Sanders, T., Parker, P., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C. (2022). Multimedia design for learning: An overview of reviews with meta-meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211052329
title: Cognitive Load Theory: learning is constrained by working memory limits and load type
description: Cognitive Load Theory describes how learning is affected by the natural limits of working memory, distinguishing intrinsic load (complexity inherent in the task, operationalised as element interactivity) from extrinsic load (complexity a teacher adds that detracts from learning). The article uses it as one of two organising theories whose hypothesised design principles are tested against meta-analytic evidence. Newer models treat germane load as "a type of intrinsic load for more complex schema construction" rather than a third load type.
requirements: Designs must reduce extraneous load so freed working memory can be directed to processes that facilitate learning
constraints: The theory applies beyond multimedia learning (e.g., goal-free effect, worked examples), per the article
target_learners: all learners of multimedia instructional materials
target_learning_goals: managing cognitive load during knowledge acquisition
key_sources: Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Harris, N. R., Sanders, T., Parker, P., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C. (2022). Multimedia design for learning: An overview of reviews with meta-meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211052329

article_title: Multimedia Design for Learning: An Overview of Reviews With Meta-Meta-Analysis
citation: Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Harris, N. R., Sanders, T., Parker, P., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C. (2022). Multimedia design for learning: An overview of reviews with meta-meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211052329
title: Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning: dual-channel, limited-capacity, active processing
description: The Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning applies Cognitive Load Theory to multimedia, assuming "two parallel systems, one for what we see and one for what we hear" (the dual-channel assumption), limited attention capacity per channel, and active processing whereby mere passive exposure is insufficient. The article tests its hypothesised design principles (modality, contiguity, signaling, etc.) against pooled meta-analytic effects and concludes the results supported many tenets of both theories.
requirements: Good multimedia should use each channel in its natural format: seeing images and hearing sounds
constraints: The theory specifically addresses multimedia combining words and pictures, not single-channel media
target_learners: learners of multimedia instructional materials across education levels
target_learning_goals: leveraging visual and auditory channels to manage cognitive load
key_sources: Noetel, M., Griffith, S., Delaney, O., Harris, N. R., Sanders, T., Parker, P., del Pozo Cruz, B., & Lonsdale, C. (2022). Multimedia design for learning: An overview of reviews with meta-meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543211052329

article_title: Meta-analysis of the modality effect
citation: Ginns, P. (2005). Meta-analysis of the modality effect. Learning and Instruction, 15(4), 313-331. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2005.07.001
title: Cognitive load theory account of the modality effect via dual working-memory channels
description: Cognitive load theory explains the modality effect through Baddeley's working-memory model: presenting graphics visually for processing in the visual cache while presenting associated text auditorily for processing in the phonological loop effectively expands working memory capacity for learning. If all information is presented visually, the learner must process everything in the visual cache, increasing the likelihood working memory is overloaded and learning impeded. The article contrasts this capacity-expansion account with Tabbers' temporal-contiguity explanation and Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning, which emphasises richer referential connections between dual-mode representations.
requirements: Applies when textual and graphical information are related and must be mentally integrated
Learners are novices for whom the material imposes high element interactivity
constraints: Tabbers' experiments found the effect disappeared or reversed under self-paced conditions, questioning the simple capacity-expansion explanation
Kalyuga et al. (2000) found the modality effect disappeared and reversed as learner expertise increased
target_learners: novice learners across primary, secondary and adult education
target_learning_goals: comprehension and schema construction from multimedia instructional materials combining graphics and text
examples: The meta-analysis tested the theory's predictions that element interactivity and pacing moderate the effect
key_sources: Ginns, P. (2005). Meta-analysis of the modality effect. Learning and Instruction, 15(4), 313-331. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2005.07.001

article_title: Integrating information: A meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects
citation: Ginns, P. (2006). Integrating information: A meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects. Learning and Instruction, 16(6), 511-525. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.10.001
title: Cognitive Load Theory account of split-attention costs
description: Cognitive load theory is an instructional design theory foregrounding human cognitive architecture: a limited working memory that can be circumvented by schemas in long-term memory. It "identifies several sources of mental effort (i.e., cognitive load) which, when acting in concert, may overload available working memory resources and retard learning" — intrinsic load from element interactivity, extraneous load from unsuitable design, and germane load from suitable design. The meta-analysis uses this account to explain why separating related elements in space or time forces extraneous search-and-match or rehearsal activity that retards schema construction.
requirements: Instructional materials must take account of the limits of students' working memory and their interaction with long-term memory schemas
constraints: Element interactivity cannot be objectively counted; it depends on learners' prior knowledge, so researchers match materials to knowledge levels
target_learning_goals: schema construction and automation from complex instructional materials
examples: The meta-analysis tests the theory's prediction that reducing split attention aids learning, especially for high element interactivity materials
key_sources: Ginns, P. (2006). Integrating information: A meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects. Learning and Instruction, 16(6), 511-525. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2006.10.001

article_title: Gender Inequality in Deliberative Participation
citation: Christopher F. Karpowitz, Tali Mendelberg, and Lee Shaker. (2012). Gender Inequality in Deliberative Participation. American Political Science Review, Volume 106, Issue 3, pp. 533-547. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055412000329
title: Gender composition interacts with decision rule to shape inequality in deliberation
description: The article proposes that inequality in deliberation is not fixed but depends on an interaction between two institutional and social features of the deliberating group. It moves "beyond the debate by hypothesizing that the group's gender composition interacts with its decision rule to exacerbate or erase the inequalities". The framework explains when deliberation equalizes women's voice and authority and when it does not, and it is tested experimentally with many groups.
requirements: Groups must vary in gender composition and operate under specified decision rules for the interaction to be observed
constraints: Tested in experimental deliberation settings with many groups, as described in the article
target_learning_goals: equal voice and authority in group deliberation
examples: The article tests the hypothesis and alternatives using experimental data with many groups and links between individuals' attitudes and speech.
key_sources: Christopher F. Karpowitz, Tali Mendelberg, and Lee Shaker. (2012). Gender Inequality in Deliberative Participation. American Political Science Review, Volume 106, Issue 3, pp. 533-547. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055412000329

article_title: Cooperative Learning and Academic Achievement: Why Does Groupwork Work?. [Aprendizaje cooperativo y rendimiento académico: ¿por qué funciona el trabajo en grupo?]
citation: Slavin, R. E. (2014). Cooperative Learning and Academic Achievement: Why Does Groupwork Work?. Anales De Psicología, 30(3), 785–791. https://doi.org/10.6018/analesps.30.3.201201
title: Cooperative learning as small-group instructional methods
description: Cooperative learning is defined as "instructional methods in which students work in small groups to help each other learn." It is the instructional category whose achievement effects the chapter reviews, encompassing methods derived from the motivational, social cohesion, developmental, and cognitive elaboration perspectives.
requirements: Students must work in small groups with the aim of helping each other learn
target_learning_goals: academic achievement through peer helping

article_title: Constructivism in Science Education
citation: Michael R. Matthews (ed.). (1998). Constructivism in Science Education: A Philosophical Examination. Kluwer Academic Publishers. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-011-5032-3
title: Educational constructivism spans three distinct kinds of theory: theories of learning, theories of teaching, and constructivist epistemologies
description: The volume's organizing taxonomy distinguishes three constructivist strands that are frequently conflated. As the preface states, "there are constructivist theories of learning - originally the personal constructivism of Piaget and the social constructivism of Vygotsky; there are constructivist theories of teaching" echoing Socratic and progressivist pedagogy, "and there are constructivist theories of knowledge, or constructivist epistemologies." The book's project is to untangle and evaluate these varied positions through philosophical analysis.
requirements: Philosophical analysis to disentangle the varieties before evaluation
constraints: The preface notes the varieties are frequently confused in educational literature
target_learning_goals: understanding the nature of science
epistemological foundations of science teaching
examples: Chapters by von Glasersfeld (radical constructivist epistemology), Nola and Suchting (critiques), Bickhard (taxonomy of constructivisms), and Grandy (cognitive vs metaphysical constructivism) each treat one strand
key_sources: Michael R. Matthews (ed.). (1998). Constructivism in Science Education: A Philosophical Examination. Kluwer Academic Publishers. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-011-5032-3

article_title: Effective Educational Videos: Principles and Guidelines for Maximizing Student Learning from Video Content
citation: Brame Cynthia J. (2016). Effective Educational Videos: Principles and Guidelines for Maximizing Student Learning from Video Content. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-03-0125
title: Cognitive load theory and the cognitive theory of multimedia learning as the framework for educational video design
description: The essay organizes video design around cognitive load theory (Sweller) and the cognitive theory of multimedia learning (Mayer). It describes sensory, working, and long-term memory, and states that "any learning experience has three components": intrinsic load, germane load, and extraneous load. Multimedia learning adds two limited-capacity channels, visual/pictorial and auditory/verbal, whose combined use maximizes working memory capacity. Instructors should minimize extraneous load, manage intrinsic load, and optimize germane load.
requirements: Designers must consider the intrinsic load of the subject and structure high-load material carefully
Working memory must be prompted to process only the most crucial information for encoding into long-term memory
constraints: Either channel can be overwhelmed by high cognitive load
What counts as extraneous information changes as learners move from novice toward expert status
target_learning_goals: effective learning from educational video content
examples: The essay illustrates intrinsic load with word pairs versus grammar, and naming mitosis stages versus understanding cell cycle control
key_sources: Brame Cynthia J. (2016). Effective Educational Videos: Principles and Guidelines for Maximizing Student Learning from Video Content. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.16-03-0125

article_title: BEYOND EXPLICIT RULE LEARNING
citation: Robert M. DeKeyser. (1997). Beyond Explicit Rule Learning: Automatizing Second Language Morphosyntax. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 19, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263197002040
title: Computer-controlled comprehension and production practice environment for L2 morphosyntax
description: A computer-controlled practice environment in which learners engage in systematic comprehension and production practice of taught L2 rules. In comprehension practice, learners choose between pictures displayed on the computer screen to match a sentence; in production practice, learners type the correct sentence corresponding to a picture. The environment delivered 8 weeks of systematic practice after learners reached criterion on metalinguistic tests of grammar and vocabulary.
requirements: Prior instruction bringing learners to criterion on metalinguistic tests of the target grammar and vocabulary
constraints: As described, the environment was used with an artificial language, four morphosyntactic rules, and 32 vocabulary items
target_learners: adult second language learners in experimental or instructional settings
target_learning_goals: automatizing explicitly learned morphosyntactic rules in comprehension and production
examples: Production practice consisted of typing the correct sentence corresponding to a picture

article_title: Students as Radical Agents of Change
citation: Fielding, M. (2001). Students as Radical Agents of Change. Journal of Educational Change, 2, 123–141. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1017949213447
title: Overarching conceptual re-appraisal of the student-voice domain
description: Alongside the evaluation questions, the article provides a second framework that re-appraises the whole student-voice domain conceptually. The abstract states it "provides an overarching conceptual re-appraisal of the domain", situating consultation practices and the Students as Researchers approach within a transformed understanding of students' role in schooling. It frames the project's "transformational nature".
requirements: Use as a conceptual lens for interpreting student-voice practices and their aims
target_learning_goals: understanding the transformative potential of student voice in schooling

article_title: Focus-on-Form and Corrective Feedback in Communicative Language Teaching
citation: Patsy M. Lightbown and Nina Spada. (1990). Focus-on-Form and Corrective Feedback in Communicative Language Teaching: Effects on Second Language Learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 12, Issue 4. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263100009517
title: Competing views of the role of form-focused instruction in second language learning as an interpretive framework
description: The article frames its findings within what it calls "current competing views of the role of form-focused instruction in second language learning". This framework contrasts positions on whether explicit attention to linguistic form is needed within communicative language teaching, and the study's between-class accuracy differences are used as evidence brought to bear on that debate. The article positions its observational findings as informing this theoretical controversy rather than testing a single model.
requirements: Classroom observation data capable of characterizing teachers' form-focused instruction and learner accuracy outcomes
constraints: The framework is applied to communicative language teaching contexts with young learners in intensive ESL programs
target_learners: Elementary school students aged 10–12 in intensive ESL programs

examples: The study discusses its between-class accuracy findings in terms of the competing views rather than endorsing one position outright

article_title: BEYOND STUDENT PERCEPTIONS: ISSUES OF INTERACTION, PRESENCE, AND PERFORMANCE IN AN ONLINE COURSE
citation: Picciano, A. G. (2002). Beyond Student Perceptions: Issues of Interaction, Presence, and Performance in an Online Course. Online Learning, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v6i1.1870
title: Course-objective-specific performance measures going beyond grades and withdrawal rates
description: This element is the article's approach to measuring online course performance: rather than relying only on typical institutional indicators, the study developed measures "specifically related to course objectives." The article states that "An attempt was made to go beyond typical institutional performance measures such as grades and withdrawal rates," positioning objective-aligned measures as a way to capture learning effectiveness more directly than institutional proxies.
requirements: Performance measures must be tied to the specific objectives of the course being evaluated rather than only to institutional indicators such as grades and withdrawal rates.
target_learners: students in an online higher education course
target_learning_goals: measuring learning effectiveness and course performance in online learning
examples: The study collected dependent performance measures specifically related to the online course's objectives, in addition to grades and withdrawal rates.

article_title: Assimilating complex information
citation: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813
title: Cognitive load theory as the generative framework of the thesis
description: The thesis is grounded in cognitive load theory, which is based on the assumption that features of human cognitive architecture have important implications for how we learn and understand. The theory distinguishes sources of cognitive load, including intrinsic load tied to element interactivity and extraneous load imposed by instructional design, and generates instructional techniques such as goal-free problems, worked examples, and split-attention, redundancy and modality effects. The five experiments reported in the thesis were generated by this theory.
requirements: Assumptions about human cognitive architecture, particularly limited working memory and long-term memory schema storage
constraints: The supplied text presents the theory as background framework; its detailed treatment of load sources lies in Chapter 2, not fully included in the supplied excerpt
target_learners: Learners of complex information across educational and training settings
target_learning_goals: Effective learning and understanding of complex material under working memory constraints
examples: The thesis's Chapter 2 lists instructional techniques generated by the theory, including goal free problems, worked examples, and the split attention, redundancy and modality effects
key_sources: Pollock, Edwina Jane. (2000). Assimilating Complex Information. PhD thesis, School of Education, University of New South Wales. https://hdl.handle.net/1959.4/17813

article_title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design
citation: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205
title: Cognitive load theory's model of human cognitive architecture: limited working memory with modality-based subcomponents and unlimited long-term memory holding schemas
description: The article's organizing framework is a model of human cognitive architecture underpinning cognitive load theory. It assumes "a limited capacity working memory that includes partially independent subcomponents to deal with auditory/verbal material and visual/2- or 3-dimensional information" alongside "an effectively unlimited long-term memory, holding schemas that vary in their degree of automation." These structures and functions are the basis from which the theory derives its instructional guidelines.
requirements: Instructional applications must respect the limited capacity of working memory when presenting information
constraints: The architecture is stated as the theory's assumption, not as a directly tested finding in the text available
target_learners: All learners processing new instructional material
target_learning_goals: Schema construction and automation in domain learning
key_sources: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J.J.G. & Paas, F.G.W.C. (1998). Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1022193728205

article_title: Benefits and Pitfalls of Multimedia and Interactive Features in Technology-Enhanced Storybooks
citation: Takacs, Z. K., Swart, E. K., & Bus, A. G. (2015). Benefits and Pitfalls of Multimedia and Interactive Features in Technology-Enhanced Storybooks: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 85(4), 698-739. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654314566989
title: Cognitive processing account: dual-channel multimedia integration helps, extraneous interactivity overloads young children's working memory
description: The article interprets its findings through the cognitive theory of multimedia learning and cognitive load theory. Dual coding theory holds that "verbal and nonverbal information are processed in two separate but interconnected channels," so congruent animation, music, and sound support comprehension rather than overload. Conversely, the coherence effect predicts deeper learning when extraneous materials are excluded; interactive features such as games and hotspots may act as seductive extraneous material, forcing task switching between story comprehension and play that places excessive load on young children's limited working memory.
requirements: Multimedia additions must be congruent with the narration to support rather than distract from comprehension
constraints: Even story-relevant interactive features may disturb comprehension because comprehending and playing are fundamentally different tasks requiring switching
target_learning_goals: story comprehension
vocabulary learning
code-related literacy skills
examples: The meta-analysis tested these predictions by contrasting multimedia-only, interactive-only, and multimedia-interactive stories across 43 studies
key_sources: Takacs, Z. K., Swart, E. K., & Bus, A. G. (2015). Benefits and Pitfalls of Multimedia and Interactive Features in Technology-Enhanced Storybooks: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 85(4), 698-739. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654314566989

article_title: Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives
citation: Tzuriel, D. (2000). Dynamic Assessment of Young Children: Educational and Intervention Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009032414088
title: Cognitive Modifiability Battery (CMB): a dynamic assessment and intervention instrument
description: The Cognitive Modifiability Battery (CMB) is a dynamic instrument named in the review's reference list as "The Cognitive Modifiability Battery (CMB): Assessment and Intervention-Instruction Manual" (Tzuriel, 1995a). It is cited both as a dynamic assessment instrument and, in conference papers listed by the review, as an intervention tool used in clinical and educational work with children with complex learning difficulties and in speech language therapy.
requirements: Use requires the instrument's instruction manual and training in dynamic assessment procedures.
target_learning_goals: assessment of cognitive modifiability
dynamic assessment-based intervention
