article_title: Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model
citation: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Clark, R.E. & de Croock, M.B.M. (2002). Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model. ETR&D. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504993
title: Couple instructional methods for each component to the basic learning processes involved in complex learning
description: In the 4C/ID approach, instructional methods are not chosen arbitrarily for each blueprint component; the article states that "Instructional methods for each component are coupled to the basic learning processes involved in complex learning". This principle directs designers to select methods for learning tasks, supportive information, just-in-time information, and part-task practice by reference to the learning processes those methods must support.
requirements: Designers must identify the basic learning processes involved in complex learning before selecting instructional methods for each component
target_learning_goals: complex skill acquisition
examples: The article's worked-out training blueprint for searching for literature applies this coupling of methods to learning processes
key_sources: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Clark, R.E. & de Croock, M.B.M. (2002). Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model. ETR&D. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504993

article_title: Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model
citation: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Clark, R.E. & de Croock, M.B.M. (2002). Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model. ETR&D. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504993
title: Training blueprint structure for complex learning with associated instructional methods
description: The article discusses "the structure of training blueprints for complex learning and associated instructional methods". A blueprint in this pattern is a design document that lays out the four interrelated components — learning tasks, supportive information, just-in-time information, and part-task practice — together with the instructional methods attached to each, providing the overall architecture for a training program for complex skills.
requirements: Blueprints must include the four interrelated components and associated instructional methods
constraints: Applies to complex learning rather than simple task training
target_learners: learners in training programs for complex skills
target_learning_goals: complex learning
key_sources: van Merriënboer, J.J.G., Clark, R.E. & de Croock, M.B.M. (2002). Blueprints for complex learning: The 4C/ID-model. ETR&D. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02504993

article_title: Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality
citation: Abry, T., Rimm-Kaufman, S.E. & Curby, T.W. (2017). Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality. Prevention Science, 18, 193–203. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-016-0743-3
title: Examine individual program components to identify active ingredients for intervention optimization and teacher professional development
description: Rather than treating a social and emotional learning program as an undifferentiated package, the article recommends analyzing variation in teachers' implementation of individual program components to find which carry the greatest leverage. As the authors state, "Results highlight the value of examining individual program components toward the identification of program active ingredients that can inform intervention optimization and teacher professional development." This component-level lens showed the four Responsive Classroom components were not equally related to interaction quality.
requirements: Implementation data on individual program components, derived from teacher-reported surveys and classroom observations
constraints: Findings come from variation in implementation among treatment teachers within one randomized controlled trial, not from manipulating components experimentally
target_learners: Elementary school students in grade 3–5 classrooms
target_learning_goals: Improving emotional, organizational, and instructional quality of teacher–student interactions
examples: The study indexed four Responsive Classroom components and found Morning Meeting, Rule Creation, Interactive Modeling, and Academic Choice differed in their relations to interaction quality.
key_sources: Abry, T., Rimm-Kaufman, S.E. & Curby, T.W. (2017). Are All Program Elements Created Equal? Relations Between Specific Social and Emotional Learning Components and Teacher–Student Classroom Interaction Quality. Prevention Science, 18, 193–203. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11121-016-0743-3

article_title: The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations
citation: Susanne Carroll, Merrill Swain, and Yves Roberge. (1992). The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations. Applied Psycholinguistics, Volume 13, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400005555
title: Expect explicit correction to improve performance on corrected items, not to guarantee generalized rule learning
description: This principle captures the study's central dissociation: correction improved responses on the corrected items themselves, yet "comparisons of guessing responses between experimental and comparison groups showed no evidence of learned generalizations." Designers of feedback activities should therefore treat explicit correction as supporting item-level accuracy, and should not assume that corrected practice alone produces learners' generalization of a morphological rule to new items.
requirements: Learners must encounter the corrected items in a feedback session and then be probed with novel stimuli to check whether generalization occurred
constraints: Demonstrated only for adult English speakers learning two rules of French suffixation in an experimental setting; generalization was not observed even with correction
target_learning_goals: morphological generalizations in a second language
examples: In the experiment, corrected learners outperformed comparison learners on feedback items while guessing responses to novel stimuli showed no learned generalizations in either group
key_sources: Susanne Carroll, Merrill Swain, and Yves Roberge. (1992). The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations. Applied Psycholinguistics, Volume 13, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400005555

article_title: Component-levels theory of the effects of spacing of repetitions on recall and recognition
citation: Glenberg, A. M. (1979). Component-level theory of the effects of spacing of repetitions on recall and recognition. Memory & Cognition, 7(2), 95-112. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03197564
title: Component-levels theory of spacing effects: three informational components plus encoding and retrieval principles
description: The theory proposes that episodic traces contain three types of components: contextual, structural, and descriptive. The name derives from the fact that "The theory specifies three types of components that represent three types of information assumed to be important in most verbal learning and memory tasks." Two abstract principles govern spacing effects: "arepetition is potentially effective to the degree that the second presentation allows for the storage of information distinct from that stored at the first presentation," and realization of this potential "is controlled by the conditions at the time of the memory test, the retrieval environment." Contextual components are encoded automatically; structural and descriptive encoding depends on control processes. Cue-trace component matching, following the encoding specificity principle, determines retrieval.
requirements: Requires verbal learning and memory tasks in which repeated stimuli are encoded into multicomponent episodic traces
Requires a retrieval environment whose cues can be characterized by their component content and bias
constraints: The theory is designed for distributed practice and spacing effects with verbal stimuli in verbal learning and memory paradigms
The article notes that most reviewed experiments were not specifically designed to test the theory, so some analyses are post hoc
target_learners: Adult learners in verbal memory experiments (introductory psychology students)
target_learning_goals: Recall and recognition of repeated verbal material as a function of spacing of repetitions
examples: The theory integrates encoding variability approaches and predicts monotonically increasing, inverted U-shaped, or decreasing lag functions depending on cue bias, as illustrated in Figure 1
key_sources: Glenberg, A. M. (1979). Component-level theory of the effects of spacing of repetitions on recall and recognition. Memory & Cognition, 7(2), 95-112. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03197590

article_title: DECONSTRUCTING COMPREHENSIBILITY
citation: Talia Isaacs and Pavel Trofimovich. (2012). DECONSTRUCTING COMPREHENSIBILITY: Identifying the Linguistic Influences on Listeners' L2 Comprehensibility Ratings. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 34, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263112000150
title: Comprehensibility as listeners' perceptions of how easily they understand L2 speech
description: The article treats comprehensibility as "a major concept in second language (L2) pronunciation research that denotes listeners' perceptions of how easily they understand L2 speech." It is presented as "central to interlocutors' communicative success in real-world contexts" and as a construct modeled in oral proficiency scales such as TOEFL and IELTS. The study operationalizes it through native listeners' scalar judgments of L2 speakers' speech, which are then related to linguistic measures of the speech itself.
requirements: Listeners provide scalar judgments of L2 speech samples that can be correlated with quantitative linguistic measures of those samples.
target_learning_goals: L2 speaking and pronunciation proficiency as perceived by listeners
examples: The study elicited scalar comprehensibility judgments from 60 native English listeners on speech samples of 40 native French learners of English.
key_sources: Talia Isaacs and Pavel Trofimovich. (2012). DECONSTRUCTING COMPREHENSIBILITY: Identifying the Linguistic Influences on Listeners' L2 Comprehensibility Ratings. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 34, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263112000150

article_title: Expertise reversal effect and its instructional implications: introduction to the special issue
citation: Slava Kalyuga, Alexander Renkl. (2010). Expertise reversal effect and its instructional implications: introduction to the special issue. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9102-0
title: Cognitive load imbalance account of the expertise reversal effect
description: Within cognitive load theory, the expertise reversal effect is explained by imbalances between the learner's organized knowledge base and provided instructional guidance. For novices, knowledge gaps not compensated by guidance cause unsupported search and excessive extraneous load; for advanced learners, overlaps between available knowledge and guidance mean redundant explanations must be integrated and cross-referenced, consuming additional resources. The article states that "instructional guidance that is essential for novices may inhibit learning for more experienced learners by interfering with retrieval and application of their available knowledge structures."
requirements: Instructional support must be matched to the learner's current level of domain expertise to optimize cognitive load
constraints: The account rests on a cognitive architecture of limited working memory and unlimited long-term memory, and was supported by subjective mental-load rating measures
target_learners: learners at varying levels of prior domain knowledge, from novices to experts
target_learning_goals: efficient acquisition of domain knowledge and skills under manageable cognitive load
key_sources: Slava Kalyuga, Alexander Renkl. (2010). Expertise reversal effect and its instructional implications: introduction to the special issue. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9102-0

article_title: Exploring the Assistance Dilemma in Experiments with Cognitive Tutors
citation: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Vincent Aleven. (2007). Exploring the Assistance Dilemma in Experiments with Cognitive Tutors. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9049-0
title: Cognitive Tutors: interactive problem-solving environments with step-by-step feedback, error messages, hints, and problem selection
description: Cognitive Tutors are intelligent tutors "based on cognitive psychology theory of problem solving and learning." They "provide a rich problem-solving environment with tutorial guidance in the form of step-by-step feedback, specific messages in response to common errors, and on-demand instructional hints" and "also select problems based on individual student performance." As they matured and spread to new subject-matter areas, they have been used as a research platform, particularly to explore interactive methods supporting metacognition.
requirements: Individual student performance data to drive problem selection
target_learners: Students in subject-matter courses using Cognitive Tutor software
target_learning_goals: Problem-solving skill acquisition supported by tutorial guidance
key_sources: Kenneth R. Koedinger, Vincent Aleven. (2007). Exploring the Assistance Dilemma in Experiments with Cognitive Tutors. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-007-9049-0

article_title: INTERACTIONAL FEEDBACK AND INSTRUCTIONAL COUNTERBALANCE
citation: Roy Lyster and Hirohide Mori. (2006). Interactional feedback and instructional counterbalance. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 28(2), 269-300. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060128
title: The counterbalance hypothesis
description: The counterbalance hypothesis holds that "instructional activities and interactional feedback that act as a counterbalance to a classroom's predominant communicative orientation are likely to prove more effective than instructional activities and interactional feedback that are congruent with its predominant communicative orientation." It was introduced by Lyster and Mori based on their finding of distinctively varied uptake and repair patterns across French and Japanese immersion, supported by an analysis of each setting's overall communicative orientation. It functions as an explanatory account of why the same feedback types produced different repair outcomes in different instructional settings.
requirements: Knowledge of the classroom's predominant communicative orientation, established through analysis of the instructional setting
constraints: Effectiveness claims are framed as likelihood ("are likely to prove more effective"), grounded in the two immersion settings analyzed
target_learners: Elementary-school immersion students learning a second language
target_learning_goals: Second language accuracy and repair of learner errors during communicative interaction
examples: The authors derived the hypothesis from contrasting French immersion, where prompts produced the most repair, with Japanese immersion, where recasts did
key_sources: Roy Lyster and Hirohide Mori. (2006). Interactional feedback and instructional counterbalance. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 28(2), 269-300. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060128

article_title: INTERACTIONAL FEEDBACK AND INSTRUCTIONAL COUNTERBALANCE
citation: Roy Lyster and Hirohide Mori. (2006). Interactional feedback and instructional counterbalance. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 28(2), 269-300. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060128
title: Select instructional activities and interactional feedback that counterbalance, rather than match, a classroom's predominant communicative orientation
description: This principle translates the counterbalance hypothesis into design guidance: because feedback congruent with a classroom's dominant communicative orientation is predicted to be less effective, teachers should choose "instructional activities and interactional feedback that act as a counterbalance to a classroom's predominant communicative orientation." The article grounds this in its comparative finding that repair patterns differed by setting, and in its analysis of each setting's overall communicative orientation. It implies first diagnosing the orientation, then selecting the feedback type that offsets it.
requirements: An analysis of the instructional setting's overall communicative orientation before selecting feedback types
constraints: The article states the hypothesis as a likelihood of greater effectiveness, not a demonstrated optimum
target_learners: Elementary-school second language learners in immersion settings
target_learning_goals: Learner uptake and repair following corrective feedback
examples: In French immersion, where recasts predominated but prompts produced the largest proportion of repair, prompts act as the counterbalancing feedback type
key_sources: Roy Lyster and Hirohide Mori. (2006). Interactional feedback and instructional counterbalance. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 28(2), 269-300. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263106060128

article_title: Cognitive ease at a cost: LLMs reduce mental effort but compromise depth in student scientific inquiry
citation: Matthias Stadler, Maria Bannert, Michael Sailer. (2024). Cognitive ease at a cost: LLMs reduce mental effort but compromise depth in student scientific inquiry. Computers in Human Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2024.108386
title: Cognitive load–self-regulation tradeoff account of information-search tool effects on learning quality
description: The article frames its findings with cognitive load theory (Sweller) and self-regulated learning (Zimmerman), synthesised via Seufert et al.'s tradeoff between cognitive load and cognitive resources: "learnersengageinself-regulatedlearningtothefullestextentwhenconfrontedwithtasks ofmediumdifficulty". Tasks that are too simple (like LLM research, in the authors' interpretation) evoke little strategic processing, while moderately demanding search fosters germane load and deeper processing. The study uses this account to explain why reduced load with LLMs co-occurred with lower-quality justifications.
requirements: The account presupposes that the task is within learners' capability range — the article notes it is unlikely an information search task is too difficult for educated adults, but it may be experienced as too simple to require much self-regulation.
constraints: The mediation test of this account was explicitly exploratory and dependent on the H2 result.
target_learning_goals: quality of argumentation and justification in socio-scientific reasoning
examples: The study interpreted the LLM condition's lower GCL and lower justification quality through this tradeoff model.
key_sources: Matthias Stadler, Maria Bannert, Michael Sailer. (2024). Cognitive ease at a cost: LLMs reduce mental effort but compromise depth in student scientific inquiry. Computers in Human Behavior. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2024.108386

article_title: Social relationships and motivation in middle school: The role of parents, teachers, and peers.
citation: DUPONT, S., Galand, B., & Nils, F. (2015). The impact of different sources of social support on academic performance: Intervening factors and mediated pathways in the case of master's thesis. Revue Européenne de Psychologie Appliquée, 65, 227-237. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.90.2.202
title: Consider multiple sources of perceived social support simultaneously when studying or supporting thesis students
description: The article argues that research and practice should examine several sources of perceived social support at once rather than in isolation, because their specific contributions differ. It states that results "underline the importance of considering different sources of perceived social support at the same time", and that findings "underline the importance of the supervisor and the institution" for master's thesis students.
requirements: Support from different sources (e.g., supervisor, institution) must be measured or provided distinctly so their specific contributions can be distinguished
constraints: Evidence comes from last-year university students working on a master's thesis; generalization to other populations is not established in the article
target_learning_goals: academic performance on the master's thesis
motivation and engagement during thesis work
examples: The study modeled institutional support, supervisor support, motivational beliefs and three engagement forms together in one SEM of 226 students
