The impact of different sources of social support on academic performance: Intervening factors and mediated pathways in the case of master's thesis. Revue Européenne de Psychologie Appliquée, 65, 227-237. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.90.2.202

article_title: Testing beyond words: Using tests to enhance visuospatial map learning
citation: Shana K. Carpenter and Harold Pashler. (2007). Testing beyond words: Using tests to enhance visuospatial map learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 14 (3), 474-478. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03194009
title: Covert retrieval with self-scoring as a method for extending the testing effect to nonverbal, visuospatial materials
description: The article introduces a method in which a learner views a map with one feature deleted, forms a mental image of the missing feature and its location, then presses a key to view the complete map and self-scores as correct or incorrect, as with flash cards. The authors note that "the testing effect may not always require overt retrieval" and that "when a person is motivated to learn, he or she can score his or her own responses". The method allows tests to be applied where verbal responses cannot easily be collected and scored.
requirements: A computer or display that can present the complete material and versions with individual features deleted
Learners motivated to honestly self-score whether they retrieved the missing feature and its location
constraints: The direct benefit of retrieval versus the indirect benefit of diagnosing unlearned items was not separated in the study
Subjects could probably base covert retrievals partly on working memory to some degree
target_learning_goals: visuospatial map knowledge such as locations of roads, rivers, and buildings
examples: Subjects studied a map for 20 sec, then repeatedly saw it with one of 12 features missing for 100 sec of test trials, forming a mental image before the complete map reappeared
key_sources: Shana K. Carpenter and Harold Pashler. (2007). Testing beyond words: Using tests to enhance visuospatial map learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 14 (3), 474-478. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03194092

article_title: The influence of concept mapping on achievement, self-regulation, and self-efficacy in students of English as a second language
citation: Pasana Chularut. (2001). The Influence of Concept Mapping on Achievement, Self-Regulation, and Self-Efficacy in Students of English as a Second Language. Doctoral dissertation, University of Oklahoma. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED3004889
title: Concept mapping as a metacognitive learning strategy grounded in Ausubel's assimilation theory of meaningful learning
description: The article frames concept mapping as a technique rooted in Ausubel's assimilation theory: "meaningful learning occurs when new knowledge is related to existing concepts in the learner's cognitive structure." A concept map is "a graphic arrangement of the key concepts in a body of subject matter with connecting lines labelled to show valid and meaningful relationships," and concept mapping is treated as a metacognitive strategy assisting learners in understanding concepts, relationships, and the hierarchical nature of knowledge. The study applies this framework to ESL students learning from English text.
requirements: Learners must choose to relate new knowledge to relevant concepts and propositions they already know, rather than incorporating it arbitrarily (rote learning).
constraints: The article notes rotely learned material is more easily forgotten since it lacks linkages to existing concepts.
target_learners: ESL students in university intensive English programs
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension and meaningful learning from English text
examples: Participants constructed concept maps from reading passages during strategy training and practice phases.
key_sources: Pasana Chularut. (2001). The Influence of Concept Mapping on Achievement, Self-Regulation, and Self-Efficacy in Students of English as a Second Language. Doctoral dissertation, University of Oklahoma. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED3004889

article_title: The influence of concept mapping on achievement, self-regulation, and self-efficacy in students of English as a second language
citation: Pasana Chularut. (2001). The Influence of Concept Mapping on Achievement, Self-Regulation, and Self-Efficacy in Students of English as a Second Language. Doctoral dissertation, University of Oklahoma. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED3004889
title: Provide explicit learning-strategy training and sustained practice when introducing concept mapping to language learners
description: The article's treatment phases show that concept mapping was introduced through structured instruction followed by practice rather than mere exposure: the procedure included pre-testing, learning strategy training, learning strategy practice, and post-testing. Related reviewed studies gave experimental groups "two one-hour lessons and two one-hour practice sessions on concept mapping" before requiring maps every lesson. The principle is that ESL students, who may have little experience using learning strategies in English, benefit from explicit training and repeated practice in the strategy before it supports learning from text.
requirements: Classroom teachers or instructors must first be trained in the use of mapping before providing it to students.
target_learners: ESL students with limited experience using learning strategies in English
target_learning_goals: Learning from text in English
examples: The study ran during a seven-week session with training and practice phases preceding post-testing.
key_sources: Pasana Chularut. (2001). The Influence of Concept Mapping on Achievement, Self-Regulation, and Self-Efficacy in Students of English as a Second Language. Doctoral dissertation, University of Oklahoma. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED3004889

article_title: Scientific Discovery Learning with Computer Simulations of Conceptual Domains
citation: Ton de Jong, Wouter R. van Joolingen. (1998). Scientific Discovery Learning with Computer Simulations of Conceptual Domains. Review of Educational Research. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190680v1
title: Provide domain information concurrently with the simulation, not before it
description: Learners in discovery learning with simulations benefit from direct access to domain knowledge (concepts, facts, rules, principles) while interacting with the simulation, e.g., via hypertext dictionaries. The review concludes such access "seems effective as long as the information is presented concurrently with the simulation so that the information is available at the appropriate moment". Pre-simulation information delivery was not effective in the studies reviewed.
requirements: Information must be available at the moment the learner needs it during interaction with the simulation
constraints: Information provided before interaction with the simulation was not effective in Leutner's and Elshout and Veenman's studies
target_learners: Learners with insufficient prior knowledge working with simulations
target_learning_goals: Domain knowledge of concepts, rules, and principles
Functional knowledge of the simulated system
examples: Shute's ITS on electricity let learners request definitions via hypertext links, with positive effects on a composite post-test
Leutner's agricultural simulation study found permanently available information helped domain knowledge acquisition
key_sources: Ton de Jong, Wouter R. van Joolingen. (1998). Scientific Discovery Learning with Computer Simulations of Conceptual Domains. Review of Educational Research. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190680v1

article_title: Spacing repetitions over 1 week
citation: Glenberg, A. M., & Lehmann, T. S. (1980). Spacing repetitions over 1 week. Memory & Cognition, 8(6), 528-538. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03213734
title: Component-levels theory: spacing effects arise from differential storage of contextual components and their match with the retrieval context
description: Component-levels theory (Glenberg, 1979) proposes that study encodes three component types—descriptive, structural (interitem associations), and contextual—and that "the variability in the encoding of all components increases as a function of repetition spacing", termed differential storage. Contextual components are aligned on a rate-of-change continuum from local (quickly changing) to global (slowly changing). Retrieval constructs a cue from the test context; traces activate in proportion to shared components, with cue overload making global components weaker cues. The theory explains the proportionality rule by applying the same storage-retrieval processes at different points on the context-change continuum.
requirements: Retrieval depends on the match between stored contextual components and the context available at the test; the account presumes free-recall testing without experimenter-provided cues
constraints: Differential storage of descriptive components was shown to have little effect on free-recall spacing effects
Within-list lag effects persist when structural (interitem) components are stored, since associative cues are independent of test context
target_learning_goals: free recall of repeated verbal material over retention intervals up to 2 weeks
examples: The theory predicted a four-way interaction in Experiment 1's within-list data that was significant, and predicted no same-different task interaction in Experiment 3, which was observed (F < 1).
key_sources: Glenberg, A. M., & Lehmann, T. S. (1980). Spacing repetitions over 1 week. Memory & Cognition, 8(6), 528-538. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03213772

article_title: Individual differences, rereading, and self-explanation: Concurrent processing and cue validity as constraints on metacomprehension accuracy
citation: Griffin, T. D., Wiley, J., & Thiede, K. W. (2008). Individual differences, rereading, and self-explanation: Concurrent processing and cue validity as constraints on metacomprehension accuracy. Memory & Cognition, 36(1), 93-103. https://doi.org/10.3758/MC.36.1.93
title: Concurrent-processing and cue-validity account of metacomprehension accuracy
description: The article proposes that metacomprehension accuracy is constrained by two factors: the concurrent-processing demand of monitoring while comprehending, and the validity and accessibility of cues. Its core assumptions are "that metacognitive monitoring is a distinct process secondary to the processes being monitored," and that some comprehension-predicting cues are less accessible after reading than during reading. Rereading reduces low-level text-processing demands, letting lower-ability and lower-WMC readers attend to metalevel cues; self-explanation increases access to inference-level cues valid for situation-model-level tests, improving accuracy for all readers.
requirements: Accurate concurrent monitoring requires available attentional resources, which vary with reading ability and working memory capacity
constraints: The article states the results may be particular to situations with relatively long texts explaining complex causal or logical relations, with inference- and situation-model-level tests
The article states it did not directly observe when readers were monitoring, and the evidence that accuracy was impacted by the ability to attend to the metalevel while reading is indirect
target_learning_goals: Accurate monitoring of one's own text comprehension
examples: Experiments 1 and 2 with explanatory natural/social-science texts and inference verification tests
Comparison to prejudgment generation tasks (summary/keyword listing) that also push readers toward situation-model cues
key_sources: Griffin, T. D., Wiley, J., & Thiede, K. W. (2008). Individual differences, rereading, and self-explanation: Concurrent processing and cue validity as constraints on metacomprehension accuracy. Memory & Cognition, 36(1), 93-103. https://doi.org/10.3758/MC.36.1.93

article_title: An examination of the seductive details effect in terms of working memory capacity
citation: Sanchez, C. A., & Wiley, J. (2006). An examination of the seductive details effect in terms of working memory capacity. Memory & Cognition, 34(2), 344-355. https://link.springer.com/journal/13421
title: Controlled attention perspective of working memory capacity
description: The article contrasts the controlled attention view with the traditional limited-capacity view of working memory. From this perspective, "WMC from the controlled attention perspective is the ability to control attention and deal with irrelevant information, and not simply the amount of information that can reside in working memory." Individual differences arise from the ability to ignore irrelevant information on the basis of a specific relevant goal, not from a limited amount of activation. Both experiments support this view: the seduction deficit appeared only for low-WMC readers and only when irrelevant illustrations were present, and eye-tracking showed high-WMC readers selectively ignored the seductive images.
requirements: Requires tasks containing irrelevant or interfering information, since differences between WMC groups emerge only when irrelevant information must be ignored
constraints: The article notes this account was tested with seductive images; the diversion hypothesis had already been ruled out for seductive images by prior work cited in the article
target_learners: undergraduate readers of expository scientific text
target_learning_goals: comprehension and situation-model construction from illustrated expository text
examples: Experiment 1 compared low- and high-WMC readers (prescreened with OSPAN and RSPAN) across nonillustrated, conceptually illustrated, and seductively illustrated conditions; Experiment 2 tracked their eye movements while reading the seductively illustrated text.
key_sources: Sanchez, C. A., & Wiley, J. (2006). An examination of the seductive details effect in terms of working memory capacity. Memory & Cognition, 34(2), 344-355. https://link.springer.com/journal/13421

article_title: Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives
citation: Tamara van Gog & Nikol Rummel. (2010). Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9134-7
title: Cognitive load explanation of why worked examples outperform unsupported problem solving for novices
description: The review explains the worked example effect via cognitive load theory: conventional problems force novices into weak strategies like means-ends analysis, which "imposes a high load on working memory but is not effective for learning", contributing little to schema construction. Worked examples prevent these weak strategies, allowing learners to devote cognitive capacity to studying the worked-out solution procedure and constructing a cognitive schema. The same theory underpins design guidelines (split-attention, redundancy) and delivery strategies such as fading and random sequencing.
requirements: Examples designed to avoid split-attention and redundancy so capacity goes to schema construction
constraints: Effect applies to novices; guidance reverses for knowledgeable learners
target_learning_goals: building cognitive schemas for problem solving
key_sources: Tamara van Gog & Nikol Rummel. (2010). Example-Based Learning: Integrating Cognitive and Social-Cognitive Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9134-7

article_title: Coaching effectiveness: the coach–athlete relationship at its heart
citation: Jowett, S. (2017). Coaching Effectiveness: The Coach-Athlete Relationship at its Heart. Current Opinion in Psychology, 16, 154-158. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2017.05.006
title: Adopt a coach-athlete-centred rather than solely athlete-centred or coach-centred view of coaching
description: The article recommends viewing coaching as coach-athlete-centred rather than athlete-centred or coach-centred. It argues that when coaching is viewed as either athlete-centred or coach-centred, its scope, quality and functions become restricted, whereas the coach-athlete-centred view is inclusive and mutually empowering, and that neither the coach nor the athlete can do it alone. The relationship becomes the medium that motivates, assures, satisfies, comforts and supports both parties to enhance sport experience, performance and well-being.
requirements: Coaches and athletes must develop and maintain a relationship in which both engage with one another, since effective coaching is understood through the quality of the connections they develop
constraints: The article frames this as a conceptual proposal supported by anecdotal and empirical evidence rather than a tested intervention
target_learning_goals: coaching effectiveness
long-term development, personal growth and transformation
examples: The review cites Nash and colleagues' finding that expert coaches plan and execute training sessions with individual athletes' needs in mind, which it argues is achievable only when coaches and athletes connect in ways that allow trust, commitment, and mutual understanding
key_sources: Jowett, S. (2017). Coaching Effectiveness: The Coach-Athlete Relationship at its Heart. Current Opinion in Psychology, 16, 154-158. http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2017.05.006

article_title: Adverse childhood experiences and trajectories of internalizing, externalizing, and prosocial behaviors from childhood to adolescence
citation: Leonardo Bevilacqua, Yvonne Kelly, Anja Heilmann, Naomi Priest, Rebecca E. Lacey. (2021). Adverse childhood experiences and trajectories of internalizing, externalizing, and prosocial behaviors from childhood to adolescence. Child Abuse & Neglect 112 (2021) 104890. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2020.104890
title: Consider both the number and the specific type of early stressors when predicting and intervening on children's mental health development
description: The article's conclusions state that accounting for both the count of stressors and their specific type helps predict mental health development and guide intervention. It reports that "taking into account not only the number of stressors that individuals are exposed to from very early age, but also the specific type of stressors, is helpful in predicting an individual's mental health development, and thus implement appropriate intervention programmes". This rests on the study's finding that ACE scores and individual ACEs each added information, with different ACEs showing different outcome-specific associations.
requirements: ACE information collected prospectively from early childhood, ideally from multiple informants
constraints: The study measured ACEs only at 9 months and 3 years and lacked data on sexual abuse, racial discrimination, and family antisocial behavior
target_learners: children from early childhood through adolescence
target_learning_goals: social-emotional development, including internalizing, externalizing, and prosocial behavior
examples: The study compared ACE score, individual ACE, and LCA cluster operationalisations against SDQ trajectories at ages 3, 5, 7, 11, and 14 in the Millennium Cohort Study
key_sources: Leonardo Bevilacqua, Yvonne Kelly, Anja Heilmann, Naomi Priest, Rebecca E. Lacey. (2021). Adverse childhood experiences and trajectories of internalizing, externalizing, and prosocial behaviors from childhood to adolescence. Child Abuse & Neglect 112 (2021) 104890. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2020.104890

article_title: The Association Between Cognitive Performance and Speech-in-Noise Perception for Adult Listeners: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Dryden Adam, Allen Harriet A., Henshaw Helen, Heinrich Antje. (2017). The Association Between Cognitive Performance and Speech-in-Noise Perception for Adult Listeners: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis. Trends in Hearing. https://doi.org/10.1177/2331216517744675
title: Dual classification framework: cognitive domains/subdomains and a speech-target-by-masker matrix for systematizing cognition–SiN studies
description: The review organizes the heterogeneous literature with two categorization systems. Cognitive measures are abstracted from individual tests into "five cognitive domains (attention, executive processes, memory, intelligence, and processing speed) and nine cognitive subdomains" based on established theories. SiN tests are classified by target lexical complexity (phonemes/syllables, words, sentences) and by masker type ordered on a continuum of decreasing energetic and increasing informational masking (unmodulated noise, modulated noise, >2-talker babble, ≤2-talker babble). This matrix enables fine-grained meta-analysis of specific cognition-by-listening-situation combinations.
requirements: Cognitive tests must be assignable to a single main subdomain; tests loading on multiple domains or not readily definable (e.g., the Text reception threshold) were excluded
constraints: Intelligibility levels, adaptive versus nonadaptive paradigms, and signal presentation are not distinguished within categories, a simplification the authors state was necessary given test heterogeneity
target_learners: Adult listeners (18+) with hearing from normal sensitivity to moderate hearing loss, unaided
target_learning_goals: Understanding the role of cognitive abilities in speech-in-noise perception
examples: The 25 included studies' 59 cognitive measures and eight target–masker combinations were mapped onto this framework before meta-analysis
key_sources: Dryden Adam, Allen Harriet A., Henshaw Helen, Heinrich Antje. (2017). The Association Between Cognitive Performance and Speech-in-Noise Perception for Adult Listeners: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis. Trends in Hearing. https://doi.org/10.1177/2331216517744675

article_title: Training Inhibition and Social Cognition in the Classrooms
citation: Honoré N, Houssa M, Volckaert A, Noël M-P and Nader-Grosbois N (2020) Training Inhibition and Social Cognition in the Classrooms. Front. Psychol. 11:1974. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01974
title: Combine inhibition and social cognition content in a single classroom-delivered EF training for young children
description: The article argues that because inhibition and social cognition are interdependent — perspective taking requires inhibitory control and both recruit the frontal lobe — a training program should address both together. It states that "it seems important to address social and emotional issues in an EF training program", and implemented this by pairing inhibition games with ToM and SIP activities in each of the 18 classroom sessions.
requirements: Sessions delivered weekly over a sustained period (6 months, 18 sessions), since longer programs yield better EF outcomes per the authors' review of Diamond and Ling
Group format in the classroom to allow socio-cognitive conflicts to emerge
constraints: Effects demonstrated for typically developing 5- and 6-year-olds in conventional-teaching schools in French-speaking Belgium
target_learners: Kindergarten and early primary school children
target_learning_goals: Inhibitory control
Theory of Mind
Social information processing
examples: Each session trained both inhibition and social cognition, with characters reminding children to activate inhibition strategies before each activity
key_sources: Honoré N, Houssa M, Volckaert A, Noël M-P and Nader-Grosbois N (2020) Training Inhibition and Social Cognition in the Classrooms. Front. Psychol. 11:1974. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.01974

article_title: Selective attention within the foveola
citation: Poletti Martina, Rucci Michele, Carrasco Marisa. (2017). Selective attention within the foveola. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.4622
title: Covert attention as a global selection mechanism operating across the entire visual field, including the foveola
description: The article proposes that covert attention is not a process that operates only away from the center of gaze but "the manifestation of a more general mechanism evolved for selectively improving and accelerating processing throughout the visual field, including the region of highest acuity." Selective enhancement can be restricted to very narrow regions and shifted across locations separated by minutes of arc, with allocation varying with task demands and stimulus characteristics. The authors infer the underlying neural processes need high-resolution saliency maps of the central field, continual updating during fixational instability, and spatial updating mechanisms with much higher resolution than those studied in the periphery.
requirements: High-resolution representations of the central visual field and mechanisms for continually updating them during fixational instability, as the article states the controlling processes must include
constraints: The account is grounded in psychophysical experiments with small observer samples (N=5 per experiment) using gaze-contingent retinal stabilization
target_learners: adult observers in visual perception tasks
target_learning_goals: selective spatial attention and fine spatial vision
examples: Experiments 2–4 showed valid-cue benefits and invalid-cue costs within the foveola at 20′ separations, under both stabilized and normal fixation
key_sources: Poletti Martina, Rucci Michele, Carrasco Marisa. (2017). Selective attention within the foveola. Nature Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1038/nn.4622

article_title: Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education
citation: Rivas SF, Saiz C and Ossa C (2022) Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education. Front. Psychol. 13:913219. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.913219
title: Components-of-critical-thinking model: cognitive skills, non-cognitive dispositions, and metacognition as a bridging process
description: The article presents a model (Figure 1, Saiz 2020) in which critical thinking comprises cognitive components (perception, learning, memory, and the core skills of reasoning, decision-making, and problem-solving) and non-cognitive components (motivation and interests), with metacognition sharing aspects of both because it "incorporates aspects of both judgment (evaluation) and disposition (control/efficiency) about thoughts." Motivation activates skills while metacognition makes them more effective; the authors argue neither cognitive skills nor dispositions alone suffice to train critical thinking, and relations among components are bidirectional.
requirements: Instruction must address both cognitive and non-cognitive components, since one component is incomplete without the other
constraints: Figure 1 shows only unidirectional relations for didactic reasons, although the authors state relations are in general bidirectional
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
metacognitive awareness and self-regulation
examples: The ARDESOS-DIAPROVE program operationalizes this model by directly teaching reasoning, decision-making, and problem-solving skills while incorporating motivational and metacognitive variables.
key_sources: Rivas SF, Saiz C and Ossa C (2022) Metacognitive Strategies and Development of Critical Thinking in Higher Education. Front. Psychol. 13:913219. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.913219

article_title: Think-Pair-Share and Roundtable: Two Cooperative Learning Structures to Enhance Critical Thinking Skills of 4th Graders
citation: Silva, H., Lopes, J., Dominguez, C., & Morais, E. (2022). Think-Pair-Share and Roundtable: Two Cooperative Learning Structures to Enhance Critical Thinking Skills of 4th Graders. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 15(1), 11-21. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2022.274
title: Cooperative learning rests on five basic elements that together promote critical thinking
description: The article describes cooperative learning as small heterogeneous groups cooperating toward common goals, structured by five elements: "positive interdependence, individual and group accountability, promotive interaction, social skills, and group processing". When these are present, students share and synthesize ideas, argue about viewpoints, and establish agreements, which the authors hold promotes critical thinking skills. The study's activities were structured so these characteristics were always present.
requirements: Students organized in small heterogeneous groups by achievement and gender
Social skills such as turn-taking, attentive listening, conflict management
Evaluation procedures for group processing
constraints: A lack of social skills is described as probably the main inhibiting factor to success of cooperative groups
target_learners: 4th grade primary students (1st cycle of basic education)
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking skills: observation, interpretation, analysis (inferences), argumentation
examples: The experimental teacher organized heterogeneous groups of four, assigned rotating roles, and ran 21 cooperative activities across Language Arts, Environment Study and Mathematics
key_sources: Silva, H., Lopes, J., Dominguez, C., & Morais, E. (2022). Think-Pair-Share and Roundtable: Two Cooperative Learning Structures to Enhance Critical Thinking Skills of 4th Graders. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 15(1), 11-21. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2022.274

article_title: Development of Affective Theory of Mind Across Adolescence: Disentangling the Role of Executive Functions
citation: Vetter, Nora C.; Altgassen, Mareike; Phillips, Louise; Mahy, Caitlin; Kliegel, Matthias. (2013). Development of Affective Theory of Mind Across Adolescence: Disentangling the Role of Executive Functions. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2012.733786
title: Theory of mind comprises cognitive and affective components distinguished by mental-state type
description: The article frames theory of mind, "the ability to understand mental states", as involving two kinds of inference: inferences about others' cognitive mental states (cognitive theory of mind) and inferences about others' emotional mental states (affective theory of mind). The study focuses on the affective component and its development across adolescence.
requirements: Measures must distinguish affective from cognitive theory-of-mind inference when assessing development.
target_learning_goals: understanding others' emotional mental states
understanding others' cognitive mental states
examples: The study measured affective theory of mind alongside three executive-function subcomponents in an adolescent sample.
key_sources: Vetter, Nora C.; Altgassen, Mareike; Phillips, Louise; Mahy, Caitlin; Kliegel, Matthias. (2013). Development of Affective Theory of Mind Across Adolescence: Disentangling the Role of Executive Functions. Developmental Neuropsychology. https://doi.org/10.1080/87565641.2012.733786

article_title: On the relationship between cultural diversity and creativity in education: The moderating role of communal versus divisional mindset
citation: Vezzali, L., Goclowska, M., Crisp, R. J., & Stathi, S. (2016). On the Relationship between Cultural Diversity and Creativity in Education: The Moderating Role of Communal versus Divisional Mindset. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/
title: Communal versus divisional mindset account of the diversity–creativity link
description: The article proposes that diversity benefits creativity because it disrupts stereotype use and prompts generative thinking, but a salient "divisional mindset" focused on group distinctions activates intergroup differentiation processes at odds with this way of thinking. A "communal mindset" that does not mention group differences leaves the beneficial cognitive effects of diversity intact. In the study, the two mindsets were manipulated orthogonally to group composition via fictional story framings.
requirements: The mindset manipulation must be orthogonal to the actual diversity of the group so its moderating role can be isolated.
constraints: The account was tested only for originality of ideas in children; the specific cognitive process (e.g., flexibility) underlying the effect was not measured.
target_learning_goals: creative thinking (originality of ideas)
examples: Children in the divisional condition imagined two opposing fictional groups (Sun and Moon) with different skin colors; those in the communal condition imagined one cooperative group on planet Astra.
key_sources: Vezzali, L., Goclowska, M., Crisp, R. J., & Stathi, S. (2016). On the Relationship between Cultural Diversity and Creativity in Education: The Moderating Role of Communal versus Divisional Mindset. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/

article_title: Video games can develop graduate skills in higher education students: A randomised trial
citation: Matthew Barr. (2017). Video games can develop graduate skills in higher education students: A randomised trial. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.05.016
title: Suite of eight selected commercial video games played in supervised drop-in game labs
description: The intervention material was a suite of commercial entertainment titles (Borderlands 2, Minecraft, Portal 2, Lara Croft and the Guardian of Light, Warcraft III, Team Fortress 2, Gone Home, Papers, Please) played on twelve Windows PCs in university game labs. Selection required that "no game with a Metacritic score of less than 80 out of 100 was considered", and all but Gone Home and Papers, Please included a substantial multiplayer component. Participants logged about 120 minutes per game (60 minutes each for Gone Home and Papers, Please).
requirements: Games must run on modestly-specified Windows PCs and be relatively inexpensive
A local network setup supporting multiplayer play without an internet connection
constraints: MMORPG titles were excluded because network ports could not be opened and their learning curve exceeded the 2 h allocated per game
target_learners: year one and year two undergraduate students in the College of Arts
target_learning_goals: communication skill
adaptability
resourcefulness
examples: Participants played Portal 2 in pairs with printed hosting instructions; Team Fortress 2 ran on a local dedicated server to avoid Steam matchmaking restrictions
key_sources: Matthew Barr. (2017). Video games can develop graduate skills in higher education students: A randomised trial. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2017.05.016

article_title: Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context
citation: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216
title: Cognitive Task Analysis: a three-phase approach to eliciting expert cognition in context
description: CTA is a collection of interview-based qualitative methods for identifying the cognitive processes and skills required to perform complex tasks in demanding, contextually dependent work domains. The article organizes it around three phases: "(i) knowledge elicitation; (ii) data analysis; (iii) knowledge representation" — interviewing or observing experts to break down task steps, eliciting the cognitive processes used during task completion, and mapping knowledge requirements, cues, strategies, and skills into a digestible format that enhances workplace knowledge transfer. It is presented as complementary to existing managerial cognition methods, with a specific focus on the role of context.
requirements: Access to expert participants whose knowledge is the elicitation target
Interviewers familiar with the specifics of the research domain, striving for quasi-expert status
constraints: Unlikely to be suited to studies aiming to elicit generalizable knowledge or quantitatively compare two distinct groups
Lends itself to initial phases of theory development rather than theory testing and confirmation
target_learners: Experts and experienced practitioners in complex work domains
target_learning_goals: Understanding expert cognitive processes, cues, strategies, and knowledge requirements in complex tasks
examples: Applied to emergency command decision-making via the Critical Decision Method and to global leadership via Applied Cognitive Task Analysis
key_sources: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216

article_title: Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens
citation: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522
title: Conceptual models as interactive visual learning objects for conceptual learning
description: A conceptual model is defined as a particular kind of learning object: an interactive and visual multimedia representation designed to depict a concept or connected concepts and support conceptual learning. The article describes it as a representation that lets learners manipulate and interrogate represented properties and relationships, drawing on Norman's and Mayer's notions of a conceptual model as a representation designed for teaching and understanding. The author positions it as reusable across purposes, student groups, and delivery devices.
requirements: Should be used in the context of a learning task that triggers conceptually demanding cognitive processing
constraints: The article notes readers should not expect detailed descriptions of data collection and analysis in this paper
target_learning_goals: conceptual learning of curriculum concepts and their properties and relationships
examples: The Explore Triangle conceptual model lets students drag sliders for base and height, redrawing the triangle and updating values such as the hypotenuse, and can be reused from lower-grade exploration of right-angled triangles to senior work on Pythagorean theorem and trigonometric functions
key_sources: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522

article_title: Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens
citation: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522
title: Design for presentation: visual, interactive, single-screen conceptual models
description: This pattern is the article's first set of recommendations for the content, screen and interface design of a conceptual model. It specifies presenting information predominantly visually, designing for interaction so users manipulate parameters and observe outcomes, arranging elements into a holistic scenario, presenting on a single screen within a small space (most models within 640 by 480 pixels per the author's experience), using audio and video only when necessary, moderating color, avoiding decorative elements, using a single font, and framing functional screen areas.
requirements: Design elements should integrate into a holistic presentational scenario depicting the represented concept
All display elements should serve the purpose of representing a concept
constraints: These recommendations alone do not address instructional uses and are, as the article states, of little use to teachers without the learning-uses set
target_learning_goals: multimedia representation and manipulation of conceptual knowledge
examples: Reviewers described features of reviewed conceptual models against criteria drawn from the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, and the River model was later designed with a single screen, Arial font only, limited colors, and no decorative elements
key_sources: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522

article_title: Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens
citation: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522
title: Design for small screens: full-screen, landscape, one-step interaction with zooming and floating panels
description: This pattern is the article's second recommendation set, addressing the limited screen area of handheld devices (about 3.5 inches, 320 by 240 pixels at the time). It recommends full-screen and landscape presentation, minimizing scrolling, task-centered design for short contacts, one-step interaction with immediately noticeable updates, a zooming facility to reach display areas beyond the physical screen, and movable, collapsible, overlapping, semi-transparent interactive panels to maximize presented information.
requirements: Single interactions such as changing a slider position should result in immediate, perceptually noticeable screen updates
constraints: Screen size continues to present design challenges; text legibility and the nature of interactions limit design possibilities, as the article reports from prior work
target_learning_goals: access to conceptual model content and interaction on small-screen devices
examples: The River conceptual model was displayed full-screen in landscape mode on the HP iPAQ rw6828 with content designed so scrolling was not required, though zooming was not yet utilized and was planned for a redesigned version
key_sources: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522

article_title: Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens
citation: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522
title: Design for learning uses: observation, analysis, experimentation, thinking, and reuse
description: This pattern is the article's third recommendation set, derived from classroom and fieldwork observations, interviews, and review of student work with teachers and students. It classifies learning uses of conceptual models into emerging categories and maps each to a design recommendation: design for observation (linking real world and represented properties), analytical use (inputting real-environment data for processing), experimentation (manipulating parameters and testing generalizations), thinking (triggers and cues supporting mental-model linking), and reuse across environments, devices, and collaborating users.
requirements: Reuse requires that interactivity be supported by a variety of devices and that large-screen presentation not cause split attention problems
constraints: The article states these recommendations present possibilities for learning-task-related uses and must complement the presentation and small-screen sets
target_learning_goals: linking theory to the world outside the classroom
inquiry
analysis
experimentation
reflection and collaboration
examples: Table 1 of the article lists each recommendation against identified learning uses such as aid to observations, analytical tool, experimentation environment, external cognitive supplement, preparation tool, collaboration tool, and reflective tool
key_sources: Daniel Churchill. (2011). Conceptual Model Learning Objects and Design Recommendations for Small Screens. Educational Technology & Society, 14(1), 203-216. https://www.worldcat.org/issn/1436-4522

article_title: Quiet or questioning? Students' discussion behaviors in student-centered education across cultures
citation: Janneke M. Frambach, Erik W. Driessen, Philip Beh and Cees P.M. van der Vleuten. (2014). Quiet or questioning? Students' discussion behaviors in student-centered education across cultures. Studies in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/03075079.2012.754865
title: Conceptual model of cultural and contextual factors shaping students' discussion behaviors in student-centered education
description: The study built a conceptual model (Figure 2) linking cultural and contextual factors to students' discussion behaviors and skills in PBL. It holds that students externalize cultural backgrounds and internalize the discussion aspect of PBL, so that 'students' discussion behaviors and skills and their development from the first to the third year were shaped by complex interactions between contextual factors, cultural factors, and the PBL discussion sessions.' The model organizes four cultural factors and six mediating contextual factors.
requirements: Data from interviews, observations, documents and contextual information across multiple institutions to populate the model
constraints: Derived from a qualitative comparative case study in three medical schools; findings do not lend themselves to generalization
target_learning_goals: discussion and communication skills in small-group student-centered learning
key_sources: Janneke M. Frambach, Erik W. Driessen, Philip Beh and Cees P.M. van der Vleuten. (2014). Quiet or questioning? Students' discussion behaviors in student-centered education across cultures. Studies in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1080/03075079.2012.754865

article_title: Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition?
citation: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0
title: Complex problems are defined by complexity, connectivity, dynamics, intransparency and polytely
description: The article defines a complex problem as one whose solution demands operations on systems with five characteristics drawn from Dörner et al. (1983): "Elements relevant to the solution process are large ( complexity), highly interconnected ( connectivity), and dynamically changing over time ( dynamics). Neither structure nor dynamics are disclosed ( intransparency)" and the goal structure is polytelic, requiring the weighting and coordination of multiple goal facets. This definition distinguishes CPS from simple problem solving and organizes the review.
requirements: Assessment scenarios must realize these characteristics, e.g. computer-simulated microworlds
constraints: The definition is presented as the European research tradition's characterization, not a formally measured taxonomy
target_learners: adult problem solvers in laboratory and real-world decision settings
target_learning_goals: problem solving in complex dynamic systems
examples: Tailorshop and Lohhausen microworlds were built to realize these characteristics under lab conditions
key_sources: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0

article_title: Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition?
citation: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0
title: Complex cognition as goal-directed derivation of new information, contrasted with simple cognition on a hierarchy of explanation levels
description: Following Knauff and Wolf, the article states that "complex cognition deals with all mental processes that are used by an individual for deriving new information out of given information, with the intention to make decisions, solve problems, and plan actions." Simple cognition studies elementary processes like perception, memory or learning in isolation; complex cognition is a shift in hierarchy level of explanation (signal, sign, broader regulation concept), and the whole follows the Gestalt principle of being more than the sum of its parts. Mental processes here include motivational and emotional processes.
requirements: A definition of complexity going beyond difficulty, which the article notes remains open
constraints: The border between simple and complex cognition is explicitly not a clear-cut one with a sharp border
target_learning_goals: deriving new information, decision making, action planning
examples: A ship's captain overseeing a red warning light illustrates complex cognition embedding perception into action regulation
key_sources: Joachim Funke. (2009). Complex problem solving: a case for complex cognition? Cogn Process. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-009-0345-0

article_title: Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research
citation: Graham LA, Gray C, Wagner TH, Illarmo S, Hawn MT, Wren SM, Iannuzzi J, Harris AHS. (2023). Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research. Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-6773.14106
title: Cognitive Demands Tables and process flow diagrams as CTA deliverables
description: The article identifies tables, diagrams, and lists of cognitive functions, cues, and subprocesses as common CTA deliverables. Process flow diagrams document cognitive steps to complete a task, while tables breaking out required cognitive tasks by event type are "frequently referred to as “Cognitive Demands Tables” when used in the context of CTA." These tables can include task types, actors, cues, and barriers and facilitators. Fishbone, flowchart, and network diagrams can detail task sequences and potential error points.
requirements: Decisions about which deliverables are most appropriate should be made based on the research audience
Systematic qualitative coding to increase validity, transparency, and reproducibility
target_learning_goals: documenting and communicating the cognitive demands of a task
examples: The pilot drafted a task flow diagram of the discharge process, a table of key actors, and a table of frequently occurring cues that a patient is ready for discharge
key_sources: Graham LA, Gray C, Wagner TH, Illarmo S, Hawn MT, Wren SM, Iannuzzi J, Harris AHS. (2023). Applying cognitive task analysis to health services research. Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-6773.14106

article_title: Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive #x0022;Quantified Self #x0022;
citation: Kai Kunze, Masakazu Iwamura, Koichi Kise, Seiichi Uchida, and Shinichiro Omachi. (2013). Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive “Quantified Self.” Computer, IEEE Computer Society, October 2013. http://kaikunze.de/papers/2013Kunze-1.pdf
title: Cognitive quantified self: mobile sensing applied to cognitive tasks such as reading
description: The article proposes extending activity tracking from physical movement to cognitive tasks, using mobile eye tracking because eye movements are "strongly correlated with cognitive tasks". Just as fitness apps record physical activity, a reading-habits app could record "the number of words read, types of documents read, and periods of concentrated reading to help users become better thinkers". The long-term goal is tracking mental processes to enable self-reflection and optimize mental fitness and well-being.
requirements: Mobile eye-tracking hardware (EOG electrodes or infrared stereo cameras) that can record gaze in real-life settings
constraints: Eye movements also encode attentiveness, fatigue, and emotional state, making it difficult to isolate the object of interest
The authors note the research "raises numerous ethical questions—for example, who should know what we read or how much we understand?"
target_learning_goals: self-reflection on reading habits
learning-progress awareness
examples: Figure 1 shows a mockup interface for a hypothetical Readit service that records and analyzes reading habits, much like a fitness service such as Fitbit
key_sources: Kai Kunze, Masakazu Iwamura, Koichi Kise, Seiichi Uchida, and Shinichiro Omachi. (2013). Activity Recognition for the Mind: Toward a Cognitive “Quantified Self.” Computer, IEEE Computer Society, October 2013. http://kaikunze.de/papers/2013Kunze-1.pdf

article_title: Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs
citation: Chris Piech, Jonathan Huang, Zhenghao Chen, Chuong Do, Andrew Ng, Daphne Koller. (2013). Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.2579
title: Coursera HCI peer grading dataset: 63,199 peer grades from 7,240 students across two course offerings
description: Two consecutive Coursera offerings of the Human Computer Interaction course taught by Scott Klemmer, using a calibrated peer grading system. Per assignment, each student evaluated five randomly selected submissions (one a ground-truth submission) on a rubric and was evaluated by four classmates; the final score was the median of peer grades. The dataset comprises 3,607 students (HCI1) and 3,633 students (HCI2), 13,972 submissions, and 63,199 peer grades — described as "the largest peer grading networks analysed to date".
constraints: HCI2 was used as a hold-out set; models were formulated only on HCI1
A small number (3-5) of submissions per assignment were marked as ground truth and supergraded with on average 160 assessments
target_learners: MOOC students in the HCI course offerings
target_learning_goals: Peer assessment of creative web-site design assignments
examples: Ground-truth submissions were graded by course staff and students were not told which submissions belonged to the ground truth set
key_sources: Chris Piech, Jonathan Huang, Zhenghao Chen, Chuong Do, Andrew Ng, Daphne Koller. (2013). Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/1307.2579

article_title: Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education
citation: Ritter, S., Anderson, J. R., Koedinger, K. R., & Corbett, A. (2007). Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2007, 14 (2), 249-255. https://www.carnegielearning.com
title: Carnegie Learning Cognitive Tutor curricula (text plus software plus teacher training)
description: A complete middle- and high-school mathematics course combining text, Cognitive Tutor software, ancillary materials, and teacher training. The inclusion of text supports activities such as "collaboration, diagramming, and writing about mathematics" that are easier on paper, and positions the software as part of primary instruction rather than a bonus or review activity. Pilot implementations led to a model in which students used the software 2 days per week, with classroom activities structured by the text on the other 3 days each week.
requirements: Teacher training and integration into broader classroom goals, since earlier tutors' success appeared highly dependent on the teacher's ability to integrate the software
target_learners: middle and high school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: algebra and geometry skills, problem solving, and multiple representations
examples: Students used the software 2 days per week with text-structured classroom activities on the other 3 days each week
key_sources: Ritter, S., Anderson, J. R., Koedinger, K. R., & Corbett, A. (2007). Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2007, 14 (2), 249-255. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03194060

article_title: Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education
citation: Ritter, S., Anderson, J. R., Koedinger, K. R., & Corbett, A. (2007). Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2007, 14 (2), 249-255. https://www.carnegielearning.com
title: Large-scale Cognitive Tutor log dataset from over 7,000 pre-algebra students
description: The article reports a collected dataset from over 7,000 students using Cognitive Tutor in a pre-algebra class, comprising over 35 million observations, amounting to observing an action for each student about every 9.5 sec. The authors expect this database will let them detect subtler factors affecting learning, including the effectiveness of individual tasks, hints, and feedback patterns, and they are starting to apply microgenetic methods to identify key learning experiences.
requirements: Aggregation of student data over the Internet and an expanded customer base to enable deep and broad analysis of student cognition
target_learning_goals: understanding students' mathematical cognition and improving instruction
examples: The authors are applying microgenetic methods to identify key learning experiences that could contribute to better cognitive models of individual differences
key_sources: Ritter, S., Anderson, J. R., Koedinger, K. R., & Corbett, A. (2007). Cognitive Tutor: Applied research in mathematics education. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 2007, 14 (2), 249-255. https://doi.org/10.3758/bf03194060

article_title: Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities
citation: Keith Topping. (1998). Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543068003249
title: Computer-assisted peer assessment systems and studies
description: The review identifies computer-assisted peer assessment as "an emerging growth area", enabled by wider availability of word processing and electronic mail. Described implementations include the MUCH (Many Using and Creating Hypermedia) system used in nursing and computer science education, which showed good correspondence with staff assessment though many computer science students were skeptical; Brock's comparison of computerized text analysis with peer feedback for 48 ESL writers; peer assessment of class presentations with computer tools; and University of Portsmouth software that randomly allocated peer assessors, integrated peer and staff marks, calculated weighted final marks, and generated feedback. Few outcome data were yet available.
requirements: Access to word processing, electronic mail or dedicated software; organizational and record-keeping functions for allocation and mark integration
constraints: Few outcome data yet available; student skepticism about computer-mediated peer assessment reported in some settings
target_learning_goals: formative feedback on writing and hypermedia products
examples: Brock (1993) found both computerized-feedback and peer-supported ESL groups showed significant writing growth, with peer interaction rated higher for helpfulness in improving content
key_sources: Keith Topping. (1998). Peer Assessment Between Students in Colleges and Universities. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543068003249

article_title: Learning in a global society
citation: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org
title: Complex cognition: cognition as individually owned and socially shared, evolving according to the laws of complex adaptive systems
description: Complex cognition is a concept proposed by the author at a Santa Fe Institute seminar (J. Visser, 2000, November). It holds that cognition is a complex phenomenon evolving according to the laws governing complex adaptive systems, whose conditions the author says are well known, citing Gell-Mann (1995) and Holland (1995). The concept integrates the spectrum of views on distributed cognitions described by Salomon (1993), resolving their juxtaposition: "Cognition is individually owned and socially shared at the same time." It underpins the chapter's argument that learning must be understood broadly to remain relevant to adaptive human behavior regarding global issues.
requirements: Account must be taken of the entire developing transdisciplinary knowledge base rooted in disciplines from cognitive science and neuroscience to anthropology and research on effective teaching
constraints: The author presents it as a conceptual proposal rather than an empirically tested model
target_learners: learners at all levels of complex organization, individual and social
target_learning_goals: constructive interaction with change through intelligent behavior
key_sources: Jan Visser. (2006). Learning in a Global Society. Learning Development Institute. https://www.learndev.org

article_title: Learning from others at work: communities of practice and informal learning
citation: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202.
title: Communities of practice are a useful but insufficient framework for informal workplace learning; loosely and tightly coupled variants and additional conceptualisations are needed
description: The article evaluates Lave and Wenger's and Wenger's communities of practice framework against qualitative data from four workgroups. It finds the framework "provides useful ways of accounting for the phenomenon we are considering", but is "not sufficient for our purposes of dealing with informal learning at work", because some learning networks are more loosely coupled groupings that do not build identity and meaning. The authors propose degrees of coupling, Bernstein's framing, and Engeström's expansive learning as complementary lenses.
requirements: The framework presupposes sustained relationships, shared ways of engaging, and mutual familiarity among members, as in the tightly coupled tiling teachers and HR group.
constraints: Communities of practice form naturally, are often strongly bounded, and may not be easily cultivated; an exclusive focus on them may limit accounts of workplace learning and the kinds of intervention possible.
target_learning_goals: Informal workplace learning, including mastering organisational processes, negotiating the political, and dealing with the atypical
examples: The tiling teachers and HR group were described as tightly coupled communities of practice; the educational planners, with more frequent reformation and changing membership, were looser and possibly more representative of contemporary organisations.
key_sources: David Boud and Heather Middleton. (2003). Learning from Others at Work: Communities of Practice and Informal Learning. Journal of Workplace Learning, 15, 5, 194-202. https://doi.org/10.1108/13665620310483895

article_title: Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience
citation: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003
title: Cognitive flexibility as an emergent property of efficient executive function, measured by set shifting and task switching
description: The review defines cognitive flexibility as "the ability to appropriately adjust one's behavior according to a changing environment" and as "an emergent property of efficient executive function" typically measured with set shifting or task switching paradigms. It adopts Bunge and Zelazo's hierarchy in which set shifting is a lower-level form and task switching the most complex form. Both produce switch costs, reflecting inhibition of the previous response set and reconfiguration to the new task.
requirements: Tasks must produce a switch cost to be valid measures of cognitive flexibility
Consistent operationalization across studies is required
constraints: The construct is difficult to examine due to the multitude of ways it has been described in the literature
target_learning_goals: flexible adjustment of behavior to changing environments
set shifting and task switching
key_sources: Dajani, D. R., & Uddin, L. Q. (2015). Demystifying cognitive flexibility: Implications for clinical and developmental neuroscience. Trends in Neurosciences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tins.2015.07.003

article_title: Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy
citation: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf
title: Computer anxiety as a concept-specific anxiety type within a trait–state–concept-specific taxonomy
description: The article organizes anxiety into three types: trait anxiety (pervasive across life experience), state anxiety (fluctuating, responsive to situations), and concept-specific anxiety (associated with a specific situation). Computer anxiety is classified as concept-specific because it "is a feeling that is associated with a person's interaction with computers". The authors later suggest adapting the anxiety construct into these three sub-dimensions for future e-learning research.
requirements: Measuring computer anxiety requires recognizing it as situation-specific rather than a general personality trait
constraints: The study measured anxiety with only four general items; only two (ANX3, ANX4) loaded cleanly on the construct
target_learning_goals: understanding and mitigating computer anxiety in e-learning contexts
key_sources: Saadé, R. G., & Kira, D. (2009). Computer Anxiety in E-Learning: The Effect of Computer Self-Efficacy. Journal of Information Technology Education, 8. https://jite.org/documents/Vol8/JITEv8p177-191Saade708.pdf

article_title: Anxiety and Reading Difficulties in Early Elementary School: Evidence for Unidirectional- or Bi-Directional Relations?
citation: Grills-Taquechel, Amie E.; Fletcher, Jack M.; Vaughn, Sharon R.; Stuebing, Karla K. (2012). Anxiety and Reading Difficulties in Early Elementary School: Evidence for Unidirectional- or Bi-Directional Relations? Child Psychiatry and Human Development, 43(1), 35-47. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10578-011-0246-1
title: Competing-models framework of anxiety-reading achievement relations
description: The article organizes the anxiety-achievement association into two competing causal models plus a bidirectional variant: Model 1 holds that increased anxiety interferes with concentration, memory, and information processing, lowering achievement; Model 2 holds that children develop anxiety symptoms in response to repeated classroom failure. The authors note a cycle may develop in which anxiety and learning difficulties continue to influence each other and worsen over time. The study tests these models longitudinally with multidimensional anxiety and two reading domains (decoding and fluency).
requirements: Longitudinal data with anxiety and achievement measured at two or more time points to test predictive direction
constraints: The article states longitudinal data is required to more clearly examine these potential relations; the pilot design cannot establish causal direction
target_learners: Early elementary school children (first grade) in general education classes
target_learning_goals: Reading achievement (decoding and oral reading fluency)
Understanding and reducing anxiety symptoms that co-occur with reading difficulties
examples: The study evaluated 153 first-graders in winter and spring using the MASC anxiety scale, WJBR decoding composite, and CMERS fluency passages, testing each model via hierarchical linear regression
key_sources: Grills-Taquechel, Amie E.; Fletcher, Jack M.; Vaughn, Sharon R.; Stuebing, Karla K. (2012). Anxiety and Reading Difficulties in Early Elementary School: Evidence for Unidirectional- or Bi-Directional Relations? Child Psychiatry and Human Development, 43(1), 35-47. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10578-011-0246-1

article_title: The Relation of Obesity to Performance in Verbal Abilities, Processing Speed, and Cognitive Flexibility in Old Age: The Role of Cognitive Reserve
citation: Ihle, Andreas; Mons, Ute; Perna, Laura; Oris, Michel; Fagot, Delphine; Gabriel, Rainer; Kliegel, Matthias (2016). The Relation of Obesity to Performance in Verbal Abilities, Processing Speed, and Cognitive Flexibility in Old Age: The Role of Cognitive Reserve. Dementia and Geriatric Cognitive Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1159/000448916
title: Cognitive reserve accumulated across the life course buffers detrimental influences of obesity on cognitive functioning in old age
description: The study applies the cognitive reserve framework to explain how accumulated life-course resources (educational attainment, occupation, engagement in activities throughout adulthood) may offset the detrimental influence of obesity on cognitive functioning in old age. The authors conclude that "cognitive reserve accumulated during the life course may reduce the detrimental influences of obesity on cognitive functioning in old age." In this study, cognitive reserve is operationalized through proxies measured across early life and midlife, and its buffering role is tested via moderation and hierarchical regression analyses.
requirements: Cognitive reserve proxies (educational attainment, occupation, engagement in activities throughout adulthood) must be measured to operationalize reserve accumulated in early and midlife.
constraints: The study is cross-sectional; the conclusion that reserve "may reduce" detrimental influences is stated as a suggestion rather than a demonstrated causal mechanism.
target_learning_goals: maintaining cognitive functioning (verbal abilities, processing speed, cognitive flexibility) in old age
examples: The study tested whether obesity's relation to processing speed and cognitive flexibility was moderated by engagement in activities and education, and whether the association disappeared when reserve proxies were added to regression models.
key_sources: Ihle, Andreas; Mons, Ute; Perna, Laura; Oris, Michel; Fagot, Delphine; Gabriel, Rainer; Kliegel, Matthias (2016). The Relation of Obesity to Performance in Verbal Abilities, Processing Speed, and Cognitive Flexibility in Old Age: The Role of Cognitive Reserve. Dementia and Geriatric Cognitive Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1159/000448916

article_title: Kindergarten predictors of third grade writing
citation: Kim Young-Suk, Al Otaiba Stephanie, Wanzek Jeanne. (2015). Kindergarten Predictors of Third Grade Writing. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.009
title: Simple view and not-so-simple view of writing as frameworks of component skills for developing writers
description: The article organizes its predictor selection around named theoretical models of writing. The simple view of writing holds that "writing is a function of two necessary component skills, ideation and transcription," while the not-so-simple view clusters skills into transcription, text generation, and executive functions/self-regulation, with working memory coordinating them. The knowledge-telling model adds that young children's writing transcribes what they know about topic and genre. The study operationalized these as transcription, oral language, attention, and word-reading predictors.
requirements: The framework assumes writing outcomes can be decomposed into measurable component skills assessed separately from writing quality itself
constraints: The article notes most prior supporting studies were concurrent predictions, and longitudinal predictive studies were lacking before this work
target_learners: children in kindergarten through elementary grades
target_learning_goals: written composition quality in narrative and expository genres
examples: The study selected kindergarten predictors (letter writing automaticity, spelling, oral language, word reading, attention) based on the simple view and not-so-simple view of writing and tested them longitudinally against third-grade writing quality.
key_sources: Kim Young-Suk, Al Otaiba Stephanie, Wanzek Jeanne. (2015). Kindergarten Predictors of Third Grade Writing. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2014.11.009

article_title: When do socioeconomic resources matter most in early childhood?
citation: Mollborn, S., Lawrence, E., James-Hawkins, L., & Fomby, P. (2014). When Do Socioeconomic Resources Matter Most in Early Childhood? Advances in Life Course Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.alcr.2014.03.001
title: Three competing hypotheses about change in the SES–development relationship across early childhood: constant, decreasing, and increasing.
description: The article articulates three hypotheses drawn from prior literature about how the SES–child development relationship changes across early childhood: (1) a constant relationship, (2) a decreasing relationship (stronger in infancy, per cumulative advantage/path-dependency and fetal-origins logic), and (3) an increasing relationship (stronger at school entry, per school-transition theory). The authors state: "we articulated three competing hypotheses about change in the relationship between SES and cognitive and behavioral development across early childhood."
requirements: Testing requires longitudinal within-child data spanning infancy through kindergarten entry.
constraints: The findings did not neatly support any single hypothesis; the curvilinear peak pattern required a modified version of Hypothesis 3.
target_learners: Children from infancy through kindergarten entry
target_learning_goals: Understanding when socioeconomic resources most influence developmental trajectories
examples: Figure 1 of the article illustrates the three hypothesized forms of the SES–outcome relationship across early childhood.
key_sources: Mollborn, S., Lawrence, E., James-Hawkins, L., & Fomby, P. (2014). When Do Socioeconomic Resources Matter Most in Early Childhood? Advances in Life Course Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.alcr.2014.03.001

article_title: The interplay between math anxiety and working memory on math performance: a longitudinal study
citation: Pellizzoni, S., Cargnelutti, E., Cuder, A., & Passolunghi, M.C. (2021). The interplay between math anxiety and working memory on math performance: a longitudinal study. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1111/nyas.14722
title: Interventions for math difficulties should combine math training with support for managing anxiety
description: The article recommends that support for children with math difficulties address emotional and cognitive factors together. It states that "rehabilitation programs that focus only on improving math skills and their cognitive precursors might be ineffective if children do not learn how to handle their negative emotional states at the same time." Intervention should therefore pair math-specific training with activities that help children contain and cope with anxiety.
requirements: Assessment of children's anxiety (ideally including teacher ratings) alongside math skills to identify who needs emotional support
constraints: Based on a longitudinal correlational path analysis of 146 Italian third graders; intervention effectiveness was not directly tested in this study
target_learners: primary school children (grades 3–4) with math difficulties
target_learning_goals: math achievement
emotional regulation of math anxiety
examples: The study found anxiety impaired math attainment from an early age via WM, with MA's role emerging later, motivating combined early intervention
key_sources: Pellizzoni, S., Cargnelutti, E., Cuder, A., & Passolunghi, M.C. (2021). The interplay between math anxiety and working memory on math performance: a longitudinal study. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1111/nyas.14722

article_title: Episodic memory contributions to autobiographical memory and open-ended problem-solving specificity in younger and older adults
citation: Peters, S. L., Fan, C. L., & Sheldon, S. (2019). Episodic memory contributions to autobiographical memory and open-ended problem-solving specificity in younger and older adults. Memory & Cognition, 47, 1592–1605. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-019-00953-1
title: Constructive episodic simulation hypothesis: episodic memory processes support both remembering and imagining hypothetical solutions
description: The constructive episodic simulation hypothesis holds that "episodic memory processes – that are affected by aging – are required to construct both past and hypothetical future events by accessing and associating together autobiographical details into a coherent mental representation" (Schacter & Addis). The article uses this framework to interpret age-related declines in both detail elaboration and event generation across memory and problem-solving tasks.
requirements: Episodic memory processes must be intact for constructing detailed representations of past and hypothetical events
constraints: The article notes executive processes also contribute, particularly to generation, and the study did not include executive function measures
target_learning_goals: autobiographical memory retrieval
open-ended problem solving
key_sources: Peters, S. L., Fan, C. L., & Sheldon, S. (2019). Episodic memory contributions to autobiographical memory and open-ended problem-solving specificity in younger and older adults. Memory & Cognition, 47, 1592–1605. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-019-00953-1

article_title: What explains the link between childhood ADHD and adolescent depression? Investigating the role of peer relationships and academic attainment
citation: Powell V, Riglin L, Hammerton G, Eyre O, Martin J, Anney R, Thapar A, Rice F. (2020). What explains the link between childhood ADHD and adolescent depression? Investigating the role of peer relationships and academic attainment. European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-019-01463-w
title: Competency-based failure model: struggles with peers and academics confer depression risk
description: The article draws on theories suggesting that a child's sense of competency or failure in peer and academic domains is important in conferring later depression risk. The authors note that "young people who struggle in their school and social lives are more likely to experience feelings of failure and rejection, which leave them more vulnerable to depression and emotional problems". This framework motivated testing peer relationships and academic attainment as mediators between childhood ADHD and adolescent depression.
requirements: Longitudinal data with time-lags between exposure, mediator and outcome to test mediation
constraints: Mediators may represent person-effects on the environment, environment-effects on the person, or both; shared genetic liability cannot be ruled out
target_learning_goals: understanding pathways to adolescent depression
examples: The hypothesised mediation model (Fig. 1) positioned peer relationships and academic attainment at 16 years between childhood ADHD and adolescent depression
