Investigating the role of peer relationships and academic attainment. European Child & Adolescent Psychiatry. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00787-019-01463-w

article_title: Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults
citation: Rogge, A.-K., Röder, B., Zech, A., Nagel, V., Hollander, K., Braumann, K.-M. & Hötting, K. (2017). Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults. Scientific Reports 7:5661. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06071-9
title: Physical exercise programs can improve cognition without increasing cardiorespiratory fitness
description: The article concludes that "an increase in cardiorespiratory fitness does not seem to be necessary to induce beneficial effects of physical exercise on cognition". Twelve weeks of balance training improved memory and spatial cognition while VO2peak remained unchanged in both groups, implying multiple mechanisms mediate exercise effects on cognition. This supports prescribing non-aerobic exercise forms for cognitive benefits.
requirements: Exercise form must plausibly engage other physiological systems (here the vestibular system) since fitness gains are not the mediating route
constraints: Demonstrated for balance versus relaxation training in healthy adults; executive functions were unaffected, so benefits may be restricted to memory and spatial functioning
target_learners: individuals unable to participate in aerobic training due to health restrictions
target_learning_goals: memory improvement
spatial cognition
examples: The randomized trial compared 12 weeks of balance circuit training against relaxation training, with neither group changing VO2peak
key_sources: Rogge, A.-K., Röder, B., Zech, A., Nagel, V., Hollander, K., Braumann, K.-M. & Hötting, K. (2017). Balance training improves memory and spatial cognition in healthy adults. Scientific Reports 7:5661. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-06071-9

article_title: Acute stress impairs cognitive flexibility in men, not women
citation: Shields Grant S., Trainor Brian C., Lam Jovian C. W., Yonelinas Andrew P. (2016). Acute Stress Impairs Cognitive Flexibility in Men, Not Women. Stress. https://doi.org/10.1080/10253890.2016.1192603
title: Consider sex as a moderating factor when studying or designing for stress effects on cognition
description: The article argues that stress research and application should not presume males and females respond alike: "stress should not be presumed to influence males and females similarly". Its randomized experiment found stress impaired cognitive flexibility in men but not women, supporting routine analysis of sex as a moderator. The authors also suggest women "may be more suited to high-stress environments requiring cognitive flexibility than men", offered as a tentative implication.
requirements: Studies or design decisions about stress and cognition must record and analyze participant sex rather than assuming uniform stress effects.
constraints: The evidence base is a single acute-stress experiment with undergraduate participants; the article states it is unknown whether chronic stress or nonstudent populations would show the same sex-specific pattern.
target_learners: adult learners in high-stress performance settings
target_learning_goals: maintaining cognitive flexibility under acute stress
examples: 113 healthy adults were randomly assigned to the TSST-G stress induction or a reading/counting control task, then completed the Berg Card Sorting Test.
key_sources: Shields Grant S., Trainor Brian C., Lam Jovian C. W., Yonelinas Andrew P. (2016). Acute Stress Impairs Cognitive Flexibility in Men, Not Women. Stress. https://doi.org/10.1080/10253890.2016.1192603

article_title: The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A Critical Review
citation: Reid Smith, Pamela Snow, Tanya Serry & Lorraine Hammond (2021) The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A Critical Review, Reading Psychology, 42:3, 214-240, https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2021.1888348
title: Construction-Integration model of reading comprehension (textbase and situation model)
description: The review adopts the Construction-Integration model (Kintsch, 1998; Kintsch & Van Dijk, 1978), in which reading comprises interactions between the literal, propositional representation of a text (the textbase) and a schema formed from background knowledge. The textbase is held in working memory and integrated with preexisting schemata in long-term memory to form a situation model, a dynamically constructed representation that is cumulative and changes through growth, reorganization and error correction. The review uses this framework to interpret differential effects of knowledge on skilled vs. low-skilled readers.
requirements: Working memory must not be too heavily burdened for integration to occur
constraints: Low-skilled readers typically construct less detailed situation models due to less coherent textbase and/or less well-formed schemata
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension of extended texts
key_sources: Reid Smith, Pamela Snow, Tanya Serry & Lorraine Hammond (2021) The Role of Background Knowledge in Reading Comprehension: A Critical Review, Reading Psychology, 42:3, 214-240, https://doi.org/10.1080/02702711.2021.1888348

article_title: Age-Related Changes in Sentence Production Abilities and Their Relation to Working-Memory Capacity: Evidence from a Verb-Final Language
citation: Sung JE (2015) Age-Related Changes in Sentence Production Abilities and Their Relation to Working-Memory Capacity: Evidence from a Verb-Final Language. PLoS ONE 10(4): e0119424. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0119424
title: Constrained sentence-production tasks with limited color vocabulary (syntactic-priming and sentence-completion tasks)
description: Two novel controlled production instruments for eliciting Korean passive sentences. The syntactic-priming task presents a two-part picture; the examiner describes the prime and the participant produces a target sentence after hearing a primed passive. The sentence-completion task provides the nouns and verb on the picture, with the examiner initiating the first noun phrase. Both use humanized color symbols ("the Red," "the Blue," and "the Yellow") as arguments to control lexical-semantic influence, with 40 stimuli total (20 per task, 10 per canonicity condition).
requirements: Responses are coded correct only when participants construct a passive with correct grammatical markers and verb inflection; using an active voice counts as an error
constraints: Designed to focus only on syntactic features by minimizing semantic-lexical top-down processing, so they do not sample spontaneous or semantically rich production
target_learners: adult Korean speakers, including elderly adults
target_learning_goals: measuring passive-sentence production accuracy
isolating syntactic planning from lexical-semantic processing
examples: Each task was administered as a block with canonical and noncanonical sentences randomly presented, and task order counterbalanced across participants
key_sources: Sung JE (2015) Age-Related Changes in Sentence Production Abilities and Their Relation to Working-Memory Capacity: Evidence from a Verb-Final Language. PLoS ONE 10(4): e0119424. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0119424

article_title: Examining the Relationships of Component Reading Skills to Reading Comprehension in Struggling Adult Readers
citation: Tighe, Elizabeth L.; Schatschneider, Christopher. (2016). Examining the Relationships of Component Reading Skills to Reading Comprehension in Struggling Adult Readers: A Meta-Analysis. Journal of Learning Disabilities. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219414555415
title: Assess and instruct component reading skills, not just global reading measures, in adult literacy programs
description: The article argues that ABE programs should move beyond global reading measures when evaluating and instructing adult learners. It states that global assessments "do not assess component skills" and "provide very limited reading skill profiles of adult learners," and that the identified strong and moderate component skills "should be considered during instructional practices and targeted in intervention and assessment research."
requirements: Component skill measures must be available alongside the global assessments currently used for grade-level equivalency placement.
constraints: The evidence base is limited to 16 studies with high heterogeneity, so the authors advise cautious interpretation.
target_learners: struggling adult readers in Adult Basic Education programs
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
examples: The meta-analysis identified six strongly and three moderately related component skills as candidates for instruction and assessment in ABE settings.

article_title: Family ethnic socialization and ethnic identity: A family-driven, youth-driven, or reciprocal process?
citation: Umaña-Taylor Adriana J., Zeiders Katharine H., Updegraff Kimberly A. (2013). Family Ethnic Socialization and Ethnic Identity: A Family-Driven, Youth-Driven, or Reciprocal Process? Journal of Family Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031105
title: Family ethnic socialization and youth ethnic identity form a context-sensitive developmental process whose direction depends on family nativity status
description: This framework, grounded in ecological theory (Bronfenbrenner, 1989) and Spencer's PVEST, holds that the direction of effects between family ethnic socialization and youth ethnic identity is not fixed but depends on cultural context, specifically the immigrant status of the family. The article states that 'the association between family ethnic socialization and ethnic identity is context sensitive, with family nativity status being a critical factor that must be considered when determining the stages at which youth and parent forces are most pronounced in this process.' This challenges the implied directional bias in prior work that treated the process as exclusively family-driven.
requirements: Longitudinal data with repeated measures of both family ethnic socialization and youth ethnic identity to test directional paths
constraints: Findings are specific to Mexican-origin youth transitioning from late adolescence to emerging adulthood and based on youths' perceptions of family ethnic socialization
target_learners: Mexican-origin and Latino adolescents and emerging adults
target_learning_goals: Understanding how family ethnic socialization and youth ethnic identity inform one another during development
examples: The study tested three competing models (family-driven, youth-driven, reciprocal) using multiple-group cross-lagged panel analyses across nativity groups
key_sources: Umaña-Taylor Adriana J., Zeiders Katharine H., Updegraff Kimberly A. (2013). Family Ethnic Socialization and Ethnic Identity: A Family-Driven, Youth-Driven, or Reciprocal Process? Journal of Family Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0031105

article_title: Chronic Stereotype Threat Is Associated With Mathematical Achievement on Representative Sample of Secondary Schoolgirls: The Role of Gender Identification, Working Memory, and Intellectual Helplessness
citation: Bedyńska S, Krejtz I and Sedek G (2018) Chronic Stereotype Threat Is Associated With Mathematical Achievement on Representative Sample of Secondary Schoolgirls: The Role of Gender Identification, Working Memory, and Intellectual Helplessness. Front. Psychol. 9:428. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.00428
title: Cognitive exhaustion model of learned helplessness applied to chronic stereotype threat
description: The article proposes a new mechanism by which chronic stereotype threat decreases school achievement, namely intellectual helplessness. It assumes that "repeated experience of stereotype threat works as intellectual helplessness training." After the phase of cognitive mobilization, cognitive exhaustion appears because the individual has no gain from intense cognitive effort. This integrates motivational and cognitive processes as two phases: mobilization and cognitive exhaustion.
requirements: Repeated experience of stereotype threat in a domain such as mathematics
constraints: The mechanism was tested in a cross-sectional design with secondary schoolgirls
target_learning_goals: mathematical achievement
examples: The study measured chronic stereotype threat, intellectual helplessness, and working memory functions in a representative sample of secondary schoolgirls
key_sources: Bedyńska S, Krejtz I and Sedek G (2018) Chronic Stereotype Threat Is Associated With Mathematical Achievement on Representative Sample of Secondary Schoolgirls: The Role of Gender Identification, Working Memory, and Intellectual Helplessness. Front. Psychol. 9:428. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.00428

article_title: Associations between preschool language and first grade reading outcomes in bilingual children
citation: Davison, Megan Dunn; Hammer, Carol; Lawrence, Frank R. (2011). Associations between Preschool Language and First Grade Reading Outcomes in Bilingual Children. Journal of Communication Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3138808/
title: Common Underlying Proficiency (CUP) model of bilingual language and literacy development
description: The CUP model, proposed by Cummins, holds that bilingual children's experience with either language promotes a shared proficiency underlying both languages, which in turn supports literacy in each. The article states that "experience with either language can promote development of the proficiency underlying both languages, given adequate motivation and exposure to both either in school or in the wider environment." This study's cross-language findings—English language growth predicting Spanish reading and vice versa—are presented as empirical support for the model. McSwan and Rolstad's refinement holds that both languages access the same store of knowledge, so transfer occurs as a natural consequence of mental architecture rather than as movement between languages.
requirements: Children need adequate motivation and exposure to both languages for experience in either to promote the shared underlying proficiency
constraints: The article notes application of the CUP model to bilingual preschoolers and later reading outcomes had received relatively little attention before this study
target_learners: bilingual preschool children developing two languages simultaneously
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension and word identification in both first and second language
examples: The study's finding that growth in English receptive language predicted Spanish reading outcomes and Spanish growth predicted English reading outcomes is presented as evidence for the CUP model
key_sources: Davison, Megan Dunn; Hammer, Carol; Lawrence, Frank R. (2011). Associations between Preschool Language and First Grade Reading Outcomes in Bilingual Children. Journal of Communication Disorders. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3138808/

article_title: Development of Metacognition in Adolescence: The Congruency-Based Metacognition Scale
citation: dos Santos Kawata KH, Ueno Y, Hashimoto R, Yoshino S, Ohta K, Nishida A, Ando S, Nakatani H, Kasai K and Koike S (2021) Development of Metacognition in Adolescence: The Congruency-Based Metacognition Scale. Front. Psychol. 11:565231. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.565231
title: The Congruency-based Metacognition Scale (CMS)
description: The CMS is a questionnaire measuring metacognitive ability and self-judgment accuracy in children and adolescents through perspective-taking congruency. The CMS metacognition score is computed as the sum of absolute differences between the child's third-person-perspective self-report (3PP_Self, e.g., "Does your mother/father think you are kind?") and the parent's first-person-perspective report (1PP_Other, e.g., "Do you think your son/daughter is kind?"). The self-judgment accuracy score is the sum of absolute differences between the child's 1PP_Self and 3PP_Self reports. Lower scores indicate greater capacity on both measures. The scale uses 20 trait adjectives (10 positive, 10 negative) rated on a four-point Likert scale.
requirements: Requires paired child-parent responses: the child completes 1PP_Self and 3PP_Self conditions while the parent completes the 1PP_Other condition
Uses 20 familiar personality-trait adjectives counterbalanced between positive and negative words, rated on a four-point Likert-type scale
constraints: The majority of "other/parents" were represented by maternal rather than paternal figures
The questionnaire may be more reliable for measuring for adolescents, as the sample of children over age 22 was small
target_learners: children and adolescents (age range 10.8-29.3 years in the validation sample)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive ability (awareness and understanding of one's own cognitive status)
self-judgment accuracy
examples: Administered to 633 child-parent pairs across three surveys in Tokyo prefecture between September 2013 and January 2020
key_sources: dos Santos Kawata KH, Ueno Y, Hashimoto R, Yoshino S, Ohta K, Nishida A, Ando S, Nakatani H, Kasai K and Koike S (2021) Development of Metacognition in Adolescence: The Congruency-Based Metacognition Scale. Front. Psychol. 11:565231. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.565231

article_title: Age and Verbal Fluency: The Mediating Effect of Speed of Processing
citation: Safa A. Elgamal, MBBCh, PhD, Eric A. Roy, PhD, Michael T. Sharratt, PhD. (2011). Age and Verbal Fluency: The Mediating Effect of Speed of Processing. Canadian Geriatrics Journal, Volume 14, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.5770/cgj.v14i3.17
title: Control for processing speed when interpreting similarly timed cognitive tasks across age groups
description: The article recommends that researchers and clinicians controlling for processing speed should be considered essential when interpreting results from similarly timed cognitive tasks, especially when the between-group variable suggests a possible effect for speed of performance. The study demonstrates why: apparent age effects on fluency depended on whether processing speed was controlled, with letter fluency differences emerging only after covariate adjustment. The authors argue that tasks measuring the same cognitive construct may employ different brain processes, so task psychological properties must be appreciated to avoid misinterpreting results.
requirements: Tasks that are similarly timed across comparison groups
A between-group variable that suggests a possible effect for speed of performance
constraints: The article frames this for similarly timed cognitive tasks; it does not claim the recommendation extends to untimed measures
target_learners: healthy adults across the adult lifespan
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of age-related differences in verbal fluency and other timed cognitive measures
examples: The study's ANCOVA models revealed significant letter fluency differences between age groups that the initial ANOVA had not shown, after controlling for the processing speed composite and NART-estimated IQ
key_sources: Safa A. Elgamal, MBBCh, PhD, Eric A. Roy, PhD, Michael T. Sharratt, PhD. (2011). Age and Verbal Fluency: The Mediating Effect of Speed of Processing. Canadian Geriatrics Journal, Volume 14, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.5770/cgj.v14i3.17

article_title: High Cognitive Flexibility Learners Perform Better in Probabilistic Rule Learning
citation: Feng X, Perceval GJ, Feng W and Feng C (2020) High Cognitive Flexibility Learners Perform Better in Probabilistic Rule Learning. Front. Psychol. 11:415. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00415
title: Cognitive flexibility as the ability to switch quickly between tasks and stimulus sets, measured by switch cost
description: The article adopts the understanding that cognitive flexibility refers to "the ability of switching between tasks and stimulus sets in a quick and ﬂexible manner". It operationalizes this construct with the number-letter task, in which the latency difference between switching and non-switching trials is the switch cost, and uses switch cost to divide learners into high and low flexibility groups. The article notes there is still no clear common definition of cognitive flexibility, which influences how the construct is operationalized.
requirements: Measurement requires a task-switching paradigm such as the number-letter task from which a switch cost can be computed; the article argues task-switching paradigms give a purer measure than the WCST by reducing demands for working memory, classified learning and rule reasoning.
constraints: The article states there is still no clear common definition of cognitive flexibility, which can influence how the construct is operationalized in research.
target_learning_goals: probabilistic rule learning and rule-based decision making
examples: Participants were ranked by switch cost on the number-letter task; the lower 27th percentile formed the high flexibility group and the upper 27th percentile the low flexibility group.
key_sources: Feng X, Perceval GJ, Feng W and Feng C (2020) High Cognitive Flexibility Learners Perform Better in Probabilistic Rule Learning. Front. Psychol. 11:415. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00415

article_title: Stroop task performance across the lifespan: High cognitive reserve in older age is associated with enhanced proactive and reactive interference control
citation: Patrick D. Gajewski, Michael Falkenstein, Sven Th€ones, Edmund Wascher. (2020). Stroop task performance across the lifespan: High cognitive reserve in older age is associated with enhanced proactive and reactive interference control. NeuroImage 207 (2020) 116430. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2019.116430
title: Cognitive reserve as inter-individual differences in neural networks underlying task performance
description: The article adopts the notion of cognitive reserve, which "postulates that inter-individual differences in neural networks underlying task performance allow some people to perform better than others". Reserve accrues from interactions between genetics and environmental factors such as education, physical activity, use of foreign languages, playing an instrument or dancing, skills mediated by neuronal plasticity. High reserve allows compensation for cognitive decline and dementia in older age. The study operationalizes reserve proxies as IQ, education level and foreign language usage, and interprets the enhanced CNV and P2/N2 amplitudes of old high performers as the electrophysiological underpinning of reserve in terms of efficiency, capacity or flexibility.
requirements: Environmental or lifestyle factors that stimulate neuronal plasticity, such as education or cognitively stimulating activities
constraints: The article states inter- and intra-individual differences accrue from complex interactions between genetics and environmental factors, representing widely stable individual properties in old age
target_learning_goals: maintaining executive function and interference control in aging
examples: Old participants were subdivided into low, mid and high performers via inverse efficiency scores, validated against drift-diffusion-model drift rates (r = -.846)

Stroop task performance across the lifespan: High cognitive reserve in older age is associated with enhanced proactive and reactive interference control. article_title: The structure of working memory in young children and its relation to intelligence
citation: Gray Shelley, Green Samuel, Alt Mary, Hogan Tiffany P., Kuo Trudy, Brinkley Shara, Cowan Nelson. (2016). The Structure of Working Memory in Young Children and Its Relation to Intelligence. Journal of Memory and Language. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5157932/
title: Cowan's embedded processes model of working memory with central executive, focus of attention, and phonological storage-and-rehearsal factors
description: Cowan's embedded processes model treats working memory as including all components used to hold information temporarily, with "the temporarily activated portion of long-term memory" at its core and, within it, a focus of attention holding several highly processed integrated items at once. The model specifies three factors: central executive, focus of attention, and phonological storage-and-rehearsal. Verbal rehearsal can make maintenance somewhat automatic and less reliant on attention, while nonverbal information that cannot easily be rehearsed requires more attention for maintenance. This study operationalized the model with 13 tasks and found it fit young children's data best.
requirements: Requires tasks that distinguish attention-dependent storage from rehearsal-supported phonological storage, such as running span tasks with unpredictable endpoints
constraints: Verbal rehearsal reduces reliance on the focus of attention only in children old enough, older than about 7 years, to begin rehearsing simple verbal stimuli
target_learners: young school-age children aged 7-9 with typical development
target_learning_goals: understanding the structure of working memory as it supports learning and assessment of working memory components
examples: The study specified the model with central executive tasks (n-back auditory and visual, number updating), focus of attention indicators including digit span running and binding tasks, and phonological storage tasks (digit span, nonword repetition)
key_sources: Gray Shelley, Green Samuel, Alt Mary, Hogan Tiffany P., Kuo Trudy, Brinkley Shara, Cowan Nelson. (2016). The Structure of Working Memory in Young Children and Its Relation to Intelligence. Journal of Memory and Language. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5157932/

article_title: A Randomized Control Study of Instructional Approaches for Struggling Adult Readers
citation: Greenberg Daphne, Wise Justin, Morris Robin, Fredrick Laura, Nanda Alice O., Pae Hye-K. (2011). A randomized control study of instructional approaches for struggling adult readers. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3237050/
title: SRA/McGraw-Hill Direct Instruction Corrective Reading program adapted for struggling adult readers
description: The Corrective Reading program is the explicit instructional intervention used in the DF, DCF, and DCEF conditions. In the Decoding component, "students learned skills such as phonemic relationships, new sound combinations, word endings and letter and sound combinations." In the Comprehension component, students learned to organize related facts and use analogies, classifications, deductions, inductions, descriptions, conclusions, contradictions, and written directions. Placement tests assigned students to levels: 94% started in Decoding B2 and 6% in Decoding B1; 85% started in Comprehension B1 and 15% in Comprehension A. The program includes frequent mastery tests and decision rules for providing additional instruction.
requirements: Instructor scripts, placement tests, mastery tests, and decision rules; teachers received one week of training plus coaching observations five times during the year
constraints: The authors state the programs are based on what is known about remediation for children and question whether that knowledge completely applies to struggling adult readers
target_learners: Adults reading single words at 3.0–5.9 grade equivalency
target_learning_goals: Decoding and comprehension skills
examples: Average decoding lessons completed: 35.88 in DCEF, 47.75 in DCF, and 75.37 in DF; comprehension lessons: 30.88 in DCEF and 33.85 in DCF

article_title: Life-span changes to adults' language: Effects of memory and genre
citation: Kemper, S., Kynette, D., Rash, S., O'Brien, K., & Sprott, R. (1989). Life-span changes to adults' language: Effects of memory and genre. Applied Psycholinguistics, 10, 49-66. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400008419
title: Trade-off between syntactic complexity and clarity/interest of prose in adult language production
description: The article proposes that producing complex syntactic structures competes with producing clear and interesting prose. Elderly adults lost left-branching clauses and showed reduced complexity, yet judges found their statements "more interesting and clearer than those from the young adults." The authors treat this pattern as evidence that syntactic elaboration and communicative clarity trade off in adult language production.
requirements: Language samples from speakers of different ages or ability levels
Ratings or judgments of clarity and interest alongside syntactic complexity measures
constraints: The trade-off is the authors' interpretation of the rating and complexity patterns, not a directly tested mechanism
target_learning_goals: oral and written expression
syntactic complexity in language production
examples: Elderly adults' written and oral statements were rated more interesting and clearer despite lower syntactic complexity

article_title: Promoting a Sense of Belonging in Online Learning Communities of Inquiry
citation: Peacock, S., & Cowan, J. (2019). Promoting a Sense of Belonging in Online Learning Communities of Inquiry. Online Learning, 23(2). https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v23i2.1488
title: Adapted Community of Inquiry Framework organised around three overlapping Influences: Trusting, Meaning-making and Deepening understanding
description: The article adapts the well-known Community of Inquiry Framework, shifting attention from the three Presences to their overlapping intersections, which the authors entitle Influences. As the abstract states, "This revision of the well-known Framework focuses upon the overlapping intersections of the three Presences, entitled Influences: 'Trusting', 'Meaning-making' and 'Deepening understanding'." Each Influence is treated as a locus of tutor facilitative activity through which online learners' sense of belonging can be nurtured, with guidance and examples offered for each.
requirements: Tutors must treat the Influences as overlapping intersections of the three Presences rather than as separate categories
constraints: The framework is framed specifically for online learning communities of inquiry
target_learning_goals: nurturing online learners' sense of belonging to promote and consolidate learning
examples: For each Influence, guidance illustrated by examples is offered, leading to particular suggestions for the online tutor's facilitative activities
key_sources: Peacock, S., & Cowan, J. (2019). Promoting a Sense of Belonging in Online Learning Communities of Inquiry. Online Learning, 23(2). https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v23i2.1488

article_title: Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity
citation: Preiss David D. (2022). Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9500634/
title: Framework: managing the interaction between metacognition and mind wandering is the main role of cognitive flexibility in creativity
description: The article advances a general framework in which cognitive flexibility during the creative process involves a strategic use of mind wandering by means of metacognitive regulation. Creators alternate between spontaneous cognition, which feeds originality during idea generation, and controlled cognition, which feeds appropriateness during idea evaluation. The author states that "managing the interaction between metacognition and mind wandering is the main role of cognitive flexibility in creativity" and that balancing metacognition during generation and exploration of pre-inventive structures is a quintessential part of creativity. The framework applies specifically to creative production involving generation and exploration of ideas, not to trial-and-error or serendipity.
requirements: Applies only to creative production involving generation and exploration of ideas
constraints: Does not fit cases involving trial-and-error or serendipity, which the author notes do not fit this conception very well
target_learning_goals: understanding the role of cognitive flexibility in creative processes
managing attention and metacognition during idea generation and evaluation
examples: Figure 1 summarizes the process of alternating between spontaneous and controlled cognition across idea generation and idea evaluation
key_sources: Preiss David D. (2022). Metacognition, Mind Wandering, and Cognitive Flexibility: Understanding Creativity. Journal of Intelligence. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9500634/

article_title: Being right is its own reward: Load and performance related ventral striatum activation to correct responses during a working memory task in youth
citation: Satterthwaite Theodore D. M.D., M.A.; Ruparel Kosha M.S.; Loughead James Ph.D; Elliott Mark A. Ph.D.; Gerraty Raphael T. B.A.; Calkins Monica E. Ph.D.; Hakonarson Hakon M.D. Ph.D.; Gur Ruben C. Ph.D.; Gur Raquel E. M.D., Ph.D.; Wolf Daniel H. M.D., Ph.D. (2012). Being Right Is Its Own Reward: Load and Performance Related Ventral Striatum Activation to Correct Responses During a Working Memory Task in Youth. Neuroimage. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3358426/
title: Account for developmental differences in in-scanner motion when analyzing youth neuroimaging data
description: The article demonstrates that age and in-scanner head motion remain related even after excluding subjects with gross motion, which can systematically bias developmental neuroimaging results. The authors "re-conducted both the across-level voxelwise analysis and the between-level VS ROI analysis including mean relative displacement as a confound variable in the models" to verify results were unchanged. This practice guards against mistaking motion-related artifacts for developmental effects.
requirements: Measuring mean relative displacement for each subject
Including motion as a confound variable in group-level models when age and motion are correlated
constraints: Even after excluding subjects with gross in-scanner motion, age and motion remained significantly related (r=−0.35)
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of brain activation differences across development
examples: The authors excluded 29 subjects for excessive motion (relative mean displacement >0.5mm or relative maximum displacement >6mm) and then re-ran analyses with motion as a confound

article_title: Sleep Patterns and School Readiness of Pre-Kindergarteners from Racially and Ethnically Diverse, Low-Income Backgrounds
citation: Turnbull Khara L. P. PhD; Mateus Deiby Mayaris Cubides; LoCasale-Crouch Jennifer PhD; Lewin Daniel S. Ph.D., D.ABSM; CBSM; Williford Amanda P. PhD. (2022). Sleep Patterns and School Readiness of Pre-Kindergarteners from Racially/Ethnically Diverse, Low-Income Backgrounds: A Secondary Data Analysis. The Journal of Pediatrics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10621568/
title: Consistent sleep routines and more optimal sleep health may serve as a protective mechanism for language, social-emotional-behavioral regulation, and approaches to learning of low-income pre-kindergarteners
description: This principle holds that predictable, consistent morning and bedtime routines and more optimal sleep health support school readiness development in children from low-income backgrounds, regardless of family income level. The article states "Consistent sleep routines and more optimal sleep health may serve as a protective mechanism for the language development, social-emotional-behavioral regulation and approaches to learning of pre-kindergarteners from racially/ethnically diverse, low-income backgrounds." It is grounded in the study's latent class and regression findings linking the earlier, longer, consistent class to stronger expressive vocabulary, emotion regulation, assertiveness, and approaches to learning.
requirements: Requires parent-reported sleep health information covering timing, nighttime sleep duration, and sleep-related behaviors
constraints: The overarching study design does not permit causal inference
Results are not generalizable beyond the study sample
Naps were not measured in a way that would permit calculating total 24-hour sleep duration
target_learners: Pre-kindergarteners from racially/ethnically diverse, low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Language development
Social-emotional-behavioral regulation
Approaches to learning
examples: Latent class analysis identified an earlier, longer, consistent sleep health class comprising 87% of the sample, whose members had earlier bedtimes, longer nighttime sleep, more consistent routines, and less pre-bedtime caffeine

article_title: Auditory Processing in Noise: A Preschool Biomarker for Literacy
citation: White-Schwoch T, Woodruff Carr K, Thompson EC, Anderson S, Nicol T, Bradlow AR, et al. (2015) Auditory Processing in Noise: A Preschool Biomarker for Literacy. PLoS Biol 13(7): e1002196. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1002196
title: Consonants-in-noise neural coding biomarker framework: timing, stability, and spectral-feature measures of the frequency-following response index literacy-relevant auditory precision
description: The article proposes that the precision of subcortical neural coding of speech in noise, measured with the frequency-following response (FFR, also called cABR), underlies language and reading development. It combines three measures from a single recording — "trial-by-trial stability, neural timing, and representation of spectral features that convey phonemic identity" — into a consonants-in-noise score. The framework holds that background noise taxes neural synchrony, so children with poor processing in noise may lag in language development, and that this brain–behavior link precedes reading instruction.
requirements: A standardized FFR recording paradigm: a 170 ms [da] syllable presented against six-talker babble at +10 SNR, with timing, stability, and spectral measures extracted blind to behavioral performance
constraints: The authors state the mechanistic account of inhibitory function and corticocollicular circuitry is speculative: "we must infer midbrain function from far-field electrophysiological recordings"; replication in a larger sample is stated as necessary
target_learners: preschool children ages 3–5 who have not yet learned to read
target_learning_goals: phonological processing
emergent literacy and reading achievement
examples: The framework was operationalized as a regression model whose predictions were applied unchanged to new cohorts in Experiments 2–4.
key_sources: White-Schwoch T, Woodruff Carr K, Thompson EC, Anderson S, Nicol T, Bradlow AR, et al. (2015) Auditory Processing in Noise: A Preschool Biomarker for Literacy. PLoS Biol 13(7): e1002196. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.1002196

article_title: The Neural Development of an Abstract Concept of Number
citation: Cantlon Jessica F., Libertus Melissa E., Pinel Philippe, Dehaene Stanislas, Brannon Elizabeth M., Pelphrey Kevin A. (2009). The Neural Development of an Abstract Concept of Number. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn.2008.21159
title: A core notation-independent neural system for number with developmental frontal mediation
description: The article proposes that "a core neural system integrates notation-independent numerical representations throughout development but, early in development, higher-order brain mechanisms mediate this process." Drawing on primate single-cell work and computational modeling, it suggests "children recruit inferior frontal cortex at an early stage of development to form associations among numerical values at a notation-independent level of abstraction," with parietal cortex becoming the automatic substrate in adulthood. The IFG's role may be domain-general (cognitive control) or task-specific (forming abstract numerical categories).
requirements: Requires an initial period of associative learning between symbolic and nonsymbolic numerical representations, per the modeling studies the article cites
constraints: The article states the precise role of inferior frontal cortex in notation-independent numerical processing cannot be determined by its data alone
The study did not address the specificity of cortical regions for numerical processing
target_learning_goals: abstract, notation-independent understanding of numerical values
symbolic number learning (Arabic numerals)
examples: Children showed a positive IFG response to both notations, a robust numerical ratio effect, and a strong correlation with behavioral performance, whereas adults showed no above-baseline IFG activity
key_sources: Cantlon Jessica F., Libertus Melissa E., Pinel Philippe, Dehaene Stanislas, Brannon Elizabeth M., Pelphrey Kevin A. (2009). The Neural Development of an Abstract Concept of Number. Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1162/jocn.2008.21159

article_title: Defective number module or impaired access? Numerical magnitude processing in first graders with mathematical difficulties
citation: Bert De Smedt, Camilla K. Gilmore. (2011). Defective number module or impaired access? Numerical magnitude processing in first graders with mathematical difficulties. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 108, 278–292. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2010.09.003
title: Teaching should provide rich opportunities to connect symbols with the quantities they represent
description: Because children with mathematical difficulties are impaired in accessing numerical meaning from symbols, the authors recommend that teaching and intervention "provide plenty of opportunities where children learn to connect symbols and the quantities they represent in rich and meaningful ways." They cite Number Worlds (Griffin, 2004) as a program developed to teach this, and linear number board games (Ramani & Siegler, 2008) as providing multimodal cues linking symbols to quantities.
requirements: Interventions must target the mapping between symbols and quantities rather than numerosity representation per se
constraints: Generalization of board-game findings to children with mathematical difficulties needs further investigation, as the authors note
target_learners: first graders and kindergarteners, particularly children with mathematical difficulties or from low-income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: connecting Arabic numerals to the quantities they represent
numerical magnitude understanding
early arithmetic development
examples: The article cites Ramani and Siegler (2008) showing linear board games enhanced numerical magnitude understanding in kindergarteners from low-income backgrounds, and Booth and Siegler (2008) showing accurate visual number-line representations improved first graders' math learning.
key_sources: Bert De Smedt, Camilla K. Gilmore. (2011). Defective number module or impaired access? Numerical magnitude processing in first graders with mathematical difficulties. Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, 108, 278–292. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jecp.2010.09.003

article_title: Some types of parent number talk count more than others: relations between parents’ input and children’s cardinal-number knowledge
citation: Gunderson Elizabeth A., Levine Susan C. (2011). Some types of parent number talk count more than others: Relations between parents' input and children's cardinal-number knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2011.01050.x
title: Encourage parents of preschoolers to count and label not only small sets but also larger sets (4–10) of present, visible objects
description: The article's policy discussion recommends that, if experimental studies corroborate its findings, parents be encouraged to engage in counting and labeling "not only very small sets of objects but also somewhat larger sets of objects," because such talk may help children figure out the relationship between counting and the cardinal meanings of number words. It notes parents often overestimate children's numerical knowledge and are unsure how to promote early mathematics, and that unlike literacy there has been no concerted effort to inform parents about supportive numerical interactions.
requirements: Experimental corroboration of the correlational findings before making firm recommendations, as the article itself stipulates
constraints: The current evidence is correlational; the authors state controlled experimental studies are critical before concluding causality
target_learning_goals: early number knowledge, especially the cardinal principle
examples: In the study, large-set present-object talk was rare (8.3 percent of number talk instances) yet accounted for 15.7 percent of variance in cardinal knowledge over and above SES
key_sources: Gunderson Elizabeth A., Levine Susan C. (2011). Some types of parent number talk count more than others: Relations between parents' input and children's cardinal-number knowledge. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-7687.2011.01050.x

article_title: The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students
citation: Lewallen TC, Hunt H, Potts-Datema W, Zaza S, Giles W. (2015). The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12310
title: Coordinate policy, process, and practice—with administrator support—when integrating learning and health in schools
description: The WSCC model makes coordination of policy, process, and practice an explicit ring around the student, because prior approaches did not describe these facilitative factors. The article states that "The key to moving from model to action is collaborative development of local school policies, processes, and practices," and that district and school wellness teams working closely with the school administrator combine both sectors' goals most effectively. It recommends starting from a common understanding of the interrelatedness of learning and health.
requirements: Administrator support, particularly principals; joint collaborative policy development followed by implementation into routine practice
constraints: Without coordination, policies, practices, and processes in place, the model would not be effective in achieving its intended outcomes (consultation team observation)
target_learners: K-12 students in schools and districts implementing the model
target_learning_goals: Integration of learning and health outcomes through coordinated school policies, practices, and processes
examples: The consultation team observed that CSH efforts succeeded when viewed as integral to the school's mission and when wellness teams worked with the school administrator
key_sources: Lewallen TC, Hunt H, Potts-Datema W, Zaza S, Giles W. (2015). The Whole School, Whole Community, Whole Child Model: A New Approach for Improving Educational Attainment and Healthy Development for Students. Journal of School Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/josh.12310

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives
citation: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8
title: Cognitive load theory: instructional control of working memory load based on the human cognitive architecture
description: CLT is concerned with learning complex cognitive tasks in which learners are overwhelmed by interactive information elements. It uses knowledge of human cognitive architecture — an effectively unlimited long-term memory interacting with a working memory that is "very limited in both capacity and duration" — to generate instructional techniques. Instructional control of excessively high load imposed by complex tasks provides the theory's focus.
requirements: Instruction must be structured around the characteristics of working memory, since WM processes information before it can be stored in long-term memory
constraints: The theory concerns complex cognitive tasks where learners are often overwhelmed by the number of interactive information elements
target_learning_goals: schema acquisition in long-term memory
complex problem-solving skill
examples: The article cites worked-example study, part-whole task simplification, task variability, and self-explanation as CLT-generated instructional techniques
key_sources: Fred Paas, Tamara van Gog, John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: New Conceptualizations, Specifications, and Integrated Research Perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 115-121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9133-8

article_title: Sixth-grade students’ reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis
citation: Maike Schindler, Stephan Hußmann, Per Nilsson, Arthur Bakker. (2017). Sixth-grade students' reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis. Math Ed Res J 29:471–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13394-017-0202-x
title: Design lesson series on negative numbers around a rich out-of-school context plus the number line as origins for students' inferences
description: From an inferentialist perspective, the article argues learning environments should encourage students to be involved in the game of giving and asking for reasons, drawing on out-of-school experiences and relating reasoning to external representations. The debts-and-assets context is chosen because students have experiences with it and use it more often than temperatures or heights, while the number line serves as origin for inferences on the existence, position, and mathematically correct order of negative numbers.
requirements: A rich, authentic out-of-school context students have prior experience with, and extensive use of the number line as a model
constraints: Students' ability to use the number line depends on their prior experiences with the number line (citing Bruno 2001)
target_learners: sixth-grade students encountering negative numbers for the first time
target_learning_goals: reasoning on the order relation for integers
examples: The 'Out of the Debts' lesson series began with the board game, followed by problems inviting reflection on the account bar and the minus sign, with many activities practicing changing representations
key_sources: Maike Schindler, Stephan Hußmann, Per Nilsson, Arthur Bakker. (2017). Sixth-grade students' reasoning on the order relation of integers as influenced by prior experience: an inferentialist analysis. Math Ed Res J 29:471–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13394-017-0202-x

article_title: Learning multiplication: An integrated analysis of the multiplication ability of primary school children and the difficulty of single digit and multidigit multiplication problems
citation: S.H.G. van der Ven, M. Straatemeier, B.R.J. Jansen, S. Klinkenberg, H.L.J. van der Maas. (2015). Learning multiplication: An integrated analysis of the multiplication ability of primary school children and the difficulty of single digit and multidigit multiplication problems. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2015.08.013
title: The computational efficiency model of multiplication problem difficulty
description: The computational efficiency model is an explanatory account of multiplication problem difficulty that the article evaluates against item data. It was contrasted with alternatives using data from two tasks: one in which children used predominantly computational strategies and one in which they were expected to rely mostly on retrieval. The article reports that "In both tasks we found most support for the computational efficiency model", making it the best-supported account of the models compared for both kinds of task data.
requirements: Item-level difficulty data from multiplication tasks, including tasks expected to elicit retrieval as well as tasks eliciting computational strategies, to test the model against alternatives.
target_learning_goals: mental multiplication ability and problem difficulty
examples: The article tested the model with data from two contrasted tasks and found most support for it in both.
key_sources: S.H.G. van der Ven, M. Straatemeier, B.R.J. Jansen, S. Klinkenberg, H.L.J. van der Maas. (2015). Learning multiplication: An integrated analysis of the multiplication ability of primary school children and the difficulty of single digit and multidigit multiplication problems. Learning and Individual Differences. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2015.08.013

article_title: (In)equitable Schooling and Mathematics of Marginalized Students: Through the Voices of Urban Latinas/os
citation: Maura Varley Gutiérrez, Craig Willey, & Lena L. Khisty. (2011). (In)equitable Schooling and Mathematics of Marginalized Students: Through the Voices of Urban Latinas/os. Journal of Urban Mathematics Education, 4(2), 26–43. http://education.gsu.edu/JUME
title: Counterstorytelling within critical race theory as a framework for understanding marginalized students' mathematics experiences
description: The article grounds its analysis in critical race theory and counterstorytelling, the practice of People of Color naming their own realities. A counterstory 'serves to illuminate these biases and the processes by which they operate and influence educational acts.' The authors combine counterstory with critical ethnography, weaving individual student stories into a collective voice of Latinas/os' lived experiences in mathematics education to counter deficit-based perspectives.
requirements: Experiential knowledge of non-dominant students must be treated as legitimate and critical data, per the article's key tenet of critical race theory
constraints: The counterstories represent a particular group of students across two urban sites and are presented as a collective reflection of shared systemic exclusion
target_learners: Urban Latina/o elementary and middle-grade students
target_learning_goals: Understanding students' perspectives on mathematics learning and schooling conditions
examples: The authors present four salient themes from students' spontaneous and structured comments across three years of after-school participation
key_sources: Maura Varley Gutiérrez, Craig Willey, & Lena L. Khisty. (2011). (In)equitable Schooling and Mathematics of Marginalized Students: Through the Voices of Urban Latinas/os. Journal of Urban Mathematics Education, 4(2), 26–43. http://education.gsu.edu/JUME

article_title: Comorbidity Between Reading Disability and Math Disability
citation: Willcutt, E. G., Petrill, S. A., Wu, S., Boada, R., DeFries, J. C., Olson, R. K., & Pennington, B. F. (2013). Comorbidity between reading disability and math disability: Concurrent psychopathology, functional impairment, and neuropsychological functioning. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 46(6), 500-516. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219413477476
title: Correlated liabilities model of RD and MD comorbidity within a multiple-deficit framework
description: The correlated liabilities model holds that RD and MD co-occur more often than chance due to shared etiological influences, while additional disorder-specific influences distinguish them. The article's results "provide the strongest support for a correlated liabilities model in which shared weaknesses in working memory, verbal comprehension, and processing speed increase risk for both RD and MD," with distinct profiles on phoneme awareness, naming speed, and set shifting. This sits within the broader multiple-deficit framework in which developmental disorders arise from additive and interactive effects of multiple neuropsychological weaknesses rather than a single primary deficit.
requirements: Requires a 2 X 2 (RD X MD) group design with groups defined by each disorder alone, comorbid, and neither, plus measures spanning multiple neuropsychological constructs
constraints: The article notes results derive from word reading and math calculations definitions; results might differ for reading comprehension, word problems, or fluency measures
target_learners: children and adolescents ages 8-15 with reading disability, math disability, or both
target_learning_goals: understanding the neuropsychological and etiological basis of reading and math learning disabilities
examples: The CLDRC twin study compared 241 RD-only, 183 MD-only, 188 RD+MD, and 411 control participants, rejecting alternate forms, phenocopy, and three independent disorders models
key_sources: Willcutt, E. G., Petrill, S. A., Wu, S., Boada, R., DeFries, J. C., Olson, R. K., & Pennington, B. F. (2013). Comorbidity between reading disability and math disability: Concurrent psychopathology, functional impairment, and neuropsychological functioning. Journal of Learning Disabilities, 46(6), 500-516. https://doi.org/10.1177/0022219413477476

article_title: Computational Thinking for All: Pedagogical Approaches to Embedding 21st Century Problem Solving in K-12 Classrooms
citation: Yadav, A., Hong, H., & Stephenson, C. (2016). Computational Thinking for All: Pedagogical Approaches to Embedding 21st Century Problem Solving in K-12 Classrooms. TechTrends. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11528-016-0087-7
title: Professional development for embedding CT should be continuous, collaborative, and tied to teachers' curricular needs
description: The article argues teachers cannot incorporate CT concepts "without support and opportunities to apply these ideas to authentic tasks," and that support mechanisms "need to be continuous rather than one- or two-time professional development events." Professional development must go hand-in-hand with curriculum and lesson development plans that work within the local classroom context, with computer science educators, teacher educators, and educational technology faculty collaborating with teachers to develop activities that make visible the overlap of CT with subject-area concepts.
requirements: Collaboration between CS educators, teacher educators, educational technology faculty, and classroom teachers
constraints: Requires administrator buy-in and resources such as release time and access to computing tools
target_learning_goals: integrating computational thinking into subject-area teaching
examples: Michigan State University's MAET course has teachers work collaboratively on a semester-long project to develop CT activities relevant to their own contexts
key_sources: Yadav, A., Hong, H., & Stephenson, C. (2016). Computational Thinking for All: Pedagogical Approaches to Embedding 21st Century Problem Solving in K-12 Classrooms. TechTrends. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11528-016-0087-7

article_title: A cognitive-ecological approach to preventing aggression in urban settings: Initial outcomes for high-risk children.
citation: Metropolitan Area Child Study Research Group. (2002). A Cognitive–Ecological Approach to Preventing Aggression in Urban Settings: Initial Outcomes for High-Risk Children. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037//0022-006X.70.1.179
title: Cognitive–ecological model of aggression prevention
description: The cognitive–ecological model holds that aggression is learned and maintained across multiple social contexts, so prevention must modify both individual cognition and context. The article states its "preventive intervention is directed at modifying both individual social–cognitive and contextual factors relevant to the learning of aggression. We called this approach a cognitive–ecological model." In the MACS trial this translated into stacked intervention levels adding classroom, peer-group, and family contexts, with effectiveness expected to rise as more targeted contexts are added.
requirements: Interventions must target multiple socialization contexts (classroom, peers, family) rather than a single context or component
constraints: The article notes single-component or single-context interventions have limited effectiveness, motivating the multi-context design
target_learners: Elementary school children in inner-city and urban poor communities, especially those at high risk for aggression
target_learning_goals: Reduce aggressive behavior and increase protective factors such as school achievement and social–cognitive skills
examples: The MACS trial assigned 16 schools to control, classroom-only (Level A), classroom plus small-group peer-skills (Level B), and classroom plus peer-skills plus family (Level C) conditions
key_sources: Metropolitan Area Child Study Research Group. (2002). A Cognitive–Ecological Approach to Preventing Aggression in Urban Settings: Initial Outcomes for High-Risk Children. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-006x.70.1.179

article_title: From Design to Implementation to Practice a Learning by Teaching System: Betty’s Brain
citation: Gautam Biswas, James R. Segedy, Kritya Bunchongchit. (2016). From Design to Implementation to Practice: a Learning by Teaching System: Betty's Brain. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0057-9
title: Coherence analysis framework and its six activity-trace measures
description: Coherence analysis (CA) is the paper's approach to analyzing learners' problem-solving processes in OELEs by "combining information gleaned from sequences of student actions to produce measures of action coherence." CA assumes that when students encounter information that could improve their solution, they should act on it; edits not justified by recent views are labeled unsupported edits. Six measures are derived from activity traces: edits/annotations per minute, unsupported edit percentage, information viewing percentage, potential generation percentage, used potential percentage, and disengaged percentage.
requirements: The redesigned interface makes only one of the reading, teaching, and quiz interfaces visible at a time, enabling the system to track shifts between activity types
constraints: View counts count toward potential only if page views lasted at least 10 s and quiz results at least 2 s, to filter out irrelevant actions
target_learning_goals: characterizing self-regulated learning behavior in open-ended problem solving
examples: CA-derived metrics predicted students' task performance and learning gains and correlated significantly with prior skill levels in the classroom study.
key_sources: Gautam Biswas, James R. Segedy, Kritya Bunchongchit. (2016). From Design to Implementation to Practice: a Learning by Teaching System: Betty's Brain. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0057-9

article_title: Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis
citation: Castro-Alonso, J. C., Wong, R. M., Adesope, O. O., & Paas, F. (2021). Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09587-1
title: Computers are social actors hypothesis as the account predicting that most agent characteristics do not moderate effectiveness
description: The article tests the computers are social actors hypothesis, which predicts that learners' responses to on-screen characters do not depend strongly on most surface characteristics of the agent. The meta-analysis is described as showing, "As predicted by the computers are social actors hypothesis, most of the agents' characteristics, including nonverbal communication, motion, and voice, appeared not to moderate their effectiveness." This account explains why students may learn similarly from different types of agents despite variation in social cues such as motion and voice.
requirements: Applies to multimedia environments where agents deliver instruction and their social characteristics could plausibly be varied.
constraints: The article's support is a pattern of null moderator results, hedged with appeared not to; it does not establish that no characteristic ever matters.
target_learning_goals: Multimedia learning outcomes across varied agent designs
examples: The meta-analysis tested moderator effects of nonverbal communication, motion, and voice and found they appeared not to moderate effectiveness.
key_sources: Castro-Alonso, J. C., Wong, R. M., Adesope, O. O., & Paas, F. (2021). Effectiveness of Multimedia Pedagogical Agents Predicted by Diverse Theories: a Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09587-1

article_title: Conjecture Mapping: An Approach to Systematic Educational Design Research
citation: Simon Lecuyer-Chardevel, Isabelle Girault, Christian Hoffmann. (2024). Modeling and supporting goal setting and planning in the regulation of learning activities in a CSCL environment. 19th European Conference on Technology Enhanced Learning (Doctoral Consortium). https://hal.science/hal-04999910v2
title: Conjecture map linking planning-tool design to self-regulation outcomes in CSCL
description: The article uses a conjecture map, described as "A representation of the design and theoretical conjectures concerning the planning phase of self-regulation." Its design conjectures state that if students engage in a team activity with goal-setting and planning tools, a time of debate and organization of the collective activity will be observed and students will create intermediate milestones and task lists. Its theoretical conjecture holds that clarifying task representations and adapting work plans leads students to share task conditions and use them in execution and adaptation. The map connects the tool design to the research questions.
requirements: Design-based research setting with mixed methods to test the conjectures
constraints: Conjectures are stated as expected outcomes, not yet empirically confirmed
target_learners: higher education students in CSCL science activities
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning, specifically goal setting and planning
examples: Design conjecture: if students use goal-setting and planning tools in a team activity, they will create intermediate milestones in the calendar and explicit task lists
key_sources: Simon Lecuyer-Chardevel, Isabelle Girault, Christian Hoffmann. (2024). Modeling and supporting goal setting and planning in the regulation of learning activities in a CSCL environment. 19th European Conference on Technology Enhanced Learning (Doctoral Consortium). https://hal.science/hal-04999910v2

article_title: Theories of learning as theories of society: A contrapuntal approach to expanding disciplinary authenticity in computing
citation: Philip, T., & Sengupta, P. (2020). Theories of Learning as Theories of Society: A Contrapuntal Approach to Expanding Disciplinary Authenticity in Computing. Journal of the Learning Sciences. http://www.isls.org/
title: Contrapuntal reading: juxtaposing designs and theories with histories of empire
description: Building on Said (1993), the article defines contrapuntal reading as drawing out "the logics of and resistances to empire and imperialism that are silent or marginally present" in designs and theories. It complements, rather than replaces, contextual and consequential readings by adding a sharpened analysis of imperialism, asking "Who is simultaneously integral and invisiblized through imperialism in our conceptualizations of learning?" The article demonstrates the lens by reading disciplinary authenticity in computing education alongside sociology of immigrant tech workers.
requirements: An explicit juxtaposition of designs and theories with histories and contemporary processes of imperialism, as Said (1993) outlined
constraints: The authors state contrapuntality is meant to complement, not replace, contextual and consequential readings
target_learners: Learning Sciences researchers and graduate students
target_learning_goals: Analyzing learning designs and theories for their entanglement with empire and imperialism
examples: The article's Said-inspired reading of Mansfield Park surfacing the labor of endarkened people in Antigua, and its juxtaposition of computing education's authenticity construct with Banerjee and Rincon's (2019) study of immigrant tech workers
key_sources: Philip, T., & Sengupta, P. (2020). Theories of Learning as Theories of Society: A Contrapuntal Approach to Expanding Disciplinary Authenticity in Computing. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2020.1828089

article_title: Do Master Narratives Change Among High School Students? A Characterization of How National History Is Represented
citation: Mario Carretero & Floor van Alphen. (2014). Do Master Narratives Change Among High School Students? A Characterization of How National History Is Represented. Cognition and Instruction, 32(3), 290-312. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2014.919298
title: Teach a constructivist nation concept first, then use it to historicize the national subject and events
description: The article proposes that history education aiming at historical understanding of a national past should first aim at a constructivist concept of nation and then use that concept to reflect on the national historical subject and events in the narrative. This sequencing follows from the finding that the nation concept was the master narrative characteristic showing the greatest change and least resistance, while identification remained constant. The authors state this approach 'might help produce historical understanding of a national past.'
requirements: Instruction that addresses the nation concept explicitly before the historical subject and events
constraints: The authors note whether identity construction and critical historical understanding are complementary 'is a matter in need of further research'
target_learning_goals: historical understanding of the national past
overcoming an essentialist concept of nation
examples: In the study, 75% of 11th graders versus 33% of 8th graders demonstrated a constructivist nation concept, and Table 6 suggested the constructivist nation concept was the historical content most often and perhaps most easily appropriated
key_sources: Mario Carretero & Floor van Alphen. (2014). Do Master Narratives Change Among High School Students? A Characterization of How National History Is Represented. Cognition and Instruction, 32(3), 290-312. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2014.919298

article_title: Making Space to Sensemake: Epistemic Distancing in Small Group Physics Discussions
citation: Conlin, L. D., & Scherr, R. E. (2012). Making Space to Sensemake: Epistemic Distancing in Small Group Physics Discussions. Preprint under review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Making+Space+to+Sensemake
title: Design collaborative learning environments to support management of affective risk, since epistemology and affect are coupled in sensemaking discussions
description: The article argues that inquiry discussions pose an essential tension between generating ideas and critiquing them, and that both sides carry affective risks such as embarrassment. It concludes that research and instruction should consider "the coupled dynamics of epistemology and affect in collaborative sensemaking discussions," and that implications for instruction include "novel ways of encouraging classroom discussion" such as epistemic distancing.
requirements: Collaborative discussions in which students both contribute ideas and critically evaluate each other's ideas
constraints: Groups that distance too much may align against the goals of inquiry curriculum
target_learning_goals: collaborative scientific sensemaking and argumentation
examples: Tutorial groups used hedging, ironic reading, and question-form disagreements to ease into saying what they think
key_sources: Conlin, L. D., & Scherr, R. E. (2012). Making Space to Sensemake: Epistemic Distancing in Small Group Physics Discussions. Preprint under review. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Making+Space+to+Sensemake

article_title: An international research community
citation: Stahl, G., Law, N., & Hesse, F. (2012). An international research community. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 341–345. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9155-y
title: Cognitive Work Analysis as a method for analyzing the socio-technical context of educational research settings
description: The editorial describes Cognitive Work Analysis as a technique drawn from engineering fields that Kim MacKinnon applies to educational research. It is offered as a response to recognized weaknesses of design-based research, including that "there is no specified methodology for analyzing the collaborative student usage of CSCL technologies" and the difficulty of generalizing from single case studies. By characterizing a case study's context, the technique is intended to help judge its broader relevance.
requirements: A case-study research setting whose socio-technical context must be characterized to judge broader relevance
constraints: The editors present it as addressing the problem that design-based research rarely yields direct implications for technology re-design and is hard to generalize from a single case-study context
target_learning_goals: Analyzing and generalizing from case-study research on collaborative learning technologies
examples: MacKinnon's article in the issue illustrates applying the technique to analyzing the socio-technical context of an educational research setting.
key_sources: Stahl, G., Law, N., & Hesse, F. (2012). An international research community. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 7, 341–345. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-012-9155-y

article_title: Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 139-145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9118-8
title: Co-referencing typology and coding scheme for analyzing collaborative interaction around external representations
description: The Evans, Feenstra, Ryon and McNeill article provides analytic tools for collaborative interactions around external representations, honing in on "co-referencing": multiple people referencing the same thing through a deictic word, a pointing gesture, or any verbal, physical, or virtual action referencing something as intended by more than one person. The editorial reports that "a systematic typology of forms and levels of co-reference is sketched and a method of coding co-references in their temporality is proposed and illustrated," enabling both qualitative sense of co-construction and quantitative comparison across cases.
requirements: A coding scheme applied to discourse so co-references can be tracked and compiled into quantitative measures
constraints: Illustrated on dyadic interaction; the editorial does not report validation statistics
target_learning_goals: Analyzing intersubjectivity and distributed cognition in dyadic discourse and gesture
examples: Paying attention to co-referential actions within a dyadic interaction gives an analyst a qualitative sense of the co-construction process and shared meaning making
key_sources: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2011). Let a hundred flowers bloom; let a hundred schools of thought contend. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 6, 139-145. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9118-8

article_title: ReaderBench: Automated evaluation of collaboration based on cohesion and dialogism
citation: Mihai Dascalu, Stefan Trausan-Matu, Danielle S. Mcnamara, Philippe Dessus. (2015). ReaderBench – Automated Evaluation of Collaboration based on Cohesion and Dialogism. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9226-y
title: Cohesion-graph model of collaboration as a longitudinal, social knowledge-building analysis
description: The article's first proposed model represents collaboration through "a cohesion graph" over the conversation. It can be perceived as "a longitudinal analysis of the ongoing conversation", accounting for collaboration from a social knowledge-building perspective. The model is one of the two approaches implemented and validated in ReaderBench for automated collaboration assessment in CSCL chats.
requirements: Requires a cohesion-based representation of the conversation that can be organized into a cohesion graph.
target_learning_goals: Assessing social knowledge-building collaboration
