article_title: Frameworks for mass collaboration, adaptable scripts, complex systems theory, and collaborative writing
citation: Ludvigsen, S., Law, N., Rosé, C. P., & Stahl, G. (2017). Frameworks for mass collaboration, adaptable scripts, complex systems theory, and collaborative writing. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 12, 127–131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9257-7
title: Complex adaptive systems theory as a lens for CSCL: self-organization, emergence, interdependencies, and hierarchical nesting of levels
description: The editorial positions complex adaptive systems theory as a lens for explaining complex phenomena in CSCL, listing its key concepts: "self-organization, emergence, interdependencies, and hierarchical nesting of levels". It notes the approach has been rare in CSCL apart from work inspired by Cress and Kimmerle. Self-organization is described as rare in education because "educational activities are most often heavily influenced by teacher instruction and social norms that regulate actions".
requirements: Analysis must be able to bridge gaps between individuals, groups, and the community, as the Vogler et al. study does by taking the group as a starting point
constraints: Self-organization can be rare in education because educational activities are most often heavily influenced by teacher instruction and social norms
target_learners: students in synchronous online learning environments
target_learning_goals: understanding emerging participation and meaning-making in collaborative online learning
examples: The editors state that the use of complex adaptive systems theory in the Vogler et al. study can be suggestive for the CSCL community
key_sources: Ludvigsen, S., Law, N., Rosé, C. P., & Stahl, G. (2017). Frameworks for mass collaboration, adaptable scripts, complex systems theory, and collaborative writing. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn, 12, 127–131. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9257-7

article_title: Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies
citation: Ludvigsen, S., Cress, U., Law, N., Stahl, G., & Rosé, C. P. (2017). Future direction for the CSCL field: Methodologies and eight controversies. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12, 337–341. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9268-4
title: Co-Census interactive design capturing visitor identity data to spark dialogue
description: Co-Census is software used as part of an interactive museum design; it "captures data about visitors' identities and some aspects of their lives (family and work), based on a few questions." The design idea is "that the personalized data should spark more interest and increase the quality of the dialogues that are performed during the museum visit." It lets participants control visualizations produced by their bodily movements and interact with other participants.
requirements: Participants contribute personal data about identities and aspects of their lives via a few questions for the design to personalize dialogue.
target_learners: Museum visitors in dyads and groups
target_learning_goals: Increasing dialogue quality and interest during interactive-exhibit experiences
examples: Co-Census was used in Roberts and Lyons' experimental-design study in a museum setting.

article_title: From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory
citation: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y
title: Nine collaborative cognitive load principles relating task, learner and team characteristics to extraneous transactive load
description: The article distills its analysis into a table of nine principles stating when collaboration's transactional activities cause extraneous load: task complexity, task guidance and support, domain expertise, collaboration skills, team size, team roles, team composition, prior task experience, and prior team experience. Each principle states a direction, for example that 'Effective collaboration occurs when a task is complex enough to justify the extra time and effort involved in the necessary transactional activities', and that more guidance, expertise, roles, or prior experience lower the extraneous load caused by transactive activities.
requirements: Collaborative tasks should be selected and teams configured so that transactive activities stay task-related and extraneous load is minimised
constraints: If a task is not complex enough, unnecessary transactional activities cause extraneous cognitive load and are detrimental to learning
target_learners: students learning collaboratively in classrooms or CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: acquisition of biologically secondary, domain-specific knowledge through collaboration
examples: The article derives the principles from team characteristics including 'team size, the roles learners can or must carry out, team composition, and the prior experience of team members working with each other'
key_sources: Kirschner, P. A., Sweller, J., Kirschner, F., & Zambrano R., J. (2018). From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9277-y

article_title: Different technologies, methodologies and epistemologies—is CSCL a community or communities?
citation: Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rose, Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen. (2018). Different technologies, methodologies and epistemologies—is CSCL a community or communities? Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9280-3
title: Collaborative cognitive load theory: extending cognitive load theory to collaborative learning with collective working memory and transactional costs
description: Kirschner, Sweller, Kirschner and Zambrano's theoretical treatise extends cognitive load theory to collaborative contexts to "generate principles specific to the design and study of collaborative learning". It takes a strictly information processing model of learning where working memory capacity is a primary factor. Collaborators gain access to a larger collective working memory, but part of working memory is devoted to "transactive activities involved in the collaborative process", so benefits depend on group experience working together. The authors also claim the theory "will be able to explain why CSCL does not always work".
requirements: Teachers are advised to think explicitly about the cognitive properties of the students, task characteristics and group composition when deciding whether to adopt collaborative learning
constraints: The editorial characterizes it as taking a strictly information processing model, which the editors place on the analytical end of the epistemic spectrum, misaligned with the constructivist, socio-cultural and social psychology frameworks popular in CSCL
target_learning_goals: collaborative learning outcomes in complex subject domains such as mathematics
examples: The editorial positions the treatise against Provocation #4, contrasting its analytical epistemology with the interpretive orientation of the other three papers in the issue
key_sources: Nancy Law, Carolyn P. Rose, Ulrike Cress & Sten Ludvigsen. (2018). Different technologies, methodologies and epistemologies—is CSCL a community or communities? Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9280-3

article_title: Leveraging mobile eye-trackers to capture joint visual attention in co-located collaborative learning groups
citation: Schneider, B., Sharma, K., Cuendet, S., Zufferey, G., Dillenbourg, P., & Pea, R. (2018). Leveraging mobile eye-trackers to capture joint visual attention in co-located collaborative learning groups. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 13(3), 241–261. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9281-2
title: Contrasting-cases warehouse-layout activity combining principle derivation with artifact construction
description: The experimental task pattern: dyads first "had to define some design principles for optimizing a warehouse layout by analyzing a set of Contrasting Cases, and build a small-scale layout based on those principles." This combines inductive analysis of contrasting cases with hands-on construction of a physical artifact, providing a collaborative task rich enough to generate meaningful gaze coordination and participation data.
requirements: A set of Contrasting Cases to analyze
Materials for building a small-scale layout artifact
constraints: Studied in the context of warehouse-layout design with student dyads on a Tangible User Interface
target_learning_goals: Deriving design principles from contrasting cases and applying them to build a layout
examples: Used as the collaborative task in the 27-dyad eye-tracking experiment

article_title: Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments
citation: Peter Holtz & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress. (2018). Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9285-y
title: Co-evolution model of individual learning and collective knowledge construction
description: The co-evolution model (Cress and Kimmerle) "combines the individual and the social levels." It "predicts that conflicts between individual and collective perspectives (as presented in collaboratively created artifacts) may make the two systems involved drift over time: In the case of the cognitive system, the drift can be called learning; in the case of the social system, this drift constitutes knowledge construction." The cognitive and social systems are structurally coupled and co-evolve toward greater capabilities in handling complexity, with persons and digital artifacts as the key entities.
requirements: Interactions between persons and collaboratively created digital artifacts in which conflicts between individual and collective perspectives arise
constraints: The model is presented for online environments where artifact-mediated collaboration makes acts of communication traceable in artifacts
target_learners: individuals participating in mass collaboration and CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: individual learning and collective knowledge construction as coupled, mutually triggering processes
examples: The three illustrative Wikipedia studies were framed by the co-evolution model and aimed "to identify the role of productive friction for learning and knowledge construction"
key_sources: Peter Holtz & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress. (2018). Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9285-y

article_title: Developing understanding beyond the given knowledge and new methodologies for analyses in CSCL
citation: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Carolyn P. Rosé, Nancy Law, & Gerry Stahl. (2018). Developing understanding beyond the given knowledge and new methodologies for analyses in CSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 13, 359–364. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9291-0
title: Cognitive-systemic stance: knowledge development at individual and social-system levels triggered by productive friction
description: The cognitive-systemic stance, developed by Cress and colleagues, builds on cognitive psychology and general system theory to investigate conceptual change by connecting "both individual cognitive systems and the individual’s interactions with the larger environment — the social systems." Within this framework, Holtz et al. hypothesize that "knowledge development at the levels of both individual and social system is triggered by productive friction," meaning that resolving sociocognitive conflicts is part of actions and activities. The editorial presents this as the theoretical frame for three big data methods applied to Wikipedia.
requirements: Big data analysis must be framed by a clear and well-developed theoretical framework, per the authors' emphasized stance
constraints: The framework's empirical example in this issue is Wikipedia environments
target_learners: individuals and large online communities engaged in mass collaboration
target_learning_goals: conceptual change
collaborative knowledge development
examples: Holtz, Kimmerle, and Cress present automatic text classification, cluster analysis of knowledge dynamics in Wikipedia articles, and social network analysis as three big data approaches
key_sources: Sten Ludvigsen, Ulrike Cress, Carolyn P. Rosé, Nancy Law, & Gerry Stahl. (2018). Developing understanding beyond the given knowledge and new methodologies for analyses in CSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 13, 359–364. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9291-0

article_title: Rendering controversial socioscientific issues legible through digital mapping tools
citation: Solli, A., Mäkitalo, Å., & Hillman, T. (2018). Rendering controversial socioscientific issues legible through digital mapping tools. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9286-x
title: Six-phase controversy mapping project sequence for science classrooms
description: A project-level design pattern in which students work through six phases: (1) surfing and scraping the internet on a controversial issue with Navicrawler logging visited URLs, (2) selecting and importing data to Gephi, (3) re-presenting data as a map of actors, (4) sharing and discussing maps with peers, (5) participating in a debate enacting an identified actor, and (6) a reflective seminar. The map serves as "an aid in explaining and discussing their controversy."
requirements: Teachers, researchers, and IT pedagogical developers collaborate on project design; the mapping activity is embedded in a multi-week science-in-society project with curriculum-aligned grading criteria
constraints: Tools were originally developed for university research on sociotechnical debates, not schools; students need guidance since studies indicate the need for more support when searching for SSIs online
target_learning_goals: evaluating source types, distinguishing scientific from non-scientific claims, understanding science-society relations, ethical discussion of science's role in society
examples: A three-week November 2015 project in a Swedish upper secondary school with four experienced teachers; student groups targeted electronic waste, HPV vaccine, prenatal diagnosis, or animal testing controversies
key_sources: Solli, A., Mäkitalo, Å., & Hillman, T. (2018). Rendering controversial socioscientific issues legible through digital mapping tools. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9286-x

article_title: Providing different types of group awareness information to guide collaborative learning
citation: Schnaubert, L., & Bodemer, D. (2019). Providing different types of group awareness information to guide collaborative learning. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 14, 7–51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9293-y
title: Two types of group awareness information: cognitive (assumptions) and metacognitive (confidence)
description: The article distinguishes two kinds of group awareness information meant to "guide collaborative learning activities by providing knowledge-related information to the learners." Cognitive group awareness information concerns "the learners' assumptions" (factor 1), while metacognitive group awareness information concerns "their confidence" (factor 2), treated as independent factors. The framework combines CSCL research with research on metacognition, and its effects are tested on individual metacognitive and cognitive outcome measures and on regulation of the collaborative process.
requirements: Access to learners' assumption-related and confidence-related information so it can be visualized as group awareness information
constraints: Study confined to dyads of university students discussing blood-sugar regulation and diabetes mellitus
target_learning_goals: domain knowledge about blood-sugar regulation and diabetes mellitus
metacognitive monitoring (confidence)
examples: In the experimental study the two information types were crossed as factor 1 (assumptions) and factor 2 (confidence) with individual and process outcome measures
key_sources: Schnaubert, L., & Bodemer, D. (2019). Providing different types of group awareness information to guide collaborative learning. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 14, 7–51. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-018-9293-y

article_title: Improving the quality of vocational students’ collaboration and knowledge acquisition through instruction and joint reflection
citation: Elise H. Eshuis, Judith ter Vrugte, Anjo Anjewierden, Lars Bollen, Jakob Sikken, Ton de Jong. (2019). Improving the quality of vocational students' collaboration and knowledge acquisition through instruction and joint reflection. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2019) 14:53–76. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09296-0
title: Collaboration reflection tool (feed up, feed back, feed forward)
description: An online tool that prompts and scaffolds joint reflection on collaborative behavior, structured in three phases per Hattie and Timperley's feedback model. In the "feed up" phase students rate their own and each other's collaborative behavior on a ten-point scale for each RIDE rule; in the "feed back" phase they see a graphical representation of team and individual scores; in the "feed forward" phase they discuss what went well and formulate joint improvement goals. Completion takes up to ten minutes and the tool was offered four times at set points in the CSCL environment.
requirements: All team members complete each phase (individually for feed up and feed back, collaboratively for feed forward); content is based on the RIDE rules familiar from instruction.
constraints: The tool required students to have used the CSCL environment before; there was no tool after module one so students could get used to the environment, and completion takes up to ten minutes.
target_learning_goals: Awareness of effective collaboration characteristics and improvement of students' own collaborative behavior
examples: Tool sessions at the end of modules two through five showed students their team's average scores per RIDE rule and previously formulated goals to discuss whether they had been reached.
key_sources: Elise H. Eshuis, Judith ter Vrugte, Anjo Anjewierden, Lars Bollen, Jakob Sikken, Ton de Jong. (2019). Improving the quality of vocational students' collaboration and knowledge acquisition through instruction and joint reflection. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2019) 14:53–76. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09296-0

article_title: Improving the quality of vocational students’ collaboration and knowledge acquisition through instruction and joint reflection
citation: Elise H. Eshuis, Judith ter Vrugte, Anjo Anjewierden, Lars Bollen, Jakob Sikken, Ton de Jong. (2019). Improving the quality of vocational students' collaboration and knowledge acquisition through instruction and joint reflection. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2019) 14:53–76. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09296-0
title: Combine collaboration instruction with prompted joint reflection (self- and peer-assessment plus goal setting) rather than offering instruction alone
description: The article's central design recommendation is that teaching collaboration skills requires more than instruction about effective-collaboration characteristics: only a combination of conventional instruction and a tool prompting joint reflection — through self- and peer-assessment and collaborative goal setting — affected both collaborative behavior and knowledge acquisition in this study. The results section and discussion support this: instruction alone "benefits neither their collaborative behavior nor their knowledge acquisition", whereas instruction plus reflection prompting students to connect instructed characteristics to their actual behavior did.
requirements: A reliable information source for reflection beyond self-assessment (peer-assessment), plus goal setting to connect reflection to future behavior.
constraints: The authors note it remains unclear which of the tool's working mechanisms (peer assessment vs goal setting) generated the effect; the finding is from technical vocational triads in a CSCL setting.
target_learners: Secondary vocational education students working in collaborative teams
target_learning_goals: Improving quality of collaboration and domain knowledge acquisition
examples: In the instruction-with-tool condition, students received 20 minutes of RIDE-rule instruction and completed the reflection tool four times during five CSCL sessions on electricity topics.
key_sources: Elise H. Eshuis, Judith ter Vrugte, Anjo Anjewierden, Lars Bollen, Jakob Sikken, Ton de Jong. (2019). Improving the quality of vocational students' collaboration and knowledge acquisition through instruction and joint reflection. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2019) 14:53–76. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09296-0

article_title: It is not either or: An initial investigation into combining collaborative and individual learning using an ITS
citation: Olsen, J. K., Rummel, N., & Aleven, V. (2019). It is not either or: An initial investigation into combining collaborative and individual learning using an ITS. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 14, 353-381. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09307-0
title: Combine collaborative and individual learning within ITS-supported activities rather than choosing one or the other
description: The article argues that collaborative and individual learning are often combined in classrooms and that CSCL should investigate "when a combination is beneficial compared to individual or collaborative learning alone." It proposes an initial test of combining both modes within one ITS activity, finding support in higher gains, fewer errors and hints, and higher situational interest. The principle is to treat the two modes as complementary stages of the same activity rather than alternatives.
requirements: An intelligent tutoring system activity is needed that can be run both collaboratively and individually so the two modes can be sequenced within the same learning content.
constraints: The learning-gain advantage was restricted to the 4th grade students in this initial investigation.
target_learning_goals: fraction problem-solving skills
examples: The study compared a combined condition to individual-only and collaborative-only conditions in an ITS for fractions with 382 4th and 5th grade students.
key_sources: Olsen, J. K., Rummel, N., & Aleven, V. (2019). It is not either or: An initial investigation into combining collaborative and individual learning using an ITS. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 14, 353-381. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09307-0

article_title: Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance
citation: Hayashi, Y. (2020). Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09333-3
title: Combine gaze-awareness feedback with PCA metacognitive suggestions to improve both coordination and learning gains in computer-mediated collaborative learning
description: The article's design principle is that two complementary facilitation methods — real-time partner gaze feedback supporting joint attention and a PCA providing metacognitive suggestions — should be integrated in collaborative-learning support systems. Gaze feedback improved process coordination but "does not directly scaffold metacognition", while PCA suggestions support self-regulation but lack partner-awareness information; jointly they produced the highest learning gains.
requirements: A system able to show a partner's real-time gaze on shared task materials and to deliver dynamic metacognitive suggestions during collaboration.
A collaborative task where partners hold different knowledge and must explain and integrate perspectives.
constraints: The synergy on learning gains appeared in one 2×2 experiment with psychology freshmen/sophomores in dyads on a jigsaw explanation task; no process-level interaction was found, so the combined advantage concerns gains, not process ratings.
target_learners: University students collaborating remotely or side-by-side without visual contact
target_learning_goals: Knowledge integration and mutual understanding of each partner's distinct concepts in collaborative explanation tasks
examples: In the experiment, learners in the visible-gaze/visible-agent condition achieved higher gain scores and showed the only significant process-performance correlation.
key_sources: Hayashi, Y. (2020). Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09333-3

article_title: Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis
citation: Ollesch, L., Heimbuch, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09346-6
title: Group awareness tools framework distinguishing cognitive and behavioral GA information for wiki-based CSCL
description: GATs collect, transform, and present information about group members in collaborative learning environments. The article distinguishes cognitive GATs, which visualize group members' knowledge, interest, or opinions, from behavioral GATs, which visualize activities such as contribution counts. Each type addresses a distinct wiki challenge — selecting meaningful content or stimulating active content production — while providing implicit guidance that supports self-regulated collaboration without explicit instructions. The article argues both types should be understood and designed together rather than in isolation.
requirements: Learners must be in computer-mediated collaborative settings where awareness information is not naturally salient, as the article notes GA information is often not salient enough there.
constraints: The article states that GA tool types are often examined separately or combined without disentangling their specific functions, limiting clarity about their respective roles.
target_learners: University students collaborating in wiki learning environments
target_learning_goals: Collaborative knowledge construction
Collaborative writing quality
examples: The article cites Sangin et al.'s knowledge awareness tool based on pretest scores and Janssen et al.'s participation tool as established examples of each GAT type.
key_sources: Ollesch, L., Heimbuch, S., & Bodemer, D. (2021). Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09346-6

article_title: A theory-driven reflection on context-aware support for collaborative discussions in light of analytics, affordances, and platforms
citation: Carolyn Rosé, Sanna Järvelä. (2021). A theory-driven reflection on context-aware support for collaborative discussions in light of analytics, affordances, and platforms. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09360-8
title: A collaborative version of MIT App Inventor for group programming
description: The final full article of the issue presents and evaluates a collaborative extension of MIT App Inventor (MAI), "a popular block-based programming (BBP) learning environment designed to aid new programmers in making quick progress towards producing computer programs by removing the need for as much knowledge of programming language syntax." The study explores interactions afforded by a platform not originally designed to be collaborative, applying analytics to gain visibility into behavior patterns. It contrasts individual vs. collaborative work, heterogeneous vs. homogeneous disciplinary-background teams, and team self-efficacy.
requirements: Extended from an established environment for individual learning and exploration, with analytics applied to identify collaborative behaviors of interest
constraints: The platform was not originally designed to be collaborative
target_learners: new programmers, including participants with non-computer-science backgrounds
target_learning_goals: block-based programming through group programming
examples: Hsu, Abelson, Patton, Chen, and Chang study the environment as participants experience it in both individual and collaborative modes, with teams formed heterogeneous or homogeneous in disciplinary background
key_sources: Carolyn Rosé, Sanna Järvelä. (2021). A theory-driven reflection on context-aware support for collaborative discussions in light of analytics, affordances, and platforms. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09360-8

article_title: A theory-driven reflection on context-aware support for collaborative discussions in light of analytics, affordances, and platforms
citation: Carolyn Rosé, Sanna Järvelä. (2021). A theory-driven reflection on context-aware support for collaborative discussions in light of analytics, affordances, and platforms. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09360-8
title: Combine diverse datasets across multiple timescales, mixing automatic and human analyses, to make dialogue analytics meaningful
description: The editors close by challenging the field with the question raised by Baker et al.: "how can such diverse data sets, over multiple timescales, involving a combination of automatic and human analyses, be combined in a meaningful way". The principle urges researchers designing CSCL studies and analytics to integrate analyses of discussion data across timescales rather than treating single-scale studies as sufficient, and especially welcomes "dialogue" in between data and theories for the following year's submissions.
requirements: Combining automatic and human analyses over multiple timescales in a meaningful way, guided by general theories of dialogue, cognition and collective activity
constraints: Findings from typical small-scale, traditional study environments must be bridged carefully toward societal-level, long-timescale phenomena
target_learning_goals: understanding collaborative dialogue processes across timescales
examples: Diffusion-based centrality analysis of thousands of students' interactions and the multimodal dyad profiles featured in this issue illustrate small and large scale analytics that the editors situate along one spectrum
key_sources: Carolyn Rosé, Sanna Järvelä. (2021). A theory-driven reflection on context-aware support for collaborative discussions in light of analytics, affordances, and platforms. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-021-09360-8

article_title: Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning
citation: Lenka Schnaubert · Freydis Vogel. (2022). Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09367-9
title: Cognitive and social group awareness as distinct facets of social context perception in CSCL
description: The article conceptualizes group awareness as "the perception of relevant social information within the collaborative learning situation." It distinguishes cognitive group awareness (the distribution of knowledge or opinions in the group, affecting content-oriented processes and outcomes) from social group awareness (socio-behavioral and socio-emotional aspects affecting group climate and willingness to participate). Both enable learners to regulate and adapt their collaborative learning to the social configuration.
requirements: Goal-oriented collaboration requires awareness of the social context, especially characteristics of the collaborating group and its members
constraints: Social conditions in CSCL settings are highly dynamic; the technological layer can restrict rather than enrich communication channels, making perception of the social environment harder
target_learners: learners in computer-supported collaborative learning settings
target_learning_goals: effective collaboration and regulation of collaborative learning processes
examples: Group awareness tools collect, transform, and present social context information to ease or guide collaborative learning
key_sources: Lenka Schnaubert · Freydis Vogel. (2022). Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self-regulation in computer-supported collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:1–10. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09367-9

article_title: CSsCL: the performance of collaborative learning
citation: Charles Crook. (2022). CSsCL: the performance of collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09364-y
title: Scripting collaborative learning: external prompts and roles to support regulation of joint activity
description: A collaboration script structures joint learning activity by externally prompting participants with options for action: the article defines scripting as 'structuring a joint activity such that participants are externally prompted with possible options for action', with prompts such as requesting information, checking shared agreement, and summarising progress, often tied to assigned roles. Scripts are conceived both as guides for a specific task and as resources that may cultivate collaboration as a general competence through appropriation of 'internal scripts'. The article discusses how scripting depends on self-regulation and group awareness and is central to CSCL research integrating these three concepts.
requirements: Learners require support and direction to mobilise effective discursive resources during collaboration
Scripts must be interpreted by learners; over-scripting risks mechanical execution
constraints: Consistent definition of a script has proved troublesome in the literature
The term risks being used as just a trendy word for lesson plans unless core scripting is distinguished from the didactic envelope
target_learning_goals: collaboration as a general competence
shared knowledge building across cognitive, motivational, social, and emotional domains
examples: Kielstra et al. set solitary reading between collaborative planning and review episodes
Vogel et al. offered guidance in minimal or maximal detail chosen by learners
Zimmerman and Land used an observational checklist and three assigned roles

article_title: CSsCL: the performance of collaborative learning
citation: Charles Crook. (2022). CSsCL: the performance of collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09364-y
title: Collaboration-as-performance: direction, production, and audience as extensions of the theatre metaphor of scripting
description: The article takes seriously the theatre metaphor implied by 'collaboration script' and elaborates collaboration in performance terms, proposing 'three headings under which this question might be pursued: direction, production, and audience'. Direction places teachers in the director role who help students find meaning in script lines before performing them; production concerns how an intervention is produced as an occasion integrating with classroom routine; audience concerns researchers and report readers as witnesses of the performance. Metaphors risk importing unwanted expectations, such as over-scripting, but can provocatively steer neglected themes.
requirements: Teachers' director-like engagement (e.g. preparatory sense-making discussion of script lines) is assumed if performance is productive
Research environments such as teacher dashboards may support direction within the flow of joint activity
constraints: The theatre-script imposing force might encourage over-scripting of collaborations
Post-intervention student evaluations may solicit polite, calculated answers
Describing collaboration quality from recorded talk is challenged when reliability comes from local codebooks not adopted by others
target_learners: students in scripted collaborative learning episodes; teachers as directors; researchers as audience
target_learning_goals: productive collaborative knowledge building
cultivating students' confidence and ownership in collaboration
examples: Fischer et al. describe a group wiki 'play' with scenes and per-scene scripts
A teacher dashboard for monitoring ongoing collaborations illustrates in-flow direction
key_sources: Charles Crook. (2022). CSsCL: the performance of collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09364-y

article_title: Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2007). Welcome to the future: ijCSCL volume 2. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-007-9010-8
title: Community-based CSCL: communities of practice as socio-cultural contexts for collaborative learning
description: An account the editorial frames from the issue's two articles on learning in communities, specifying the collaborative in CSCL as "community based" in the sense that communities of practice, as introduced by Lave and Wenger, provide socio-cultural contexts in which collaborative learning can take place. Fischer, Rohde and Wulf elaborate CoPs with distinctions into networks of practice and communities of interest as variants, and the approach brings CSCW and HCI considerations into the CSCL discussion at what the editorial calls the macro-scale.
requirements: A community context (CoP or variant) within which computer-supported collaboration takes place.
constraints: Illustrated by the issue's articles in relation to universities and to non-profit organizations / NGOs; the editorial notes a reviewer may dispute whether pattern-based theory is strong enough for the field.
target_learners: Members of communities of practice, university students, and volunteers in community-based organizations
target_learning_goals: Learning through participation in communities, including learning how to design and use community-based learning technology
examples: Carroll and Faroque propose frameworks as a middle layer of theoretical constructs mediating between general patterns and individual cases, based on work with non-profit community-based organizations.

article_title: Collaborative analytics-supported reflective Assessment for Scaffolding Pre-service Teachers’ collaborative Inquiry and Knowledge Building
citation: Yang, Y., Zhu, G., Sun, D., & Chan, C. K. K. (2022). Collaborative analytics-supported reflective Assessment for Scaffolding Pre-service Teachers’ collaborative Inquiry and Knowledge Building. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09372-y
title: A conceptual design framework for PST collaborative inquiry combining knowledge building principles with collaborative-analytics reflective assessment
description: The article proposes a conceptual and design framework in which knowledge building principles emphasise "epistemic agency, idea improvement, community knowledge and transformative assessment" and PSTs take epistemic agency to foster idea improvement using transformative assessment focused on metacognitive reflection. Two key design components follow: sustained idea-driven knowledge building inquiry in Knowledge Forum writing, and collaborative analytics consisting of KBDeX visualizations plus interaction rubrics and prompt questions supporting metacognitive reflection. PSTs use the analytics to reflect on and assess ongoing Knowledge Forum work for deepening inquiry and revision.
requirements: PSTs must engage in sustained idea-driven inquiry for knowledge advancement situated in Knowledge Forum writing, posing questions, co-constructing explanations, building on peers’ ideas, and revising theories
Analytics, rubrics, and prompt questions must be provided so PSTs can reflect and assess their ongoing Knowledge Forum work
constraints: The framework is designed for pre-service teachers developing collaborative inquiry and knowledge building competencies; at the start of the course most PSTs had limited knowledge of and ability in collaborative inquiry and knowledge building
target_learners: pre-service teachers in higher education teacher preparation
target_learning_goals: collaborative inquiry competencies
knowledge building and community knowledge advancement
metacognitive reflection and epistemic agency

article_title: Co-constructing knowledge with generative AI tools: Reflections from a CSCL perspective
citation: Ulrike Cress · Joachim Kimmerle. (2023). Co-constructing knowledge with generative AI tools: Reflections from a CSCL perspective. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09409-w
title: Co-evolution model: knowledge construction as structural coupling of meaning-based cognitive and social systems
description: The co-evolution model, developed by Cress and Kimmerle, describes knowledge construction as a 'structural coupling of meaning-based cognitive and social systems'. Individual cognitions form an autopoietic cognitive system, while social systems are formed by communication in which utterances lead to further utterances. Both use language as a medium and can mutually irritate each other when expectations are slightly violated, which may lead to individual learning and collective knowledge construction. The article applies this framework to human-AI interaction, asking whether knowledge construction occurs only within human agents or between both agents.
requirements: Both cognitive and social systems use language as a medium through which they can influence each other
constraints: The article leaves open whether knowledge construction happens between human and AI agents, or whether knowledge development happens only within but not between agents
target_learners: learners interacting with generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: individual learning
collective knowledge construction
examples: The authors pose the open question whether human-AI collaboration is 'still a situation where both partners stimulate and irritate each other in such a way that knowledge development happens only within but not between agents'

article_title: Studying teacher withitness in the wild: comparing a mirroring and an alerting & guiding dashboard for collaborative learning
citation: Reet Kasepalu, Pankaj Chejara, Luis P. Prieto, Tobias Ley. (2023). Studying teacher withitness in the wild: comparing a mirroring and an alerting & guiding dashboard for collaborative learning. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2023) 18:575–606. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09414-z
title: CoTrack: MMLA collaboration analytics tool combining mirroring dashboard with an AI alerting & guiding layer
description: CoTrack is a web-based collaboration analytics tool mirroring student behaviour: it "collects audio data along with logs generated by collaborative writing", processing audio in real-time via Voice Activity Detection, Speech-to-Text, Speaking time and Turn taking, plus characters added or deleted in Etherpad. The mirroring dashboard visualises a 'who is talking after whom' network, word-clouds and writing bar graphs; the alerting & guiding layer uses a CNN trained on image-encoded multimodal features to predict ACARS collaboration-quality dimensions, with coregulation suggestions drawn from the Collaboration Intervention Model.
requirements: Teacher-facing display during authentic lessons; model feedback limited to dimensions with suitable model performance
constraints: Model predictions restricted to individual task orientation, cooperative orientation and sustaining mutual understanding; guiding suggestions delivered on paper by a researcher
target_learners: in-service teachers with student groups of 12 to 30
target_learning_goals: monitoring and improving collaboration quality in group work
examples: Twenty lessons with eleven class formations ran with the tool; T17 in the guiding condition followed all groups and received 5 alerts and suggestions for two groups

article_title: The perceptions of task cohesion in collaborative learning teams
citation: Zamecnik, A., Kovanović, V., Joksimović, S., Grossmann, G., Ladjal, D., Pardo, A. (2024). The perceptions of task cohesion in collaborative learning teams. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09424-5
title: Four-group taxonomy of team cohesion perception transitions (Aligned, Multifaceted, Regressive, Progressive)
description: The article organises teams by how their shared or divergent cohesion perceptions change between Week 1 and Week 3 into four transition groups: "Aligned (SS) – Week 1: Similar; Week 3: Similar", Multifaceted (DD), Regressive (SD), and Progressive (DS). Of 194 teams, "The number of teams (N) for the Aligned, Multifaceted, Regressive, and Progressive groups were 43, 72, 25, and 54, respectively", all averaging about five members. The taxonomy serves as the grouping variable for performance, engagement and synchrony comparisons.
requirements: Two survey assessment points (Week 1 and Week 3) with team-level agreement scoring (weighted Kappa threshold 0.33) to label perceptions as similar or different
constraints: Derived within a 3-week WIL program; the weighted Kappa 0.33 threshold defines the similar/different boundary, so groups depend on that cutoff
target_learners: Adult learners in team-based work-integrated learning programs
target_learning_goals: Teamwork and collaboration skills
Task cohesion in collaborative learning teams
examples: Teams were randomly grouped into teams of about five members across 15 program sessions, then categorised into one of the four groups based on their Weeks 1 and 3 survey agreement
key_sources: Zamecnik, A., Kovanović, V., Joksimović, S., Grossmann, G., Ladjal, D., Pardo, A. (2024). The perceptions of task cohesion in collaborative learning teams. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09424-5

article_title: Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs
citation: Bo Yang. (2024). Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09426-3
title: Community of Inquiry framework as the analytical lens for cognitive and socio-emotional interaction
description: The study adopts the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework of Garrison et al. (2000) to analyze cognitive and socio-emotional interaction in danmaku and on discussion boards. The article states the framework "delineates three interconnected elements—cognitive presence, social presence, and teaching presence—that collectively contribute to a meaningful educational experience." Cognitive presence is described as having four phases (initiation, exploration, integration, resolution), which the study used to interpret learners' question-asking and knowledge sharing. The original three presences were used rather than later expansions.
requirements: The framework is applied to learner-generated text in asynchronous, video-based online environments; a coding scheme derived from Rourke et al.'s social-presence template operationalizes it
constraints: The study used the original three types of presence and did not adopt later expansions such as additional presence types
Cognitive interaction categories were limited to two categories identified in a pilot analysis
target_learners: MOOC learners, primarily Grade 10 students in an informal Chinese math course
target_learning_goals: Understanding social interaction, collaboration, and cognitive engagement in large-scale online learning
examples: The author coded 2435 danmaku messages and 739 discussion-board posts against the CoI-derived scheme and interpreted initiation/exploration phases as evident but integration/resolution as absent
key_sources: Bo Yang. (2024). Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09426-3

article_title: Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs
citation: Bo Yang. (2024). Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09426-3
title: Combine danmaku with discussion boards so MOOC environments serve both large-community connectedness and small-group exchange
description: The article argues that because the two tools organize mass participation differently—one as a video-synchronized collective space, the other as threaded small-group discussion—pairing them covers complementary learner needs. It states that "learners can simultaneously benefit from both small-group and large-community environments," and that "the combination of danmaku and the discussion board in MOOCs has the potential to address diverse aspects of individual learners' demands." In the studied lecture, different needs such as information retrieval and temporary while-learning connectedness were both satisfied at least to some extent.
requirements: Both tools available on one course webpage, with the discussion board reachable for deeper threads and danmaku switchable in the video player
constraints: Claim rests on one naturalistic lecture in one informal math MOOC; collaboration proper was rare and occurred only in a small portion of knowledge-related discussions
target_learners: Adult and K–12 MOOC learners at large scale, including lurkers
target_learning_goals: Peer support, socio-emotional connectedness, question answering, and knowledge sharing in large-scale online courses
examples: In the studied lecture, two learners wrote detailed calculation explanations on the discussion board in response to questions raised in danmaku, showing synergy between the tools

article_title: Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry
citation: Ramy Elmoazen, Mohammed Saqr, Laura Hirsto, Matti Tedre. (2025). Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09431-6
title: Community of inquiry framework as a socio-cognitive foundation for operationalizing online collaborative discourse
description: The article uses the community of inquiry (CoI) framework as the coding lens for role identification, with "three main components, 'social presence, cognitive presence, and teaching presence,' that are necessary for a successful educational experience". Social presence covers affective, interactive and cohesive expression; cognitive presence proceeds through the phases of "triggering event, exploration, integration, and resolution"; teaching presence "organizes, facilitates, and directs" the other presences. The study coded student discourse with ten CoI elements and argues CoI supplies theory that quantitative learning analytics often lacks. Students' teaching presence was included because it can improve role identification.
requirements: Discourse must be codable into the CoI social, cognitive and teaching presence indicators, with trained coders achieving acceptable intercoder agreement
constraints: The framework was developed for asynchronous text-based online discussions; the resolution phase was excluded in this study due to disproportionately few posts (23)
target_learners: higher education students in problem-based learning
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
social interaction and group cohesion
shared teaching and facilitation behaviors
examples: The authors coded 9301 Moodle posts with CoI indicators (kappa rising from 0.76 to 0.88) and used the resulting states as variables for latent class role identification.
key_sources: Ramy Elmoazen, Mohammed Saqr, Laura Hirsto, Matti Tedre. (2025). Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09431-6

article_title: CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?
citation: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4
title: Collaboration Sciences: a proposed superclass of CSCL encompassing group dynamics, communication, and organizational learning
description: The authors propose a research domain, a superclass of CSCL, called the Collaboration Sciences, related to but not identical to the Learning Sciences. Blending Learning and Collaboration Sciences would let CSCL "gain a broader perspective on learning under the conditions of technology-mediated collaboration, including forms of group learning that are not designed for in advance", examining groups as learning and interacting entities.
requirements: Shared goals and methods with the Learning Sciences and with constituent fields such as small group research, CSCW, co-design, networked learning, and collaborative creativity
constraints: The authors note the risk that an orientation broader than the LS could lead to a theoretical Tower of Babel
target_learning_goals: theorising collaboration and group learning in CSCL research
examples: Zamecnik et al. (2024) applying a group-dynamics lens to task cohesion in collaborative learning teams is given as an example of this perspective applied to CSCL.
key_sources: Baker, M., Reimann, P. (2024). CSCL: a learning and collaboration science?. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-024-09433-4

article_title: Understanding the role of I-positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment
citation: Aaron J. Peltoniemi, Joni Lämsä, Sami Lehesvuori, Raija Hämäläinen. (2025). Understanding the role of I-positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09447-6
title: The computer as a dialogical other (technological other) in CSCL
description: The article suggests the computer "can represent a dialogical other that mediates learning and identity in CSCL", intertwining social resources such as interaction with content resources such as technical language and the learning task. Students consulted the technological other (I–it), where the computer's voices included the teacher's, the animator's and other media makers'. From the DST perspective, the computer was thus "not just a knowledge artifact for learning but also a social artifact for promoting or limiting discourse... at personal and group levels".
requirements: The technological other's voices emerge only when acted upon, e.g., by clicking, so the environment must expose task directions and media outputs learners can consult
constraints: Asynchronous technological scaffolding can disrupt the overall cohesiveness of collaboration and dialogue because it can only facilitate, not actively produce learning
target_learners: university students learning with computer-based learning tasks without a teacher present
target_learning_goals: inquiry-based conceptual understanding and collaborative problem solving
examples: Students could consult the computer's displayed directions and outputs (I–it), which represented a mesh of the teacher's, animator's and media makers' voices

Understanding the role of I-positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09447-6

article_title: The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review
citation: Shihui Feng, Ziyi Wei. (2025). The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09450-x
title: CoMPAS framework: six forms modeling the multi-faceted and multi-level nature of individual participation in collaborative learning
description: The CoMPAS framework models individual participation in collaborative learning processes across six components: Cognitive interactions, Coordinative interactions, Metacognitive interactions, Passive participation, solo Active participation, and Socio-emotional interactions. It was induced from a systematic review of 66 empirical studies via reflexive thematic analysis, and the article states it captures "the multi-faceted and multi-level nature of individual participation in collaborative learning processes." The framework distinguishes solitary forms (passive and solo active participation) from interactive forms, with the first two "named as passive participation and solo active participation and the other four forms as cognitive interactions, socioemotional interactions, metacognitive interactions, and coordinative interactions." Passive participation (12 studies) involves receiving information without overt contribution; solo active participation (46 studies) involves manipulating artefacts without interacting; the four interaction forms involve coconstruction with other group members.
requirements: Analysis must use process data rather than outcome-focused approaches, since group deliverables often do not provide direct evidence of individual participation
constraints: Derived from empirical studies meeting inclusion criteria that used process data; studies relying solely on summative individual assessments or group-level artefacts were outside the review's scope
target_learners: students in higher education (38 of 66 studies) and K-12 school contexts (14 of 66 studies) engaged in collaborative learning
target_learning_goals: understanding and assessing individual engagement and contribution within collaborative learning processes
supporting individual-level assessment and personalized feedback during group work
examples: The framework was built inductively from open coding of 66 articles followed by six-phase reflexive thematic analysis, with contributions ranging from solo active participation (45 studies assessed) to cognitive interactions (61 studies) and coordinative interactions (16 studies)
key_sources: Shihui Feng, Ziyi Wei. (2025). The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09450-x

article_title: Age-related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis
citation: Shigen Shimojo, Yugo Hayashi. (2025). Age-related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09456-5
title: Collaborative memory mechanisms of cross-cuing, re-exposure, and error pruning with shared knowledge as an external resource
description: The article reviews an information-processing account of why collaboration aids memory: "Blumen et al. (2013) explain the effects of collaborative learning through three mechanisms: cross-cuing, re-exposure, and error pruning." Cross-cuing treats partners' information as retrieval cues, re-exposure functions as an additional learning session, and error pruning increases correct recall while reducing errors. The study frames older adults' reliance on reactivating memory during interaction in these terms, positioning partners' externalized knowledge as an external cognitive resource integrated with internal cognition.
requirements: Interaction partners who externalize and share knowledge, e.g. via concept maps, so their knowledge can serve as retrieval cues
constraints: The review reports that merely acquiring information about a partner's knowledge is not sufficient to improve group performance
target_learning_goals: memory retrieval, encoding, and knowledge elaboration
examples: Older adults' utterance examples include re-reading the study text ('I think it said in the textbook...') to reactivate knowledge before elaborating
key_sources: Shigen Shimojo, Yugo Hayashi. (2025). Age-related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09456-5

article_title: Learning to deal with hate speech: An online collective intelligence experiment on the Collective Learning platform
citation: Tatiana Íñiguez-Berrozpe, Carmen Elboj-Saso, Francesco Marcaletti, Pablo Bautista-Alcaine. (2025). Learning to deal with hate speech: An online collective intelligence experiment on the Collective Learning platform. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09460-9
title: Collective Learning platform: seven-phase AI-moderated online collective intelligence tool
description: Collective Learning is an online tool built by Zaragoza University researchers and Kampal Data Solutions "designed to yield high-quality solutions to a wide range of problems by applying collective intelligence following a model of successive digital interactions among participants". Participants work on a practical case across a 35-min, seven-phase session: individual responses, then iterative interaction with four neighbours, AI-driven swapping of network positions, forced copying for inactive participants, deletion of low-prestige answers, and final top-ten consensus phases. An AI moderator spreads ideas, applies a popularity/prestige factor and controls heterogeneity so collective intelligence can emerge in large groups.
requirements: An AI moderator is deemed "essential for collective intelligence to emerge among large groups", with participants connected simultaneously during the session.
constraints: Each participant sees only four neighbours in phases 2–5 to avoid information overload; the design addresses risks of unoriginal answers, low-quality drift and turn-taking monopoly the article states.
target_learners: Spanish adolescents in obligatory secondary education (14–16 years old)
target_learning_goals: Responding constructively to online hate speech situations
collaborative reasoning and consensus formation
examples: In this study participants read a fictional case about a 16-year-old girl confronting hate speech on social networks and answered four quantitative questions across all phases
key_sources: Tatiana Íñiguez-Berrozpe, Carmen Elboj-Saso, Francesco Marcaletti, Pablo Bautista-Alcaine. (2025). article_title: Learning to deal with hate speech: An online collective intelligence experiment on the Collective Learning platform
citation: Tatiana Íñiguez-Berrozpe, Carmen Elboj-Saso, Francesco Marcaletti, Pablo Bautista-Alcaine. (2025). Learning to deal with hate speech: An online collective intelligence experiment on the Collective Learning platform. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09460-9
title: Collective intelligence as group performance exceeding mean individual performance in complex-task collaboration
description: The article adopts a construct in which "collective intelligence is defined as the performance of a large group of people collaborating on a series of complex tasks, generating responses and/or solutions in an aggregative manner, based on the idea that the mean individual performance of each member is lower than the mean performance obtained by the group". It is distinguished from group learning, defined as change within a group observable in cognition, task organisation and performance. Online environments expand the problem-solving potential by increasing participant numbers and permit an AI moderator to sustain quality, originality and interaction. The construct is used to hypothesise that CI experiments can help adolescents manage hate speech situations.
requirements: Emergence requires structured online interaction with an efficient AI moderator, conditions the article ties to large groups
constraints: The authors state conditions for emergence were met in the large group G1 but not in the small groups G2 and G3 in this study
target_learners: Adolescents collaborating in online school settings
target_learning_goals: Moral reasoning and ethical decision-making in digital contexts
collective problem-solving competencies
examples: Prior experiments applied online CI to moral dilemmas, significantly elevating groups' level of moral reasoning, as the article reports of Orejudo et al. and Bautista et al.

article_title: A collaboration literacy analytics framework (CLAF): Investigating students’ perspectives on collaboration quality indicators and feedback utilization
citation: Tochukwu Dominic Eze, Lucas Zurbuchen, Khalil Anderson, Marcelo Worsley. (2026). A collaboration literacy analytics framework (CLAF): Investigating students' perspectives on collaboration quality indicators and feedback utilization. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09475-w
title: Collaboration literacy as a metacognitive-behavioral construct of monitoring, interpreting, and responding to collaboration quality
description: The article defines collaboration literacy as extending beyond collaboration skills and competence: collaboration literacy emphasizes learners' ability to interpret and self-regulate collaboration using feedback and analytic representations. It is described as 'a metacognitive-behavioral construct that bridges collaboration skills, competence, and quality,' rooted in sociocultural theory (Vygotsky) and self-regulated learning theory (Zimmerman). Whereas competence describes what learners do in collaboration, collaboration literacy describes how learners understand, monitor, and act upon information about their collaboration. The study frames it as distinct from OECD-PISA performance-framed monitoring.
requirements: Learners must have access to indicators and feedback about their collaborative processes in order to interpret and self-regulate collaboration
constraints: The construct is framed as an analytic and regulatory orientation toward collaboration itself, not as a performance capacity
target_learners: University students in collaborative group activities
target_learning_goals: Monitoring and regulating quality of collaboration
Detecting declining collaboration quality and intervening productively
examples: The article builds on Worsley and Ochoa (2020), who define collaboration literacy from a student's perspective as awareness of one's contribution and intervening when bad indicators of poor collaboration arise.
key_sources: Tochukwu Dominic Eze, Lucas Zurbuchen, Khalil Anderson, Marcelo Worsley. (2026). A collaboration literacy analytics framework (CLAF): Investigating students' perspectives on collaboration quality indicators and feedback utilization. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-026-09475-w

citation: Tochukwu Dominic Eze, Lucas Zurbuchen, Khalil Anderson, Marcelo Worsley. (2026). title: Collaboration Literacy Analytics Framework (CLAF)
description: The CLAF is a conceptual framework 'that integrates evaluation metrics, indicator interdependencies, and feedback mechanisms.' It 'captures the dynamic relationship between process and outcome measures, connects individual- and group-level indicators, and incorporates review mechanisms as student-driven quality assurance.' The framework organizes learner-valued indicators across process, outcome, and review layers and links real-time feedback for immediate self-regulation with post hoc feedback for longer-term reflection and collaboration literacy development. It is grounded in consolidated collaboration dimensions and the student survey data.
requirements: CA systems must both represent collaborative processes and empower learners to interpret and respond to them
constraints: The framework is described as conceptual, providing an analytical basis for future CSCL research and practice rather than a validated measurement instrument
target_learners: University students collaborating in group activities
CSCL researchers and CA tool designers
target_learning_goals: Collaboration quality assessment
Self-regulation of collaboration
Collaboration literacy development
examples: The framework was developed from findings of an open-ended survey of 290 students after 12 weeks of CA tool-mediated activities across three task types: Minecraft game development, accessibility design brainstorming, and webpage accessibility implementation.

title: Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning Framework: shared diagnostic spaces built via collaborative diagnostic activities
description: The Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning Framework describes how individual diagnostic content — an individual evidence space (e.g., individual observations) and an individual hypothesis space (e.g., initial hypotheses) — becomes part of shared diagnostic spaces (a shared evidence space and a shared hypothesis space) through collaborative diagnostic activities such as elicitation, sharing, and negotiation. These "shared diagnostic spaces can then be seen as the basis for generating a collaborative diagnosis", and the activities are "expected to influence the accuracy of the collaboratively generated diagnosis".
requirements: Collaborators must apply elicitation, sharing, and negotiation activities to convert individual diagnostic spaces into shared diagnostic spaces
constraints: Empirical support was recently found in a medical context; the article notes it remains ambiguous how well the framework applies to other contexts such as teacher collaboration
target_learning_goals: collaborative diagnosis of pupils' cross-domain skills such as scientific reasoning

citation: Amadeus J. Pickal, Katharina Engelmann, Clark A. Chinn, Birgit J. Neuhaus, Raimund Girwidz, Christof Wecker. (2026). title: Coding scheme for collaborative diagnostic activities across 11 scientific reasoning sub-skills
description: Elicitation (asking for evidence pertinent to the diagnosed pupil's scientific reasoning skills), sharing (sharing such evidence), and negotiation (negotiating how consistent or contradictory observations affect the joint diagnosis) were coded from screen recordings at the level of the individual, for each of 11 sub-skills spanning hypothesis formulation, experimentation, and drawing conclusions. Dyad-level coverage variables counted sub-skills for which any participant performed an activity, divided by the maximum score of 11. Inter-coder agreement was acceptable to excellent (e.g., negotiation ICCabsolute = .67 in the learning phase; elicitation ICCabsolute = 1.00).
requirements: Two trained independent coders with a detailed coding manual; about 10% of recordings double-coded
constraints: Coding was independent of the accuracy or importance of the specific piece of information elicited, shared, or negotiated
target_learning_goals: measuring collaborative diagnostic activities during diagnosis of scientific reasoning skills
examples: Sample coded utterances included an elicitation of 'precision of hypotheses' and sharing about 'holding all other variables constant'

Signaling cues and focused prompts for professional vision support: The interplay of instructional design and situational interest in preservice teachers' video analysis. Instructional Science (2024) 52:879–917. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09662-y
title: Continuum-of-authenticity approximation tasks for training core practices
description: Following the Framework for Teaching Practice in Professional Education (Grossman et al., 2009, as cited), the article organizes novices' practice opportunities along increasing authenticity and complexity. "novices rehearse a particular element of practice on a continuum of authenticity, starting with approximation tasks that focus on a reduced set of practice components and have many low-stakes practice opportunities, and gradually work up to enacting the authentic practice itself with support". The study positions video analysis of simplified, scripted tutoring scenarios as one approximation step within this continuum.
requirements: tasks approximating authentic core teaching practices, with authenticity increasing gradually toward real teaching
constraints: beginning with real teaching scenarios is "often too complex and overwhelming" for teachers in training (Syring et al., 2015, as cited)

target_learning_goals: rehearsal of specific elements of professional practice such as professional vision
examples: The article sketches a path from written cases to video analysis, role-plays and simulations, then observations during student teaching.

article_title: The effects of competitive classroom activities on undergraduates with varied levels of competitive preference
citation: Daniell DiFrancesca, Dan Spencer. (2025). The effects of competitive classroom activities on undergraduates with varied levels of competitive preference. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09741-8
title: Constructive competition within Social Interdependence Theory
description: The article frames classroom competition through Social Interdependence Theory, which defines competition as a situation in which "individuals have similar goals and each individual's performance is impacted by the actions of others." Modern views place competition and cooperation on one continuum, and treat competition as constructive to learning "when winning is relatively unimportant, in situations in which all participants have a reasonable chance to win, and under circumstances in which there are clear, specific, and fair rules, procedures, and criteria for winning." The study designed its Kahoot activities (no grade impact, immediate feedback, leaderboard with normative comparisons) to meet this definition, and examined individual-difference predispositions toward competition alongside the situational context.
requirements: Competition must be low-stakes with winning relatively unimportant, a reasonable chance for all to win, and clear, specific, and fair rules and criteria for winning
constraints: The study did not test varied competitive-activity designs; it examined one constructive implementation in a single educational psychology course without a noncompetitive control classroom
target_learning_goals: content review and comprehension monitoring in course material
examples: Eight in-class Kahoot review games worth no course credit, scored on accuracy and speed with a cumulative leaderboard rewarding monitoring accuracy
key_sources: Daniell DiFrancesca, Dan Spencer. (2025). The effects of competitive classroom activities on undergraduates with varied levels of competitive preference. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09741-8

article_title: The effects of competitive classroom activities on undergraduates with varied levels of competitive preference
citation: Daniell DiFrancesca, Dan Spencer. (2025). The effects of competitive classroom activities on undergraduates with varied levels of competitive preference. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09741-8
title: Low-stakes constructive competitive review activities did not disadvantage low-competitive students relative to high-competitive students
description: The article reports that incorporating a constructive competitive activity (Kahoot) did not advantage highly competitive students over low-competitive students on learning outcomes, monitoring, motivation, or enjoyment, supporting the instructional use of such activities. As the authors put it, "Teachers' pedagogical decision to incorporate competitive activities to increase student engagement does not disadvantage students reporting low competitive tendencies." This holds when the activities follow constructive-competition guidelines and outcomes do not affect course grades.
requirements: Competition should follow constructive guidelines (winning relatively unimportant, reasonable chance for all, clear fair rules), and assessments should not count toward grades
constraints: No noncompetitive control classroom was included, so claims concern relative impacts on low- versus high-competitive students, not competition versus no competition; the course content covered motivational and learning theories, potentially shifting perceptions
target_learning_goals: review of course content with regular feedback and metacognitive monitoring practice
examples: A semester of eight five-item Kahoot comprehension checks in which top and bottom SIS tertiles showed similar performance, monitoring, and enjoyment outcomes
