article_title: Understanding the effects of constructivist learning environments: introducing a multi-directional approach
citation: Loyens, S. M. M., & Gijbels, D. (2008). Understanding the effects of constructivist learning environments: introducing a multi-directional approach. Instructional Science, 36, 351–357. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9059-4
title: Constructivism defined by its core assumption that knowledge is actively constructed by the learner
description: The article presents a working definition of constructivism: how people create meaning is "the main concern of constructivist theories," and although definitions vary, the perspectives share one core. "In essence, constructivism is a view of learning that considers the learner as a responsible, active agent in his/her knowledge acquisition process." Learners activate prior knowledge and interpret new information against it, so understanding is a function of knowledge construction rather than mere information accumulation.
requirements: The learner must function as a responsible, active agent in his or her knowledge acquisition process
constraints: A clear, unequivocal definition of constructivism is hard to find because the concept is defined and embodied in varied ways
target_learning_goals: knowledge construction and understanding of subject matter
key_sources: Loyens, S. M. M., & Gijbels, D. (2008). Understanding the effects of constructivist learning environments: introducing a multi-directional approach. Instructional Science, 36, 351–357. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9059-4

article_title: Understanding the effects of constructivist learning environments: introducing a multi-directional approach
citation: Loyens, S. M. M., & Gijbels, D. (2008). Understanding the effects of constructivist learning environments: introducing a multi-directional approach. Instructional Science, 36, 351–357. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9059-4
title: Constructivist learning environments built around four assumed elements: active construction, cooperation, self-regulation, and authentic problems
description: The article characterizes constructivist learning environments by several features believed to promote effective learning. These are active knowledge construction building on prior knowledge, cooperative learning in which social interactions contribute to knowledge building, self-regulated learning through goal setting and monitoring, and confronting students with "complex, ill-structured problems" similar to future professional problems. Educators applying constructivism combine these elements in learning environments.
requirements: Learning situations that preferably resemble real-life or authentic situations, with prior knowledge activated and social interaction supported
constraints: The constitution of the instructional principles of constructivist theory often remains unclear, and constructivists have different opinions concerning the influence of cooperation on knowledge acquisition
target_learning_goals: deep understanding of subject matter and problem-solving skills

title: CORDTRA diagrams for visually representing the chronology of tool use and discourse in collaborative learning analysis
description: CORDTRA stands for Chronologically-ordered Representations of Discourse and Tool-Related Activity. The Hmelo-Silver, Chernobilsky, and Jordan study uses "CORDTRA diagrams in order to demonstrate how visually representing the chronology of tool use and discourse in an activity can enhance analysis of collaborative learning in a computer supported learning environment." Their analyses locate differences in how students use resources and engage in metacognitive talk and knowledge transforming activities, sometimes to the group's detriment.
requirements: A computer supported learning environment in which tool use and discourse can be logged and ordered chronologically for analysis
constraints: Differences in how groups use resources and engage in metacognitive talk can be to the group's detriment

article_title: Contact-2: a computer-assisted instructional strategy for promoting conceptual change
citation: Biemans, H.J.A., Simons, P.RJ. (1996). Contact-2: a computer-assisted instructional strategy for promoting conceptual change. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF00120487
title: The CONTACT strategy: continuous, computer-assisted activation of individual learners' conceptions to promote conceptual change
description: The CONTACT strategy is an instructional approach premised on the idea that students need guidance to activate and correct their preconceptions in text processing. It is "characterised by continuous, computer-assisted activation of the conceptions of individual learners". The article situates it within conceptual-change instruction and demonstrates it with fifth- and sixth-graders studying physical geography texts, where it helped students construct more correct conceptions, though learners attended selectively to central concepts.
requirements: Continuous computer-assisted activation operating on the conceptions of individual learners during instruction
constraints: Original version induced selective attention: students mainly focused on the central concepts from the training texts, disregarding other information
target_learners: Fifth- and sixth-grade primary education students
target_learning_goals: Conceptual change in text processing (domain: physical geography)
examples: The original CONTACT study showed that students constructed more correct conceptions from training texts in physical geography.

article_title: Exploring interconnections between communicative activities, situational stress reactions and cognitive engagement in undergraduate mathematics lesson
citation: Lehesvuori, S., Järvinen, M., Lämsä, J., Heilala, V., Hämäläinen, R. (2026). Exploring interconnections between communicative activities, situational stress reactions and cognitive engagement in undergraduate mathematics lesson. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09786-3
title: Communicative-activity coding scheme with eight teacher-level and seven individual student-level codes for mathematics lesson interaction
description: The coding scheme maps observable communicative activities in a mathematics lesson at 20-second intervals. Teacher-level codes (N = 210 intervals) include teacher presentation, scaffolding questions, correcting/complementing, and whole-class discussion; individual student-level codes (N = 3*210 intervals) include active/passive listening, student presentation, student question, and peer discussion. Codes were grounded in prior classroom-interaction research and context-specific variations of the IRF pattern, and the scheme achieved "a Cohen's kappa value of 0.70 for the teacher codes and 0.77 for the student codes, indicating substantial agreement."
requirements: Video recording of the lesson and application of the interruption rule coding any (inter)active communicative activity interrupting listening or presentation within a 20-second interval
constraints: Designed for observable communicative activities only; does not quantitatively scale levels of engagement
target_learning_goals: characterising teacher and student communicative participation in problem-solving and presentation lessons
examples: Applied to one two-hour undergraduate mathematics demonstration session where students presented homework solutions at the whiteboard

citation: Yoon, Susan A.; Anderson, Emma; Koehler-Yom, Jessica; Evans, Chad; Park, Miyoung; Sheldon, Joshua; Schoenfeld, Ilana; Wendel, Daniel J; Scheintaub, Hal; Klopfer, Eric. (2016). Teaching about complex systems is no simple matter: building effective professional development for computer-supported complex systems instruction. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-016-9388-7
title: Computer-supported complex systems curricula delivered in science classrooms
description: Computer-supported complex systems curricula are classroom science materials in which computational tools support student learning about complex systems, a topic that next generation science standards in the United States emphasize as "a core feature of science learning". The article studies teachers' delivery of such curricula in a 2-year professional development project, gathering data on teachers' abilities and perceptions. The curricula's classroom implementation is the setting in which the article's teacher-support findings arise.
requirements: Effective delivery depends on teacher-side supports, including differentiated expertise-building opportunities and addressing teacher beliefs about computational-model construction in the science classroom.
constraints: Little research has been devoted to identifying the supports teachers need to teach about complex systems in the classroom, per the article's gap statement.
target_learners: K-12 science students in classrooms using computer-supported complex systems curricula
target_learning_goals: learning about complex systems in science
examples: The 2-year professional development study examined delivery of computer-supported complex systems curricula, with students' classroom experiences and learning offered to illustrate the impact of the instructional supports.

article_title: Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners
citation: Ashlyn Pierson, D. Teo Keifert, Bethany Daniel, Sarah Lee, Tessaly Jen, Adam Bell, Heather Johnson, Rachel Askew, Andrea Henrie. (2024). Designing to support equity-as-transformation perspectives for multilingual science learners. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09674-8
title: Provide teachers explicit opportunities to connect new equity perspectives with day-to-day classroom teaching experiences
description: The article concludes that, for practice, PD must "underscore the importance of providing teachers with opportunities to explicitly connect new perspectives of equity with day-to-day experiences of classroom teaching" (Abstract, practice implications). The redesign succeeded when facilitators gave significant time for small-group discussion tying big ideas to practical, real-world stories, whereas abstract ideological debriefs alone reified deficit framings. The principle holds that transformative equity perspectives need structured occasions where teachers apply them to their own students' work, language, and classroom events.
requirements: Structured discussion time connecting concepts of equity to teachers' own teaching contexts, including student work and state assessment pressures
constraints: Applies to professional development design contexts; the article's evidence is a multi-year case study of one district partnership
target_learning_goals: Taking up equity-as-transformation perspectives in everyday science teaching
examples: In the second storybook iteration, facilitators tied discussion of big ideas to real-world stories through significant small-group discussion time

article_title: Investigating the effectiveness of a POE-based teaching activity on students’ understanding of condensation
citation: Bayram Costu, Alipasa Ayas, Mansoor Niaz. (2011). Investigating the effectiveness of a POE-based teaching activity on students' understanding of condensation. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-011-9169-2
title: Condensation Conceptual Test (CCT): a five-item diagnostic combining two-tier and open-ended formats
description: The CCT is a purpose-designed test for assessing conceptual change about condensation. The article states it "consist[ed] of five items ... developed based on the alternative conceptions derived from the literature", comprising one two-tier multiple-choice item, two true/false two-tiered items, and open-ended items. Items were piloted with 31 students and validated by a panel of three chemistry teachers and two teacher educators, then administered as pre-, post-, and delayed post-tests.
requirements: Two-tiered item scoring categories (e.g., T-T = 3 points) and open-ended categories SU 3, PU 2, SM 1, NU 0, NR 0
constraints: Open-ended response coding used two raters with about 90% agreement, differences resolved by negotiation
target_learners: first-year university primary science education students
target_learning_goals: diagnosing and measuring conceptual change on condensation
examples: Item 5 asks students to explain where water droplets on a cold bottle taken from a refrigerator come from

article_title: When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains
citation: Valentina Nachtigall · Katja Serova · Nikol Rummel. (2020). When failure fails to be productive: probing the effectiveness of productive failure for learning beyond STEM domains. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-020-09525-2
title: Instruction that contrasts four typical erroneous solution features with components of the canonical solution
description: This instructional pattern structures the delayed instruction phase of a PF lesson: the instructor walks through ways in which typical student solutions fall short of each component of a canonical solution. For the experimental-design topic, the article's Table 3 pairs four error features (e.g. "No inclusion of a control condition") with corresponding canonical components (e.g. "Inclusion of a control condition"), presented in a step-by-step explanation based on pilot-test results, so that students can recognize their specific knowledge gaps and the deep features of the concept.
requirements: Typical erroneous solution features must be identified in advance (here via pilot tests) so the standardized lesson can target them
A canonical solution with clearly definable components must exist for the targeted concept
target_learning_goals: principles of experimental design, including control conditions, systematic variation of variables, pretest administration, and measurement of control variables
examples: Table 3 contrasts student solutions lacking control conditions, systematic variation, pretests, and control-variable measurement with the corresponding canonical design components.

article_title: Examining secondary school students’ views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology
citation: Lee, S. W.-Y., Wu, H., & Chang, H. (2021). Examining secondary school students' views of model evaluation through an integrated framework of personal epistemology. Instructional Science, 49, 223–248. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09534-9
title: Contextualized model-evaluation items presenting two competing models and three epistemic assumptions
description: The study developed model-evaluation items with three design characteristics: they are "contextualized by real scientific problems," they "present at least two competing models," and they "present three epistemic positions for the students to choose from." Two item sets were built on SARS virus infection models and dinosaur-extinction models, deliberately chosen as non-textbook science contexts with high uncertainty. After reading about the two models, students chose among three epistemic assumptions and wrote justifications explaining their choice.
requirements: Item review by co-authors and by two middle school teachers and one high school teacher to ensure construct, face, and content validity
constraints: The two contexts were intentionally non-textbook and possessed high levels of uncertainty, since scientists are still attempting to understand the mechanisms or causes
target_learning_goals: assessing students' epistemic views of scientific model evaluation
examples: Two models of SARS virus infection and two explanatory models of dinosaur extinction were presented, and students chose among assumptions such as "one model is better than another" and "depends on the evidence"

article_title: Learning with concept maps: the effect of activity structure and the type of task
citation: Amante, C., Lucero, M., & Montanero, M. (2026). Learning with concept maps: the effect of activity structure and the type of task. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09764-1
title: Collective working memory account of why collaborative self-construction of concept maps supports learning
description: The article explains the advantage of collaborative map self-construction through a collective-working-memory account: dialogic conversation distributes the proposing and evaluating of representational alternatives across partners, so "the exchange and integration of information that characterizes dialogic conversation would generate a kind of collective working memory" that reduces the load on any single member's working memory. The authors link this to cognitive load theory, noting that individually constructing a map from a text requires producing and evaluating many alternatives, which overloads working memory. Peer help in the deep exploratory episodes of self-constructed CM pairs showed co-inference processes that offset this load.
requirements: Tasks complex enough that the intrinsic load justifies collaboration; the article states collaboration is only truly effective "when the task is sufficiently complex to justify the extra time and effort involved in collaborating with others".
constraints: Peer help showed no significant effect over individual work for relatively simple tasks such as completing a mutilated map, because the intrinsic load is much lighter.
target_learners: Undergraduate students with little or no experience using concept maps
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and delayed recall of academic text content
examples: Pairs who created complete maps showed deep exploratory episodes with co-inference, distributing the work of proposing and evaluating concept representations.
key_sources: Amante, C., Lucero, M., & Montanero, M. (2026). Learning with concept maps: the effect of activity structure and the type of task. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09764-1

article_title: Authentic evidence from the ‘SRL-AIDE’ simulative environment on explicitness and duration of in-class SRL teaching practices
citation: Orna Heaysman, Bracha Kramarski. (2026). Authentic evidence from the 'SRL-AIDE' simulative environment on explicitness and duration of in-class SRL teaching practices. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09787-2
title: Teacher PD for SRL should combine explicit theoretical instruction with authentic simulation-based practice, since promoting independence (KC) alone does not build metacognitive instruction capacity
description: The article recommends that effective SRL development for teachers requires "explicit theoretical instruction combined with authentic practice opportunities", because promoting independence through knowledge construction alone does not build teachers' capacity for explicit metacognitive instruction. PD programs should integrate direct and indirect SRL approaches with extended duration and simulation-based experiences allowing practice and reflection. The study's comparison of the SRL-AIDE group against a KC-focused comparison program provides the empirical basis for this recommendation.
requirements: PD programs need extended duration and simulation-based experiences allowing practice and reflection, per the article's implications section
constraints: The evidence comes from a quasi-experimental study of 70 elementary teachers in grades 3–5 in central Israel; the authors note student outcomes and other practice types remain untested
target_learning_goals: teachers' capacity to implement metacognitive strategic support and knowledge construction practices in class
examples: The SRL-AIDE group received explicit SRL theory instruction plus live-actor simulation workshops, while the comparison group received only KC-focused instruction; only the SRL-AIDE group's KC duration increased significantly

article_title: Fostering knowledge integration through individual competencies: the impacts of perspective taking, reflexivity, analogical reasoning and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty
citation: Olga Vogel, Marcel Hunecke. (2024). Fostering knowledge integration through individual competencies: the impacts of perspective taking, reflexivity, analogical reasoning and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09653-5
title: Competencies of Knowledge Integration questionnaire: four newly developed self-report scales
description: A newly developed questionnaire measuring intraindividual competencies for knowledge integration, built from theoretical definitions in the ITD context with 52 initial Likert-scale items. After item reduction and residual correlations, "The resulting model contained a total of 23 items and provided an acceptable model fit (χ 2(217) = 372.408, p < 0.001, CFI = 0.913, TLI = 0.900, RMSEA = 0.045, SRMR = 0.055)". Reflexivity retained six items, perspective taking five, analogical reasoning eight, and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty seven.
requirements: Items with factor loadings λ < 0.300 and discriminative power r it < 0.300 were stepwise excluded during scale development
constraints: Perspective taking and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty had internal consistencies of α > .600, considered low but acceptable, and AVE was below .50; the authors state low reliability could have caused low beta weights and non-significant effects in the scientific sample
target_learning_goals: assessing individual competencies that support knowledge integration in ITD work
examples: Example item for perspective taking: "It is easy for me to put myself in the perspective of other disciplines."
key_sources: Olga Vogel, Marcel Hunecke. (2024). Fostering knowledge integration through individual competencies: the impacts of perspective taking, reflexivity, analogical reasoning and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09653-5

article_title: Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant?
citation: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8
title: Design discovery tasks by deliberately covering up and constraining the problem space; more autonomy demands better task design
description: The article argues that teaching for discovery always involves deciding what to cover up and what to let students discover: "there is no teaching for discovery learning without covering up." Teachers and designers put constraints on the problem space in which students carry out tasks, and it is the designer or teacher who judges which constraints will be productive for the target knowledge or skill. The paradox is that "the more autonomy we want to give students, the better we have to design the tasks."
requirements: Designers and teachers must make professional judgments about which constraints on the problem space will be productive for the target knowledge or skill.
constraints: Some things can and should be told; discovery is appropriate only for what cannot be transmitted and must be constructed or experienced.
target_learners: Students in domain-specific didactic settings such as statistics and mathematics education
target_learning_goals: Discovering or reinventing insights that cannot simply be told
examples: Levy et al. designed constraints into the TrafficJams system to limit possible actions so as to guide and focus students on particular aspects of the system.
key_sources: Arthur Bakker. (2018). Discovery learning: zombie, phoenix, or elephant? Instructional Science, 46, 169–183. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9450-8

article_title: Preservice elementary science teachers’ argumentation competence: impact of a training programme
citation: Daniel Cebrián-Robles; Antonio-Joaquín Franco-Mariscal; Ángel Blanco-López. (2018). Preservice Elementary Science Teachers' Argumentation Competence: Impact of a Training Programme. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9446-4
title: CoRubric e-rubric tool for online peer assessment of arguments
description: CoRubric is an e-rubric designed by one of the authors of this research and available free of charge, used in the programme's second peer assessment so PESTs could assess and justify their scores through online rubrics. The article lists its advantages: peer assessment (formative assessment), which allows for multiple evaluations to check progress, role management using notes and comments and exporting results to other programmes for treatment. It supports a 360º assessment, i.e., peer assessment, self-assessment and teacher assessment of the questions.
requirements: Supports online rubrics for peer, self and teacher assessment of the same questions
target_learning_goals: Peer assessment of arguments
Formative self-monitoring of argumentation competence
examples: Used in Session 2 for a second peer assessment of the tooth decay answers, this time using the specific rubric, to check whether there was any more consistency in the results when using the specific rubric
key_sources: Daniel Cebrián-Robles; Antonio-Joaquín Franco-Mariscal; Ángel Blanco-López. (2018). Preservice Elementary Science Teachers' Argumentation Competence: Impact of a Training Programme. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-018-9446-4

article_title: Supports for preservice teachers’ metacognitive monitoring and explanations of fraction comparisons
citation: Guba, T.-P., Barbieri, C. A., Jansen, A., & Morris, A. (2026). Supports for preservice teachers' metacognitive monitoring and explanations of fraction comparisons. Instructional Science (2026) 54:18. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09773-0
title: Give preservice teachers a fully correct and complete exemplar to compare against their own mathematical explanations
description: When learners cannot receive direct instructor feedback, the article recommends providing a fully correct and complete explanation they can compare and contrast with their own draft. The authors write this "would be a proxy for getting direct feedback from their instructor on their explanation" and "is similar in design to correct examples within the worked examples literature." Their experiment found this support produced greater explanation improvement and error detection than misconception examples or a features list, informing instructional materials design for pre-service teacher mathematics content courses.
requirements: The exemplar must include the correct answer, a complete explanation of how it was obtained, and a visual representation
Learners need an explicit prompt to list differences between their draft and the exemplar before revising
target_learning_goals: revising explanations of fraction magnitude comparisons for correctness and completeness
examples: In the CE condition, the support was marked correct with a checkmark and included an equally partitioned rectangle (fraction strip) for visual comparison, and participants were asked to number and describe each difference before rewriting
key_sources: Guba, T.-P., Barbieri, C. A., Jansen, A., & Morris, A. (2026). Supports for preservice teachers' metacognitive monitoring and explanations of fraction comparisons. Instructional Science (2026) 54:18. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09773-0

article_title: Productive failure in learning from generation and invention activities
citation: Manu Kapur, Nikol Rummel. (2012). Productive failure in learning from generation and invention activities. Instr Sci 40:645-650. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9235-4
title: Provide content-general support during generation that helps without telling students the targeted content
description: Across the special issue's studies, support during the generation phase was "mainly content-general in that it does not provide speciﬁc mathematical content to students during the generation phase" — affective support, role-play support for interaction, metacognitive support, or high-ability peers. Support structures are "designed to keep students from unproductive failure experiences, while leaving a central portion of student activity unstructured, thus allowing for productive failure." This distinguishes support from direct instruction.
requirements: Support must help students without giving or telling them the targeted content knowledge directly
A central portion of student activity must remain unstructured
target_learners: 9th-grade to university students learning mathematics and statistics
target_learning_goals: generating and exploring representations and solution methods for novel concepts
examples: Kapur provided affective support and encouragement to persist; Westermann and Rummel provided the TAU role script; Roll et al. provided metacognitive prompts
key_sources: Manu Kapur, Nikol Rummel. (2012). Productive failure in learning from generation and invention activities. Instr Sci 40:645-650. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-012-9235-4

article_title: Testing the testing effect with advanced materials while accounting for individual differences
citation: Redifer, J. L., Myers, S. J., Bae, C. L., Naas, A., & Scott, A. (2026). Testing the testing effect with advanced materials while accounting for individual differences. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09758-z
title: Cognitive load balance account of the testing effect with advanced materials
description: The article proposes that retrieval practice produces two opposite effects on memory: a positive effect through more effortful learning and memory-strengthening mechanisms, and a negative effect through the additional cognitive load it imposes. The authors state that "engaging in retrieval practice is most likely leading to two opposite effects", and that a testing effect occurs only when the positive effects outweigh the load costs; when mental demands interfere with retrieval's potential benefits, retrieval practice is no longer the superior strategy. This account explains why no retrieval condition beat rereading with advanced materials.
requirements: Enough cognitive resources must remain available during retrieval practice for a substantial memory search and strengthening of memory details
constraints: With materials demanding enough (e.g., a published research article), the load cost of retrieval can cancel its memorial benefits, as observed in this study
target_learners: undergraduate students learning advanced reading materials such as published research articles
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of advanced, complex educational content
examples: In the study, all retrieval conditions rated higher cognitive load than rereading, load fully mediated the strategy-to-performance relationship, and no condition outperformed rereading on the one-week delayed test.
key_sources: Redifer, J. L., Myers, S. J., Bae, C. L., Naas, A., & Scott, A. (2026). Testing the testing effect with advanced materials while accounting for individual differences. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09758-z

article_title: Living the DReaM: The interrelations between statistical, scientific and nature of science uncertainty articulations through citizen science
citation: Aridor, K., Dvir, M., Tsybulsky, D., & Ben-Zvi, D. (2023). Living the DReaM: The interrelations between statistical, scientific and nature of science uncertainty articulations through citizen science. Instr Sci, 51, 729–762. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09626-8
title: Design learning activities to concurrently foster statistical, scientific and nature of science reasoning
description: The article recommends designing activities that address all three reasoning types at once, since responsible citizenship and decision-making require appreciating uncertainty in data-based knowledge. It examines 'the uncertainties that young students articulate as they engage in activities designed to concurrently foster all three types of reasoning'. Designing for concurrency lets students coordinate across uncertainty types.
requirements: Learning activities must engage students in authentic data-based scientific practices
target_learning_goals: uncertainty articulation
scientific reasoning
statistical reasoning
nature of science understanding
examples: The Radon Citizen Science Project interdisciplinary extended learning sequence for middle school students
key_sources: Aridor, K., Dvir, M., Tsybulsky, D., & Ben-Zvi, D. (2023). Living the DReaM: The interrelations between statistical, scientific and nature of science uncertainty articulations through citizen science. Instr Sci, 51, 729–762. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09626-8

article_title: Peer versus staff tutoring in problem-based learning
citation: Schmidt, H., van der Arend, A., Kokx, I. & Boon, L. (1995). Peer versus staff tutoring in problem-based learning. Instructional Science 22: 279-285.
title: Cognitive congruence framework for peer versus staff tutoring
description: The cognitive congruence framework holds that tutors are effective when there is congruence between their cognitive structures and those of the tutees, which "would qualify the student tutors to better understand the difficulties encountered by the tutees". It is balanced against a subject-matter knowledge argument, that student tutors' lesser knowledge risks a 'pooling of ignorance'. The article uses it to interpret why peer tutors were rated higher and equally effective in the first year, while staff tutors' subject-matter expertise becomes more important over the course of the years.
requirements: Tutors must display an understanding of the way in which students think and express themselves in their language for cognitive congruence to operate
constraints: Subject-matter expertise of the tutor becomes more important only over the course of the years, limiting congruence advantages to early curriculum years
target_learners: Higher education students in problem-based curricula
target_learning_goals: Facilitating learning in small-group problem-based tutorials
examples: The field experiment found no achievement difference in year 1, where students prefer tutors behaving 'cognitively congruent'
key_sources: Schmidt, H., van der Arend, A., Kokx, I. & Boon, L. (1995). Peer versus staff tutoring in problem-based learning. Instructional Science 22: 279-285. https://doi.org/10.1007/bf00891781

article_title: The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations
citation: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z
title: Teachers’ conceptions of teaching as a framework theory used to interpret and predict teaching situations
description: The article draws on the idea that conceptions of teaching — beliefs about teaching that underlie its purpose and strategies — form a coherent framework through which teachers read classroom events. As it puts it, “the conceptions the teacher holds form a framework theory the teacher can use in explaining and predicting teaching situations”. Conceptions range from teaching as knowledge transmission to teaching as learning facilitation, and they are linked to content-focused versus learning-focused approaches to teaching, which in turn relate to students’ surface versus deep approaches to learning. The study operationalises this lens by coding teachers’ written interpretations of scripted video trigger events.
requirements: Conceptions are measured indirectly through interpretations of authentic teaching situations rather than directly through self-report items
constraints: The article notes the relationship between approaches and conceptions is not exclusive: teachers “may adopt elements of both approaches in their teaching and hold conceptions that mirror elements of both conception categories”
target_learners: Doctoral students with or without teaching duties
target_learning_goals: Developing learning-facilitation conceptions of teaching
Interpreting teaching–learning situations in terms of student learning
examples: Participants’ interpretations of a lecture interruption were coded as knowledge transmission (e.g. postponing questions to the end of the lecture) or learning facilitation (e.g. valuing interaction and activating students).
key_sources: Henna Vilppu, Ilona Södervik, Liisa Postareff, Mari Murtonen. (2019). The effect of short online pedagogical training on university teachers’ interpretations of teaching–learning situations. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-019-09496-z

article_title: English learners learn from worked example comparison in algebra
citation: Xiaojuan Ke · Kristie J. Newton. (2024). English learners learn from worked example comparison in algebra. Instructional Science (2024) 52:831–858. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09668-6
title: Cognitive load account of mathematics learning in a second language
description: The article frames ELs' mathematics learning through cognitive load theory: working memory handles only a very limited number of novel interacting elements and retains information for only about 30 seconds, and ELs additionally use working memory to translate or code-switch between L1 and L2. Worked examples are presented as a way to reduce cognitive load, and the authors argue the goal "is not to reduce the cognitive demands of the task, but to help ELs fully utilize their bilingual strengths to learn mathematics." This account motivates the MLS-WEPs design and its language supports.
requirements: Instructional methods that reduce ELs' cognitive load in working memory, while keeping the cognitive demands of the task themselves intact
constraints: The account applies to mathematics learned in a second-language context, where translation and code-switching add working-memory demands relative to native-speaking peers
target_learners: English learners in K-12 mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: Algebraic problem solving
Mathematical reasoning and explanation
examples: The article uses this account to justify worked examples with detailed problem-solving descriptions and to interpret why ELs benefited across proficiency levels
key_sources: Xiaojuan Ke · Kristie J. Newton. (2024). English learners learn from worked example comparison in algebra. Instructional Science (2024) 52:831–858. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09668-6

article_title: The effects of scaffolding in the classroom: support contingency and student independent working time in relation to student achievement, task effort and appreciation of support
citation: van de Pol, J., Volman, M., Oort, F., & Beishuizen, J. (2015). The effects of scaffolding in the classroom: support contingency and student independent working time in relation to student achievement, task effort and appreciation of support. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9351-z
title: Contingent shift framework for measuring scaffolding contingency in classroom interaction
description: The contingent shift framework, based on Wood et al. (1978), operationalizes scaffolding as the tailored adaptation of the degree of control in teacher support to a student's demonstrated understanding. The article states: "If a teacher used more control after a student’s demonstration of poor understanding and less control after a student’s demonstration of good understanding, we labelled the support contingent." Teacher turns are coded for degree of control from zero to five, student turns for demonstrated understanding, and contingency is scored as the percentage of contingent three-turn sequences per teacher. The article uses this framework as the measure of support quality in its classroom experiment.
requirements: Coding requires transcribed teacher-student interaction fragments and a three-turn-sequence unit; diagnosing or evaluating student understanding is needed before support can be contingent.
constraints: The article notes most studies, unlike this one, did not use such a dynamic operationalization; contingency scores were class-level, so all students of a class shared the same score.
target_learners: Pre-vocational secondary students (age 12-15) working in small groups
target_learning_goals: Subject-matter achievement in social studies (European Union project)
examples: Teachers' interaction fragments were coded for degree of control (0-5) and student understanding; the contingency score was the percentage of contingent three-turn sequences per teacher per measurement occasion.
key_sources: van de Pol, J., Volman, M., Oort, F., & Beishuizen, J. (2015). The effects of scaffolding in the classroom: support contingency and student independent working time in relation to student achievement, task effort and appreciation of support. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-015-9351-z

article_title: Accommodating heterogeneity: the interaction of instructional scaffolding with student preconditions in the learning of hypothesis-based reasoning
citation: Hanna Grimm · Peter A. Edelsbrunner · Kornelia Möller. (2023). Accommodating heterogeneity: the interaction of instructional scaffolding with student preconditions in the learning of hypothesis-based reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09601-9
title: In whole-class inquiry, combine a static structuring scaffold with teacher modeling and adaptive problematizing verbal scaffolds to serve heterogeneous student preconditions
description: The article argues that scaffolding connects two ways of dealing with heterogeneity: adapting deep structures (quality of teacher-student interaction through cognitive activation) rather than only sight structures. In the experimental condition, students received a structuring scaffold in which the teacher, supported by a visual aid, modeled the reasoning process, and — as the article states — "the teacher provides cognitively activating, problematizing verbal scaffolds during students' inquiry to react adaptively to students' difficulties with the reasoning process". This combination aimed to let a static scaffold serve students with differing prior knowledge, inhibition ability, and logical reasoning.
requirements: Teachers must be trained to deliver the modeling sequence and adaptive questions; this study supplied three three-hour courses and detailed teaching scripts
The inquiry tasks must be structured, e.g., by a predetermined order of hypotheses of increasing difficulty, which was also part of the control condition
constraints: Prototypical scaffolding takes more time than is generally available in day-to-day science instruction, so similar support is often provided for all students instead of individually tailored support
Essential scaffolding elements such as consistent diagnosis and fading of support should not be neglected
target_learners: third-graders in heterogeneous whole school classes
target_learning_goals: acquiring hypothesis-based reasoning with conditionals in inquiry-based science
examples: Within an elasticity unit on 'the bouncing ball', experimental-condition teachers modeled reasoning with the sorting box, then faded problematizing questions as student pairs no longer needed them
key_sources: Hanna Grimm · Peter A. Edelsbrunner · Kornelia Möller. (2023). Accommodating heterogeneity: the interaction of instructional scaffolding with student preconditions in the learning of hypothesis-based reasoning. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09601-9

article_title: Deficit narratives as teacher foils: how vulnerability and emotional regimes shape teacher discourse
citation: Samantha A. Marshall, Grace A. Chen. (2025). Deficit narratives as teacher foils: how vulnerability and emotional regimes shape teacher discourse. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09740-9
title: Collective vulnerability as interactionally produced by destabilization of emotional regimes
description: Extending prior work that treated vulnerability as individual or as threats to group reputation, the article proposes that collective vulnerability can be interactionally produced when a group's normative emotional terrain is destabilized. If "affirmation and positivity are the normative way for teachers to relate to each other in a group, and a teacher breaches this norm through sustained negativity," the group's expectations of each other may be threatened. This account links vulnerability to face threats from video-based PD, where practice is on display with decreased room for plausible deniability.
requirements: Analysis must trace how a critique becomes a threat through the collective response to it
constraints: Proposed from two extreme cases of asset-oriented teachers; the authors state they do not know whether teacher vulnerability commonly precipitates deficit narratives
target_learners: teacher teams in video-based professional development
target_learning_goals: collaborative sensemaking about teaching practice
professional identity maintenance
examples: In both focal cases, the destabilization of emotional regimes by persistent negative self-critique produced collective vulnerability that colleagues resolved by blaming students and families
key_sources: Samantha A. Marshall, Grace A. Chen. (2025). Deficit narratives as teacher foils: how vulnerability and emotional regimes shape teacher discourse. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09740-9

article_title: Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions
citation: Sjöblom, B., & Lymer, G. (2025). Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09717-8
title: Conceptual socialization: learning a functional professional concept through its use in reflective debriefing interaction
description: The article applies Engeström's notion of conceptual socialization and Greeno's distinction between formal and functional concepts to explain how tactical knowledge develops in debriefing. Tactics is treated as a functional concept that "has meaning in a kind of activity, in which it contributes to the way participants organize their understanding of what they are doing". Learning is framed via a participation metaphor and Goodwin's professional vision: debriefing participants parse the shared domain of scrutiny of the recent game through discursive highlighting, so the concept of tactics takes on professional significance and becomes a tool for evaluating and explaining actions.
requirements: Post-simulation reflective discussion in which the concept is explicitly used and given meaning in interaction, anchored to concrete game experiences
constraints: The concept studied is not a formal concept determined by an explicit definition; the analysis concerns its situated, functional use in military debriefing settings
target_learners: military officer cadets in professional education
target_learning_goals: professional conceptual understanding of tactics
participation in professional discourse and practical reasoning
examples: Analysis of IRE sequences in which teachers specify questions as requests for tactical considerations, ratifying student replies as tactical observations
key_sources: Sjöblom, B., & Lymer, G. (2025). Conceptual socialization in debriefing: tactics as an object of knowledge in wargame interactions. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09717-8

article_title: The effects of constructivist learning environments: a commentary
citation: Remy M. J. P. Rikers, Tamara van Gog, Fred Paas. (2008). The effects of constructivist learning environments: a commentary. Instr Sci (2008) 36:463–467. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9067-4
title: CORDTRA — Chronologically-Ordered Representations of Discourse and Tool-Related Activity
description: CORDTRA is a technique introduced in the Hmelo-Silver, Chernobilsky, and Jordan study for visually representing collaborative learning processes in a computer-supported learning (CSCL) environment. By "visually representing the chronology of discourse and tool use (such as a personal notebook, electronic whiteboard) associated with an activity", it gives a better overview of collaborative learning processes in computer-mediated problem-based learning. The commentary judges it very promising but notes its outcome measures need firmer links to a constructivist theoretical framework.
requirements: Future research must establish a firm link between outcome measures and the (constructivist) theoretical framework for the technique to be most meaningful.
constraints: Many activities in a problem-based learning environment cannot be indisputably linked to the theoretical framework.
target_learners: students in computer-mediated problem-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: understanding collaborative learning processes
examples: Hmelo-Silver, Chernobilsky, and Jordan used CORDTRA to capture the dynamic nature of collaborative learning processes, representing discourse and tool use chronologically.
key_sources: Remy M. J. P. Rikers, Tamara van Gog, Fred Paas. (2008). The effects of constructivist learning environments: a commentary. Instr Sci (2008) 36:463–467. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-008-9067-4

article_title: Learning from animation enabled by collaboration
citation: Rebetez, C., Betrancourt, M., Sangin, M., & Dillenbourg, P. (2010). Learning from animation enabled by collaboration. Instructional Science, 38(5), 471–485. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9117-6
title: Collaborative learning as a design condition enabling transfer benefits from animated graphics
description: This pattern pairs animated multimedia instruction with collaborative study so that animation's potential for transfer is realised. The article notes animation "may also be used to promote interactions in computer-supported collaborative learning", and its findings show that for transfer, only dyads benefited from animated over static graphics. Collaboration thus functions as the enabling condition under which animation pays off, within the article's multimedia comprehension framework.
requirements: Learners must study in collaborative (dyad) settings for the transfer benefit of animation over static graphics to appear, per the reported findings.
constraints: Adding snapshots of critical steps was significantly detrimental for dyads, so extra static visual support should not be assumed helpful in this setting.
target_learners: Learners in computer-supported collaborative learning settings studying dynamic-system content
target_learning_goals: Transfer of understanding of how dynamic systems work
examples: The experiment assigned learners individually or in dyads to study multimedia instruction with static or animated graphics, with or without snapshots of critical steps.
key_sources: Rebetez, C., Betrancourt, M., Sangin, M., & Dillenbourg, P. (2010). Learning from animation enabled by collaboration. Instructional Science, 38(5), 471–485. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9117-6

article_title: ICT-support for grounding in the classroom
citation: Pieter J. Beers, Paul A. Kirschner, Henny P. A. Boshuizen, Wim H. Gijselaers. (2007). ICT-support for grounding in the classroom. Instructional Science 35, 535–556. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9018-5
title: Match collaboration-script coercion to learners' prior experience: when learners lack experience with collaborative complex problem-solving, coercing a formalism may be detrimental
description: The article's design recommendation is that the extent of coercion in a collaboration script must be geared toward learners' capacities: the less coercion, the more learners must themselves fulfil the prerequisites the facilitated processes require. Its conclusion from the vocational-education results is that "when learners have too little prior experience to beneﬁt from the use of a formalism, coercing such a formalism may be detrimental to the learning process." In that situation the target population may need a minimal level of prior experience with collaborative work and problem-solving before process-specific support such as NTool can be effective, and coercion would be entirely extraneous to the task.
requirements: Learners need some minimal level of prior experience with collaborative work and with problem-solving before very process-specific support can be effective
constraints: If a formalism requires unmet individual prerequisites, coercion applies it with more strength without making it easier to understand, and from a disruption-of-communication perspective may actually be detrimental
target_learners: secondary vocational education students with little prior group-work experience
target_learning_goals: effective negotiation of common ground in collaborative problem-solving
examples: Secondary vocational participants showed more regulation and 'other' communication under Stringent NTool, while university seniors in the prior study did not; the article cites Song et al. (2006) that high-school learners need more general group support
key_sources: Pieter J. Beers, Paul A. Kirschner, Henny P. A. Boshuizen, Wim H. Gijselaers. (2007). ICT-support for grounding in the classroom. Instructional Science 35, 535–556. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-007-9018-5

article_title: Constructive alignment of a mathematics methodology module
citation: Spangenberg, E. D. (2025). Constructive alignment of a mathematics methodology module. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09712-z
title: Constructive alignment (Biggs & Tang) as a student-centered framework for aligning learning outcomes, teaching-and-learning activities, and assessment tasks
description: The study is underpinned by the theory of constructive alignment coined by Biggs and Tang, derived from constructivism and advocating active involvement in creating understanding. As the article states, "CA is a student-centered model focusing on what MPTs undertake and value about learning rather than what teacher educators accomplish", with teacher educators facilitating while pre-service teachers construct knowledge through classroom activities. Aligning a module involves establishing the outcomes to achieve, the activities to engage in, and the tasks measuring achievement, so that assessment tasks mirror learning outcomes and activities and tasks inform each other.
requirements: Learning outcomes in modules must be clear for successful assessment
Teacher educators must consider LOs and ATs from both sides when designing TLAs
constraints: The article notes negative connotations persist, with CA sometimes applied top-down for quality assurance and criticized as abstract and lacking practical strategies
target_learners: mathematics pre-service teachers in higher education
target_learning_goals: specialized teaching competence in mathematics
integration of theory and practice in lesson planning and assessment
examples: The redesigned module aligned six learning outcomes with eight teaching-and-learning activities and weighted assessment tasks mirroring those outcomes
key_sources: Spangenberg, E. D. (2025). Constructive alignment of a mathematics methodology module. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09712-z

article_title: A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models
citation: Namsoo Shin, Jonathan Bowers, Steve Roderick, Cynthia McIntyre, A. Lynn Stephens, Emil Eidin, Joseph Krajcik, Daniel Damelin. (2022). A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09590-9
title: Framework for Computational Systems Modeling: five cyclic modeling practices integrating ST and CT
description: The Framework for Computational Systems Modeling organizes modeling as a cyclic process of five practices: characterize a problem or phenomenon, define system boundaries, design and construct model structure, test/evaluate/debug model behavior, and use the model to explain, predict, or design solutions. The authors state it 'elucidates the synergy between modeling, ST, and CT', with each practice drawing on aspects of both types of thinking. The process is highly iterative, with involvement in one practice influencing both future and previous practices.
requirements: Learners engage in computational (not paper-pencil) modeling so that models produce output values
Curriculum, tools, scaffolds, and assessments aligned to the five practices
constraints: Focus narrowed to a computational approach rather than modeling generally
target_learning_goals: Explaining phenomena and solving problems through modeling
Systems thinking
Computational thinking
examples: The authors illustrate each practice with example models built in SageModeler, such as dynamic time-based climate change models
key_sources: Namsoo Shin, Jonathan Bowers, Steve Roderick, Cynthia McIntyre, A. Lynn Stephens, Emil Eidin, Joseph Krajcik, Daniel Damelin. (2022). A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09590-9

article_title: A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models
citation: Namsoo Shin, Jonathan Bowers, Steve Roderick, Cynthia McIntyre, A. Lynn Stephens, Emil Eidin, Joseph Krajcik, Daniel Damelin. (2022). A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09590-9
title: Taxonomy of five computational thinking aspects with 13 sub-aspects derived from a review of 28 manuscripts
description: From a review of 28 manuscripts defining computational thinking, the authors identified five key CT aspects in the context of modeling: decomposing problems so they are computationally solvable, creating artifacts using algorithmic thinking, generating/organizing/interpreting data, testing and debugging, and making iterative refinements. Thirteen sub-aspects were synthesized, e.g., parameterizing relevant elements and encoding them into executable algorithmic form. Generic features like creativity and collaboration, disposition features, and overly broad features such as abstraction were deliberately excluded.
requirements: Aspects must pass the filters of wide description in the literature, specificity to CT, and operationalizability through observable behaviors
constraints: Generic, dispositional, and overly broad features (e.g., abstraction, creativity) were excluded from the taxonomy
target_learning_goals: Computational problem solving
Building and refining computational models
examples: Table 2 summarizes how the reviewed manuscripts described each CT aspect, with counts of authors per aspect
key_sources: Namsoo Shin, Jonathan Bowers, Steve Roderick, Cynthia McIntyre, A. Lynn Stephens, Emil Eidin, Joseph Krajcik, Daniel Damelin. (2022). A framework for supporting systems thinking and computational thinking through constructing models. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09590-9

article_title: Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others
citation: Floris M. van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2011). Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others. Instructional Science 39, 189–204. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9124-7
title: Cognitive elaborative perspective on collaborative learning
description: One of two major theoretical perspectives on collaborative learning distinguished by O'Donnell (2006), the other being socio-behavioral. It holds that "students process information at deeper levels when they learn collaboratively", stressing elaboration and recourse to prior knowledge rather than motivation or social cohesion. Elaboration is defined as higher-order thinking that connects new information with existing knowledge, producing a richer memory structure assumed to inhibit forgetting. The present experiment was designed to test this perspective by isolating explaining as the cognitive process underlying the benefit of small-group discussion.
requirements: Learners must possess relevant prior knowledge that can be activated and elaborated during the discussion
constraints: The article notes the perspective's assumptions had not previously been tested in a controlled, experimental study
target_learners: undergraduate students in small-group or problem-based settings
target_learning_goals: deep processing and long-term retention of subject-matter knowledge
examples: The experiment compared explaining, listening and irrelevant-discussion conditions with recall of a radar text tested immediately and after one month
key_sources: Floris M. van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2011). Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others. Instructional Science 39, 189–204. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9124-7

article_title: Enhancing students’ critical thinking skills: is comparing correct and erroneous examples beneficial?
citation: Lara M. van Peppen, Peter P. J. L. Verkoeijen, Anita E. G. Heijltjes, Eva M. Janssen, Tamara van Gog. (2021). Enhancing students' critical thinking skills: is comparing correct and erroneous examples beneficial? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09559-0
title: Contrasting examples as a generative-processing instructional method whose preconditions for critical-thinking transfer are questioned
description: The article frames contrasting examples—comparing fictitious students' correct and erroneous solutions side by side—as a method expected to induce generative processing, structural alignment, and focus on underlying principles, drawing on cognitive load theory and the temporal contiguity effect. It reasoned that "As contrasting can help learners to focus on key information and thereby induces generative processes directly relevant for learning". The study's null results led the authors to state that the findings "raise questions about the preconditions of contrasting examples effects".
requirements: Learners compare correct and erroneous solutions presented side by side and are prompted to indicate the erroneous solution and step, following explicit CT instruction
constraints: In this classroom study with elaborate instructions preceding practice, contrasting examples showed no advantage over correct examples, erroneous examples, or practice problems on learning or transfer
target_learners: first-year higher professional education students (Public Administration and Safety and Security Management)
target_learning_goals: avoiding biased reasoning (syllogistic, conjunction, confirmation-bias, and base-rate tasks)
transfer of critical-thinking skills to novel task types
examples: Participants compared fictitious students' correct and erroneous solutions to heuristics-and-biases tasks and indicated the erroneous solution step, after a 12-minute video-based CT instruction with two worked examples
key_sources: Lara M. van Peppen, Peter P. J. L. Verkoeijen, Anita E. G. Heijltjes, Eva M. Janssen, Tamara van Gog. (2021). Enhancing students' critical thinking skills: is comparing correct and erroneous examples beneficial? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09559-0

article_title: Two comparative studies of computer simulations and experiments as learning tools in school and out-of-school education
citation: Krüger, J. T., Höffler, T. N., Wahl, M., Knickmeier, K., & Parchmann, I. (2022). Two comparative studies of computer simulations and experiments as learning tools in school and out-of-school education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09566-1
title: Combine computer simulations and hands-on experiments so each method compensates for the other's weaknesses when teaching complex socioscientific topics
description: The article concludes that neither method dominates: simulations produced better knowledge acquisition but higher cognitive load, while experiments better fostered epistemic and value-related interest. The authors state that "working with one method may complement and supplement the weaknesses of the other" and conclude "the most effective way to communicate complex current research topics might be a combination of both methods" in school and out-of-school settings.
requirements: Both methods must convey the same content with comparable instructional support so their effects can complement each other
constraints: The conclusion is drawn from two studies on marine ecology topics with secondary students; the authors phrase it as what "might" be most effective
target_learning_goals: content knowledge of complex socioscientific issues
situational interest in science
examples: In both studies the same content was taught via experiments or simulations with identical scripts, introductions and post-tests, allowing the methods' complementary strengths to be compared directly
key_sources: Krüger, J. T., Höffler, T. N., Wahl, M., Knickmeier, K., & Parchmann, I. (2022). Two comparative studies of computer simulations and experiments as learning tools in school and out-of-school education. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09566-1

article_title: The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic
citation: Tessa Eysink, Sanne Dijkstra, Jan Kuper. (2002). The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016018210897
title: Combine guidance to all relevant problem situations with manipulable objects when designing computer-based problem-solving instruction
description: When teaching a concept through computer-based problem solving, design instruction so that guided problems lead learners to all relevant basic problem situations of the concept, while also giving them a visual representation with manipulable objects and feedback. The article's results support this combination: guidance affected immediate post-test performance and manipulation affected retention, so "guidance in combination with the possibility to manipulate objects in a domain, support the acquisition of knowledge and skills in that domain".
requirements: Problems must cover all different types of basic problem situations derivable from the target concept
The environment must give feedback so learners systematically experience the results of their actions
constraints: Demonstrated for the conditional in first-order logic with social science students; manipulation's benefit appeared on the retention test, guidance's on the post-test
target_learners: first- and second-year social science students
target_learning_goals: concept development in logic
retention of problem-solving knowledge and skills
examples: Instructions in Tarski's World were varied so guided learners encountered all basic problem situations of the conditional while manipulating or imagining to manipulate geometrical objects
key_sources: Tessa Eysink, Sanne Dijkstra, Jan Kuper. (2002). The role of guidance in computer-based problem solving for the development of concepts of logic. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1016018210897

article_title: Do students learn more from failing alone or in groups? Insights into the effects of collaborative versus individual problem solving in productive failure
citation: Charleen Brand, Christian Hartmann, Katharina Loibl, Nikol Rummel. (2023). Do students learn more from failing alone or in groups? Insights into the effects of collaborative versus individual problem solving in productive failure. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09619-7
title: Collaboration is not a necessary design component of the PF problem-solving phase for conceptual learning
description: Within the traditional PF design for secondary mathematics, individual problem solving prepared students for subsequent instruction as well as collaboration: no condition differences or mediations through the preparatory mechanisms were found. The authors conclude that "collaboration does not hold a major preparatory function in itself for the design of PF", and that collaboration "does not seem to afford elaborate discussion sufficiently" to prepare learning better than individual work. Designers need not treat group work during the PF problem-solving phase as essential.
requirements: Adherence to the remaining PF fidelity criteria: a task affording multiple solution attempts, motivational scaffolds, and instruction building on student solutions
constraints: Evidence is limited to the traditional PF setting of secondary school mathematics with the variance task; prior studies in other domains, age groups, or with fidelity violations also found no collaboration advantage
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge acquisition in mathematics
examples: In the experiment, 87 students worked in 35 groups of three and 50 worked individually on the same variance problem before identical instruction, with no post-test difference
key_sources: Charleen Brand, Christian Hartmann, Katharina Loibl, Nikol Rummel. (2023). Do students learn more from failing alone or in groups? Insights into the effects of collaborative versus individual problem solving in productive failure. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09619-7

article_title: The impact of interpersonal perceptions on the process of dealing with errors while providing and processing peer-feedback on writing
citation: Jochem E. J. Aben, Mayra Mascareño Lara, Anneke C. Timmermans, Filitsa Dingyloudi, Jan-Willem Strijbos. (2024). The impact of interpersonal perceptions on the process of dealing with errors while providing and processing peer-feedback on writing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09660-0
title: Aben et al.'s model of cognitive sub-phases in dealing with errors during feedback provision and processing
description: The article builds on a theoretical model that visualizes dealing with errors during feedback provision and processing as a sequence of cognitive sub-phases. In provision, feedback providers may "identify an error", then "decode the identified error, i.e., assign meaning to the error, by labelling the error as an error of a particular kind", followed by evaluation, encoding of a feedback remark, and sending. In processing, recipients read the feedback remark, decode it, evaluate the extent to which they agree, and may encode an output such as a correction, leading to a revised performance. The study tests whether these sub-phases can be observed empirically in peer-feedback on argumentative writing.
requirements: Feedback activities that are improvement-oriented, so that errors in a performance (e.g., a written text) are the object of the provision and processing phases
constraints: The model was theorized for dyads providing and processing feedback; the article notes Timms et al.'s related model instead covers feedback from a digital learning environment and includes a feedback-identification activity in processing that Aben et al.'s model does not
target_learners: Secondary education students (grade 11, pre-university track, ages 16-18)
target_learning_goals: Improving argumentative writing through providing and processing peer-feedback
examples: Six dyads of 11th-grade students provided and processed peer-feedback on argumentative texts while thinking aloud, and the study examined whether the model's sub-phases could be empirically observed
key_sources: Jochem E. J. Aben, Mayra Mascareño Lara, Anneke C. Timmermans, Filitsa Dingyloudi, Jan-Willem Strijbos. (2024). The impact of interpersonal perceptions on the process of dealing with errors while providing and processing peer-feedback on writing. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09660-0

article_title: Developmental relations between mathematics self-concept, interest, and achievement: A comparison of solo- and co-taught classes
citation: Lehikoinen, H., Väisänen, P., Havu-Nuutinen, S., Lappalainen, K., & Niemivirta, M. (2025). Developmental relations between mathematics self-concept, interest, and achievement: A comparison of solo- and co-taught classes. Instructional Science, 53, 239–261. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09678-4
title: Co-teaching implementation with shared planning, teaching, and evaluation supported by workshops and fidelity monitoring
description: The study implemented co-teaching as a collaborative effort of two or more educators who "share all aspects of teaching, planning, and evaluation", pairing class teachers with special education teachers in the same mathematics classes. Implementation was supported by an initial workshop for each co-teacher pair covering basics, teacher roles, and requirements for successful co-teaching, plus interviews and weekly check-list diaries. Fidelity checks showed co-teaching occurred in 70% of mathematics classes due to teacher absence, with the higher teacher-student ratio maintained via substitutes, and perceived lesson success was high (M = 4.4, SD = 0.69).
requirements: Teachers need a Master's degree in education, at least five years of teaching experience, and voluntary participation; co-teacher pairs should be formed by the teachers themselves to match interests and pedagogical views.
constraints: Co-teaching occurred in only 70% of mathematics classes due to teacher absence; joint planning and assessment were not carried out during substitute-taught lessons, and implementation is described as resource-intensive and far from straightforward.
target_learners: Sixth-grade primary school students (aged 12–13) in mathematics
target_learning_goals: Mathematics achievement and motivation (self-concept and individual interest)
examples: Co-teacher pairs received a researcher-led workshop, kept weekly check-list diaries, and used different co-teaching models such as team- and alternative teaching flexibly, spending around three quarters of an hour per week on planning and reflection.
key_sources: Lehikoinen, H., Väisänen, P., Havu-Nuutinen, S., Lappalainen, K., & Niemivirta, M. (2025). Developmental relations between mathematics self-concept, interest, and achievement: A comparison of solo- and co-taught classes. Instructional Science, 53, 239–261. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09678-4

article_title: Team learning: building shared mental models
citation: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3
title: Treat differences of opinion as windows of opportunity and manage both social and cognitive processes in teams
description: The article draws a practical implication for education and organizations: teams must "pay explicit attention to their socio-cognitive processes in order to promote team learning as an avenue to develop shared mental models". Differences of opinion "need to be seen as windows of opportunity instead of threats to progress", and an interpersonal context of psychological safety can foster these learning behaviors. Proficiency in team discussion skills — expressing ideas, asking for information and arguments, and integrating ideas — is named an important building block.
requirements: An interpersonal context characterised by psychological safety
constraints: Findings come from student teams in a two-week simulation and may not generalize directly to real project teams
target_learning_goals: developing shared mental models through constructive handling of disagreement
examples: The authors recommend training team members to monitor and strengthen their internal functioning and to build proficiency in the skills of team discussion
key_sources: Van den Bossche, P., Gijselaers, W., Segers, M., Woltjer, G., & Kirschner, P. (2011). Team learning: building shared mental models. Instructional Science, 39, 283-301. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-010-9128-3

article_title: Expert example standards but not idea unit standards help learners accurately evaluate the quality of self-generated examples
citation: Linda Froese, Julian Roelle. (2022). Expert example standards but not idea unit standards help learners accurately evaluate the quality of self-generated examples. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09293-z
title: Standards must represent concrete correct responses to enhance judgment accuracy
description: The article proposes that, following Rawson and Dunlosky's (2007) original idea, standards enhance judgment accuracy only when they are "external representations of a correct answer to a task assignment" that learners can directly compare with their own products. Idea unit and full standards fail in example generation because learners must still generate an internal standard, which can be misaligned with objective standards. Expert example standards succeed because they provide objectively correct responses.
requirements: The standard must give learners access to an objectively correct response they can directly compare with their own product
constraints: The article notes expert example standards require more interpretation than standards in retrieval or problem-solving tasks, because surface features differ and learners must transfer what a good illustration looks like, which could increase cognitive load
target_learning_goals: Accurate self-evaluation of the quality of self-generated examples
examples: In the experiment, learners compared their self-generated examples with two piloted expert examples per concept that would receive full credit, which lowered bias and improved absolute accuracy
key_sources: Linda Froese, Julian Roelle. (2022). Expert example standards but not idea unit standards help learners accurately evaluate the quality of self-generated examples. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09293-z

article_title: Evaluating false positive rates of standard and hierarchical measures of metacognitive accuracy
citation: Manuel Rausch, Michael Zehetleitner. (2023). Evaluating false positive rates of standard and hierarchical measures of metacognitive accuracy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09353-y
title: Hierarchical resampling simulation framework based on the confidence database for evaluating metacognitive measures
description: A simulation methodology in which real confidence-judgment datasets are resampled hierarchically (participants with replacement, then trials within participants) to create realistic simulated experiments without committing to a mathematical model of confidence. The article states that "The 46 datasets from the confidence database were used to simulate 5000 experiments," with a continuous predictor sampled from a Gaussian distribution for each simulated participant.
