It enables false positive rate estimation for any measure computable from binary stimulus, binary response, and confidence data.
requirements: Datasets with binary stimulus and response categories and at least 20 participants with at least 20 trials each
constraints: Computation was capped at 200 subjects and 500 trials per subject per simulated study
target_learners: Researchers evaluating statistical methods for metacognition research
target_learning_goals: Method selection for measuring metacognitive accuracy
examples: Simulated two-group comparisons and continuous-predictor analyses were run on each simulated dataset for all included measures
key_sources: Manuel Rausch, Michael Zehetleitner. (2023). Evaluating false positive rates of standard and hierarchical measures of metacognitive accuracy. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09353-y

article_title: Metacognitive judgments can potentiate new learning: The role of covert retrieval
citation: Veit Kubik, Kenneth Koslowski, Torsten Schubert, Alp Aslan. (2022). Metacognitive judgments can potentiate new learning: The role of covert retrieval. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:1057–1077. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09307-w
title: Covert retrieval account of the forward effect of metacognitive judgments
description: The article proposes that making item-based JOLs potentiates new learning to the extent that the judgment prompt elicits covert retrieval attempts before the metacognitive assessment. When only partial study information is available (word stems), "more frequent and effortful retrieval attempts and also retrieval failures are likely evoked prior to making the JOLs", engaging the same mechanisms as overt retrieval practice — retrieval-based episodic context change, list segregation, release from proactive interference, and reset of encoding. When complete study information is present, covert retrieval is unlikely and no forward benefit emerges. The account extends the forward testing effect literature to metacognitive monitoring acts.
requirements: JOLs must be delayed and based on partial cues (e.g., word stems) so that covert retrieval attempts occur prior to the judgment
constraints: Demonstrated with lists of unrelated single words; the authors note it is unclear whether JOLs with complete study information could benefit new learning with related materials
The covert-retrieval interpretation is offered speculatively: the authors write they "cannot firmly conclude" that covert retrieval was evoked
target_learners: undergraduate students in laboratory learning contexts
target_learning_goals: enhancing recall of newly studied verbal material
reducing proactive interference across successive study episodes
examples: Participants who made JOLs on word stems after each of Lists 1–4 recalled more List-5 words and produced fewer prior-list intrusions than participants who restudied the lists
key_sources: Veit Kubik, Kenneth Koslowski, Torsten Schubert, Alp Aslan. (2022). Metacognitive judgments can potentiate new learning: The role of covert retrieval. Metacognition and Learning (2022) 17:1057–1077. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09307-w

article_title: Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation
citation: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6
title: Collisions: a SimQuest-based collaborative inquiry learning environment on colliding particles
description: Collisions is a computer-simulation-based inquiry environment developed in SimQuest in which dyads work on two computers with a shared interface and communicate through chat. Students "had to uncover the relation between the momentum of a particle before and after it hits another particle" by varying mass and initial velocity and viewing results in graphs. Assignments with multiple-choice and open questions guide the inquiry across three content levels of increasing complexity: Uniform motion, Fixed wall, and Elastic collisions.
requirements: Dyads work synchronously from separate computers, communicating through a chat channel with a shared interface
constraints: Students were not familiar with Collisions, but were acquainted with the variables from their physics classes
target_learning_goals: discovering underlying physics rules of colliding particles, such as momentum relations
examples: Used with 48 dyads across three support conditions for 90-minute collaborative sessions
key_sources: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6

article_title: Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation
citation: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6
title: Collaborative Hypothesis Tool (CHT): a scaffold for jointly formulating and testing hypotheses
description: The CHT provides students with a hypothesis template supporting formulation of a syntactically correct hypothesis, plus a trust indicator scaled 0 to 100%. It "provided prompting windows with instructions on how to formulate a hypothesis together, and how to plan experiments" and a conclusion window prompting students to check whether results confirmed or rejected the hypothesis, urging re-inquiry after rejection.
requirements: Used within the SimQuest simulation environment so hypotheses can be tested with planned experiments
constraints: In this study the CHT was only provided in addition to the RIDE instruction, so its standalone effect is unknown
target_learners: secondary school students working in dyads in inquiry learning
target_learning_goals: collaborative hypothesis formulation, experiment planning, and evaluation of inquiry results
examples: Presented only to the experimental group of the second study (CHT condition, N=15 dyads) alongside the RIDE rules instruction
key_sources: Saab, N., van Joolingen, W., & van Hout-Wolters, B. (2012). Support of the collaborative inquiry learning process: influence of support on task and team regulation. Metacognition and Learning, 7, 7-23. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9068-6

article_title: Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations
citation: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6
title: Contextual factors as a key feature of SRL frameworks, extending beyond the immediate task to the larger learning context
description: The article defines contextual factors as encompassing "features of the learning environment, the learner, and their interaction". It chronicles how context appeared in early SRL frameworks as task, environment, or learning task, and argues that examining direct and indirect effects requires operationalizing the task and accounting for features of the task environment in research designs. The special issue extends consideration of context beyond the immediate learning task to the larger context in which the task is embedded.
requirements: The task must be operationally defined and features of the task environment accounted for and incorporated into research designs
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning processes
examples: Ben-Eliyahu and Linnenbrink-Garcia (2015) and McCardle and Hadwin (2015) examine contextual factors at the course-level as well as more distal factors
key_sources: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6

article_title: Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations
citation: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6
title: Contingencies as IF–THEN relations between SRL events, examined as they unfold over time
description: The article defines contingencies as "instances where one event occurs in the context of another", formalized as IF–THEN scenarios in which a learner consciously determines that, in response to a specific SRL event (the IF), a second event or process should be initiated (the THEN). An example is a metacognitive monitoring judgment that a reading passage is dense cueing the selection of note taking as a control strategy. Contingent relations are a critical assumption of process models of SRL and the basis for research on sequential and temporal characteristics of SRL.
requirements: Fine-grained data collected in sequence so that the likelihood that one event follows another can be gauged
target_learners: learners studying with hypermedia and other structured tasks
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring and control during learning
examples: Binbarasan-Tüysüzoğlu and Greene (2015) use judgments of learning made when thinking aloud to test assumptions of the COPES model and examine contingencies between monitoring and control processes
key_sources: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6

article_title: Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations
citation: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6
title: Combine multiple complementary methods to accommodate the complex structure of SRL processes
description: The article contends that while statistical methodologies for testing theorized SRL relationships have long been available, collecting sufficiently precise and comprehensive data remains a challenge. It argues that "it is often necessary to combine multiple methods in order to accommodate the complex structure of the SRL process", and intentionally includes papers demonstrating how complementary methods illuminate dynamic or contingent relations and contextual influences on SRL.
requirements: Each measurement approach must be appropriately aligned to the SRL component under investigation
target_learners: SRL researchers studying learners across contexts
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations in SRL
examples: The issue pairs think-aloud protocols with contingency analysis, embedded questionnaires with trace methodologies, and parallel context-anchored surveys with qualitative questions
key_sources: Ben-Eliyahu, A., & Bernacki, M. L. (2015). Addressing complexities in self-regulated learning: a focus on contextual factors, contingencies, and dynamic relations. Metacognition and Learning, 10, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-015-9134-6

article_title: Exploring the connection between task difficulty, task perceptions, physiological arousal and learning outcomes in collaborative learning situations
citation: Malmberg, J., Haataja, E., & Järvelä, S. (2022). Exploring the connection between task difficulty, task perceptions, physiological arousal and learning outcomes in collaborative learning situations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09320-z
title: COPES framework of self-regulated learning (Winne & Hadwin)
description: The Winne & Hadwin (1998) SRL model proposes that "regulation occurs in four loosely sequenced, recursive phases: task perceptions, goal setting, strategic enactment and adaptation". Their COPES framework (conditions, operations, products, evaluations and standards) models the conditions and identifies the facets where learners exercise SRL. External conditions (social and contextual features, task complexity, resources, time constraints) and internal cognitive conditions (metacognitive knowledge of task characteristics, judgments of task difficulty, prior domain knowledge, efficacy judgments) influence the whole process; operations create internal and external products that are compared to standards through metacognitive monitoring, and evaluations can trigger adaptations. The article uses this framework to frame how internal conditions such as task understanding and task difficulty shape regulation in collaborative learning.
requirements: Learners exercise SRL across phases in which conditions frame task perception and products are evaluated against self-set standards
constraints: The framework aims to describe how students adapt SRL to the current learning task; the article notes it provides a means to understand internal conditions in individual and collaborative learning
target_learners: students in individual and collaborative learning situations
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning across task perception, goal setting, enactment and adaptation
examples: The study operationalized internal conditions as situational ratings of task understanding and task difficulty before and after collaborative tasks
key_sources: Malmberg, J., Haataja, E., & Järvelä, S. (2022). Exploring the connection between task difficulty, task perceptions, physiological arousal and learning outcomes in collaborative learning situations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-022-09320-z

article_title: Software scaffolds to promote regulation during scientific inquiry learning
citation: Sarah Manlove, Ard W. Lazonder & Ton de Jong. (2007). Software scaffolds to promote regulation during scientific inquiry learning. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-007-9012-y
title: Cognitive regulation as a recursive three-phase process of planning, monitoring, and evaluation
description: The article frames regulation of cognition as "a recursive process which comprises three main phases: planning, monitoring, and evaluation." Planning establishes goal hierarchies that serve as strategic plans and standards for monitoring and evaluating performance; monitoring compares current knowledge or learning products to goal, task, or resource standards via self-questioning and elaboration; evaluation assesses learning processes and outcomes against whole-task goals and generalizes them to a broader context. The Process Coordinator tool was designed to scaffold exactly these three phases during inquiry learning.
requirements: Learners must be engaged in inquiry tasks whose phases (orientation, hypothesis formation, experimentation, drawing conclusions) can serve as process goals
constraints: The framework addresses regulation of cognition within self-regulated learning, not motivational or emotional aspects
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry skills
self-regulation of planning, monitoring, and evaluation during inquiry
examples: The Process Coordinator operationalized the framework with a process model, preset goal hierarchy, prompts, cues, and a report template mapped onto the three phases
key_sources: Sarah Manlove, Ard W. Lazonder & Ton de Jong. (2007). Software scaffolds to promote regulation during scientific inquiry learning. Metacognition Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-007-9012-y

article_title: Knowing how to learn: development and validation of the strategy knowledge test for self-regulated learning (SKT-SRL) for college students
citation: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Jörn R. Sparfeldt, Franziska Perels. (2024). Knowing how to learn: development and validation of the strategy knowledge test for self-regulated learning (SKT-SRL) for college students. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09379-w
title: Conditional SRL strategy knowledge as a distinct competence linked to strategy maturity deficiencies
description: The article frames conditional strategy knowledge—knowledge of when and why a strategy is useful for a specific situation—as a distinct competence, drawing on Paris et al. and Karlen's position that it is a necessary prerequisite for strategy usage. It explains knowledge-usage gaps via Hasselhorn's strategy maturity deficiencies: mediation deficiency, production deficiency, and usage deficiency. The SKT-SRL operationalizes this construct as the fit between strategies and learning situations.
requirements: Assessment must distinguish conditional knowledge from strategy usage to avoid mixing the two, as questionnaires do
constraints: Studies on the relationship between conditional strategy knowledge and strategy usage are rare, with reported correlations ranging from non-significant low to moderate
target_learning_goals: conditional self-regulated learning strategy knowledge across cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational components
examples: The SKT-SRL presents scenario vignettes and scores learners on differentiating useful from less useful strategies per scenario
key_sources: Laura Dörrenbächer-Ulrich, Jörn R. Sparfeldt, Franziska Perels. (2024). Knowing how to learn: development and validation of the strategy knowledge test for self-regulated learning (SKT-SRL) for college students. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09379-w

article_title: Age-related differences in metacognitive reactivity in younger and older adults
citation: Murphy, D. H., Rhodes, M. G., & Castel, A. D. (2024). Age-related differences in metacognitive reactivity in younger and older adults. Metacognition and Learning, 19, 863–877. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09391-0
title: Cognitive-load / dual-task account of negative JOL reactivity
description: This account explains why making judgments of learning can impair memory: making a JOL is a secondary task alongside encoding, so "making JOLs increases learners’ cognitive load, resulting in dual-task costs (see Janes et al., 2018), leading to negative reactivity". The article applies it to aging: older adults, with reduced working memory capacity and processing speed, may be unable to engage in elaborative associative encoding while judging, whereas younger adults can manage both tasks. Preserved semantic memory may mask negative reactivity for related pairs.
requirements: JOLs must be made during encoding as an additional task concurrent with studying the material
constraints: The article states the present data cannot discern whether age differences reflect greater costs or fewer benefits of making JOLs
The account is offered as one of several mechanisms; cue-strengthening and other accounts have also received support
target_learning_goals: cued recall of word-pair associations
metacognitive monitoring during encoding
examples: In the experiment, older adults recalled more pairs when each pair was followed by an unfilled 7-second inter-stimulus interval than when they made a JOL, consistent with JOLs consuming resources needed for elaborative encoding
key_sources: Murphy, D. H., Rhodes, M. G., & Castel, A. D. (2024). Age-related differences in metacognitive reactivity in younger and older adults. Metacognition and Learning, 19, 863–877. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09391-0

article_title: Metacognitive control processes in question answering: help seeking and withholding answers
citation: Monika Undorf, Iris Livneh, Rakefet Ackerman. (2021). Metacognitive control processes in question answering: help seeking and withholding answers. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09259-7
title: Metacognitive monitoring-control framework for question answering, indexed by control sensitivity
description: The article frames question answering through a metacognitive monitoring-control framework: monitoring corresponds to "people's confidence in the accuracy of the knowledge they retrieve from memory", and control corresponds to strategic regulation of the answers provided, including seeking help and withholding answers. Control sensitivity — the within-participant correlation between confidence and strategy use — indexes how strongly control processes track confidence. The study extends this framework, developed mainly for withholding answers, to help seeking as a metacognitive control process.
requirements: Confidence judgments must be collected at the level of individual questions to index monitoring-control links
constraints: The framework was examined in general-knowledge question-answering tasks with numeric answers under contingency reward systems; the article notes help seeking has been largely neglected in metacognition research
target_learners: adult learners answering knowledge questions in educational and testing contexts
target_learning_goals: accurate and informative question answering
adaptive use of help seeking and answer withholding as self-regulated learning strategies
examples: Across Experiments 1-3, control sensitivity was indexed as within-participant gamma correlations between confidence and strategy use and compared across help-seeking, don't-know, combination, and no-choice conditions
key_sources: Monika Undorf, Iris Livneh, Rakefet Ackerman. (2021). Metacognitive control processes in question answering: help seeking and withholding answers. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-021-09259-7

article_title: Reactivity to confidence ratings: evidence of impaired rule-learning
citation: Kit S. Double, Micah B. Goldwater, Damian P. Birney. (2025). Reactivity to confidence ratings: evidence of impaired rule-learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09413-5
title: Conservatism Hypothesis of reactivity to confidence ratings
description: The Conservatism Hypothesis holds that when confidence ratings are elicited, participants "become more conservative in their approach to a task", prioritizing immediate performance over mastery. Drift Diffusion Modelling evidence shows confidence ratings increase response thresholds, and participants given limited time attempt fewer items and spend longer on each. The current study interprets impaired rule-learning as support: ratings push participants toward memorization, "the strategy that maximizes short-term performance".
requirements: Confidence ratings elicited online, after each response on a primary task
constraints: The authors state the current study "is not a direct test of this hypothesis" and does not tell us why confidence ratings impede rule learning
target_learning_goals: rule-based category learning
metacognitive monitoring accuracy
examples: Participants who made confidence ratings were more likely to respond to ambiguous transfer items in ways indicating greater use of memorization strategies
key_sources: Kit S. Double, Micah B. Goldwater, Damian P. Birney. (2025). Reactivity to confidence ratings: evidence of impaired rule-learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09413-5

article_title: The impact of retrieval processes, age, general achievement level, and test scoring scheme for children’s metacognitive monitoring and controlling
citation: Krebs, S.S., Roebers, C.M. (2012). The impact of retrieval processes, age, general achievement level, and test scoring scheme for children's metacognitive monitoring and controlling. Metacognition and Learning 7, 75–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9079-3
title: Metacognitive development is fueled by both cognitive resources (achievement level) and mnemonic experience (age)
description: The article offers a two-factor explanatory account of children's metacognitive development: "Results suggest that both cognitive resources (operationalized through achievement level) and mnemonic experience (assessed through age) fuel metacognitive development." Cognitive resources are indexed by general achievement level, while mnemonic experience is indexed by age, and the account explains why both high achievers and older children showed more accurate monitoring and control. The account also carries a scope qualification: under higher retrieval demands, experience appears to take the more important role.
requirements: Both an index of cognitive resources (achievement level) and an index of mnemonic experience (age) must be available to disentangle their contributions.
constraints: When facing higher demands regarding retrieval processes, experience seems to play the more important role, qualifying the equal-weight reading of the two factors.
target_learners: Primary school children aged 9/10 and 11/12 years
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive monitoring accuracy
Metacognitive control (strategic regulation of answers)
key_sources: Krebs, S.S., Roebers, C.M. (2012). The impact of retrieval processes, age, general achievement level, and test scoring scheme for children's metacognitive monitoring and controlling. Metacognition and Learning 7, 75–90. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9079-3

article_title: Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Loyens, S. M. M., Magda, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2008). Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9082-7
title: Provide conceptual clarity and guidance to teachers and students so PBL can produce self-directed learners
description: The review concludes that PBL only brings forth self-directed learners when everyone understands what SDL means and receives support. When faculty fear content will not be covered, they supply core literature, which "completely undermined" freedom to select materials and makes SDL impossible. The article recommends "Conceptual clarity of what SDL entails and guidance for both teachers and students can help PBL to bring forth self-directed learners". Students themselves reported needing teacher support to become self-directed.
requirements: Teachers and students share a clear conception of SDL
Guidance and support are provided rather than SDL being equated with lack of support
constraints: If students or faculty interpret SDL as do-it-yourself education or lack of support, SDL becomes impossible
target_learners: PBL students including medical and higher education students
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning skills
selection and critical evaluation of learning materials
examples: Dornan et al. found students indicated they needed support by teachers to become self-directed, and when guidance was given they were motivated to plan their learning needs
key_sources: Loyens, S. M. M., Magda, J., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2008). Self-Directed Learning in Problem-Based Learning and its Relationships with Self-Regulated Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-008-9082-7

article_title: Issues of Constructs, Contexts, and Continuity: Commentary on Learning in Higher Education
citation: Patricia A. Alexander. (2017). Issues of Constructs, Contexts, and Continuity: Commentary on Learning in Higher Education. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 345–351. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9409-3
title: Constructs, context, and continuity as three barriers to an integrated theory of learning in higher education
description: Alexander's organizing framework holds that integration of models of higher-education learning is blocked by three issues: constructs (lack of explicit, shared definitions of core terms), context (insufficient characterization of what is unique about higher education as a learning environment), and continuity (neglect of learners' prior and subsequent academic development). She states the common threads across the reviews "do not forge the framework for the type of meta-theory of learning in higher education" until these questions "can be resolved," and offers ways over, around, and through these barriers.
requirements: Researchers must explicate their working definitions of key constructs in their writings and presentations for integration to proceed
constraints: The framework is argued from a commentary on five reviews, not tested empirically; the author acknowledges the developmental perspective was not the focus of the special issue
target_learning_goals: academic development and learning within higher education
examples: The commentary applies the triad to the five reviews: construct ambiguity in engagement definitions, NSSE benchmarks shared with K-12 as a context example, and unidimensional treatment of higher education without disentangling required from optional courses
key_sources: Patricia A. Alexander. (2017). Issues of Constructs, Contexts, and Continuity: Commentary on Learning in Higher Education. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 345–351. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-017-9409-3

article_title: Confounded or Controlled? A Systematic Review of Media Comparison Studies Involving Immersive Virtual Reality for STEM Education
citation: Lawson, A. P., Martella, A. M., LaBonte, K., Delgado, C. Y., Zhao, F., Gluck, J. A., Munns, M. E., LeRoy, A. W., & Mayer, R. E. (2024). Confounded or Controlled? A Systematic Review of Media Comparison Studies Involving Immersive Virtual Reality for STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09908-8
title: IVR comparison studies should control instructional methods and content between conditions before attributing learning gains to the medium
description: Building on the media methods debate, the review argues that media comparison conditions must be equivalent on instructional methods and content so that only the medium differs. It notes that active learning techniques "are not necessarily unique to the VR device and can be used in conventional media, thus potentially conflating the usefulness of VR itself." Researchers should therefore match activities, non-IVR activities, practice, time, and content, and provide complete operational definitions of both conditions.
requirements: Complete operational definitions allowing replication of both conditions; matching of activities, practice with the dependent measure, time spent learning, and content across conditions.
constraints: Active learning benefits found in meta-analyses were for methods embedded in VR, which may conflate the usefulness of VR itself rather than reflect the medium.
target_learners: K-12 and higher education students learning STEM content
target_learning_goals: Valid causal attribution of learning outcomes to instructional media
examples: The review coded 50 comparisons against its five criteria and found only 26% fully controlled, illustrating how rarely current studies meet this standard.
key_sources: Lawson, A. P., Martella, A. M., LaBonte, K., Delgado, C. Y., Zhao, F., Gluck, J. A., Munns, M. E., LeRoy, A. W., & Mayer, R. E. (2024). Confounded or Controlled? A Systematic Review of Media Comparison Studies Involving Immersive Virtual Reality for STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09908-8

article_title: Learning Mathematics Problem Solving through Test Practice: a Randomized Field Experiment on a Global Scale
citation: Avvisati, F., & Borgonovi, F. (2020). Learning Mathematics Problem Solving through Test Practice: a Randomized Field Experiment on a Global Scale. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 791–814. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09520-6
title: Use content-relevant practice tests to produce small domain-specific learning gains, without expecting improvements in general reasoning
description: The article's findings support designing practice tests that emphasize the target content domain: "the greater the proportion of mathematics problems included in the practice session, the better students performed on the target test." However, the gains are subject-specific — mathematics practice did not improve domain-general problem solving — and are small in magnitude (~2% of a standard deviation per hour of practice). Educators should therefore expect practice testing to consolidate domain-specific skills rather than to build transferable general reasoning.
requirements: Practice tasks must relate to the same content domain as the target assessment
Adequate exposure time within the practice session (effects observed across 0.5–1.5 hours of domain-relevant content)
constraints: Effects are small in magnitude
No corrective feedback was provided in this study, so gains may differ with feedback
No improvement in domain-general problem-solving ability was found
target_learners: 15-year-old secondary school students across diverse countries and educational systems
target_learning_goals: Mathematics problem solving
examples: In the PISA 2012 field experiment, students randomly assigned to forms with 1.5 hours of mathematics content outperformed those with 0.5 hours on a subsequent computer-based mathematics test covering the same content areas
key_sources: Avvisati, F., & Borgonovi, F. (2020). Learning Mathematics Problem Solving through Test Practice: a Randomized Field Experiment on a Global Scale. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 791–814. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09520-6

article_title: Single- and Multilevel Perspectives on Covariate Selection in Randomized Intervention Studies on Student Achievement
citation: Stallasch, S. E., Lüdtke, O., Artelt, C., Hedges, L. V., & Brunner, M. (2024). Single- and Multilevel Perspectives on Covariate Selection in Randomized Intervention Studies on Student Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09898-7
title: Compiled single- and multilevel design parameter database and OSF repository with R scripts and interactive Excel workbooks for RT study planning
description: The article releases an extensive compilation of empirical and meta-analytic single- and multilevel design parameters (R2 and intraclass correlations) for covariate sets varying type, combination, and 1-7 year time lag, estimated from six German probability samples totaling N = 68,502 students in grades 1-12. The repository includes "all R scripts, and instructions for accessing the analyzed data" at https://osf.io/nhx4w, with OSM A-G and interactive Excel workbooks compiling empirical, meta-analytic, and simulation results. It is accompanied by the multides R package (Stallasch, 2024).
requirements: Access to the German large-scale assessment datasets via the documented research data centers
constraints: Estimates stem from German samples whose school-system characteristics, such as early ability-based school-type-tracking, deviate markedly from those of the United States
target_learners: Students in grades 1-12 in elementary, lower secondary, and upper secondary school
target_learning_goals: Design sensitivity and statistical power of randomized trials measuring student achievement outcomes
examples: The article applies the compiled design parameters in illustrative scenarios of study planning and precision simulations conceding ρ and R2 uncertainties via a Bayesian rationale
key_sources: Stallasch, S. E., Lüdtke, O., Artelt, C., Hedges, L. V., & Brunner, M. (2024). Single- and Multilevel Perspectives on Covariate Selection in Randomized Intervention Studies on Student Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09898-7

article_title: The Role of Individual Differences in Sourcing: a Systematic Review
citation: Anmarkrud, Ø., Bråten, I., Florit, E., & Mason, L. (2022). The Role of Individual Differences in Sourcing: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09640-7
title: Conflict-driven accounts of sourcing: D-ISC and CSI models
description: The review describes two specialized models of sourcing under conflicting information. The discrepancy-induced source comprehension (D-ISC) model proposes that "when readers encounter conflicting information about a particular topic or issue and thereby experience a break in situational coherence, they may strategically pay attention to source information". The content-source integration (CSI) model adds that readers lacking prior knowledge shift from asking "what is true?" to evaluating who presents claims. Both models imply individual difference roles for topic beliefs and prior knowledge, though the review notes their opposing predictions about knowledge remain to be clarified empirically.
requirements: Conflicting information or belief-content conflict that breaks situational coherence triggers strategic source attention
constraints: The review states that whether belief-content conflicts influence sourcing "is an issue for further research"
target_learning_goals: sourcing
evaluating conflicting information
restoring coherent understanding
examples: The CSI model implies less prior knowledge may be associated with more sourcing, whereas the IF-MT implies more knowledge increases sourcing
key_sources: Anmarkrud, Ø., Bråten, I., Florit, E., & Mason, L. (2022). The Role of Individual Differences in Sourcing: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09640-7

article_title: Long-Term Effects of an Intervention Targeting Dimensional and Temporal Comparisons on Students’ Math and English Academic Self-Concepts: A Waiting-List Replication and Extension Study
citation: Hörsch, H., Schumacher, J., & Wolff, F. (2026). Long-Term Effects of an Intervention Targeting Dimensional and Temporal Comparisons on Students' Math and English Academic Self-Concepts: A Waiting-List Replication and Extension Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10137-4
title: COMPASS: a theory-driven intervention addressing dimensional and temporal comparison processes and their associated beliefs
description: COMPASS (comparison processes in students' self-concept formation) is an intervention framework that enhances subject-specific academic self-concepts by educating students about dimensional comparisons (comparisons of one's own performance across subjects) and temporal comparisons (comparisons with one's own past performance) and the beliefs moderating them. The article states that "COMPASS represents a coherent, theory-driven application of comparison theories that jointly addresses dimensional and temporal comparison processes and their associated beliefs." Its modules work with psychoeducation, exercises, and discussions, delivered in roughly 120 minutes with lectures, class discussions, group exercises, and mnemonic posters.
requirements: Delivery in regular school lessons by trained intervention leaders with group sizes limited to a maximum of 20 students to ensure active discussion engagement
constraints: The social comparison module was excluded because it did not change the targeted belief and led to an unintended decrease in students' German self-concept, and the cohort-comparison idea is not applicable in nonacademic track schools
target_learners: Students in Grades 9 to 11 at German secondary schools of the academic track
target_learning_goals: Subject-specific academic self-concepts in math or English
Belief in the positive interdependence of mathematical and verbal abilities
Belief in the changeability of abilities
examples: Students imagined performing the same in the intervention subject while performing worse in all other subjects, and reflected on how this would affect their self-concept
Students wrote down three key learnings from the past year and discussed them to emphasize their actual learning gains
key_sources: Hörsch, H., Schumacher, J., & Wolff, F. (2026). Long-Term Effects of an Intervention Targeting Dimensional and Temporal Comparisons on Students' Math and English Academic Self-Concepts: A Waiting-List Replication and Extension Study. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10137-4

article_title: Why We Might Still be Concerned About Low Cronbach’s Alphas in Domain-specific Knowledge Tests
citation: Steffen Zitzmann, Gabe A. Orona. (2025). Why We Might Still be Concerned About Low Cronbach's Alphas in Domain-specific Knowledge Tests. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10015-5
title: Report confidence or Bayesian credible intervals around estimated alpha rather than comparing a point estimate to a threshold
description: The authors propose complementing the usual reporting practice with intervals for alpha, because the real problem with thresholds is that comparing an estimated alpha to a threshold "does not properly account for sampling error." Placing a confidence interval or, preferably, a Bayesian variant around the estimate conveys the uncertainty of the value; only when the upper bound does not exceed the threshold can one reasonably infer alpha is too low. They argue this practice may counteract the inflation of seemingly high alphas in educational psychology.
requirements: Intervals for alpha might not be readily available in software; the article states they can be obtained via factor analytic methodology or resampling techniques.
target_learning_goals: Accurate measurement and reporting of the reliability of domain-specific knowledge test scores
examples: The article showcases the procedure with an estimated alpha of .61 below the 0.70 threshold whose calculated interval [0.48, 0.74] includes the threshold, suggesting a fair chance the true alpha is acceptably high.
key_sources: Steffen Zitzmann, Gabe A. Orona. (2025). Why We Might Still be Concerned About Low Cronbach's Alphas in Domain-specific Knowledge Tests. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10015-5

article_title: Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape
citation: Julia Chatain, Charlotte Müller, Keny Chatain, Leon Calabrese, Manu Kapur. (2025). Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10073-9
title: A data-driven taxonomy organizing the meanings of concrete and abstract along a learner–representation–concept dimension
description: The article proposes a taxonomy of the semantic landscape of concreteness and abstraction in mathematics education, built from qualitative coding of a corpus of 368 papers. It models learning as follows: "To learn a concept ( C ), a learner ( L ) interacts with a representation ( R) of C , designed through mapping." Axes are placed at the interaction level (learner–representation) or the mapping level (representation–concept), each running between a concrete and an abstract end, and each paired with a design question to make the taxonomy usable in research and practice.
requirements: Axes must be defined according to the representation, as it is the only element that can be acted upon when designing interventions or studies
constraints: For two axes, only codes for one end of the spectrum were found in the data; the other end was added during analysis and is indicated by dotted lines
The authors do not claim objectivity, as they offer a specific perspective
target_learners: Mathematics education researchers and designers of mathematics learning interventions
target_learning_goals: Precise use of the terms concrete and abstract in mathematics education research and intervention design
examples: The taxonomy was built by two researchers through reflexive thematic analysis, iteratively grouping codes until both agreed every code was assigned a group
key_sources: Julia Chatain, Charlotte Müller, Keny Chatain, Leon Calabrese, Manu Kapur. (2025). Concreteness and Abstraction in Mathematics Education: A Taxonomy of the Semantic Landscape. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10073-9

article_title: Classroom Active Breaks as a Physical-Educational Intervention for Executive Functions and Mathematical Outcomes: a Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis
citation: Melguizo-Ibáñez, E., Zurita-Ortega, F., Tadeu, P., Ubago-Jiménez, J. L., & Alonso Vargas, J. M. (2026). Classroom Active Breaks as a Physical-Educational Intervention for Executive Functions and Mathematical Outcomes: a Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10146-3
title: Cognitive load theory as an interpretive framework for how active-break modality relates to executive function and learning outcomes
description: The article uses cognitive load theory, with its distinction between intrinsic, extraneous and germane load, to interpret why different active-break modalities may relate differently to cognitive and academic outcomes. It distinguishes a motor-only modality of "simple physical movements that do not require decision-making", a cognitive-motor light modality with "simple rules or basic cognitive demands alongside physical movement", and a cognitive-motor high modality involving "complex decision-making, dual-task coordination or problem-solving during movement". Each modality is theorised to carry a distinct profile of element interactivity and working-memory demand.
requirements: Effects depend on how the movement modifies cognitive demands relevant to schema construction; benefits require alignment with instructional goals and control of extraneous load
constraints: Cognitive load and its components were not directly assessed in the primary studies; the framework is interpretive, not an empirically tested causal mechanism
The theory does not model physiological arousal, attentional set-shifting, or fatigue
target_learners: Primary and secondary school students aged 6–16
target_learning_goals: Executive functions (attention, inhibitory control, working memory) and mathematical achievement and fluency
examples: The meta-analysis coded each included study's active break as motor-only, cognitive-motor light, or cognitive-motor high and used these categories as prespecified moderators in exploratory RVE meta-regressions.
key_sources: Melguizo-Ibáñez, E., Zurita-Ortega, F., Tadeu, P., Ubago-Jiménez, J. L., & Alonso Vargas, J. M. (2026). Classroom Active Breaks as a Physical-Educational Intervention for Executive Functions and Mathematical Outcomes: a Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10146-3

article_title: Employing Machine Learning to Predict Medical Trainees’ Psychophysiological Responses and Self- and Socially- Shared Regulated Learning Strategies While Completing Medical Simulations
citation: Moreno, M., Grewal, K., Cutumisu, M., & Harley, J.M. (2025). Employing Machine Learning to Predict Medical Trainees’ Psychophysiological Responses, Self- and Socially-Shared Regulated Learning Strategies While Completing Medical Simulations. Education Psychology Review, 37 (70), 1-29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10044-0
title: COPES model of self-regulated learning (Winne & Hadwin)
description: The article describes COPES as a model of self-regulated learning consisting of five interconnected facets: conditions, operations, products, evaluations, and standards. Conditions include internal factors (prior knowledge, motivation, emotions) and external factors (task instructions, learning environment); operations are the cognitive and metacognitive strategies learners employ; products are outcomes such as comprehension and performance; evaluations involve assessing progress against goals or gold standards; and standards are benchmarks used to judge success. The article notes the facets are "interconnected, with feedback from one facet (e.g., evaluation) influencing earlier facets (e.g., conditions), making the model cyclical and adaptive in nature."
requirements: Learners establish goals, engage in metacognitive monitoring, and have a self-reflection mechanism to make adaptations throughout the learning process
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognitive monitoring and self-reflection
key_sources: Moreno, M., Grewal, K., Cutumisu, M., & Harley, J.M. (2025). Employing Machine Learning to Predict Medical Trainees’ Psychophysiological Responses, Self- and Socially-Shared Regulated Learning Strategies While Completing Medical Simulations. Education Psychology Review, 37 (70), 1-29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10044-0

article_title: AI-Related Threats to Information Sovereignty and Challenges for Research Ethics
citation: Skulmowski, A. (2024). AI-Related Threats to Information Sovereignty and Challenges for Research Ethics. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09939-1
title: Expand informed consent with AI- and cloud-related privacy warnings to restore consent validity
description: The article recommends incorporating additional information into informed consent forms so participants understand how their devices may collect and transfer data. For sensitive studies, it would be "recommendable to include a brief warning concerning the threats that AI-related and cloud-based data collection poses to privacy and anonymity", ideally with suggestions for changing settings or software. The author argues this restores informed consent, while cautioning that many participants do not read consent forms, so other security measures remain necessary.
requirements: Consent forms must describe device-related data-transfer risks and practical mitigations such as disabling cloud-based features.
constraints: A large part of participants do not read informed consent forms, so this measure alone is insufficient.
target_learners: remote study participants in educational research
target_learning_goals: protecting participant privacy and information sovereignty during data collection
examples: For studies involving sensitive data such as health data or learning impairments, the author recommends a warning notice with suggestions on avoiding the issues by changing settings or using different software.
key_sources: Skulmowski, A. (2024). AI-Related Threats to Information Sovereignty and Challenges for Research Ethics. Educational Psychology Review, 36, 101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09939-1

article_title: The Effects of Educational Technology Interventions on Literacy in Elementary School: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Rebecca D. Silverman, Kristin Keane, Elena Hammond, S. Khanna. (2025). The Effects of Educational Technology Interventions on Literacy in Elementary School: A Meta-Analysis. Review of Educational Research, 95(5), 972-1012. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241261073
title: Four-outcome literacy framework: constrained and unconstrained skills underlie reading comprehension and writing proficiency
description: The meta-analysis organizes literacy outcomes along two levels: two broad constructs, reading comprehension and writing proficiency, and the underlying skills that support them. It distinguishes "the constrained and unconstrained skills that underlie these two literacy constructs," allowing effects of educational technology interventions to be estimated separately for each of the four outcome categories. This framework structures both the synthesis and the moderator analyses of intervention and participant characteristics.
requirements: Studies in the corpus must measure one or more of the four literacy outcome categories so effects can be assigned within the framework.
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
writing proficiency
constrained literacy skills
unconstrained literacy skills
examples: The meta-analysis estimated effects separately for constrained skills, unconstrained skills, reading comprehension, and writing proficiency.

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Community-specific knowledge position: discourse conventions and community knowledge shape writing within tasks
description: The third position holds that even given task-specific skills, writers in different communities produce similar texts in quite different ways. Using Toulmin's argument elements, the review shows that literary criticism employs its own repertoire of persuasive tactics and topoi that "invoke the shared assumptions of the community of literary scholars, and at the same time create that community," while legal brief writing requires knowledge of the unique rhetorical demands structuring appellant-appellee relationships. The position requires conventional knowledge of the social or situational understandings governing behavior in particular circumstances.
requirements: Instruction must address conventional knowledge—tone, sources of evidence, voice—specific to the community being written for
constraints: Teachers adopting this position face the daunting problem of either instructing students to differentiate writing in seemingly unlimited ways or accepting limited influence on student writing
target_learners: students learning discipline-specific and professional writing
target_learning_goals: adapting argumentation and composing to the conventions of specific discourse communities
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543062003279

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Cognitive view of reading: active readers flexibly use general comprehension strategies
description: The review describes the cognitive view of reading offered by Dole, Duffy, Roehler, and Pearson, which contrasts with the traditional subskills view that "assumes a passive reader who has mastered a large number of subskills and automatically applies them to all texts." The cognitive view "assumes an active reader who constructs meaning through the integration of existing and new knowledge and the flexible use of strategies to foster, monitor, regulate, and maintain comprehension." The five strategies named—determining importance, summarizing, drawing inferences, generating questions, monitoring comprehension—reflect faith in general procedural knowledge at the center of the reading curriculum.
requirements: Instruction should help students gain conscious control over strategies they can adapt to any text
constraints: The review notes these researchers emphasize that good readers adapt strategies based on purpose, task and text demands, and situational context
target_learners: students learning to read across text types
target_learning_goals: comprehension monitoring and flexible strategy use in reading
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543062003279

article_title: Educational Responses Toward Community Violence: A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions
citation: van Dijk, A, de Haan, M & de Winter, M 2026, 'Educational Responses Toward Community Violence : A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions', Review of Educational Research, vol. 96, no. 3, pp. 829-869. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251324491
title: Conceptual reorientation of community violence including structural mechanisms and multilevel targeting
description: Based on imbalances in theoretical orientations among existing interventions, the paper suggests a conceptual reorientation of community violence. In the authors' words, this reorientation "includes structural mechanisms and enables a targeted approach of the many levels through which youth and communities are affected." It reframes community violence as not only a matter of individual behavior or group interaction but also of social-system structures, so that educational responses can be targeted to the multiple levels at which violence affects youth and communities.
requirements: Requires moving beyond the individual-behavior and group-interaction orientations that dominate current interventions
constraints: The paper presents this as a suggested reorientation based on the review, not as a tested intervention
target_learning_goals: violence prevention
equity
promotion of peace
examples: The reorientation is offered to policymakers and practitioners as a basis for integrating multiple strategies in a context-based and community-involved approach
key_sources: van Dijk, A, de Haan, M & de Winter, M 2026, 'Educational Responses Toward Community Violence : A Critical Analysis of Perspectives on Causes and Solutions', Review of Educational Research, vol. 96, no. 3, pp. 829-869. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251324491

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Community-specific argumentation: literary criticism and legal brief writing employ distinct argumentative conventions
description: The review argues that even shared task-specific skills operate differently across discourse communities. Fahnestock and Secor show literary criticism employs "a definable repertoire of persuasive tactics to achieve communication in its well-defined environment," including special topoi such as paradox and metaphor. Stratman's analysis of legal brief writing shows appellate brief writers must anticipate how judges and opponents read and integrate briefs, knowledge the review says is almost absent in law school instruction despite law schools' belief in transferable general critical reasoning.
requirements: Effective argumentation within a community requires "knowledge that gives background and definition to [each discipline]—not only 'facts' but the terms of art, operational concepts, canons of relevance, patterns of association, characteristic argumentative gestures."
constraints: The community-specific position creates a daunting instructional problem: teachers must either instruct students to differentiate their writing in seemingly unlimited ways or accept limited influence on student writing.
target_learners: students learning discipline-specific writing such as literary criticism or legal brief writing
target_learning_goals: argumentation adapted to the conventions of a discourse community
examples: The review contrasts Kael's film reviews and Scalia's flag-burning-case deliberations: both use defining skills of generating criteria through problematic examples, yet each requires community-specific knowledge the other lacks.
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.2307/1170740

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Cognitive view of reading: five general comprehension strategies at the center of the reading curriculum
description: The review describes the cognitive view offered by Dole, Duffy, Roehler, and Pearson, which "assumes an active reader who constructs meaning through the integration of existing and new knowledge and the flexible use of strategies to foster, monitor, regulate, and maintain comprehension," in contrast to the traditional view of a passive reader applying subskills automatically. They identify five strategies—determining importance, summarizing information, drawing inferences, generating questions, and monitoring comprehension—that ought to stand at the center of the reading curriculum.
requirements: Instruction should help students gain conscious control over strategies they can adapt to any text, with good readers adapting strategies based on purpose, task and text demands, and situational context.
constraints: The review classifies this position as reflecting faith in general procedural knowledge, since the researchers name strategies meant to apply across texts.
target_learners: students learning reading comprehension across text types
target_learning_goals: strategic, flexible reading comprehension
examples: The review contrasts this cognitive view with traditional skill instruction, which Dole et al. criticize for connoting consistency, if not rigidity.

article_title: The Effects of Co-Teaching and Related Collaborative Models of Instruction on Student Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Vembye, M. H., Weiss, F., & Bhat, B. H. (2022). The Effects of Co-Teaching and Related Collaborative Models of Instruction on Student Achievement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. https://osf.io/ur2bs
title: Three-category taxonomy of collaborative instruction models with distinct causal mechanisms
description: The review organizes two-teacher in-class interventions into three categories studied largely separately: co-teaching (general plus special education professionals), teacher assistants/aides (collaboration with adults without formal teaching qualifications), and team teaching (two general education teachers). It "broadly define[s] collaborative instruction as the simultaneous presence of two or more educators/adults working together and sharing responsibilities in instructional and/or behavioral interventions." Mechanisms include improved student-teacher ratio, freed teacher time, scaffolding, feedback, and behavior management.
requirements: Both educators at least 18 years old teaching in-class in the same physical space
At least two weeks (ten school days) of treatment
constraints: Excludes peer teaching, tutoring, and out-of-classroom two-teacher arrangements
General education setting focus; special education school settings excluded
target_learners: Students in grades one to twelve in primary and secondary schools
General education and special needs students
target_learning_goals: Academic achievement in arts, social science, and STEM subjects
examples: The review's data extraction scheme was developed in line with co-teaching literature to test these theoretical hypotheses empirically

article_title: A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis to Synthesize the Influence of                     Contexts of Scaffolding Use on Cognitive Outcomes in STEM                     Education
citation: Belland Brian R., Walker Andrew E., Kim Nam Ju. (2017). A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis to Synthesize the Influence of Contexts of Scaffolding Use on Cognitive Outcomes in STEM Education. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654317723009
title: Taxonomy of computer-based scaffolding types: conceptual, strategic, metacognitive, and motivational
description: The article presents a four-part taxonomy of computer-based scaffolding functions: scaffolding is often designed to (a) help students with what to consider when addressing a problem (conceptual scaffolding), (b) bootstrap a strategy for addressing a problem (strategic scaffolding), (c) invite students to question their own understanding (metacognitive scaffolding), and (d) enhance interest, autonomy, self-efficacy, and other motivational variables (motivational scaffolding). Specific embedded strategies include highlighting critical problem features, modeling expert processes and demonstration, and motivational support such as recruitment, direction maintenance, and controlling frustration. This taxonomy organizes the scaffolding interventions synthesized in the meta-analysis.
requirements: Computer-based scaffolding must support students addressing an ill-structured problem
target_learners: students in STEM education across educational levels
target_learning_goals: problem solving
strategy use
metacognition
motivation

article_title: Children’s Creativity: A Theoretical Framework and Systematic Review
citation: Kupers, E., Lehmann-Wermser, A., McPherson, G., & van Geert, P. (2019). Children's creativity: a theoretical framework and systematic review. Review of Educational Research, 89(1), 93-124. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654318815707
title: A complex dynamic systems framework describing and explaining children's creativity
description: The article develops a theoretical integration of children's creativity grounded in complex dynamic systems theory. The framework is offered as a model that "describes and explains children's creativity" and is used to reconcile differing views on how education contributes to creative development. It frames creativity as developing through interactions across levels rather than as a fixed trait.
requirements: The framework is intended to integrate existing theoretical views on children's creativity rather than to stand as a standalone instructional method
constraints: The framework's empirical grounding in the reviewed literature is limited by the field's predominant static, aggregated measurement of creativity, as the review itself reports
target_learning_goals: creative development
creativity as a 21st-century skill
examples: The authors use the model to explain differing views on the role of education in developing children's creativity
