article_title: Towards a new, complexity science of learning and education
citation: Jörg, T., Davis, B. & Nickmans, G. (2007). Towards a new, complexity science of learning and education. Educational Research Review, 2(2), 145–156. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2007.09.002
title: A complexity paradigm for the science of learning and education
description: The article proposes a new paradigm for education built on complexity thinking, in which learning is understood as a complex, self-organising, nonlinear process. Its stated characteristics are 'a focus on the transphenomenal resulting in a transdisciplinary and interdiscursive approach, an orientation towards self-organisation and potentiality instead of pre-specified ends and an incorporation of a theory of change'. The paradigm calls for rethought modes of inquiry, a new lexicon, and assessment practices geared to complexity.
requirements: A theory of the crisis must first be formulated so the field acknowledges the crisis and its causes
New tools of thought beyond linear causality and reductionism
constraints: The paradigm does not provide access to an ultimate truth; it is offered as better fitted to rapidly evolving times
target_learning_goals: understanding learning as a complex dynamic process
adapting to a changing world
key_sources: Jörg, T., Davis, B. & Nickmans, G. (2007). Towards a new, complexity science of learning and education. Educational Research Review, 2(2), 145–156. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2007.09.002

article_title: Professional learning of late-career teachers: A systematic literature review
citation: Brouhier, Q., Raemdonck, I., & März, V. (2026). Professional Learning of Late-career Teachers: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Research Review, 50, 100757. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100757
title: Design context-sensitive professional learning approaches that value late-career teachers' continued growth, contributions and well-being
description: The review concludes by "advocating for more nuanced, context-sensitive approaches to professional learning that value the continued growth, contributions and well-being of teachers in the later stages of their careers." This principle calls for professional development design that responds to late-career teachers' specific needs and circumstances rather than applying generic provision, and that recognises their ongoing capacity to grow and contribute.
requirements: Attention to the specific needs, context and well-being of late-career teachers when designing professional learning
constraints: The review highlights a notable gap in tailored interventions addressing late-career teachers' specific needs, so evidence on what such tailored approaches should contain is limited
target_learning_goals: Continued professional growth, contribution and well-being
examples: The review concludes with theoretical and practical implications advocating nuanced, context-sensitive approaches to professional learning for late-career teachers.
key_sources: Brouhier, Q., Raemdonck, I., & März, V. (2026). Professional Learning of Late-career Teachers: A Systematic Literature Review. Educational Research Review, 50, 100757. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2025.100757

article_title: Recalibrating impact in STEM education: Empirical benchmarks for interpreting intervention effects
citation: Mehmet Bicakci, Heidrun Stoeger, Diana Wengler, Albert Ziegler. (2026). Recalibrating impact in STEM education: Empirical benchmarks for interpreting intervention effects. Educational Research Review 52. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100803
title: Interpret STEM education intervention effects against empirically derived, context-sensitive benchmark distributions rather than Cohen's universal thresholds
description: The article argues that labeling an effect small, medium, or large with inherited conventions is insufficient because STEM effect distributions vary by field, intervention type, outcome domain, and valence. It states researchers "should instead interpret effects relative to benchmark distributions that reflect the relevant field, intervention type, and outcome orientation." The study supplies the benchmark tables that make this possible.
requirements: Researchers need access to benchmark distributions for the relevant STEM field, intervention category, outcome domain, and valence orientation.
constraints: Benchmarks reflect prior review decisions and reporting practices; subgroup coverage is uneven, with engineering, technology, collaborative learning, and nonacademic outcomes sparse.
Adjusted benchmarks are more conservative estimates, not definitive population values.
target_learning_goals: Accurate interpretation of the practical significance of STEM intervention effect sizes
examples: The study derived quartile benchmarks from 95 meta-analyses and 5,956 effect sizes, showing raw overall quartiles of 0.21, 0.48, and 0.86 that fell after bias adjustment.
key_sources: Mehmet Bicakci, Heidrun Stoeger, Diana Wengler, Albert Ziegler. (2026). Recalibrating impact in STEM education: Empirical benchmarks for interpreting intervention effects. Educational Research Review 52. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2026.100803

article_title: Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research
citation: Fagerlund, J., Palsa, L., & Mertala, P. (2025). Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research. Educational Research Review, 46, Article 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100663
title: Corpus of 77 peer-reviewed K-12 data literacy education studies yielding 611 purpose expressions
description: The review's final corpus comprises 77 peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers on K-12 data literacy education, identified through multi-database keyword searching, cleaning, two-stage screening, and a snowball search of prior reviews. From these studies the authors collected "argumentation and justification of its educational goals, intents, and/or purposes were gathered (total: 611 expressions in the 77 studies)", drawn from the early and final sections of IMRaD-structured articles. The corpus is the empirical basis for all thematic findings.
requirements: Included studies had to use the term data literacy within a K-12 or general-education context and be written in English
constraints: Book chapters, dissertations, editorials, and non-K-12 contexts (e.g., medicine, higher education) were excluded
target_learning_goals: Mapping expressed educational purposes of data literacy education
examples: Search stages included identification, cleaning in Zotero, cursory screening, content screening, and an additional snowball search revisiting prior reviews
key_sources: Fagerlund, J., Palsa, L., & Mertala, P. (2025). Exploration of domains of educational purpose in K-12 data literacy education research. Educational Research Review, 46, Article 100663. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2024.100663

article_title: An integrative review of the cognitive costs and benefits of note-taking
citation: Jansen, R. S., Lakens, D., & IJsselsteijn, W. (2017). An integrative review of the cognitive costs and benefits of note-taking. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.10.001
title: Cognitive load framework of note-taking: five recursive processes whose load explains divergent encoding effects
description: The review proposes that note-taking is a multi-stage process in which a note-taker must "(1) comprehend the lecture material, (2) identify key points, (3) link the material to prior knowledge and prior notes, (4) paraphrase or summarize, and (5) transform to written form", performed recursively during a lecture. Because note-taking induces load beyond comprehension alone, it can overload some individuals in some situations and become detrimental. The framework links lecture structure, modality, speed, note-taking style and structure, and cognitive ability to load on specific phases, integrating the divergent empirical findings reviewed.
requirements: Applicable to individual (non-collaborative) note-taking in educational settings without note review, as scoped by the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: The review states further research is warranted to test the effects of note-taking on cognitive load, and that which effect of typing (resource savings versus shallower processing) is stronger should be explored in more detail
target_learners: students in primary, secondary, and higher education attending lectures
target_learning_goals: memory for lecture content
examples: The review uses the framework to explain why organised note-taking hurt memory with an audio lecture (Bui et al., 2013) but helped with a text (Bretzing & Kulhavy, 1979): with text, phases 2 and 3 can be performed sequentially rather than simultaneously with comprehension
key_sources: Jansen, R. S., Lakens, D., & IJsselsteijn, W. (2017). An integrative review of the cognitive costs and benefits of note-taking. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.10.001

article_title: The Social Side of School: Why Teachers Need Social Psychology
citation: Gehlbach, Hunter. (2010). The social side of school: Why teachers need social psychology. Educational Psychology Review 22, no. 3: 349-362. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9138-3
title: Cognitive dissonance as a self-persuasion mechanism with free-choice and foreseeable-consequence conditions
description: The review describes cognitive dissonance (Festinger) as the finding that "the arguments we perceive to be most persuasive tend to come from our own mouths," so that preaching a position increases the likelihood of practicing it. It specifies two caveats from Cooper and Fazio (1984): dissonance requires perceived free choice and foreseeable negative consequences. Classroom applications include peer tutoring in which students advocate homework's importance, and having students voice, explain, and publicly post their goals.
requirements: People must feel they freely chose the behavior, and the behavior must have foreseeable negative consequences, for dissonance to arise
constraints: The review hedges that the preach-then-practice rule holds true only subject to a couple of caveats
target_learning_goals: bolstering student motivation and effort on homework and academic goals
examples: Eighth graders mentoring fourth graders were encouraged to stress homework's importance, with free choice established via an onerous worksheet alternative and consequences instilled through class discussion of setting a good example
key_sources: Gehlbach, Hunter. (2010). The social side of school: Why teachers need social psychology. Educational Psychology Review 22, no. 3: 349-362. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9138-3

article_title: There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy
citation: Lin Zhang, Paul A. Kirschner, William W. Cobern, John Sweller. (2022). There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09646-1
title: Cognitive load theory account of why explicit instruction outperforms inquiry for novice learners acquiring complex novel information
description: The article invokes cognitive load theory (Sweller et al., 2011, 2019) as a cognitively based theory underpinning explicit, structured instruction. Its assumptions are that humans evolved to obtain novel information from others because this is more efficient than generating it by problem solving; novel information must be processed by a limited capacity, limited duration working memory before transfer to long-term memory; and stored information governs action without known working-memory limits. On this basis the article argues "there never is a justification for engaging in inquiry-based learning or any other pedagogically identical approaches when students need to acquire complex, novel information."
requirements: Applies when students need to acquire complex, novel information
constraints: The article's argument targets acquisition of complex novel information by novices; it does not claim inquiry is never useful for other learning goals
target_learners: novice learners in a complex area
target_learning_goals: acquisition of complex novel information
science conceptual and procedural understanding
examples: The article cites the worked example effect, in which studying worked examples yields superior performance over solving equivalent problems for novices
key_sources: Lin Zhang, Paul A. Kirschner, William W. Cobern, John Sweller. (2022). There is an Evidence Crisis in Science Educational Policy. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09646-1

article_title: Practice Recommendations or Not? The LoGeT Model as Empirical Approach to Generate Localized, Generalized, and Transferable Evidence
citation: Lachner, A., Sibley, L., & Wagner, S. (2024). Practice Recommendations or Not? The LoGeT Model as Empirical Approach to Generate Localized, Generalized, and Transferable Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09876-z
title: Design transfer products co-constructively and early, using formative testing to foster acceptance and adoption
description: Within the LoGeT model's transfer stage, evidence and interventions are processed and published so other stakeholders can adopt them, with transfer activities planned from the outset and outputs tailored to the targeted audience (compact summaries, intervention descriptions, OER materials; print, multimedia, social media formats). The article recommends that "co-constructive, formative design and testing could contribute to the acceptance and adoption of the different transfer products," and suggests presentation in application-related specialist outlets and practice-related conferences. In the example projects, materials were published as OER in repositories and scaled through professional networks and practice journals.
requirements: Transfer activities considered early in the localization and generalization stages
Professionals to effectively communicate the obtained evidence
constraints: Cascade-transfer strategies via clearing houses may create a natural bottleneck for in-time, state-of-the-art evidence
OER materials vary greatly in quality and may not integrate empirical research testing their effectiveness
target_learners: Schools not participating in the original design studies
target_learning_goals: Adoption of evidence-based instructional practices in educational practice
examples: The TPACK and adaptive-teaching projects published materials as OER in repositories; non-interactive teaching findings were incorporated into federal professional development programs and short explanation videos for German teachers.
key_sources: Lachner, A., Sibley, L., & Wagner, S. (2024). Practice Recommendations or Not? The LoGeT Model as Empirical Approach to Generate Localized, Generalized, and Transferable Evidence. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09876-z

article_title: The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion
citation: John Sweller. (2023). The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09817-2
title: Current cognitive load theory: biologically secondary knowledge, limited working memory, vast long-term memory, and element interactivity determining intrinsic and extraneous load
description: The article outlines the current version of cognitive load theory, which is 'concerned with the acquisition of biologically secondary knowledge and is based on the cognitive architecture associated with the acquisition of such knowledge'. Novel information is processed by a working memory with severe capacity and duration limits and stored in long-term memory with no known limits. Element interactivity determines working memory load: high interactivity yields intrinsic cognitive load, while presentation-driven complexity yields extraneous load that instruction should minimise.
requirements: Instruction must be designed to minimise or eliminate extraneous cognitive load
The theory applies to biologically secondary knowledge that requires explicit teaching
constraints: Germane cognitive load is no longer considered an independent source of load
Element interactivity cannot be accurately measured because it relies on knowledge of the exact contents of long-term memory, but it can be estimated
target_learners: students acquiring biologically secondary knowledge in educational institutions
target_learning_goals: acquisition of biologically secondary knowledge such as reading, writing, and mathematics
key_sources: John Sweller. (2023). The Development of Cognitive Load Theory: Replication Crises and Incorporation of Other Theories Can Lead to Theory Expansion. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09817-2

article_title: The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects
citation: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1
title: Common-core definition of curiosity as recognition of an information gap combined with a sense that closing it is possible and intrinsically valuable
description: The article proposes deriving definitions from the common core of typical usages. On this approach, curiosity is defined as a psychological state including recognition of an information gap, anticipation that it may be possible to close it, and an intrinsically motivated desire to do so. The article argues that information gaps alone are insufficient, since gaps may alternatively cause surprise, confusion, or frustration, so a sense of control must be added.
requirements: The definition treats perception of an information gap as a necessary constituent, plus a sense of control that the gap can be closed and intrinsic value of closure
constraints: At this stage of research, the article states there is insufficient evidence to consider additional components, such as negative deprivation affect, as necessary constituents of curiosity
target_learning_goals: fostering curiosity and knowledge acquisition
key_sources: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1

article_title: The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects
citation: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1
title: Common-core definition of interest as intrinsically motivated engagement with a specific activity, object, or content
description: The article defines interest as intrinsically motivated engagement with any specific object, content, or activity. The common core of definitions is engagement with an activity, object, or content because such engagement is intrinsically valuable. Additional components such as positive emotion are treated as possible but not necessary ingredients, since situational interest can be associated with either positive or negative feelings.
requirements: Definitions of interest should be derived from the common core of typical usages, with engagement and intrinsic value as the core elements
constraints: Positive emotion is not a necessary component; the article notes cases in which interest involves negative emotions, such as students' disgust when fascinated by dissecting frogs
target_learners: students across age groups and cultural contexts
target_learning_goals: fostering interest and engagement in learning
key_sources: Pekrun, R. (2019). The Murky Distinction Between Curiosity and Interest: State of the Art and Future Prospects. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 905–914. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09512-1

article_title: The Forward Effect of Judgements of Learning on Memory and Transfer in Inductive Learning
citation: Ritter, C., Hausman, H., Gaschler, R., Tiffin-Richards, S. P., & Kubik, V. (2025). The Forward Effect of Judgements of Learning on Memory and Transfer in Inductive Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10094-4
title: Covert-retrieval account of forward effects of judgments of learning
description: The article advances and tests the account that JOLs benefit new learning "by inducing covert retrieval—that is, causing learners to search their memory for the target information to judge the likelihood they will be able to recall on a later test." Cue-only JOLs, given when only partial information is present, should trigger more retrieval than cue–target JOLs, which can rest on familiarity. The two-stage model holds that a JOL involves an initial familiarity assessment followed by retrieval only when familiarity is moderate, producing the inverted U-shaped JOL–RT relationship observed for cue-only JOLs.
requirements: JOL prompts must be item-level and cue-only (target information absent) to engage retrieval-based monitoring
constraints: The truncated search hypothesis warns that retrieval efforts that stop prematurely will fail to support future learning
Aggregate JOLs rely on broader heuristics and may be less sensitive to retrieval-based mechanisms
target_learners: university students learning visual natural categories
target_learning_goals: inductive learning of natural categories (memory and transfer of category memberships)
examples: Experiment 1 compared overt retrieval, cue-only JOLs, cue–target JOLs, and restudy as interim tasks between study phases
Experiment 2 added a feedback manipulation to cue-only JOLs to test retrieval-based versus metacognitive-effort explanations
key_sources: Ritter, C., Hausman, H., Gaschler, R., Tiffin-Richards, S. P., & Kubik, V. (2025). The Forward Effect of Judgements of Learning on Memory and Transfer in Inductive Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10094-4

article_title: Special Issue on Cognitive Load Theory: Editorial
citation: Paul Ginns & Jimmie Leppink. (2019). Special Issue on Cognitive Load Theory: Editorial. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 255–259. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09474-4
title: Cognitive load theory: working-memory limits and schema-based instructional design
description: Cognitive load theory draws on models of cognitive architecture, including a working memory whose limits are reduced when domain-specific schemas are activated from long-term memory, to generate and test instructional design hypotheses. The editorial states that "When working memory is overloaded by the competing demands of these processes, CLT argues, student learning is impaired." Researchers have typically used experimental methods to test designs targeting obstructions such as split attention or circumventing them with worked examples.
requirements: Instructional designs must be tested against models of human cognitive architecture, particularly working memory capacity and duration limits
target_learning_goals: schema construction and automation
problem solving
comprehension
examples: The Special Issue presents theoretical reviews, meta-analyses, and intervention studies all focused on advancement of CLT
key_sources: Paul Ginns & Jimmie Leppink. (2019). Special Issue on Cognitive Load Theory: Editorial. Educational Psychology Review, 31, 255–259. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09474-4

article_title: One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education
citation: Tommi Kokkonen & Lennart Schalk. (2021). One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09581-7
title: Biology's complex systems hierarchy of components, interactions, and emergent behaviors as a framework for representational levels
description: For biology, the article presents a framework conceptualizing three levels of complex systems. It states the framework "conceptualizes three levels of complex systems: components, interactions, and emergent behaviors (Buckley and Quellmalz 2013)." The component level corresponds to the concrete level, capturing phenomena as experienced; the interaction level consists of descriptions or dynamic models of interactions between components with significant idealization; the emergent behavior level may consist of mathematical descriptions such as population dynamics devoid of contextual details. The article argues the biochemical level constitutes its own conceptual sphere rather than a more idealized representation of macro-level phenomena, and that biology spans nested hierarchies of multiple entities.
requirements: Learners must make sense of complex interdependencies and causalities within and across levels
constraints: The article notes emergent phenomena are counterintuitive with non-linear interaction patterns, and cross-level relations are not present in mathematical descriptions of population-level dynamics
target_learning_goals: understanding hierarchical and complex biological systems and emergent phenomena
examples: Buckley and Quellmalz use an animation with life-like depictions of organisms such as grass, lizards, and crickets to illustrate ecosystem components
key_sources: Tommi Kokkonen & Lennart Schalk. (2021). One Instructional Sequence Fits all? A Conceptual Analysis of the Applicability of Concreteness Fading in Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, and Biology Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09581-7

article_title: Commentary on the Special Issue
citation: Gary D. Phye. (2012). Commentary on the Special Issue. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9211-1
title: Gibson's correspondence principle: research findings should correspond across levels of analysis
description: The commentary invokes Gibson (1994)'s correspondence principle to address poor communication between basic and applied psychologists. Different specialties study the same human behavior "from quite different levels of observation and analysis" but "there should be a correspondence among levels in terms of research findings." The author explicitly rejects a reductionist reading, framing the principle as correspondence between levels rather than a prescriptive cause-effect chain, and applies it to educational research on classroom learning.
requirements: Researchers studying the same behavior at different levels must seek correspondence among their findings rather than treating levels as incommensurable
constraints: The author states this is not a reductionist view proposing a prescriptive cause-effect relationship from brain cell to classroom performance
target_learning_goals: Academic learning and classroom performance
examples: The commentary contrasts a global constructivist analysis of fourth-grade academic growth with the more precise functional study of memory and cognition conducted by applied cognitive psychologists
key_sources: Gary D. Phye. (2012). Commentary on the Special Issue. Educ Psychol Rev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9211-1

article_title: The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development
citation: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5
title: Design epistemic learning environments by creating opportunities for learners and teachers to collaboratively notice, articulate, elaborate, and evaluate epistemic ideals and processes
description: This design principle from the Apt-AIR framework addresses growth in metacognitive understanding of epistemic performance. The article states that "a key design principle for supporting growth in metacognitive understanding of epistemic performance is creating opportunities for learners and teachers to collaboratively notice, articulate, elaborate, and evaluate epistemic ideals and processes." The authors implemented this by encouraging middle school students to develop and refine their own class lists of criteria for evaluating models, arguments, or sources, and by prompting students to evaluate source trustworthiness and discuss their justifications.
requirements: Learners need appropriate materials and prompts that scaffold the articulation and evaluation of epistemic ideals and processes
constraints: More research is needed to examine how designs for supporting learners' epistemic growth can be adapted to different educational levels and contexts
target_learners: middle school students through undergraduates and teacher education students
target_learning_goals: metacognitive understanding of epistemic aims, ideals, and processes including why they are valuable and how to apply them
examples: Encouraging middle school students to develop and refine class lists of criteria for evaluating models, arguments, or sources; prompting students to evaluate source trustworthiness and discuss justifications
key_sources: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5

article_title: Compositional Analysis of Writing Instructional Practices Performed with Digital Tools: A Meta-Analysis
citation: López, P., Fidalgo, R., Álvarez-Moreno, C., Díaz-Tejedor, R., van den Bergh, H., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2026). Compositional Analysis of Writing Instructional Practices Performed with Digital Tools: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10153-4
title: Component-based instructional design framework for analyzing ICT-supported writing interventions
description: The article adopts a component-based instructional design perspective, coding each intervention on four design aspects: Merrill's instructional principles (problem centered, activation, demonstration, application, integration), the instructional activities that operationalize them, the types of feedback, and the types of scaffolding. Each element is additionally coded by delivery agent (teacher, ICT, or both). The article argues that "analyzing ICT-supported writing interventions at a fine-grained, componential level provides clearer insight into how instructional design shapes learning outcomes" than aggregating interventions as a single category.
requirements: Studies must report sufficient description of the instructional intervention to code principles, activities, feedback, scaffolding, and delivery agent
constraints: Applied to ICT-supported writing interventions targeting higher-level cognitive writing processes (planning, drafting, revising, genre-based text structuring) in typically developing students
target_learners: typically developing students in primary, secondary, and higher education writing instruction
target_learning_goals: improvement of writing quality through higher-level writing processes such as planning, text structuring, and revision
examples: The framework was applied to 42 empirical studies contributing 53 effect sizes, coded with interrater reliability (Cohen's kappa ranging from 0.805 to 1.00)
key_sources: López, P., Fidalgo, R., Álvarez-Moreno, C., Díaz-Tejedor, R., van den Bergh, H., & Rijlaarsdam, G. (2026). Compositional Analysis of Writing Instructional Practices Performed with Digital Tools: A Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10153-4

article_title: Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: T. Vessonen, M. Dahlberg, H. Hellstrand, A. Widlund, J. Korhonen, P. Aunio, A. Laine. (2024). Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09954-2
title: Cognitive load account of word problem-solving task difficulty
description: The article frames task characteristics as moderators of the cognitive demands of word problem-solving: solving requires integrating multiple linguistic and numerical elements simultaneously, drawing on limited working memory, executive functions, and reading comprehension. "According to such theory, performing learning tasks imposes cognitive demands (or load) on a student's limited cognitive capacity (e.g., working memory)". The amount of demand is determined by element interactivity, so characteristics such as irrelevant information, lexical inconsistency, and multiple operations increase the elements to process and may especially challenge elementary schoolers whose cognitive capacity is still developing.
requirements: Applies to tasks requiring simultaneous integration of linguistic and numerical elements within limited working memory
constraints: The article presents this as a theoretical framing for interpreting associations, not as a tested mechanism in the meta-analysis itself
target_learners: Elementary school-aged children in Grades 1 to 6
target_learning_goals: Mathematical word problem-solving
key_sources: T. Vessonen, M. Dahlberg, H. Hellstrand, A. Widlund, J. Korhonen, P. Aunio, A. Laine. (2024). Task Characteristics Associated with Mathematical Word Problem-Solving Performance Among Elementary School-Aged Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09954-2

article_title: The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis
citation: Achraf Ammar, Khaled Trabelsi, Mohamed Ali Boujelbane, Atef Salem, Omar Boukhris, Jordan M. Glenn, Piotr Zmijewski, Haitham A. Jahrami, Hamdi Chtourou, Wolfgang I. Schöllhorn. (2024). The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09892-z
title: The contextual interference (CI) paradox model of practice scheduling
description: The CI model holds that "When practice trials are interrupted by the execution of other tasks, detrimental effects can be observed immediately after the acquisition phase but are followed by greater benefits in the subsequent retention phase compared to uninterrupted sequence." Two mechanisms are proposed: the "elaborative hypothesis" (deeper, more elaborate information processing during random practice) and the "forgetting/reconstruction hypothesis" (increased forcing retrieval practice and reconstruction of tasks' plans-of-action); working-memory overload during random practice is suggested to hinder acquisition. This meta-analysis tests and largely fails to support the model's generalization to gross motor skills.
requirements: A design contrasting low CI (blocked) practice with high CI (random/serial) practice, with acquisition and retention test phases, to exhibit the paradoxical pattern.
constraints: The article reports the effect "could only be systematically demonstrated for sequences of fine motor movements with a high visual-spatial component," and finds very limited evidence for generalization to PE and sports practices.
target_learners: learners of gross motor and sports skills in physical education settings
target_learning_goals: skill acquisition and relatively permanent retention of motor skills
examples: Blocked practice completes all trials of a task before moving to a different task in predictable patterns; random practice interleaves tasks in unpredictable order.
key_sources: Achraf Ammar, Khaled Trabelsi, Mohamed Ali Boujelbane, Atef Salem, Omar Boukhris, Jordan M. Glenn, Piotr Zmijewski, Haitham A. Jahrami, Hamdi Chtourou, Wolfgang I. Schöllhorn. (2024). The Effects of Contextual Interference Learning on the Acquisition and Relatively Permanent Gains in Skilled Performance: A Critical Systematic Review with Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09892-z

article_title: Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load
citation: Alexander Skulmowski & Kate Man Xu. (2022). Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09624-7
title: Cost-benefit model links specific design factors to extraneous load types with associated germane processing benefits
description: The review's organizing framework treats design factors as cognitive costs (extraneous load) paired with benefits (germane processing). "The cost-benefit model links different design factors to extraneous load types that feature associated forms of germane processing." Digital learning often involves "a trade-off between risks of exposing learners to extraneous load and the benefit of letting them profit from novel and engaging experiences", so a small extraneous investment can be worthwhile when its germane benefit exceeds the cost.
requirements: Designers must identify which germane process a given extraneous load component supports and compare cost against benefit for the specific task
constraints: The review states a cost-benefit approach alone does not suffice to explain divergent effects on different outcome measures such as retention versus transfer
target_learners: learners using digital and online learning environments
target_learning_goals: balancing engagement and cognitive load in digital learning design
key_sources: Alexander Skulmowski & Kate Man Xu. (2022). Understanding Cognitive Load in Digital and Online Learning: a New Perspective on Extraneous Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09624-7

article_title: The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning
citation: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1
title: Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning (CTML): dual channels, limited capacity, active processing
description: CTML is an evidence-based account of how people learn academic material from words and graphics. Its three guiding assumptions are that "dual channels (i.e., humans have separate information processing channels for verbal and visual information)", that "processing capacity is severely limited", and that meaningful learning involves active selecting, organizing, and integrating of material in working memory with prior knowledge from long-term memory. The theory is depicted in a stable flowchart with sensory, working, and long-term memory stores and yields multimedia design principles.
requirements: Applies to academic material consisting of words and graphics presented as multimedia instructional messages
constraints: The theory focuses on how to help people learn academic content rather than on the capabilities of the latest educational technologies
target_learners: students learning academic material from multimedia lessons
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning that transfers to new situations
examples: The theory is represented in Fig. 8 with an auditory row across the top and a visual row across the bottom, boxes for sensory, working, and long-term memory, and arrows for selecting, organizing, and integrating.
key_sources: Richard E. Mayer. (2024). The Past, Present, and Future of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09842-1

article_title: Interrelations Among Achievement Goals and Achievement Emotions: A Meta-Analytic Examination
citation: Tanja Bross, Ulrike Elisabeth Nett, & Martin Daumiller. (2024). Interrelations Among Achievement Goals and Achievement Emotions: A Meta-Analytic Examination. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09931-9
title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions with activity/outcome object focus
description: Control-value theory defines achievement emotions as "emotions tied directly to achievement activities or achievement outcomes" and explains them via control- and value-appraisals. Emotions are classified by valence and by object focus into activity emotions (e.g., enjoyment, boredom, anger during an activity) and outcome emotions (e.g., hope, pride, shame, hopelessness regarding outcomes), each with prospective, concurrent, or retrospective temporal relations. The article uses this taxonomy to differentiate goal-emotion associations at a specific level rather than only at the affective valence level, and predicts mastery-approach goals correlate positively with enjoyment and negatively with boredom and anger, while performance-approach goals link to positive outcome emotions such as hope and pride.
requirements: Achievement emotions must be measured with their object focus (activity vs. outcome) and temporal relation distinguished, not only by valence
constraints: The article notes the relationships among work-avoidance goals and emotions as well as among relational goals and emotions are not addressed in either theoretical model it reviews
target_learning_goals: understanding how achievement goals relate to achievement emotions in educational settings
examples: The article's Table 2 maps emotions such as anticipatory joy, hope, hopelessness, anxiety, enjoyment, boredom, anger and frustration onto object focus, value and control appraisals
key_sources: Tanja Bross, Ulrike Elisabeth Nett, & Martin Daumiller. (2024). Interrelations Among Achievement Goals and Achievement Emotions: A Meta-Analytic Examination. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09931-9

article_title: A Computational Model of School Achievement
citation: Brendan A. Schuetze. (2024). A Computational Model of School Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09853-6
title: CoMSA: A computational model of school achievement unifying cognitive, metacognitive, and motivational theory
description: The CoMSA is a formal mathematical model of the relationship between learning over time and exam achievement. It simulates individual student trajectories using logistic learning curves with three parameters (slope, intercept, inflection point), modulated by metacognitive bias and precision, and bounded by motivational circuit breakers (norm of study and maximum willingness to study). The model acts as an interface between construct-focused educational psychology and achievement outcomes by modeling the downstream behavioral effects of cognition, motivation, and metacognition.
requirements: Explicit encoding of assumptions in computer code enabling modification, theory testing, and novel predictions
Assumption that the S-shaped logistic curve is generally acceptable for modeling learning
constraints: The three steps (curve establishment, metacognitive modulation, stopping rule) are laid out in strict sequence for tractability; in real-world settings contingencies exist between steps
All inputs are assumed to be set once at the beginning of the study session and do not change over the course of the learning period
The analyses do not directly test the ability of the CoMSA to model individual-level data
target_learning_goals: Exam achievement
Self-regulated learning
examples: The model was used to simulate classroom-level data from two meta-analytic sources: Godwin et al. (2021) on time-on-task and Simonsmeier et al. (2022) on prior knowledge
key_sources: Brendan A. Schuetze. (2024). A Computational Model of School Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09853-6

article_title: A Computational Model of School Achievement
citation: Brendan A. Schuetze. (2024). A Computational Model of School Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09853-6
title: CoMSA simulation database of 184,032 simulation runs representing over 1.8 billion simulated students
description: A publicly available database hosted on OSF (https://osf.io/z8n3a/) containing the full simulation output from the CoMSA project. It includes N = 184,032 simulation runs representing over 1.8 billion individual simulated students, including runs rejected due to the second and third filtering criteria. The database can be queried, filtered, plotted, and analyzed to understand effects of different individual and contextual factors.
requirements: Access to the OSF project at https://osf.io/z8n3a/
constraints: Includes runs rejected due to the second and third filtering criteria, not just the final 100,000 used in analyses
target_learning_goals: Understanding effects of individual and contextual factors on achievement
examples: The database was used for proof-of-concept analyses comparing simulated correlations to two meta-analytic sources
key_sources: Brendan A. Schuetze. (2024). A Computational Model of School Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09853-6

article_title: A Computational Model of School Achievement
citation: Brendan A. Schuetze. (2024). A Computational Model of School Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09853-6
title: Learning curve parameterization: slope, intercept, and inflection point map to distinct educational constructs
description: The CoMSA conceptualizes educational differences through three logistic curve parameters. Slope (Logis a) represents learning rate per unit of time invested. Intercept (Logis c) represents floor performance when time spent studying is zero, associated with prior knowledge and guessing floors. Inflection point (Logis d) determines the amount of prerequisite learning needed before performance gains appear on the tested material. Interventions are modeled as modifications to these parameters.
requirements: Assumption that learning follows a logistic (S-shaped) curve within the 0-100 percent grading scale
Three-parameter logistic (3PL) model from psychometrics
constraints: Slope and all parameters are not directly mappable to any one contextual or psychological variable
The relationship between floor and prior knowledge also depends on the inflection point
target_learning_goals: Predicting exam achievement from student and contextual characteristics
examples: A medical student studying for a licensing exam would have a much shallower learning curve than a fifth-grade student studying for a ten-word vocabulary quiz
key_sources: Brendan A. Schuetze. (2024). A Computational Model of School Achievement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09853-6

article_title: Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework
citation: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6
title: CoDiL framework: a cognitive process framework on the learning mechanisms of digital tools in educational settings
description: CoDiL is a high-level conceptual integration of the KLI framework, the SOI model, and the ULO framework explaining how learning with digital tools succeeds. It distinguishes external instructional events and student-tool interactions from internal cognitive processes and knowledge components. Instructional features offer learning opportunities that, if utilized, trigger learning activities which—mediated by selecting, organizing, and integrating and in interaction with prior knowledge—lead to knowledge gains. The authors state it "can be used to theoretically ground, firstly, the design of digital tools for learning, and secondly, the empirical analysis of students' learning activities in digitally enriched educational settings via the analysis of specific student-tool interactions."
requirements: The framework's degrees of freedom must be specified for the concrete educational scenario of interest, since it is a high-level conceptual integration requiring more detailed empirical integration into specific studies
constraints: The authors state the current framework represents a high-level conceptual integration of KLI, SOI, and ULO, providing a basic starting point but requiring further empirical integration
target_learners: students in digitally enriched educational settings across subject domains
target_learning_goals: subject-matter knowledge acquisition with digital tools
examples: The authors frame Koedinger et al. (2010) formative assessment study and Lalley et al. (2010) virtual frog dissection study through the framework
key_sources: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6

article_title: Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework
citation: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6
title: Taxonomy of learning activities relevant for digitally enriched educational settings
description: The CoDiL framework enumerates learning activities that digital instructional features may initiate and stimulate, each with an external behavioral side (observable student-tool interactions) and an internal cognitive side. The article lists abstraction, conducting experiments, creating examples, exploration, formulating hypothesis, refinement, revision, and self-explanation, each defined with cited literature. These activities function as a link between external behavior and internal cognitive processes and are understood as theoretical predictors of learning outcomes. The authors state that "students' engagement in these learning activities as necessity for successful learning—in line with the ULO framework and generative learning theory."
requirements: Content-specific analysis of knowledge components as a fundamental basis for understanding which learning activities are at play
constraints: The article notes such content-specific learning activities are often not specified in detail in educational research, especially research on learning with digital tools
target_learners: students learning with digital tools in educational settings
target_learning_goals: engagement in generative learning activities leading to knowledge component acquisition
examples: The framework's discussion section centers the model on learning activities shown relevant to digital learning, e.g., abstraction, conducting experiments, creating examples, exploration, formulating hypothesis, refinement, revision, self-explanation
key_sources: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6

article_title: Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework
citation: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6
title: Digitally enriched instructional features as affordance-and-constraint learning opportunities
description: The framework conceptualizes instructional features as digitally enriched instructional events that have the potential to stimulate learning activities, are subject of affordances and constraints, and should be designed to lower extraneous load and increase generative processing. The article argues, in line with the media debate, that it is not the digital tool itself but the implemented features that initiate learning. It enumerates essential features: adaptive feedback, opportunities to try and fail (PS-I), prompting, prompting to summarize and explain, and contrasting cases, each mapped to the learning activities it may stimulate.
requirements: Features should be designed to foster learning activities, i.e., to lower extraneous load and increase generative processing compared to non-digitally enriched settings
constraints: Some of these instructional features can be included in classical non-digital classroom instruction as well; digital implementation is described as potentially particularly promising, not uniquely effective
target_learners: students in digitally enriched educational settings
target_learning_goals: stimulation of content-specific generative learning activities
examples: Adaptive feedback may stimulate refinement and revision activities by revealing the limits of students' prior knowledge; contrasting cases may stimulate revision by comparing examples
key_sources: Frank Reinhold, Timo Leuders, Katharina Loibl, Matthias Nückles, Maik Beege, Jan M. Boelmann (2024). Learning Mechanisms Explaining Learning With Digital Tools in Educational Settings: a Cognitive Process Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09845-6

article_title: The Associations Between Discrete Emotions and Political Learning: A Cross-Disciplinary Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Elisabeth Graf, Johanna L. Donath, Elouise Botes, Martin Voracek, Thomas Goetz. (2024). The Associations Between Discrete Emotions and Political Learning: A Cross-Disciplinary Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09893-y
title: Control-value theory four-category framework (activation × valence) applied to political learning
description: The article applies the control-value theory of achievement emotions (Pekrun, 2006) to political learning by sorting discrete emotions into four categories: "(1) positive-activating, (2) positive-deactivating, (3) negative-activating, and (4) negative-deactivating emotions". The theory proposes that positive-activating emotions foster learning while negative-deactivating emotions hinder it, with variable expectations for the other two categories. Using this framework let the authors "combine multiple discrete emotions to these categories with uniform expectations regarding their associations with learning" and derive Hypotheses 1 and 2 for the meta-analysis.
requirements: Emotions must be classifiable along the activation and valence dimensions, and discrete emotion measures must be available or categorizable into one of the four emotion groups
constraints: The article notes consequences for learning are not clear for positive-deactivating and negative-activating emotions, as they "often depend on the specific emotion or learning aspect considered"; the framework was developed for achievement settings and applied to politics as a novel context
target_learners: adults and university students in political learning contexts
target_learning_goals: political knowledge and knowledge gain
attention to politics
political information seeking
political discussions
examples: The meta-analysis tested Hypothesis 1 on positive-activating emotions and Hypothesis 2 on negative-deactivating emotions, and explored negative-activating emotions (anxiety, anger) separately by design type
key_sources: Elisabeth Graf, Johanna L. Donath, Elouise Botes, Martin Voracek, Thomas Goetz. (2024). The Associations Between Discrete Emotions and Political Learning: A Cross-Disciplinary Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09893-y

article_title: Why Do Learners (Under)Utilize Interleaving in Learning Confusable Categories? The Role of Metastrategic Knowledge and Utility Value of Distinguishing
citation: Roman Abel, Anique de Bruin, Erdem Onan, Julian Roelle. (2024). Why Do Learners (Under)Utilize Interleaving in Learning Confusable Categories? The Role of Metastrategic Knowledge and Utility Value of Distinguishing. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09902-0
title: Conditional-knowledge framework of learners' (under)utilization of interleaving in confusable category learning
description: The article models learners' spontaneous interleaving as depending on conditional (if–then) links among motivational and metacognitive processes. Learners first need "awareness-that-differences-matter": "learners need to be aware that detecting differences is essential for being able to distinguish confusable categories". Second, they need "awareness-that-interleaving-highlights-differences": awareness "that interleaving is supportive in detecting subtle differences between confusable categories". A motivational gap — low utility value of distinguishing — can break the first link, so that even aware learners do not invest effort in finding differences.
requirements: Learners must hold both conditional knowledge components — that differences matter for distinguishing and that interleaving highlights differences — for the if–then links to translate into spontaneous interleaving use.
constraints: The framework is stated for adult learners with advanced learning skills such as university students, for whom a mediation deficiency (not knowing how to execute interleaving) appears unlikely.
target_learning_goals: distinguishing easily confusable categories by detecting their predictive differences
examples: Experiment 1 factorially varied utility value of distinguishing (poisonous/edible vs. soil labels) and the differences-matter instruction; Experiment 2 additionally varied the instruction that interleaving highlights differences.
key_sources: Roman Abel, Anique de Bruin, Erdem Onan, Julian Roelle. (2024). Why Do Learners (Under)Utilize Interleaving in Learning Confusable Categories? The Role of Metastrategic Knowledge and Utility Value of Distinguishing. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09902-0

article_title: The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023))
citation: Zitzmann, S., Machts, N., Hübner, N., Schauber, S., Möller, J., & Lindner, C. (2023). The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023)). Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09776-8
title: Communicate findings from educational trials to stakeholders in a way they can easily understand, because recommendations derive from the findings
description: The article argues that researchers should report findings to teachers, schools, school authorities, and policy makers in a meaningful, understandable form. It states that "recommendations are derived from the findings, and a correct understanding of them is essential for stakeholders to evaluate the usefulness of recommendations and strengthen stakeholders' beliefs in their added value." Practical recommendations should be preceded by a stakeholder-appropriate summary of findings.
requirements: A summary of findings that is meaningful to stakeholders and communicated so these persons will easily understand them
target_learners: teachers, schools, school authorities, and policy makers as research stakeholders
target_learning_goals: stakeholder understanding and evaluation of research-based recommendations
examples: The authors precede their own recommendation by summarizing findings in plain terms and propose responder rates as an understandable summary format

The Yet Underestimated Importance of Communicating Findings from Educational Trials to Teachers, Schools, School Authorities, or Policy Makers (Comment on Brady et al. (2023)).
