article_title: On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging
citation: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2
title: Counterspaces with three processes for sustaining marginalized students' belonging
description: Counterspaces are relational spaces where students with shared marginalization share, affirm, and analyze counter-stories, satisfying relational and cultural place-belongingness needs. The article describes them as psychological and relational sites of resistance that reshape dominant power structures 'through three distinct processes: narrative identity work, direct relational transactions, and acts of resistance (Case & Hunter, 2012).' Many institutional spaces, including research labs and ethnic studies courses, can function as counterspaces, though they sit outside the main fabric of the institution.
requirements: Participants must be able to feel accepted within safe parameters while a critical approach heightens awareness of the politics of belonging
constraints: Counterspaces are considered 'counter' because they do not exist within the main fabric of the institution
target_learners: marginalized undergraduate students, e.g., undergraduate women of color in STEM at a predominantly white institution
target_learning_goals: fostering belonging, navigational competence in dominant culture, and resistance to structural marginalization
examples: A year-long community initiative at a PWI served as a counterspace and fostered belonging for undergraduate women of color in STEM (Wilkins-Yel et al., 2022); a counterspace for first-generation students of color mobilized navigational and resistance capital
key_sources: Rebecca Covarrubias. (2024). On Being Accepted: Interrogating How University Cultural Scripts Shape Personal and Political Facets of Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09970-2

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory: Advances in Research on Worked Examples, Animations, and Cognitive Load Measurement
citation: Tamara van Gog & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: Advances in Research on Worked Examples, Animations, and Cognitive Load Measurement. Educ Psychol Rev (2010) 22:375–378. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9145-4
title: Cognitive load theory: instruction should optimize intrinsic load, reduce extraneous load, and foster germane load
description: Cognitive load theory concerns learning complex cognitive tasks in which learners may be overwhelmed by "the number of interactive information elements that need to be processed simultaneously". Its central tenet is that instruction should be designed at an optimal level of complexity (intrinsic load), reduce load from processes not contributing to learning (extraneous load), and optimize load from processes fostering learning (germane load). This editorial uses the framework to organize advances in example-based learning, animation design, and load measurement.
requirements: Instruction must be designed so complexity is at an optimal level for the learner's working memory capacity
constraints: Applies to complex cognitive tasks where interactive elements must be processed simultaneously before meaningful learning can commence
target_learners: novice learners of complex cognitive tasks
target_learning_goals: learning and transfer of complex cognitive task skills
examples: The special issue applies the theory to worked examples in tutoring systems, animation segmentation, and EEG load measurement
key_sources: Tamara van Gog & Fred Paas & John Sweller. (2010). Cognitive Load Theory: Advances in Research on Worked Examples, Animations, and Cognitive Load Measurement. Educ Psychol Rev (2010) 22:375–378. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9145-4

article_title: Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives:Commentary on the Special Issue Papers
citation: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1
title: Concreteness fading: systematic shift from enactive to iconic to symbolic representations to support generalization of deep structure
description: Concreteness fading is an instructional approach in which representations systematically become more abstract over instruction: learners begin with enactive (physical) representations, move through iconic intermediaries, and end with symbolic ones. The commentary describes it as seeking "an appropriate level of instructional guidance" and notes that, unlike providing multiple external representations, "concreteness fading requires that the representations systematically become more abstract". It is grounded in long-standing interest dating to Bruner (1964) and is exemplified in the special issue by Fyfe et al.'s math and science strategy.
requirements: Representations must shift systematically from enactive to symbolic, with iconic representations as an intermediary
constraints: After a period of instruction with external representations learners often fail to generalize learning, which the approach is designed to address; model breaking points may impede transfer when deep structure implied by manipulatives fails to generalize
target_learners: Elementary and secondary mathematics and science learners
target_learning_goals: Generalization of the deep structure of mathematical and scientific concepts to related circumstances
examples: Fyfe et al. (2014/this issue) develop and empirically test a mathematics and science instructional strategy based on concreteness fading; related reading and listening comprehension research used imagined manipulation as an iconic intermediary
key_sources: Scott C. Marley & Kira J. Carbonneau. (2014). Future Directions for Theory and Research with Instructional Manipulatives: Commentary on the Special Issue Papers. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9259-1

article_title: Comments on Integration, Theory Conflicts, and Practical Implementations: Some Contrarian Ideas for Consideration
citation: Richard M. Ryan. (2024). Comments on Integration, Theory Conflicts, and Practical Implementations: Some Contrarian Ideas for Consideration. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09858-1
title: Coordinate distinct theories within interventions when their techniques are compatible and non-contradictory
description: The article argues that practical integration in interventions differs from theoretical integration: distinct theories can be combined in interventions "as long as techniques and processes within different theories can be coordinated and are not contradictory to one another". Different theories address different aspects of the classroom, and applying multiple frameworks is common in professions like engineering and psychotherapy. The author cites pairings such as teacher expectation theory with SDT, and SDT with socio-emotional learning strategies, as readily combined in practice.
requirements: Techniques and processes from the combined theories must be coordinable and non-contradictory
constraints: Some theories cannot be easily integrated and some may be contradictory, e.g. differing definitions of basic psychological need
Social cognitive theory could not incorporate SDT's views of competence growth without radical change in its philosophical foundations
target_learning_goals: Supporting student motivation, engagement, and classroom climate
examples: The article cites Hornstra et al. (2023) combining teacher expectation theory with SDT around positive classroom climate, and Ng (2023) pairing SDT with SEL strategies
key_sources: Richard M. Ryan. (2024). Comments on Integration, Theory Conflicts, and Practical Implementations: Some Contrarian Ideas for Consideration. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09858-1

article_title: Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories?
citation: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5
title: Core motivation: mental processes that directly influence goal direction, intensity, and persistence of behavior
description: The article argues that broad energy-and-direction definitions of motivation are overinclusive, implying that neurohormonal processes, nutrition, and emotions would all count as motivation. It instead proposes "core motivation, defined as mental processes that directly influence goal direction, intensity, and persistence of behavior," comprising proximal mental determinants such as goals, expectancies, values, and intentions combined with feelings of desire. The author recommends defining the conceptual space theoretically before integrating theories located in it.
requirements: The conceptual space of motivation should be defined theoretically rather than by lists of theories that happen to exist
constraints: The author presents core motivation as one possibility among several, not the only defensible definition
target_learning_goals: academic motivation
examples: The theories synthesized in the collection focus on mental representations such as goals, ability beliefs, expectancies, attributions, values, and needs
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5

article_title: The Effect of Testing on the Retention of Coherent and Incoherent Text Material
citation: de Jonge, M., Tabbers, H. K., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2015). The Effect of Testing on the Retention of Coherent and Incoherent Text Material. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9300-z
title: Use completion tests for retention of unconnected materials rather than highly structured texts
description: The article's central design implication is that the benefit of fill-in-the-blank testing depends on material connectedness. As the abstract states, "Testing with a completion test seems most beneficial for unconnected materials and less so for highly structured materials." When material is already coherent and structured, the text's organization may serve as a retrieval cue, leaving the completion test little additional processing to add; when material is a list of facts, testing slows forgetting relative to restudy.
requirements: Material whose connectedness is low (e.g., lists of facts) for the testing benefit to emerge.
constraints: Conclusions are limited to the short-answer (fill-in-the-blank) test format; the authors state they "would not want to imply that testing as a general learning activity might not be a useful tool for learning texts."
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of learned material
examples: Experiment 2 presented the black hole text as a scrambled list of facts and found testing slowed forgetting; Experiment 1 with the coherent text found no benefit.
key_sources: de Jonge, M., Tabbers, H. K., & Rikers, R. M. J. P. (2015). The Effect of Testing on the Retention of Coherent and Incoherent Text Material. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9300-z

article_title: Emotional Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
citation: Heng Zhang, Yuhan Liu, Meilin Jiang, Juanjuan Chen, Minhong Wang, Fred Paas. (2025). Emotional Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10086-4
title: Control-value theory as an explanatory framework for AI-based cognitive and emotional support effects
description: The review interprets effects of AI-based learning support through Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions, which "posits that achievement emotions stem from learners’ appraisals of control over tasks and the value they assign to those tasks." In AI-supported learning, cognitive support such as personalized feedback can raise perceived control, while emotional support can stabilize achievement emotions; the authors therefore expected the largest knowledge and skill effects when supports are integrated. This framework organizes the meta-analysis's directional expectations and its interpretation of why integrated supports outperformed emotional-only support on cognitive outcomes.
requirements: AI-based cognitive support that raises perceived task control and emotional support that regulates achievement emotions must be distinguishable and combinable in the intervention design
constraints: The authors describe their expectations as "theory-informed expectations rather than confirmatory hypotheses"; heterogeneity suggests mechanisms depend on task complexity, adaptivity, and how tightly emotional signals are coupled to instructional actions
target_learners: students across pre-school, elementary, secondary, and tertiary education
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition
skill acquisition
affective experience regulation
examples: The review expected integrated support to outperform emotional-only support on cognitive outcomes by increasing perceived control while regulating emotions
key_sources: Heng Zhang, Yuhan Liu, Meilin Jiang, Juanjuan Chen, Minhong Wang, Fred Paas. (2025). Emotional Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10086-4

article_title: The Cognitive Architecture of Digital Externalization
citation: Alexander Skulmowski. (2023). The Cognitive Architecture of Digital Externalization. Educational Psychology Review, 35:101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09818-1
title: Cognitive architecture of digital externalization: cognitive load determines when learners offload information
description: The article presents a model of digital externalization grounded in cognitive load theory, in which the decision to externalize information is driven by five factors: lower actual or perceived working memory capacity, higher extraneous cognitive load, higher intrinsic cognitive load, and the perceived value of information. As the article states, "the model presented in Fig. 1 presents extraneous cognitive load as a triple barrier for information in the selection, offloading, and long-term memorization stages." Extraneous load can block information from entering working memory, from being stored in long-term memory, and from being externalized via complex artifact controls. Strategy selection is metacognitive, drawing on learners' beliefs about their capabilities and the task.
requirements: Grounded in the current iteration of cognitive load theory distinguishing intrinsic and extraneous cognitive load
Learners make metacognitive strategy-selection decisions based on beliefs about capabilities and task demands
constraints: The article notes memory and intention offloading "might need to be considered as distinct phenomena following their own sets of rules"
The model is a synthesis of prior studies rather than a directly tested prediction
target_learners: learners using digital technologies for learning
target_learning_goals: understanding when learners internalize versus externalize information
key_sources: Alexander Skulmowski. (2023). The Cognitive Architecture of Digital Externalization. Educational Psychology Review, 35:101. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09818-1

article_title: The Relationship Between Cognitive Offloading and the Transient Information Effect
citation: Chen, O., Allen, R., Waterman, A., & Sweller, J. (2026). The Relationship Between Cognitive Offloading and the Transient Information Effect. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10132-9
title: Cognitive offloading is a learner-driven process of externalising internal information onto the environment
description: The article defines cognitive offloading as the use of physical action to alter the information processing requirements of a task so as to reduce cognitive demand. It distinguishes two forms: environmental adjustments or external normalisation, and direct externalisation of to-be-remembered information to the environment such as note-taking or setting reminders. The learner is active and drives the offloading behaviour.
requirements: Learners must have access to external tools or representations to offload information onto
constraints: Offloading can become problematic if overused or if it distracts from learning
target_learners: children and adults across a range of educational and everyday contexts
target_learning_goals: reducing memory and processing demands during task performance
key_sources: Chen, O., Allen, R., Waterman, A., & Sweller, J. (2026). The Relationship Between Cognitive Offloading and the Transient Information Effect. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10132-9

article_title: Editor’s Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno
citation: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2
title: Moreno's cognitive–affective theory of learning with media incorporates motivational and metacognitive factors within cognitive theories of multimedia learning
description: This editorial describes the cognitive–affective theory of learning with media as Roxana Moreno's extension of emerging cognitive theories of multimedia learning. According to Mayer's tribute, along the way she was able to "incorporate motivational and metacognitive factors within the emerging cognitive theories of multimedia learning, creating her cognitive – affective theory of learning with media." The theory integrates affective and motivational processes with the cognitive account of learning from words and pictures, and Park and Brünken note a final paper she valued because it "integrates the cognitive and affective perspectives on learning with multimedia instruction."
requirements: The theory is presented as an extension of cognitive theories of multimedia learning, building on that prior theoretical base as the article describes
target_learning_goals: learning from words and pictures in multimedia environments
examples: The editorial reports that Moreno applied the theory across media ranging from narrated animation to virtual reality to educational games to training video
key_sources: Robinson, D. (2010). Editor's Note: Remembering Roxana Moreno. Educational Psychology Review, 22, 363–374. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-010-9147-2

article_title: Inhibitory Control and Mathematical Ability in Elementary School Children: A Preregistered Meta-Analysis
citation: Zhu, X., Tang, Y., Lu, J., Song, M., Yang, C., & Zhao, X. (2025). Inhibitory Control and Mathematical Ability in Elementary School Children: A Preregistered Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 37(1), 1. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09976-w
title: Constrained and unconstrained model of mathematical skills
description: The constrained and unconstrained model categorizes mathematical skills by whether they can be mastered and automated. The article states that "constrained skills involve a relatively small and finite pool of knowledge (e.g., counting, single-digit arithmetic), which can be fully automated through learning or experience", whereas "unconstrained skills involve an infinite pool of knowledge (e.g., word problem-solving), which may be slow or even impossible to automate". It integrates intrinsic cognitive load theory and dual-processing theory, predicting that the inhibitory control–mathematical ability relationship is weaker for constrained skills and stable for unconstrained skills. The meta-analysis uses it to motivate the mathematical-domain moderator and to interpret the weaker elementary-school correlation.
requirements: Requires distinguishing mathematical skills that can be automated from those that cannot
constraints: The meta-analysis found no significant moderation by mathematical ability domain, which runs against the model's prediction of domain-dependent correlations
target_learning_goals: mathematical ability
inhibitory control development
examples: The meta-analysis coded six domains of mathematical ability, including numerical ability, arithmetical ability, logical reasoning ability, geometric ability, standardized mathematics tests scores, and school examinations scores, to test the model's predictions
key_sources: Zhu, X., Tang, Y., Lu, J., Song, M., Yang, C., & Zhao, X. (2025). Inhibitory Control and Mathematical Ability in Elementary School Children: A Preregistered Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 37(1), 1. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09976-w

article_title: Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations
citation: Skulmowski, A., Nebel, S., Remmele, M., & Rey, G. D. (2022). Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09638-1
title: Cognitive model of learning with realistic visualizations: perception, schema construction, and testing stages
description: The article's cognitive model traces learning outcomes with realistic visualizations through three stages: perception, schema construction, and testing. In the perceptual stage learners segment contents and form a 3D representation; realism dimensions contribute to a perceptual load that can be lightened with cues. At schema construction, elements and their visual relationships form a primarily visual form of element interactivity integrated into long-term memory, moderated by learner characteristics such as spatial ability. At testing, the realism level of the learned visualization interacts with test type in determining performance.
requirements: The model assumes stages may be completed in a different order or in a continuous loop, for example in virtual reality environments where several objects are perceived and learned in succession
constraints: The model is presented as a framework for formulating predictions and guiding research, not as directly tested in this article
target_learners: learners using realistic visualizations, e.g., in anatomy learning and virtual reality environments
target_learning_goals: retention and transfer of visually presented learning content
examples: The model explains how realistic details created using shading and texture maps induce perceptual load that can be lowered using cues, and how learning goals can transform realistic details from extraneous load towards intrinsic load
key_sources: Skulmowski, A., Nebel, S., Remmele, M., & Rey, G. D. (2022). Is a Preference for Realism Really Naive After All? A Cognitive Model of Learning with Realistic Visualizations. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09638-1

article_title: Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis
citation: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2
title: Collaboration scripts as scaffolds structuring interactive processes between learning partners
description: The article defines collaboration scripts as instructional scaffolds for collaborative learning. As the abstract states, collaboration scripts are scaffolds that aim to improve collaboration through structuring the interactive processes between two or more learning partners. The concept is grounded in the script notion from Schank and Abelson and applied to both face-to-face and computer-mediated collaborative learning settings.
requirements: At least two learning partners whose interactive processes are to be structured
target_learners: Collaborative learners in face-to-face or computer-mediated settings
target_learning_goals: Improved collaboration and individual knowledge acquisition
key_sources: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2

article_title: Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis
citation: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2
title: Five-component taxonomy of collaboration scripts
description: The article proposes that collaboration scripts can be analyzed into five components, which serve as a basis for comparing different script approaches. As printed, collaboration scripts consist of at least five components: (a) learning objectives, (b) type of activities, (c) sequencing, (d) role distribution, and (e) type of representation. These components function as an analytical taxonomy for describing and comparing prototypical script approaches.
requirements: A script design must specify each of the five components to be fully described
constraints: The list is stated as a minimum: at least five components
target_learners: Designers and researchers of collaborative learning environments
target_learning_goals: Systematic design and comparison of collaboration scripts
key_sources: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2

article_title: Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis
citation: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2
title: Design collaboration scripts that support both participation and coordination and induce individual knowledge acquisition and metacognition
description: The article recommends consolidating the two research lines so that scripts both support participation and coordination, as well as induce learning activities closely related to individual knowledge acquisition and metacognition. This design principle follows directly from the analysis showing that face-to-face scripts emphasize acquisition activities while computer-mediated scripts emphasize coordination, so integrated scripts should address both functions.
requirements: Script designers must address both the communicative-coordinative dimension and the individual knowledge acquisition dimension
target_learners: Collaborative learners in face-to-face and computer-mediated settings
target_learning_goals: Collaboration quality, individual knowledge acquisition, and metacognition
key_sources: Kollar, I., Fischer, F. & Hesse, F.W. (2006). Collaboration Scripts – A Conceptual Analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 18, 159–185. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-006-9007-2

article_title: Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective
citation: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2
title: Teachers can combine load-reducing instructional strategies with an autonomy-supportive, structured motivating style, since the same strategies reduce cognitive load and support autonomous motivation
description: The article concludes that strategies for motivating students and strategies for reducing cognitive load are not antagonistic: "the same strategies that support students' autonomous motivation can also be those that minimize extraneous cognitive load." Teachers should use load reduction instruction (reducing difficulty, scaffolding, practice, feedback, guided independent work) while adopting motivating styles high in autonomy support and structure, because control and chaos pose risks of increased load and reduced motivation and engagement.
requirements: Teachers able to enact load reduction instruction principles and autonomy-supportive, structured motivating styles in whole-class settings
constraints: Evidence is cross-sectional and correlational; the article notes minimal risk for motivation and engagement from load-reducing strategies but causal conclusions await longitudinal designs
target_learning_goals: reducing extraneous cognitive load while fostering autonomous motivation, engagement, and achievement
examples: In the survey of 88 classes, student-perceived load reduction instruction correlated negatively with extraneous load (r = -.679) and positively with engagement (r = .646).
key_sources: Evans, P., Vansteenkiste, M., Parker, P., Kingsford-Smith, A., & Zhou, S. (2024). Cognitive Load Theory and Its Relationships with Motivation: a Self-Determination Theory Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09841-2

article_title: The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education
citation: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y
title: Systematic review corpus of 46 STEM studies on more than two external representations
description: The article's evidence base is a systematic review corpus of 46 eligible studies identified through searches of Scopus, ERIC, and PsycINFO plus conference proceedings (AERA, EARLI, ICLS, ESERA, NARST), "comprising 170 individual measurements." Studies were screened by two independent raters against eight predefined inclusion criteria using Rayyan. Of the 46 studies, 23 were selected for the meta-analysis based on having a control group with two or fewer representations, sufficient data to calculate effect sizes, and a focus on students' learning. Publication years spanned 1984 to 2022, and contexts included mathematics, electrical engineering, chemistry, biology, physics, and computer science.
requirements: Included studies required a comparative design, students of any age, STEM scope, cognitive outcomes, at least one condition with more than two external representations, and data allowing effect-size calculation.
constraints: Only a few of the included studies investigate students' problem-solving with MERs, and studies solely investigating learning with different types of more than two representations are sparse.
target_learners: Students of any age in STEM education
target_learning_goals: Learning and problem-solving with multiple external representations
examples: The Results section reports a subset of 20 studies for the meta-analysis, while the Method section states 23 studies were selected; the article prints both figures.
key_sources: Rexigel, E., Kuhn, J., Becker, S., & Malone, S. (2024). The More the Better? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of the Benefits of More than Two External Representations in STEM Education. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09958-y

article_title: Benefits of Taking a Virtual Field Trip in Immersive Virtual Reality: Evidence for the Immersion Principle in Multimedia Learning
citation: Guido Makransky · Richard E. Mayer. (2022). Benefits of Taking a Virtual Field Trip in Immersive Virtual Reality: Evidence for the Immersion Principle in Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1771–1798. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09675-4
title: Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL)
description: CAMIL describes how the level of immersion influences learning through affective factors. "According to the CAMIL ..., the main affordances of learning in immersive environments are a higher sense of presence (the psychological sense of 'being there') and agency (being in control of one's actions)". The model links immersion to presence, presence to enjoyment and interest, and these affective factors to immediate and delayed retention. The study's SEM provided "evidence for two pathways within the cognitive affective model of immersive learning—the enjoyment pathway and the interest pathway".
requirements: Structural equation modeling of the hypothesized links between immersion, presence, enjoyment, interest, and retention measures.
constraints: Cognitive load is identified as a potential limitation of learning with IVR; boundary conditions include cognitive load, reflection opportunities, and self-regulated learning support.
target_learning_goals: retention of instructional content
affective outcomes (presence, enjoyment, interest)
examples: Figure 1's hypothesized model with nine links (immersion→presence; presence→enjoyment and interest; enjoyment and interest→immediate and delayed retention) was tested via SEM in the Greenland virtual field trip experiment.
key_sources: Guido Makransky · Richard E. Mayer. (2022). Benefits of Taking a Virtual Field Trip in Immersive Virtual Reality: Evidence for the Immersion Principle in Multimedia Learning. Educational Psychology Review (2022) 34:1771–1798. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09675-4

article_title: Promoting Social Inclusion in Educational Settings: Challenges and Opportunities
citation: Juvonen, J., Lessard, L.M., Rastogi, R., Schacter, H.L., & Smith, D.S. (2019). Promoting social inclusion in educational settings: Challenges and opportunities. Educational Psychologist, 54, 250-270. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2019.1655645
title: Conceptual accounts of peer exclusion: homophily, social norms, and intergroup dynamics
description: The article's explanatory framework for why classmates bully, reject, and avoid befriending some peers, approached from the perspective of those showing prejudice rather than presuming something is wrong with excluded students. It integrates three accounts. First, ingroup favoritism and homophily: "Students of all ages gravitate toward similar peers and away from dissimilar classmates, thereby contributing to lack of integration." Second, social norms: deviation from classroom behavioral norms predicts rejection, and high-status peers police norms, making attributes salient. Third, intergroup dynamics: lack of proximity, unequal status, competition, and absence of authority sanctioning maintain prejudice and exclusionary behaviors.
requirements: Educators must comprehend these dynamics to prevent and decrease social exclusion
constraints: The article states homophily does not promote inclusion for groups small in number and students with stigmatized identities and attributes
target_learners: K-12 students, particularly those with stigmatized identities or attributes
target_learning_goals: Understanding and preventing peer victimization, rejection, and friendlessness
examples: The review cites experiments and classroom observations showing aggressive boys in non-aggressive groups and socially withdrawn boys in aggressive groups are most likely to be rejected
key_sources: Juvonen, J., Lessard, L.M., Rastogi, R., Schacter, H.L., & Smith, D.S. (2019). Promoting social inclusion in educational settings: Challenges and opportunities. Educational Psychologist, 54, 250-270. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2019.1655645

article_title: A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate
citation: Murayama, K., & von Keyserlingk, L. (2025). A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate.
title: The common formula of motivation theories: core constructs with antecedents and outcomes
description: The article describes a shared structural scheme across major motivation theories (Figure 1): each theory posits one or more core motivation constructs (e.g., need satisfaction, self-efficacy, achievement goals, expectancy and task values), plus antecedents (e.g., school environment, social support) and outcomes (e.g., achievement, engagement). "Usually, some adaptive form of motivation ... is posited to positively predict some adaptive outcome(s)", while maladaptive forms predict maladaptive outcomes. The authors argue most empirical motivation research, including person-centered profile approaches, largely adheres to this formula, which maps readily onto regression models.
requirements: A core motivation construct or set of constructs
Posited antecedents and outcomes of those constructs
constraints: The article notes theories are "far more complex and nuanced" than this general scheme, which captures only part of them
target_learning_goals: understanding motivated behavior such as engagement, achievement, and educational choice
examples: The article illustrates the formula with adaptive constructs (need satisfaction, mastery goals, self-efficacy, subjective task values) predicting positive outcomes and maladaptive constructs (amotivation, performance-avoidance goals) predicting negative ones
key_sources: Murayama, K., & von Keyserlingk, L. (2025). A critical analysis of the current motivation theories in educational psychology: Why the same theories continue to dominate. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2025.2473894

article_title: Beyond Amplification: Using the computer to Reorganize Mental Functioning
citation: Roy D. Pea. (1985). Beyond Amplification: Using the Computer to Reorganize Mental Functioning. Educational Psychologist, 20(4), pp.167-182. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190536
title: Computer as reorganizer of mental functioning: an alternative to the amplifier view of computing in cognition
description: Pea contrasts two conceptualizations of the computer's role in cognition. The classical view treats computers as "amplifiers of cognition," while his alternative treats the computer as a "reorganizer of mental functioning," meaning that cognitive technologies change what people do and thus who they become, rather than merely speeding up existing processes. He argues this reframing opens new visions of the potential cognitive benefits of computers in education.
requirements: Educational software and cognitive technologies must be analyzed in terms of how they restructure activity, not only how much faster or more of it learners produce.
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptualization supported by software analyses, not as a tested experimental result.
target_learners: learners using computers in educational settings
target_learning_goals: general cognitive skills and reorganized mental functioning
examples: The article reports software analyses used to illuminate the advantages of the reorganizer view over the amplifier view.
key_sources: Roy D. Pea. (1985). Beyond Amplification: Using the Computer to Reorganize Mental Functioning. Educational Psychologist, 20(4), pp.167-182. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190536

article_title: Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research
citation: Reinhard Pekrun, Thomas Goetz, Wolfram Titz, & Raymond P. Perry. (2002). Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep3702_4
title: Cognitive-motivational model of academic emotion effects: valence × activation categories influence motivation, learning strategies, cognitive resources, and self-regulation
description: Pekrun's cognitive-motivational model assumes emotion effects on learning and achievement are mediated by motivation to learn, learning strategies, cognitive resources, and self-regulation. It distinguishes four emotion categories by valence and activation: "positiveactivatingemotions (such as enjoyment of learning, hope for success, or pride); positive deactivating emotions (e.g., relief...); negative activatingemotions (such as anger, anxiety, and shame); and negative deactivating emotions(e.g., boredom, hopelessness)." Positive activating emotions are hypothesized to enhance motivation and flexible learning; negative deactivating emotions to be detrimental; the other two categories to have ambivalent effects.
requirements: Mediating mechanisms of motivation, strategies, cognitive resources, and self-regulation link emotions to achievement
constraints: The valence-activation simplification has stated exceptions: anxiety may lead to behavioral freezing, and some boredom variants may be arousing
target_learning_goals: understanding how emotions shape self-regulated learning and achievement
examples: The model explains why test anxiety-achievement correlations rarely explain more than 10% of achievement variance
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun, Thomas Goetz, Wolfram Titz, & Raymond P. Perry. (2002). Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep3702_4

article_title: Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research
citation: Reinhard Pekrun, Thomas Goetz, Wolfram Titz, & Raymond P. Perry. (2002). Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep3702_4
title: Control-value theory of academic emotion antecedents: control-related and value-related appraisals are main sources of students' academic emotions
description: The control-value theory integrates expectancy-value and attributional theories, holding that "control-related and value-related appraisals are main sources of students' academic emotions." Control cognitions take forms of retrospective attributions, state control cognitions, or future expectancies (self-efficacy, situation-outcome, action-outcome), interacting with intrinsic and extrinsic values such that, for most emotions, both control and values are necessary antecedents. Environmental factors (instruction quality, autonomy support, expectancies, feedback, social support) are assumed to affect emotions indirectly via these appraisals.
requirements: Both control and value appraisals are necessary antecedents for most academic emotions
constraints: The authors state they have not yet tested the mediational assumptions implied by control-value theory in more direct ways
target_learning_goals: understanding origins of academic emotions to inform prevention and instructional design
examples: In a statistics-course study, enjoyment was high when both control and value were high, whereas anxiety showed a pattern of low control combined with high value
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun, Thomas Goetz, Wolfram Titz, & Raymond P. Perry. (2002). Academic Emotions in Students' Self-Regulated Learning and Achievement: A Program of Qualitative and Quantitative Research. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326985ep3702_4

article_title: Emotions in flipped and lecture-based math courses
citation: Hartikainen, S., Nokelainen, P., Puhakka, I., & Kangaslampi, R. (2026). Emotions in flipped and lecture-based math courses. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102474
title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions as the study's organizing framework
description: The study is organized around the control-value theory (CVT) of achievement emotions, which "views individual appraisals of control and value as antecedents of emotions". CVT categorizes achievement emotions by valence (positive/negative) and arousal (activating/deactivating) plus object focus, and holds that positive activating emotions are most beneficial to learning while negative deactivating emotions may hinder it. The article uses CVT to select the measured emotions (hope, joy, relief, anxiety, hopelessness before events; joy, pride, contentment, relief, shame, anger, sadness, disappointment, gratitude after), to code arousal, and to interpret learning-mode and implementation differences as differences in perceived control, value, autonomy, and support.
requirements: Appraisal of control and value as antecedents: emotions arise from students' perceived control over actions and outcomes and the perceived value of the activity
constraints: The article notes negative activating emotions such as anxiety may sometimes mobilize effort, so their effects are context-dependent
target_learning_goals: achievement emotions in mathematics learning events
examples: The study coded each self-reported emotion into CVT valence × arousal quadrants, finding positive–activating emotions most common before events (48.2%) and positive–deactivating most common after (49.3%)
key_sources: Hartikainen, S., Nokelainen, P., Puhakka, I., & Kangaslampi, R. (2026). Emotions in flipped and lecture-based math courses. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102474

article_title: Fostering teenagers' assessment of information reliability: Effects of a classroom intervention focused on critical source dimensions
citation: Ana Pérez, Anna Potocki, Marc Stadtler, Mônica Macedo-Rouet, Johanna Paul, Ladislao Salmerón, Jean-François Rouet. (2018). Fostering Teenagers' Assessment of Information Reliability: Effects of a Classroom Intervention focused on Critical Source Dimensions. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.04.006
title: Content-Source Integration (CSI) model of processing conflicting documents
description: The Content-Source Integration model, attributed to Stadtler and Bromme (2014), explains how readers handle conflicting texts. It "posits that content-source integration involves three processing stages": detection of a conflict, regulation of the conflict (e.g., attributing the contradiction to different sources), and resolution of the conflict (e.g., evaluating information reliability). The article uses it, together with the D-ISC effect, to justify building the training workshops on the presentation and discussion of documents providing conflicting views, and predicts that readers with low prior knowledge rely on second-hand evaluation of source trustworthiness.
requirements: Readers must notice contradictions across texts dealing with the same topic for content-source integration to be triggered
constraints: When prior knowledge is low, readers may rather evaluate the trustworthiness of the sources (second-hand evaluation) rather than judge truth value from subject matter
target_learning_goals: evaluating information reliability when comprehending multiple conflicting documents
examples: The three workshops were largely based on the presentation and discussion of short documents providing conflicting views on a given topic
key_sources: Ana Pérez, Anna Potocki, Marc Stadtler, Mônica Macedo-Rouet, Johanna Paul, Ladislao Salmerón, Jean-François Rouet. (2018). Fostering Teenagers' Assessment of Information Reliability: Effects of a Classroom Intervention focused on Critical Source Dimensions. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.04.006

article_title: Early childcare enrollment and the pursuit of higher education: A Canadian longitudinal study
citation: Garon-Carrier, G., Ansari, A., Letarte, M.-J., & Fitzpatrick, C. (2022). Early childcare enrollment and the pursuit of higher education: A Canadian longitudinal study. Learning and Instruction, 80. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101615
title: Compensatory effect and lost-resource effect accounts of childcare outcomes
description: The article uses two explanatory accounts for heterogeneous childcare effects. The compensatory hypothesis "suggests that childcare may be particularly beneficial for children from low-income families", which the authors see supported by the finding that childcare attendance increased enrollment probability for children from low-income and non-working families. The lost-resource effect (Desai et al., 1989) describes how "children with cognitively and linguistically stimulating home environment may be comparatively deprived of learning opportunities when receiving formal out of home childcare", which the authors invoke for higher-income children in formal care.
requirements: Distinguishing family contexts (e.g., household income, parental employment) to identify which children benefit from which arrangement
constraints: The authors present these as interpretations of observational matched data, not tested mechanisms; unmeasured factors could also account for the associations
target_learners: Children from low-income or non-working families
target_learning_goals: Long-term educational attainment (enrollment in higher education)
examples: The study found formal childcare attendance mitigated disparities in pursuit of higher education for vulnerable children while being associated with reduced chances for children from higher-income, fully-employed families
key_sources: Garon-Carrier, G., Ansari, A., Letarte, M.-J., & Fitzpatrick, C. (2022). Early childcare enrollment and the pursuit of higher education: A Canadian longitudinal study. Learning and Instruction, 80. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101615

article_title: Complexity affects performance, cognitive load, and awareness
citation: Ines Zeitlhofer, Joerg Zumbach, Judith Schweppe. (2024). Complexity affects performance, cognitive load, and awareness. Learning and Instruction 94 (2024) 102001. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.102001
title: Expose learners to consistently high task complexity to stimulate germane processing without harming intrinsic interest
description: This principle holds that, contrary to the standard cognitive load recommendation of gradually increasing complexity, presenting learners with consistently high complexity problem-solving tasks can stimulate germane cognitive processing and metacognitive engagement. The authors conclude that "exposing learners to consistently high complexity tasks can have beneficial effects on learning without negatively influencing intrinsic interest." It applies to problem-solving tasks where complexity can be manipulated, such as the Tower of Hanoi task used in the study.
requirements: Learners must tackle problem-solving tasks whose complexity can be manipulated, such as varying the number of disks in the Tower of Hanoi task
constraints: The immediate-performance advantage did not carry over to a delayed post-test two days later
Only germane cognitive load was assessed, not overall cognitive load
The study used a standardized problem-solving activity rather than authentic learning materials
target_learners: university students with no prior familiarity with the learning task
target_learning_goals: problem-solving schema construction
metacognitive awareness of solution strategies
examples: Participants repeatedly solved a six-disk Tower of Hanoi task (consistently high complexity) or progressed from four to six disks (gradually increasing), with performance assessed by time and number of moves
key_sources: Ines Zeitlhofer, Joerg Zumbach, Judith Schweppe. (2024). Complexity affects performance, cognitive load, and awareness. Learning and Instruction 94 (2024) 102001. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.102001

article_title: How feedback affects emotions, performance and self-concept in mathematics
citation: Van der Beek, J.P.J.; Van der Ven, S.H.G.; Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E.; Kroesbergen, E.H. (2025). How feedback affects emotions, performance and self-concept in mathematics. Learning and Instruction 99, 102169. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102169
title: Control-Value Theory as framework for feedback effects on achievement emotions, performance and self-concept
description: The study is framed by Pekrun's Control-Value Theory, in which "performance feedback is regarded as an important antecedent of achievement emotions, which subsequently affect performance and self-concept". Emotions are classified as positive or negative, activating or deactivating, and activity- or outcome-focused; feedback effects are shaped by control appraisals, value appraisals and achievement goals. The article's findings on hope as the key mediator are interpreted within this framework.
requirements: Feedback must be appraised by students through control and value appraisals for emotional effects to arise, per the theory's structure as described
constraints: The article notes control-value appraisals, achievement goals and emotions can be domain- and even situation-specific, so effects need not generalize across subjects
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement emotions
math performance
math self-concept
examples: The experiment operationalized feedback as an antecedent and measured anxiety, anger, enjoyment and hope as mediators of performance and self-concept effects
key_sources: Van der Beek, J.P.J.; Van der Ven, S.H.G.; Van de Weijer-Bergsma, E.; Kroesbergen, E.H. (2025). How feedback affects emotions, performance and self-concept in mathematics. Learning and Instruction 99, 102169. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102169

article_title: Self-regulated learning processes vary as a function of epistemic beliefs and contexts: Mixed method evidence from eye tracking and concurrent and retrospective reports
citation: Gregory Trevors, Reza Feyzi-Behnagh, Roger Azevedo, François Bouchet. Self-Regulated Learning Processes Vary as a Function of Epistemic Beliefs and Contexts: Mixed Method Evidence from Eye Tracking and Concurrent and Retrospective Reports. Learning and Instruction, 2016, 42, pp.31-46. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.11.003
title: Science content with conceptual discrepancies as a learning task for studying epistemic cognition in SRL
description: The studies used science content deliberately designed to relay conceptual discrepancies, presented to university students within a multi-study mixed method design. The authors state they "presented university students with science content that relayed conceptual discrepancies and collected quantitative and qualitative data to study how students responded to discrepancies." This material serves as the stimulus context in which eye tracking, study times, metacognitive ratings, think-aloud protocols, and retrospective interviews were collected.
requirements: Content must relay conceptual discrepancies so that learners' responses to discrepancies can be observed
target_learning_goals: responding to conceptual discrepancies in science content
examples: Both Study 1 (n = 42) and Study 2 (n = 20) presented this discrepant science content to university students.
key_sources: Gregory Trevors, Reza Feyzi-Behnagh, Roger Azevedo, François Bouchet. Self-Regulated Learning Processes Vary as a Function of Epistemic Beliefs and Contexts: Mixed Method Evidence from Eye Tracking and Concurrent and Retrospective Reports. Learning and Instruction, 2016, 42, pp.31-46. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.11.003

article_title: School grades and students’ emotions: Longitudinal models of within-person reciprocal effects
citation: Reinhard Pekrun, Herbert W. Marsh, Felix Suessenbach, Anne C. Frenzel, Thomas Goetz. (2022). School grades and students' emotions: Longitudinal models of within-person reciprocal effects. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101626
title: Control-value theory reciprocal effects model of achievement feedback and emotions
description: Control-value theory (CVT) proposes that feedback about achievement drives achievement emotions via appraisals of control and value, and that these emotions in turn affect performance and subsequent feedback, producing reciprocal effects over time. As the article states, "CVT proposes that feedback about achievement is a prime driver of achievement emotions, due to its impact on appraisals of control and value related to achievement." Positive emotions are triggered by high control and high value, negative emotions by low control and high value. The present study used CVT to derive preregistered hypotheses about within-person reciprocal links between grades and emotions.
requirements: Feedback interpreted as success or failure must be appraised by students in terms of control and value for emotions to be aroused as theorized
constraints: The article notes positive emotions can occasionally undermine performance and negative emotions can sometimes support performance, so overall effects are described as typically positive or negative
target_learning_goals: achievement emotions such as enjoyment, pride, anger, anxiety, shame, boredom, and hopelessness in mathematics
examples: The study operationalized feedback as end-of-the-year mathematics grades across five annual assessments in the PALMA study
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun, Herbert W. Marsh, Felix Suessenbach, Anne C. Frenzel, Thomas Goetz. (2022). School grades and students' emotions: Longitudinal models of within-person reciprocal effects. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101626

article_title: Linking parental scaffolding with self-regulated learning in Chinese kindergarten children
citation: Heyi Zhang, David Whitebread. (2014). Linking parental scaffolding with self-regulated learning in Chinese kindergarten children. Faculty of Education, University of Cambridge. https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk
title: Support children's problem solving contingently: adjust instructional demand to the child's ongoing evidence of task understanding
description: The article's findings indicate that the effectiveness of parental scaffolding lies in its contingency rather than its quantity: parents should provide "less specific instructions and higher cognitive demand after a child's success and more specific instructions and lower cognitive demand after a child's failure". In the study, contingency was the only independent scaffolding predictor of children's SRL strategic behaviours and task performance, and it mediated the effect of parental education. This principle applies the shift rule to any adult supporting a child's problem solving.
requirements: The adult must monitor the child's ongoing evidence of task understanding and adjust demand level accordingly
constraints: Evidence comes from parent-child problem-solving tasks with Chinese kindergarten children; the longer-term influence the authors propose needs testing in longitudinal studies
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategic behaviours
independent problem-solving performance
examples: In the study, parents' contingent instructional demand (D1-D3 matched to children's understanding levels U0-U4) was coded utterance-by-utterance in puzzle and origami tasks
key_sources: Heyi Zhang, David Whitebread. (2014). Linking parental scaffolding with self-regulated learning in Chinese kindergarten children. Faculty of Education, University of Cambridge. https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk

article_title: Intraindividual relations between achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions: An experience sampling approach
citation: Goetz, T., Sticca, F., Pekrun, R., Murayama, K., & Elliot, A. J. (2016). Intraindividual relations between achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions: An experience sampling approach. Learning and Instruction, 41, 115-125. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.10.007
title: Pekrun et al.'s control-value-based model linking trichotomous achievement goals to discrete achievement emotions
description: The article tests and supports a theoretical model grounding goal-emotion links in "control-value theory which posits that the perceived controllability and the subjective value of achievement activities and outcomes function as proximal antecedents of achievement emotions." Within this model, mastery goals focus attention on the controllability and positive value of activities (fostering enjoyment, reducing boredom and anger), performance-approach goals on success outcomes (fostering pride), and performance-avoidance goals on possible failure and uncontrollability (fostering anxiety and shame). The study's experience sampling design provides the first direct intraindividual test of these propositions in classrooms.
requirements: Assessment of both state (or trait) achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions so goal-emotion propositions can be tested at the intended level of analysis
constraints: The model posits goals influencing emotions, but the article notes reciprocal causation (emotions influencing goal adoption) cannot be ruled out and the ESM design did not allow causal analysis
target_learning_goals: Fostering adaptive achievement emotions (enjoyment, pride) and reducing maladaptive emotions (boredom, anger, anxiety, shame) through goal foci
examples: The study assessed mastery, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance goals against six emotions (enjoyment, pride, anxiety, shame, anger, boredom) in mathematics, German, English, and French classrooms
key_sources: Goetz, T., Sticca, F., Pekrun, R., Murayama, K., & Elliot, A. J. (2016). Intraindividual relations between achievement goals and discrete achievement emotions: An experience sampling approach. Learning and Instruction, 41, 115-125. https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2015.10.007

article_title: Do you play in class? Board games to promote cognitive and educational development in primary school: A cluster randomized controlled trial
citation: Nuria Vita-Barrull, Verónica Estrada-Plana, Jaume March-Llanes, Pablo Sotoca-Orgaz, Núria Guzmán, Rosa Ayesa, Jorge Moya-Higueras. (2024). Do you play in class? Board games to promote cognitive and educational development in primary school: A cluster randomized controlled trial. Learning and Instruction, 93. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101946
title: Conectar Jugando classroom board-game programme
description: Conectar Jugando (Connecting Through Play) is a school intervention programme in which students play commercial analogue board games during school hours to train basic executive functions and support academic skills. "The Conectar Jugando Group received 12 gaming sessions over six weeks", each lasting one hour and held twice a week, with students in groups of three to five playing two games face-to-face. Teachers received a manual specifying session organisation and which games to use; commercial games were selected by an expert committee for the executive functions and curriculum competencies they could train.
requirements: Teachers receive a programme manual and a preliminary game session covering objectives, implementation details and the games used
Games must fit the educational competencies of the Spanish curriculum and suit recommended ages and durations
constraints: Games varied between first grade and second-to-sixth grades to adapt to recommended ages
target_learners: primary school students from first to sixth grade
target_learning_goals: executive functions (updating, inhibition, flexibility)
reading and maths skills
examples: In the trial, students played games such as Monster Match and La Morada Maldita, chosen for cognitive domains like working memory updating, inhibition and shifting
key_sources: Nuria Vita-Barrull, Verónica Estrada-Plana, Jaume March-Llanes, Pablo Sotoca-Orgaz, Núria Guzmán, Rosa Ayesa, Jorge Moya-Higueras. (2024). Do you play in class? Board games to promote cognitive and educational development in primary school: A cluster randomized controlled trial. Learning and Instruction, 93. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101946

article_title: The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving
citation: Strohmaier, A. R., Schons, C., Knabbe, A., Vogel, M., Saado, K., & Obersteiner, A. (2025). The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving. Learning and Instruction, 101, 102235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102235
title: Teach word-problem text-comprehension strategies that prepare the mathematical model rather than strip away the story context
description: Because the study found that linguistic and mathematical processes share a joint mental representation, the authors argue that "teaching text-comprehension strategies for word-problem solving should be particularly valuable if those strategies are working towards preparing the mathematical model". Strategies aimed merely at identifying keywords or removing the context risk building an incomplete mental representation that takes longer to transform into an adequate mathematical model.
requirements: Instruction should connect comprehension of the problem text to the construction of the mathematical model, since both draw on one shared mental representation
constraints: The authors warn that supporting text comprehension superficially "might initially lead to quicker linguistic processing, but might result in an incomplete mental representation"
target_learning_goals: mathematical word-problem solving
examples: The study found question-first placement accelerated initial processing but lengthened the second solution phase, which the authors read as evidence that superficial comprehension support can backfire
key_sources: Strohmaier, A. R., Schons, C., Knabbe, A., Vogel, M., Saado, K., & Obersteiner, A. (2025). The relation between text comprehension and computation in mathematical word-problem solving. Learning and Instruction, 101, 102235. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102235

article_title: The happy-fish-little-pond effect on enjoyment: Generalizability across multiple domains and countries
citation: Basarkod, G., Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Parker, P. D., Dicke, T., & Pekrun, R. (2023). The Happy-Fish-Little-Pond Effect on Enjoyment: Generalizability Across Multiple Domains and Countries. https://osf.io/kb29h/
title: Control-value theory and the relative universality principle as the framework for achievement-emotion formation
description: Control-value theory (CVT; Pekrun, 2006, 2018) holds that emotions are a consequence of cognitive appraisals of control over, and subjective value placed on, achievement activities and outcomes. The article applies CVT to enjoyment: success in a valued, controllable subject raises control appraisals and thus enjoyment, while high class-average achievement lowers relative control via social comparison. CVT assumes "general functional mechanisms of human emotions are universal", with contents and intensities varying across individuals and groups — the relative universality principle this study tests.
requirements: Emotions arise from control and value appraisals, so testing CVT-based predictions requires measures of achievement contexts and appraisals
constraints: CVT assumes functional relations are universal but levels of emotions may differ across domains and cultural contexts
target_learning_goals: Academic enjoyment in mathematics, science, and reading
examples: The study tested CVT-derived hypotheses that student-level achievement positively and class-average achievement negatively predict enjoyment across three domains and 37 countries.
key_sources: Basarkod, G., Marsh, H. W., Guo, J., Parker, P. D., Dicke, T., & Pekrun, R. (2023). The Happy-Fish-Little-Pond Effect on Enjoyment: Generalizability Across Multiple Domains and Countries. https://osf.io/kb29h/

article_title: Feedback complexities interact with prior knowledge
citation: Fynn Töllner, Poldi Kuhl, Michael Besser. (2026). Feedback complexities interact with prior knowledge. Learning and Instruction 105 (2026) 102413. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2026.102413
title: Provide elaborated feedback, especially conceptual feedback, to learners with low prior knowledge
description: The article recommends that teachers give elaborated feedback and, for struggling learners, base it on conceptual knowledge, because conceptual feedback nearly nullified the effect of prior knowledge on achievement in their RCT. As the authors put it, "especially those learners who perform poorly in class should receive teacher feedback based on conceptual knowledge." This addresses heterogeneity by reducing achievement differences between low- and high-prior-knowledge students.
requirements: Feedback must be elaborated with conceptual knowledge explaining why the procedure works, e.g. visualized fraction representations
constraints: Transferability to other subjects and contexts is unknown per the article's limitations; the study was underpowered
target_learners: seventh-grade secondary mathematics students, especially those with low prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: fraction addition; conceptual and procedural knowledge of adding fractions
examples: In the study, students in the conceptual feedback group received illustrated explanations of why fraction addition works after incorrect answers, and low-prior-knowledge students in this group reached posttest scores similar to their more knowledgeable peers.

article_title: Getting along and feeling good: Reciprocal associations between student-teacher relationship quality and students’ emotions
citation: Goetz, T., Bieleke, M., Gogol, K., van Tartwijk, J., Mainhard, T., Lipnevich, A. A., & Pekrun, R. (2021). Getting along and feeling good: Reciprocal associations between student-teacher relationship quality and students' emotions. Learning and Instruction, 71, 101349. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101349
title: Control-value theory applied to student-teacher relationships and emotions
description: Control-value theory (CVT; Pekrun, 2006) is a comprehensive account of the antecedents and effects of achievement emotions that the article uses to motivate reciprocal hypotheses. According to the article, "the learning environment is a core antecedent of students' emotions in the classroom", which in turn affect the learning environment, implying possible downward spirals (e.g., poor relationship quality and boredom) and upward spirals (e.g., positive relationship quality and enjoyment). The article operationalizes relationship quality as interpersonal closeness, a social facet of the learning environment whose effects on emotions are mediated by control and value appraisals.
requirements: Relationship quality must be conceptualized as a facet of the learning environment whose effects on emotions operate through changes in cognitive appraisals of control and value
constraints: The article states CVT does not yield specific assumptions about differences in associations across discrete emotions, making hypotheses about emotion-specific strengths difficult to formulate
target_learning_goals: students' achievement emotions in academic domains
quality of dyadic student-teacher relationships
examples: The study tested CVT-derived reciprocity hypotheses with cross-lagged panel models across four school domains and six discrete emotions
key_sources: Goetz, T., Bieleke, M., Gogol, K., van Tartwijk, J., Mainhard, T., Lipnevich, A. A., & Pekrun, R. (2021). Getting along and feeling good: Reciprocal associations between student-teacher relationship quality and students' emotions. Learning and Instruction, 71, 101349. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2020.101349

article_title: Understanding the structure of the set of rational numbers: a conceptual change approach
citation: Xenia Vamvakoussi, Stella Vosniadou. (2004). Understanding the structure of the set of rational numbers: a conceptual change approach. Learning and Instruction. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190233
title: The conceptual change approach to learning can apply to mathematics learning
description: The article argues that conceptual change, a framework usually applied to science learning, extends to mathematics. It states that "the conceptual change approach to learning can apply in the case of mathematics", provided the account takes into consideration "the particular nature of mathematical knowledge and the neurobiological bases of mathematical cognition". The framework is then used to interpret ninth graders' understanding of rational numbers.
requirements: The application must take into consideration the particular nature of mathematical knowledge and the neurobiological bases of mathematical cognition, as the article states.
target_learning_goals: understanding the structure of the set of rational numbers
examples: The authors use the conceptual change perspective to investigate ninth graders' understanding of algebraic and structural properties of rational numbers.
key_sources: Xenia Vamvakoussi, Stella Vosniadou. (2004). Understanding the structure of the set of rational numbers: a conceptual change approach. Learning and Instruction. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190233

article_title: Achievement emotions and arithmetic fluency – Development and parallel processes during the early school years
citation: Rawlings, A. M., Niemivirta, M., Korhonen, J., Lindskog, M., Tuominen, H., & Mononen, R. (2023). Achievement emotions and arithmetic fluency – Development and parallel processes during the early school years. Preprint Version 3, Accepted for publication, 27 March 2023.
title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions as the framework for mathematics emotions
description: The article adopts Pekrun's control-value theory, in which "emotions directly related to achievement activities or outcomes that are judged on competence-related standards are defined as achievement emotions". Emotions arise from appraisals of perceived control over task demands and the subjective value of the activity or outcome. The theory organises emotions along a three-dimensional taxonomy of object focus, valence, and arousal level, which the study uses to select enjoyment, anxiety, and boredom as the emotions representing its main dimensions.
requirements: Measurement of domain-specific emotions tied to mathematics activities and outcomes, as the theory treats achievement emotions as domain-specific
constraints: The study measures only three emotions representing the taxonomy's main dimensions, within the mathematics domain of early primary school
target_learning_goals: mathematics-related achievement emotions (enjoyment, anxiety, boredom) and arithmetic fluency development
examples: The study used the framework to hypothesise that enjoyment is instigated by high control and value appraisals, anxiety by high value but low control, and boredom when both are low
key_sources: Rawlings, A. M., Niemivirta, M., Korhonen, J., Lindskog, M., Tuominen, H., & Mononen, R. (2023). Achievement emotions and arithmetic fluency – Development and parallel processes during the early school years. article_title: Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning
citation: Kirschner, P.A. (2002). Cognitive load theory: implications of cognitive load theory on the design of learning. https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/16884
title: A cognitive theory of multimedia learning (Mayer & Moreno)
description: The editorial announces that the special issue includes "a cognitive theory of multimedia learning (Mayer & Moreno)". Within the issue's framing, this theory addresses how multimedia instruction relates to the cognitive architecture of limited working memory with partly independent visual and audio processing units, making modality-relevant presentation a central design concern. The editorial itself does not describe the theory's mechanisms beyond naming it as part of the issue's coverage.
requirements: A multimedia learning theory under this framing must connect presentation formats to the load limits of working memory
constraints: The editorial names the theory but does not describe its content
target_learners: learners generally, across the domains covered in the special issue
target_learning_goals: learning from multimedia presentations under working-memory constraints
examples: The special issue includes the Mayer and Moreno article on a cognitive theory of multimedia learning

article_title: Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning
citation: Baxter, P.A.; Bekkering, H.; Dijkstra, A.F.J.; Droop, W.; Hurk, M.M. van den; Léoné, F.T.M. (2022). Contrasting orthographically similar words facilitates adult second language vocabulary learning. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101582
title: Use contrasting of orthographically similar new L2 words to sharpen form representations
description: When teaching new L2 vocabulary, present orthographically similar words together so learners must contrast them, because contrasting "underspecified representations serves as a learning mechanism that guides attention to relevant lexical information." In Experiment 1 this improved recall of orthographically similar words and made errors more target-like. The benefit is dimension-specific: it applied to orthographically similar L2 words, not semantically similar ones, and appeared in recall rather than recognition.
requirements: The contrasted words should be new, underspecified L2 forms whose distinctive features learners must attend to
constraints: The benefit appeared in recall posttests but not recognition, and contrasting lowered accuracy during the learning phase itself
target_learning_goals: productive L2 vocabulary recall and representational specificity
examples: Participants in the sorted condition saw triplets of orthographically similar pseudowords (e.g., maximum Levenshtein distance 2) as answer options and had to carefully compare them to select the correct translation
