E., França, T., González-Fernández, B., Hall, R., Inasius, F., Kar, S. K., Keržič, D., Lazányi, K., Lazăr, F., Machin-Mastromatteo, J. D., Marôco, J., Marques, B. P., Mejía-Rodríguez, O., Méndez Prado, S. M., Mishra, A., Mollica, C., Navarro Jiménez, S. G., Obadić, A., Mamun-ur-Rashid, M., Ravšelj, D., Tatalović Vorkapić, S., Tomaževič, N., Uleanya, C., Umek, L., Vicentini, G., Yorulmaz, Ö., Zamfir, A.-M., & Aristovnik, A. (2022). Higher education students' achievement emotions and their antecedents in e-learning amid COVID-19 pandemic: A multi-country survey. Learning and Instruction, 80, 101629. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2022.101629
title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions extended to e-learning
description: The control-value theory (CVT) is an integrative framework describing interrelations between achievement emotions, their antecedents, and outcomes. It defines achievement emotions as "those emotions which are felt in relation to learning activities and outcomes", organized by valence and activation into four categories (e.g., positive activating emotions such as enjoyment; negative deactivating emotions such as boredom). It differentiates proximal individual antecedents such as control appraisals and self-efficacy, which act directly, from distal environmental antecedents such as cognitive and motivational quality of tasks, which act through mediation, and proposes the relative universality of these links across individuals, genders, areas of study, and cultures. This study tested and largely confirmed the CVT's mediation structure for e-learning during the COVID-19 pandemic.
requirements: Students' perceptions of task structure, clarity, demands, and social support as antecedent conditions
Self-efficacy beliefs (e-learning and computer) as proximal control appraisals
constraints: Cross-country comparability was limited: only configural invariance held across the 13 countries
target_learners: Higher education students in e-learning contexts
target_learning_goals: Emotional wellbeing and performance in academic learning
examples: The study tested a CVT-based SEM with 17019 students from 13 countries during the first COVID-19 wave

article_title: Teacher self-efficacy and burnout: Determining the directions of prediction through an autoregressive cross-lagged panel model.
citation: Kim, Lisa E. and Burić, Irena. (2020). Teacher self-efficacy and burnout: Determining the directions of prediction through an autoregressive cross-lagged panel model. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000424
title: Conservation of Resources theory account of the TSE–burnout relationship
description: The article uses Hobfoll's (1989) Conservation of Resources theory to explain why burnout may precede low self-efficacy rather than only the reverse. Under this account, "prolonged exposure to stressors (e.g., lack of collegiality) results in resource depletion, which can be manifested as burnout symptoms," and depleted resources hinder confidence and self-efficacy. The theory also permits the reverse cycle: exhausted, disengaged individuals are less able to restore personal resources, perpetuating a cycle in which low-resource teachers concurrently experience exhaustion, disengagement, and low self-efficacy. The article presents this theory as the framework consistent with its finding that burnout predicts future TSE.
requirements: The account presupposes that individuals strive to obtain, conserve, and build resources for their positive well-being, and that prolonged stressor exposure occurs without resource replacement
constraints: The theory is offered as an interpretation of the observed cross-lagged paths, not as a mechanism directly tested in the study
target_learners: teachers across elementary, middle, and secondary educational levels
target_learning_goals: understanding the directional relationship between teacher well-being (burnout) and teacher self-efficacy beliefs
examples: The article invokes the theory in its Discussion to explain why experiencing burnout more strongly colors future TSE levels than TSE colors future burnout levels
key_sources: Kim, Lisa E. and Burić, Irena. (2020). Teacher self-efficacy and burnout: Determining the directions of prediction through an autoregressive cross-lagged panel model. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000424

article_title: The potential of relevance interventions for scaling up: A cluster-randomized trial testing the effectiveness of a relevance intervention in math classrooms.
citation: Gaspard, H., Parrisius, C., Piesch, H., Kleinhansl, M., Wille, E., Nagengast, B., Trautwein, U., & Hulleman, C. S. (2021). The potential of relevance interventions for scaling up: A cluster-randomized trial testing the effectiveness of a relevance intervention in math classrooms. Journal of Educational Psychology. Advance online publication. https://dx.doi.org/10.1037/edu0000663
title: Combine direct communication of utility value with relevance-inducing reflection tasks and an expectancy component to reach more students
description: The article argues that neither intervention approach alone serves all students: directly communicating utility value benefits students with high interest or expectancies but can backfire for students with low expectancies, whereas relevance-inducing reflection tasks particularly benefit students with low expectancies. It therefore recommends that "One potential approach might be to combine the communication of utility value with relevance-inducing reflection tasks" and to add an expectancy component such as a growth-mindset element, so that as many students as possible benefit. MoMa operationalizes this by pairing a utility-communication presentation with individual reflection tasks and an effort/mindset segment.
requirements: An expectancy component (e.g., emphasizing effort over talent) to prevent utility communication from backfiring for students with low expectancies
constraints: Directly communicated utility value alone can undermine interest and performance for students with low expectancies, per prior lab studies the article cites
target_learners: secondary school students in mathematics classrooms
target_learning_goals: perceived relevance and utility value of school content
expectancies for success
examples: MoMa's psychoeducational presentation first inoculates students against negative effects of relevance highlighting for low-expectancy students, then presents utility examples, followed by individual quotation-evaluation reflection tasks

title: Knowledge quizzes for the social, dimensional, and temporal comparison modules
description: Table S6 documents a knowledge test for each comparison module (social, dimensional, temporal), administered separately for math and German. "Each item was a sentence that was to be completed, with three possible answers", with one correct answer marked per item, covering e.g. whether self-concept rises after comparing with better, worse, or similar performers. "Students were only presented with the knowledge quiz whose module they actually attended."
requirements: Each student receives only the quiz matching the module they attended

examples: One social-module item asks whether math self-concept increases when comparing with others who perform better, worse, or similarly.

article_title: Cooperative learning in middle school: A means to improve peer relations and reduce victimization, bullying, and related outcomes.
citation: Van Ryzin, M. J., & Roseth, C. J. (2018). Cooperative Learning in Middle School: A Means to Improve Peer Relations and Reduce Victimization, Bullying, and Related Outcomes. Journal of Educational Psychology, 110(8), 1192-1201. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000265
title: Use cooperative learning as a sustainable, stand-alone component of bullying prevention that does not sacrifice instructional time
description: The article recommends embedding cooperative learning in everyday classroom instruction as a prevention approach, rather than adding a separate anti-bullying curriculum. It argues this "does not require the sacrifice of instructional time, and can be used in any subject," and that techniques "can be shared among staff members, modified to fit new academic curricula and learning objectives, and taught to new teachers by existing staff," sustaining implementation despite teacher turnover.
requirements: Teacher training in the cooperative learning approach (the trial used 3 half-day in-person sessions plus videoconference check-ins)
constraints: Evidence comes from a relatively homogeneous rural sample that was about three-quarters White, limiting external validity; all measures were self-report, some with low reliability
target_learning_goals: reduced bullying and victimization
positive peer relations
academic achievement alongside social outcomes
examples: The trial trained intervention-school staff with 3 half-day sessions using Cooperation in the Classroom, 9th Edition, and teachers applied cooperative learning within existing curricula

article_title: Mental fatigue in day school children as measured by immediate memory: Part I.
citation: W. H. Winch. (1910). Mental Fatigue in Day School Children as Measured by Immediate Memory. Part I. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://books.google.com
title: Visual immediate-memory test of twelve consonants used as a fatigue measure in day school children
description: A mechanical memory test used by Winch to measure fatigue: "Twelve consonants, arranged in the following way" were "exposed to view for 25 seconds", after which boys wrote down as much as they could remember with 1 minute 35 seconds for writing and rest. Ten tests formed a 20-minute exercise, scored three marks per correctly remembered and rightly placed consonant, two for one place out, one for two places out. Study was visual, audible articulation not permitted.
requirements: New material each test so "the process can be mechanized, but the acquisition required is always a new matter"
A preliminary series of tests to establish steady performance before fatigue comparisons
constraints: Contemporary opinion held that immediate memory tests "will not give satisfactory indices of fatigue" in children, due to irregularity in the first exercises of a series
target_learners: School children around 13 years of age (Standard VI class)
target_learning_goals: Immediate memory for visual percepts of non-connotative material
examples: Used with 45 boys in a municipal boys' school in a poor London neighborhood, morning tests following Scripture lessons and afternoon tests after spelling, drill, recreation and algebra

article_title: School instruction in matters of sex.
citation: Foster, W. S. (1911). School Instruction in Matters of Sex. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22School+Instruction+in+Matters+of+Sex%22+Foster
title: Sex instruction should be continuous, progressive, and suited to the learner's development, beginning at home with the mother before school age.
description: The essay organizes instruction into three periods—home and kindergarten, pre-pubertal, and adolescent—insisting that "Sexual enlightenment, like any other enlightenment, should be continuous, progressive and suited to the development and needs of the learner." Because "the mother is the natural teacher in early years," she should begin instruction before the child meets sources of misinformation, with the school supplementing her teaching. Marking off one specific time for complete instruction is explicitly not recommended.
requirements: A groundwork satisfying all insistent curiosity should be secured before the child goes to school or becomes open to misinformation.
constraints: If early information has not been given, the teacher is no longer so free to speak nor so influential, so words are left unsaid or come with little force.
target_learning_goals: developmentally appropriate sexual knowledge
preparation for puberty changes
rational attitudes toward marriage, prostitution and venereal disease
examples: The essay assigns habit formation and simple facts to the mother in the first stage, puberty preparation to the pre-pubertal stage, and facts of marriage, prostitution and venereal disease before school leaving.
key_sources: Foster, W. S. (1911). School Instruction in Matters of Sex. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22School+Instruction+in+Matters+of+Sex%22+Foster

article_title: The benefits of combining value for the self and others in utility-value interventions.
citation: Priniski, S. J., Rosenzweig, E. Q., Canning, E. A., Hecht, C. A., Tibbetts, Y., Hyde, J. S., & Harackiewicz, J. M. (2019). The Benefits of Combining Value for the Self and Others in Utility-Value Interventions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000343
title: Combine self-focused and other-focused utility-value assignments through variety or choice rather than repeating one assignment type
description: The article recommends that when implementing utility-value writing interventions, instructors expose students to both self-focused essays and other-focused letters, either by assigning a fixed variety of both types or by letting students choose between them each time. The authors state that students "benefitted most from the UV intervention when the assignment structure exposed them to both types of UV assignments, rather than instructing them to complete the same type of assignment three times."
requirements: Assignments must be authentic coursework integrated into the curriculum, graded for scientific accuracy, and returned before unit exams, as in the study procedure.
constraints: Evidence comes from one introductory biology course for prospective majors at a single institution; the article states more work is needed to determine whether other assignment structures generalize, and the overall intervention contrast versus control was not significant.
target_learners: Undergraduate students in introductory college science courses
target_learning_goals: Course performance in introductory science
Motivation, interest, and perceived utility value of course material
examples: Students were randomly assigned to six conditions: control summaries, self-first variety, other-first variety, self-focused only, other-focused only, or choice between essay and letter on each of three assignments.

article_title: Test boredom: Exploring a neglected emotion.
citation: Goetz, T., Bieleke, M., Yanagida, T., Krannich, M., Roos, A.-L., Frenzel, A. C., Lipnevich, A. A., & Pekrun, R. (2023). Test boredom: Exploring a neglected emotion. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/ftr4g/?view_only=beac4ca87987492294aeac4a1bb96c86
title: Control-value theory account of test boredom and its antecedents
description: The article applies Pekrun's control-value theory (CVT) of achievement emotions to testing situations, defining test boredom as a subtype of academic boredom: "Test boredom is the experience of boredom in situations that are labeled and/or experienced as tests." CVT posits that perceived control and perceived value are the key psychosocial antecedents: the control-boredom relation is curvilinear (boredom rises at very low and very high control), and "CVT posits a negative relation between perceived value and test boredom." The theory's relative universality assumption holds that structural relations with antecedents and outcomes are similar across academic settings, while test-specific features (task difficulty spread, low stakes) shape boredom magnitude.
requirements: Assessment of students' control and value appraisals (e.g., over-/underchallenge, intrinsic and extrinsic value) alongside boredom measures
constraints: The article notes the predicted curvilinear control relation has only partial support; perceived control was commonly found to relate linearly and negatively to boredom in prior studies
target_learners: school students in achievement testing situations
target_learning_goals: understanding and managing achievement emotions during tests
examples: Study 1 induced non-optimal control by splitting a low-stakes math test into easy and difficult blocks and assessing state boredom during each
key_sources: Goetz, T., Bieleke, M., Yanagida, T., Krannich, M., Roos, A.-L., Frenzel, A. C., Lipnevich, A. A., & Pekrun, R. (2023). Test boredom: Exploring a neglected emotion. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://osf.io/ftr4g/?view_only=beac4ca87987492294aeac4a1bb96c86

article_title: Verbal and abstract elements in intelligence examinations.
citation: Herring, J. P. (1923). Verbal and Abstract Elements in Intelligence Examinations. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Two continuous scales, C (concrete–abstract) and N (non-verbal–verbal), for describing and rating test content and behavior
description: The article proposes that human behavior and test content be described on two continuous seven-point scales rather than dualistic categories: scale C runs from concrete (pertaining to things or objects) to abstract (pertaining to relations between objects, involving analytic and synthetic thinking), and scale N from non-verbal to verbal (involving use of words and symbols). The article states it is "false to classify human behavior dualistically" and that responses are distributed "continuous throughout both scale C and scale N." Five judges rated 63 test units on both scales, producing subjective scales against which any homogeneous portion of test material may be rated for abstractness and symbolism.
requirements: Judged classification of test units by multiple judges, with each judge given a voice in determining the meaning of the concepts as well as classifying material
constraints: The definitions of abstract, concrete, and verbal are not regarded as final or even as necessarily valid, but as starting points for classification
target_learners: School children in grades IV–VII assessed with group intelligence examinations
target_learning_goals: Measurement and prediction of general intelligence
examples: Digit symbol tests were rated distinctly concrete and very non-symbolic; the Army Beta Maze Test as concrete as anything found; arithmetical problems rated very abstract.
key_sources: Herring, J. P. (1923). Verbal and Abstract Elements in Intelligence Examinations. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org

article_title: Differential effects of the classroom on African American and non-African American’s mathematics achievement.
citation: Schenke, K., Nguyen, T., Watts, T. W., Sarama, J. H., & Clements, D. H. (2017). Differential effects of the classroom on African American and non-African American’s mathematics achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(6), 794–811. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000165
title: COEMET — Classroom Observation of Early Mathematics Environment and Teaching
description: The COEMET is a live classroom observation instrument used to measure the quality of early mathematics environments. Its first section documents the number of computers and the start and end times of all activities via interval coding; its second section contains 28 indicators rated on a 5-point Likert scale during each mathematics activity, covering constructs such as supporting children's conceptual understanding, teaching strategies, and expectations. In this study, inter-rater reliability was 88% of Likert items coded identically, and coefficient alpha ranged from .95 to .97 in previous research.
requirements: Observers who spend about half a day in each classroom and are blind to experimental condition; pair visits for reliability checking
constraints: Ratings for each mathematics activity are averaged to obtain mean scores; the instrument was used with preschool classrooms in this study
target_learning_goals: early mathematics instruction quality
examples: Observations were conducted twice during the school year (October–December and March–May) and averaged to obtain a school-year rating of the classroom environment
key_sources: Schenke, K., Nguyen, T., Watts, T. W., Sarama, J. H., & Clements, D. H. (2017). Differential effects of the classroom on African American and non-African American’s mathematics achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(6), 794–811. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000165

article_title: 'Bright' and 'slow' pupils in elementary and high school.
citation: Cummins, R. A. (1917). 'Bright' and 'Slow' Pupils in Elementary and High School. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Equalize high/low mark ratios across subjects by combining adjusted subject-matter difficulty with within-class ranking and curve-based mark distribution
description: The author proposes that schools make the relative frequency of high and low marks practically the same across subjects by combining two methods: introducing more difficult subject-matter where ratios are high and less difficult material where they are low, and ranking class members from best to poorest using all available information, then distributing marks along a curve approximating the normal surface of frequency. He states this should be done "in all cases where there are as many as 50 pupils in a subject".
requirements: At least 50 pupils in a subject (the author notes theoretically there should be at least 100)
constraints: Due allowance is needed for exceptional cases in which the selection of pupils in the class is other than random
target_learners: secondary school pupils in subjects with sufficiently large enrollments
target_learning_goals: consistent marking standards across subject departments
examples: The author lists three possible methods for equalizing ratios and recommends combining methods (2) and (3) rather than simply liberalizing or exacting marking
key_sources: Cummins, R. A. (1917). 'Bright' and 'Slow' Pupils in Elementary and High School. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org

article_title: A Survey of the Three First Grades of the Horace Mann School by Means of Psychological Tests and Teachers' Estimates, and a Statistical Evaluation of the Methods Employed.
citation: Chassell, C. F., & Chassell, L. M. (1921). A survey of the three first grades of the Horace Mann School by means of psychological tests and teachers' estimates, and a statistical evaluation of the methods employed. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 12(5), 243-252.
title: Composite of all measures as criterion for evaluating classification measures
description: The article constructs a composite mental age as the standard against which each survey measure is evaluated. As printed, "this composite is the average mental age found by adding the mental ages obtained from the Stanford Revision, the two group tests, and the teachers' estimates, the Terman mental age being doubled". Each measure's worth for classification and promotion is judged by its correlation with this composite. The authors acknowledge the composite cannot be evaluated against an independent criterion in this survey.
requirements: Requires mental ages from all component measures for each child, with the Terman mental age counted as two measures
constraints: The measures compared are contained within the composite itself, so correlations with it are far higher than they would otherwise be; no independent criterion was available
target_learning_goals: classification and promotion of pupils into relatively homogeneous groups
examples: The survey of three first grades at the Horace Mann School used this composite to evaluate the Stanford Revision, the Pressey Primer Scale, the Meyer Tests, and teachers' estimates
key_sources: Chassell, C. F., & Chassell, L. M. (1921). A survey of the three first grades of the Horace Mann School by means of psychological tests and teachers' estimates, and a statistical evaluation of the methods employed. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 12(5), 243-252. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0068285

article_title: Achievement emotions and academic achievement: Reciprocal relations and the moderating influence of academic buoyancy.
citation: Putwain, D. W., Wood, P., & Pekrun, R. (2021). Achievement emotions and academic achievement: Reciprocal relations and the moderating influence of academic buoyancy. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000671
title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions
description: Control-value theory (CVT) is a framework incorporating the antecedents and outcomes of achievement emotions. Appraisals of value (importance of activities/outcomes) and control (expectancies and attributions) are proximal antecedents of emotions; emotions influence cognitive and motivational processes underpinning performance, and performance outcomes reciprocally influence emotions in "a cycle of reciprocal causation". The present study tested CVT's reciprocal predictions for enjoyment, boredom, and anxiety in primary mathematics.
requirements: Requires measurement of both emotion appraisals (control and value) and achievement outcomes over time to test reciprocal relations
constraints: The article notes effects of emotions on learning may be complex, depending on interactions of mediating mechanisms with task demands
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
academic emotional development
examples: The study tested CVT-predicted reciprocal relations between three classroom emotions and mathematics test performance over four waves in Year 5 students
key_sources: Putwain, D. W., Wood, P., & Pekrun, R. (2021). Achievement emotions and academic achievement: Reciprocal relations and the moderating influence of academic buoyancy. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000637

article_title: Promoting positive attitudes toward peers with disabilities: The role of information and imagined contact.
citation: Ginevra, M. C.; Vezzali, Loris; Camussi, E.; Capozza, D.; Nota, L.. (2021). Promoting positive attitudes toward peers with disabilities: The role of information and imagined contact. JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000661
title: Combine positive information about disabilities with imagined contact exercises to strengthen improvement of children's attitudes toward peers with disabilities
description: The article's implication statement recommends providing positive information about disabilities together with imagination exercises. It reports that "The combination of the 2 interventions (information about disability and imagination) allows to get stronger effects." This principle supports pairing informational content about peers with sensory disability, intellectual disability, or behavioral difficulties with guided imagined interactions.
requirements: Provide positive information about the disabilities and strategies to encourage participation in educational and extracurricular activities.
constraints: Tested with typically developing elementary school children; effects on other populations are not established in this study.
target_learning_goals: positive attitudes toward peers with disabilities
intentions to engage in contact with peers with disabilities
examples: The study randomly assigned 142 typically developing children to a cognitive intervention, a behavioral intervention, a combined intervention, or a no-intervention control condition.
key_sources: Ginevra, M. C.; Vezzali, Loris; Camussi, E.; Capozza, D.; Nota, L.. (2021). Promoting positive attitudes toward peers with disabilities: The role of information and imagined contact. JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000661

article_title: A tentative standardization of a completion test.
citation: Walter R. Miles and Julian E. Butterworth. (1912). A Tentative Standardization of a Completion Test. The Journal of Educational Psychology, pp. 329-336. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Tentative+Standardization+of+a+Completion+Test%22
title: A standardization method for completion tests combining per-unit timing with subjects' introspective difficulty marking of elisions
description: The article develops a method for assigning differential credit to the blanks of a completion test. Subjects complete sentence units under timing, then "immediately underline the words which gave difficulty," marking especially hard words twice. The relative difficulty of each elision is "estimated by the frequency with which it was marked by all subjects as of one of the three degrees of difficulty," combined with unit times to produce per-elision values. The authors offer it as an approach "which may be applied to any test of this character."
requirements: Subjects must complete units one at a time and retrospectively mark three degrees of word difficulty after each sentence, with marking time measured and deducted from total test time.
constraints: The authors note it was originally intended to correlate difficulty with correctness but no way was found to determine time for absolutely correct work, so the two elements were kept separate.
target_learners: students or faculty at the State University of Iowa
target_learning_goals: accurate scoring of completion (cloze) test performance
examples: Twenty-five university subjects completed the test with telegraph-key signalling to a time-recording apparatus in an adjoining sound-proof room; values were then validated with 100 first-year normal school girls as a mass test.
key_sources: Walter R. Miles and Julian E. Butterworth. (1912). A Tentative Standardization of a Completion Test. The Journal of Educational Psychology, pp. 329-336. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Tentative+Standardization+of+a+Completion+Test%22

article_title: The correlation between college grades and the Alpha Intelligence Tests.
citation: Bridges, J. W. (1920). The correlation between college grades and the Alpha intelligence tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 11(7), 361-369.
title: Intelligence tests used to predict college grades should be standardized separately for each college, with weak subtests improved or dropped
description: From the finding that Alpha subtests and total-score correlations differ sharply across colleges, Bridges recommends that "tests for university students should be selected and standardized for the various colleges separately; or, that in addition to a general intelligence test for all students there should be specific tests for the students of different colleges." He also argues weak predictors should be removed. The article grounds this in the college-by-college correlations of Table IV.
requirements: Correlations between test scores and academic standing must be computed for each college or subgroup separately before selecting or weighting tests
constraints: The article states it is difficult to draw definite conclusions from the figures, and the Agriculture advantage is only partially explained by supervision
target_learning_goals: prediction of academic standing from intelligence testing
examples: Bridges computed separate product-moment correlations for Arts, Engineering, Agriculture and Education students against the total Alpha score and each of the eight subtests
key_sources: Bridges, J. W. (1920). The correlation between college grades and the Alpha intelligence tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 11(7), 361-369. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071462

article_title: Acquiring science and social studies knowledge in kindergarten through fourth grade: Conceptualization, design, implementation, and efficacy testing of content-area literacy instruction (CALI).
citation: Dombek, J., Crowe, E. C., Spencer, M., Tighe, E. L., Coffinger, S., Zargar, E., Wood, T., Petscher, Y., & Connor, C. M. (2017). Acquiring Science and Social Studies Knowledge in Kindergarten Through Fourth Grade: Conceptualization, Design, Implementation, and Efficacy Testing of Content-Area Literacy Instruction (CALI). Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(3), 301-320. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000128
title: Deliver content-area (science and social studies) instruction during the existing literacy block to build content knowledge without sacrificing reading instruction time.
description: Because the literacy block monopolizes early elementary instructional time and excludes science and social studies, this principle embeds content-area literacy instruction within that block. The article developed CALI "to be implemented in general education classrooms" during the literacy block, aiming to improve content knowledge "without negatively affecting students' reading gains (i.e., no opportunity cost)." The efficacy RCT supported this: comprehension gains were positive, not negative.
requirements: Alignment with state and Common Core standards so educational leaders accept the content as literacy instruction
A principal goal of reading and understanding expository text
constraints: What can be taught during the literacy block may be limited by district core reading curriculum definitions
target_learning_goals: Science and social studies content knowledge
Reading and learning from expository text
examples: CALI units were implemented 4 days/week for 30 minutes (whole class) or 15-20 minutes per small group during the literacy block
key_sources: Dombek, J., Crowe, E. C., Spencer, M., Tighe, E. L., Coffinger, S., Zargar, E., Wood, T., Petscher, Y., & Connor, C. M. (2017). Acquiring Science and Social Studies Knowledge in Kindergarten Through Fourth Grade: Conceptualization, Design, Implementation, and Efficacy Testing of Content-Area Literacy Instruction (CALI). Journal of Educational Psychology, 109(3), 301-320. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000128

article_title: Practice and transference in normal and feeble-minded children.
citation: Woodrow, H. (1915). Practice and transference in normal and feeble-minded children. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Practice+and+Transference+in+Normal+and+Feeble-Minded+Children%22
title: Compare learners of different ability groups at the same mental age, not the same chronological age, to isolate differences in learning capacity
description: The author argues that comparing feeble-minded children with normal children of the same chronological age reveals only differences attributable to developmental level, not to feeble-mindedness itself. Characteristics such as inability to learn, lack of attention, and incapacity for sustained effort "characterize a six-year-old child compared with a ten-year-old child." Only by matching on mental age and initial ability can genuine differences in learning capacity be detected, which is how the four groups in this study were constructed.
requirements: An independent measure of mental age, such as a Binet-scale revision, must be available for matching groups
constraints: The author notes matching on exact mental age may require sacrificing exact equality of mental age in favor of equal initial ability
target_learning_goals: valid comparison of learning and practice effects across ability groups
examples: The four groups (feeble-minded and normal, each with practice and control) were selected so as to give about the same average mental age, namely nine years, and equality in initial ability
key_sources: Woodrow, H. (1915). Practice and transference in normal and feeble-minded children. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22Practice+and+Transference+in+Normal+and+Feeble-Minded+Children%22

article_title: The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: Beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies.
citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281
title: Build pure self-efficacy items so the frame of reference and context are contained in the item itself
description: The article's design recommendation for self-belief instrumentation is that self-efficacy items should supply their own explicit criterion: 'if the appropriate frame of reference and context are fully contained in the self-efficacy item itself, then social and dimensional comparison effects should be substantially attenuated'. Operationally this means showing students example tasks (test-like or everyday functional problems) and asking for confidence in accomplishing them, with a stated standard of successful performance, rather than asking generalized evaluations of performing well.
requirements: Items must specify a clear criterion of successful performance and the specific task or referent against which competence is judged
constraints: The article warns this distinction depends on item wording, and generalized items without explicit criteria behave like self-concept measures
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of self-efficacy distinct from self-concept
examples: The PISA2003 functional math self-efficacy measure asked confidence about concrete tasks such as using a train timetable or calculating a discounted price
key_sources: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., Parker, P. D., Murayama, K., Guo, J., Dicke, T. and Arens, A. K. (2019). The murky distinction between self-concept and self-efficacy: beware of lurking jingle-jangle fallacies. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111 (2). pp. 331-353. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000281

article_title: Language-independent and language-specific aspects of early literacy: An evaluation of the common underlying proficiency model.
citation: Goodrich J. Marc, Lonigan Christopher J. (2017). Language-Independent and Language-Specific Aspects of Early Literacy: An Evaluation of the Common Underlying Proficiency Model. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000179
title: Common Underlying Proficiency Model (Cummins)
description: The common underlying proficiency model holds that proficiencies in a first and second language are not separate abilities: "As proficiency in one language develops, so does language-independent knowledge (i.e., the common underlying proficiency) that supports the development of skills in both languages." Exposure to either language contributes to this shared proficiency, which may permit cross-language transfer. This study evaluated the model empirically for the first time using bifactor confirmatory factor analysis with language-minority preschoolers.
requirements: Sustained exposure to both languages so that language-independent knowledge can develop in either
constraints: The article notes evidence of a common underlying proficiency is not necessarily evidence of cross-language transfer; further research is needed on conditions under which transfer occurs
target_learning_goals: Early literacy: phonological awareness, print knowledge, oral language
examples: The study estimated bifactor models in which Spanish and English items loaded on language-specific factors and all items also loaded on a general factor for each skill
key_sources: Goodrich J. Marc, Lonigan Christopher J. (2017). Language-Independent and Language-Specific Aspects of Early Literacy: An Evaluation of the Common Underlying Proficiency Model. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000179

article_title: Identifying reciprocities in school motivation research: A review of issues and solutions associated with cross-lagged effects models.
citation: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Jacques Juhel, Pascal Bressoux, Cécile Nurra. (2021). Identifying Reciprocities in School Motivation Research: A Review of Issues and Solutions Associated With Cross-Lagged Effects Models. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114 (5), pp.945-965. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000700
title: Violating the convergence assumption of cross-lagged models confounds between- and within-person processes of change
description: The review's central explanatory account is that the reliability of cross-lagged models "rests on the assumption that students do not differ in their trajectories of growth over time". When this convergence assumption is violated — for example, when high- or low-achievers follow different growth trajectories — the estimated cross-lagged effects become unreliable because they mix between-person differences with within-person processes of change. The article frames this as the core methodological issue underlying questionable findings in school motivation research.
requirements: Longitudinal panel data with repeated measures of the constructs across occasions
constraints: Standard cross-lagged models are unreliable when students differ in their trajectories of growth over time
target_learning_goals: school motivation
academic self-concept
school achievement
key_sources: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Jacques Juhel, Pascal Bressoux, Cécile Nurra. (2021). Identifying Reciprocities in School Motivation Research: A Review of Issues and Solutions Associated With Cross-Lagged Effects Models. Journal of Educational Psychology, 114 (5), pp.945-965. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000700

article_title: An absolute point scale for the group measurement of intelligence.- Part II.
citation: Arthur S. Otis. (1917). An Absolute Point Scale for the Group Measurement of Intelligence.—Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org
title: Correlational-spread account: the sums of a test's intercorrelations with all other tests measure the relative degree to which it shares a common factor
description: In Appendix III, Otis develops a mathematical argument that if each test measures a general factor plus specifics, the relative degrees to which two tests correlate with the general factor are expressed by their relative correlations with the other tests. He demonstrates with a four-test example that "the sums of the correlations of each of the tests with all of the others afford meaures of the relative correlational spread of the tests," and shows average intercorrelations can be derived from each test's correlation with the composite without computing all pairwise coefficients.
requirements: Assumes each test measures only a general factor common to all tests plus factors specific to that test alone, so that the general factor is the only source of correlation.
constraints: The derivation assumes equal weights and standard deviations where stated, and the author notes the ratios hold only subject to the chance errors of the coefficients.
target_learners: pupils administered group intelligence tests in grades 3 through 8
target_learning_goals: measurement of general intelligence via group-administered point scales
examples: Otis illustrates the argument with a hypothetical four-test group whose elements overlap in known proportions, showing correlation sums of 1.80 : 1.80 : 1.60 : 1.20 match the elemental-overlap proportions 9 : 9 : 8 : 6.
key_sources: Arthur S. Otis. (1917). An Absolute Point Scale for the Group Measurement of Intelligence.—Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0074753

article_title: A report on the teaching and practice of hygiene in the public normal schools of the United States.
citation: Arthur Heche. (1909). A Report on the Teaching and Practice of Hygiene in the Public Normal Schools of the United States. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducreducpsyc
title: Correlate hygiene throughout the whole curriculum so prospective teachers habitually consider school problems from the point of view of hygiene
description: The article recommends that hygiene pervade the whole curriculum rather than appear only in physiology. It describes one school that "offers several courses in hygiene, and in addition deals in various other courses with the hygienic aspects of school problems," including sanitation with school administration and hygiene in practice-school observation. The author states that "Such correlation of hygiene with other courses unifies the student's knowledge and instils the habit of considering all school problems" hygienically.
requirements: Every instructor must be awake to the problems involved, according to the article, for such a program to be carried out successfully
target_learning_goals: personal, school, and community hygiene; habitual hygienic evaluation of school problems such as discipline, daily programs, and pupil classification
examples: One surveyed school deals with hygienic aspects of school problems in courses on school administration, practice-school observation, educational psychology, and child psychology.
key_sources: Arthur Heche. (1909). A Report on the Teaching and Practice of Hygiene in the Public Normal Schools of the United States. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org/journal/jeducreducpsyc

article_title: Effects of peers’ emotions on students’ emotions, achievement goals, mental effort, and performance.
citation: Hu, Y., Elliot, A. J., Wouters, P., van der Schaaf, M., Kester, L., & Pekrun, R. (2024). Effects of peers' emotions on students' emotions, achievement goals, mental effort, and performance. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(7), 1283–1299. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000895
title: CosmiClean game and peer-model emotion videos
description: CosmiClean is a game "designed ... to teach secondary school and university students the principles of separation processes for recycling materials", in which players build separation chains of conveyors, separators, and receptors across cargo levels with corrective feedback. For the intervention, three recorded videos (about 23 minutes each, 13 game levels) showed a male peer model playing the same script with enjoyment, frustration, or a neutral expression, filmed from a first-person perspective and hosted on Edpuzzle.
requirements: Participants watch the video carefully and cannot skip it; a manipulation check after the posttest verifies perceived emotion
constraints: The study used a virtual peer participants did not know, and an online rather than classroom format, to keep exposure to a single emotion clearly controlled
target_learning_goals: Chemistry separation processes: using nine separators, twelve materials, and eight properties
examples: Videos asked multiple-answer questions about which separators to use, gave corrective feedback, then the peer model explained and ran the recycling
key_sources: Hu, Y., Elliot, A. J., Wouters, P., van der Schaaf, M., Kester, L., & Pekrun, R. (2024). Effects of peers' emotions on students' emotions, achievement goals, mental effort, and performance. Journal of Educational Psychology, 116(7), 1283–1299. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000895

article_title: Parents’ academic expectations and aspirations predict students’ achievement emotions.
citation: Sakaki, M., Murayama, K., Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Marsh, H. W., Lichtenfeld, S., Wünsch, M., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Parents' academic expectations and aspirations predict students' achievement emotions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000959
title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions
description: Control-value theory explains achievement emotions through students' appraisals: 'achievement emotions are based on students' appraisals of control and value of the learning activities and achievement outcomes.' It distinguishes activity emotions (enjoyment, boredom, anger) from outcome emotions (pride, anxiety, shame, hopelessness), tying activity emotions mainly to intrinsic value and outcome emotions to achievement value. The study invokes it to predict how parental expectations and over-aspiration shift perceived control and the value of failure.
requirements: Learners hold appraisals of perceived control and of intrinsic and achievement value regarding learning activities and outcomes
constraints: The article notes boredom can also occur when perceived control is too high, making its relation to control non-linear
target_learning_goals: achievement emotions in mathematics (enjoyment, pride, anger, boredom, anxiety, shame, hopelessness)
examples: The study used the theory to predict that high expectations raise perceived control, increasing positive and reducing negative emotions, while over-aspiration shifts outcome appraisals toward failure.
key_sources: Sakaki, M., Murayama, K., Frenzel, A. C., Goetz, T., Marsh, H. W., Lichtenfeld, S., Wünsch, M., & Pekrun, R. (2025). Parents' academic expectations and aspirations predict students' achievement emotions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000959

article_title: The writing abilities of the elementary and grammar school pupils of a city school system measured by the Ayres scale.
citation: King, I., and Johnson, H. (1914). The Writing Abilities of the Elementary and Grammar School Pupils of a City School System Measured by the Ayres Scale. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072531
title: Compare pupils' writing across grades, ages and schools using a common scale applied uniformly by judges blind to those characteristics
description: The article's core design principle: apply a standard scale to writing produced under ordinary conditions, and have judges grade without knowledge of the child's age or grade, so that resulting grades reveal age, grade and school variations. The authors state that if samples were judged by one person without reference to age or grade and still showed progression, this would indicate "the scale is really workable" and could throw light on the relative efficiency of writing supervision in different schools.
requirements: A common standard scale applied to all specimens
Judges must not attend to or think of the age or grade of the child when ranking
constraints: Grading is subjective and judge variation cannot be wholly eliminated; consistency should be checked by having multiple judges grade a random subsample
target_learning_goals: handwriting legibility
examples: Teachers had pupils copy a typewritten sentence at the regular writing period; 34 specimens were re-graded by eight judges to check consistency
key_sources: King, I., and Johnson, H. (1914). The Writing Abilities of the Elementary and Grammar School Pupils of a City School System Measured by the Ayres Scale. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072531

article_title: No evidence that playing a linear number board game improves numerical skills beyond teaching as usual: A randomized controlled trial in 4- to 5-year-old primary school children.
citation: James-Brabham, E., Jay, T., & Sella, F. (2024). No evidence that playing a linear number board game improves numerical skills beyond teaching as usual: a randomized controlled trial in four- to five-year-old primary school children. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000857
title: Co-developed linear number board game with forward-only and bidirectional conditions
description: A classroom number game in which pairs of children place number food cards in order on a tablecloth-shaped mat to feed a monster, building a linear number line. Children in the forward condition placed cards ascending (e.g., 1-10 or 6-15); bidirectional children placed cards forward then backward (e.g., 10-1 or 15-6). The interval moved from 1-10 in the first three sessions to 6-15 in the remaining five after pilot testing. The game was designed to "required limited input from adults to play, and children found highly playable, fun, and engaging."
requirements: Played in small pairs in a quiet corner of the classroom with an experimenter prompting children to find the successive or preceding number and checking card order with scaffolded support
constraints: The article notes it used a one-size-fits-all difficulty level, with all children playing the same number intervals
target_learners: four- to five-year-old children in primary schools in socioeconomically disadvantaged areas
target_learning_goals: early numerical skills: counting, number naming, number order, number line estimation, number comparison
examples: Eight gameplay sessions across five weeks (twice weekly for four weeks with a one-week break), approximately ten minutes per session, with number-game pairs playing twice per session to match card placements with the alphabet control
key_sources: James-Brabham, E., Jay, T., & Sella, F. (2024). No evidence that playing a linear number board game improves numerical skills beyond teaching as usual: a randomized controlled trial in four- to five-year-old primary school children. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000857

article_title: Between- and within-domain relations of students' academic emotions.
citation: Goetz, T., Frenzel, A. C., Pekrun, R., Hall, N. C., & Lüdtke, O. (2006). Between- and Within-Domain Relations of Students' Academic Emotions. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu
title: Control–value theory of achievement emotions as an explanatory framework for domain-specific academic emotions
description: Pekrun's control–value theory holds that academic emotions are joint products of two appraisal types: appraisals of control over achievement activities and outcomes, and appraisals of their value. The article states that "any emotion related to academic achievement can be understood as a joint product of control and value appraisals, including students' enjoyment, pride, anxiety, anger, and boredom." Because control- and value-related constructs (self-efficacy, attributions, self-concepts, task values, achievement goals) are organized domain-specifically, the theory implies academic emotions should show weak between-domain relations — a corollary the study's results corroborate.
requirements: Appraisal of control and of value are both needed for the arousal of academic emotions, per the theory's account.
constraints: The theory's domain-specificity corollary applies to the extent that control- and value-related constructs are themselves organized in domain-specific ways, as the article states.
target_learners: secondary school students (Grades 8 and 11 in the study)
target_learning_goals: academic emotions related to classroom learning and achievement in specific subject domains
examples: The study tested the theory's corollary that academic emotions should show weak between-domain relations, finding disattenuated cross-domain emotion correlations that were generally weak.
key_sources: Goetz, T., Frenzel, A. C., Pekrun, R., Hall, N. C., & Lüdtke, O. (2006). Between- and Within-Domain Relations of Students' Academic Emotions. https://psycnet.apa.org/journals/edu

article_title: The Significance of Alpha in Colleges.
citation: Stone, Charles Leonard. (1920). The significance of alpha in colleges. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+significance+of+alpha+in+colleges%22+Stone
title: Compare intelligence percentiles with scholarship percentiles to identify students whose achievement diverges from measured ability
description: The article recommends pairing intelligence-test percentiles with scholarship percentiles for individual students to flag extreme disparity between ability and achievement. It names the candidates this surfaces: "idlers, men too heavily loaded with extra-curricular activities, and men with unusual capacity to develop their potential." Disparity cases should then be eliminated or explained, with motivation and accessory case-study data considered. The author presents this as a step toward scientific educational administration rather than a tested finding.
requirements: Intelligence test percentiles and scholarship percentiles for the same individual students, plus accessory data such as case studies and instinct tests.
constraints: The article bases the recommendation on tentative trust in intelligence tests; it is offered as a direction for educational administration, not a tested procedure.
target_learning_goals: Identifying students whose scholarship diverges from measured ability, including underperformers and students with undeveloped potential
examples: The Dartmouth study compared Alpha test performance with scholarship quarters and reported 18.2 per cent of A men below the class Alpha average and 32.8 per cent of E men above it.
key_sources: Stone, Charles Leonard. (1920). The significance of alpha in colleges. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+significance+of+alpha+in+colleges%22+Stone

article_title: Problems in the scientific study of the teaching of arithmetic.
citation: Stone, C. W. (1913). Problems in the Scientific Study of the Teaching of Arithmetic. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IV(1). https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Courtis standardized tests for measuring and interpreting results in the four fundamental operations and in simple reasoning
description: The article identifies the tests of Mr. Courtis as the best available standardized tests for arithmetic, noting in a footnote that "They afford means of measuring and interpreting results in the four fundamental operations and in simple reasoning." The tests are presented as usable by class teachers without special psychological or statistical training, both for evaluating teaching methods and for determining the needs and progress of pupils relative to definite standards for boys and girls of the same age and grade.
requirements: Standardized tests in a form the class teacher can readily utilize without special psychological or statistical training
target_learners: elementary school pupils in arithmetic classes
target_learning_goals: measuring addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and simple reasoning performance against definite standards
examples: The article recommends that adequate testing at the beginning of a term shows where the class stands as a class and where pupils stand as individuals, so the teacher can plan to meet class and individual needs
key_sources: Stone, C. W. (1913). Problems in the Scientific Study of the Teaching of Arithmetic. The Journal of Educational Psychology, IV(1). https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu

article_title: Why grades engender performance-avoidance goals: The mediating role of autonomous motivation.
citation: Pulfrey, C., Buchs, C., & Butera, F. (2011). Why grades engender performance-avoidance goals: The mediating role of autonomous motivation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 683–700. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0023911
title: Use comment-only formative feedback rather than grades when the aim is to avoid fostering performance-avoidance goals
description: Because expecting a grade raised performance-avoidance goals even when accompanied by formative comments, while comment-only assessment did not, the article's findings support assessing student work with individualized comments alone where avoidance-oriented motivation is a concern. In the experiment, "Assessment based uniquely on comments produced lower levels of performance avoidance than the other two conditions", i.e., than grade-only and grade-with-comment feedback. Comments specified mastered areas and how to improve, following the formative-assessment tradition the authors cite.
requirements: Comments must be individualized, specifying areas of the work mastered and giving indications how to improve, as in the comment-only condition.
constraints: The effect was demonstrated for in-class EFL exercises in Swiss professional schools; comment-based feedback could still be perceived as potentially threatening, per the literature the authors cite.
target_learners: secondary and postsecondary students in graded courses
target_learning_goals: reducing performance-avoidance goal adoption prior to assessment tasks
examples: In Experiment 2, comment-only students received an individualized comment such as 'You have shown you have understood the main theme of the discussion. Now try to distinguish more precisely the viewpoint of each speaker' with no grade, and showed lower performance-avoidance goal adoption (M = 4.95) than graded students (M = 5.73).
key_sources: Pulfrey, C., Buchs, C., & Butera, F. (2011). Why grades engender performance-avoidance goals: The mediating role of autonomous motivation. Journal of Educational Psychology, 103(3), 683–700. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0023911

article_title: Intelligence and its measurement: A symposium--IV.
citation: Colvin, S. S., & Pintner, R. (1921). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu
title: Colvin's definition of intelligence as the capacity to learn
description: Colvin proposes that intelligence is best understood as learning capacity: an individual possesses intelligence insofar as he has learned, or can learn, to adjust to his environment. He argues this view avoids overemphasizing the problem aspect of intelligence and rightly attributes intelligence to animals whose learning is confined to trial and error. As he writes, intelligence "is equivalent to the capacity to learn." The article presents this as a definitional position, not a tested result.
requirements: The definition is offered as a conceptual viewpoint for considering intelligence, to guide how intelligence examinations are interpreted.
constraints: Colvin notes the broader definition of intelligence as mental adaptability to environment is too broad because it includes instinctive adaptations as well as those acquired through experience.
target_learners: school and college students assessed with intelligence tests
target_learning_goals: understanding and measuring general intelligence as learning ability
examples: Colvin points to existing intelligence examinations, which measure intelligence largely in terms of what the examinee has learned, as practical acceptance of this definition.
key_sources: Colvin, S. S., & Pintner, R. (1921). Intelligence and Its Measurement. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu

article_title: Constancy of the I.Q. in Mental Defectives According to the Stanford Revision of Binet Tests.
citation: Poull, L. E. (1921). Constancy of I. Q. in mental defectives, according to the Stanford-revision of Binet tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Use composite ratings combining non-language and performance scales with the Stanford-Binet for truer evaluation of problem cases
description: The article recommends that classification decisions about persons with suspected mental defect should not rest on a single Stanford-Binet administration. Instead, "Composite ratings, including non-language and performance scales, together with the Stanford-Binet, have been found to give truer evaluations of problem cases", because they weight manual abilities that language inhibitions can hide. This is offered as an assessment practice for problem cases in institutional settings.
requirements: Trained psychologists accustomed to the reactions of mental defectives administer and interpret the tests
constraints: The advantage is stated for problem cases above the obvious imbecile type, where language inhibitions may hide intelligence
target_learners: persons under suspicion of mental defect, including institutionalized mental defectives aged four to 28
target_learning_goals: accurate classification of intellectual level and identification of individuals requiring permanent supervision or institutional care
examples: The author's retest data from 126 institutional cases showed variations large enough to change classification, motivating the composite-rating recommendation.
key_sources: Poull, L. E. (1921). Constancy of I. Q. in mental defectives, according to the Stanford-revision of Binet tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0071851

article_title: Mental fatigue in day school children as measured by immediate memory. Part II.
citation: W. H. Winch. (1911). Mental Fatigue in Day School Children as Measured by Immediate Memory. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology
title: Auditory consonant-span immediate memory test with positional scoring (3/2/1 marks)
description: The measuring instrument of the experiment: sets of six consonants called out twice in 25 seconds by the class teacher, with 1 minute 5 seconds for written recall in two lines of three. Ten sets constituted one 15-minute test. Scoring gave "Three marks for each consonant correctly remembered and rightly placed", two for one place out, and one for two places out, with spaces left for forgotten consonants.
requirements: Administered by the class teacher whose voice and enunciation are familiar to the children
constraints: The author judged these tests relatively, as well as absolutely, easier than those given in the previous experiment with older and abler boys
target_learners: Standard IV school class, boys averaging 11 years
target_learning_goals: Measuring immediate memory for auditory percepts as an index of mental fatigue
examples: Four preliminary tests (June 13–20, 1911) used to divide the class into two equal groups, then four final tests (July 5–14) taken mornings by one group and afternoons by the other
key_sources: W. H. Winch. (1911). Mental Fatigue in Day School Children as Measured by Immediate Memory. Part II. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journal_of_Educational_Psychology

article_title: Trajectories of the expression of negative emotion from kindergarten to first grade: Associations with academic outcomes.
citation: Hernández, M. M., Eisenberg, N., Valiente, C., Thompson, M. S., Spinrad, T. L., Grimm, K. J., VanSchyndel, S. K., Berger, R. H., Silva, K. M., Pina, A. A., Southworth, J., & Gal, D. E. (2018). Trajectories of the Expression of Negative Emotion from Kindergarten to First Grade: Associations with Academic Outcomes. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000213
title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions as a framework linking negative emotion to academic functioning
description: The article draws on Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions, in which achievement emotions are "emotions directly tied to achievement activities or achievement outcomes" and are proposed to affect cognitive resources, motivation, learning strategies, self-regulated learning, and subsequent achievement. The study uses this framework, alongside temperament perspectives, to motivate testing whether observed classroom negative expressivity predicts academic outcomes. It frames negative expression as limiting attention and interest relevant to academic tasks.
requirements: Emotions measured in the academic setting itself, since the article argues classroom-context expression has more direct implications for classroom functioning than general expressivity
constraints: The article treats the theory as a guiding perspective; it did not experimentally test the theory's mechanisms, and notes mediator variables such as working memory, attention, and social interactions were not measured
target_learners: kindergarten and first-grade children in elementary school classrooms
target_learning_goals: school engagement
academic skills
reading passage comprehension
examples: The study tested the theory's prediction longitudinally by modeling observed negative expressivity trajectories from kindergarten to first grade and relating them to three academic outcomes while controlling for prior academic levels

(2018). Trajectories of the Expression of Negative Emotion from Kindergarten to First Grade: Associations with Academic Outcomes. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000213

article_title: Neurocognitive academic training to improve symptoms executive functions and Chinese handwriting in children with ADHD
citation: Han Jiang, Stuart J. Johnstone, Yingxin Li, Jinjin Lu & Bo-Bei Mao. (2026). Neurocognitive Academic Training to Improve Symptoms Executive Functions and Chinese Handwriting in Children with ADHD. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00415-9
title: Cognitive-energetic model grounding of NAT: synergistic engagement of cognitive mechanisms, energetic pools, and executive functions
description: The article grounds NAT in the cognitive-energetic model, which "posits that ADHD involves deficits across three interrelated levels: cognitive mechanisms, energetic mechanisms, and EFs". NAT's efficacy is interpreted as synergistic: NCT trains core cognitive efficiency, progressively structured handwriting tasks challenge and regulate the child's arousal, activation, and effort pools, and phased teacher positive feedback modulates the effort pool via reward sensitivity. Enhanced cognitive efficiency alone is described as insufficient for transfer; it must be supported by an optimal energetic state and deployed under executive control within a meaningful academic context.
requirements: Simultaneous engagement of all three levels — cognitive training, scaffolded ecologically valid tasks, and motivational feedback — rather than EF training in isolation
constraints: The article states enhanced cognitive efficiency alone "is insufficient for far-transfer" without optimal energetic state and meaningful context
target_learning_goals: Executive function efficiency
Transfer of trained cognitive skills to academic tasks such as Chinese handwriting
examples: NAT's three components are mapped onto the model's three levels: NCT for cognitive mechanisms, scaffolded handwriting tasks for energetic pools, teacher feedback for effort regulation
key_sources: Han Jiang, Stuart J. Johnstone, Yingxin Li, Jinjin Lu & Bo-Bei Mao. (2026). Neurocognitive Academic Training to Improve Symptoms Executive Functions and Chinese Handwriting in Children with ADHD. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00415-9

article_title: Interbrain neural correlates of self and other integration in joint statistical learning
citation: Zheng Zheng & Jun Wang. (2024). Interbrain neural correlates of self and other integration in joint statistical learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00280-4
title: Co-representation account of joint statistical learning
description: The article frames its findings within the co-representation account, in which people act so that "actions at another person's command are represented just as if they were at one's own command". On this view, participants implicitly represent their co-actor's task information even when no response is required, coupling self-task and other-task information, which produces the observed joint statistical learning effect. The authors argue this challenges the traditional view that task relevance is a prerequisite for statistical learning, since co-representation rendered the irrelevant co-actor's stimuli salient.
requirements: A joint action setup in which co-actors share a complementary task with pre-assigned targets so that each co-actor's task information can be co-represented
constraints: Observed with only female participants in female–female pairings, so the authors caution against generalizing to female–male or male–male pairings
target_learning_goals: implicit extraction of statistical regularities from sequences
self-other integration in joint action
examples: Dyads performed a complementary SRTT in which a fixed 12-step stimulus sequence was divided between co-actors, with all participants reporting they were unaware of any sequence or pattern
key_sources: Zheng Zheng & Jun Wang. (2024). Interbrain neural correlates of self and other integration in joint statistical learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00280-4

article_title: Cognitive training enhances growth mindset in children through plasticity of cortico-striatal circuits
citation: Lang Chen, Hyesang Chang, Jeremy Rudoler, Eydis Arnardottir, Yuan Zhang, Carlo de los Angeles and Vinod Menon. (2022). Cognitive training enhances growth mindset in children through plasticity of cortico-striatal circuits. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00146-7
title: Cortico-striatal plasticity account of growth-mindset malleability
description: The article proposes that plasticity of cortico-striatal circuitry is "a key neurobiological mechanism underlying cognitive-training-induced changes in growth mindset." In this account, the dorsal ACC supports cognitive control processes such as implementation and correction of action plans, while the striatum is implicated in value-based action selection; together they may "facilitate more effective goal-directed actions to support learning and growth mindset." The account also draws on the expected value of control framework, in which the dorsal ACC weighs effort costs against potential rewards when allocating cognitive resources.
requirements: Longitudinal training data with task-based fMRI at pre- and post-training visits to observe circuit plasticity
constraints: Neuroimaging evidence comes from the training group only; the smaller control neuroimaging sample limited specificity analysis, and the authors call for larger control samples and active control groups matched for expectation of improvement
target_learners: children ages 7–10 in early elementary school
target_learning_goals: growth mindset
cognitive control and math skill acquisition
examples: Whole-brain fMRI and gPPI connectivity analyses during a parametrically modulated addition task showed activation and connectivity changes in dACC, striatum, and hippocampus tracking growth-mindset gains
key_sources: Lang Chen, Hyesang Chang, Jeremy Rudoler, Eydis Arnardottir, Yuan Zhang, Carlo de los Angeles and Vinod Menon. (2022). Cognitive training enhances growth mindset in children through plasticity of cortico-striatal circuits. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00146-7

article_title: Multi-stakeholder perspective on responsible artificial intelligence and acceptability in education
citation: Alexander John Karran, Patrick Charland, Joé Trempe-Martineau, Ana Ortiz de Guinea Lopez de Arana, Anne-Marie Lesage, Sylvain Sénécal & Pierre-Majorique Léger. (2025). Multi-stakeholder perspective on responsible artificial intelligence and acceptability in education. npj Science of Learning 10:44. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00333-2
title: Multi-stakeholder confidence-trust framework for AI acceptability in education
description: The article proposes that acceptance of AI in education hinges on a balance of agency, confidence, and trust underpinned by explainability and transparency. Confidence and trust are described as "inextricably linked, representing a feedback loop wherein conﬁdence builds towards trust and trust instils conﬁdence". Trust is an umbrella construct relying on transparency of AI processes, alignment with educational ethics, explainability, privacy protection, and evidence of effectiveness. The study operationalises this framework through vignette-manipulated variables (agency, transparency, explainability, privacy) and mediators (global utility, individual usefulness, justice, confidence, risk) predicting intention to use.
requirements: AI systems must exhibit reliability, assessment accuracy, and transparent and explainable decision-making, requiring robust design, testing, and ongoing monitoring
constraints: The framework was tested with vignette methodology on hypothetical AI applications not yet widely deployed; school director data were excluded from mediation analysis due to small sample size
target_learning_goals: Responsible and ethical deployment of AI in education
Stakeholder acceptance and intention to use educational AI applications
examples: Four ecologically valid vignette scenarios (Correct-AI, Answer-AI, Tutor-AI, Emotion-AI) in a 2 x 2 x 2 × 2 counterbalanced design with manipulation checks
key_sources: Alexander John Karran, Patrick Charland, Joé Trempe-Martineau, Ana Ortiz de Guinea Lopez de Arana, Anne-Marie Lesage, Sylvain Sénécal & Pierre-Majorique Léger. (2025). Multi-stakeholder perspective on responsible artificial intelligence and acceptability in education. npj Science of Learning 10:44. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00333-2

article_title: An fMRI study of scientists with a Ph.D. in physics confronted with naive ideas in science
citation: Geneviève Allaire-Duquette, Lorie-Marlène Brault Foisy, Patrice Potvin, Martin Riopel, Marilyne Larose, Steve Masson. (2021). An fMRI study of scientists with a Ph.D. in physics confronted with naive ideas in science. npj Science of Learning 6:11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00091-x
title: Coordination account of conceptual change: naive and scientific ideas coexist and must be coordinated rather than replaced
description: This account, proposed in the article's discussion, holds that learning science does not erase naive ideas: "Conceptual change might instead yield multiple ideas of each given natural phenomena, including scienti ﬁc and naive ideas, which then have to be coordinated to demonstrate appropriate conceptual understanding." Expert performance then depends on inhibitory control to suppress the dominant naive idea when the context demands a scientific judgment, framed as "a dynamic vigilance, allowing active control of thoughts when the context requires for it". The fMRI evidence shows frontal inhibitory-control activations for incongruent statements in both physics and biology among Ph.D. physicists.
requirements: Learners must have both naive and scientific ideas coexisting in memory for coordination-based conceptual change to apply
constraints: The article states its interpretation relies on reverse inference from brain activity to mental processes and recommends the findings be treated with considerable caution
target_learning_goals: conceptual change in science
overcoming naive ideas and misconceptions
examples: Physicists with a Ph.D. judging incongruent statements recruited MFG and IFG associated with inhibitory control, while congruent statements showed more focal posterior activations consistent with automatic processing
key_sources: Geneviève Allaire-Duquette, Lorie-Marlène Brault Foisy, Patrice Potvin, Martin Riopel, Marilyne Larose, Steve Masson. (2021). An fMRI study of scientists with a Ph.D. in physics confronted with naive ideas in science. npj Science of Learning 6:11. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00091-x

article_title: Anticipated variability increases generalization of predictive learning
citation: Hadar Ram, Guy Grinfeld & Nira Liberman. (2024). Anticipated variability increases generalization of predictive learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00269-z
title: Construal Level Theory link: psychological distance cues variability and abstraction
description: The article invokes Construal Level Theory (CLT), which holds that distancing an object in time, space, social distance or hypotheticality changes how we think about it, and that "distance introduces variability": distal objects are less similar to current experience, more uncertain, and therefore represented more abstractly. The paper proposes that psychological distance to the anticipated application of learning serves as a subtle cue for potential variability, eliciting more abstract, broader representations and thus broader generalization, complementing explicitly instructed variability expectations.
