requirements: A perceived temporal (or other psychological) distance between the learning situation and the anticipated application context
constraints: The CLT-based hypothesis rests on the premise that distance increases the range and variability of possibilities; Experiment 2 tested only the distance–expected-variability link, using time distance
target_learners: adult learners anticipating future application of learning
target_learning_goals: abstract, broader category formation and generalization from limited learning experience
examples: Experiment 3 told participants the actual task would occur immediately or a week later, without any difference in the actual learning and generalization procedures
key_sources: Hadar Ram, Guy Grinfeld & Nira Liberman. (2024). Anticipated variability increases generalization of predictive learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00269-z

article_title: The neural and cognitive basis of expository text comprehension
citation: Keller, T. A., Mason, R. A., Legg, A. E., & Just, M. A. (2024). The neural and cognitive basis of expository text comprehension. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00232-y
title: Make instructional technical texts more cohesive by explicitly relating different types of information across sentences and paragraphs
description: Because passage difficulty was modulated by processes that bind together different types of information from distributed cortical areas, the authors recommend engineering texts so such relations are explicit. They suggest "Explicit cohesive devices that can be incorporated across sentences and paragraphs include overlap of arguments and clear indications of causal, temporal, and spatial relations that are not overtly stated." Cohesion facilitates coherence and improves discourse comprehension, consistent with prior educational research.
requirements: Texts must make relations among different types of information explicit, using argument overlap and clear causal, temporal, and spatial relation indicators.
constraints: The present study did not find reliable correlations between passage comprehension and cohesion measures; the materials were not designed to vary greatly in cohesion.
target_learners: Readers of technical instructional texts in STEM and technical education
target_learning_goals: Improved comprehensibility and retention of technical text content
examples: Passages that were harder to comprehend "inadequately interrelate different types of information, evoking additional integrative and inferential processing" in the study.
key_sources: Keller, T. A., Mason, R. A., Legg, A. E., & Just, M. A. (2024). The neural and cognitive basis of expository text comprehension. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00232-y

article_title: The method of educational assessment affects children’s neural processing and performance: behavioural and fMRI Evidence
citation: Howard, S. J., Burianová, H., Calleia, A., Fynes-Clinton, S., Kervin, L. and Bokosmaty, S. (2017). The method of educational assessment affects children's neural processing and performance: behavioural and fMRI Evidence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0010-9
title: Cognitive Load Theory extends from learning and instructional design to the design of educational assessment
description: The article applies Cognitive Load Theory's distinction between intrinsic and extraneous load to standardised testing: information varies in the demands it places on learners' working memory "as a function of its inherent complexity (intrinsic load) and complexity with which information is presented (extraneous load)". It argues the mode of information delivery in a test can influence WM demands, and that its behavioural and neuroanatomical data suggest "these principles may also apply to the assessment of children's knowledge and skills" rather than only to acquisition of competencies.
requirements: Assessment items must be equated in content complexity for extraneous-load differences between methods to be interpretable
constraints: Cognitive Load Theory's foremost concern has thus far been learning and instructional design; application to assessment rests on the article's own behavioural and neuroanatomical data
target_learners: school-aged children taking standardised assessments (Grade 2, age 7-8 in the study)
target_learning_goals: accurate measurement of domain-specific competencies such as spelling, reading comprehension and numeracy
examples: The proofreading condition, modelled on Australia's NAPLAN, recruited dorsal attentional and WM-related activations, which the article maps onto increased intrinsic load via Whelan's fMRI-to-load mapping
key_sources: Howard, S. J., Burianová, H., Calleia, A., Fynes-Clinton, S., Kervin, L. and Bokosmaty, S. (2017). The method of educational assessment affects children's neural processing and performance: behavioural and fMRI Evidence. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0010-9

article_title: Metacognition: ideas and insights from neuro- and educational sciences
citation: Damien S. Fleur, Bert Bredeweg and Wouter van den Bos. (2021). Metacognition: ideas and insights from neuro- and educational sciences. npj Science of Learning 6:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00089-5
title: Design metacognitive instruction that combines strategy instruction with strategy knowledge and extends over a longer duration
description: This design principle holds that metacognitive instruction works best when it pairs offline meta-control training with offline meta-knowledge development. The article reports interventions "lead to the highest effect sizes when they both (i) instructed a combination of metacognitive strategies with an emphasis on planning strategies" and provided knowledge about strategies, and that "The longer the duration of the intervention, the more effective they were", with the strongest academic effects in mathematics.
requirements: Instruction must combine metacognitive strategies with an emphasis on planning strategies together with knowledge about strategies, illustrating benefits of applying trained strategies
constraints: Effects of metacognitive training interventions are often difficult to evaluate due to a lack of randomised control designs in the literature
target_learning_goals: learning strategies, planning, and academic achievement
examples: Meta-analyses of direct metacognitive instruction showed the strongest effects on academic performance in mathematics, followed by reading and writing
key_sources: Damien S. Fleur, Bert Bredeweg and Wouter van den Bos. (2021). Metacognition: ideas and insights from neuro- and educational sciences. npj Science of Learning 6:13. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00089-5

article_title: Change by challenge: A common genetic basis behind childhood cognitive development and cognitive training
citation: Bruno Sauce, John Wiedenhoeft, Nicholas Judd and Torkel Klingberg. (2021). Change by challenge: A common genetic basis behind childhood cognitive development and cognitive training. npj Science of Learning 6:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00096-6
title: The cognitive challenge hypothesis: developmental genes rely heavily on cognitive experiences (contrasted with the maturation hypothesis)
description: The article frames two accounts of gene-environment interplay in cognitive development. Under the "maturation hypothesis (also known as experience-expectant)", genes set a "default course" of development needing only common supporting experiences. Under the "cognitive challenge hypothesis (also known as skill learning or experience-dependent)", the effect of developmental genes "relies heavily on cognitive experiences", so variation in cognitive change arises from genes interplaying with idiosyncratic cognitive challenges. The study tests the prediction that cogPGS explains WM change in both development and training.
requirements: Requires intervention designs that create deliberate and trackable cognitive experiences to distinguish it from the maturation hypothesis, because typical-development studies confound the two hypotheses
constraints: The two processes are not mutually exclusive and could coexist or dominate at different points during childhood, as the article states
target_learners: children and adolescents (ages 6–25 in the developmental sample, 7–19 in the training sample)
target_learning_goals: working memory and general cognitive abilities (reasoning, attention, learning)
examples: The study combined a longitudinal developmental sample with an intervention sample of 25-day intense WM training to contrast the two hypotheses using the same polygenic score
key_sources: Bruno Sauce, John Wiedenhoeft, Nicholas Judd and Torkel Klingberg. (2021). Change by challenge: A common genetic basis behind childhood cognitive development and cognitive training. npj Science of Learning 6:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00096-6

article_title: The effect of classroom environment on literacy development
citation: Gary Rance, Richard C. Dowell and Dani Tomlin. (2023). The effect of classroom environment on literacy development. npj Science of Learning 8:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00157-y
title: Cognitive resource allocation and the Irrelevant Sound Effect as explanations for open-plan learning disadvantage
description: The article draws on the theory of cognitive resource allocation, which "proposes that a ﬁnite, interactive pool of cognitive resources, including memory and attention, are ﬂexibly allocated to an activity depending on the demands of the task." When an auditory signal is masked or degraded, listeners compensate with top-down, knowledge-based processing, increasing cognitive load; comprehension may be restricted if resource limits are exceeded. The article also invokes the Irrelevant Sound Effect (ISE), whereby meaningful noise impacts non-auditory tasks such as reading through an increased attention burden, and links both accounts to its finding that children with poorer attention and speech-in-noise skills showed the greatest open-plan disadvantage.
requirements: A masked or degraded auditory signal that requires compensatory top-down listening
Meaningful (speech) noise sources competing with the target signal
constraints: The article states the present work cannot be taken as proof of the listening-effort relationship as there were no direct measures of listening effort
The lack of significant interaction between working memory and reading development suggests more than cognitive resource limitations may underlie the observed effect
target_learning_goals: Reading fluency development
Speech perception and attention in classroom listening conditions
examples: Students demonstrating the poorest listening in noise skills tended to be those with the greatest negative academic impact in the noisier open-plan study phases
key_sources: Gary Rance, Richard C. Dowell and Dani Tomlin. (2023). The effect of classroom environment on literacy development. npj Science of Learning 8:9. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00157-y

article_title: The challenge of explicit learning in life skill education
citation: Dominik M. Piehlmaier & Dee Warmath. (2025). The challenge of explicit learning in life skill education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00375-6
title: Continuum of knowledge from factual through inflexible, semi-flexible, to flexible knowledge
description: The article introduces a continuum of knowledge ordering forms by transferability. Factual knowledge is memorized content the individual "struggles to apply what they know, even to decisions in the knowledge domain". Inflexible knowledge applies within a domain but not beyond it; semi-flexible knowledge (e.g., statistical methods) transcends domains but is limited to a specific method; flexible knowledge (e.g., strategic thinking) applies broadly across domains with few constraints. The continuum frames the argument that collegiate financial education over-relies on the inflexible end.
requirements: Flexible knowledge is described as developing through instruction that gives learners tacit or procedural understanding of decision processes, not just declarative content
constraints: The article notes a three-month course cannot cover all eventualities a financial decision-maker will face, limiting inflexible knowledge's transferability to ill-structured real-world decisions
target_learners: undergraduate students in collegiate life skills or financial education courses
target_learning_goals: applying knowledge to optimal real-world financial decision-making
transferring learning across domains and unfamiliar problems
examples: The RCT taught semi-flexible knowledge via an applied statistics course and flexible knowledge via a design thinking/strategic planning course, compared against an explicit personal finance course
key_sources: Dominik M. Piehlmaier & Dee Warmath. (2025). The challenge of explicit learning in life skill education. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00375-6

article_title: Genetic associations with learning over 100 days of practice
citation: Cherry Youn, Andrew D. Grotzinger, Christina M. Lill, Lars Bertram, Florian Schmiedek, Martin Lövdén, Ulman Lindenberger, Michel Nivard, K. Paige Harden, Elliot M. Tucker-Drob. (2022). Genetic associations with learning over 100 days of practice. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00121-2
title: COGITO 100-day intensive cognitive practice protocol with individualized task difficulty
description: The COGITO study protocol consists of "an extensive pre-test evaluation, a practice phase of ~100 days (M = 101) on 12 cognitive tasks, and a post-test evaluation". For all tasks except perceptual speed comparison tasks, "difficulty levels at the practice phase were individualized by using different presentation time based on the average accuracies achieved at four different presentation times pre-test". The authors argue this individualization experimentally deconfounds rate and shape of learning by tailoring difficulty to individual pre-test scores.
requirements: Genetic or other participant data availability; participants completed 10 days of pre-testing used to set individualized presentation times
constraints: Data are not publicly available due to German privacy regulation and are available only upon reasonable request with COGITO study permission
target_learning_goals: Episodic memory
Working memory
Perceptual speed
examples: 131 COGITO participants (51 younger, 80 older) completed daily practice sessions on twelve tasks, with three choice reaction time tasks excluded, leaving nine tasks for analyses
key_sources: Cherry Youn, Andrew D. Grotzinger, Christina M. Lill, Lars Bertram, Florian Schmiedek, Martin Lövdén, Ulman Lindenberger, Michel Nivard, K. Paige Harden, Elliot M. Tucker-Drob. (2022). Genetic associations with learning over 100 days of practice. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00121-2

article_title: How to capture developmental brain dynamics: gaps and solutions
citation: van Atteveldt, N., Vandermosten, M., Weeda, W. & Bonte, M. (2021). How to capture developmental brain dynamics: gaps and solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00088-6
title: Use a common developmental framework spanning levels, functions, and time across studies and disciplines
description: The article recommends that a framework encompassing multiple levels, functional networks, and their dynamic interactions across time (illustrated by its Fig. 1) be used across studies and disciplines. It states "a common framework is essential in order to allow communication between the experts at each level", enabling researchers to specify which levels and networks their study addresses and take into account constraints and modulatory influences from other levels. It also supports exploratory research by relating findings to specific parts of the multilevel model.
requirements: Multidisciplinary, multisite studies involving researchers from different levels and disciplines
Measures comparable across studies
constraints: Studies encompassing different levels and functions at multiple time points are currently scarce
target_learners: Children and adolescents in developmental research
target_learning_goals: Reading, math, executive function and broader developmental outcomes
examples: Workshop participants used the framework to map each presenter's work onto levels and functions (Table 1)
key_sources: van Atteveldt, N., Vandermosten, M., Weeda, W. & Bonte, M. (2021). How to capture developmental brain dynamics: gaps and solutions. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00088-6

article_title: Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education
citation: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z
title: Consider the implicit norms embedded in empirical evaluations of educational inequality
description: Evaluations of inequality embed norms about which outcomes matter and for whom. The article proposes "consideration of the implicit norms that forms of evaluation set for the pursuit of equality in education," including "consideration of the potential reinforcement of inequality through the normativity of pursuing certain outcomes." Group-level indicators (e.g., explained variance by background) and individual-level learning-gain indicators embody different norms about what equality requires.
requirements: Reflection must include consideration of the potential reinforcement of inequality through the normativity of pursuing certain outcomes
constraints: The article notes a narrow focus on cognitive outcomes may in fact perpetuate or even increase inequality
target_learning_goals: Choosing and interpreting indicators of educational equality with awareness of their normative repercussions
examples: The article cites critical discussions such as the works of Au and Hogg as aids for researchers considering implicit norms embedded in particular evaluations
key_sources: Louise Elffers, Eddie Denessen and Monique Volman. (2024). Combining perspectives in multidisciplinary research on inequality in education. npj Science of Learning 9:5. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00215-z

article_title: Reading and writing habits compensate for aging effects in speech connectedness
citation: Malcorra, B. L. C., Mota, N. B., Weissheimer, J., Schilling, L. P., Wilson, M. A. & Hübner, L. C. (2022). Reading and writing habits compensate for aging effects in speech connectedness. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00129-8
title: Cognitive reserve: cognitively stimulating activities increase brain resilience to cope with cognitive-processing changes in typical and atypical aging
description: The article frames education and frequency of reading and writing habits under "the concept of cognitive reserve which establishes the theory that activities that stimulate the brain are linked to an increase in brain resilience to cope with changes in cognitive processing resulting from typical and atypical aging". It uses this framework to interpret its finding that RWH's coefficient compensated for the aging effect in speech connectedness, aligning with longitudinal evidence that reading activity prevents long-term cognitive decline.
requirements: The framework presumes activities that stimulate the brain, such as formal education and frequent reading and writing habits, are present across the lifespan
constraints: The article notes its own correlational design "could not be taken as a causality effect"
target_learners: typical adults and older adults, predominantly with low educational level and low to middle-low SES
target_learning_goals: maintenance of speech connectedness and cognitive efficiency in aging
examples: The study measured oral narratives of 118 healthy individuals aged 51–82 as word-graphs and found the strength of RWH's coefficient compensated for the aging effect.
key_sources: Malcorra, B. L. C., Mota, N. B., Weissheimer, J., Schilling, L. P., Wilson, M. A. & Hübner, L. C. (2022). Reading and writing habits compensate for aging effects in speech connectedness. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00129-8

article_title: The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students
citation: Shiels, L., Carew, P., Tomlin, D. & Rance, G. (2025). The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00350-1
title: Cognitive Resource Allocation theory as an explanation for greater SFA benefit among lower-IQ students
description: The article invokes Cognitive Resource Allocation theory to explain why lower-IQ children gained more reading fluency benefit from sound field amplification. The theory "proposes a limited pool of resources that are flexibly allocated depending on task demands". Under poor listening conditions, perception of the acoustic signal requires more resources, compromising the cognitive processing left for the task; individuals with higher intelligence can allocate more resources to demanding tasks, explaining the observed IQ–benefit relationship in this study.
requirements: Applies to listening tasks where degraded acoustic conditions increase the perceptual resource requirement, as stated in the article's account.
constraints: The article presents it as a proposed explanation for the observed IQ–SFA benefit relationship, not as a directly tested mechanism.
target_learning_goals: reading fluency development under degraded classroom listening conditions
key_sources: Shiels, L., Carew, P., Tomlin, D. & Rance, G. (2025). The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00350-1

article_title: Counting days is a spacing incentive that unlocks the potential of low GPA students
citation: Iman YeckehZaare & Paul Resnick. (2025). Counting days is a spacing incentive that unlocks the potential of low GPA students. npj Science of Learning 10:35. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00322-5
title: Counting Days grading incentive in the Runestone retrieval practice tool
description: A grade-based incentive implemented in a retrieval practice tool built into the Runestone online textbook platform. In the treatment condition, "students earn a ﬁxed increment of points for every day on which they correctly answer at least ten practice questions, thereby promoting spaced learning", whereas the control condition awards points per question without any distribution requirement. The tool uses an adaptive spacing algorithm inspired by the SuperMemo 2 algorithm, presenting multiple-choice and active-code questions from a topic-based bank. The design rewards spaced activity so that an equivalent amount of activity massed near exams earns fewer course points.
requirements: Activity must be measurable and delivered and tracked through a course management system so days of activity can be counted
A set of practice questions per day (ten in the within-class experiment) as the threshold for earning the day's points
Points capped so students can earn the maximum with about 40 days of activity, roughly three days per week
constraints: Results may be specific to the domain and level of introductory programming
Impact may depend on using similar question types for assessing learning outcomes as those used in the practice activity
May depend on students having internalized the norm of doing activities the instructor assigns points for, so it may be more effective in more elite institutions
Does not provide complete autonomy, since students do not set their own goals for how much practice to do on how many days
target_learners: high school and college students in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: spaced retrieval practice
long-term retention of course material
examples: In the within-class experiment, 10% of the course grade (100 points) was based on the practice tool; treatment students earned 2.5 points per day for correctly answering ten practice questions, for up to 40 days
In the between-instructor experiment, 71 instructors teaching 97 courses to 1,648 students randomized at the instructor level configured the points per day and questions per day themselves
key_sources: Iman YeckehZaare & Paul Resnick. (2025). Counting days is a spacing incentive that unlocks the potential of low GPA students. npj Science of Learning 10:35. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00322-5

article_title: Effects of described demonstrator ability on brain and behavior when learning from others
citation: Selbing, I., Becker, N., Pan, Y., Lindström, B., & Olsson, A. (2025). Effects of described demonstrator ability on brain and behavior when learning from others. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00292-0
title: Two-form framework of observational learning: copying versus observational outcome learning
description: The article organizes social learning by distinguishing two forms of learning from observation. The authors write that learning about others' actions is "commonly divided into two forms of learning: 1) learning by observing the action of the demonstrator, and 2) learning by observing the outcome of a demonstrator's actions", referred to as "copying" and "observational outcome learning" respectively. The framework structures their hypotheses and RL models: copying is modeled as a tendency to make the same choice as the demonstrator, while observational outcome learning is modeled as Q-value updating from observed outcomes. In this study the framework guided which parameters could vary with described demonstrator ability.
requirements: Requires that both the demonstrator's action and the outcome of that action are available to the observer, as in the article's task, for both forms of learning to be possible
constraints: The authors note that for observational outcome learning the link between demonstrator ability and learning efficiency is less straightforward, since observers can also learn from the outcomes of poor decisions
target_learners: Adult university students learning probabilistic avoidance tasks through observation
target_learning_goals: Learning which of two choice options is optimal from observing another person's choices and their outcomes
examples: Fifty Q-learning-based RL models were generated varying whether copying and/or observational outcome learning were included and whether their parameters were description-sensitive
key_sources: Selbing, I., Becker, N., Pan, Y., Lindström, B., & Olsson, A. (2025). Effects of described demonstrator ability on brain and behavior when learning from others. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00292-0

article_title: Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions
citation: Inmaculada Márquez & Mario Treviño. (2025). Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions. npj Science of Learning 10:85. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00377-4
title: Compartmentalized, context-dependent predictive control in human sensorimotor function
description: The article proposes that predictive processing in sensorimotor control is not a unified hierarchical architecture but a set of specialized, task-specific computations. As the authors state, "predictive control relies on specialized, context-dependent mechanisms, in which task-speci ﬁc computations adaptively integrate context and internal state dynamics". The framework holds that sensory detection, motor execution, and visuomotor adaptation operate as loosely coupled, domain-specific subsystems, with angular and speed errors engaging distinct control policies. It is supported by the study's weak cross-task associations and dominant within-subject variability, and is offered as useful for understanding adaptive control in real-world behaviors such as sports, driving, or human–machine interaction.
requirements: Within-task performance must be measured with task-specific metrics; the framework was built from a within-subject, multi-task battery in the same participants.
constraints: The design emphasized rapid, trial-level corrections to transient perturbations rather than long-term adaptation.
With only 54 participants, statistical power may have been insufficient to detect small cross-domain effects.
target_learning_goals: sensorimotor prediction and adaptation
perceptual detection of prediction errors
motor consistency
examples: The study combined a visuomotor interception task with angular or speed perturbations, a sensory detection task, and a no-feedback motor variability task in the same 54 participants.
key_sources: Inmaculada Márquez & Mario Treviño. (2025). Dissociable sensory, motor, and visuomotor predictive functions. npj Science of Learning 10:85. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00377-4

article_title: The influence of task and interpersonal interdependence on cooperative behavior and its neural mechanisms
citation: Zijun Yin, Bin Xuan, Chengchi Liu, Jingchao Yi, Xiaoyan Zheng & Mingming Zhang. (2025). The influence of task and interpersonal interdependence on cooperative behavior and its neural mechanisms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00303-8
title: Adapted cooperation key-pressing paradigm distinguishing HICT and LICT with fNIRS hyperscanning
description: A two-task experimental element adapted from a prior cooperation key-pressing paradigm and administered under fNIRS hyperscanning. In HICT, "if |RTleft − RTright |<| R Tleft + RTright |/8, they could receive 1 point" rewarding synchronous key-pressing; in LICT, each participant pressed faster than a personally calibrated standard time derived from practice trials. Each round comprised 20 formal trials with per-trial fast/slow feedback, and neural data were collected from 21 channels covering PFC.R, DLPFC.L, DLPFC.R and TPJ.R.
requirements: Two NIRSport fNIRS systems; E-prime 3.0 stimulus control; participants refrained from verbal or non-verbal communication
constraints: The fNIRS device's limited channel capacity conﬁned the study to the PFC and the TPJ.R, and the authors note the generalizability of the ﬁndings may be limited because real-world cooperative situations are often more complex.
target_learning_goals: cooperative behavior and neural coordination during joint tasks
examples: The HICT scoring rule awarded 1 point when response times were close; the LICT awarded 1 point when both participants pressed faster than their respective standard times
key_sources: Zijun Yin, Bin Xuan, Chengchi Liu, Jingchao Yi, Xiaoyan Zheng & Mingming Zhang. (2025). The influence of task and interpersonal interdependence on cooperative behavior and its neural mechanisms. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00303-8

article_title: Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning
citation: Zhu, J.-P., Xie, X.-Y., Yu, C. & Zhang, J.-Y. (2026). Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00396-1
title: COVIS dual-systems framework and its continuum refinement for category learning
description: The article describes the Competition between Verbal and Implicit Systems (COVIS) framework, which "posits two partially distinct systems: an explicit, prefrontal-dependent rule-based (RB) system and an implicit, basal ganglia-dependent information-integration (II) system". RB learning engages verbalizable rules on a single dimension and depends on working memory and executive attention; II learning combines multiple incommensurable dimensions implicitly via striatal-based feedback learning. The article argues recent evidence refines rather than refutes this view, supporting a continuum of partially overlapping explicit and implicit processes.
requirements: Distinguishing rule-based from information-integration category structures, as the framework's predictions concern these two learning types
constraints: The article states the separation between systems is relative rather than absolute, with partially overlapping neural activations
target_learners: Adults learning perceptual categories in laboratory visual tasks
target_learning_goals: Implicit information-integration category learning and explicit rule-based category learning
examples: The study used a four-category II structure defined by spatial frequency and orientation (categories F, D, K, J) with trial-by-trial feedback
key_sources: Zhu, J.-P., Xie, X.-Y., Yu, C. & Zhang, J.-Y. (2026). Double training promotes retinotopic transfer of category learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00396-1

article_title: Targeted memory reactivation with sleep disruption does not weaken week-old memories
citation: Nathan W. Whitmore, Erika M. Yamazaki & Ken A. Paller. (2024). Targeted memory reactivation with sleep disruption does not weaken week-old memories. npj Science of Learning 9, 64. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00276-0
title: Time-dependent memory resilience account: TMR-SD weakens memories only when consolidation has not yet transformed them
description: The article proposes that sleep-based consolidation progressively makes memories resistant to the harm caused by reactivation combined with sleep disruption. Reactivation via cue sounds is described as involving selection of a memory followed by modification of storage, and the authors write that "sleep disruption weakens memories specifically by interfering with consolidation that would otherwise transpire." On this account, week-old memories survive TMR-SD whereas newly formed memories are degraded, aligning with amnestic-drug and electroconvulsive-therapy findings of temporally graded vulnerability, which the authors call "one of the main hallmarks of systems consolidation."
requirements: A memory reactivation procedure (auditory cues linked during learning) and a sleep period during which cues can be delivered at arousal-provoking intensity
constraints: Findings derive from afternoon naps; the authors state further research is needed to determine generalization beyond afternoon naps, and they did not examine TMR without sleep disruption for week-old memories directly
target_learners: adult learners (undergraduate and community participants aged 18-33)
target_learning_goals: declarative spatial memory for object locations
examples: The article compares a 1-hour-delay study where TMR-SD weakened spatial memories with the present 1-week-delay study where it did not, using identical procedures aside from the delay
key_sources: Nathan W. Whitmore, Erika M. Yamazaki & Ken A. Paller. (2024). Targeted memory reactivation with sleep disruption does not weaken week-old memories. npj Science of Learning 9, 64. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00276-0

article_title: Enhancing learning and retention with distinctive virtual reality environments and mental context reinstatement
citation: Joey Ka-Yee Essoe, Nicco Reggente, Ai Aileen Ohno, Younji Hera Baek, John Dell'Italia and Jesse Rissman. (2022). Enhancing learning and retention with distinctive virtual reality environments and mental context reinstatement. npj Science of Learning 7:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00147-6
title: Context-dependence harnessing account: distinctive contexts, contextual crutch, and mental reinstatement jointly optimise learning of interference-prone material
description: The article proposes that learning protocols can harness context-dependence by pairing distinctive encoding contexts with mental reinstatement at retrieval. Distinctive contexts provide unique cues bound to each information set, "reducing interference between the sets", while the "contextual crutch" phenomenon accelerates acquisition but risks context-dependent forgetting, which cued mental reinstatement mitigates because it "can be nearly as effective as physically returning to the learning context". The fMRI results supply a mechanism: neural pattern similarity to the encoding context during retrieval indexes contextually supported recall.
requirements: Participants must subjectively experience the VR-based contexts as environments they inhabit (high sense of presence) for context effects to emerge
constraints: Context-to-content relationship was arbitrary in this study; benefits were evaluated only immediately and at one week, so the time course of the advantage remains undetermined
target_learners: Adult monolingual or bilingual English speakers learning foreign vocabulary
target_learning_goals: Retention and transfer of interference-prone paired-associate material such as foreign vocabulary
examples: Participants learnt Swahili and Chinyanja words in two custom VR contexts (Fairyland Garden and Moon Base), with expanding retrieval practice and cued mental reinstatement before each recall trial
key_sources: Joey Ka-Yee Essoe, Nicco Reggente, Ai Aileen Ohno, Younji Hera Baek, John Dell'Italia and Jesse Rissman. (2022). Enhancing learning and retention with distinctive virtual reality environments and mental context reinstatement. npj Science of Learning 7:31. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00147-6

article_title: Context-based learning for Inhibition of alternative conceptions: the next step forward in science education
citation: Alexandra Renouard and Yves Mazabraud. (2018). Context-based learning for Inhibition of alternative conceptions: the next step forward in science education. npj Science of Learning 3:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0026-9
title: Interaction-centered context-based learning model for inhibiting alternative conceptions
description: The article proposes a synthetic learning model in which learning is driven by interactions between individuals and their contextual elements. Context "designates each element with which we interact specifically, such as the people around us, media, teaching and learning resources, or our living environment". Rather than the classical transformist tradition of conceptual change, the approach "focuses on the learning context rather than on conceptions themselves", aiming to act on brain inhibition processes by identifying environmental factors that impede scientific learning.
requirements: Individual contexts must be describable, requiring survey of teacher, student, media, textbook and environment interactions
constraints: The model is a proposal in a perspective article; no empirical test of the model is reported in the article
target_learning_goals: acquisition of scientific conceptions
scientific literacy
examples: The authors thank students and parents who accepted to participate to the testing of the model, though no test results are reported
key_sources: Alexandra Renouard and Yves Mazabraud. (2018). Context-based learning for Inhibition of alternative conceptions: the next step forward in science education. npj Science of Learning 3:10. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-018-0026-9

article_title: Dissipation of reactive inhibition is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements in motor sequence learning
citation: Mohan W. Gupta and Timothy C. Rickard. (2022). Dissipation of reactive inhibition is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements in motor sequence learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00140-z
title: Control for reactive inhibition when inferring offline consolidation from post-rest improvements in motor learning studies
description: Because RI builds during continuous performance and dissipates during breaks, post-rest RT improvements can be illusory learning rather than offline consolidation. The article argues RI "is clearly a necessary factor in understanding motor performance, whereas facilitating consolidation does not appear to be necessary". Studies comparing practice schedules should equate or manipulate break-to-trial ratios before attributing gains to consolidation.
requirements: Manipulation or measurement of on-task trial time and break time, as in the 2×2 design used here
constraints: Findings concern short breaks and rest periods (10–300 s); the article notes RI is a short-lasting phenomenon
target_learning_goals: accurate attribution of motor skill gains to online versus offline processes
examples: The 10 s trial, 10 s break group—analogous to groups in two recent studies—showed RI both within trial and across the rest, raising the possibility that inferred consolidation reflects solely RI dissipation
key_sources: Mohan W. Gupta and Timothy C. Rickard. (2022). Dissipation of reactive inhibition is sufficient to explain post-rest improvements in motor sequence learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00140-z

article_title: Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice
citation: Gupta, M.W., Pan, S.C., & Rickard, T.C. (2026). Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00416-8
title: Correlated-strengths account of reduced testing efficacy for highly related materials
description: The article proposes that for highly related cue–target pairs, "study and test memories are formed by partially overlapping features drawn from pre -existing semantic associations between the cue and target," so that study and test memory strengths become positively correlated across items rather than independent. This shared representational substrate is captured by a single free parameter ρ in a simulated extension of the dual-memory model. The account explains why the independent-routes model overpredicts testing efficacy for high relatedness while remaining adequate for low relatedness materials.
requirements: A sufficiently high degree of cue–target semantic relatedness so that study and test memories recruit overlapping semantic features
constraints: The article states the account is one interpretation consistent with the model; ρ acts as a scaling parameter for mean predictions, so only distribution fits are informative
It is plausible that for low relatedness pairs ρ is ≤ .1, making the extension empirically indistinguishable from the independence case there
target_learners: Adult learners studying verbal paired materials
target_learning_goals: Understanding when retrieval practice enhances long-term retention
examples: The authors predict that neural pattern similarity between study and test, and item-level embedding cosine similarity, should track the model-estimated ρ
key_sources: Gupta, M.W., Pan, S.C., & Rickard, T.C. (2026). Semantic relatedness and the efficacy of retrieval practice. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-026-00416-8

article_title: The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages
citation: Lawson, A. P., & Mayer, R. E. (2022). The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00282-y
title: Cognitive-affective model of e-learning: emotion recognition as the first link in a chain from instructor tone to learning outcome
description: The cognitive-affective model of e-learning is the authors' framework, derived from CATLM and consistent with ICAMLM, for how emotional elements in online lessons affect learners. As printed, "the model posits that learners recognize the emotional tone displayed by the instructor (i.e., first link in Fig. 3), which triggers an emotional response within the learner such as feeling the same emotion as the instructor (i.e., second link in Fig. 3)", which then primes cognitive effort and better learning outcomes. The present study tests only the first link, whether the instructor's voice alone suffices for the learner to recognize emotional tone, which the authors call crucial for initiating the chain of affective and cognitive processes.
requirements: The first link requires that emotional cues in the instructional message, such as the instructor's voice, are calibrated so learners can recognize the emotional tone
constraints: The study examined only the first link and did not examine effects on learning processes and outcomes
target_learners: adult online learners in multimedia instructional settings
target_learning_goals: recognizing the emotional tone of an instructor during online multimedia learning
key_sources: Lawson, A. P., & Mayer, R. E. (2022). The Power of Voice to Convey Emotion in Multimedia Instructional Messages. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00282-y

article_title: Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing
citation: Chih-Yueh Chou & Tak-Wai Chan. (2015). Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0083-7
title: Cognitive Load Sharing (CLS) approach for designing reciprocal tutoring systems
description: CLS is a design approach for reciprocal tutoring systems in which a complex learning task is decomposed into sub-tasks that are distributed to various agents (human students, virtual tutors or tutees) and computer scaffolding tools, so each learner focuses on an assigned sub-task while others handle the rest. The authors state its rationale is to Bdivide and conquer^ and which entails distributing sub-tasks to computer scaffolding tools or various agents. From the perspective of cognitive load theory, the objective of CLS is to alter the intrinsic cognitive load of students by adaptively dividing learning tasks among various agents.
requirements: A learning task must be analyzable and partitionable into sub-tasks that different agents can complete
constraints: The benefit of cognitive load reduced by sharing should be greater than the damage of the increased effort resulting from sharing sub-tasks and collaboration among agents
Other agents must be able to complete their sub-tasks
target_learners: Students in one-to-one classrooms learning with personal computing devices
target_learning_goals: Complex learning tasks such as solving problems and writing programs
examples: In the Distributed Reciprocal Tutoring system, a Petal-Like-System tool assisted tutees constructing recursive Lisp programs and a Diagnosis-Hint-Tree assisted tutors in locating errors and providing hints
key_sources: Chih-Yueh Chou & Tak-Wai Chan. (2015). Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0083-7

article_title: Automatic Classification of Online Discussions and Other Learning Traces to Detect Cognitive Presence
citation: Dornauer, V., Netzer, M., Kaczkó, É., Norz, L.-M., & Ammenwerth, E. (2024). Automatic Classification of Online Discussions and Other Learning Traces to Detect Cognitive Presence. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00335-4
title: Community of Inquiry framework with cognitive presence as the four-phase Practical Inquiry Model
description: The Community of Inquiry framework describes how to achieve meaningful educational experiences in collaborative online learning through three presences: cognitive, social, and teaching. Cognitive presence, developed by Garrison et al. (2001) from Dewey's Practical Inquiry Model, "comprises four phases a student goes through in the critical thinking process": triggering event, exploration, integration, and resolution. The article uses this construct as its target of automatic measurement, coding student posts into these phases to build a classifier for a future teacher dashboard.
requirements: Manual coding of posts or meaningful units into the four phases (via a CoI codebook) to ground automatic measurement
Asynchronous forum discussion data from a collaborative online course
constraints: The phases are not always sequential; students may move back and forth through them (Garrison, 2017)
Triggering events may be rare in a given course: in this study the triggering phase appeared in only one post and was excluded from analysis
target_learning_goals: critical thinking and construction of meaning through sustained reflection and discourse
examples: The study coded 1,521 meaningful units from 1,147 German-language posts into the phases to train and evaluate automatic classifiers
key_sources: Dornauer, V., Netzer, M., Kaczkó, É., Norz, L.-M., & Ammenwerth, E. (2024). Automatic Classification of Online Discussions and Other Learning Traces to Detect Cognitive Presence. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00335-4

article_title: MetaLinks: Authoring and Affordances for Conceptual and Narrative Flow in Adaptive Hyperbooks
citation: Tom Murray. (2003). MetaLinks: Authoring and Affordances for Conceptual and Narrative Flow in Adaptive Hyperbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.199-233. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197317
title: Conceptual and narrative flow as a design concern for open-ended hyperbook learning
description: The article frames hyperbook design around the problem that flexible, idiosyncratic navigation can break "conceptual and narrative flow". It treats learner reading as opportunistic and active, so the system must supply adaptive smoothing and linkage structures to keep a coherent storyline and concept structure intact across non-linear paths through richly interconnected material.
requirements: Adaptive methods and interface features such as narrative smoothing, custom depth control, and thematic links
constraints: Applies to open-ended learning environments where users navigate flexibly and idiosyncratically
target_learning_goals: sustained comprehension across non-linear navigation
examples: The article discusses a number of hyperbook design issues arising from flexible navigation through interconnected content.
key_sources: Tom Murray. (2003). MetaLinks: Authoring and Affordances for Conceptual and Narrative Flow in Adaptive Hyperbooks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 13, pp.199-233. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197317

article_title: Designing Academic Writing Analytics for Civil Law Student Self-Assessment
citation: Knight, S., Buckingham Shum, S., Ryan, P., Sándor, Á., & Wang, X. (2016). Designing Academic Writing Analytics for Civil Law Student Self-Assessment. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0121-0
title: Confusion-matrix annotation by a domain expert as a rapid parser-refinement methodology
description: A practical methodology for refining analytics tools with time-poor domain experts: the lecturer annotates AWA output pasted into Word using signal detection theory codes (True/False Positives/Negatives) in a 2×2 confusion matrix, with margin comments; the linguist responds in the shared document. The article describes this as "a rapid version of the more systematic coding that a qualitative data analyst would normally perform on a large corpus". The structured exchange builds a corpus from which precision, recall and F1 could in principle be calculated.
requirements: A domain expert willing to annotate parser output against agreed TP/FP/TN/FN codes
A familiar tool (Word) and simple 2×2 representation requiring no training
constraints: The corpus from this exercise is not yet large enough to calculate precision, recall and F1 reliably
target_learners: not applicable (methodology for analytics development teams and domain academics)
target_learning_goals: refining NLP analytics for disciplinary validity
examples: The law academic annotated essays with known grades; misclassifications were counted as another form of failure to spot an important move; the process doubled as a test of whether label names and short explanations were intuitively understandable
key_sources: Knight, S., Buckingham Shum, S., Ryan, P., Sándor, Á., & Wang, X. (2016). Designing Academic Writing Analytics for Civil Law Student Self-Assessment. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0121-0

article_title: A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management
citation: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y
title: Four event types in the competence ontology: resource use, event participation, interaction with a person, and accomplishment of an evaluation test
description: MultCComp specifies its competence-domain ontology by instantiating the Event class with the activities workers can perform to advance competences: '(1) Resource Use', '(2) Participation of Event', and '(3) Interaction with Person' with a higher-level-competence user. Because recorded activity alone cannot establish that a competence improved, a fourth instance was added: '(4) Accomplishment of Evaluation Test'. Each activity performed registers a ptrail on the worker's trail; without a passed test the proficiency level is marked as partially developed rather than developed.
requirements: Each of the five proficiency levels may have an evaluation test associated with it; a person in charge applies tests and informs grades via the Administrative Website
constraints: The authors state they 'have no concrete data to affirm that the tests will enable a viable approach' to confirm competence development, and note alternatives such as peer or supervisor review
target_learners: workers developing professional competences in organizations
target_learning_goals: validating attainment of proficiency levels in competences
examples: Interaction with Person is confirmed by asking the interacted person whether they really helped; if they respond no, the information is not registered in the trail
key_sources: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y

article_title: A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management
citation: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y
title: Trigger recommendations from context changes and always inform users when a contextualized opportunity is detected
description: MultCComp's Competences Agent triggers its recommendation capability only when one of the user's contexts changes, dividing recommendation into capabilities initiated by different perceptions (events update, resources update, locations update, profile update, competences update). The authors 'adopted this strategy because we believe that the contextualized opportunities are very dynamic and must be mapped continuously', since 'the opportunities may arise at anytime and anywhere'. When several recommendations match the same context, all options are shown so users can choose.
requirements: Continuous monitoring of context changes (events, resources, locations, profiles, competences map) feeding the agent's perceptions
constraints: The authors report applying this approach in prior context-aware systems in Commerce, Health and Education that 'received good evaluation of users' acceptance', but the article prints no direct test of this design choice in MultCComp
target_learners: mobile workers in organizations using context-aware systems
target_learning_goals: taking advantage of contextualized learning opportunities to develop competences
examples: A locations-update perception triggers filtering of users in the same location by complementary competences, messaging selected users about the newly arrived person who can assist them
key_sources: João H. Rosa, Jorge L. V. Barbosa, Marcos Kich, Lucas Brito. (2015). A Multi-Temporal Context-aware System for Competences Management. Int J Artif Intell Educ 25:455–492. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0047-y

article_title: Investigating the Effect of Agency on Learning from Worked Examples, Erroneous Examples and Problem Solving
citation: Xingliang Chen & Antonija Mitrovic & Moffat Mathews. (2019). Investigating the Effect of Agency on Learning from Worked Examples, Erroneous Examples and Problem Solving. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2019) 29:396–424. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00179-x
title: Cognitive Efficiency-based adaptive strategy for selecting preparatory learning activities in SQL-Tutor
description: The article describes an adaptive strategy that selects each preparatory task (worked example, 1- or 2-error erroneous example, problem, or skip) based on the student's Cognitive Efficiency: "CE is computed as the quotient between the problem-solving score on the most recent problem (P) and the self-reported mental effort score (R), CE = P ÷ R". Performance P is derived from constraint violations per SQL clause, and CE thresholds, combined with prior-knowledge level (LPK/HPK), determine the next preparation task. The strategy extends Kalyuga and Sweller's (2005) cognitive efficiency measure to activity selection in an ITS.
requirements: Per-problem performance scoring based on violated vs relevant constraints, and a self-reported mental effort rating after each task
constraints: Performance is computed from the first submission only, so students could ask for feedback by submitting an empty solution initially; the strategy does not consider how well the student knows each constraint
target_learners: Second-year university database students with low or high prior SQL knowledge
target_learning_goals: SQL query writing: conceptual, procedural, and debugging knowledge
examples: For HPK students CE > 1 led to skipping the preparation task; for LPK students CE below 0.25 led to a worked example
key_sources: Xingliang Chen & Antonija Mitrovic & Moffat Mathews. (2019). Investigating the Effect of Agency on Learning from Worked Examples, Erroneous Examples and Problem Solving. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2019) 29:396–424. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00179-x

article_title: Carelessness and Affect in an Intelligent Tutoring System for Mathematics
citation: Maria Ofelia Z. San Pedro, Ryan S. J. d. Baker, & Ma. Mercedes T. Rodrigo. (2014). Carelessness and Affect in an Intelligent Tutoring System for Mathematics. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0015-y
title: Contextual Slip model of carelessness within Bayesian Knowledge Tracing
description: The Contextual Slip model operationalizes carelessness as the probability that an incorrect action is a slip rather than a knowledge failure. Built on Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, it "contextually estimates the probability that a specific student action indicates a slip/carelessness, whenever the student reaches a problem step requiring a specific skill, but answers incorrectly". First-step slip estimates using future actions train a linear regression model that predicts slip in real time from action features such as action speed, help-seeking history, and p-know. The article applies it to a Cognitive Tutor for scatterplots.
requirements: Requires BKT parameter estimates per skill and log features of each student action to compute slip probabilities
constraints: First-step estimates use future information (actions N+1, N+2), making them unusable in real time; the regression approximation is needed for real-time use
target_learners: middle school and high school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: reducing careless errors in mathematics problem-solving
examples: Detectors trained per condition achieved cross-validated correlations of r=0.886 (NoScooter) and r=0.836 (Scooter) with training labels
key_sources: Maria Ofelia Z. San Pedro, Ryan S. J. d. Baker, & Ma. Mercedes T. Rodrigo. (2014). Carelessness and Affect in an Intelligent Tutoring System for Mathematics. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0015-y

article_title: BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics
citation: Dzikovska, M., Steinhauser, N., Farrow, E., Moore, J., & Campbell, G. (2014). BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24, 284–332. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0017-9
title: Conceptual change instructional approach for countering naïve science conceptions
description: The conceptual change method is a science-instruction framework the article adopts as the organizing approach for its electricity curriculum. It has two key processes: students are "presented with unavoidable and incontrovertible evidence that explicitly contradicts their existing na¨ıve conception(s)" and are then "guided just enough to allow them to generate an accurate conceptualization" of the domain. BEETLE II implements it with simulation exercises that contradict misconceptions followed by reflective dialogue, leveraging Socratic tutoring and self-explanation research.
requirements: Instruction must present evidence that directly contradicts students' existing naïve conceptions
A guided reflection stage must help students generate accurate new conceptualizations
constraints: The article applies it to the sub-topic of electricity and electric circuits
target_learners: students with no prior knowledge of electronics and electricity
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of basic electricity and electric circuits
overcoming common physics misconceptions
examples: BEETLE II curriculum exercises use varied circuit configurations designed to show that sequential circuit analysis fails and global reasoning is required
key_sources: Dzikovska, M., Steinhauser, N., Farrow, E., Moore, J., & Campbell, G. (2014). BEETLE II: Deep Natural Language Understanding and Automatic Feedback Generation for Intelligent Tutoring in Basic Electricity and Electronics. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 24, 284–332. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0017-9

article_title: Calibration Discrepancy Predicts Students’ Subsequent Metacognitive Strategy Use in Computer-based Learning Environments
citation: HaeJin Lee · Nigel Bosch. (2025). Calibration Discrepancy Predicts Students’ Subsequent Metacognitive Strategy Use in Computer-based Learning Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00514-5
title: Coherence analysis (CA) as a theory-driven measure of metacognitive strategy use from trace data
description: Coherence analysis is a method that evaluates metacognitive strategies by examining the sequential alignment of students' learning actions within online learning contexts. The article states CA "examines how learning activities are sequentially connected in a way that indicates metacognitive strategies such as self-reflection and planning". In this study, the authors use CA to quantify coherent reading (reviewing material after a quiz) and coherent quiz (preparatory engagement before a quiz) as metacognitive strategies, counting time devoted to related content within a five-minute window.
requirements: Trace data recording each interaction with timestamps at activity and page levels
A defined time window limiting the gap between learning activities (five minutes in this study)
constraints: Suited to short-term, online learning environments with constrained task scope and duration, as in this study
target_learners: College students in computer-based learning environments
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive strategy use (planning, monitoring, reflection) during self-paced learning
examples: Coherent reading was measured by summing time spent reviewing material related to missed quiz questions within five minutes after the quiz; coherent quiz summed reading-related time in the five minutes before attempting quizzes.
key_sources: HaeJin Lee · Nigel Bosch. (2025). Calibration Discrepancy Predicts Students’ Subsequent Metacognitive Strategy Use in Computer-based Learning Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00514-5

article_title: Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability
citation: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6
title: Complexity-matching framework for authoring tool usability
description: The article proposes that ITS authoring tool design should be grounded in coordinating three kinds of complexity: tool complexity, task complexity, and user complexity capacity. As the article states, "one way to do this is to match the complexity of tool design to the complexity of authoring tasks and the complexity capacity of users and user communities". This entails estimating the complexity of the mental models users must build to use a tool as intended, with the goal of designing tools that meet realistic user audiences rather than maximizing power.
requirements: Designers must estimate the complexity of the mental models a user is expected to build to use the tool as intended
constraints: The framework is explicitly exploratory and speculative; the author notes the suggestions are preliminary and many details remain to be worked out beyond the paper
target_learners: authoring tool user communities (teachers, domain experts, instructional designers, knowledge engineers)
target_learning_goals: usable design of complex educational authoring tools
key_sources: Tom Murray. (2015). Coordinating the Complexity of Tools, Tasks, and Users: On Theory-based Approaches to Authoring Tool Usability. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:37–71. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0076-6

article_title: Learning Analytics to Reveal Links Between Learning Design and Self-Regulated Learning
citation: Yizhou Fan, Wannisa Matcha, Nora’ayu Ahmad Uzir, Qiong Wang, Dragan Gašević. (2021). Learning Analytics to Reveal Links Between Learning Design and Self-Regulated Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 980–1021. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00249-z
title: Learning analytics method combining cluster analysis, process mining, and epistemic network analysis to link learning design and learning tactics
description: The article proposes "a novel learning analytic method that combines three data analytic techniques, including a cluster analysis, a process mining technique, and an epistemic network analysis". Clustering detects learning tactics within sessions using the EM algorithm; process mining examines tactic usage across sessions; ENA visualises and statistically analyses connections between tactics and learning-design units for each performance group. The combination is offered as a new methodological approach for studying links between learning design and learning tactics.
requirements: Trace data from an online learning environment, course design metadata, and performance data; a learning design that varies across units so tactic–design links can be observed
constraints: Applied to one MOOC (Flipped Classroom) with adult teacher-learners on a Chinese platform; learners active for more than three sessions and three weeks were included
target_learners: pre-service and in-service teachers in a MOOC
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
use of learning tactics aligned with learning design
examples: Applied to a flipped-classroom MOOC with 97,475 registrants, analysing 4,664,214 unique events split into 201,038 learning sessions
key_sources: Yizhou Fan, Wannisa Matcha, Nora’ayu Ahmad Uzir, Qiong Wang, Dragan Gašević. (2021). Learning Analytics to Reveal Links Between Learning Design and Self-Regulated Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 31, 980–1021. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00249-z

article_title: AI Versus Human Feedback in Mixed Reality Simulations: Comparing LLM and Expert Mentoring in Preservice Teacher Education on Controversial Issues
citation: Nygren, T., Samuelsson, M., Hansson, P.-O., Efimova, E., & Bachelder, S. (2025). AI Versus Human Feedback in Mixed Reality Simulations: Comparing LLM and Expert Mentoring in Preservice Teacher Education on Controversial Issues. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00484-8
title: Combine AI feedback with human expert insight when using AI in teacher training simulations
description: The study concludes that AI can help scale mixed reality simulations for teacher education, but AI-generated feedback should be balanced by human expertise. It finds "it should be carefully evaluated and balanced by human expertise in teacher education", since AI misses missed opportunities and contextual understanding that experts provide. AI mentoring is preferable to no feedback but should complement rather than replace expert mentoring.
requirements: AI feedback should be paired with human expert review to catch missed teaching opportunities and contextual nuances the AI does not identify
constraints: AI systems in the study did not identify missed opportunities unless directly instructed and lacked contextual understanding of preservice teachers' development
target_learning_goals: teaching controversial issues
receiving feedback on classroom discussion facilitation
examples: The study compared AI and expert feedback on the same simulation transcripts and found AI useful for structure, respect/discussion rules, and pupil misconceptions but not for missed opportunities
key_sources: Nygren, T., Samuelsson, M., Hansson, P.-O., Efimova, E., & Bachelder, S. (2025). AI Versus Human Feedback in Mixed Reality Simulations: Comparing LLM and Expert Mentoring in Preservice Teacher Education on Controversial Issues. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00484-8

article_title: Navigating the Ethical Frontier: Graduate Students’ Experiences with Generative AI-Mediated Scholarship
citation: Soroush Sabbaghan, & Sarah Elaine Eaton. (2025). Navigating the Ethical Frontier: Graduate Students' Experiences with Generative AI-Mediated Scholarship. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00454-6
title: COREI: a seven-application GenAI-powered research support suite for graduate students
description: COREI (Collaborative Research Environment and Intelligence) is a suite of seven GenAI-powered tools developed to support academic research: LEO (literature exploration and research-gap identification), NORA (research-plan guidance with pre-set methodologies), OMAR (manuscript outline generation), SARA (citation-backed literature search), VIDA (web-based information retrieval), SADI (context-aware document interaction), and CESAR (APA 7th edition-compliant copyediting). Built with Python and OpenAI's GPT-4o and deployed via Streamlit, it integrates external APIs including Elsevier Scopus, SerpAPI, and Crossref. The authors describe it as "a comprehensive suite of GenAI-powered tools developed by the first author to support various aspects of academic research."
requirements: Students must critically evaluate AI suggestions and refine them with their own expertise and judgment, as the article repeatedly states for each tool.
constraints: Pre-set methodologies in NORA are "not meant to be viewed as a one-size-fits-all solution"; automated tools like SADI and CESAR may not fully capture the nuances of documents or academic writing.
target_learning_goals: academic research skills
academic writing
literature review
examples: Participants used LEO to find research questions, OMAR for personalized suggestions, and CESAR to polish writing in APA 7th edition style, logging 13,122 total interactions across the seven applications.
key_sources: Soroush Sabbaghan, & Sarah Elaine Eaton. (2025). Navigating the Ethical Frontier: Graduate Students' Experiences with Generative AI-Mediated Scholarship. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00454-6

article_title: Fostering Transversal Skills Through Open Schooling Supported by the CARE-KNOW-DO Pedagogical Model and the UNESCO AI Competencies Framework
citation: Okada, A., Sherborne, T., Panselinas, G., & Kolionis, G. (2024). AI in Education: A Cross-National Study of Open Schooling Using the CARE-KNOW-DO Framework for Sustainable Development Goals. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-3960164/v1
title: CONNECT transversal skills self-report instrument
description: The CONNECT transversal skills instrument is a validated self-report questionnaire with a Likert scale and an open-ended question, distributed via Qualtrics. It was "validated by international educators, ensuring content, face and construct validity, with ethical adherence to the AERA, APA, and NCME standards" and met International Test Commission translation standards. The instrument produced automated, personalized feedback reports reflecting geographic, age, and gender insights.
requirements: International Test Commission translation standards for multilingual delivery
target_learners: Secondary school students aged 15 to 17 in public state schools
target_learning_goals: Assessment of transversal skills in science education
examples: Used with 330 students across the UK, Greece, and Brazil
key_sources: Okada, A., Sherborne, T., Panselinas, G., & Kolionis, G. (2024). AI in Education: A Cross-National Study of Open Schooling Using the CARE-KNOW-DO Framework for Sustainable Development Goals. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-3960164/v1

article_title: Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward
citation: McManus, M. M., & Aiken, R. M. (2015). Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 365–377. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0068-6
title: Collaborative Skills Network: mapping sentence openers to collaborative skills and subskills
description: The Collaborative Skills Network was a conceptualization of collaborative skills, their subskills, and the sentence openers that signal them, grounded in Johnson and Johnson's collaborative learning framework. As the authors explain, 'Each sentence opener in a discussion was related to a particular CL skill (Communication, Trust, Leadership and Creative Conflict) or subskill (Openness for the Communication skill) as defined by Johnson and Johnson (1991).' Selecting the opener 'I think' indicated openness of the sending subskill of communication, letting the GL Tutor interpret which skill a student was using and compare it to the optimal skills defined in the network.
requirements: Sentence openers whose association with particular skills and subskills is predefined in the network, so the tutor can trace discussion through a finite state machine
constraints: The network was operationalized through scripted, menu-driven sentence openers, a later-recognized insufficiency for identifying and guiding collaborative skills
target_learners: students working collaboratively in networked group projects
target_learning_goals: developing collaborative skills and subskills during group discussion
examples: A student's opener 'I think' was interpreted as the openness attribute of the sending subskill of the communication skill, as in 'I think that the counter needs to be set to zero.'
key_sources: McManus, M. M., & Aiken, R. M. (2015). Supporting Effective Collaboration: Using a Rearview Mirror to Look Forward. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 365–377. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0068-6

article_title: Intelligent Feedback on Hypothesis Testing
citation: Tacoma, S., Heeren, B., Jeuring, J., & Drijvers, P. (2020). Intelligent Feedback on Hypothesis Testing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00218-y
title: Combining model tracing and constraint-based modeling to generate feedback on multistep reasoning
description: This framework combines two ITS design paradigms so that constraints check the internal consistency of a (partial) solution — identifying missing elements and inconsistencies — while model-tracing elements provide hints on appropriate next steps and diagnose specific common errors via buggy rules. In this article the combination was implemented in a domain module for hypothesis testing with 36 expert rules, 16 buggy rules, and 49 constraints. The authors found "constraints to be very useful for identifying missing elements and inconsistencies in students’ solutions", while model tracing allowed addressing specific errors and providing hints. Unlike prior systems (ActiveMath, Invention Lab) where the paradigms reasoned about separate domain aspects, this design integrates them to cooperatively reason about the domain as a whole.
requirements: A domain module containing expert rules, buggy rules, and constraints, with a reasoning engine that prioritizes rules and constraints when more than one is applicable
constraints: In this implementation no distinction was made between rules following the expert strategy and rules not following it
The possibility of generating worked-out solutions was not exploited
target_learners: first-year university social sciences students in introductory statistics
target_learning_goals: carrying out hypothesis tests and understanding the logic of hypothesis testing
examples: The domain module used constraints to flag a rejection region without hypotheses, and buggy rules to distinguish a t-test for independent groups from other test-type errors
key_sources: Tacoma, S., Heeren, B., Jeuring, J., & Drijvers, P. (2020). Intelligent Feedback on Hypothesis Testing. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00218-y

article_title: Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support
citation: Rummel, N., Walker, E., & Aleven, V. (2016). Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0102-3
title: Comprehensive instructional framework for ACLS integrating collaborative learning theory, instructional theory, and instructional design principles
description: The article's central proposal is a comprehensive instructional framework, rooted in educational theory, to guide nuanced and flexible ACLS and prevent the Dystopian future. Its development "encompasses three components: 1. The integration of theories of collaborative learning to create a comprehensive framework that, alongside data-driven models, can inform support; 2.
