The derivation of principles of when, how, and what support to provide...; 3. The derivation of methods for balancing adaptivity and adaptability within support." Such a framework would orchestrate support across the multiple dimensions (timing, realm, mode, locus, target, type) in a coordinated and transparent manner, and its explainable models would underpin system transparency and shared control.
requirements: Rigorous empirical research and theory-building within each support dimension
Coordination of decision-making across all support dimensions
constraints: The authors expect that by 2040 the field will likely not yet have a comprehensive and actionable instructional framework, though substantial progress is possible
target_learning_goals: domain-level learning and learning of collaboration skills
examples: In the Utopian scenario, the framework lets the system coordinate motivational and social support (a break suggestion) with the goal of helping students progress at the domain level
key_sources: Rummel, N., Walker, E., & Aleven, V. (2016). Different Futures of Adaptive Collaborative Learning Support. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0102-3

article_title: Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations
citation: Mirko Marras, Ludovico Boratto, Guilherme Ramos, Gianni Fenu. (2022). Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00271-1
title: Fairness metric combining consistency (complement of weighted Manhattan distance) and equality (complement of Gini index) across learners
description: The paper formalizes consistency as the similarity between the targeted degree p_u(m) each platform sets for each principle m and the degree q(m) achieved in a learner's recommended list, measured as the complement of a weighted Manhattan distance. It then defines equality as "the complement of the Gini index over the consistencies across learners", where a value of 1 means the recommender is perfectly equal across learners in terms of consistency. Unlike prior individual-fairness work, learners count as positively treated when they achieve high consistency regardless of their past interactions, and no sensitive demographic attributes are used.
requirements: The targeted degree for each principle for each learner must be set by or known by the educational platform, requiring stakeholders empowered with decision-making capabilities to configure the platform
constraints: The notion assumes principles are context-sensitive and may provide different target degrees per learner or time period; quantifying student-specific target degrees from training-set preferences may be unreliable because preferences may have been biased by the recommender itself
target_learning_goals: monitoring and ensuring equality of recommended learning opportunities across learners
examples: The metric is computed locally on each ranked list so it can be optimized on a pre-computed recommended list through a post-processing function.
key_sources: Mirko Marras, Ludovico Boratto, Guilherme Ramos, Gianni Fenu. (2022). Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00271-1

article_title: Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations
citation: Mirko Marras, Ludovico Boratto, Guilherme Ramos, Gianni Fenu. (2022). Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00271-1
title: COCO educational dataset from an online course platform
description: COCO (Dessì et al., 2018) is, to the authors' knowledge, the widest educational dataset carrying all attributes required to model the proposed principles. "Collected from an online course platform, it includes 43,045 courses and 4,123,127 learners who gave 6,564,870 ratings." The authors note other educational datasets generally include only (learner, course, rating) triplets. For evaluation, a fixed-timestamp split at 2017-06-08 "led to 43,021 learners, 24,321 courses, and 529,857 interactions".
requirements: Requires course attributes such as category, last update timestamp, instructional level, enrolment counts, price, and asset types to model the principles
target_learning_goals: evaluating equality and personalization of course recommendations
examples: Used to evaluate ten recommendation algorithms and the post-processing equality approach.
key_sources: Mirko Marras, Ludovico Boratto, Guilherme Ramos, Gianni Fenu. (2022). Equality of Learning Opportunity via Individual Fairness in Personalized Recommendations. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00271-1

article_title: A Teachable Agent Game Engaging Primary School Children to Learn Arithmetic Concepts and Reasoning
citation: Pareto, L. (2014). A Teachable Agent Game Engaging Primary School Children to Learn Arithmetic Concepts and Reasoning. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0018-8
title: Teaching scheme based on cognitive-apprentice model with three scaffolding steps
description: The student tutor teaches the agent through a cognitive-apprentice model (Collins et al. 1989) with three steps: 1) show how to play while the agent observes, 2) let the agent try playing while providing corrective feedback, or 3) let the agent play by itself. These steps correspond to gradual withdrawal of support, where scaffolding is temporary and removed as the apprentice masters more of the task. This design was chosen because formulating general explanations of good choices would be too difficult for primary school students.
requirements: The tutor must have the option to show, provide corrective feedback, or step back
Scaffolding should be temporary and gradually removed
target_learning_goals: learning-by-teaching of arithmetic reasoning
examples: In try-mode the agent selects a card and the tutor has the final decision via go and stop signs; if rejected the tutor must provide an alternative card
key_sources: Pareto, L. (2014). A Teachable Agent Game Engaging Primary School Children to Learn Arithmetic Concepts and Reasoning. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0018-8

article_title: Revealing Rubric Relations: Investigating the Interdependence of a Research-Informed and a Machine Learning-Based Rubric in Assessing Student Reasoning in Chemistry
citation: Martin, P. P., Kranz, D., & Graulich, N. (2025). Revealing Rubric Relations: Investigating the Interdependence of a Research-Informed and a Machine Learning-Based Rubric in Assessing Student Reasoning in Chemistry. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 1465–1503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00440-y
title: Computational grounded theory: a three-step framework integrating unsupervised ML pattern detection, human refinement, and quantitative confirmation for rubric development
description: Computational grounded theory integrates qualitative research with computational techniques to analyze large datasets systematically for theory development, addressing grounded theory's subjective interpretation and replication difficulties. The article describes it as outlining "a three-step process to guide researchers in rubric design and application": pattern detection (unsupervised ML converts text into interpretable, data-driven categories), pattern refinement (human experts interpret and refine the data-driven categories via thematic content analysis, merging or adding categories), and pattern confirmation (computational methods such as supervised ML test reliability and generalizability). This study examines the validity of the first two steps.
requirements: Human experts must interpret the data-driven categories, since pattern detection only assigns numerical labels to responses
constraints: The article examines the validity of only the first two steps; developing an automatic ML classifier is beyond its scope
target_learning_goals: mechanistic reasoning about reaction rates in organic chemistry
examples: The authors applied HDBSCAN to extract categories from student reasoning, interpreted the categories via the concepts students integrated, and quantitatively compared the resulting rubric with a research-informed one
key_sources: Martin, P. P., Kranz, D., & Graulich, N. (2025). Revealing Rubric Relations: Investigating the Interdependence of a Research-Informed and a Machine Learning-Based Rubric in Assessing Student Reasoning in Chemistry. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 1465–1503. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00440-y

article_title: Implementing CBM: SQL-Tutor After Fifteen Years
citation: Mitrovic, A., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Implementing CBM: SQL-Tutor After Fifteen Years. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0049-9
title: Constraint-based modelling (CBM): student modelling via constraints on correct solutions
description: CBM is a student modelling approach proposed by Ohlsson as a way to overcome limitations of earlier approaches such as bug libraries. The article states that "A constraint-based tutor only needs a set of constraints that describe features of correct solutions", eliminating the need for bug libraries and for a runnable domain module. Because CBM does not require a problem solver, it "can be applied to open-ended tasks for which there is no algorithmic solution or executable expert model". SQL-Tutor was built to test whether CBM was as promising as it seemed, and the approach was later adopted by many researchers beyond the authors' group.
requirements: A set of constraints describing features of correct solutions, with relevance and satisfaction conditions
constraints: The constraint formalism is difficult to grasp and, per the authors, is the aspect of CBM most often misunderstood, including the mistaken idea of buggy constraints
target_learning_goals: SQL querying and other well-defined and ill-defined tasks modelled with constraints
examples: SQL-Tutor operationalized CBM with syntax and semantic constraints, all problem-independent, so new problems require only problem text and one correct solution
key_sources: Mitrovic, A., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Implementing CBM: SQL-Tutor After Fifteen Years. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0049-9

article_title: The Impact of Contextualized Emotions on Self-Regulated Learning and Scientific Reasoning during Learning with a Game-Based Learning Environment
citation: Michelle Taub, Robert Sawyer, James Lester, Roger Azevedo. (2019). The Impact of Contextualized Emotions on Self-Regulated Learning and Scientific Reasoning during Learning with a Game-Based Learning Environment. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00191-1
title: Contextualizing learner emotions within in-game action outcomes
description: This framework defines emotional context in terms of the outcomes of specific in-game actions rather than general session-level affect. The article states: "we define context in terms of different in-game outcomes (i.e., a relevant vs. irrelevant book for solving the mystery, a positive vs. negative scan outcome, a correct vs. incorrect final diagnosis)". Emotions are measured as duration proportions in a five-second window after feedback (or during reading) using facial detection software, then compared across positive and negative outcomes. The approach addresses prior methods (e.g., BROMP) that produced instantaneous rather than continuous measures not tied to specific gameplay events.
requirements: Facial detection software capable of continuous emotion measurement, and in-game actions that produce identifiable positive or negative feedback outcomes
constraints: The study excluded the temporal component of context and could not detect engagement or boredom due to facial-detection software restrictions, using joy as a proxy for positive state
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
scientific reasoning
microbiology content learning
examples: In CRYSTAL ISLAND, emotions were contextualized around scanning food items, reading books, and submitting diagnosis worksheets, with outcomes dichotomized as positive or negative
key_sources: Michelle Taub, Robert Sawyer, James Lester, Roger Azevedo. (2019). The Impact of Contextualized Emotions on Self-Regulated Learning and Scientific Reasoning during Learning with a Game-Based Learning Environment. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-019-00191-1

article_title: Examining the Effect of Assessment Construct Characteristics on Machine Learning Scoring of Scientific Argumentation
citation: Haudek, K. C., & Zhai, X. (2024). Examining the Effect of Assessment Construct Characteristics on Machine Learning Scoring of Scientific Argumentation. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00385-8
title: Three-dimensional framework of assessment construct characteristics for ML-based science assessment: Complexity, Diversity, and Structure
description: The article adopts and empirically tests a framework abstracting three fundamental features of the assessment construct for ML-based science assessments. "Complexity" captures the cognitive processes students must engage in, from identifying provided information to evaluating multiple pieces of data. "Diversity" reflects the combinations of different cognitive demands, specifically the number of dimensions of three-dimensional science learning engaged. "Structure" reflects cognitive developmental features, operationalized as alignment to levels of a validated learning progression for scientific argumentation. The framework was used to code 19 assessment items and examine associations with ML scoring accuracy.
requirements: Assessment items must be codable on all three dimensions by trained human raters using a defined coding scheme
constraints: The three characteristics were not independent in this sample of items (all pairwise Fisher's exact tests p < .01), preventing combination into a single statistical model
target_learning_goals: scientific argumentation competence
examples: Items were coded on all three dimensions: e.g., item S4 was coded Complexity level 4, Diversity level 3, Structure level 3; item G1 was coded level 1 on all three characteristics
key_sources: Haudek, K. C., & Zhai, X. (2024). Examining the Effect of Assessment Construct Characteristics on Machine Learning Scoring of Scientific Argumentation. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00385-8

article_title: Examining the Effect of Assessment Construct Characteristics on Machine Learning Scoring of Scientific Argumentation
citation: Haudek, K. C., & Zhai, X. (2024). Examining the Effect of Assessment Construct Characteristics on Machine Learning Scoring of Scientific Argumentation. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00385-8
title: When developing ML scoring models, consider assessment construct characteristics—particularly for higher complexity and multidimensional items
description: The article recommends that developers of ML scoring models for science assessments should attend to the Complexity, Diversity, and Structure of assessment constructs. The authors state these findings "highlight the importance of considering these construct characteristics when developing ML models for scoring assessments, particularly for higher complexity items and multidimensional assessments." Lower-level items (level 1 on any characteristic) consistently achieved substantial agreement, while higher-level items showed decreased and more variable performance.
requirements: Awareness of the cognitive complexity, number of learning dimensions, and learning progression level of assessment items before ML model development
constraints: The study used a consistent set of ML parameters across all models; tuning parameters might improve performance for mid-level constructs more than higher-level ones, as the authors note
target_learning_goals: scientific argumentation competence
examples: The study held training set size constant at 361 responses and used identical text processing parameters across all 17 models to isolate the role of construct characteristics
key_sources: Haudek, K. C., & Zhai, X. (2024). Examining the Effect of Assessment Construct Characteristics on Machine Learning Scoring of Scientific Argumentation. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00385-8

article_title: Are We There Yet? Evaluating the Effectiveness of a Recurrent Neural Network-Based Stopping Algorithm for an Adaptive Assessment
citation: Matayoshi, J., Cosyn, E., & Uzun, H. (2021). Are We There Yet? Evaluating the Effectiveness of a Recurrent Neural Network-Based Stopping Algorithm for an Adaptive Assessment. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00240-8
title: Combining deep learning with existing AIED models rather than replacing them
description: The article proposes augmenting rather than replacing established AIED models with deep learning. Rather than directly comparing RNNs with other models, the authors "are instead interested in the results when deep learning is used in combination with one of these models." Specifically, they augment the KST-powered ALEKS assessment with the classification strengths of an RNN model, motivated by evidence that deep learning models are not guaranteed to outperform existing educational models. This approach leverages the complementary strengths of knowledge-structure-based assessment and sequence-based prediction.
requirements: An existing well-vetted AIED model or system whose outputs can serve as features or targets for a deep learning component
Sufficient sequential data to train the deep learning component
constraints: The article notes deep learning models are by no means guaranteed to outperform other educational models, citing Wilson et al. (2016)
The approach is demonstrated specifically for a placement assessment where coarse category prediction suffices rather than full knowledge state identification
target_learners: post-secondary mathematics students taking placement assessments
target_learning_goals: accurate course placement recommendation
examples: The authors combine an RNN classifier with the ALEKS PPL assessment to predict final course placement from partial assessment data, enabling a stopping algorithm that reduces average assessment length by over 26%
key_sources: Matayoshi, J., Cosyn, E., & Uzun, H. (2021). Are We There Yet? Evaluating the Effectiveness of a Recurrent Neural Network-Based Stopping Algorithm for an Adaptive Assessment. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00240-8

article_title: An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments
citation: Heindrich, L., Consul, S., & Lieder, F. (2025). An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3095–3127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00493-7
title: Intelligent cognitive tutor for planning in partially observable environments
description: An intelligent tutoring system that teaches MGPO-discovered planning strategies through interactive practice with metacognitive feedback. "To teach people the planning strategies discovered by MGPO, we developed a cognitive tutor" that presents learners with highlighted planning-action choices, provides feedback on suboptimal selections with delay penalties proportional to the VOC difference, and demonstrates the optimal strategy through step-by-step videos. Unlike prior tutors using dynamic programming with cached Q-values, this tutor computes VOC values online via MGPO, enabling application to large, partially observable environments where pre-computing feedback is infeasible.
requirements: The MGPO algorithm for online VOC computation
A set of precomputed observation samples for the environment
constraints: Delay penalty uses a fixed 0.05 VOC threshold rather than exact Q-value differences
Premature termination triggers a delay penalty rather than actual termination when MGPO would continue planning
target_learning_goals: planning strategies
metacognitive skill
resource-rational information search
examples: Used in a flight-planning scenario where participants route an airplane over 60 airports, inspecting nodes to reveal stochastic observations of profitability
key_sources: Heindrich, L., Consul, S., & Lieder, F. (2025). An Intelligent Tutor for Planning in Large Partially Observable Environments. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 35, 3095–3127. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00493-7

article_title: Examinations of the relationships between self-efficacy, self-regulation, teaching, cognitive presences, and learning engagement during COVID-19
citation: Doo, M. Y., Bonk, C. J., & Heo, H. (2023). Examinations of the relationships between self-efficacy, self-regulation, teaching, cognitive presences, and learning engagement during COVID-19. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10187-3
title: Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework as organizing framework for online learning relationships
description: The study applies the community of inquiry (CoI) framework, in which learning occurs through the intersection of teaching presence, cognitive presence, and social presence. The authors define cognitive presence as "the extent to which learners are able to construct and confirm meaning through sustained reflection and discourse in a critical community of inquiry" and treat teaching presence as the "binding" element of CoI. The framework structured the study's nine hypotheses and research model.
requirements: Measurement of teaching and cognitive presence using the CoI survey instrument (Arbaugh et al., 2008)
constraints: The study focused on cognitive presence and teaching presence; social presence was not modeled
target_learners: undergraduate students in online and blended courses
target_learning_goals: constructing and confirming meaning through sustained reflection and discourse

article_title: Towards minding the disability achievement gap: the case of technology-enhanced inclusive embodied design for integer arithmetic
citation: Anton, J., Cosentino, G., Gelsomini, M., Sharma, K., Giannakos, M. N., & Abrahamson, D. (2026). Towards minding the disability achievement gap: the case of technology-enhanced inclusive embodied design for integer arithmetic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10704-0
title: Design inclusive embodied mathematics activities that coordinate egocentric action with allocentric semiotic displays
description: The article proposes that students best learn to connect traditional allocentric manipulation of symbolic forms with their own embodied egocentric experiences when their egocentric actions actively generate, inscribe, or transform their allocentric semiotic correlates on mathematical displays. Technological tools can support this integration by allowing students to perceive and track their proximal egocentric motor actions as these result in visible, distal effects on semiotic displays, fostering mathematical learning as perception–action semiosis.
requirements: Designs must provide opportunities for students to coordinate full-body egocentric experiences with typical, allocentric classroom tasks
constraints: The article notes the design poses challenges for scaling to full-class instruction in its current individual-usage form
target_learners: middle-school students with and without disabilities
target_learning_goals: grounding integer arithmetic procedures in embodied experience
examples: Students walked a floor-projected number line while a wall-projected avatar concurrently mimicked their actions, providing an allocentric depiction of their egocentric movements
key_sources: Anton, J., Cosentino, G., Gelsomini, M., Sharma, K., Giannakos, M. N., & Abrahamson, D. (2026). Towards minding the disability achievement gap: the case of technology-enhanced inclusive embodied design for integer arithmetic. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10704-0

article_title: The positivity principle: do positive instructors improve learning from video lectures?
citation: Lawson, A. P., Mayer, R. E., Adamo-Villani, N., Benes, B., Lei, X., & Cheng, J. (2021). The positivity principle: do positive instructors improve learning from video lectures? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10057-w
title: The cognitive-affective model of e-learning: a four-step model linking instructor emotion to learning outcomes.
description: The cognitive-affective model of e-learning proposes that "there are 4 steps that lead from the emotion displayed by an instructor to an effect on learning outcome." First the learner recognizes the instructor's emotional stance (step 1), then feels a social partnership with the instructor (step 2), then works hard to learn the lesson (step 3), and thus performs better on learning outcome tests (step 4). The article describes it as a set of to-be-tested steps rather than an established set of findings.
requirements: The instructor must display a positive emotion during the lesson as the model's first step.
constraints: The authors acknowledge affective interactions between student and teacher are more complex than this linear model, and the study is a preliminary step in establishing basic relations.
target_learners: university students learning from video lectures
target_learning_goals: improved learning outcomes from computer-based instruction
key_sources: Lawson, A. P., Mayer, R. E., Adamo-Villani, N., Benes, B., Lei, X., & Cheng, J. (2021). The positivity principle: do positive instructors improve learning from video lectures? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10057-w

article_title: The positivity principle: do positive instructors improve learning from video lectures?
citation: Lawson, A. P., Mayer, R. E., Adamo-Villani, N., Benes, B., Lei, X., & Cheng, J. (2021). The positivity principle: do positive instructors improve learning from video lectures? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10057-w
title: Adapted core-affect framework: instructor emotions classified along valence and activity dimensions.
description: The study adapts Russell's model of core affect, which displays "two orthogonal dimensions: valence (which runs from positive to nega- tive) and arousal, or what we have called activity (which runs from active to passive)." These dimensions create four quadrants represented as happy (positive/active), content (positive/passive), frustrated (negative/active), and bored (negative/passive), which are the four emotions displayed by instructors in the study's videos.
requirements: Emotions must be portrayed so learners can perceive differences along both the valence and activity dimensions.
constraints: The authors prefer the term activity over arousal because they focus on the instructor's portrayed emotion; cultural background can affect how learners interpret displayed emotion, which the study did not address.
target_learning_goals: recognizing instructor emotional tone during video lectures
key_sources: Lawson, A. P., Mayer, R. E., Adamo-Villani, N., Benes, B., Lei, X., & Cheng, J. (2021). The positivity principle: do positive instructors improve learning from video lectures? Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10057-w

article_title: Context and agency: complementarity and interactivity
citation: Elen, J. (2021). Context and agency: complementarity and interactivity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09850-w
title: Context and agency as complementary and interacting perspectives on educational technology research
description: In this reaction to Joo, Kim and Kim's study of mobile learning management system use, Elen argues that "their study can be approached from to complementary and interacting perspectives: context and agency." The framework treats contextual factors and learner agency as two lenses that jointly explain technology use rather than competing accounts. It is offered as a way of interpreting research on technology acceptance and continuance intention in learning settings.
requirements: Research on technology use in learning should be interpreted through both contextual and agency perspectives
target_learning_goals: use of mobile learning management systems
examples: The reaction reads Joo, Kim and Kim's finding that perceived usefulness plays a pivotal role in m-LMS use through the lenses of context and agency
key_sources: Elen, J. (2021). Context and agency: complementarity and interactivity. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09850-w

article_title: The effect of programming on primary school students’ mathematical and scientific understanding: educational use of mBot
citation: Sáez-López, J.-M., Sevillano-García, M.-L., & Vazquez-Cano, E. (2019). The effect of programming on primary school students’ mathematical and scientific understanding: educational use of mBot. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 1405–1425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09648-5
title: Constructionist rationale for robotics and programming in primary education
description: The article grounds its design in Papert's constructionist theory, which "holds that when children work with materials that allow them to design and construct meaningful artifacts, they learn better", alongside meaningful learning and sociocultural-constructivist foundations. Learning occurs through creating and sharing meaningful artifacts with tools such as robots and computers, in opposition to passive instruction. This frames the project-based, learning-by-doing activities with the mBot.
requirements: Active methodologies and student participation rather than traditional passive instruction
constraints: The authors note robotics have not been found to statistically improve academic outcomes in some prior work (Fagin and Merkle 2003)
target_learning_goals: computational thinking
problem solving and logical-mathematical understanding
examples: mBot activities in which students program motion and sensors within math and science didactic units
key_sources: Sáez-López, J.-M., Sevillano-García, M.-L., & Vazquez-Cano, E. (2019). The effect of programming on primary school students’ mathematical and scientific understanding: educational use of mBot. Education Tech Research Dev, 67, 1405–1425. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09648-5

article_title: Promoting preservice teachers’ multiperspective professional vision in virtual learning environments – On the effects of modeling videos and prompts during video-based lesson analysis
citation: Janeczko, J. M., Lehmkuhl, A., Junker, R., Zucker, V., Meschede, N., & Holodynski, M. (2026). Promoting preservice teachers' multiperspective professional vision in virtual learning environments – On the effects of modeling videos and prompts during video-based lesson analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10546-2
title: Cognitive apprenticeship approach as a didactic framework for designing digital support tools in video-based learning
description: The article draws on the cognitive apprenticeship approach, which focuses on learning through guided experience and describes support activities including modeling, scaffolding, and coaching. Modeling means that an expert performs an exemplary task while verbalizing their perceptions, thoughts, and strategies. Scaffolding and coaching can be embodied in prompts that stimulate cognitive, metacognitive, volitional, or cooperative activities during learning.
requirements: Support tools derived from this approach must be designed according to multimedia learning principles to avoid increasing extraneous cognitive load.
constraints: Scaffolding types with high levels of guidance, such as modeling, are particularly effective for less advanced learners, and combined scaffolds may not be supportive for everyone.
target_learners: preservice teachers with diverse entry levels
target_learning_goals: effective video-based lesson analysis
examples: The study implemented modeling videos showing an expert's screencast thinking aloud during video analysis, and written prompts guiding planning and conducting of analyses.
key_sources: Janeczko, J. M., Lehmkuhl, A., Junker, R., Zucker, V., Meschede, N., & Holodynski, M. (2026). Promoting preservice teachers' multiperspective professional vision in virtual learning environments – On the effects of modeling videos and prompts during video-based lesson analysis. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10546-2

article_title: The crucial role of theoretical scholarship for learning design and technology
citation: Richard E. West, Peg Ertmer, Susan McKenney. (2020). The crucial role of theoretical scholarship for learning design and technology. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09770-9
title: Communities of engagement framework for online learning
description: The final special-issue paper by Borup, Graham, West, Archambault, and Spring presents a communities of engagement framework. The editorial describes it as "a collection of ideas and principles that explain how students engage affectively, behaviorally, and cognitively in online learning environments". The framework also describes the roles that various actors within students' personal and course communities play in increasing students' engagement and learning, making it a framework for understanding and supporting online student engagement.
requirements: Actors within students' personal and course communities are understood as playing roles in engagement
constraints: The framework is presented in the context of online learning environments
target_learning_goals: affective, behavioral, and cognitive engagement in online learning
examples: The editorial describes the framework as explaining how students engage in online environments and the roles various actors play in increasing engagement and learning
key_sources: Richard E. West, Peg Ertmer, Susan McKenney. (2020). The crucial role of theoretical scholarship for learning design and technology. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09770-9

article_title: Analyzing learners’ engagement and behavior in MOOCs on programming with the Codeboard IDE
citation: Gallego-Romero, J.M., Alario-Hoyos, C., Estévez-Ayres, I. et al. (2020). Analyzing learners' engagement and behavior in MOOCs on programming with the Codeboard IDE. Education Tech Research Dev 68, 2505–2528 (2020). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09773-6
title: Codeboard web-based IDE integrated into MOOCs via IMS LTI
description: Codeboard is an open-source, web-based development environment that lets learners "code directly in Codeboard without installing any additional software locally", supporting multiple languages (Java, C, C++, Python). Teachers provide base code and test cases; activities integrate into MOOC learning sequences through the IMS LTI standard and scale to thousands of concurrent learners. In this study a modified local instance collected compilation, execution, access and code data across 117 activities in three Java MOOCs on edX.
requirements: A local installation with code modifications is needed for low-level data collection, as Codeboard has no API for data collection
IMS LTI support in both platform and tool for seamless integration
constraints: Activity logs originally lack compilation/execution results, requiring an added description field
target_learners: MOOC learners on introductory Java programming
target_learning_goals: Learning-by-doing programming skills in Java
examples: Three 5-week Java MOOCs on edX used 38, 25 and 54 Codeboard activities respectively, all formative, with base code and weekly solutions provided
key_sources: Gallego-Romero, J.M., Alario-Hoyos, C., Estévez-Ayres, I. et al. (2020). Analyzing learners' engagement and behavior in MOOCs on programming with the Codeboard IDE. Education Tech Research Dev 68, 2505–2528 (2020). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09773-6

article_title: Concept-guided development of technology in ‘traditional’ and ‘innovative’ schools: quantitative and qualitative differences in technology integration
citation: Sandra de Koster, Monique Volman, Els Kuiper. (2017). Concept-guided development of technology in 'traditional' and 'innovative' schools: quantitative and qualitative differences in technology integration. Education Tech Research Dev 65:1325–1344. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9527-0
title: Concept-guided development of technology use: a pedagogy-driven approach taking the school's educational concept as the starting point for developing technology use
description: The article proposes concept-guided development of technology use, in which school teams develop and implement forms of technology use in line with the school's educational concept, encompassing both pedagogical practices and the beliefs and perspectives motivating them. It is "a pedagogy-driven approach that aims to promote this ﬁt" between proposed technology use and the school's educational concept. The approach calls for a definition of technology integration that gives room to a variety of educational concepts and encompasses teachers' perceptions, so that integration depends on fit with existing or desired classroom practices rather than on the school's pedagogy type.
requirements: A team of teachers supported to reflect on the school's educational concept and design learning arrangements as they see best fit
A definition of technology integration that encompasses the perceptions of the teachers who carry out the concepts
constraints: The labeling of school types as 'traditional' or 'innovative' is indicative rather than conclusive
To what extent achieved integration can be attributed to the approach cannot be concluded from the exploratory study
target_learning_goals: integration of technology use into classroom practice in line with the school's educational concept
examples: Five Dutch primary schools each designed and realized up to four technology-supported learning arrangements over two school years, coached by external educational counsellors
key_sources: Sandra de Koster, Monique Volman, Els Kuiper. (2017). Concept-guided development of technology in 'traditional' and 'innovative' schools: quantitative and qualitative differences in technology integration. Education Tech Research Dev 65:1325–1344. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9527-0

article_title: Contextualized-OLPC education project in rural India: measuring learning impact and mediation of computer self-efficacy
citation: Ale, K., Loh, Y. A.-C., & Chib, A. (2017). Contextualized-OLPC education project in rural India: measuring learning impact and mediation of computer self-efficacy. Education Tech Research Dev, 65, 769–794. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-017-9517-2
title: Contextualized-OLPC education project in rural India
description: A technology-implementation project in which OLPC laptops were introduced in nine rural Indian primary schools within a longitudinal quasi-experimental design (test n = 126, control n = 79) with pre- and post-experiment measures. The project "utilized strategies identified by the Technology-Community-Management model to address contextually germane factors of teacher training, unbiased gender access, and local language use."
requirements: Strategies from the Technology-Community-Management model addressing teacher training, unbiased gender access, and local language use.
constraints: Evaluated in rural Indian primary school contexts; the article does not claim generalizability beyond that setting.
target_learners: rural primary school students in India
target_learning_goals: technological literacy
functional literacy

description: The editorial identifies control-value theory of achievement emotions as the strong theoretical framework adopted by the Jarrell et al. (2017) study of medical students' emotions in computer-based learning environments. It frames emotions as theoretically and empirically linked to engagement and learning outcomes across many domains and settings. The theory anchors the special issue's call to explore whether emotions are malleable factors that can be harnessed to support engagement, persistence, and achievement.

article_title: The influence of pre-reading purpose and extra-textual networks with summary writing on multiple document concept network integration: a replication of Wei et al. (2024)
citation: Ziqian Wei, Shuting Yin, Roy B. Clariana, Xuqian Chen. (2025). The influence of pre-reading purpose and extra-textual networks with summary writing on multiple document concept network integration: a replication of Wei et al. (2024). Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10508-8
title: Concept network analysis as a measure of multiple document integration quantity and quality
description: The article describes concept network analysis (aka knowledge structure analysis) as a method for measuring multiple document integration by converting students' learning products, such as summary essays, into networks with nodes representing core concepts and edges representing semantic relationships. Quantity of integration is the proportion of integrative links, semantic quality is the similarity of integrative links to an expert referent network, and structural quality is graph centrality similarity (GCsim) to the expert network form. The article uses this approach to evaluate how reading purpose and expert networks influence integration.
requirements: Essays must be converted to concept networks using ALA and the Pathfinder network algorithm with pre-selected core concepts
constraints: The requirement of the similarity of integrative links might be too stringent for many reasons, for example, due to issues such as using different terms for the same concept across documents
target_learning_goals: multiple document comprehension and integration

article_title: Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research
citation: Weidlich, J., Hicks, B., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10241-0
title: Control for confounders but not for mediators or colliders
description: The paper derives three configuration-specific recommendations: for a fork (confounder), "control for Z"; for a chain (mediator), "do not control for Z" because doing so blocks the causal pathway and induces overcontrol bias; and for an inverted fork (collider), "do not control for Z" because conditioning opens a spurious path and induces endogenous selection bias. These rules follow directly from the graphical structure of each configuration.
requirements: Researchers must classify each third variable as a confounder, mediator, or collider within the assumed DAG before deciding whether to adjust for it.
constraints: The recommendations hold only under the assumed causal structure; if the true graph differs, the classification and the resulting adjustment decision may be wrong.
target_learning_goals: choosing covariates for statistical adjustment
avoiding overcontrol and collider bias
examples: The paper's mediator example shows that controlling for a mediator blocks the path X → Z → Y and can yield a false-negative; its collider example shows that conditioning on a collider opens the path X ← Z → Y and can yield a false-positive.
key_sources: Weidlich, J., Hicks, B., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Causal reasoning with causal graphs in educational technology research. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10241-0

article_title: Can videos affect learning outcomes? Evidence from an actual learning environment
citation: Tani, M., Manuguerra, M., & Khan, S. (2022). Can videos affect learning outcomes? Evidence from an actual learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10147-3
title: Cognitive load theory as a framework for multimedia learning effects
description: The article uses cognitive load theory to explain how multimedia presentations affect knowledge acquisition. Its tenets include that "learners can only process a limited amount at any one time" and that learners handle knowledge construction "through at least two processors, depending on whether the form of representation is verbal or pictorial". Offloading cognitive demands via cues such as textbooks, instructor feedback, and multimedia is associated with better retention and transfer, freeing capacity to detect distinctions and coordinate ideas with evidence.
requirements: Materials should be designed with instructor awareness of "the impacts of instructional tasks on students' cognitive load".
constraints: The theory's basic model has remained constant for 20 years, with emphasis shifting toward cognitive processes and longer-term outcomes.
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of declarative, conceptual, procedural, and evaluative knowledge

article_title: Cheating in the second year of generative AI chatbots: a follow-up study on high school student cheating behaviors
citation: Ruishi Chen, Victor R. Lee, Annie Camey Kuo, Denise Clark Pope, Sarah Miles. (2026). Cheating in the second year of generative AI chatbots: a follow-up study on high school student cheating behaviors. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10587-1
title: Academic integrity as a long-standing coevolutionary negotiation between student practices and educator expectations, with generative AI as a new iteration rather than a new pattern
description: The article frames cheating not as a new AI-driven phenomenon but as part of a "long-standing coevolutionary pattern in education, in which students continually explore new ways to gain academic advantage while educators respond by developing new norms, policies, and instructional strategies to maintain academic integrity." Under this lens, generative AI represents "a new iteration of an ongoing negotiation between students' practices and educators' expectations" rather than a novel form of dishonesty. The framework draws on prior scholarship (McCabe et al., 2001; Whitley, 1998; Stephens & Wangaard, 2013) and is used to interpret the finding that cheating rates remained stable while AI use grew.
requirements: Self-report survey instrumentation that tracks specific dishonest behaviors over time, enabling comparison against historical baselines
constraints: The article notes specific technologies change over time, so the framework addresses the general negotiation pattern rather than predicting effects of any single technology
target_learning_goals: academic integrity
appropriate technology use norms
examples: The authors apply this lens to interpret stable cheating rates alongside increasing AI chatbot exposure and use in the 2023-24 survey

article_title: Supporting children’s engagement through learning experience design, situational interest, and user experience: implementing a blended learning math experience in the classroom

Supporting children's engagement through learning experience design, situational interest, and user experience: implementing a blended learning math experience in the classroom. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10637-8
title: Cognitive apprenticeship model combined with Mayer's multimedia learning principles as the pedagogical basis of the video-based blended lesson
description: The article describes the cognitive apprenticeship model (CAM) as founded on the principle that learning is best achieved through active engagement and practical application, with key components of "content knowledge, modeling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, and exploration". Pre-recorded videos of authentic math lessons taught in a real classroom embed these CAM elements. The authors also adopted Mayer's multimedia learning principles—segmenting, coherence, signaling, and pre-training—integrated throughout the video design to enhance comprehension and retention.
requirements: Videos must reflect a realistic classroom context capturing natural student-teacher interactions to embed CAM elements
constraints: The article states the synergy between CAM and Mayer's multimedia principles was applied specifically to the video-based blended learning approach for classroom settings
target_learning_goals: proportional reasoning strategies
flexible use of multiple solution strategies
examples: An hour-long video lesson was segmented into ten parts, and students engaged in embedded practice problems with worked examples and free-response reflection questions

citation: Kosmas, P., Nisiforou, E. A., Kounnapi, E., Sophocleous, S., & Theophanous, G. (2025). Integrating artificial intelligence in literacy lessons for elementary classrooms: a co-design approach. Education Tech Research Dev (2025) 73:2589–2615. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10492-z
title: Co-designed AI-integrated literacy lesson plans with three AI tool categories
description: Three co-created lesson plans for grades 1–2, 3–4, and 5–6 on the curriculum theme "The Summer", each integrating at least three AI tools drawn from three categories: text tools (ChatGPT, Gemini), image tools (Copilot, Ideogram, Muse.ai), and video tools (VideoGen, Fliki, Invideo AI). The article states that "Tools like ChatGPT are used to create, edit, and summarise text so that students can compare it with their "humanised" texts and identify language errors", image tools let students "create images based on their texts", and video tools support collaborative video creation and discussion. Each plan follows a standardized, adaptable structure with learning objectives, brainstorming, hands-on AI tasks, differentiation options, and assessment.

At least three different AI tools integrated per lesson plan
Alignment with the national elementary curriculum

Designed for Greek language literacy in elementary grades 1–6

Writing, reading, and speaking skills
Familiarity with AI concepts

citation: Kosmas, P., Nisiforou, E. A., Kounnapi, E., Sophocleous, S., & Theophanous, G. (2025). Integrating artificial intelligence in literacy lessons for elementary classrooms: a co-design approach. Education Tech Research Dev (2025) 73:2589–2615. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10492-z
title: Use a co-design approach with teachers and researchers to develop AI-integrated classroom materials
description: The article advocates involving in-service teachers collaboratively with researchers to design AI-integrated learning materials, so that deliverables are innovative and tailored to students' needs. It states that "The co-design method in educational settings and environments provides a valuable framework for teachers and researchers to promote the sharing of knowledge, fruitful collaboration, and foster innovation". In this study the method was implemented as a six-hour workshop with presentations, group discussions, and hands-on AI tool practice, followed by classroom piloting and reflection.

Researcher facilitation with guidelines, sample lesson plans, and practical AI tool information
Sufficient workshop time for discussion and feedback exchange

24% of teachers needed more time to practice and understand the AI tools

Teacher professional development in AI use

citation: Zhai, X. (2021). Advancing automatic guidance in virtual science inquiry: from ease of use to personalization. Education Tech Research Dev, 69, 255–258. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09917-8
title: CoSIL with appropriate guidance as an approach for shifting science education to digital when in-person schooling is not viable
description: Computer-supported inquiry learning (CoSIL) with appropriate guidance is presented as an approach for moving science education online when in-person schooling is not viable, as highlighted by COVID-19. The author writes that "one approach to facilitate this shift, as reviewed by Zacharia et al. (2015), is to involve students in computer supported inquiry learning (CoSIL) with appropriate guidance." With knowledge of guidance forms and efficacy across inquiry phases, educators may "develop decent guidance so that students can experience scientific inquiry virtually as they used to do in-person."

article_title: Shifting digital, shifting context: (re)considering teacher professional development for online and blended learning in the COVID-19 era
citation: Barbara B. Lockee. (2021). Shifting digital, shifting context: (re)considering teacher professional development for online and blended learning in the COVID-19 era. Education Tech Research Dev 69. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09836-8
title: Context as a multilevel body of factors embedding learning and performance
description: The article invokes Tessmer and Richey's (1997) account of context as central to designing learning solutions including TPD for OBL: "Context is then a multilevel body of factors in which learning and performance are embedded." These factors' physical, social, and instructional aspects interplay to influence learning. The author uses this account to argue that the unprecedented pandemic context—mandated digital shift, changed logistics, and teacher emotion—must be considered when applying or extending the Philipsen et al. TPD framework.
requirements: Design of learning solutions, including TPD for OBL, must acknowledge the existing context regarding OBL
constraints: The framework's factors were ascertained from pre-pandemic studies, so context-dependent needs may differ under mandated crisis shifts
target_learning_goals: understanding how contextual factors shape teacher professional development for online and blended learning
examples: The author applies the context account to argue that educators' unprecedented, no-choice shift to digital introduced new influencing factors for TPD for OBL needs

article_title: An investigation of blended learning to support reading instruction in elementary schools
citation: Paul Macaruso, Shani Wilkes, Jen Elise Prescott. (2020). An investigation of blended learning to support reading instruction in elementary schools. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09785-2

Teachers use real-time performance data from the digital component to provide individualized instruction targeting skill gaps, which the article links to promising results for at-risk students. In this study, teachers were encouraged to track daily online progress via an implementation dashboard and deliver Lexia Lessons to small groups accordingly.

constraints: The article notes control schools used digital technology in a less integrated way, and the study did not probe which program elements contributed to gains
target_learners: elementary school students, including at-risk students experiencing early literacy struggles
target_learning_goals: reading development and closing skill gaps in early literacy
examples: Lexia Lessons were typically administered by the teacher to a small group as a center activity in the ELA block or by an interventionist in a pull-out session

title: Coach roles of coordinator, facilitator, and curator in video coaching for ECTs
description: The article distinguishes three roles for coaches supporting early career teachers, plus the learner role. "The coordinator is responsible for organizing learning opportunities and determines the appropriate task complexity." The facilitator stimulates learning, scaffolds support, prompts thinking, and provides cognitive feedback. The curator "is responsible for selecting relevant and high-quality learning materials and determines the authenticity of the task". Learners manage their own learning behavior and may act as co-facilitators.

Coordination among the three roles so tasks, support, and materials align

article_title: Improving metacognition through self-explication in a digital self-regulated learning tool
citation: Eelco Braad, Nick Degens, Wolmet Barendregt, Wijnand IJsselsteijn. (2022). Improving metacognition through self-explication in a digital self-regulated learning tool. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10156-2
title: Conceptual model of metacognition during self-regulated learning combining SRL phases with five facets of learning
description: The article derives a conceptual model of metacognition during SRL from the COPES model (Winne & Hadwin, 1998), combining the preparatory, performance, and appraisal phases with five facets: conditions, operations, (meta)cognitive products, evaluations, and standards. It defines two adaptation routes: "metacognitive monitoring and control lead to adaptations of the current task definition, goals and performance expectations, and plans (local update)" and reflection leading to a global update of metacognitive knowledge. The model structures the tool's design rationale of encouraging informed local and global updates via self-explication.

constraints: The model is a metacognitive perspective that the article says must be seen within the broader construct of SRL
target_learning_goals: metacognitive knowledge and skills for self-regulated learning
examples: The tool's five prompt categories (ideas about learning, goals, plans, checks, improvements) map onto the model's phases and facets
