article_title: Role of organisational readiness and stakeholder acceptance: an implementation framework of adaptive learning for higher education
citation: Mirata, V., & Bergamin, P. (2023). Role of organisational readiness and stakeholder acceptance: an implementation framework of adaptive learning for higher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10248-7
title: Build stakeholder acceptance of adaptive learning by communicating its advantages and presenting evidence-based results
description: Because acceptability by all stakeholders was the most frequently mentioned outcome and was strongly connected to recognition of adaptive learning's advantages, the article supports communicating advantages and presenting evidence-based results as implementation strategies. Participants suggested "the communication of the advantages and presentation of evidence-based results on the influence of adaptive learning on the success and drop-out rate of students and the satisfaction of stakeholders" as the most effective strategies, alongside didactically sound course design, skilled staff, and favourable working conditions.
requirements: Strategies must address the determinant of insufficient recognition of the advantages of adaptive learning for students, instructors, and the institution
constraints: The connection was identified from qualitative expert statements, particularly salient for the Swiss university panel
target_learning_goals: stakeholder acceptability of adaptive learning
scaled implementation of adaptive learning
examples: The implementation team communicates the advantages and added value of adaptive learning among all stakeholders, and the research team presents intermediate research results demonstrating effects on student success, dropouts, satisfaction, and inclusiveness
key_sources: Mirata, V., & Bergamin, P. (2023). Role of organisational readiness and stakeholder acceptance: an implementation framework of adaptive learning for higher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10248-7

article_title: Towards emotion awareness tools to support emotion and appraisal regulation in academic contexts
citation: Elise Lavoué, Maedeh Kazemitabar, Tenzin Doleck, Susanne P. Lajoie, Rubiela Carrillo, et al.. (2019). Towards emotion awareness tools to support emotion and appraisal regulation in academic contexts. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09688-x
title: Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions as an analytic framework for emotion awareness data
description: The study uses Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions as the framework for a quantitative descriptive analysis of students' retrospective emotion interviews. The abstract states: "A quantitative descriptive analysis of these retrospective interviews was conducted based on Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions." Within this framework, transcripts are coded along three axes: the focus of emotions, the causes students attribute, and their appraisals of value and control. The theory thus organizes both the emotional experience and the situational appraisals that antecede it.
requirements: Student emotion reports (transcripts of retrospective interviews) to code
constraints: Applied to university-level academic emotion episodes in this study
target_learning_goals: understanding achievement emotions
appraisal of value and control in learning situations
examples: Student transcripts were coded for emotion focus, attributed causes, and value/control appraisals
key_sources: Elise Lavoué, Maedeh Kazemitabar, Tenzin Doleck, Susanne P. Lajoie, Rubiela Carrillo, et al.. (2019). Towards emotion awareness tools to support emotion and appraisal regulation in academic contexts. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09688-x

article_title: Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach
citation: Susan Verbunt-Janssen, Carolien A. N. Knoop-van Campen, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar. (2026). Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10632-z
title: COPES model of self-regulated learning as the organizing framework for SRL teacher dashboard indicators
description: The COPES model (Winne & Hadwin, 1998) frames SRL as unfolding in four phases: task definition, goal setting, enactment, and adaptation. The article states "in the enactment phase, students execute their plans, monitor, and control their progress". The study used COPES as the theory-driven coding scheme for focus group data, compared teacher-generated indicators against it to identify gaps, and structured the dashboard prototype's widgets around its phases.
requirements: Metacognitive indicators must be mapped to specific COPES phases to structure dashboard information
constraints: Teachers in this study did not spontaneously mention task definition indicators, creating a gap between teacher needs and the theory-based indicator set
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognition
examples: The prototype dashboard has five widgets, one per COPES phase, including a task definition widget with prior knowledge and motivation indicators teachers did not request
key_sources: Susan Verbunt-Janssen, Carolien A. N. Knoop-van Campen, Martine Baars, Inge Molenaar. (2026). Teacher dashboard design for self-regulated learning: a participatory approach. Educational technology research and development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10632-z

article_title: Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses
citation: Poquet, O., Trenholm, S., & Santolini, M. (2024). Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10262-9
title: Design forum tasks that combine individual participation and interactivity to create conditions for learner relationship formation
description: The article's synthesis argues that forum designs eliciting both individual posting and engagement with others were most likely to foster relational structures. It reports that "courses with high participation and high interactivity were more likely to create conditions for relationship formation among learners," whereas courses focusing only on interactivity without individual participation were less successful at developing relational structures. The principle guides instructors choosing forum task designs when relationship formation is a goal.
requirements: Forum tasks must elicit both individual participation and engagement with others
constraints: Inference rests on log data without self-reports to verify whether frequent pairs experienced social presence
Only one course (D, with fixed small groups and weekly group tasks) showed the full group-formation pattern
target_learners: university students in online and blended courses
target_learning_goals: relationship formation among learners
participation in discussion forums
examples: Course D assigned learners to fixed small groups with weekly group tasks and showed the highest participation, interactivity, and the only significant Simmelian-tie pattern
key_sources: Poquet, O., Trenholm, S., & Santolini, M. (2024). Forum posts, communication patterns, and relational structures: A multi-level view of discussions in online courses. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10262-9

article_title: Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age
citation: Joke Voogt, Gerald Knezek. (2021). Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09985-4
title: Connected learning reframes learning in the digital age through self-driven action across formal and non-formal contexts
description: Prestridge and colleagues describe connected learning environments facilitated by digital technologies. Core to connected learning is that it "emphasizes self-driven actions and interactions for learning with a diversity of (digital) tools, people and ways of knowing." It spans formal and non-formal contexts and is examined through three concepts: open and bounded context, prescribed and emergent curriculum, and the rise of a new class of influencer.
requirements: Diversity of digital tools, people and ways of knowing for self-driven learning
constraints: Complexities around open versus bounded contexts and prescribed versus emergent curriculum
target_learners: learners in formal and non-formal digital contexts
target_learning_goals: self-driven learning in the digital age
examples: The authors envision connected learning as a new alignment for learning in the digital age
key_sources: Joke Voogt, Gerald Knezek. (2021). Learners and learning contexts: international perspectives on new alignments for the digital age. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-09985-4

article_title: Linking self-regulated learning to community of inquiry in online undergraduate courses: A person-centered approach
citation: Chungsoo Na, Soojeong Jeong, Jody Clarke-Midura, Youngin Shin. (2024). Linking self-regulated learning to community of inquiry in online undergraduate courses: A person-centered approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10380-y
title: Extended Community of Inquiry framework incorporating self-regulated learning as a learning presence
description: The article extends the CoI framework (social, cognitive, teaching presence) by situating SRL as a fourth, 'learning presence' construct, following Shea and Bidjerano (2010). In the extended conceptual model, SRL comprises seven sub-constructs including goal setting, environmental structuring, task strategies, help-seeking, time management, and two forms of self-evaluation, and is hypothesized to relate to all three original presences. The study's empirical findings support that 'SRL skills as a learning presence are critical components under the framework of the community of inquiry.'
requirements: Empirical measurement of SRL strategy use (e.g., OSLQ) alongside CoI perceptions to test the extended model
constraints: Theoretical controversy on integrating a new presence into CoI still exists (Akyol & Garrison, 2011a; Garrison & Akyol, 2013), as the article notes
target_learners: undergraduate students in online higher education courses
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning strategy use
online learning engagement and perceived presence
examples: The study tested the extended model with 750 undergraduates in an online introductory mathematics course using latent profile analysis and MANOVA
key_sources: Chungsoo Na, Soojeong Jeong, Jody Clarke-Midura, Youngin Shin. (2024). Linking self-regulated learning to community of inquiry in online undergraduate courses: A person-centered approach. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10380-y

article_title: Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners
citation: Ding, S. L., & Chew, E. (2019). Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09651-w
title: Adapt feedback modes and strategies to learners' cultural, educational and personality differences rather than assuming one strategy fits all
description: The article argues that because learners differ in cultural background, educational history and personality (e.g., introversion), educators should be context-sensitive when choosing feedback modes. It states: "Strategies need to be adapted for different learn ers in various learning situations" and that "no one strategy is applicable to all learners". The study's metaphoric method itself exemplifies adapting elicitation to restrained expressers.
requirements: Educators need to build their skills and be flexible and open-minded, and academic training should attend to student differences, learning outcomes, and contextual realities
constraints: Findings from a Confucian-influenced background may not be applicable to learners from different backgrounds, per the authors' own limitation
target_learners: introverted or culturally reticent higher-education language learners
target_learning_goals: effective uptake of feedback on second-language writing
examples: The study used metaphoric elicitation in Mandarin instead of direct questioning because participants were restrained in open expression; online feedback was chosen to avoid public embarrassment.
key_sources: Ding, S. L., & Chew, E. (2019). Thy word is a lamp unto my feet: A study via metaphoric perceptions on how online feedback benefited Chinese learners. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-019-09651-w

article_title: Monitoring student progress using virtual appliances: A case study
citation: Romero-Zaldivar, V.-A., Pardo, A., Burgos, D., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2012). Monitoring student progress using virtual appliances: A case study. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1058–1067. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.003
title: Coverage measure (covs) quantifying the extent of monitoring per student
description: The coverage measure covs is a per-student figure of merit computed from version control server logs as 1 − UPf/(UPe + UPf), where UPe is the number of event upload operations and UPf the number of file update operations. The article states "a coverage value of 0.5 denotes a fully monitored user environment" and values above 0.5 are possible. It is used both to answer the feasibility question and to select the students included in the correlation and regression analyses. A copy of recorded events is kept in the student's own folder so students may review, amend or delete collected events.
requirements: A version control system (Subversion) whose server logs record event-upload and file-update operations separately per user
constraints: Students may disable monitoring at any time, so coverage varies from student to student; the article reports a significant number of students with covs below 0.5
target_learning_goals: monitoring student engagement with course practical activities to predict academic achievement
examples: In the Fall 2010 course, only students with covs ≥ 0.40 (79 students) were included in the correlation and regression analyses
key_sources: Romero-Zaldivar, V.-A., Pardo, A., Burgos, D., & Delgado Kloos, C. (2012). Monitoring student progress using virtual appliances: A case study. Computers & Education, 58(4), 1058–1067. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.003

article_title: Split-attention and redundancy effects on mobile learning in physical environments
citation: Liu, T.-C., Lin, Y.-C., Tsai, M.-J., & Paas, F. (2011). Split-attention and redundancy effects on mobile learning in physical environments. Computers & Education. https://ro.uow.edu.au/edupapers/784
title: Cognitive load theory applied to mobile learning: split-attention and redundancy effects from combining texts, pictures, and real objects
description: The article extends cognitive load theory to mobile learning in rich physical environments, where at least three visual media co-occur: texts, pictures on the mobile device, and real objects outside it. It argues that "Split-attention effects may result from the difficult integration of physically separated media" and that "Redundancy effects may result from the similarity of the pictures and objects, which may force students to process the same information more than once." Because all media are visual, both effects compete for the same visual/pictorial channel capacity.
requirements: Learning must occur in a rich physical environment with multiple visual media whose combination can be varied (texts and/or pictures on a mobile device, plus real objects).
constraints: The study's test of these effects applies to the specific media configurations used (texts, pictures, real objects) with primary-school children learning leaf morphology; the authors note other media configurations "need to be investigated before reliable conclusions can be drawn".
target_learners: Elementary school students (fifth grade, about 11 years old)
target_learning_goals: Science content knowledge, specifically plant leaf morphology (venation, margin, phyllotaxy)
examples: The study operationalized the theory with three material versions: TP (text and picture on the tablet), TO (text on tablet plus real plants), and TPO (text, picture, and real plants).
key_sources: Liu, T.-C., Lin, Y.-C., Tsai, M.-J., & Paas, F. (2011). Split-attention and redundancy effects on mobile learning in physical environments. Computers & Education. https://ro.uow.edu.au/edupapers/784

article_title: Split-attention and redundancy effects on mobile learning in physical environments
citation: Liu, T.-C., Lin, Y.-C., Tsai, M.-J., & Paas, F. (2011). Split-attention and redundancy effects on mobile learning in physical environments. Computers & Education. https://ro.uow.edu.au/edupapers/784
title: Provide complementary rather than similar information when combining media in mobile learning environments
description: When designing mobile learning in rich physical environments, media combined with necessary real objects should convey different, complementary information rather than similar information. The article states that "providing students with complementary learning information is the recommended method to avoid this effect," because redundant media oblige students "to invest extra effort to process similar information from different media," harming comprehension and efficiency.
requirements: Mobile learning settings where objects and texts are necessary media, so additional on-device media must be selected deliberately.
constraints: The authors caution the results "can only be subscribed to the specific configuration of different media" and that many media configurations in mobile learning still need investigation before reliable guidelines can be formulated.
target_learners: Primary school children using mobile devices in physical learning environments
target_learning_goals: Comprehension of observable object characteristics (e.g., plant morphology) and efficient acquisition of that knowledge
examples: In the experiment, the TPO condition combined pictures on the device with highly similar real plants and produced the lowest comprehension (7.22) and efficiency (1.44), illustrating the redundancy the principle avoids.
key_sources: Liu, T.-C., Lin, Y.-C., Tsai, M.-J., & Paas, F. (2011). Split-attention and redundancy effects on mobile learning in physical environments. Computers & Education. https://ro.uow.edu.au/edupapers/784

article_title: To capture the research landscape of lecture capture in university education
citation: Banerjee, S. (2021). To capture the research landscape of lecture capture in university education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104032
title: Constructivist framing of lecture capture as a technology-enhanced learning design
description: The review conceptualises lecture capture through the lens of learning theories, positioning behaviourism and constructivism as "the two key paradigms that lie at opposite ends of the spectrum." According to constructivism, students who are self-regulated actively construct their own understanding of reality by linking new information to their prior experiences. The paper argues that watching lecture capture after attending face-to-face lectures is likely to help students in knowledge building from half-baked notions.
requirements: Students attend the face-to-face sessions and use recordings to build knowledge afterwards
constraints: The scope is trained on in vivo lecture capture, where live face-to-face lectures in front of students are captured in real time
target_learning_goals: knowledge building and complex problem solving
key_sources: Banerjee, S. (2021). To capture the research landscape of lecture capture in university education. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.104032

article_title: Towards reliable generative AI-driven scaffolding: Reducing hallucinations and enhancing quality in self-regulated learning support
citation: Qian, K., Liu, S., Li, T., Raković, M., Li, X., Guan, R., Molenaar, I., Nawaz, S., Swiecki, Z., Yan, L., & Gašević, D. (2025). Towards Reliable Generative AI-Driven Scaffolding: Reducing Hallucinations and Enhancing Quality in Self-Regulated Learning Support. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05929
title: COPES model of self-regulated learning as a framework for parsing SRL processes in scaffolds
description: The COPES model (Conditions, Operations, Products, Evaluations, Standards) from Winne and Hadwin provides a detailed depiction of the learning process that underscores the significance of SRL. The article uses COPES to derive a process library of 15 SRL processes that could be explicitly scaffolded, which forms the basis for evaluating whether LLM-generated scaffolds target the correct SRL processes. Two indistinguishable SRL processes (C.STR.2 and C.MTR.2) were merged during expert coding, reducing the final count to 14.
requirements: A process library derived from COPES that maps SRL processes to observable trace action patterns
constraints: Two SRL processes (C.STR.2 and C.MTR.2) were indistinguishable from trace data and had to be merged into a single category
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning processes including goal setting, self-monitoring, and strategic planning
examples: The article constructed a process library of 15 SRL processes derived from the COPES model, following principles proposed by Fan et al. (2022), to evaluate scaffold reliability.
key_sources: Qian, K., Liu, S., Li, T., Raković, M., Li, X., Guan, R., Molenaar, I., Nawaz, S., Swiecki, Z., Yan, L., & Gašević, D. (2025). Towards Reliable Generative AI-Driven Scaffolding: Reducing Hallucinations and Enhancing Quality in Self-Regulated Learning Support. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05929

article_title: An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS
citation: Angelides, M. C. & Agius, H. W. (2001). An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS. https://www.brunel.ac.uk/~cssthwa/
title: COSMOS: Content Oriented Semantic Modelling Overlay Scheme
description: COSMOS is a content-modelling scheme for multimedia that uses the multimedia frame (m-frame) as its basis, a 'slot-and-filler' type structure with perspectives and instances. It defines three m-frame types: syntactic m-frames (SYMs) for spatial relationships, semantic m-frames (SEMs) for events, actions and object properties, and temporal m-frames (TEMs) for temporal relationships using Allen's 13 primitives. It has been used to develop several educational multimedia systems.
requirements: A formal definition language (COSMOS-DL) and query language (COSMOS-QL) support creation, population and querying of the model
target_learning_goals: understanding of VLSI products and processes
key_sources: Angelides, M. C. & Agius, H. W. (2001). An interactive multimedia learning environment for VLSI built with COSMOS. https://www.brunel.ac.uk/~cssthwa/

article_title: Re-thinking physics teaching with web-based learning
citation: Chandra, Vinesh & Watters, James J. (2012). Re-thinking physics teaching with web-based learning. Computers and Education, 58(1), 631-640. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.09.010
title: Electronic cognitive apprenticeship as a design framework for web-based physics learning
description: The study draws on the cognitive apprenticeship model, which proposes that learners should be exposed to "a variety of methods that systematically encourage student exploration and independence" while teachers scaffold and gradually fade support. Its instructional methods — modelling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, exploration, questioning, and performance feedback — were each embedded in the Getsmart website (Table 1). The framework framed both the design of web-based lessons and the interpretation of results.
requirements: Teachers or designers embed each instructional method (modelling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, exploration, questioning, feedback) in the web environment
constraints: Chat sessions required a teacher moderator to be present
target_learning_goals: conceptual knowledge of physics topics such as electronics and atomic physics
examples: Table 1 maps each method to its Getsmart implementation, e.g. scaffolding via emails, chats, online quizzes, and hypertext
key_sources: Chandra, Vinesh & Watters, James J. (2012). Re-thinking physics teaching with web-based learning. Computers and Education, 58(1), 631-640. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.09.010

article_title: Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation
citation: Reynolds, R., Walker, K., & Speight, C. (2010). Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.04.010
title: Socio-constructivist evaluation framework combining Falk and Dierking's Contextual Model with activity theory
description: The article's summative evaluation used a hybrid analytical model based on Falk and Dierking's Contextual Model, which considers personal, physical, and sociocultural contexts of museum learners, augmented with activity theory focusing on how tools mediate visitors' experience with artefacts. The overall framework drew from socio-constructivist perspectives, in which learners become collaborative meaning makers within a community of shared practice. The authors note the Contextual Model was applied mainly to informal family visits and science centres, hence the augmentation.
requirements: Analysis of trail structure and content, student-generated data, prior findings, and interviews with project personnel.
constraints: The Contextual Model has been applied mainly to informal family visits and primarily to science centres.
target_learning_goals: meaning making with museum collections
examples: The summative stage analysed data using this hybrid model, carried out independently by one of the authors.
key_sources: Reynolds, R., Walker, K., & Speight, C. (2010). Web-based museum trails on PDAs for university-level design students: Design and evaluation. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2010.04.010

article_title: High-quality digital distance teaching during COVID-19 school closures: Does familiarity with technology matter?
citation: Fütterer, T., Hoch, E., Lachner, A., Scheiter, K., & Stürmer, K. (2023). High-quality digital distance teaching during COVID-19 school closures: Does familiarity with technology matter? Computers & Education, 199, 104788. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104788
title: Providing opportunities for cognitively activating instruction matters more than device familiarity for quality digital distance teaching
description: The study concludes that "infrastructural measures, such as equipping schools with digital devices so that teachers and students can familiarize themselves with technology, do not seem to be decisive for high-quality digital (distance) teaching." Instead, the quality of technology integration—whether students perceive teaching as cognitively activating—drives effort in learning. This suggests that instructional design for cognitive activation should be prioritized over mere device provision.
requirements: Teachers must design instruction that students perceive as cognitively activating, using technologies to initiate higher-level learning activities
constraints: This finding applies to short-term change from face-to-face to digital distance teaching, as occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic
target_learners: Secondary school students in digital distance teaching
target_learning_goals: Effort in learning
Cognitive engagement
key_sources: Fütterer, T., Hoch, E., Lachner, A., Scheiter, K., & Stürmer, K. (2023). High-quality digital distance teaching during COVID-19 school closures: Does familiarity with technology matter? Computers & Education, 199, 104788. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104788

article_title: Cartoons beyond clipart: A computer tool for storyboarding and storywriting
citation: M. Madden, P.W.H. Chung and C.W. Dawson. (2007). Cartoon beyond clipart: a computer tool for storyboarding and storywriting. Loughborough University. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: Content-centred versus build-centred software taxonomy for visual story tools
description: The article proposes a taxonomy distinguishing 'content-centred' software, whose defining feature is "a primary reliance on pre-supplied characters and artwork", from 'build-centred' software providing tools for user-created content to take an equal or dominant role. Content-centred tools offer low range and high support; build-centred tools offer high range and low support. The review found no tool offering both range and support.
requirements: Analysis criteria include characterisation flexibility and the camera's role in shot distances and types
constraints: The boundary between categories is described as blurred
target_learning_goals: Moving image production
Visual storytelling
key_sources: M. Madden, P.W.H. Chung and C.W. Dawson. (2007). Cartoon beyond clipart: a computer tool for storyboarding and storywriting. Loughborough University. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/

article_title: A study of motivations, behavior, and contributions quality in online communities of teachers: A data analytics approach
citation: Gutiérrez-Páez, N. F., Santos, P., Hernández-Leo, D., & Carrió, M. (2023). A study of motivations, behavior, and contributions quality in online communities of teachers: A data analytics approach. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2023.104829
title: Community analytics layer of the Analytics Layers for Learning Design framework
description: The Analytics Layers for Learning Design framework proposes "three layers of data analytics to support and inform decision-making in learning design: learning experience (learning analytics), learning design elements (design analytics) and community of educators (community analytics)." This study's cross-case analysis of motivations, behavior, and contribution quality contributes to the community analytics layer, using data to inform stakeholders in online communities of teachers.

constraints: The study contributes specifically to the community analytics layer rather than the other two layers
target_learners: teacher community stakeholders, including platform developers and facilitators
target_learning_goals: data-informed decision-making about learning design communities
examples: Applied to analyze motivations, engagement behavior, and learning design quality in a pre-service teacher online community

article_title: Between the lines: documenting the multiple dimensions of computer-supported collaborations
citation: Luckin, Rosemary (2003). Between the lines: documenting the multiple dimensions of computer-supported collaborations. Computers & Education, 41 (4). http://sro.sussex.ac.uk/id/eprint/1366/
title: CORDFU chart for two-dimensional collaboration documentation
description: The Chronologically Ordered Dialogue & Features Used (CORDFU) chart is the development of the original annotated user log from the Ecolab evaluation for group use of multimedia. Its vertical axis records CD-ROM features above a bold horizontal line and categories of talk below it, while the horizontal axis records the amount of attention paid to a feature or dialogue category in text units of up to 24 characters. For each X recording a CD-ROM feature there is a O indicating the type of talk that occurred whilst this feature was in use.
requirements: Interactions were captured via two video sources, one of the computer screen and the other of the learners, and the video data was then transcribed and coded
target_learning_goals: collaborative construction of understanding with multimedia
examples: In the example CORDFU extract the group of learners used the notepad in conjunction with the introductory section whilst discussing their reactions to the multimedia

article_title: Training pre-service teachers to deal with cyberbullying: Collective intelligence as a mode of learning
citation: Bautista Alcaine, P., Vicente Sánchez, E., Orejudo Hernández, S., & Cano Escoriaza, J. (2024). Training pre-service teachers to deal with cyberbullying: Collective intelligence as a mode of learning. Computers & Education, 220, 105123. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105123
title: Collective Learning online platform
description: Collective Learning is an online collective intelligence tool developed by the Institute for Biocomputation and Physics of Complex Systems (BIFI) and Kampal Data Solutions, "designed to apply collective intelligence to certain problems or tasks with the aim of achieving high-quality solutions through a model of successive social interactions". It deploys actions such as edit, view, copy, permutation of users, modifying responses and response deletion across seven phases, with an AI acting as moderator selecting Top 10 answers.
requirements: An initial individual response phase followed by six successive interaction phases, with each user seeing responses of four randomized anonymized "neighbours" in phases 2–5
constraints: The popularity or prestige effect can lead to "responses of lower quality or diversity that have been endorsed by less competent leaders"
target_learning_goals: complex problem resolution
moral dilemmas
mathematics and physics problems
examples: Used with 221 pre-service teachers working on an adolescent sexting case across seven phases

article_title: Training pre-service teachers to deal with cyberbullying: Collective intelligence as a mode of learning
citation: Bautista Alcaine, P., Vicente Sánchez, E., Orejudo Hernández, S., & Cano Escoriaza, J. (2024). Training pre-service teachers to deal with cyberbullying: Collective intelligence as a mode of learning. Computers & Education, 220, 105123. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2024.105123
title: Collective intelligence as a construct for group performance on complex tasks
description: The article describes collective intelligence as "the shared effort of a large group of people confronted with diverse complex tasks", where "it is presumed that the average performance of the individual is lower than the performance achieved by the group as a whole". Building on Woolley et al. (2010), the article distinguishes top-down analysis (interaction processes such as group heterogeneity, diversity of responses, order of turns) from bottom-up analysis (gender, emotional intelligence, individual intelligence, cognitive diversity, social sensitivity).
requirements: A facilitator or moderator role to manage interaction and control the prestige effect
constraints: Conditions that lead to quality results remain open to debate, and online environments face dispersal of answers, lack of collaboration, and lack of originality
target_learning_goals: collaborative problem resolution
complex task performance
examples: Applied via the Collective Learning platform to a cyberbullying case with pre-service teachers

article_title: A comparison of structured and unstructured navigation through a CBT package
citation: Stanton, N. A. and Stammers, R. B. (1990). A comparison of structured and unstructured navigation through a CBT package. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ414518
title: Cognitive style taxonomy of serialist, holist, top-down and bottom-up navigation strategies
description: The article organizes trainee navigation behaviour through cognitive style classifications drawn from Pask's distinction between a "serialist" (a step-by-step approach in a linear fashion, increasing understanding by small increments) and a "holist" (a more global approach, involving testing assumptions of the overall structure of the task). Because the task under investigation had a hierarchical structure, the authors add two further styles: a "top down" strategy (starting with higher-order procedures, moving down to lower-order procedures) and a "bottomup" strategy (starting with lower-order procedures, moving up to higher-order procedures). These styles were used to classify unstructured-condition trainees and interpret differences in modules viewed.
requirements: Classification of trainee styles relied on self-report of navigation approach, for example "I looked at the most important things first" (top down)
constraints: The taxonomy was applied only to trainees in the unstructured condition, who were measured using the Embedded Figures Test
target_learning_goals: navigation and sequencing of instruction in hierarchical computer-based training tasks
key_sources: Stanton, N. A. and Stammers, R. B. (1990). A comparison of structured and unstructured navigation through a CBT package. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ414518

article_title: A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies
citation: Tondeur, Jo; Aesaert, Koen; Prestridge, Sarah; Consuegra, Els. (2018). A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.002
title: Combine multiple institutional strategies, rather than a single strategy, when preparing pre-service teachers for ICT integration
description: Because the study found that the more strategy occurrences pre-service teachers perceive, the higher their perceived ICT competence, the article recommends that results "can provide guidance for the preparation of pre-service teachers for the 21st century learning environments with new technologies". It motivates this by noting prior research is generally limited to the impact of one single strategy, whereas the model integrates multiple strategies simultaneously.
requirements: Institutional strategies must be experienced by pre-service teachers during their teacher education programme
constraints: Evidence base is a cross-sectional survey of perceived competence among final-year pre-service teachers in Flanders
target_learning_goals: ICT integration in learning processes and instructional practice
examples: The survey measured the six strategies — role models, reflection, learning technology by design, peer collaboration, scaffolding authentic experiences, and continuous feedback — as perceived occurrences among 931 final-year pre-service teachers
key_sources: Tondeur, Jo; Aesaert, Koen; Prestridge, Sarah; Consuegra, Els. (2018). A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.002

article_title: Improving the quality of teaching by utilising written student feedback: A streamlined process
citation: Hujala, M., Knutas, A., Hynninen, T., & Arminen, H. (2020). Improving the quality of teaching by utilising written student feedback: A streamlined process. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103965
title: Combine topic modelling with thematic analysis to make qualitative analysis of large feedback datasets practical
description: The article argues that large-scale analysis of written student feedback is easily dismissed as too time-consuming when done purely by hand, and that purely automatic methods lose richness. Combining the two addresses both problems: "Topic modelling allows pre-sorting large document sets into topic categories and finding most characteristic documents from each category", while thematic analysis assigns expert human themes to those categories. This makes thematic analysis practical in larger datasets and speeds up the analysis.
requirements: Requires a corpus of open-ended feedback large enough that manual analysis alone would be impractical.
constraints: The authors note that the drawback of automated text mining compared to manual analysis is loss in the richness of the data.
For small datasets, the authors agree the automated step can be skipped in favour of a fully manual thematic analysis.
target_learning_goals: evaluation of teaching quality
quality assurance of degree programmes
examples: In the article's demonstration, the authors coded the 12 most characteristic feedback texts per topic (72 total) rather than the full corpus, requiring about 70 coded rows to achieve beneficial results.
key_sources: Hujala, M., Knutas, A., Hynninen, T., & Arminen, H. (2020). Improving the quality of teaching by utilising written student feedback: A streamlined process. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103965

article_title: Automated multimodal visual analytics of social and epistemic dimensions in team communication for reflective practice in healthcare simulation
citation: Zhao, L., Echeverria, V., Gašević, D., Yan, L., Alfredo, R., Li, X., & Martinez-Maldonado, R. (2026). Automated multimodal visual analytics of social and epistemic dimensions in team communication for reflective practice in healthcare simulation. Computers & Education, 252, 105655. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105655
title: Co-designed network visualisation design decisions for debriefing evidence
description: The article enumerates design decisions for the social and epistemic networks established through co-design with nursing educators: role-based colour coding of learner nodes, fixed node sizes and hidden edges for non-learners, absolute speech duration and absolute co-occurrence frequency for node and edge sizes, and an abstracted content view that summarises dialogue without raw transcripts. These choices were made "to highlight the communication among learners by reducing unnecessary information and cognitive load" and to allow comparison of communication across phases.
requirements: Co-design with educators to select relevant codes and visual encodings
Use of absolute rather than normalised metrics so educators can compare durations and co-occurrences across phases
constraints: Reducing the epistemic network from seven to four behaviours focused the debriefing on closed-loop communication and escalation, although it also reduced the network's informational richness
target_learning_goals: Reflecting on team communication roles, engagement and closed-loop communication strategies
examples: Educators suggested refining the epistemic network by dropping and merging behaviours, leaving four codes: task allocation, questioning, acknowledging, and escalation
key_sources: Zhao, L., Echeverria, V., Gašević, D., Yan, L., Alfredo, R., Li, X., & Martinez-Maldonado, R. (2026). Automated multimodal visual analytics of social and epistemic dimensions in team communication for reflective practice in healthcare simulation. Computers & Education, 252, 105655. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2026.105655

article_title: Effects of Manipulative Use on PK-12 Mathematics Achievement: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Amy B. Holmes, Vanderbilt University. (2013). Effects of Manipulative Use on PK-12 Mathematics Achievement: A Meta-Analysis. SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Constructivist account of manipulatives as concrete objects supporting progression to abstract mathematical thinking
description: The article frames manipulatives through constructivist theories of learning, which postulate that students build increasingly complex knowledge through active engagement with concrete materials. Manipulatives are defined as "objects that appeal to several senses and that can be touched, moved about, rearranged, and otherwise handled by children", including physical items and virtual applets. The framework holds that manipulating such objects supports students' progression from concrete to increasingly abstract ways of thinking about diverse mathematical ideas, motivating the meta-analysis of manipulative interventions.
requirements: Manipulative use must introduce or reinforce mathematical concepts and be accompanied by instruction supporting model-based reasoning, which the article says necessitates extensive teacher preparation and professional development
constraints: Critics cited in the article note that simple provision of manipulative materials is not likely to result in learning without specific supporting instruction
target_learning_goals: conceptual and procedural understanding of mathematics
examples: The meta-analysis operationalized this framework by including interventions with physical or virtual manipulative materials during school-based mathematics instruction compared to nonuse or business-as-usual controls
key_sources: Amy B. Holmes, Vanderbilt University. (2013). Effects of Manipulative Use on PK-12 Mathematics Achievement: A Meta-Analysis. SREE Spring 2013 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563072

article_title: Effects of Integrated Literacy and Content-Area Instruction on Vocabulary and Comprehension in the Elementary Years: A Meta-Analysis
citation: HyeJin Hwang, Sonia Q. Cabell & Rachel E. Joyner (2021). Effects of Integrated Literacy and Content-area Instruction on Vocabulary and Comprehension in the Elementary Years: A Meta-analysis. Scientific Studies of Reading. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888438.2021.1954005
title: Present connected content ideas explicitly and cumulatively, and revisit content-related words across sessions
description: In integrated literacy and content-area instruction, the logical organization of the science or social studies content guides design: "Connected ideas from science or social studies content are presented to students explicitly and cumulatively within and across class sessions." Text sequences reflect connections among content ideas, and content-related words appear repeatedly within and across sessions, with meanings taught in relation to content rather than in isolation. The article presents this organization as the mechanism leveraged by the interventions it meta-analyzes.
requirements: Students regularly interact with multiple texts coherently connected to one another around science or social studies content
target_learners: Elementary students in kindergarten through fifth grade
target_learning_goals: Building content knowledge through text
Vocabulary learning of content-related words
Comprehension of connected texts
examples: The article gives the example of a text explaining the process of pollination followed by a text about animals assisting with plant pollination, with words like pollen, flower, and bees recurring across sessions
key_sources: HyeJin Hwang, Sonia Q. Cabell & Rachel E. Joyner (2021). Effects of Integrated Literacy and Content-area Instruction on Vocabulary and Comprehension in the Elementary Years: A Meta-analysis. Scientific Studies of Reading. https://doi.org/10.1080/10888438.2021.1954005

article_title: Comparing Effects of Different Applications on Pre-Service Teachers: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Şenel Elaldı, Veli Batdı. (2016). Comparing Effects of Different Applications on Pre-Service Teachers: A Meta–Analysis. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i7.1456
title: In teacher education, select teaching methods appropriate to learners' social and cultural context to develop the process of learning to teach
description: The article concludes that no single instructional approach dominates once learner dispositions and classroom interaction are considered, recommending that teacher educators match methods to context. It states that "in teacher education, providing appropriate selection of teaching methods within their socia l and cultural context, teachers will enable students to develop and refine the process of learning to teach". This rests on its finding that effect sizes varied widely across applications and that pre-service teachers' prior beliefs filter new methodologies.
requirements: Knowledge of pre-service teachers' predispositions toward subject matter, which the article says include beliefs about how a subject should be taught and learned
constraints: The article states "the impact of a certain classroom instructional approach on pre -service teachers’ retention and attitude scores is outweighed by teachers’ preferences or the nature of the interactions occurring in the classrooms"
The article notes pre-service teachers are drawn to "perceived practicality", which may constrain receptiveness to methods they see as impractical
target_learners: Pre-service teachers in education faculties in Turkey
target_learning_goals: Retention of learning
Attitudes toward teaching and their subject areas
examples: The meta-analysis compared nine retention applications and fourteen attitude applications, finding effect sizes ranged from d=2,0606 to d=-0,3949, supporting the claim that no single method dominates across contexts
key_sources: Şenel Elaldı, Veli Batdı. (2016). Comparing Effects of Different Applications on Pre-Service Teachers: A Meta–Analysis. Journal of Education and Training Studies. http://dx.doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i7.1456

article_title: Does Context-Based Learning Increase Academic Achievement and Learning Retention?: A Review Based on Meta-Analysis
citation: Tutal, Ö (2023). Does Context-Based Learning Increase Academic Achievement and Learning Retention?: A Review based on Meta-Analysis. Journal of Practical Studies in Education, 4(5), 1-16. https://doi.org/10.46809/jpse.v4i5.71
title: Context-based learning as a constructivist instructional approach using real-world contexts to build and understand concepts
description: CBL is an instructional approach that recognizes the importance of both the social context within the learning environment and the practical, real-world context in knowledge acquisition. It promotes active student engagement, using "context as a powerful tool for constructing and understanding concepts," and aligns with a constructivist view of learning. Knowledge construction is stimulated through the recognition of the need-to-know within a given context, and contexts act as integrators bringing "coherence, connection, meaning, and relevance to the learning experience."
requirements: Contexts should be relevant and relatable to students' lives, drawing from real-life experiences, social events, or scientifically valid situations
constraints: The article notes CBL differs from traditional education in that content is situated within the learner's horizon from the outset rather than presented first and applied later
target_learners: Elementary, middle, high school and tertiary students
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding
Knowledge construction and application in real-life contexts
examples: The article describes a spiral curriculum approach where ideas introduced in one context are further developed and reinforced in other contexts
key_sources: Tutal, Ö (2023). Does Context-Based Learning Increase Academic Achievement and Learning Retention?: A Review based on Meta-Analysis. Journal of Practical Studies in Education, 4(5), 1-16. https://doi.org/10.46809/jpse.v4i5.71

article_title: Clinical teaching models for the instruction of healthcare trainees in the 21(st) century: a scoping review.
citation: Munguiko Clement, Masereka Enos Mirembe, Atukwatse Joseph, Smitha Joseph, Kateregga James, Nankinga Clare, Collete Alice Alum, Namujju Josephine, Akello Safina, Nalubega Sylivia. (2026). Clinical teaching models for the instruction of healthcare trainees in the 21st century: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09710-w
title: Clinical teaching models share common design features: structured stepwise approaches, learner-centred instruction, active participation, feedback, and clinical reasoning promotion
description: Across the eight mapped models, the review identifies a recurring set of design features: "structured stepwise approaches, learner-centred instruction, active participation, feedback, and the promotion of clinical reasoning and competency development." The pattern operates as a design template for clinical teaching sessions: a defined step sequence guides the encounter, the learner is placed in an active role, and feedback and reasoning prompts are embedded within routine patient care. Most models additionally aim to improve teaching effectiveness, diagnostic accuracy, and learner engagement through experiential and reflective learning.
requirements: Implementation requires clinical educators who can deliver the structured steps and provide feedback within real clinical encounters
constraints: The review notes most models aim to improve teaching effectiveness, diagnostic accuracy, and learner engagement, but does not report outcome evidence for the pattern itself
target_learners: healthcare trainees in medicine, nursing, midwifery, and allied health disciplines
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
competency development
learner engagement
examples: OMP operationalizes the pattern with five microteaching skills (get a commitment, probe for supporting evidence, teach general rules, reinforce what is done well, correct errors) within brief clinical encounters
key_sources: Munguiko Clement, Masereka Enos Mirembe, Atukwatse Joseph, Smitha Joseph, Kateregga James, Nankinga Clare, Collete Alice Alum, Namujju Josephine, Akello Safina, Nalubega Sylivia. (2026). Clinical teaching models for the instruction of healthcare trainees in the 21st century: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09710-w

article_title: Mapping the evidence on public health competency assessment strategies in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review.
citation: Hernández Rincón Erwin Hernando, González Garcés Mariana, Montoya Jerónimo Cárdenas, Fernández Valeria Concha, Torres Mario Andrés Torres, Vargas Villafañe Nicolle Valeria, Chaves Natalia Castaño. (2026). Mapping the evidence on public health competency assessment strategies in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09976-0
title: Continuum of evaluative complexity spanning ten levels from cognitive assessment to normative/consensus assessment
description: The review establishes a continuum of evaluative complexity (Table 4) ranking assessment approaches from knowledge-centred measurement to assessment at educational-systems level. As printed: "Analysis of the identified strategies allowed establishment of a continuum of evaluative complexity, from approaches centred on knowledge to integrated models of assessment in real contexts (Table 4)." The ten levels run from cognitive assessment (low complexity), through skills, attitudinal, real performance-based, applied clinical, programmatic, population/institutional, and validated-instrument assessment, to longitudinal assessment and normative/consensus assessment. Levels were assigned by degree of contextual authenticity, integration of multiple competency domains, educational scope and proximity to real-world professional performance.
requirements: Intended to facilitate understanding of the progressive sophistication of assessment strategies in undergraduate medical education
constraints: Inductively derived from the included studies and explicitly "should not be interpreted as a validated assessment framework"; implementation of the highest-level consensus approaches remains limited
target_learning_goals: Public health competencies including knowledge, skills, attitudes and integrated applied competencies
examples: The review places examinations and questionnaires at Level 1, OSCEs and standardised patients at Level 2, and community projects, service learning and clinical rotations at Levels 4–5
key_sources: Hernández Rincón Erwin Hernando, González Garcés Mariana, Montoya Jerónimo Cárdenas, Fernández Valeria Concha, Torres Mario Andrés Torres, Vargas Villafañe Nicolle Valeria, Chaves Natalia Castaño. (2026). Mapping the evidence on public health competency assessment strategies in undergraduate medical education: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09976-0

article_title: Mapping competencies of family physicians in primary healthcare: a scoping review.
citation: Saza Salas Laura Daniela, Hernandez Rincon July Andrea, Hernandez Rincon Erwin Hernando, Ulloa Rodriguez Mauricio Fernando, Diaz Quijano Diana Marcela, Jaimes Peñuela Claudia Liliana. (2026). Mapping competencies of family physicians in primary healthcare: a scoping review. Family Medicine and Community Health. https://doi.org/10.1136/fmch-2025-003528
title: Competency categorisation pattern: eight domains each specified by component lists of skills, attitudes and knowledge
description: The review organises professional competence as eight broad categories, each elaborated with a component list in Table 4 — for example, knowledge management comprises "Use of evidence for clinical decision-making", clinical reasoning, practical skills of correct diagnosis and treatment, and an interdisciplinary approach to mental, organic and end-of-life pathologies. This category-plus-components structure, based on PAHO and WONCA frameworks, maps how each domain is decomposed into observable professional behaviours.
requirements: Categorisation determined by the authors based on PAHO and WONCA documents; some articles covered more than one category and were categorised accordingly
constraints: Components were recorded "according to the information available" in the included studies
target_learning_goals: defining the family physician professional profile
structuring competency-based training and assessment
examples: Communication components include reporting bad news, maintaining clear language, empowering the patient for shared decision-making, obtaining clinical data and conflict resolution

article_title: Efficacy of mind maps and concept maps in enhancing academic performance among undergraduate medical students in the preclinical stage: a systematic review.
citation: Aljamal Husam, Alawneh Rama, Derbas Afnan, Edaibes Mohammad, Ahmed Aya, Amer Lama, Alzoubi Hiba, Serhan Hashem Abu Habuser. (2025). Efficacy of mind maps and concept maps in enhancing academic performance among undergraduate medical students in the preclinical stage: a systematic review. Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-025-10437-4
title: Two-feature taxonomy distinguishing concept maps from mind maps: hierarchy and explicit link naming
description: The review organizes the two visual mapping tools by two differentiating characteristics drawn from Santiago (2011). Concept maps are "hierarchical with the most important concept shown first", with subsidiary and tertiary concepts placed below, and they require "explicit naming of links" through verbs such as "includes" or "is part of", aiding accurate interpretation. Mind maps place the main idea at the center with ideas radiating outward with no obvious hierarchy, and their links are unnamed, leaving relationships implicit. The review includes both tools because they share the goal of enhancing knowledge organization and retention, and builds on the account that concept mapping rests on Ausubel's assimilation theory of learning.
requirements: Concept mapping requires links between concepts to be named explicitly through linking verbs
constraints: The two tools differ structurally despite a shared purpose of knowledge organization and retention
target_learning_goals: knowledge organization
knowledge retention
comprehension of complex medical information
examples: The review's included RCTs used concept mapping with clinical cases, mind mapping of neuroanatomy topics, and online testable pathogenesis maps
key_sources: Aljamal Husam, Alawneh Rama, Derbas Afnan, Edaibes Mohammad, Ahmed Aya, Amer Lama, Alzoubi Hiba, Serhan Hashem Abu Habuser. (2025). article_title: Nurse Managers' Awareness of and Competence in Palliative Care in Municipal Care Settings: A Systematic Mixed Studies Review.
citation: Xu Hongxuan, Möllerberg Marie-Louise, Dalhammar Karin, Bengtsson Mariette, Sjögren Forss Katarina. (2026). Nurse Managers' Awareness of and Competence in Palliative Care in Municipal Care Settings: A Systematic Mixed Studies Review. Nursing & Health Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1111/nhs.70352
title: Competence-confidence framework: confidence shapes how nurse managers develop and demonstrate palliative care competence
description: The review frames competence in palliative care as encompassing knowledge, skills, abilities, values, beliefs, attributes and behaviors, and links it to self-efficacy or confidence. It states that "Published research widely recognizes the role of confidence in both the development of competence and its demonstration in evaluative contexts", drawing on Bandura's account of self-efficacy shaped through social and environmental influences. In the synthesis, nurse managers' competence was demonstrated in performing diverse responsibilities and was closely tied to their confidence in leading complex care processes.
requirements: NMs must possess adequate awareness of and robust competence in palliative care grounded in clinical practice for the framework to support effective leadership practices
constraints: The review aimed to compile existing evidence rather than develop or test the framework empirically
target_learners: nurse managers in municipal care settings
target_learning_goals: palliative care competence
leadership of complex palliative care processes
examples: The synthesis reports that confidence influenced how nurse managers performed their complex palliative care responsibilities
key_sources: Xu Hongxuan, Möllerberg Marie-Louise, Dalhammar Karin, Bengtsson Mariette, Sjögren Forss Katarina. (2026). Nurse Managers' Awareness of and Competence in Palliative Care in Municipal Care Settings: A Systematic Mixed Studies Review. Nursing & Health Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1111/nhs.70352

article_title: A systematic review of the use of human body donor models for postgraduate laparoscopic surgical training.
citation: Pinar Sedat Alp, Morrow Joseph J., Kong Chia Yew. (2025). A systematic review of the use of human body donor models for postgraduate laparoscopic surgical training. Anatomical Science International. https://doi.org/10.1007/s12565-025-00872-z
title: Systematic review corpus of 55 studies of body donor models for laparoscopic training
description: A PRISMA-guided systematic review corpus of "Fifty-five studies" identified via a July 2023 search of MEDLINE, EMBASE, ClinicalTrials.gov and Cochrane, registered on PROSPERO (NIHR CRD42023437230). Studies span "15 different countries", with 28 in general surgery, 12 in obstetrics and gynaecology and 6 in urology. Fifteen types of body donor were used, with Thiel embalmed (15 studies) and fresh frozen (11 studies) the most frequent. Quality was assessed with the Modified MERSQI, yielding a median scaled score of 10.2 across 48 scored studies.
requirements: Eligibility restricted to studies reporting educational outcomes of postgraduate doctors on body donor models for laparoscopic surgery, or detailed descriptive feasibility studies
constraints: Conference abstracts, animal-model studies with veterinary trainees, undergraduate medical students, robotic and natural-orifice procedures were excluded
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic surgical skills
examples: Quality assessment scored 48 studies on the Modified MERSQI, with scaled scores ranging from 5.4 to 16.4 and no study achieving the maximum

article_title: Augmented Reality in Surgical Training: Systematic Review of Its Impact on Technical Performance in Surgical Trainees.
citation: El Ashry M, El Ashry A, Khalique H, Abdalle Y, Yeung T. (2026). Augmented Reality in Surgical Training: Systematic Review of Its Impact on Technical Performance in Surgical Trainees. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/71572
title: Cognitive load and gaze-guidance account of AR's training benefit
description: The review frames AR's educational value through cognitive load theory: instruction should "minimize extraneous cognitive load while maximizing germane load, the mental effort directed toward schema formation". AR telestration and anatomical overlays bypass the cognitive translation step of converting verbal descriptions into spatial awareness by providing visual guidance colocated with the task. The expertise reversal effect predicts the same overlays that scaffold novices may act as extraneous load for experts with robust internal schemas. Eye-tracking evidence on reduced gaze latency is presented as the most direct experimental support for this mechanism.
requirements: AR overlays must be colocated with the task being performed to bypass the cognitive translation step
constraints: The review strictly defines AR as unidirectional overlay of digital data onto a physical field, excluding bidirectional spatially mapped mixed reality interactions
The same overlays may function as extraneous cognitive load for experts who have already developed robust internal schemas
target_learners: surgical trainees: medical students, residents, and fellows
target_learning_goals: technical surgical skill acquisition
spatial anatomical understanding
procedural accuracy
examples: Felinska et al's eye-tracking data showed AR reduced gaze latency from 2.04 to 0.21 seconds (P<.01, ηp²=0.95), which the review cites as confirming that AR telestration directs trainees' visual attention to operationally relevant structures more rapidly than verbal instruction
key_sources: El Ashry M, El Ashry A, Khalique H, Abdalle Y, Yeung T. (2026). Augmented Reality in Surgical Training: Systematic Review of Its Impact on Technical Performance in Surgical Trainees. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/71572

article_title: Sport Participation and Nutrition in Students: A Scoping Review of Neuroendocrine and Autonomic Mechanisms Linking Lifestyle Behaviors to Cognitive and Academic Outcomes.
citation: Tafuri Maria Giovanna, Monda Vincenzo, La Marra Marco, Tafuri Francesco, Messina Antonietta, Monda Antonietta, Casillo Maria, Di Maio Girolamo, Tafuri Domenico, Latino Francesca, Moscatelli Fiorenzo, Polito Rita, Messina Giovanni. (2026). Sport Participation and Nutrition in Students: A Scoping Review of Neuroendocrine and Autonomic Mechanisms Linking Lifestyle Behaviors to Cognitive and Academic Outcomes. Nutrients. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu18111651
title: Educational programs should adopt combined strategies targeting movement behaviors and dietary habits together rather than as independent domains
description: Because physical activity and nutrition likely interact through shared biological pathways, the review recommends integrated lifestyle approaches in educational and public health settings. It states that "Educational programs and public health initiatives would benefit from adopting combined strategies that simultaneously target movement behaviors and dietary habits, rather than treating them as independent domains." This follows its finding that only a small proportion of studies examined physical activity and nutrition within the same analytical framework.
requirements: Programs should simultaneously target movement behaviors and dietary habits rather than addressing them separately
constraints: The review cautions that findings from predominantly observational evidence should be translated into practice with appropriate caution and not interpreted as definitive proof of causal academic benefit
target_learning_goals: cognitive function
academic achievement
healthy lifestyle behaviors
examples: The review notes integrated physical activity-nutrition models were comparatively limited in the included literature, motivating the combined-strategy recommendation

article_title: The Implementation of Data-Driven Assessment into Laparoscopic Skills Training: A Systematic Review.
citation: Hardon Sem F., Horeman Tim, Reijers Sophie J. M., Schoonmade Linda J., Daams Freek, van der Peet Donald L. (2025). The Implementation of Data-Driven Assessment into Laparoscopic Skills Training: A Systematic Review. Surgical Innovation. https://doi.org/10.1177/15533506251336824
title: Combine force- and motion-based assessment tools for comprehensive evaluation of technical skills in minimally invasive surgery
description: The review recommends that trainers "utilize combined force- and motion-based assessment as objective measures of technical competency, to ensure patient safety and to improve surgical outcomes." This addresses the identified gap where most tools assess instrument handling while tissue manipulation assessment is limited. The authors argue each tool has strengths and limitations, and tool choice should depend on specific learning objectives and context.
requirements: Assessment metrics must have established validity and reliability
Feedback and guidance must be provided to trainees based on assessment results
constraints: Development and validation of force-based safety metrics is relatively new and integration into existing devices takes time and money
target_learning_goals: Laparoscopic technical skills
Tissue manipulation
Instrument handling
examples: The review found only three studies evaluated tissue handling skills using metrics like knot quality, tissue handling forces, and anastomotic integrity
key_sources: Hardon Sem F., Horeman Tim, Reijers Sophie J. M., Schoonmade Linda J., Daams Freek, van der Peet Donald L. (2025). The Implementation of Data-Driven Assessment into Laparoscopic Skills Training: A Systematic Review. Surgical Innovation. https://doi.org/10.1177/15533506251336824

article_title: Assessing effectiveness and skill transferability in multi-platform simulated training for robotic surgical skills: a systematic review.
citation: Liu Wai Miu Emma, Burr Katy-Anne, Dave Charvi, Pearse Callum, Li Yang, Quarez Julien, Granados Alejandro, Challacombe Ben, Dasgupta Prokar, Raison Nicholas. (2026). Assessing effectiveness and skill transferability in multi-platform simulated training for robotic surgical skills: a systematic review. Journal of Robotic Surgery 20(1):121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-03090-x
title: Cognitive Flexibility Theory as a framework for multi-platform robotic surgical training
description: The review invokes Cognitive Flexibility Theory as the explanatory framework for why multi-platform training may benefit trainees: "exposure to multiple representations of similar content across differing contexts promotes deeper understanding and adaptability". Applied to robotic surgery education, the framework suggests multi-platform training could strengthen understanding of fundamental robotic principles and facilitate smoother transfer of skills between systems.
requirements: Exposure to multiple representations of similar content across differing contexts
constraints: The review presents this as an alignment rather than a tested prediction; it calls for randomised controlled trials to isolate causal effects of such curricula
target_learners: surgical trainees in robotic skills training
target_learning_goals: adaptive expertise and cross-platform skill transfer in robotic surgery
examples: The review aligns multi-platform training with Cognitive Flexibility Theory, citing the framework's premise about exposure to multiple representations across contexts

Assessing effectiveness and skill transferability in multi-platform simulated training for robotic surgical skills: a systematic review. Journal of Robotic Surgery 20(1):121. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-03090-x

article_title: The who, how and what of educational outcome research for autistic students published in the last decade: A systematic quantitative literature review.
citation: Smart, R., Adams, D., & Simpson, K. (2026). The who, how and what of educational outcome research for autistic students published in the last decade: A systematic quantitative literature review. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 96, 286–305. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70015
title: Researchers should comprehensively report demographic data including co-occurring conditions, gender beyond the binary, and race and ethnicity to support intersectional analysis
description: A design recommendation from the review's conclusions: educational outcome researchers should "collect and report on characteristics of participants in their research to ensure it is applicable for practice". The review argues comprehensive demographic reporting, including co-occurring conditions, gender identity beyond the binary, and personal and perceived racial and ethnic identity, is necessary for intersectional analysis and for including marginalised subgroups of autistic people. It further recommends combining large administrative datasets with primary data collection and collaborative, co-produced research design.
requirements: Reporting of co-occurring conditions, gender beyond the binary, and race and ethnicity in primary data collection
constraints: Information on co-occurring conditions may not always be available in secondary datasets
Small sample sizes for specific subgroups may limit statistical power even in population-level datasets
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
school attendance
disciplinary outcomes
examples: The review found only 25.0% of items reported co-occurring conditions and no attendance items reported race and ethnicity
key_sources: Smart, R., Adams, D., & Simpson, K. (2026). The who, how and what of educational outcome research for autistic students published in the last decade: A systematic quantitative literature review. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 96, 286–305. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70015

article_title: Virtual reality for assessment in undergraduate nursing and medical education - a systematic review.
citation: Neher Andrea N., Bühlmann Florian, Müller Martin, Berendonk Christoph, Sauter Thomas C., Birrenbach Tanja. (2025). Virtual reality for assessment in undergraduate nursing and medical education – a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06867-8
title: Align VR assessments with learning objectives and teaching methods through constructive alignment
description: The review concludes VR assessments should be integrated thoughtfully into a comprehensive pedagogical strategy rather than added as technology for its own sake. It states that "it is crucial to ensure that the technology is thoughtfully integrated into a comprehensive pedagogical strategy", guided by constructive alignment between learning objectives, teaching methods, and assessment. The review warns that complex VR scenarios ending in a single multiple-choice question waste the technology's potential.
requirements: Learning objectives, teaching methods, and VR assessments must be aligned; the review states "it is important to determine which learning objectives should be assessed in VR and train accordingly to achieve alignment between learning objectives, teaching, and assessment".
constraints: The review notes that simply integrating new technology into a training program does not inherently enhance its value.
target_learning_goals: Clinical competencies assessed in VR, e.g., Patient Care, communication skills, medical knowledge
examples: The review criticizes designing complex VR scenarios with detailed action sequences only to assess learners at the end with a single multiple-choice question answered by controller click.
key_sources: Neher Andrea N., Bühlmann Florian, Müller Martin, Berendonk Christoph, Sauter Thomas C., Birrenbach Tanja. (2025). Virtual reality for assessment in undergraduate nursing and medical education – a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06867-8

article_title: Determining the metrics of competence in robotic hysterectomy: a systematic review.
citation: Arcamo K, Murugappan S, Larkins K, Mohan H, Costello A, Pendlebury A, McNally O, McBain R. (2025). Determining the metrics of competence in robotic hysterectomy: a systematic review. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02471-6
title: A metric- or competence-based educational pathway improves trainee performance and reduces intraoperative complications compared to a time- or case-based curriculum.
description: The review asserts that a metric- or competence-based educational pathway ensures learners reach the required knowledge, skills, and attitudes before progressing. It states that "Compared to a time- or case-based curriculum, a metric-based system has been shown to improve trainee performance and reduce intraoperative complications." The authors emphasize competency-based progression as an essential component of robotic hysterectomy training, straying from conventional volume-based training requirements.
requirements: Valid, procedure-specific performance metrics that reliably assess skill progression.
target_learning_goals: achieving competency-based progression in robotic surgical skills
key_sources: Arcamo K, Murugappan S, Larkins K, Mohan H, Costello A, Pendlebury A, McNally O, McBain R. (2025). Determining the metrics of competence in robotic hysterectomy: a systematic review. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02471-6

article_title: Freely available, online videos to support neurological physiotherapists and students in task-specific training skill acquisition: a scoping review.
citation: Towersey Nicola C.M., Sasse Kelvin, Stavric Verna, Alder Gemma, Saywell Nicola L. (2024). Freely available, online videos to support neurological physiotherapists and students in task-specific training skill acquisition: a scoping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05545-5
title: Neurological physiotherapists and students should consider the uploading source when judging the educational quality of online videos
description: Because search results are ranked by likes, views and popularity rather than suitability for skill acquisition, learners cannot rely on search ranking to find quality videos. The article advises that "Neurological physiotherapists and students should consider the source of online videos to assist them to assess the educational quality of video resources", since videos from educational institutions or private clinics were more suitable in this review, and prior studies found uploading source valuable for predicting quality.
requirements: Learners must critically evaluate video content rather than trusting search ranking or popularity metrics
constraints: Video duration and likes/dislikes ratio were found unreliable as quality predictors
target_learning_goals: selecting educationally suitable online videos for clinical skill acquisition
examples: Seven of the ten included videos were uploaded by universities and two by clinicians in private practice

Freely available, online videos to support neurological physiotherapists and students in task-specific training skill acquisition: a scoping review.
