article_title: The effectiveness of problem-based learning and case-based learning teaching methods in clinical practical teaching in TACE treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma in China: a bayesian network meta-analysis.
citation: Yan Jingxin, Wen Yonghao, Liu Xinlian, Deng Manjun, Ye Bin, Li Ting, Wang Huanwei, Jia Cui, Liao Jinsong, Zhang Lushun. (2024). The effectiveness of problem-based learning and case-based learning teaching methods in clinical practical teaching in TACE treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma in China: a bayesian network meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05615-8
title: Combine problem-based learning with case-based learning when designing clinical practical teaching for interventional procedures such as TACE
description: The article recommends the combined PBL+CBL teaching mode for TACE clinical education, concluding it "significantly improves the teaching effect and significantly improves the theoretical and surgical operations, meeting the requirements of clinical education." PBL supplies student-centered, question-guided group work while CBL anchors learning in real clinical cases that students investigate before teacher-led analysis. The authors suggest the combination allows more student-teacher interaction and helps forge a preliminary mind of clinical logic.
requirements: Teaching must combine question-guided problem-based group work with real clinical cases that students inquire into before the teacher systematically explains, as the article describes both methods.
constraints: The evidence base is 7 small Chinese studies mixing RCTs and observational designs with subjective outcome measures; the authors state researchers outside China should interpret results with caution and that further high-quality studies are needed.
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge of TACE
practical operational skills
clinical thinking capacity
examples: The meta-analysis pooled studies in which medical students and surgical trainees were assigned to PBL+CBL, PBL, CBL, PBL+TBL or lecture-based learning conditions in TACE teaching in China.
key_sources: Yan Jingxin, Wen Yonghao, Liu Xinlian, Deng Manjun, Ye Bin, Li Ting, Wang Huanwei, Jia Cui, Liao Jinsong, Zhang Lushun. (2024). The effectiveness of problem-based learning and case-based learning teaching methods in clinical practical teaching in TACE treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma in China: a bayesian network meta-analysis. article_title: Essential core competencies for health policy graduates: a multi-method consensus type study.
citation: Doshmangir Leila, Alipouri Sakha Minoo, Mostafavi Hakimeh, Kabiri Neda, Ghaffarifar Saeideh, Takian Amirhossein. (2024). Essential core competencies for health policy graduates: a multi-method consensus type study. Health Research Policy and Systems. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12961-024-01221-8
title: Health policy curricula should be contextually tailored to foster multi-dimensional competencies complementing graduates' specific disciplines
description: The article concludes that curriculum appropriateness and contextual tailoring are crucial to foster multi-dimensional competencies that complement the specific disciplines of future health policy scholars, enabling them to serve their health systems towards health-system goals and sustainable development. This follows from the consensus finding that competencies span research, policy analysis, education, decision-making and multidisciplinary work, and from the observation that graduates often cannot secure positions matching their training.
requirements: Educational content should be continuously updated and identified by stakeholders from diverse disciplines
constraints: The article notes a paucity of attention to modifying higher education curricula in numerous countries, including Iran
target_learning_goals: preparation for academic and non-academic roles
serving health-system goals and sustainable development
examples: Iran's first health policy doctoral curriculum, developed over a decade ago, drew from nursing, medicine, midwifery, health education, social welfare, rehabilitation and management disciplines across four universities.
key_sources: Doshmangir Leila, Alipouri Sakha Minoo, Mostafavi Hakimeh, Kabiri Neda, Ghaffarifar Saeideh, Takian Amirhossein. (2024). Essential core competencies for health policy graduates: a multi-method consensus type study. Health Research Policy and Systems. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12961-024-01221-8

article_title: The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review.
citation: Zhou Haixia, Xian Chengyao, Zhang Kai-Jun, Yang Zhouwen, Li Wei, Tian Jing. (2022). The frequency of assessment tools in arthroscopic training: a systematic review. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2022.2085317
title: Combine subjective and objective assessment tools when evaluating arthroscopic skills training
description: The review recommends that assessment of arthroscopic skill training should not rely on a single tool class. Because objective metrics cannot identify weaknesses in specific skills and subjective scales have context limits, the authors conclude that "combined use of subjective and objective assessment tools can be applied to more situations and skills and can be the optimal way for assessment." Most reviewed studies (60.7%) already combined the two.
requirements: Both tool types must be available: objective metrics for measurable performance and GRS or checklists for rated performance
constraints: Heterogeneity in study designs, methodology and outcome measures precluded quantitative statistical analysis, and no included study directly compared objective with subjective measures
Evidence for other joints besides knee and shoulder was insufficient
target_learning_goals: arthroscopic technical skills, from basic diagnostic arthroscopy to advanced procedures such as meniscectomy
examples: Studies such as Waterman et al. used simulator completion time and probe distance alongside a 14-point diagnostic arthroscopy checklist and ASSET for patient performance.

article_title: GENESISS 2-Generating Standards for In-Situ Simulation project: a systematic mapping review.
citation: Evans Kerry, Woodruff Jenny, Cowley Alison, Bramley Louise, Miles Giulia, Ross Alastair, Cooper Joanne, Baxendale Bryn. (2022). GENESISS 2—Generating Standards for In-Situ Simulation project: a systematic mapping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03401-y
title: Conceptual model of in-situ simulation in healthcare proposing four main ISS functions
description: The GENESISS project's phase-one conceptual model of ISS in healthcare proposes four main ISS functions, depicted in Figure 1 of this review. The model underpins the review's aim to develop evidence-based standards for healthcare professionals, educators and managers implementing ISS interventions in clinical practice. The review states that "A conceptual model of ISS was developed in phase one [33] which proposed four main ISS functions (Fig. 1)", and the mapping review's four evidence categories reflect these functions.
requirements: ISS terms and concepts require standardisation and integrated models of learning are required to provide a more comprehensive and cohesive strategic approach, as the review states
constraints: The model was developed in phase one of the GENESISS project and this article reports its use to frame a mapping review, not a direct empirical validation of the model
target_learning_goals: teamwork and non-technical skills
clinical skills and patient safety
system readiness and safety culture
examples: The review organised 69 included studies into categories reflecting the model's functions: assessment, system readiness and safety cultures, clinical skills and outcomes, and non-technical skills and confidence

GENESISS 2—Generating Standards for In-Situ Simulation project: a systematic mapping review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03401-y

article_title: Advances in e-learning in undergraduate clinical medicine: a systematic review.
citation: Delungahawatta T., Dunne S. S., Hyde S., Halpenny L., McGrath D., O'Regan A., Dunne C. P. (2022). Advances in e-learning in undergraduate clinical medicine: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03773-1
title: Connectivism as the learning-theoretic framing for e-learning in medical education
description: The review frames e-learning as "a pedagogical approach supported by the principles of connectivism learning theory", in which knowledge is "a fluid entity circulated through technology enabled networks". Learners filter information, develop perspectives, log into networks to share understanding, and repeat the cycle. The review uses this framework to analyse how individual e-learning elements collectively affect learning, and notes only 7 of 25 higher-impact studies described theoretical underpinnings.
requirements: Effective e-learning strategies should consider potential learning challenges encountered by the e-learner, and the roles of e-learner, e-teacher and host institution should be defined
constraints: Only 7 of 25 higher-impact reviewed studies (28%) described theoretical underpinnings; the review calls for future work to reference theoretical principles
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in clinical medicine
target_learning_goals: knowledge and skill acquisition in clinical medicine disciplines
examples: The review applied connectivism in its data extraction, examining how and when to use e-learning in undergraduate clinical medical education
key_sources: Delungahawatta T., Dunne S. S., Hyde S., Halpenny L., McGrath D., O'Regan A., Dunne C. P. (2022). Advances in e-learning in undergraduate clinical medicine: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03773-1

article_title: Descriptors for unprofessional behaviours of medical students: a systematic review and categorisation.
citation: Mak-van der Vossen M, van Mook W, van der Burgt S, Kors J, Ket JCF, Croiset G, Kusurkar R. (2017). Descriptors for unprofessional behaviours of medical students: a systematic review and categorisation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0997-x
title: Give educators a common language of behaviour descriptors so unprofessional behaviour is acknowledged and reported
description: The review proposes its framework of 30 descriptors in four themes as a shared vocabulary for medical educators. It argues that a common understanding among educators about denominating unprofessional behaviours could lead to greater consistency in observing, describing and evaluating them, and that the list "might facilitate teachers to see and report unprofessional behaviours, and thus help to solve the problem of 'failure to fail'". Explicitly denominating behaviour serves two goals: creating a culture in which unprofessional behaviour is acknowledged, and targeting students who need extra guidance.
requirements: Educators conduct a conversation with the student about observed behaviours rather than only giving a fail
constraints: Only giving a fail is not enough; the behaviour list indicates which behaviours should prompt a discussion, aiming for contextual interpretation
target_learners: preclinical and clinical undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: professionalism
timely identification and remediation of unprofessional behaviour
examples: The review's Table 1 lists implications: a common language facilitates acknowledgment and discussion among teachers and students, and the behaviour list facilitates teachers to see and report unprofessional behaviours
key_sources: Mak-van der Vossen M, van Mook W, van der Burgt S, Kors J, Ket JCF, Croiset G, Kusurkar R. (2017). Descriptors for unprofessional behaviours of medical students: a systematic review and categorisation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-0997-x

article_title: A systematic review of serious games in medical education: quality of evidence and pedagogical strategy.
citation: Gorbanev Iouri, Agudelo-Londoño Sandra, González Rafael A., Cortes Ariel, Pomares Alexandra, Delgadillo Vivian, Yepes Francisco J., Muñoz Óscar. (2018). A systematic review of serious games in medical education: quality of evidence and pedagogical strategy. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2018.1438718
title: Corpus of 21 peer-reviewed studies of serious games in medical education (2011–2015)
description: A systematically assembled corpus of 21 peer-reviewed journal articles describing or assessing serious games or gamified apps in under- and postgraduate medical education, published 2011–2015 in English, Spanish, or Portuguese. From 494 initial records, 108 duplicates and 365 non-qualifying articles were excluded, leaving 21 studies. The corpus spans specialties including "phono audiology, laboratory, surgery, forensics, pathology, neurosurgery, and urology", with six games in physiology and anatomy, and was coded for study design, MERSQI quality, game attributes, pedagogical strategy, and pedagogical role.
requirements: Articles had to be peer-reviewed and describe or assess serious games or gamified apps in medical education for medical students and doctors, excluding patient-education games and non-gamified apps
constraints: The 5-year time frame was chosen due to high speed of innovation and obsolescence in games; no Spanish- or Portuguese-language games were found despite targeted searching
target_learning_goals: knowledge acquisition and retention
clinical skill development
perceptions and motivation
examples: Games coded in Table 3 include Mediman, Uro Island, DKA simulator, Triage Trainer, and NeuroTouch simulator, classified by type, platform, genre, pedagogical role, and strategy

article_title: Do final-year medical students have sufficient prescribing competencies? A systematic literature review.
citation: Brinkman, D. J., Tichelaar, J., Graaf, S., Otten, R. H. J., Richir, M. C., and van Agtmael, M. A. (2018). Do final‐year medical students have sufficient prescribing competencies? A systematic literature review. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.13491
title: Core drug and disease lists for prescribing curricula
description: Several descriptive articles reviewed define core lists of drugs and diseases that medical students should know for prescribing education. Orme et al. described "a list of 120 ‘core drugs’ that students should know in detail, and 47 drugs that students should be familiar with" plus core disease lists; Maxwell and Walley described 201 core drugs and 148 core diseases; Ross and Maxwell refined this into 98 drug classes and 125 therapeutic problems; Baker et al. developed a validated list of 100 commonly prescribed drugs based on prescribing data and a survey of 148 FY1 doctors.
requirements: Intended for use in undergraduate CPT curriculum design and prescribing teaching
constraints: Most descriptive articles (96%) were based on expert opinion rather than empirical evaluation
target_learning_goals: knowledge of core drugs and diseases for safe prescribing
examples: Baker et al. (2011) built a core list of 100 commonly prescribed drugs from a retrospective analysis of prescribing data from primary and secondary care combined with a cross-sectional survey among 148 FY1 doctors

A systematic literature review. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.13491

article_title: A meta-analytic perspective on the valid use of subjective human judgement to make medical school admission decisions.
citation: Kreiter Clare, O'Shea Marie, Bruen Catherine, Murphy Paul, Pawlikowska Teresa. (2018). A meta-analytic perspective on the valid use of subjective human judgement to make medical school admission decisions. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2018.1522225
title: Use constrained optimization rather than holistic review to incorporate subjective policy judgements transparently in admission decisions
description: The review argues that mechanical methods can incorporate subjective judgements in quantitative form, with weights reflecting explicitly stated values. It identifies constrained optimization (CO) as the most explicit and versatile such framework: 'CO methods are preferable to holistic review because they are transparent and treat all applicants equally while providing flexibility for programmes seeking to implement both subjective and objective policy decisions'. This follows from the meta-analytic finding that mechanical combination outperforms clinical judgement.
requirements: Subjective decisions about class composition and applicant attributes must be encoded as explicit weights or constraints within the optimization
constraints: Decisions about the relative importance of attributes such as communication skills, intellectual ability, and ethnicity/race remain inherently subjective because objective evidence of their relative importance does not exist
target_learning_goals: fair, transparent, and valid selection decisions incorporating subjective policy values
examples: The article cites the authors' prior work applying constrained optimization to admission decisions, including generating an alternate list when using constrained optimization to make admission decisions
key_sources: Kreiter Clare, O'Shea Marie, Bruen Catherine, Murphy Paul, Pawlikowska Teresa. (2018). A meta-analytic perspective on the valid use of subjective human judgement to make medical school admission decisions. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2018.1522225

article_title: Use of Commercial Off-The-Shelf Devices for the Detection of Manual Gestures in Surgery: Systematic Literature Review.
citation: Alvarez-Lopez F, Maina MF, Saigí-Rubió F. (2019). Use of Commercial Off-The-Shelf Devices for the Detection of Manual Gestures in Surgery: Systematic Literature Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/11925
title: Commercial off-the-shelf touchless gesture-based interfaces as a solution for sterile surgical human-computer interaction
description: The review organizes its field around COTS devices enabling touchless gesture-based human-computer interaction in surgical environments, where touching a mouse, keyboard or touchscreen breaks asepsis and antisepsis protocols. The article defines the category: "The term COTS refers to a device that can be taken from a shelf, that is, sold over the counter", noting they are low-cost, wireless, ergonomic, and allow manipulation with 6 degrees of freedom. The review uses this framework to classify 86 studies by device (Microsoft Kinect, Leap Motion Controller, Myo armband, cameras), clinical area, and type of use.
requirements: Sterile environments requiring touchless interaction, since hand contact with input devices alters the pace of surgery and breaks asepsis protocols
constraints: Studies on COTS devices requiring hand contact (ie, Wii) were excluded from the analysis
Early touchless systems were very expensive and inaccurate and required calibration and a complex setup
target_learning_goals: motor skills learning in minimally invasive surgery
touchless interaction with medical images and systems
examples: The review's Tables 1-3 summarize included studies by device: 43 on Microsoft Kinect, 31 on the Leap Motion Controller, and others on cameras, the Myo armband, and general touchless interaction
key_sources: Alvarez-Lopez F, Maina MF, Saigí-Rubió F. (2019). Use of Commercial Off-The-Shelf Devices for the Detection of Manual Gestures in Surgery: Systematic Literature Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/11925

article_title: Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges
citation: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661
title: Cognitive load theory applied to AR-based learning: germane load fostered, extraneous load minimized, intrinsic load adjusted
description: The review presents cognitive load theory as a relevant theory for AR-based physics learning: working memory is very limited in capacity and duration and may become overloaded, impeding learning. Learning environments induce three mutually additive load types — germane load from learning processes relevant to constructing target knowledge, extraneous load from information not relevant to learning, and intrinsic load from the inherent complexity of the task. For effective learning, "germane load should be fostered, extraneous load should be minimized and intrinsic load should be adjusted (e.g., by segmenting information)". The review links this to AR design via Mayer's multimedia principles, particularly spatial and temporal contiguity and segmenting.
requirements: AR learning environments must foster germane load, minimize extraneous load, and adjust intrinsic load, e.g., by segmenting information.
constraints: If learning with multiple representations is not introduced carefully, it may result in cognitive overload, per Ainsworth's account cited in the review.
target_learners: physics students at school and university level using AR applications
target_learning_goals: managing cognitive load when learning physics concepts with AR visualizations
examples: The review notes AR tools can place words and images near animated or physical objects, e.g., overlaying textual descriptions on real-world car engine parts, consistent with spatial contiguity.
key_sources: Andrej Vidak, Iva Movre Šapić, Vanes Mešić, Vjeran Gomzi. (2023). Augmented Reality Technology in Teaching about Physics: A systematic review of opportunities and challenges. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci11110661

article_title: Effects of Physics Teaching Materials on Student Critical Thinking and Creative Thinking Skills: A Meta-Analysis
citation: Serli Ahzari, Asrizal, Usmeldi. (2024). Effects of Physics Teaching Materials on Student' Critical Thinking and Creative Thinking Skills: A Meta-Analysis. Jurnal Penelitian Pembelajaran Fisika (JPPF). https://jppf.ppj.unp.ac.id/index.php/jppf/article/view/129627
title: Constructivist learning theory as the explanatory account for high effect sizes of modules and worksheets
description: The article interprets its meta-analytic findings through constructivist learning theory, which it describes as positing that "active engagement in knowledge construction is crucial for deep learning." It argues well-designed physics modules promote deeper cognitive processing through guided exploration and reflection, and that student worksheets scaffold higher-order thinking when they include explicit prompts for analysis and evaluation. This account is offered as the authors' interpretation of why modules and worksheets showed the largest effects.
requirements: Materials must actively engage learners in knowledge construction rather than passive reading
constraints: The article presents this as an interpretive alignment with literature, not as a mechanism tested within the meta-analysis
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
creative thinking skills
examples: The discussion links the module effect size (ES = 3.93) to constructivist principles citing Chen (2023), and worksheet scaffolding to Yulkifli et al. (2022)
key_sources: Serli Ahzari, Asrizal, Usmeldi. (2024). Effects of Physics Teaching Materials on Student' Critical Thinking and Creative Thinking Skills: A Meta-Analysis. Jurnal Penelitian Pembelajaran Fisika (JPPF). https://jppf.ppj.unp.ac.id/index.php/jppf/article/view/129627

article_title: Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review.
citation: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/
title: Combine or alternate assessment tools because no single tool covers all patient safety competency domains
description: The review states that each tool has its own strengths and limitations, so complementing methods must be sought to overcome these weaknesses. Because "no tool covered all the patient safety competency domains", the review recommends that tools should be combined or alternated, while noting that the various tools cover the domains unevenly.
requirements: Multiple assessment tools must be available covering complementary patient safety domains.
constraints: The various tools cover the domains unevenly, and more work is needed on 'contributing to safety culture', 'optimizing human and environmental factors', and 'recognizing, responding to, and disclosing adverse events'.
target_learners: Physicians, residents, medical students, nurses, and nursing students in hospital settings
target_learning_goals: Comprehensive assessment of patient safety competencies across all six Canadian Safety Competencies Framework domains
examples: The review found 25 tools assessing 'managing safety risks' but only four measuring 'optimising human and environmental factors', illustrating the uneven coverage that motivates combining tools.
key_sources: Okuyama Ayako, Martowirono Kartinie, Bijnen Bart. (2011). Assessing the patient safety competencies of healthcare professionals: a systematic review. BMJ Quality & Safety. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3203526/

article_title: Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review.
citation: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/
title: Competence-performance gap in simulated procedural skills assessment
description: The review raises the concern that certifying competence in a simulated setting does not guarantee the skill transfers to the workplace, framing the challenge of teaching for transfer. It states that "The assertion of competence in a simulated setting does not, however, guarantee the transferability of the skill to the workplace", and that medical educators must facilitate students to be consistent in competent performance irrespective of whether the setting is simulated or an emotionally charged clinical area. Engum's tool, in which students performed real rather than simulated cannulation, is presented as addressing this potential gap.
requirements: Assessment approaches must consider whether simulated competence reflects actual clinical performance
constraints: The transfer claim is supported by unpublished data cited by the authors (MM, PFR, 2012)
target_learners: medical students assessed in simulated settings before practice
target_learning_goals: transfer of procedural skills from simulation to clinical practice
examples: Engum's IV cannulation tool assessed students performing real rather than simulated procedures, which the review says addresses the potential competence-performance gap
key_sources: Morris Marie C., Gallagher Tom K., Ridgway Paul F. (2012). Tools used to assess medical students competence in procedural skills at the end of a primary medical degree: a systematic review. Medical Education Online. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3427596/

article_title: Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies.
citation: McManus IC, Dewberry Chris, Nicholson Sandra, Dowell Jonathan S, Woolf Katherine, Potts Henry WW. (2013). Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3827328/
title: Construct-level predictive validity (CLPV) framework for interpreting selection-measure validity
description: The article develops and applies the construct-level predictive validity framework following Hunter, Schmidt and Le (2006): the estimate of the "true predictor-outcome correlation" between the underlying construct measured by a selection test and the underlying knowledge measured in later examinations, correcting for restriction of range, measurement unreliability and right-censorship. It argues that raw correlations within selected entrants are of "little real interest" because selectors need to know how all applicants would have performed. The framework is operationalized via an MCMC-adapted HSL method that yields standard errors and confidence intervals, and is applied in a meta-regression of 57 coefficients from six UK cohorts.
requirements: Requires predictor distributions in both entrants and applicants, plus reliability estimates for predictor (in applicants) and outcome (in entrants)
Requires the Hunter-Schmidt-Le method adapted for right-censored predictors and ordinal/binary outcomes via MCMC
constraints: The Hunter et al. method can produce erroneous results if the predictor measure is heavily right-censored, as with A-levels where many candidates hold maximum grades
CLPV standard errors must be estimated from MCMC chain variability; equivalent N is about a quarter of actual N
target_learners: medical school applicants and entrants in UK selection contexts
target_learning_goals: predicting subsequent undergraduate and postgraduate medical training performance from selection measures
examples: Applied to six UK cohorts (Westminster, 1980, 1985, 1990, UCLMS, UKCAT-12) covering entry years 1972–2009, yielding 57 CLPV coefficients meta-regressed by predictor, outcome stage and year of entry
key_sources: McManus IC, Dewberry Chris, Nicholson Sandra, Dowell Jonathan S, Woolf Katherine, Potts Henry WW. (2013). Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3827328/

article_title: Educating medical trainees on medication reconciliation: a systematic review.
citation: Ramjaun Aliya, Sudarshan Monisha, Patakfalvi Laura, Tamblyn Robyn, Meguerditchian Ari N. (2015). Educating medical trainees on medication reconciliation: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4373246/
title: Combine didactic sessions, role-play and experiential learning to educate medical students in medication reconciliation
description: The review concludes that a combination of didactic sessions, role-play exercises and experiential learning at the undergraduate level may be effective in educating medical students in how to conduct medication reconciliation. None of the studies concerning the education of medical students relied solely on didactic methods, and 5 out of 7 included an experiential component.
requirements: Interventions should combine didactic teaching with active practice components rather than relying solely on didactic methods
constraints: None of the included student studies assessed more objective outcomes such as increase in skill or accuracy in performing medication reconciliation
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students (clerkship and pre-clinical years)
target_learning_goals: Conducting accurate medication reconciliation
Safe patient transitions of care
examples: Bray-Hall et al. combined introductory didactic sessions, faculty role-play demonstration, self-study, direct patient care and small-group reflection
Lindquist et al. used pharmacist instruction, a standardized patient demonstration, small-group medication history-taking and class reflection
key_sources: Ramjaun Aliya, Sudarshan Monisha, Patakfalvi Laura, Tamblyn Robyn, Meguerditchian Ari N. (2015). Educating medical trainees on medication reconciliation: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4373246/

article_title: Use of theory in computer-based interventions to reduce alcohol use among adolescents and young adults: a systematic review.
citation: Tebb Kathleen P., Erenrich Rebecca K., Jasik Carolyn Bradner, Berna Mark S., Lester James C., Ozer Elizabeth M. (2016). Use of theory in computer-based interventions to reduce alcohol use among adolescents and young adults: a systematic review. BMC Public Health 16, 517. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-016-3183-x
title: Corpus of 42 unique computer-based alcohol interventions for youth (100 articles, 1999–2014)
description: The review assembles a corpus of 42 unique computer-based interventions targeting alcohol use among adolescents and young adults, drawn from 100 retained articles published between 1999 and 2014. The search "yielded a total of 600 unique articles", of which 500 were excluded. Thirty of the 42 interventions were studied exclusively in the United States; 33 were delivered in school settings and the remainder in home or clinic settings, with study sample sizes ranging from 59 to 20,150 participants.
requirements: Included interventions delivered their main component via computer, tablet or smartphone and targeted alcohol use among ages 12-21
constraints: Interventions intended to treat a substance use disorder, non-English articles, protocols, and studies without outcomes were excluded
target_learning_goals: alcohol use prevention and reduction
examples: Nearly all interventions had at least one study measuring alcohol use as a primary outcome (n = 37); other common outcomes included binge drinking (n = 17) and perceived alcohol norms (n = 14)
key_sources: Tebb Kathleen P., Erenrich Rebecca K., Jasik Carolyn Bradner, Berna Mark S., Lester James C., Ozer Elizabeth M. (2016). Use of theory in computer-based interventions to reduce alcohol use among adolescents and young adults: a systematic review. BMC Public Health 16, 517. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-016-3183-x

article_title: Systematic review of the effect of training interventions on the skills of health professionals in promoting health behaviour, with meta-analysis of subsequent effects on patient health behaviours.
citation: Hatfield Thomas G., Withers Thomas M., Greaves Colin J. (2020). Systematic review of the effect of training interventions on the skills of health professionals in promoting health behaviour, with meta-analysis of subsequent effects on patient health behaviours. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-020-05420-1
title: Healthcare professional training for behaviour change interventions should combine educational and practical elements rather than education alone
description: The review concludes that effective training of healthcare professionals who deliver health behaviour change interventions should include both educational components (e.g. presentations, workshops) and practical components (e.g. opportunities to practise techniques learnt, case study evaluation). In the narrative synthesis, "Training using both educational and practical elements seemed to be more effective, significantly improving 52% of outcomes, whereas education only training significantly improved only 23% of outcomes." The review advises policymakers that education-only components are unlikely to suffice.
requirements: Training must be delivered to healthcare professionals whose role involves contact with patients and delivery of care or treatment
Practical elements must provide opportunities to practise techniques learnt, such as case study evaluation or practising taught elements
constraints: Evidence base is 12 RCTs all judged high risk of bias for delivery-quality outcomes
The advantage of combined training is a descriptive percentage comparison, not a tested difference
target_learners: Physiotherapists and other healthcare professionals delivering health behaviour change interventions
target_learning_goals: Communication skills for behaviour change counselling
Delivery of intended intervention content
examples: Nine of the 12 included studies added practical elements such as providing opportunities to practice techniques learnt on top of educational elements like presentations and workshops
key_sources: Hatfield Thomas G., Withers Thomas M., Greaves Colin J. (2020). Systematic review of the effect of training interventions on the skills of health professionals in promoting health behaviour, with meta-analysis of subsequent effects on patient health behaviours. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-020-05420-1

article_title: A meta-analysis of the effects of non-traditional teaching methods on the critical thinking abilities of nursing students.
citation: Lee JuHee, Lee Yoonju, Gong SaeLom, Bae Juyeon, Choi Moonki. (2016). A meta-analysis of the effects of non-traditional teaching methods on the critical thinking abilities of nursing students. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5025580/
title: Implement critical thinking education continuously throughout a curriculum rather than in a single course
description: The article concludes that non-traditional teaching methods improve critical thinking dispositions, but that gains fade without reinforcement: disposition scores "gradually decreased as time passed, showing no significant difference after 2 years" in the one long-term follow-up. It therefore recommends that "teaching and learning methods for the improvement of critical thinking must be implemented continuously throughout a curriculum." This principle distributes critical-thinking interventions across multiple courses rather than concentrating them in one.
requirements: Interventions must use non-traditional teaching and learning methods (i.e., no lectures) targeting critical thinking outcomes
constraints: Effects were not sustained after two years in the single study measuring long-term outcomes; the article states sufficient effects cannot be anticipated after one or two semesters in a single course
target_learning_goals: critical thinking dispositions
critical thinking skills
examples: The meta-analysis included interventions lasting from 8 weeks to two semesters, such as PBL spanning two semesters at 3–6 h weekly for 28 weeks, and concept mapping lessons of 40 min biweekly for 16 weeks
key_sources: Lee JuHee, Lee Yoonju, Gong SaeLom, Bae Juyeon, Choi Moonki. (2016). A meta-analysis of the effects of non-traditional teaching methods on the critical thinking abilities of nursing students. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5025580/

article_title: Comparing a Program Implemented under the Constraints of an RCT and in the Wild
citation: Newman, D., Lazarev, V., & Zacamy, J. (2016). Comparing a Program Implemented Under the Constraints of an RCT and in the Wild. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Content-literacy instructional framework centered on metacognitive conversation with teacher-leader team meetings
description: The program evaluated in both contexts is an instructional framework helping teachers support discipline-specific literacy and learning in content areas. At its center is metacognitive conversation, carried on internally through reading and reasoning routines and externally as teacher and students talk about reading, with extensive reading including increased in-class opportunities to practice academic texts. It targets learning dispositions as well as literacy skills and knowledge. For the i3 project it was modified for scalability: teachers of ELA, biology, and history were included to build a school-wide teacher community, and teacher leaders were developed to convene monthly team meetings supporting implementation.
requirements: Each teacher was offered 10 days (65 hours) of subject-specific professional development over twelve months, delivered through a summer institute
constraints: A constraint on RCT schools was that teachers could not have participated in program training prior to the project, whereas Scale-up schools included teachers who may have already been familiar with the program
target_learners: high school students in ELA, biology, and history classes
target_learning_goals: discipline-specific literacy skills, knowledge, and learning dispositions
examples: The professional development was designed to change teachers' understanding of their role in adolescent literacy development and to build capacity for literacy instruction in the academic disciplines.
key_sources: Newman, D., Lazarev, V., & Zacamy, J. (2016). Comparing a Program Implemented Under the Constraints of an RCT and in the Wild. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567633

article_title: Testing the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Mathematics Intervention: A Conceptual Replication Study
citation: Doabler, C. T., Clarke, B., Kosty, D. B., Kurtz-Nelson, E., Fien, H., Smolkowski, K., & Baker, S. K. (2016). Testing the efficacy of a tier 2 mathematics intervention: A conceptual replication study. Exceptional Children, 83, 92–110. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402916660084
title: Counterfactual variability account of replication outcomes in intervention research
description: The article advances the account that the control condition, or counterfactual, is an essential component of intervention research because it lets researchers rule out alternative explanations of treatment effects, but that its nature and strength vary by location and improve over time. As the article puts it, "an intervention implemented in a similar fashion to the same population may produce vastly different results based on the nature and strength of the counterfactual." It applies this account by deliberately varying the counterfactual's instructional context in the Boston replication, where core programs were WWC-rated effective, and treats a strengthened counterfactual as capable of attenuating observed treatment effects.
requirements: Replication studies must document the instructional dimensions of the counterfactual, as this study did through teacher surveys and direct observations of core mathematics instruction
constraints: The article notes a study establishing an intervention as evidence based relative to one counterfactual could lose its treatment effect if the counterfactual shifts or strengthens in a subsequent replication
target_learning_goals: whole-number concepts and early number sense
examples: The replication documented its counterfactual via surveys and observations: District A primarily used Scott Foresman and District B enVisionMath, both WWC-rated effective, and ROOTS materials were not used during core instruction
key_sources: Doabler, C. T., Clarke, B., Kosty, D. B., Kurtz-Nelson, E., Fien, H., Smolkowski, K., & Baker, S. K. (2016). Testing the efficacy of a tier 2 mathematics intervention: A conceptual replication study. Exceptional Children, 83, 92–110. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402916660084

article_title: Use of Portfolio Assessment Technique in Teaching Map Sketching and Location in Secondary School Geography in Jos, Nigeria
citation: Ugodulunwa, C., & Wakjissa, S. (2015). Use of Portfolio Assessment Technique in Teaching Map Sketching and Location in Secondary School Geography in Jos, Nigeria. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(17). http://www.iiste.org
title: Constructivism as the theoretical basis for portfolio assessment
description: The article grounds portfolio assessment in constructivist theory attributed to Piaget and Vygotsky, in which learners actively build knowledge. It states that "human beings generate and build their own knowledge and meaning from an interaction between their ideas and experiences", and that the teacher dialogues with learners until mastery is attained. Portfolio assessment is presented as a student-centred strategy in which instruction and assessment are planned together, with portfolios serving reflection and demonstration of responsibility for learning.
requirements: Instruction and assessment should be built together, with what is assessed and how planned alongside instruction
target_learning_goals: map sketching and location skills
constructing geography knowledge from experience
examples: The experimental group submitted work samples over 12 weeks; the best sample out of every four submissions was selected, scored, evaluated and recorded for each student.
key_sources: Ugodulunwa, C., & Wakjissa, S. (2015). Use of Portfolio Assessment Technique in Teaching Map Sketching and Location in Secondary School Geography in Jos, Nigeria. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(17). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1079911

article_title: Effects of an E-Learning Module on Students' Attitudes in an Electronics Class
citation: Daniel M. Getuno, Joel K. Kiboss, Johnson M. Changeiywo, & Leo B. Ogola. (2015). Effects of an E-Learning Module on Students' Attitudes in an Electronics Class. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.36. https://www.iiste.org
title: Cognitive flexibility theory as the guiding framework for the e-learning module's instructional design
description: The study is based on Spiro's theory of cognitive flexibility, which the authors say "enables teachers to promote the use of educational technologies in the learning process" and which guided the instructional design of the Transistors e-learning module. Following Kearsley (2000), the article sums up its principles as four: learning activities must provide multiple representations of content; instructional materials should avoid oversimplifying the content domain and support context-dependent knowledge; instruction should be case-based and emphasise knowledge construction rather than transmission of information; and knowledge sources should be highly interconnected rather than compartmentalised. The theory encourages learners to integrate various aspects or perspectives of knowledge across different learning contexts.
requirements: A flexible teaching environment providing the variability needed to present complex and ill-structured knowledge domains
constraints: The article applies it to one topic, Transistors, in a Kenyan polytechnic Electronics course
target_learners: first-year Electronic Engineering diploma students in Kenyan National Polytechnics
target_learning_goals: flexible integration of multiple perspectives on Electronics content
positive attitudes toward the topic studied
examples: The e-learning module's instructional design in the topic Transistors was guided by the theory's four principles as summarised by Kearsley (2000)
key_sources: Daniel M. Getuno, Joel K. Kiboss, Johnson M. Changeiywo, & Leo B. Ogola. (2015). Effects of an E-Learning Module on Students' Attitudes in an Electronics Class. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.36. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1086475

article_title: The Effects of Two Different Instructional Programmes on Literacy Skills of Kindergarten Children
citation: Gahwaji, N. (2016). The Effects Of Two Different Instructional Programmes On Literacy Skills Of Kindergarten Children. Journal of International Education Research, 12(1). https://journals.cluteonline.com/index.php/JIER
title: Computerized literacy skill assessment test of 25 questions
description: The author designed a literacy skill assessment test based on concepts taught in both instructional programmes, hosted on computers as a standalone programme so it appeared similar to the TIP and game content. "The skill assessment test contained 25 questions, which enable us in evaluating the literacy skills of the participating children", covering letters, words, rhymes, missing letters and pictures without names. It was reviewed by MOE officials and kindergarten teachers and updated from their feedback.
requirements: Content was the same for children instructed with TIP and with the educational games programme
constraints: The test was centered on the postulates of development theory, with continuous reinforcement and hints provided during administration
target_learning_goals: recognizing letters by shape and phonics and other emergent literacy concepts
examples: Each child spent 15 minutes in the computer lab taking the test in the presence of a teacher and the author
key_sources: Gahwaji, N. (2016). The Effects Of Two Different Instructional Programmes On Literacy Skills Of Kindergarten Children. Journal of International Education Research, 12(1). https://journals.cluteonline.com/index.php/JIER

article_title: Technology Integration and the Effect on Mathematics Fact Fluency in the Middle East
citation: Letwinsky, K. M., & Berry, M. D. (2017). Technology Integration and the Effect on Mathematics Fact Fluency in the Middle East. Journal of International Education and Leadership, 7(1). http://www.jielusa.org/
title: Combine technology-based and traditional practice rather than replacing traditional drill with technology when building basic fact fluency
description: The article recommends that educators deeply examine the value and use of technology for mathematics and adopt a combination of teaching and learning experiences with consistency over time. The authors state results indicated a "both…and" approach, rather than an "either…or" perspective, because technology did not outperform traditional practice for fact fluency.
requirements: Consistent reinforcement of basic facts over time, since the article states consistent reinforcement of basic facts is important in developing mathematical fluency.
constraints: The study found technology did not significantly improve learning of the treatment group, so technology alone is not supported as a replacement for traditional practice.
target_learning_goals: automatic recall of basic multiplication facts (fluency in speed and accuracy)
examples: The treatment group used Mathletics.com three times a week for 15 minutes over three weeks while the control used paper-and-pencil drill on the same schedule; both improved in accuracy, and the control improved more in speed.
key_sources: Letwinsky, K. M., & Berry, M. D. (2017). Technology Integration and the Effect on Mathematics Fact Fluency in the Middle East. Journal of International Education and Leadership, 7(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1153618

article_title: Effectiveness of Constructivist Approach on Academic Achievement in Science at Secondary Level
citation: Samaresh Adak. (2017). Effectiveness of constructivist approach on academic achievement in science at secondary level. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2017.3298
title: The constructivist 7E instructional model
description: The 7E model is an instructional model for constructivism developed by the BSCS team with Roger Bybee, extending the 5Es model for science teaching. The article states that "the process is explained by employing 7 E's. They are Elicit, Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate and Expand." In this study it was operationalised as unit-wise lesson plans with teaching aids such as pictures, chart papers and models, implemented over three weeks with Class IX physical science students.
requirements: Unit-wise lesson plans based on the 7E model, supplemented with teaching aids such as pictures, chart papers and models
constraints: In this study the model was implemented only with Class IX students, in physical science, over three weeks, at one Bengali-medium school
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in physical science concepts
examples: Unit-wise 7E lesson plans were taught to the experimental section for three weeks while the control section received traditional instruction
key_sources: Samaresh Adak. (2017). Effectiveness of constructivist approach on academic achievement in science at secondary level. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2017.3298

article_title: Textbooks Thematic Based Character Education on Thematic Learning Primary School: An Influence
citation: Wuryani, M. T., Roemintoyo, & Yamtinah, S. (2018). Textbooks thematic based character education on thematic learning primary school: An influence. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 4(2), 75-81. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.4.2.75
title: Contextual learning theory as the design basis for character-embedded thematic textbooks
description: The article grounds its textbook development in contextual theory, under which "learning will meaningful when associated with daily life." The teaching materials are therefore built by showing illustrations of daily events containing character education, and every theme lesson is related to character-education elements, producing reciprocity between thematic learning and character education. The authors also invoke Piaget's constructivist theory, emphasizing students actively building their own knowledge through problem-solving, drawing conclusions, and formulating ideas in their own words.
requirements: Learning content must be associated with daily life for meaning to arise
target_learning_goals: meaningful thematic learning
character formation
examples: The developed textbook shows illustrations of daily events containing character education and links each theme lesson to character-education elements
key_sources: Wuryani, M. T., Roemintoyo, & Yamtinah, S. (2018). Textbooks thematic based character education on thematic learning primary school: An influence. International Journal of Educational Methodology, 4(2), 75-81. https://doi.org/10.12973/ijem.4.2.75

article_title: Effects of Inquiry-Based Agriscience Instruction and Subject Matter-Based Instruction on Student Argumentation Skills
citation: Andrew C. Thoron, Brian E. Myers. (2012). Effects of Inquiry–based Agriscience Instruction and Subject Matter–based Instruction on Student Argumentation Skills. Journal of Agricultural Education, 53(2), 58–69. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2012.02058
title: Constructivism as the guiding philosophical perspective for inquiry-based agriscience instruction
description: The study adopts constructivism as its guiding philosophical perspective, grounded in Piaget's Theory of Cognitive Development and Vygotsky's Sociocultural Theory. Constructivism concerns the role of the learner with the teacher as facilitator, and shifts the focus from "how knowledge is acquired" to "how it [knowledge] is constructed" (Schunk, 2004, as cited). The article uses this framework to explain why inquiry-based instruction, which places students first in the learning process, should develop argumentation skills.
requirements: Teachers act as facilitators who manage interactions and keep teams focused on progress rather than dominating classroom conversation.
constraints: The framework is applied to secondary agriscience education contexts in this study.
target_learning_goals: argumentation skills
evidence-based reasoning in science
examples: The study's conceptual model depicts interactions in an inquiry-based classroom, with static attributes collected during the investigation and the teaching and learning process describing the inquiry-based process.
key_sources: Andrew C. Thoron, Brian E. Myers. (2012). Effects of Inquiry–based Agriscience Instruction and Subject Matter–based Instruction on Student Argumentation Skills. Journal of Agricultural Education, 53(2), 58–69. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2012.02058

article_title: Testing the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention: Findings of Year 1
citation: Christian Doabler, Ben Clarke, Keith Smolkowski, Hank Fien, Scott Baker. (2014). Testing the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention: Findings of Year 1. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://www.sree.org/
title: COSTI observation instrument for instructional intensity
description: The Classroom Observations of Student-Teacher Interactions (COSTI) is "a low-inference, frequency-based observation instrument" used to measure instructional intensity in ROOTS groups. It targets seven instructional behaviors: teacher demonstrations, guided practice for groups and individuals, independent practice for groups and individuals, student mistakes, and teacher-provided academic feedback. Trained observers conducted all observations, with each ROOTS group observed three times across the 10 intervention weeks.
requirements: Trained observers meeting acceptable reliability criteria
Three observations per group across the intervention period
constraints: Previous evidence links COSTI behaviors to reading and mathematics gains, which the article describes as preliminary
target_learners: kindergarten students in small-group math interventions
target_learning_goals: measuring student-teacher instructional interactions
examples: Round-1 observations yielded rate-per-minute descriptive statistics for each of the seven behaviors in both group-size conditions
key_sources: Christian Doabler, Ben Clarke, Keith Smolkowski, Hank Fien, Scott Baker. (2014). Testing the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention: Findings of Year 1. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562831

article_title: Reporting Randomized Controlled Trials in Education
citation: Evan Mayo-Wilson, Sean Grant, Paul Montgomery. (2014). Reporting Randomized Controlled Trials in Education. SREE Fall 2014 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: CONSORT-SPI: an extension of the CONSORT Statement for social and psychological intervention trials, developed in five phases
description: CONSORT-SPI is an official Extension of the CONSORT Statement for Social and Psychological Interventions, under development "to provide tailored guidance for reporting RCTs in education and related fields". It is being built through five phases: a literature review of guidelines and reporting quality, a modified Delphi process, a formal consensus meeting, writing of guideline documents including an explanation and elaboration (E&E) document, and dissemination with simultaneous publication and endorsement in multiple journals. At submission, three phases were complete and the Delphi process and consensus meeting had yielded a checklist of reporting items for the essential content of reports of social and psychological intervention RCTs.
requirements: Items in the checklist are based on empirical evidence of and expert consensus opinion about their importance to RCTs in education and related disciplines
constraints: At the time of this submission, only three of the five phases (literature review, Delphi process, consensus meeting) had been completed; the E&E document and dissemination were still pending
target_learning_goals: accurate, comprehensive, and transparent reporting of randomised controlled trials in education
examples: A modified Delphi process with 384 stakeholders from 32 countries (including 46 education researchers, 19 of them journal editors) ranked items on a 10-point Likert scale across two rounds; a three-day consensus meeting in Oxford in March 2014 with 31 participants finalised the checklist via anonymous voting
key_sources: Evan Mayo-Wilson, Sean Grant, Paul Montgomery. (2014). Reporting Randomized Controlled Trials in Education. SREE Fall 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562867

article_title: Testing the Immediate and Long-Term Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention
citation: Ben Clarke, Christian Doabler, Keith Smolkowski, Evangeline Kurtz Nelson, Hank Fien, Scott K. Baker & Derek Kosty (2016). Testing the Immediate and Long-Term Efficacy of a Tier 2 Kindergarten Mathematics Intervention. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2015.1116034
title: Conceptual understanding and procedural fluency as interdependent constructs developing reciprocally
description: The article's framework for how the ROOTS curriculum supports mathematics development holds that focused whole-number content and explicit instructional design jointly impact two knowledge forms. The authors "consider conceptual understanding and procedural fluency as interdependent constructs that develop in tandem and reciprocally," citing Rittle-Johnson, Siegler, and Alibali (2001) and Wu (1999), and hold that these in turn impact overall mathematics achievement. ROOTS instruction is designed to build both forms simultaneously.
requirements: Instruction addressing both conceptual understanding and procedural fluency rather than one in isolation
target_learners: Kindergarten students at risk in mathematics
target_learning_goals: Whole-number conceptual understanding
Procedural fluency
examples: ROOTS lessons pair work with counting blocks and ten frames (conceptual) with writing and solving single-digit addition expressions (procedural), as assessed by the RAENS items

article_title: Using a Concept Cartoon© Method to Address Elementary School Students' Ideas about Natural Phenomena
citation: Michaela Minárechová. (2016). Using a concept cartoon© method to address elementary school students' ideas about natural phenomena. European Journal of Science and Mathematics Education, Vol. 4, No. 2, 214-228. https://ejmste.com
title: Concept cartoons© as a visual, cognitive-conflict-based method for inducing conceptual change
description: Concept cartoons© present an everyday situation visually with dialog bubbles from 3–5 fictional characters whose differing views create conflict that leads discussants to argumentation. The article states "Individual statements of these characters support formation of conflicts which lead discussants to argumentation", aiming to induce cognitive conflict that disturbs students' current expectations and drives conceptual change. Most character views are naïve but appear logical, and one is usually scientifically acceptable; statements are drawn from research on the most common children's views.

constraints: The article notes conceptual change is a very complex process and students' ideas are very resistant to change

argumentation and reasoning with evidence

article_title: Congruence in Parent-Teacher Communication: Implications for the Efficacy of CBC for Students with Behavioral Concerns
citation: S. Andrew Garbacz, Susan M. Sheridan, Natalie A. Koziol, Kyongboon Kwon, Shannon R. Holmes. (2015). Congruence in Parent–Teacher Communication: Implications for the Efficacy of CBC for Students With Behavioral Concerns. School Psychology Review, 44(2), 150–168. https://www.nasponline.org/publications/periodicals/spr
title: Congruent communication as a specific form of relational congruence in the parent–teacher relationship
description: The article defines congruent communication as "a special form of relational congruence; it is the degree to which parents and teachers view their communication in a similar fashion." It extends global relational congruence (Sheridan et al., 2004; Minke et al., 2014) by isolating communication as a specific relationship element, and operationalizes it dyadically with a distance score computed from parent and teacher responses to the PTRS-II Communication-to-Other items, where higher scores indicate less congruence. The construct is framed as a main process feature of CBC and a candidate active ingredient.
requirements: Requires parallel self-report items from both dyad members (parent and teacher) at each time point
constraints: Measurement relied on one subscale whose full psychometric properties have not been established; the construct's operationalization is novel and alternative conceptualizations exist
target_learners: Kindergarten through third-grade children with behavioral concerns
target_learning_goals: Social skills (cooperation, assertion, self-control) across home and school settings
examples: Congruence scores were computed as the square root of the sum of squared differences between parent and teacher responses to the five PTRS-II Communication-to-Other items

title: Apply corpora in class only with adequate instruction and pedagogical mediation
description: The article argues that direct classroom use of corpora succeeds only when embedded in adequate instruction. It adopts Flowerdew's four improvement aspects: "1) the combination of the bottom-up and top-down fashion, 2) pedagogical mediation for revealing the embedded context, 3) the intervention of teachers, and 4) the use of a suitable corpus." Its own findings indicate corpus application "with adequate instruction" improved learners' vocabulary, supporting teacher-facilitated rather than bare corpus exposure.

A suitable corpus matched to learner needs
Combination of top-down and bottom-up teaching styles

informed, curious, and critical engagement in lexical learning
examples: The experimental condition combined instructor-edited new-GSL data, KWIC display, and the OHE cycle rather than unmediated corpus search.

article_title: In Search of a More Effective Strategy: Using the 5E Instructional Strategy to Teach Civic Education in Senior Secondary Schools in Ilorin, Nigeria
citation: AbdulRaheem, Y., Bello, M. B., & Odutayo, A. O. (2018). In Search of a More Effective Strategy: Using the 5E Instructional Strategy to Teach Civic Education in Senior Secondary Schools in Ilorin, Nigeria. Journal of International Social Studies, 8(1), 62-85. http://www.iajiss.org
title: Constructivist theory of learning as the framework for the 5Es classroom
description: The study is underpinned by constructivism: learners must individually discover and transform complex information to make it their own, connecting new experience with existing knowledge. The article characterizes the view through three propositions: understanding arises in engagement with the environment; "Cognitive conflict or puzzlement is the stimulus for learning"; and knowledge evolves through social negotiation and evaluation of the viability of learners' understandings. When new experience does not overlap with prior knowledge, learners may destroy, modify, or reject knowledge. In the 5Es classroom the teacher leads exploratory activities in which students investigate on their own.
requirements: Task-oriented environments enhancing hands-on and minds-on learning with authentic tasks
A social environment in which other individuals test understanding
constraints: The article frames this as a philosophical view of how we come to know, most closely attuned to Richard Rorty's pragmatic philosophy
target_learning_goals: internalized civic concepts
social awareness and social understanding
higher-order thinking skills
examples: The article describes the constructivist classroom as focusing on problem-based learning, real-life problem solving, independent investigation, simulation, discussion, collaborative learning, and think-pair-share

citation: Stephen Akinyemi Omotayo & Joshua Oluwatoyin Adeleke. (2017). The 5E Instructional Model: A Constructivist Approach for Enhancing Students' Learning Outcomes in Mathematics. JISTE, Vol. 21, No. 2, 2017.
title: Adopt constructivist instructional approaches that guide learners to develop their own understanding rather than rote memorization
description: The article recommends that teachers move beyond teacher-centered, rote-oriented instruction and instead guide students to construct their own understanding through exploration, hands-on activity, and teacher facilitation. Teachers are "encouraged to adopt constructivist instructional approaches that discourage rote memorization and guide learners to develop their own understanding." The 5E model is presented as one such approach, with students fully involved in teaching and learning processes.
requirements: Teachers must be well trained; the article states a constructivist-based approach may not yield the desired result if not adequately utilized and implemented by a well-trained teacher
constraints: The article cites evidence that constructivist/hands-on instruction did not produce superior gains in some studies (Alsup & Sprigler, 2003; McNeil & Jarvin, 2007; Ivers & Helton, 2016; White, 2012), and manipulatives can be challenging and potentially ineffective if teachers lack confidence
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
interest in mathematics
conceptual understanding
examples: The experimental group's teachers were trained for two weeks and taught with the 5E model for six weeks, while control teachers used traditional methods covering the same concepts

title: Contextualized unit design: same fundamental concepts taught through real-world application, video, and authentic tasks
description: In the experimental treatment, slideshow content presented the same fundamental concepts as the comparison treatment but applied them to real-world situations highlighting how technologies operate in industry. Lessons used "extensive use of video presentations such as virtual field trips and how–to type documentaries", and activities included case studies, problem-solving scenarios, and team-based exercises, several requiring students to produce artifacts a teacher would create in a job-related scenario. Assessment likewise employed authentic tasks.

constraints: Delivered via distance education through Moodle; results limited to one course at one university with small class sizes

application of content to real-world agricultural contexts

article_title: Concept Cat: A Two-Armed Cluster Randomised Controlled Trial. Evaluation Report. Updated
citation: Miguel Subosa, Fin Oades, Erin Dysart, Louise Tracey, Anna Brian, and Elena Rosa Speciani. (2025). Concept Cat: A two-armed cluster randomised controlled trial — Evaluation report. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Concept Cat programme: a 30-week whole-class early verbal concepts intervention built on the STAR approach
description: Concept Cat is a whole-class intervention for three- to four-year-olds teaching early verbal concepts such as 'first', 'wide', and 'empty' that are integral to the maths and science curriculum. It delivers one new word per week over approximately 30 weeks through four components: "a whole-class introduction to the word, meaningful play sessions, parent-child tasks, and a whole-class review". Its structure is "based on the STAR methodology", in which a concept is selected, taught, activated implicitly through play and home activities, and reviewed. Delivery is by EYPs trained remotely, supported by seven in-setting coach visits.
requirements: Lead EYPs complete a three-hour remote training session and other EY staff a one-hour remote session; settings receive seven in-setting support visits from Concept Cat coaches
Key materials include the Word Aware 2 book, Concept Cat soft toy, word bag, Picky Puppet, Lift Lessons animated videos, and printed word-of-the-week materials
constraints: Focus children are identified by staff judgement against informal criteria with no formal assessments conducted
target_learners: Children aged three to four in early years settings, including focus children with below-average language skills
target_learning_goals: Early conceptual vocabulary linked to the mathematics and science curriculum
Early numeracy development
examples: In the trial, if the target word was 'empty', sand and water trays were made available and staff incorporated the word 'empty' during playtime; families received home tasks such as looking out for roads that are narrow and not narrow

article_title: Academic Controversy in Macroeconomics: An Active and Collaborative Method to Increase Student Learning
citation: Craig F. Santicola. (2015). Academic Controversy In Macroeconomics: An Active And Collaborative Method To Increase Student Learning. American Journal Of Business Education – Third Quarter 2015 Volume 8, Number 3. https://www.clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE
title: Conceptual conflict and epistemic curiosity process model of academic controversy's achievement benefits
description: Johnson and Johnson's theoretical account, as presented in the article, explains why controversy produces achievement benefits. When individuals present conclusions based on incomplete information and are "confronted by other people with different conclusions," they "become uncertain as to the correctness of their views" and a state of conceptual conflict or disequilibrium is aroused. This uncertainty motivates an active search for more information (epistemic curiosity), and by accommodating others' perspectives learners derive a reconceptualized, qualitatively better conclusion.
requirements: Presentation of ideas or concepts that are not in alignment with learners' current knowledge, creating uncertainty
constraints: Hypothesized process offered by the model's creators; not directly tested in this study
target_learning_goals: deeper understanding of course concepts
higher-level reasoning strategies
divergent thinking
examples: The article's discussion interprets its significant post-test result as consistent with this process: conceptual conflict "unleashes their epistemic curiosity," prompting students to seek new information

article_title: Effects of Student Teams-Achievement Divisions Cooperative Learning with Models on Students' Understanding of Electrochemical Cells
citation: Ataman Karaçöp. (2016). Effects of Student Teams-Achievement Divisions Cooperative Learning with Models on Students' Understanding of Electrochemical Cells. International Education Studies, 9(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n11p104
title: Combine STAD cooperative learning with physical models when teaching chemistry topics involving molecular-level processes
description: The article recommends pairing the STAD cooperative learning method with concrete models so that teams can visualise particulate-level processes while learning socially. The authors conclude: "we believe that teachers and researchers can use the method of cooperative learning student team achievement divisions along with the models in teaching of chemistry subjects containing processes that occur at the molecular level." Models support understanding of visual processes at the molecular (particulate) level that text-based sources and two-dimensional diagrams do not convey as well.
requirements: Models that represent the molecular-level events of the topic, such as three-dimensional molecule models and play dough used in this study
Cooperative group organisation following the STAD structure
constraints: Use of models could not fully remove students' misunderstandings; some molecular-level misconceptions persisted in all groups
target_learning_goals: understanding electrochemical cells and other chemistry topics with molecular-level processes
examples: In CLMG, student teams used three-dimensional molecule models and play dough to show the events occurring at the molecular level in electrochemical cells during a two-week instructional period.

description: The article recommends that language teachers employ computers to enhance preschool children's vocabulary knowledge because computer assisted instruction provides encouraging, motivating contexts for foreign language learning. constraints: The study found CAVI may not always provide children with superior involvement in vocabulary learning compared with traditional instruction

title: Constructivist open learning environments realized through learning at workstations
description: The article frames learning at workstations as a constructivist, open learning environment in which students individually and actively construct new knowledge influenced by prior conceptions. Open environments provide "situations favourable for constructivist approaches by opening teaching method, social form, learning atmosphere and material environment". Workstations allow working with self-instructional material at the individuals' pace, with the teacher shifting towards being a supporter while students work autonomously and cooperatively in small groups.
requirements: Sufficient reading skills are named in the article as a precondition for student-oriented approaches, a main problem for low achievers
constraints: The article reports that teachers reject workstations arguing they are not practicable due to excessive demand on students, and that only high achievers were said to benefit unless materials and support are adapted
target_learners: secondary school students, specifically low achievers
target_learning_goals: active knowledge construction
self-determination and self-sufficiency
cooperative learning of subject matter
examples: The study operationalised this framework with eight cannabis-prevention workstations using information texts, audio texts, experiments, hands-on activities and a movie, each student receiving an individual workbook

citation: Surya, E., Putri, F.A., & Mukhtar. (2017). Improving Mathematical Problem-Solving Ability and Self-Confidence of High School Students through Contextual Learning Model. Journal on Mathematics Education, 8(1), 85-94. https://jme.ejournal.ums.ac.id/index.php/jme

description: The article presents contextual learning as an approach that "recognizes and shows the natural conditions of knowledge", linking classroom material to real contexts so experience becomes relevant and meaningful. In the study it is implemented as the experimental teaching model contrasted with expository instruction.

constraints: The article's empirical support is a single quasi-experiment in one Indonesian junior high school
target_learners: grade VIII junior high school mathematics students
target_learning_goals: mathematical problem-solving ability
self-confidence
examples: The experimental class at SMP Muhammadiyah 11 Pangkalan Brandan was taught with the contextual learning model while the control class received expository teaching

description: The study's conceptual framework combines constructivism theory with Fathom-based instruction to explain how teaching approach affects students' statistical reasoning ability. The framework guided the design of active, student-centred, self-directed lessons in which students construct knowledge rather than receive it, with teachers facilitating rather than telling.

citation: Sare Şengül. (2011). Effects of Concept Cartoons on Mathematics Self-Efficacy of 7th Grade Students. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 11(4), 2305-2313. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/estp
title: Concept-cartoon discussion cycle with homogeneous four-person groups and teacher questioning
description: The implementation pattern places students in "Four-person homogeneous groups" so they can "create a social learning environment and discuss the concepts more comprehensively". Each activity sheet presents a problem with characters holding different statements, one scientifically correct; groups answer, a different group shares dialogues with the class, and distinctive answers spark inter-group discussion. The teacher then asks questions such as "What happened? How did you understand?" to prompt self-questioning about which character was right and why disagreements arose.

introduction of the cartoons as a method before application
teacher questioning after the discussion session
constraints: Applied in a 7th-grade mathematics unit over four weeks in this study

meaningful restructuring of mathematical concepts
examples: After discussion the teacher asked "Which character's opinion turned out to be true? Where did we go wrong?" to make students question themselves
