article_title: Effects of Concept Cartoons on Mathematics Self-Efficacy of 7th Grade Students
citation: Sare Şengül. (2011). Effects of Concept Cartoons on Mathematics Self-Efficacy of 7th Grade Students. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 11(4), 2305-2313. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/estp
title: Concept cartoons as multiple-perspective dialogue depictions for discussion-based learning
description: Concept cartoons, first designed for science classes by Naylor and McMurdo (1990), are defined in the article as "depiction of dialogues in which 3 or more students are involved". Each character holds a different perspective and statement; one statement is scientifically accepted as true while the rest are plausible misconceptions students may hold. Ideas appear in dialogue boxes so opinions are justified through discussion among the characters, and teachers guide students by involving them in that discussion. The article uses them as visual tools creating a discussion environment consistent with the constructivist approach.
requirements: At least three characters with differing perspectives
one scientifically correct statement among the alternatives
dialogue boxes presenting the ideas
constraints: Originally designed for science classes; in this study adapted to 7th-grade algebra
target_learning_goals: revealing and eliminating misconceptions
critical evaluation of new information against existing knowledge
examples: In the study's cartoons, characters proposed alternative answers to algebra problems and groups debated which statement was scientifically true

article_title: Exploring the Use of Discussion Strategies and Labels in Asynchronous Online Discussion
citation: Fei Gao. (2013). Exploring the Use of Discussion Strategies and Labels in Asynchronous Online Discussion. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Exploring+the+Use+of+Discussion+Strategies+and+Labels+in+Asynchronous+Online+Discussion
title: Combine explicit discussion strategy instruction with post type labels in a constrained online discussion environment to promote desired types of posts
description: The article proposes an approach that "combined the use of labels with strategy instruction" to improve online discussion quality. Instructors teach strategies one or two per module via written mini-lectures, model good use, give whole-class feedback, and require students to label posts with the strategy used (EC, MC, CH, BLD, QST). The quasi-experiment found increased use of four of five strategies and gains in Phases I–II of discussion quality.

The discussion forum must support post type labels adjacent to post titles
constraints: Labels were sometimes used incorrectly (e.g., building posts showing mere agreement), and some students found it hard to choose the right label
The approach was studied in non-argumentative discussions in a master's-level course with non-random assignment
target_learners: master's-level online students, mostly K–12 teachers and nursing students
target_learning_goals: quality of asynchronous online discussion, including elaborating, connecting, challenging, building, and questioning
examples: In the study, the instructor introduced one or two strategies per module over six weeks, students labeled posts in Modules 1–4, and the introduction unit served as a baseline

article_title: Challenge in Enhancing the Teaching and Learning of Variable Measurements in Quantitative Research
citation: Chang Peng Kee, Kamisah Osman & Fauziah Ahmad. (2013). Challenge in Enhancing the Teaching and Learning of Variable Measurements in Quantitative Research. International Education Studies, 6(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v6n6p15
title: Constructivist learning intervention grounded in Vygotsky's zone of proximal development
description: The article frames its interventions with Vygotsky's constructivism, "a theory that explains how learning takes place" as students use past experience to build understanding, promoting active learning in which students recall and interpret active experiences. It describes the teacher as facilitator rather than deductive instructor, learning as an active and collaborative social process, and challenging students one level above their current proximal development zone. The challenge the challenger technique is presented as an instantiation of this challenging of students' minds.
requirements: A dynamic teacher-student interaction and student-centered, active and interactive learning situations
constraints: The article presents this as the most appropriate related theory for stimulating students' minds in a quantitative teaching class, not as a tested component of the design
target_learning_goals: constructing understanding of research concepts through active, collaborative challenge
examples: The challenge the challenger group engaged in self-access learning with group cooperation, creating and posing questions to peers

article_title: Examining the Effect of Teacher Guidance on Collaborative Argumentation in Middle Level Classrooms
citation: Hsu, P.-S., Van Dyke, M., & Chen, Y. (2015). Examining the effect of teacher guidance on collaborative argumentation in middle level classrooms. RMLE Online, 38(9). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Examining+the+Effect+of+Teacher+Guidance+on+Collaborative+Argumentation+in+Middle+Level+Classrooms
title: Collaborative argumentation as a group technique for arriving at an agreed-upon position, distinct from debate
description: The article defines collaborative argumentation, citing Andriessen (2006), as "a technique for arriving at an agreed-upon position among members of a group." It distinguishes it from debate, where students learn to prevail over an opponent; collaborative argumentation is emphasized in the scientific domain, where scientists build on and refute one another's theories to reach conclusions. The authors treat it as a key way students learn critical thinking, reasoning, and problem solving and develop individual argumentation skills.
requirements: Requires a group setting in which members build on and refute one another's positions toward a shared conclusion
target_learners: middle level students in science classrooms
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
reasoning
argumentation skills
examples: Seventh graders argued the issue "Do you think that cell phones should be banned in school?" in whole-class discussion

article_title: Teaching Aids a Special Pedagogy Tool of Brain Development in School Children, Interest and Academic Achievement to Enhance Future Technology
citation: Joseph, O. C. (2015). Teaching Aids a Special Pedagogy Tool of Brain Development in School Children, Interest and Academic Achievement to Enhance Future Technology. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(29). https://www.iiste.org
title: Constructivism (Piaget) as the framework for how teaching aids support children's brain development
description: The article anchors its account of brain development in constructivism, which holds that "Children learn thr ough adaptation, but not passive in knowledge but active at making meaningful testing senses out of theories". Citing Piaget via Mcleod, it describes children building "cognitive structure like mental maps, schema and network conc epts" that increase in sophistication from innate reflexes to complex mental activities. Teaching aids are positioned as objects and technology that let children touch, taste, see, hear and smell, supporting this active construction.
requirements: Children need opportunities to actively interact with objects and teaching aids rather than receive passive instruction
constraints: The framework is applied specifically to elementary school children aged 5-6 in the study
target_learning_goals: interest in learning
academic achievement
brain and cognitive development
examples: The study exposed experimental-group pupils to one week of teaching with aids such as computers, audio-visual aids, power point presentation and animated software
key_sources: Joseph, O. C. (2015). Teaching Aids a Special Pedagogy Tool of Brain Development in School Children, Interest and Academic Achievement to Enhance Future Technology. Journal of Education and Practice, 6(29). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1081258

article_title: An Insight into a School's Readiness to Implement a CAPS Related Indigenous Knowledge Curriculum for Meteorological Sciences
citation: Alvin Daniel Riffel. (2015). An Insight into a School's Readiness to Implement a CAPS Related Indigenous Knowledge Curriculum for Meteorological Sciences. Universal Journal of Educational Research 3(11): 906-916. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2015.031117
title: Contiguity Argumentation Theory (CAT)
description: CAT, proposed by Ogunniyi to mediate between Western/school science and indigenous knowledge, holds that "two distinct co -existing thought systems" such as science and IK "tend to rea dily couple with, or recall each other to create an optimum cognitive state". Unlike TAP, it addresses both logical scientific arguments and non-logical metaphysical discourses embraced by IKS. The study used CAT as one of two theoretical frameworks to analyse learners' meteorological conceptions and pre-test attitude data.
requirements: Applicable to classroom discourse dealing with phenomena about which learners hold conflicting worldviews
constraints: Addresses metaphysical IK-related beliefs that TAP does not address, per the article's account of subsequent research
target_learning_goals: Integrating indigenous knowledge with Western meteorological science concepts
examples: The study applied CAT to inform and describe findings from the survey and pre-test descriptive data in the Grade 9 geography classroom

article_title: Effects of Concept Mapping Instruction Approach on Students' Achievement in Basic Science
citation: Ukpai Patricia Ogonnaya, Gabriel Okafor, Okechukwu S. Abonyi, J.O Ugama. (2016). Effects of Concept Mapping Instruction Approach on Students’ Achievement in Basic Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.8. https://www.iiste.org
title: Concept mapping as a diagrammatic representation of conceptual structure derived from Ausubel's meaningful learning theory
description: The article describes the concept map as "a diagrammatic devise used to represent the conceptual structure of a subject discipline in a two dimensional form" analogous to a road map. Developed by J.D. Novak in the early 1980s, it derives from Ausubel's learning theory, which places central emphasis on the influence of students' prior knowledge on subsequent meaningful learning. Maps are constructed in hierarchical and/or linear order with the most inclusive concept on top and the most specific at the bottom, and propositions are two or more concept labels linked by words describing connections.
requirements: Concepts must be linked to show relationships, since each concept depends on its relationship to many others for meaning
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning of science concepts
understanding relationships among concepts in a discipline
examples: The treatment group was taught the living components of the environment, grouping of living things and classification of living things using concept mapping for four weeks.
key_sources: Ukpai Patricia Ogonnaya, Gabriel Okafor, Okechukwu S. Abonyi, J.O Ugama. (2016). Effects of Concept Mapping Instruction Approach on Students’ Achievement in Basic Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.8. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1095361

article_title: Concept Cartoons Supported Problem Based Learning Method in Middle School Science Classrooms
citation: Balım, A. G., İnel-Ekici, D., & Özcan, E. (2016). Concept Cartoons Supported Problem Based Learning Method in Middle School Science Classrooms. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n2p272
title: Concept cartoons as visual discussion tools presenting alternative views
description: Concept cartoons are visual tools in which cartoon characters declare views about an event from daily life, using short dialogue texts to encourage students to discuss and solve issues. The article describes them as presenting "logical thoughts about daily life from different points of view", guiding learners to inquire about reasons for their answers, compare their views to the characters, and search for evidence. In this study they were integrated into PBL scenarios as a support tool connecting PBL to younger learners.
requirements: Cartoon characters present multiple alternative views, including scientifically correct ideas, to route students into discussion
constraints: The article notes concept cartoons include a limited number of views, which teachers interviewed said might limit students
target_learners: middle school science students (sixth grade, ages 13-14)
target_learning_goals: inquiry learning skills
conceptual change and misconception removal
discussion and questioning in science
examples: In experiment group 1, scenarios such as the shirt-in-the-sun problem were paired with concept cartoons whose characters voiced different views, and students searched for solutions in terms of the views in the cartoons
key_sources: Balım, A. G., İnel-Ekici, D., & Özcan, E. (2016). Concept Cartoons Supported Problem Based Learning Method in Middle School Science Classrooms. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n2p272

article_title: Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues
citation: Elif Ozata Yucel, Muhlis Ozkan. (2015). Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.4.2579
title: Teach ecosystem, biodiversity, and environmental issues through context-based learning that connects content to daily life
description: The design grounded the unit in context-based learning, creating environments that put students at the center and let them learn by doing and experiencing. Content was rewritten with daily-life examples so students could associate it with their own surroundings. The authors report that "it was considered that "context-based" learning would be appropriate and effective for having students achieve the intended learning and level of consciousness".
requirements: Learning environments that put students at the center and allow learning by doing and experiencing
Content rewritten and enriched with daily-life examples so students can associate it with their surroundings
constraints: Teachers had to be at the center from time to time
target_learning_goals: Understanding ecosystem, biodiversity, and environmental issues
Developing environmental awareness and consciousness
examples: Activities included experiments, observations, field surveys, drama, poster-making, videos, animations, and writing petitions to authorities
key_sources: Elif Ozata Yucel, Muhlis Ozkan. (2015). Development and Implementation of an Instructional Design for Effective Teaching of Ecosystem, Biodiversity, and Environmental Issues. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.4.2579

article_title: The Effects of the Comprehensive Inductive Educational Approach on the Social Behaviour of Preschool Children in Kindergarten
citation: Robi Kroflič and Helena Smrtnik Vitulić. (2015). The Effects of the Comprehensive Inductive Educational Approach on the Social Behaviour of Preschool Children in Kindergarten. c e p s Journal, Vol.5, No1. https://journals.cepsj.si/index.php/cepsj
title: The comprehensive inductive educational approach (CIEA): a three-step relational model of prosocial and moral development
description: The CIEA is an educational framework, built on Levinas's ethics and Hoffman's inductive discipline, holding that moral education proceeds through genuine relationships characterised by love and friendship rather than submission to norms. Its basic structure holds that "children are capable of entering relations characterised by love and friendship already in early childhood", then develops respect towards specific persons and actions, and finally builds awareness of ethical principles used for democratic negotiation of conflicts. In kindergarten it combines inductive discipline in conflicts with prosocial activity, teamwork and education through art.
requirements: Teachers must be trained to distinguish the CIEA from classic fostering of psychoanalytic guilt with love withdrawal

Teachers should prevent children from avoiding the other person's emotional distress and refrain from explaining why an action is inappropriate, letting children grasp the cause-effect connection themselves
constraints: The article states the approach's effects were measured only over a five-month period in a single kindergarten
target_learners: preschool and kindergarten children aged roughly 2.5 to 6 years
target_learning_goals: prosocial and moral development
social competence
emotion regulation and respectful relationships
examples: Experimental kindergarten teachers attended three lectures with discussions on the theoretical framework and evaluated implementation examples monthly with three trained pedagogues
key_sources: Robi Kroflič and Helena Smrtnik Vitulić. (2015). The Effects of the Comprehensive Inductive Educational Approach on the Social Behaviour of Preschool Children in Kindergarten. c e p s Journal, Vol.5, No1. https://journals.cepsj.si/index.php/cepsj

article_title: Orientation and Mobility Training in Special Education Curriculum for Social Adjustment Problems of Visually Impaired Children in Pakistan
citation: Malik, S., Abd Manaf, U. K., Ahmad, N. A., & Ismail, M. (2018). Orientation and Mobility Training in Special Education Curriculum for Social Adjustment Problems of Visually Impaired Children in Pakistan. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 185-202. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11213a
title: Corn's (1983) three-dimensional visual functioning model
description: The article presents Corn's (1983) visual functioning model as an educational-rehabilitative framework in which a person's low-vision functioning is not determined by the level of disability alone. As printed, "Corn (1983) proposed a three -dimensional hypothetical model by which a man's low vision working is not just dictated by the level of the disability additionally by different variables as identity, environment and so forth." Its three dimensions are visual capacities, stored and available individuality, and ecological cues; working on one dimension can improve performance on the others.
requirements: Used as an instrument for examining and assessing the functioning level of a person with low vision, per the article's account of the model
constraints: The article frames it as a hypothetical model for individuals with low vision, applied from an educational-rehabilitative point of view
target_learners: visually impaired children and persons with low vision
target_learning_goals: functional performance of visual tasks presupposed during learning
rehabilitative planning to augment individual functioning
examples: The article uses the model in its literature review to argue that functioning depends on identity and environment as well as visual capacity

Orientation and Mobility Training in Special Education Curriculum for Social Adjustment Problems of Visually Impaired Children in Pakistan. article_title: Helping Students to Automatize Multiplication Facts: A Pilot Study
citation: Barbara Allen-Lyall. (2018). Helping Students to Automatize Multiplication Facts: A Pilot Study. IEJEE, Volume 10, Issue 4, 391-396. https://doi.org/10.26822/iejee.2018438128
title: Combine concept development with dedicated automaticity practice rather than relying on a concept-based only approach
description: The article concludes that schools should not rely on concept-based instruction alone for multiplication facts: “we must seek to successfully combine concept development with real automaticity for optimum student achievement.” It recommends systematically supporting automatization through dedicated time blocks, with conceptual understanding of multiplication as repeated addition established before memorization, and reports teachers felt that with professional development they could institute such an approach without compromising an already full teaching schedule.
requirements: Dedicated 30-minute weekly time blocks for facts acquisition; teacher professional development in efficient, flexible, exploratory instructional methods
constraints: Teachers would need professional development; principals noted teachers could not take on increased teaching load without various approvals
target_learning_goals: multiplication facts automaticity supporting computation, number sense, and mathematics self-concept
examples: Ten 30-minute sessions of facts exploration and practice were inserted before or after regular mathematics instruction in seven Grade 3 classrooms

article_title: Adventures with Sport Rivalry Man: Initial Testing of a Classroom Method Using Comics and Cartoons to Teach about Rivalry and Fan Behavior
citation: Cody T. Havard & Skylar S. Workman. (2018). Adventures With Sport Rivalry Man: Initial Testing of a Classroom Method Using Comics and Cartoons to Teach about Rivalry and Fan Behavior. The University of Memphis. https://www.SportRivalry.com
title: Extra-credit exposure-and-learning program with note-taking and guided discussion
description: The study's treatment was worked into normal class structure: students could earn extra credit by reading or watching and summarizing eight comic strips or cartoons (three historical, five Sport Rivalry Man). To foster comprehension and retention, the class first watched one story of each type together and was "led in a brief discussion of rivalry and the stories." Notes required describing characters and scenarios and explaining in their own words what the comics meant.
requirements: students turn in notes on the assigned comics or cartoons
an in-class viewing and brief discussion to model note-taking and foster retention
constraints: offered as extra credit within on-campus classes; online classes serving as controls received no exposure
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate students in sport management classes
target_learning_goals: learning about the rivalry phenomenon
modeling appropriate behavior toward out-group members
examples: Students provided descriptions of main characters and scenarios and explained the psychological term or theory or the moral of the story in their own words

article_title: On the Effectiveness of Team Teaching in Promoting Learners' Grammatical Proficiency
citation: Mohammad Aliakbari and Ali Mansouri Nejad. (2013). On the Effectiveness of Team Teaching in Promoting Learners' Grammatical Proficiency. Canadian Journal of Education / Revue canadienne de l'éducation 36:3. https://www.cje-rce.ca
title: Co-teaching as a shared pedagogical arrangement defined by distinct structural features
description: The article frames co-teaching (also called collaborative or cooperative teaching) as "a general term referring to the pedagogical setting where two teachers share their pedagogy, information, and assessment", with team teaching as one distinct instructional model within that framework. Drawing on Cook (2004), it lists the features that distinguish a co-teaching system from traditional single-teacher instruction, including "a contract to share instructional responsibility", "mutual ownership, pooled resources, and joint accountability", and variable individual participation levels. The study uses this framework to position its team-teaching treatment against single-teacher instruction.
requirements: Two (or more) educators or certified staff, a single group of students, primarily a single classroom or workspace, and specific content objectives, per the article's feature list
constraints: The article notes every co-teaching model may not be suitable in all educational settings because students and teachers do not possess similar features
target_learners: students in inclusive and mainstream classrooms
target_learning_goals: grammar instruction
general subject-matter teaching
examples: The study operationalized co-teaching as the team-teaching model, with two teachers delivering the same grammar structure simultaneously through different modes (whiteboard and oral examples)
key_sources: Mohammad Aliakbari and Ali Mansouri Nejad. (2013). On the Effectiveness of Team Teaching in Promoting Learners' Grammatical Proficiency. Canadian Journal of Education / Revue canadienne de l'éducation 36:3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057969

article_title: On the Effectiveness of Team Teaching in Promoting Learners' Grammatical Proficiency
citation: Mohammad Aliakbari and Ali Mansouri Nejad. (2013). On the Effectiveness of Team Teaching in Promoting Learners' Grammatical Proficiency. Canadian Journal of Education / Revue canadienne de l'éducation 36:3. https://www.cje-rce.ca
title: Effective co-teaching requires collaboration and consensus between co-teachers in planning, teaching, and evaluation
description: The article states that co-teaching "does not take place haphazardly in the classroom": collaboration and consensus between co-teachers must determine every issue of planning, teaching, and evaluation of student performance. It grounds this in the study's own procedure, where co-teachers cautiously planned in advance how each grammar part would be taught and mutually shared opinions about when and how each would fulfill their role, and in Olsen, Chamers, and Hoover's (1997) attributes of effective co-teachers, such as being "tolerant, reflective, and flexible" and maintaining positive relationships.
requirements: Co-teachers should plan instruction in advance, share decisions about roles, and exhibit tolerant, reflective, flexible attitudes with positive mutual relationships
constraints: Time limits are a salient obstacle; the article quotes Bullough and Birrell that there was "simply insufficient time and resources" to maintain a good program and positive relationships
target_learning_goals: grammar instruction
collaborative delivery of any subject content
examples: Before the treatment, the study's co-teachers taught grammar together in an assimilated classroom for at least one week to familiarize themselves with the method and enhance mutual trust
key_sources: Mohammad Aliakbari and Ali Mansouri Nejad. (2013). On the Effectiveness of Team Teaching in Promoting Learners' Grammatical Proficiency. Canadian Journal of Education / Revue canadienne de l'éducation 36:3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057969

article_title: Effectiveness of Co-Operative Learning Method in Learning of Mathematics among Eighth Standard Students
citation: K. Thiyagu. (2012). Effectiveness of Co-operative Learning Method in Learning of Mathematics among Eighth Standard Students. i-manager's Journal on Educational Psychology, Vol. 5 No. 4, February - April 2012. https://imanagerpublications.com
title: Cooperative learning as small stable groups working toward group goals unattainable alone or competitively
description: The article frames cooperative learning as students working together to "attain groups goals that cannot be obtained by working alone or competitively". Operationally, a large class is divided into small groups of about three or four students assigned for the duration of the course, who then complete activities such as homework and practical assignments as a group. The stated purpose is actively involving students in the learning process, a level of empowerment the author says is not possible in a lecture format.
requirements: Small groups of roughly three or four students assigned for the duration of the course
Group tasks such as homework assignments and practical assignments performed cooperatively
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement across knowledge, understanding and application objectives
examples: The investigator taught the 20-student experimental group with cooperative learning for 60 minutes per day over fifteen days, with corrective feedback given where necessary.
key_sources: K. Thiyagu. (2012). Effectiveness of Co-operative Learning Method in Learning of Mathematics among Eighth Standard Students. i-manager's Journal on Educational Psychology, Vol. 5 No. 4, February - April 2012. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102329

article_title: Effectiveness of Co-Operative Learning Method in Learning of Mathematics among Eighth Standard Students
citation: K. Thiyagu. (2012). Effectiveness of Co-operative Learning Method in Learning of Mathematics among Eighth Standard Students. i-manager's Journal on Educational Psychology, Vol. 5 No. 4, February - April 2012. https://imanagerpublications.com
title: Use cooperative learning as an alternative to traditional lecture-based mathematics teaching, combined with whole-group instruction and individual work
description: The article concludes that cooperative learning "may serve as an alternative to traditional method of teaching" in science and mathematics, while cautioning that it cannot cure all the problems teachers face. It recommends teachers give less emphasis to lecturing and recitation of acquired knowledge and more emphasis on active learning, discussion, elaboration and working with peers and teachers. It also recommends staff development: needs analysis before courses, hands-on courses covering basic concepts and the rationale for cooperative learning.
requirements: Staff development courses that are hands-on and include basic concepts of cooperative learning and its rationale
Needs analysis study done before running any courses
constraints: Cooperative learning cannot cure all the problems faced by teachers in teaching and learning science and mathematics
target_learners: eighth-standard mathematics students in Indian schools
target_learning_goals: mathematics conceptual understanding
student discussion and elaboration skills
examples: The article cites the NCTM recommendation that students work together cooperatively in large and small groups on significant problems arising from their experiences, combining new knowledge with prior knowledge within the group.
key_sources: K. Thiyagu. (2012). Effectiveness of Co-operative Learning Method in Learning of Mathematics among Eighth Standard Students. i-manager's Journal on Educational Psychology, Vol. 5 No. 4, February - April 2012. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102329

article_title: An Empirical Study Investigating Interdisciplinary Teaching of Biology and Physical Education
citation: Katharina Spintzyk, Friederike Strehlke, Stephanie Ohlberger, Bernd Gröben, and Claas Wegner. (2016). An Empirical Study Investigating Interdisciplinary Teaching of Biology and Physical Education. Science Educator, Vol. 25, No. 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=An+Empirical+Study+Investigating+Interdisciplinary+Teaching+of+Biology+and+Physical+Education
title: Complementary interdisciplinary lesson pairing in which biology explains PE processes and PE visualises biology content
description: In this pattern, two subjects' lessons are designed to complement each other: "the biology lesson supplies explanations for processes occurring in PE, whereas the PE lesson provides a visualisation of the theoretical biology content". The test group received interdisciplinary block-classes of three lessons a week in the fitness studio, combining a short theoretical introduction with a practical phase in which scientific input was applied to physical perceptions, observed and reflected upon. In combination the lessons offer a physical experience and critical reflection on what was learned theoretically and practically.
requirements: Both groups must deal with the same content so lessons differ only in teaching method
constraints: The pattern was studied in human biology topics such as muscle build-up, the cardiovascular system, nutrition and endurance training
target_learners: German grammar school students in fifth and sixth form
target_learning_goals: Connecting theoretical biology content with practical physical experience
Applicable knowledge of training and human biology
examples: Table 1 pairs theoretical components such as muscle contraction and ATP with practical components such as guided and autonomous training and training-log reflection

article_title: Holy Psychopathology Batman: The Pedagogical Use of Comic Books in the Teaching of Abnormal Psychology
citation: Rahman, R. O. & Zeglin, R. J. (2014). Holy psychopathology Batman: The pedagogical use of comic books in the teaching of abnormal psychology. Psychology Teaching Review, 20(1). https://www.bps.org.uk/journals/psychology-teaching-review
title: Comic-book character diagnostic evaluation assignment
description: An instructional element in which students select an instructor-approved graphic novel, choose a character, "perform a m ock clinical evalu ation, and provide a written psychological report". The report must include client demographics, referral reason, psychosocial history, assessment procedures, differential diagnosis with rule-out rationale, DSM-IV-TR multiaxial diagnoses, case formulation, prevalence and incidence, treatments, treatment recommendations, and prognosis. Comic books were chosen because symptomatology is not presented as straightforwardly as in film, challenging students to develop clinical acumen.
requirements: Students submit their chosen graphic novel for instructor approval; the instructor provided a list of potential comic books in the syllabus and arranged for a local comic book store's employees to offer selection assistance
constraints: The version used was possible because of the authors' familiarity with the medium; none of the experimental students selected a graphic novel the authors had not read, which the authors note will not hold for all instructors
target_learners: undergraduate psychology majors in an abnormal psychology course
target_learning_goals: diagnostic evaluation skills
DSM-IV-TR diagnosis
clinical report writing
examples: Students were encouraged to consult outside references, such as a character's fan page, to obtain information not found in the graphic novel

article_title: The Effects of Training and Other Factors on Problem Solving in Students
citation: Robabeh Puran, Mohamad Hasan Behzadi, Ahmad Shahvarani, Farhad Hosseinzadeh Lotfi. (2017). The Effects of Training and Other Factors on Problem Solving in Students. European Journal of Contemporary Education, 6(3): 448-460. https://doi.org/10.13187/ejced.2017.3.448
title: Concrete teaching aids (coloured counters and bracelets) for teaching permutations and combinations
description: A set of physical manipulables used in the active-method condition: equal numbers of red, blue, and green counters, thread for making bracelets, and a container for random draws. Students "made a bracelet using a thread and the counters" to distinguish circular from gyrate permutation, and drew numbered counters from a container to enumerate two-counter combinations, obtaining 15 possibilities before confirming with the formula. The article reports students said "now we can easily understand why there are so many possibilities."
requirements: An equal number of counters in each colour and a container for random selection
constraints: Used with second-grade science students learning combinational mathematics in this study
target_learning_goals: understanding linear, circular, and gyrate permutation
understanding combinations c(n,r)
examples: Students numbered counters R1, R2, B, G1, G2, G3, drew two at random, and wrote out combinations such as R1G3 before referring back to the formula

article_title: Community-Based Instructional Strategies, School Location, and Primary School Pupils' Environmental Knowledge
citation: Ajitoni, S. O., & Gbadamosi, T. V. (2015). Community-Based Instructional Strategies, School Location, and Primary School Pupils' Environmental Knowledge. JISTE Vol. 19, No. 2. https://www.jiste.org
title: Use community-based strategies (service learning and educational trips) to connect school with the community in teaching environmental content
description: Because both community-based instructional modes produced significantly better environmental knowledge than conventional expository teaching, the article recommends that social studies teachers adopt them and that curriculum developers promote them. The authors call for "total re-orientation of teachers on the use of community-based strategies in teaching and learning of environmental issues and problems in social studies to enhance learning", so that learners learn in and for the environment.
requirements: Teachers need re-orientation/training in community-based strategies; trips require adult supervision and planning skills
constraints: The evidence base is one quasi-experiment with primary-5 pupils in Oyo Metropolis, Nigeria
target_learning_goals: environmental knowledge and problem solving in social studies
examples: Schools in each local government were assigned randomly to treatment groups and pupils received eight weeks of instruction in service learning, educational trips, or conventional teaching
key_sources: Ajitoni, S. O., & Gbadamosi, T. V. (2015). Community-Based Instructional Strategies, School Location, and Primary School Pupils' Environmental Knowledge. JISTE Vol. 19, No. 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1177058

article_title: Getting Teachers Excited about Student Feedback: It's All in the Ask
citation: Robinson, C.; Finefter-Rosenblum, I.; Benshoof, C.; Gehlbach, H. (2016). Getting Teachers Excited about Student Feedback: It's all in the Ask. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Cognitive dissonance as a mechanism for shifting teachers' beliefs about student feedback
description: The article applies Festinger's cognitive dissonance theory to teacher evaluation: people "strive for internal consistency and feel discomfort when holding contradictory, or dissonant, beliefs", and may change a belief to reduce the discomfort. By juxtaposing teachers' likely favorable views of teacher perception surveys with skeptical views of student surveys, the intervention arouses dissonance that should push teachers toward more favorable views of student feedback. The split-ballot experiment tests this account.
requirements: The learner must hold both beliefs simultaneously — favorable views of giving feedback to administrators and skeptical views of receiving feedback from students — so that juxtaposing them arouses dissonance.
constraints: Tested only in a low-stakes survey; the authors note teachers' opinions may vary greatly when the practice is actually implemented at their school, particularly if stakes are attached.
target_learning_goals: Openness to learning from student feedback; malleability of beliefs about student perception surveys
examples: The treatment condition asked teachers a mirrored 5-item scale about teacher perception surveys of administrators before the student perception survey scale.
key_sources: Robinson, C.; Finefter-Rosenblum, I.; Benshoof, C.; Gehlbach, H. (2016). Getting Teachers Excited about Student Feedback: It's all in the Ask. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567735

article_title: The Effects of Cooperative Learning on the Academic Achievement and Knowledge Retention
citation: Van Dat Tran. (2014). The Effects of Cooperative Learning on the Academic Achievement and Knowledge Retention. International Journal of Higher Education, 3(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v3n2p131
title: Adopt cooperative learning as an alternative to lecture-based teaching in Vietnamese higher education
description: Based on its experimental results, the article concludes that "cooperative learning is highly recommended as an alternative instructional pedagogy in the current wave of educational reform in Vietnamese higher education." It argues the approach stimulated cognitive activities and promoted higher achievement and retention, and that students accustomed to teacher-centered instruction adapted to the cooperative style within eight weeks.
requirements: Both lecturers and students would need to undergo a training course in this kind of learning to promote effective implementation.
constraints: The sample of this study is restricted to only 110 participants, which the author states as a limitation warranting future studies with more participants.
target_learning_goals: academic achievement
knowledge retention
examples: The study compared Learning Together with lecture-based teaching in two intact classes taught by the same lecturer over eight weeks of psychology instruction.

article_title: The Power of Graphic Organizers: Effects on Students' Word-Learning and Achievement Emotions in Social Studies
citation: İlter, İ. (2016). The Power of Graphic Organizers: Effects on Students' Word-Learning and Achievement Emotions in Social Studies. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 41(1). http://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajte/vol41/iss1/3
title: Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions as a model linking vocabulary instruction to emotions
description: The study builds on Pekrun's (2006) control-value theory, a cognitive-motivational model in which "emotions interact with language and cognitive process, and can profoundly affect students' motivation and learning outcomes". The article uses it to posit that instruction with different types of graphic organizers enhances word-learning and subsequent achievement emotions, framing effective vocabulary instruction as information about students' achievement goals, beliefs and performance.
requirements: A rich learning environment that is appropriate for students' current development, per the article's account of the theory
constraints: Applied here specifically to word-learning and achievement emotions in fourth-grade social studies vocabulary instruction
target_learning_goals: word-learning and the development of positive achievement emotions such as enjoyment, hope and pride
examples: The authors interpret the GOs group's higher pride, hope and enjoyment as consistent with control-value theory, positing mediating mechanisms such as academic feedback

article_title: The Prevalence of Reading Fluency and Vocabulary Difficulties among Adolescents Struggling with Reading Comprehension
citation: Nathan H. Clemens, Deborah Simmons, Leslie E. Simmons, Huan Wang, and Oi-man Kwok. (2017). The Prevalence of Reading Fluency and Vocabulary Difficulties Among Adolescents Struggling With Reading Comprehension. Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment. https://doi.org/10.1177/0734282916662120
title: Assess struggling adolescent readers comprehensively, including foundational fluency and vocabulary skills, not only comprehension
description: The article argues that assessment of adolescents' reading must go beyond comprehension tests to component skills, because most struggling comprehenders in the study had foundational deficits. It states that "the assessment of adolescents' reading skills must be sufficiently comprehensive to identify weaknesses in foundational skills that may be implicated in their reading comprehension difficulties." Without fine-grained component data, educators cannot tell whether comprehension problems stem from foundational deficits or higher-order processing difficulties.
requirements: Assessment batteries must include measures of text reading fluency and vocabulary alongside comprehension measures
constraints: Group-administered vocabulary measures require independent word reading and may be somewhat confounded by decoding skills, per the article's limitations
target_learners: adolescents in middle and secondary grades struggling with reading comprehension
target_learning_goals: identifying sources of reading comprehension difficulty
aligning intervention to student skill profiles
examples: The study administered the GMRT-4, GRADE, GORT-5, and an easyCBM passage reading fluency probe to capture comprehension, vocabulary, and text reading fluency separately
key_sources: Nathan H. Clemens, Deborah Simmons, Leslie E. Simmons, Huan Wang, and Oi-man Kwok. (2017). The Prevalence of Reading Fluency and Vocabulary Difficulties Among Adolescents Struggling With Reading Comprehension. article_title: Estimating the Effect of a Teacher Training Program on Advanced Placement® Outcomes
citation: Richard S. Brown & Emily Anne Brown. (2019). Estimating the Effect of a Teacher Training Program on Advanced Placement® Outcomes. International Journal of Computer Science Education in Schools, 2(4). https://www.csesjournal.org/
title: Code.org Professional Learning Program for CS Principles teachers
description: A year-long professional development program supporting teachers implementing the Code.org CS Principles curriculum. It coordinates three efforts — Regional Partners, Facilitator Development, and Professional Development Workshops — and "offers both in-person and online support for teachers before and during their first year teaching the Code.org curriculum." It begins with a five-day summer in-person workshop and continues with academic-year workshops run by trained facilitators, plus ongoing supports such as the Code.org Forum online professional learning community.
requirements: Admission requires a stated commitment from the district, or teacher and school principal, to offer and teach the course in the upcoming school year
constraints: Teachers are not required to offer the course as an AP course for admission; in 2016-17 roughly half of teachers self-reported offering CS Principles as an AP course
target_learners: High school teachers new to computer science instruction
target_learning_goals: Implementing the AP Computer Science Principles curriculum
Equitable teaching practices
Student recruitment representative of school population
examples: Teachers apply through a Regional Partner beginning in January; the summer workshop explores the curriculum and learning tools, practices classroom management and teaching strategies, and builds a community of educators
key_sources: Richard S. Brown & Emily Anne Brown. (2019). Estimating the Effect of a Teacher Training Program on Advanced Placement® Outcomes. International Journal of Computer Science Education in Schools, 2(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1207479

article_title: Improving Teacher Perceptions of Parent Involvement Patterns: Findings from a Group Randomized Trial
citation: Keith C. Herman and Wendy M. Reinke. (2016). Improving Teacher Perceptions of Parent Involvement Patterns: Findings From a Group Randomized Trial. School Psychology Quarterly. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/spq0000169
title: A person-centered, two-dimensional profile approach to teacher-perceived parent involvement (contact and comfort)
description: The article conceptualizes teacher-perceived parent involvement as co-occurring patterns of two dimensions: contact (frequency of interaction with school personnel) and comfort (relationship quality, including perceived alignment of goals and values). Using latent profile analysis and latent transition analysis, it identifies four involvement profiles and tracks transitions between them, arguing that "it is the combination of contact and comfort, not either in isolation, that may determine how adaptive they are." The authors state this dimensional, profile approach "adds a more nuanced portrayal of involvement patterns than can be captured by single indicators."
requirements: Teacher ratings of both parent contact and parent comfort are needed (e.g., the 21-item Parent Involvement Measure – Teacher with Contact and Comfort subscales) to define the profiles
Latent profile and transition analyses in MPlus with adequate covariance coverage for model convergence
constraints: The fourth class differed between time points (Medium Contact/Medium Comfort at baseline, Low Contact/High Comfort at follow-up) and was treated as comparable for transition purposes
The study measured teacher perceptions only, not parent perceptions or observed parent behavior
target_learners: Kindergarten to third grade students in urban elementary schools
Parents of students with academic and behavior problems
target_learning_goals: Improve teacher perceptions of parent involvement
Foster positive parent-teacher relationships and parent participation in education
examples: LPA at baseline and follow-up identified four classes; LTA then tested whether intervention condition predicted follow-up class membership and transitions among classes.
key_sources: Keith C. Herman and Wendy M. Reinke. (2016). Improving Teacher Perceptions of Parent Involvement Patterns: Findings From a Group Randomized Trial. School Psychology Quarterly. http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/spq0000169

article_title: The Effect of Computerized Instructional Program in the Intermediate First Grade Students Achievement in Arabic Language Grammar in Iraq
citation: Ibtesam Al-Mashaqbeh, Mushtak Neama. (2015). The Effect of Computerized Instructional Program in the Intermediate First Grade Students Achievement in Arabic language Grammar in Iraq. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.32. https://www.iiste.org
title: Computerized Grammar Program for seventh-grade Arabic grammar unit
description: A researcher-designed computerized instructional program covering one unit from the seventh-grade Arabic grammar textbook, built with computer applications. It "includes a set of general and specific unit objectives, new concepts,  activities, educational games, and evaluation", with "sequential steps from easy to difficult and immediate feedback". Validity was checked by university professors and supervisors from Jordan and Iraq, whose comments led to modifications of objectives and activities.
requirements: Content analyzed into measurable behavioral goals according to the first three levels of Bloom's Taxonomy
Expert validation by professors, supervisors and teachers, with revisions made in response to their comments
constraints: Designed for one unit from the seventh-grade Arabic grammar textbook, not the whole curriculum
target_learning_goals: Arabic language grammar achievement
examples: Experimental-group boys and girls used the program during the six-week treatment while control groups studied the same material the usual way
key_sources: Ibtesam Al-Mashaqbeh, Mushtak Neama. (2015). The Effect of Computerized Instructional Program in the Intermediate First Grade Students Achievement in Arabic language Grammar in Iraq. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.32. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1083567

article_title: Concept Map Technique as a New Method for Whole Text Translation
citation: Tamara Mohd Altabieri Krishan. (2017). Concept Map Technique as a New Method for Whole Text Translation. English Language Teaching, 10(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n4p62
title: Concept maps as graphical tools for organizing and representing knowledge
description: Concept maps are graphical tools for organizing and representing knowledge: they include concepts, usually enclosed in circles or boxes, and relationships between concepts indicated by a connecting line linking two concepts. Words on the line, called linking words or linking phrases, specify the relationship between two concepts. The article applies this representation to translation training, arguing that when concepts are placed in order some words are more inclusive than others and concepts are connected by linkers, which supports whole-text comprehension.
requirements: Concepts represented as nodes and relationships made explicit with linking words or phrases on connecting lines
constraints: The article describes the tool as web-based and desktop-oriented, not for tapping-based tablets and smartphones
target_learners: Foreign language learners translating English texts
target_learning_goals: Text comprehension
Translation skill development
examples: The study's experiment design used concept map tools in which students organized text concepts before summarizing and translating
key_sources: Tamara Mohd Altabieri Krishan. (2017). Concept Map Technique as a New Method for Whole Text Translation. English Language Teaching, 10(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n4p62

article_title: Improving English Language Learners' Idiomatic Competence: Does Mode of Teaching Play a Role?
citation: Zainab Abolfazli Khonbi & Karim Sadeghi. (2017). Improving English Language Learners’ Idiomatic Competence: Does Mode of Teaching Play a Role? Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research 5(3), 61-79. http://ijltr.urmia.ac.ir
title: Context-proportionality account of idiom comprehension
description: The authors invoke the proportionality theory (Qualls, O’Brien, Blood, & Hammer, 2003) to explain why groups receiving richer context learned more idioms. The theory 'predicts that idiom comprehension will decrease proportionally as the amount of context decreases'. They pair it with the lexical representation model (Swinney & Cutler, 1979), in which the amount of context provided determines whether the correct meaning is retrieved during concurrent processing of literal and figurative meanings. In this study, the Role-play, Movie, and Sentence-use groups had access to more context than the Definition Group.
requirements: Sufficient context must accompany idioms for comprehension to be supported; comprehension falls as context is reduced.
constraints: Offered by the authors as an explanatory framework drawn from prior literature, not tested directly in this study.
target_learning_goals: idiom comprehension and interpretation
examples: The Definition Group received only PowerPoint definitions, while the other three groups encountered idioms in movie clips, sentences, or conversational stories, giving them more context.
key_sources: Zainab Abolfazli Khonbi & Karim Sadeghi. (2017). Improving English Language Learners’ Idiomatic Competence: Does Mode of Teaching Play a Role? Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research 5(3), 61-79. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1156202

article_title: Effectiveness of Cognitive Conflict Strategy in Improving Academic Achievement and Modifying Sex Education Misconceptions in Science Course among Intermediate Second-Grade Students
citation: Subahi, N. H. (2019). Effectiveness of Cognitive Conflict Strategy in Improving Academic Achievement and Modifying Sex Education Misconceptions in Science Course among Intermediate Second-Grade Students. World Journal of Education, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v9n2p90
title: Cognitive conflict strategy as a constructivist approach to replacing misconceptions
description: The cognitive conflict strategy is a constructivism-based teaching approach grounded in Piaget's theory of cognitive development, in which conflict in the learner's mind leads to learning. It is used by the teacher as an educational tool for replacing misconceptions with alternative correct conceptions. The article describes three stages: creating conflict through an unexpected event, searching for a solution through active observation and experimentation, and solving the conflict so that "a misconception is replaced by a sound scientific one."
requirements: The teacher identifies students' misconceptions before teaching and creates cognitive uncertainty concerning the target concepts
Students play an active role through participating in discussions, making hypotheses and constructing visions
constraints: The article states the teacher plays a key and intrinsic role in the success of cognitive conflict instruction, based on experience and professionalism
target_learning_goals: correct scientific concepts in Science
modification of sex education misconceptions
examples: The study applied the strategy to the Family Planning and Reproduction chapter via a prepared teacher guide with tailored lessons
key_sources: Subahi, N. H. (2019). Effectiveness of Cognitive Conflict Strategy in Improving Academic Achievement and Modifying Sex Education Misconceptions in Science Course among Intermediate Second-Grade Students. World Journal of Education, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v9n2p90

article_title: Effectiveness of Cognitive Conflict Strategy in Improving Academic Achievement and Modifying Sex Education Misconceptions in Science Course among Intermediate Second-Grade Students
citation: Subahi, N. H. (2019). Effectiveness of Cognitive Conflict Strategy in Improving Academic Achievement and Modifying Sex Education Misconceptions in Science Course among Intermediate Second-Grade Students. World Journal of Education, 9(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v9n2p90
title: Teacher guide for teaching sex education concepts via cognitive conflict strategy
description: A teacher guide was prepared based on the cognitive conflict strategy for the Family Planning and Reproduction chapter. It includes an introduction, objective, significance, the unit's objective and significance, and a proposed teaching plan, plus an overview of the strategy's role in modifying sex education misconceptions. Each tailored lesson was formed to achieve learning outcomes and "include questions which measure misconceptions, evaluation and homework."
requirements: Lessons were reviewed by specialists in Science for accuracy, appropriateness to students' level, and consistency with the cognitive conflict strategy
constraints: Developed for the Family Planning and Reproduction chapter of the intermediate second-grade Science course in Jeddah
target_learning_goals: sex education concepts
modification of sexual misconceptions
examples: A pilot study with 14 intermediate second-grade students on 9/2/2017 checked the strategy's appropriateness before finalizing the guide
