article_title: The Effect of Using Concept Mapping on Student's Attitude and Achievement When Learning the Physics Topic of Circular and Rotational Motion
citation: Dennis Luchembe, Kaumba Chinyama, Jack Jumbe. (2014). The Effect of Using Concept Mapping on Student's Attitude and Achievement When Learning the Physics Topic of Circular and Rotational Motion. European J of Physics Education, Volume 5 Issue 4. https://www.ejp-e.com/
title: Concept-mapping instructional sequence: train map construction on a familiar topic, then apply hierarchies, link words and cross-links to the target topic in groups
description: The article's experimental treatment followed a staged sequence: a whole-class lecture, explicit training in constructing a concept map on the familiar topic of Ohm's law, then group construction of maps on circular and rotational motion. Students first arranged ideas into categories and "put them in hierarchical order within the categories", connected words with "Link words and linking phrases", and finally added cross-links, which the article defines as "a relationship that exists between two concepts in different vertical segments of the map". The sequence ended with group presentations after four days.
requirements: Students must first be taught to define, construct and correctly link concept maps, using link phrases, on a familiar topic before applying maps to the target topic
constraints: The sequence was implemented with a single class of 70 first-year prospective physics teachers at one university, so the authors note a lack of external validity from not randomly selecting the class
target_learners: first-year undergraduate prospective physics teachers taking introductory physics
target_learning_goals: understanding concepts of circular and rotational motion
meaningful learning by relating new information to existing knowledge
examples: Students practised constructing concept maps on any physics topic within class in about 45 minutes, then worked in seven sub-groups of five to build and present maps on circular and rotational motion in a 3-hour tutorial session
key_sources: Dennis Luchembe, Kaumba Chinyama, Jack Jumbe. (2014). The Effect of Using Concept Mapping on Student's Attitude and Achievement When Learning the Physics Topic of Circular and Rotational Motion. European J of Physics Education, Volume 5 Issue 4. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068159

article_title: The Effect of Using Concept Mapping on Student's Attitude and Achievement When Learning the Physics Topic of Circular and Rotational Motion
citation: Dennis Luchembe, Kaumba Chinyama, Jack Jumbe. (2014). The Effect of Using Concept Mapping on Student's Attitude and Achievement When Learning the Physics Topic of Circular and Rotational Motion. European J of Physics Education, Volume 5 Issue 4. https://www.ejp-e.com/
title: Concept mapping as a tool for meaningful learning grounded in assimilation theory
description: The article frames concept mapping as a learner-centred strategy that supports meaningful learning, citing the claim that "concept mapping can increase the capacity for meaningful learning" (Novak and Gowin, 1984). It interprets its questionnaire finding that students related new information to what they already knew as consistent with "Ausubel's assimilation theory and Novak's theory of learning", under which "students learn new things by making use of their existing knowledge and finding ways to assimilate the newly acquired knowledge". Cross-links in a map are treated as evidence of understanding relationships between concepts.
requirements: Learners must possess existing knowledge to which new concepts can be assimilated, which the article says requires some interest
constraints: The article presents this framework as a rationale and interpretation rather than testing the mechanism directly
target_learning_goals: meaningful learning of physics concepts
relating new information to prior knowledge
examples: The experimental group constructed hierarchical maps of Ohm's law and circular and rotational motion with link words and cross-links as the operationalisation of this framework
key_sources: Dennis Luchembe, Kaumba Chinyama, Jack Jumbe. (2014). The Effect of Using Concept Mapping on Student's Attitude and Achievement When Learning the Physics Topic of Circular and Rotational Motion. European J of Physics Education, Volume 5 Issue 4. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068159

article_title: The Effects of the Use of Microsoft Math Tool (Graphical Calculator) Instruction on Students' Performance in Linear Functions
citation: Philip Siaw Kissi, Opoku Gyabaah and Sampson Kwadwo Boateng. (2016). The Effects of the use of Microsoft Math Tool (Graphical Calculator) instruction on students' performance in linear functions. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.21. http://www.iiste.org
title: Constructivist theory of learning as active construction of knowledge through engagement
description: The article frames the study in constructivist theory, which "believe[s] in active engagement of students in activities to generate their personal knowledge but not transfer from the teacher". Learning occurs when students construct new understanding from active participation with old and new experience, through engagement in activities and reflection on their outcomes. In the constructivist classroom teaching is student-centred, with teachers acting as facilitators who organise engaging activities rather than detail explainers.
requirements: An environment that engages students' interest and connects new knowledge to existing knowledge
constraints: The article notes teachers have difficulty introducing concepts without detailed explanation and arranging such engaging environments
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of mathematics concepts
examples: The article cites studies indicating constructivist learning environments affected students' performance positively compared with other instructional methods
key_sources: Philip Siaw Kissi, Opoku Gyabaah and Sampson Kwadwo Boateng. (2016). The Effects of the use of Microsoft Math Tool (Graphical Calculator) instruction on students' performance in linear functions. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.21. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1109378

article_title: Investigating the Effectiveness of Group Work in Mathematics
citation: Anastasia Sofroniou and Konstantinos Poutos. (2016). Investigating the Effectiveness of Group Work in Mathematics. Educ. Sci. 2016, 6, 30. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci6030030
title: Collaborative versus cooperative group work as constructivist learning structures in mathematics
description: The article frames group work within the constructivism model of learning and distinguishes two structurally different forms. In collaborative learning, participants "tackle the same problem together continuously within their groups and learn from each other", whereas cooperative learning involves "specific role assignments in a group" and divisible subtasks processed in parallel, with each student responsible for the final result. The study's intervention deliberately mixed both modes.
requirements: Two or more learners interacting synchronously to negotiate shared meaning and jointly solve problems
target_learning_goals: deepen understanding of mathematics module content
develop critical and analytical thinking skills
examples: In the intervention, students worked collaboratively on the same problems and cooperatively on role-assigned tasks such as plotting a curve and determining the bounded area, with each student responsible for the concluding solution.
key_sources: Anastasia Sofroniou and Konstantinos Poutos. (2016). Investigating the Effectiveness of Group Work in Mathematics. Educ. Sci. 2016, 6, 30. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci6030030

article_title: Concept Attainment Teaching Methodology (CATM)--An Effective Approach for Training Workers on Chemicals Health Hazards
citation: Abdulqadir Mohamad Suleiman. (2016). Concept Attainment Teaching Methodology (CATM) – An Effective Approach for Training Workers on Chemicals Health Hazards. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(11): 2677-2685. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.041122
title: Concept attainment teaching methodology (CATM) as an inductive information-processing teaching model
description: CATM is an information-processing teaching model in which learners construct concepts inductively by comparing exemplars labelled YES with non-exemplars labelled NO. As the article explains, concept attainment is "an inductive thinking process by which learners decipher attributes of a concept by comparing and contrasting data presented as exemplars with that presented as non-exemplars". It proceeds through presentation and hypothesis formulation, hypothesis testing with additional unlabelled data, and analysis of the thinking that led to the conclusion, and can be run in a selection-based paradigm (learners gather unlabelled information themselves) or a reception-based paradigm (discriminate units are presented). The article applies it to workplace safety training for cleaning workers.
requirements: Training materials must present both positive examples carrying the concept's attributes and non-examples lacking them, plus additional attributes substantiating the YES attributes
constraints: Earlier studies cited by the article generalize that the reception method is more effective on difficult conceptual tasks while the selection method suits less difficult ones
target_learners: adult workers with low-level formal education
target_learning_goals: understanding of chemicals health hazards
concept formation and categorization of hazard information
examples: Labelled chemical containers served as YES examples and unlabelled containers as NO examples in PowerPoint presentations; printed pictures and information cards with hazard and precautionary statements were used for the selection strategy
key_sources: Abdulqadir Mohamad Suleiman. (2016). Concept Attainment Teaching Methodology (CATM) – An Effective Approach for Training Workers on Chemicals Health Hazards. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(11): 2677-2685. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.041122

article_title: Mathematical Critical Thinking and Curiosity Attitude in Problem Based Learning and Cognitive Conflict Strategy: A Study in Number Theory Course
citation: Zetriuslita, Wahyudin & Jarnawi. (2017). Mathematical Critical Thinking and Curiosity Attitude in Problem Based Learning and Cognitive Conflict Strategy: A Study in Number Theory course. International Education Studies, 10(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n7p65
title: Cognitive conflict strategy pattern: expose alternative framework, create conceptual conflict, request cognitive accommodation
description: Ismaimuza (2010), as reported in the article, describes cognitive conflict strategy as having "a common pattern which include exposing alternative framework (revealing initial conc ept), creating conceptual cognitive (creating conceptual conflict), and enco uraging cognitive accommodati on (requesting cognitive accommodation)". The article illustrates it with an integral calculus question whose computed area of zero is implausible, prompting students to check assumptions and draw the function graph. In the study this pattern was embedded in the PBLCCS orientation step.
requirements: Problems must present results that conflict with learners' initial concepts so they are willing to find out more using critical thinking
constraints: Jarnawi (2012) is cited arguing cognitive conflict occurs less frequently in collaborative than personal contexts
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
conceptual reorganization via assimilation and accommodation
examples: The article's integral calculus example asks whether the bounded area is zero, then prompts: are you sure with the obtained result? Check again more carefully, is there anything wrong.
key_sources: Zetriuslita, Wahyudin & Jarnawi. (2017). Mathematical Critical Thinking and Curiosity Attitude in Problem Based Learning and Cognitive Conflict Strategy: A Study in Number Theory course. International Education Studies, 10(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n7p65

article_title: The Effect of a Group Approach on the Performance of High School Mathematics Learners
citation: Dhlamini, J., & Mogari, D. (2013). The effect of a group approach on the performance of high school mathematics learners. Pythagoras, 34(2), Art. #198. https://doi.org/10.4102/pythagoras.v34i2.198
title: Cognitive load account of collaborative learning: distributing processing across group members' working memories
description: The article frames the group approach within cognitive load theory: because individual working memory is limited in capacity and duration, dividing information processing across group members expands the collective working memory reservoir and lowers the risk of overload. The article states that "dividing the processing of information in the working memory across individuals in a group approach environment is useful because this technique allows information to be divided across a larger reservoir of cognitive capacity". Within a group, processing is characterised by sharing, discussing and remembering task-relevant information, and schemas constructed jointly promote performance.
requirements: Communication and coordination between group members so that information elements and cognitive load can be shared
constraints: The account is used interpretively; the study did not measure collective working memory directly
target_learning_goals: financial mathematics problem solving (simple and compound interest, hire purchase, inflation, exchange rates)
examples: Experimental classrooms arranged desks in groups of five to seven mixed-achievement learners with assigned leader, explainer and recorder roles, and used worked-out example worksheets as springboards for group discussion
key_sources: Dhlamini, J., & Mogari, D. (2013). The effect of a group approach on the performance of high school mathematics learners. Pythagoras, 34(2), Art. #198. https://doi.org/10.4102/pythagoras.v34i2.198

article_title: Can We Improve Preschool Classroom Quality in Chile? A Cluster-Randomized Trial Evaluation of a Professional Development Program
citation: Leyva, D., Yoshikawa, H., Snow, C. E., Treviño, E., Rolla, A., Barata, M. C., & Weiland, C. (2014). Can we improve preschool classroom quality in Chile? A cluster-randomized trial evaluation of a professional development program. SREE Spring 2014 Conference abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Professional development that pairs content-focused training with continuous classroom coaching can improve teaching practices where minimal supports fail
description: The article recommends incorporating research-based teaching practices into existing classroom practices and curricula, supported by an intensive coaching model in which teachers and aides not only learn and practice strategies but are continuously supported by coaches in improving their classroom practices. The authors note this professional development model with intensive coaching is relatively rare in Chile and other Latin American countries, and that paired with an emphasis on content expertise, such models have shown promising results in North America.
requirements: Continuous coach support in the classroom, including modeling, observation, and immediate post-observation feedback meetings
An emphasis on content expertise alongside coaching
constraints: The article reports no significant child-level outcome effects after two years, so improved classroom practices did not translate to measured child gains within the program duration
target_learners: Prekindergarten and kindergarten teachers and aides
target_learning_goals: Improving classroom interaction quality
Enhancing children's language, literacy, and socio-emotional learning experiences
examples: UBC coaches modeled strategies, observed teacher implementation or co-implemented with teachers, and held immediate post-observation meetings to discuss what went well and what could be improved
key_sources: Leyva, D., Yoshikawa, H., Snow, C. E., Treviño, E., Rolla, A., Barata, M. C., & Weiland, C. (2014). Can we improve preschool classroom quality in Chile? A cluster-randomized trial evaluation of a professional development program. SREE Spring 2014 Conference abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562728

article_title: Use of Mobile Testing System PeLe for Developing Language Skills
citation: Titova, S. (2015). Use of mobile testing system PeLe for developing language skills. Critical CALL – Proceedings of the 2015 EUROCALL Conference, Padova, Italy. http://dx.doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2015.000387
title: Post-test collaborative enquiry activities following mobile formative tests
description: A lesson-level design pattern in which each mobile test is followed by interactive post-test activities that turn assessment into learning. The article's framework lists "collaborative and peer learning post-test activities, brainstorming, problem solving activities, group discussions" as the enquiry-based component, operationalized through 24 post-test activity grids completed by teachers after each of the eight tests. The study suggests this combination engaged students in enquiry-based tasks and produced more output in the target language.
requirements: A mobile testing system providing immediate feedback so post-test activities can build on test results
Teacher-prepared post-test activity grids for each test
constraints: Some participants commented on the challenging nature of weekly tests and post-test activities
target_learners: University EFL students at B1 level
target_learning_goals: Target-language output production
Collaboration and peer learning skills
examples: Teachers of the experimental groups completed 24 grids of post-test activities used after each of the eight PeLe tests between September and December 2013
key_sources: Titova, S. (2015). Use of mobile testing system PeLe for developing language skills. Critical CALL – Proceedings of the 2015 EUROCALL Conference, Padova, Italy. http://dx.doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2015.000387

article_title: The Practices of Critical Thinking Component and Its Impact in Malaysian Nurses Health Education
citation: Abdul Ghani Kanesan Abdullah, Naser Jamil Alzaidiyeen, Ng Mooi Yee. (2010). The Practices of Critical Thinking Component and Its Impact in Malaysian Nurses Health Education. International Education Studies, 3(1). https://journals.ccsenet.org/index.php/ies
title: De Bono's CoRT 1 thinking method as a teachable set of critical thinking tools for nursing decisions
description: The article presents the CoRT 1 thinking method (de Bono, 1972) as a set of thinking tools developed from different aspects of thinking, grounded in de Bono's belief that "thinking skills can be taught". The seven tools are P.M.I. (Plus, Minus, Interesting), C.A.F. (Consider All Factors), O.P.V. (Other People's Views), F.I.P. (First Important Priorities), A.G.O. (Aims, Goals, Objectives), A.P.C. (Alternatives, Possibilities, Choices) and C&S (Consequences and Sequel). In this study these tools structured both the critical thinking module and the analysis of students' health talks with patients.
requirements: The article states the tools must be taught, as in the module's instructional strategies, for students to know the how of thinking for specific situations
constraints: The article notes reflection cannot take place in an emergency situation since the nurse needs to follow standard protocols in such situations
target_learners: year-2 nursing students in a private medical college in Malaysia
target_learning_goals: critical thinking and decision-making for delivering patient-tailored health education
examples: The critical thinking module taught the tools and had students apply them to context-free problems and then to real health talks with chronic-illness patients
key_sources: Abdul Ghani Kanesan Abdullah, Naser Jamil Alzaidiyeen, Ng Mooi Yee. (2010). The Practices of Critical Thinking Component and Its Impact in Malaysian Nurses Health Education. International Education Studies, 3(1). https://journals.ccsenet.org/index.php/ies

article_title: A Comparative Study of the Effectiveness of Two Methods of Teaching Resumptive Pronouns in Writing: TBLT and Blended Learning
citation: Rajabi, B., & Hashemian, M. (2015). A Comparative Study of the Effectiveness of Two Methods of Teaching Resumptive Pronouns in Writing: TBLT and Blended Learning. English Language Teaching, 8(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n9p196
title: Combine traditional task-based methodology with technology-supported blended delivery rather than relying on technology alone
description: The article's concluding design recommendation is that technology should complement, not replace, teacher-led task-based instruction. It states that "it is the combination of traditional methodology and using tasks that results in better and more fruitful results," and that although the Internet and computer improved writing performance, learner-teacher interaction, tasks, and brainstorming must also be taken into account. It cites Nunan (1987) and Williams (1998) that computers cannot replace the teacher's presence.
requirements: Teacher presence and interaction must be retained alongside online components; teachers select activities, prepare students, give feedback, and review and reteach as needed.
constraints: The article notes every method has its own benefits and limitations, so curriculum redesign should match the method to the compatibility of the lesson and the learners.
target_learners: Intermediate EFL learners in intensive English writing programs
target_learning_goals: Learning problematic grammatical points such as resumptive pronouns in L2 writing
examples: In the study, the task-based group received teacher-led planning instruction in class, while the blended group split lessons between a Weblog and the classroom; both improved, with the task-based group's posttest effect described as more noticeable.
key_sources: Rajabi, B., & Hashemian, M. (2015). A Comparative Study of the Effectiveness of Two Methods of Teaching Resumptive Pronouns in Writing: TBLT and Blended Learning. English Language Teaching, 8(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n9p196

article_title: A Fitness Intervention Program within a Physical Education Class on Cardiovascular Endurance among Malaysia Secondary School Students
citation: Shabeshan Rengasamy, Subramaniam Raju, Wee Akina Sia Seng Lee, Ramachandran Roa. (2011). A Fitness Intervention Program within a Physical Education Class on Cardiovascular Endurance among Malaysia Secondary School Students. The Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Science, 2(1). http://www.moj-es.net
title: Cooper's Twelve Minute Run test for measuring cardiovascular endurance
description: Cardiovascular endurance was measured with Cooper's Twelve Minute Run, administered on a 400-meter track before and after the ten-week program. The article reports "a reliability of 0.95 and the validity coefficients of .65" and that the test "possesses a high correlation with VO2max of r = .90". Students ran in pairs, with a partner recording laps to the nearest 25 meters, aiming to cover maximum distance in twelve minutes.
requirements: A 400 meter track in the school field, as recommended by Baumgartner and Jackson (1991)
Paired runners with lap scorers and a whistle at the twelfth minute
target_learning_goals: Assessment of cardiovascular endurance (aerobic fitness)
examples: Pretest and posttest were conducted prior to treatment initiation and following the ten-week intervention program
key_sources: Shabeshan Rengasamy, Subramaniam Raju, Wee Akina Sia Seng Lee, Ramachandran Roa. (2011). A Fitness Intervention Program within a Physical Education Class on Cardiovascular Endurance among Malaysia Secondary School Students. The Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Science, 2(1). http://www.moj-es.net

article_title: Vocabulary Learning through an Online Computerized Flashcard Site
citation: McLean, S., Hogg, N., & Rush, T. W. (2013). Vocabulary learning through an online computerized flashcard site. The JALT CALL Journal, 9(1), 79-98. https://jaltcall.org
title: Design computerized flashcard programs to implement retrieval grading, adaptive sequencing, and expanded rehearsal
description: The article argues computers can augment paired-associate vocabulary study by automating word selection, card making, and card use according to research-based principles. Retrieval should progress in difficulty, since "the greater the effort made to successfully retrieve information the greater memory of it is enhanced"; adaptive sequencing returns unrecalled items for more practice; and expanded rehearsal, "a review method whereby the time between reviews increases", is judged the most effective sequencing method. A well-designed program automates these so learners spend effort on learning rather than organization.
requirements: A program must track per-item retrieval success to automate adaptive sequencing judgments and schedule expanding review intervals
constraints: With paper flashcards expanded rehearsal is "highly impractical owing to the large amount of time that would be taken from learning words to managing the learning of words", and adaptive sequencing relies on learners honestly judging their own knowledge
target_learners: second language learners doing deliberate vocabulary study
target_learning_goals: efficient acquisition of form-meaning mappings for second language vocabulary
examples: The article evaluates Word Engine against Nakata's flashcard creation and learning criteria, finding it supports retrieval mode, receptive recall and recognition, progressive retrieval effort, adapted sequencing, and expanded rehearsal
key_sources: McLean, S., Hogg, N., & Rush, T. W. (2013). Vocabulary learning through an online computerized flashcard site. The JALT CALL Journal, 9(1), 79-98. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1108008

article_title: Effects of Mathematics Integration in a Teaching Methods Course on Mathematics Ability of Preservice Agricultural Education Teachers
citation: Christopher T. Stripling and T. Grady Roberts. (2014). Effects of Mathematics Integration in a Teaching Methods Course on Mathematics Ability of Preservice Agricultural Education Teachers. Journal of Agricultural Education, 55(3), 1-16. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2014.03001
title: Consider the MTIS treatment in agricultural teaching methods courses to increase preservice teachers' mathematics ability
description: Based on the study's findings, the authors recommend that teacher educators integrate mathematics content and mathematics instruction into teacher education courses. Their first recommendation states: "The MTIS treatment should be considered for use in an agricultural teaching methods course to increase the mathematics ability of preservice agricultural teachers." The recommendation rests on the significant ANCOVA result and large effect size reported in the study.
requirements: A lecture on the seven components of a math-enhanced lesson delivered within the methods course
Lab sections in which preservice teachers deliver micro-teachings to peers
constraints: The authors call for replication with preservice teachers from other teacher education programs before broader generalization, given the limited scope and small sample
target_learning_goals: mathematics ability
integrating mathematics into agricultural instruction
examples: The MTIS treatment was implemented in two randomly assigned lab sections of the University of Florida teaching methods course in Fall 2011
key_sources: Christopher T. Stripling and T. Grady Roberts. (2014). Effects of Mathematics Integration in a Teaching Methods Course on Mathematics Ability of Preservice Agricultural Education Teachers. Journal of Agricultural Education, 55(3), 1-16. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2014.03001

article_title: Inside the Black Box: Examining Mediators and Moderators of a Middle School Science Intervention
citation: Laura M. Desimone, Kirsten Lee Hill. (2017). Inside the Black Box: Examining Mediators and Moderators of a Middle School Science Intervention. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373717697842
title: Cognitive Science Casebook: researcher-constructed curriculum materials embedding three cognitive science principles
description: The Cognitive Science Casebook is a researcher-constructed supplement of approximately 500 pages provided to teachers in the CS treatment condition alongside summer professional development. It provided "step-by-step lesson plans, including detailed explanations, warm-ups, activi- ties, and PowerPoint slides" aligned to the Holt Science and Technology units (Cells, Inside the Restless Earth, Introduction to Matter), and was "to be used in place of the districts' planning guides." Interviewed teachers credited it with pacing and streamlined planning.
requirements: Teachers received accompanying summer PD on how and why the three CS principles should be integrated into the curriculum during classroom lessons
constraints: The Casebook was specific to the three Holt curriculum units studied and aligned to district curricular guidelines
target_learners: middle school science students in seventh and eighth grade
target_learning_goals: science achievement on Cells, Inside the Restless Earth, and Introduction to Matter units
examples: CS-condition teachers taught the three Holt units using Casebook lessons reflecting contrasting cases, visualization, and spaced testing, with monthly PLC follow-up sessions
key_sources: Laura M. Desimone, Kirsten Lee Hill. (2017). Inside the Black Box: Examining Mediators and Moderators of a Middle School Science Intervention. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373717697842

article_title: Effectiveness of Flipped Learning: Improving Pre-Service Teachers' Prowess in Producing Videos
citation: Faisal M. Almutairi, Abdullah A. Almodaires & Alaa J. Zeyab. (2020). Effectiveness of Flipped Learning: Improving Pre-Service Teachers' Prowess in Producing Videos. International Education Studies, 13(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v13n7p163
title: Constructivism and Kolb's experiential learning as the theoretical framework for flipped learning in pre-service teacher education
description: The article grounds flipped learning in two theories: constructivism and Kolb's experiential learning. It states that "The two theories underpinning this study are Kolb's experiential learning and constructivism", framing flipped learning as learner-centred, facilitative and socially constructivist, with in-class dialogic discourse and out-of-class monologic engagement with videos and readings. The framework reconceptualises Kolb's philosophy from a constructivist perspective, mapping experiential phases (concrete experience, reflection, abstract conceptualisation, experimentation) onto before-, during- and after-class flipped activities.
requirements: Flipped learning must be structured so students actively engage with, manipulate and apply content, per the introduction's citation of Yough et al. (2017)
constraints: The framework is applied to a single six-week video-production unit in a Kuwaiti teacher-education programme
target_learners: pre-service teachers in teacher education programmes
target_learning_goals: digital video production and editing skills and knowledge
examples: The experimental group watched demonstration videos and read materials before class, then spent class time on hands-on, collaborative activities guided by the instructor and peers
key_sources: Faisal M. Almutairi, Abdullah A. Almodaires & Alaa J. Zeyab. (2020). Effectiveness of Flipped Learning: Improving Pre-Service Teachers' Prowess in Producing Videos. International Education Studies, 13(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v13n7p163

article_title: Summer Outreach with Near-Age Peer Mentors: A Randomized Experiment to Improve the Transition to College
citation: Schneider, B., Broda, M., & Judy, J. (2013). Summer Outreach with Near-Age Peer Mentors: A Randomized Experiment to Improve the Transition to College. SREE Spring 2013 Conference abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Summer+Outreach+with+Near-Age+Peer+Mentors
title: Design college-going interventions that comprehensively connect several aspects of the college-going process rather than targeting one aspect
description: The authors contrast typical interventions—counselor training, tutoring and mentoring staff, financial aid form assistance, college visits—which "typically focus on one aspect of the college-going process", with CAP, which is "specifically designed to be an intervention that comprehensively connects several important aspects of the college-going process". They also note few interventions deliver training for accessing and using the information parents and students receive. The summer outreach study extends this comprehensive approach into the summer months.
requirements: Components should cover multiple aspects of the college-going process, including information use, not only information provision
constraints: The authors state existing one-dimensional reforms are helpful but limited; the comprehensive design claim rests on CAP's preliminary positive results (Authors, 2012), with summer effects still forthcoming
target_learners: high school students, especially those with limited family resources and first-generation college-goers
target_learning_goals: college knowledge and navigation skills
successful matriculation to postsecondary education
examples: CAP operated as a whole-school quasi-experimental design in four treatment and four matched comparison schools, with a CAP center whose visit frequency was used as a take-up measure
key_sources: Schneider, B., Broda, M., & Judy, J. (2013). Summer Outreach with Near-Age Peer Mentors: A Randomized Experiment to Improve the Transition to College. SREE Spring 2013 Conference abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED564094

article_title: Focusing on Mathematical Knowledge: The Impact of Content-Intensive Teacher Professional Development. Executive Summary. NCEE 2016-4009
citation: Garet, M. S., Heppen, J. B., Walters, K., Parkinson, J., Smith, T. M., Song, M., Garrett, R., Yang, R., & Borman, G. D. (2016). Focusing on mathematical knowledge: The impact of content-intensive teacher professional development, executive summary (NCEE 2016-4009). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee
title: Content-Intensive Math PD Program: Intel Math plus Mathematics Learning Community plus Video Feedback Cycles
description: A 93-hour professional development program for grade 4 teachers with three interrelated components. The core is Intel Math, "an intensive 80-hour workshop delivered in summer 2013 that focused on deepening teachers' knowledge of grades K–8 mathematics." Two school-year components reinforce it: the Mathematics Learning Community, "a series of five 2-hour collaborative meetings focused on analyzing student work," and Video Feedback Cycles, three one-on-one coaching sessions where lessons were observed and critiqued using the MQI instrument. The program was evaluated in a randomized trial across six districts and five states.
requirements: Delivered by experienced instructors (one mathematician and one math educator per district) for Intel Math and trained district-based facilitators for the school-year components
Video feedback based on lessons on topics covered in Intel Math and the Mathematics Learning Community, coded with the MQI instrument
constraints: Evaluated with grade 4 teachers in self-contained classes across six districts and five states
The report states the PD did not improve student achievement despite improving teacher knowledge and one practice dimension
target_learning_goals: Deepen teachers' conceptual understanding of grades K–8 mathematics
Improve mathematical quality of instruction
examples: In each district, grade 4 treatment teachers were joined by about 10 teachers in grades K–3 and 5–8 to emulate typical Intel Math implementation
District-based facilitators delivered both the five Mathematics Learning Community meetings and the three Video Feedback Cycles during 2013–14
key_sources: Garet, M. S., Heppen, J. B., Walters, K., Parkinson, J., Smith, T. M., Song, M., Garrett, R., Yang, R., & Borman, G. D. (2016). Focusing on mathematical knowledge: The impact of content-intensive teacher professional development, executive summary (NCEE 2016-4009). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee

article_title: Focusing on Teachers' Mathematical Knowledge: The Impact of Content-Intensive Professional Development. Study Snapshot. NCEE 2016-4011
citation: Garet, M. S., Heppen, J. B., Walters, K., Parkinson, J., Smith, T. M., Song, M., Garrett, R., Yang, R., & Borman, G. D. (2016). Focusing on teachers' mathematical knowledge: The impact of content-intensive professional development (NCEE 2016-4010). Washington, D.C.: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/pubs/20164010
title: Content-intensive 93-hour math PD program combining Intel Math, Mathematics Learning Community, and Video Feedback Cycles
description: A 93-hour professional development program focused on deepening grade 4 teachers' general math knowledge and some math knowledge for teaching. Its core was "Intel Math , an intensive 80 -hour workshop delivered in summer 2013 that focused on deepening teachers' knowledge of grades K–8 math". Two school-year components totaling 13 hours reinforced the content: five structured 2-hour collaborative meetings reviewing math content and analyzing student work, and three rounds of individualized video-based coaching with feedback on mathematical explanations using the MQI rubric.
requirements: Summer workshop plus school-year reinforcement components delivered during the 2013–14 school year
Coaching feedback based on video analysis of lessons using the MQI rubric
constraints: The program targeted elementary teachers' K–8 math content knowledge; it did not improve student achievement in this study
target_learning_goals: deepening teachers' general math content knowledge
improving quality and clarity of teachers' mathematical explanations
examples: Grade 4 teachers from 94 schools in six districts and five states were randomly assigned within schools to receive the PD or business-as-usual PD
key_sources: Garet, M. S., Heppen, J. B., Walters, K., Parkinson, J., Smith, T. M., Song, M., Garrett, R., Yang, R., & Borman, G. D. (2016). article_title: Effects of Using Model Robots in the Education of Programming
citation: Attila PÁSZTOR, Róbert PAP-SZIGETI, Erika LAKATOS TÖRÖK. (2010). Effects of Using Model Robots in the Education of Programming. Informatics in Education, 9(1), 133–140. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2010.09
title: Piagetian/neo-Piagetian concrete-operations framework for supporting abstract programming learning with concrete tools
description: The article grounds its intervention in Piaget's stage model and the neo-Piagetian approach, which refuses Piaget's rigorous age borders and rearranges curriculum with tools that provide concrete experiences. Its core hypothesis is that mastering abstract programming elements is easier when students "use a real tool and learn at the level of concrete operations". The article cites the CASE program's measurable permanent effects and Hungarian curriculum-rearrangement work as supporting precedents.
requirements: Devices must be concrete and curriculum-compatible so students can operate at the level of concrete operations
constraints: The article notes many researchers criticize Piaget's theory for its rigorous age borders and idea of universal development
target_learning_goals: algorithmic thinking
basic programming structures and problem solving
examples: The Model Robot Programming subject had students write algorithms and programs and build LEGO NXT robots controlled by their programs, working in small groups
key_sources: Attila PÁSZTOR, Róbert PAP-SZIGETI, Erika LAKATOS TÖRÖK. (2010). Effects of Using Model Robots in the Education of Programming. Informatics in Education, 9(1), 133–140. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2010.09

article_title: An Integrated Approach to Teaching Literature in an EFL Classroom
citation: Supaporn Yimwilai. (2015). An Integrated Approach to Teaching Literature in an EFL Classroom. English Language Teaching, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p14
title: Literature instructors and educators should consider the benefits of the integrated approach when teaching literature in EFL classrooms
description: Based on the study's findings, the author recommends that "literature instructors and educators should consider the benefits of the integrated approach" when teaching literature to EFL students. The principle rests on the study's evidence that the integrated approach outperformed the conventional method on achievement, critical thinking, and attitudes, and that teaching literature can be useful "if it is taught properly". The author cautions that more research is needed to support this claim.
requirements: Teaching methods and approaches should aim toward the all-around development and welfare of students
constraints: The author states more research is needed to support the claim; evidence comes from one study at two Thai universities
target_learning_goals: literature achievement
critical thinking skills
positive attitudes toward reading literature
examples: Experimental groups at two Thai universities outperformed controls on achievement, critical thinking improvement, and attitudes after eight weeks of integrated-approach instruction
key_sources: Supaporn Yimwilai. (2015). An Integrated Approach to Teaching Literature in an EFL Classroom. English Language Teaching, 8(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n2p14

article_title: Citation as a Stimulus to Boost Students' Communication Skills at the English Lessons
citation: Sadykova, A. G., Yashina, M. E., & Sharafieva, A. D. (2014). Citation as a Stimulus to Boost Students' Communication Skills at the English Lessons. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p12
title: Communicative orientation: foreign language teaching aims at willingness and ability to carry out cross-cultural communication
description: The article frames citation use within a communicative orientation to foreign-language teaching. Its stated main purpose is "the formation of communicative competence, that is, the willingness and ability to carry out cross-cultural communication in a foreign language with native speakers". Communicative competence involves the knowledge and skills needed to understand foreign-language dialogue and generate one's own model of verbal behavior adequate to the situation. The authors distinguish communicative speech skills, which are creative and require re-selection of linguistic means in new situations, from stereotyped verbal skills, and argue that citation-based communicative activities supply real communication in educational settings.
requirements: Two related factors are paramount for communicative activities: interest in the subject and maximal involvement of students in active discussion
constraints: The authors note that in real situations with native speakers, students' speech intentions often take unnatural form or are blocked, which communicative activities aim to overcome
target_learning_goals: cross-cultural communication
communicative competence
expressing one's own opinions in English
examples: The article cites Edelsky's notion of authentic assignments and Krashen's comprehensible input as supporting ideas for meaningful, purposeful communication activities
key_sources: Sadykova, A. G., Yashina, M. E., & Sharafieva, A. D. (2014). Citation as a Stimulus to Boost Students' Communication Skills at the English Lessons. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p12

article_title: Effectiveness of Computer-Assisted STAD Cooperative Learning Strategy on Physics Problem Solving, Achievement and Retention
citation: Amosa Isiaka Gambarı, Mudasiru Olalere Yusuf. (2015). Effectiveness of Computer-Assisted Stad Cooperative Learning Strategy on Physics Problem Solving, Achievement and Retention. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, 3(3). https://www.mojet.net
title: Computer-assisted STAD activity structure: team tasks, individual and team quizzes, team scores, and recognition
description: The article's experimental treatment followed a five-step STAD routine around the CALP package: "Each team consists of three members assigned to one computer", teammates complete reading and tasks as a team, students take an individual quiz, each team takes the same quiz and reaches consensus with one answer sheet earning a shared team score, individual and team scores count equally toward the grade, and high-scoring teams are recognized and rewarded. Groups were heterogeneous by gender and achievement level with rotating roles to avoid free riders.
requirements: Heterogeneous three-member teams with role assignment and rotation; teachers trained in cooperative learning elements (positive interdependence, face-to-face interaction, individual accountability, social skills, group processing)
constraints: Treatment lasted six weeks within a twelve-week study; teams shared one standalone computer
target_learners: senior secondary school year two (SS II) physics students in mixed-gender, mixed-ability teams
target_learning_goals: physics problem solving, achievement, and retention
examples: The experimental group completed team reading and tasks on CALP, individual quizzes, consensus team quizzes with a single submitted answer sheet, and class recognition of high-scoring teams
key_sources: Amosa Isiaka Gambarı, Mudasiru Olalere Yusuf. (2015). Effectiveness of Computer-Assisted Stad Cooperative Learning Strategy on Physics Problem Solving, Achievement and Retention. Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Technology, 3(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085945

article_title: Use of Jigsaw Technique to Teach the Unit "Science within Time" in Secondary 7th Grade Social Sciences Course and Students' Views on This Technique
citation: Hakkı Yapıcı. (2016). Use of jigsaw technique to teach the unit "science within time" in secondary 7th grade social sciences course and students' views on this technique. Educational Research and Reviews, 11(8), 773-780. https://www.academicjournals.org/ERR
title: Collaborative learning defined by five basic principles of positive dependency, interaction, responsibility, social skills, and group-process evaluation
description: The article presents collaborative (cooperative) learning as a teaching approach in which students form small heterogeneous groups and work together on a topic or problem, with the teacher as guide and students as active participants. It lists the features distinguishing it from other methods: "a. Positive dependency b. Face to face interaction c. Individual responsibility d. Social skills and e. Evaluation of the group process", regarded as five basic principles enabling collaboration among group members.
requirements: Students must be motivated to study together; merely splitting students into groups will not improve learning or collaboration
constraints: The article notes cooperative learning is not students sitting together studying separately, nor one student doing the whole work unaided
target_learning_goals: academic achievement, social skills, motivation
key_sources: Hakkı Yapıcı. (2016). Use of jigsaw technique to teach the unit "science within time" in secondary 7th grade social sciences course and students' views on this technique. Educational Research and Reviews, 11(8), 773-780. https://www.academicjournals.org/ERR

article_title: The Effects of the First Part of the CoRT Program for Teaching Thinking (BREADTH) on the Development of Communication Skills among a Sample of Students from Al al-Bayt University in Jordan
citation: Wael Mohammad Alshurman. (2017). The effects of the first part of the CoRT program for teaching thinking (BREADTH) on the development of communication skills among a sample of students from Al al-Bayt University in Jordan. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.3069
title: CoRT BREADTH ten-lesson training program
description: The first part of De Bono's CoRT program, delivered here as ten training sessions over four weeks at three hours per week, each lesson with a plan and a worksheet for each group. The lessons teach thinking tools applied to communication: PMI (plus, minus, interesting), CAF (consider all factors), rules, C&S (consequence and sequel), AGO (aims, goals, objectives), planning, FIP (first important priorities), APC (alternatives, possibilities, choices), decisions, and OPV (other people's views). The article describes it as "Ten consecutive sequential lessons selected from the CoRT program for teaching thinking, which includes tools, objectives, examples, exercises, discussion, and follow-up".
requirements: Delivered as sessions and workshops with a plan and a worksheet for each group, as in the study's four-week format
constraints: The article treats BREADTH as the part that must be studied before any other CoRT parts, as the fundamental basis for future lessons
target_learners: university students from different specializations and academic levels
target_learning_goals: thinking tools such as considering all factors, priorities, alternatives, decisions, and other people's views
examples: The researcher implemented the ten-session program on 36 university students over four weeks, with a pretest a week before and a posttest a week after the program.
key_sources: Wael Mohammad Alshurman. (2017). The effects of the first part of the CoRT program for teaching thinking (BREADTH) on the development of communication skills among a sample of students from Al al-Bayt University in Jordan. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.3069

article_title: The Effects of the First Part of the CoRT Program for Teaching Thinking (BREADTH) on the Development of Communication Skills among a Sample of Students from Al al-Bayt University in Jordan
citation: Wael Mohammad Alshurman. (2017). The effects of the first part of the CoRT program for teaching thinking (BREADTH) on the development of communication skills among a sample of students from Al al-Bayt University in Jordan. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.3069
title: Researcher-built communication skills scale for university students
description: A 40-item self-report scale prepared by the researcher to measure communication skills including clarity, realism, briefing, honesty, consistency, friendliness and the whole message, across university settings such as the lecture, cafeteria, library, laboratories and university areas. Items use a three-point estimation scale (always, sometimes, rarely) scored 1-3. Validity was checked by 10 specialized university professors who judged each item, and reliability was estimated by test-retest and internal consistency.
requirements: Validity and reliability extracted in this study, as the article states for the scale prepared by the researcher
constraints: The test-retest reliability of 0.88 was computed on 30 university students not included in the study sample
target_learning_goals: effective communication skills
examples: The Pearson correlation between two administrations two weeks apart was 0.88, and Cronbach's alpha was 0.83, values the author considered appropriate.

article_title: The Effects of the First Part of the CoRT Program for Teaching Thinking (BREADTH) on the Development of Communication Skills among a Sample of Students from Al al-Bayt University in Jordan
citation: Wael Mohammad Alshurman. (2017). The effects of the first part of the CoRT program for teaching thinking (BREADTH) on the development of communication skills among a sample of students from Al al-Bayt University in Jordan. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.3069
title: CoRT six-part taxonomy for teaching thinking
description: De Bono's CoRT (Cognitive Research Trust) program organizes the teaching of thinking into sixty lessons distributed in six parts of ten lessons each, each part handling one aspect of thinking: breadth (broadening the circle of understanding), organization (identifying problem landmarks and developing solution strategies), interaction (discussion and negotiation, evidence and agreement), creativity (escaping limiting ideas and producing new ideas), information (collecting and providing information effectively), and action (the process of thinking as a whole from choosing the goal to forming an implementation plan). The article states "The CoRT program consists of sixty lessons distributed in six parts, each of which contains ten lessons" and describes each part's purpose and lesson topics.
requirements: Each part has a name signaling a purpose that should be achieved when ending this part, and breadth must be studied before any other parts
constraints: The first five parts are concerned with private aspects of thinking, while CoRT6 is interested in the process of thinking as a whole
target_learners: students across educational stages, including university students
target_learning_goals: thinking skills in their different types, including creative thinking, critical thinking, and decision making
examples: The study used only CoRT 1 (breadth), whose lessons cover handling ideas, considering all factors, laws, consequences, goals, planning, priorities, alternatives, decisions, and the views of others.
