The effects of the first part of the CoRT program for teaching thinking (BREADTH) on the development of communication skills among a sample of students from Al al-Bayt University in Jordan. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.3069

article_title: Teaching High-Value Pronunciation Features: Contrastive Stress for Intermediate Learners
citation: John M. Levis & Greta Muller Levis. (2018). Teaching High-Value Pronunciation Features: Contrastive Stress for Intermediate Learners. The CATESOL Journal, 30(1). https://www.catesoljournal.org
title: Teach contrastive stress together with grammatical frames for comparison and contrast
description: This lesson-level pattern combines prosodic prominence practice with explicit lexicogrammatical frames (e.g., but, while, first/second, on the left/right) and grammatical parallelism. The article states that to express comparisons efficiently, "contrastive stress needed to be taught in conjunction with these patterns," and that the frames "helped make productions of contrastive stress more noticeable." Frames were paired with pictures to bridge between sentence reading and free speech.
requirements: Grammatical frames provided during class
Pairing frames with pictures to bridge from sentence reading toward free speech
Feedback and encouragement of correct forms during practice
constraints: The article states it could not distinguish whether pronunciation, grammar, or both drove the comprehensibility gains
target_learning_goals: expressing contrasts efficiently in speech
producing noticeable contrastive stress
examples: Table 1 frames such as "The first house is gray, but the second house is red" were practiced with picture prompts in PowerPoint slides
key_sources: John M. Levis & Greta Muller Levis. (2018). Teaching High-Value Pronunciation Features: Contrastive Stress for Intermediate Learners. The CATESOL Journal, 30(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1174193

article_title: The Effectiveness of Content-Based Instruction in English Language Teaching
citation: Evangelin Arulselvi. (2016). The Effectiveness of Content-Based Instruction in English Language Teaching. Excellence in Education Journal, 5(2). https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+Effectiveness+of+Content-Based+Instruction+in+English+Language+Teaching%22
title: Content-based instruction (CBI) as an approach integrating language and content learning
description: CBI is an approach to language teaching in which "the student learns the target language by using it to learn new content"; language is the medium, not the object, of instruction. It integrates language learning with academic subject matter, treats the four skills as integrated rather than separate, and draws on Krashen's emphasis on comprehensible, low-anxiety input. The article uses CBI as the experimental treatment, operationalized through dictogloss, graphic organizers, and process writing with heterogeneous team groupings.
requirements: Teachers knowledgeable in the subject matter who can elicit that knowledge from learners
Authentic, linguistically simplified materials drawn from real-life sources
Learner-centered classrooms with context and comprehensibility kept foremost
constraints: The article notes application issues such as assessment of language and content and teacher education in EFL contexts
target_learners: non-native English speaker pre-service teachers (B.Ed. students)
target_learning_goals: English language skills
academic content knowledge in Optional 1 English
examples: The experimental group learned units 5 and 6 of Optional I English through group research tasks, dictogloss, graphic organizers, and process writing
key_sources: Evangelin Arulselvi. (2016). The Effectiveness of Content-Based Instruction in English Language Teaching. Excellence in Education Journal, 5(2). https://www.google.com/search?q=%22The+Effectiveness+of+Content-Based+Instruction+in+English+Language+Teaching%22

article_title: Preschool Teachers Can Use a PBS KIDS Transmedia Curriculum Supplement to Support Young Children's Mathematics Learning: Results of a Randomized Controlled Trial
citation: Llorente, C., Pasnik, S., Moorthy, S., Hupert, N., Rosenfeld, D., & Gerard, S. (2015). Preschool Teachers Can Use a PBS KIDS Transmedia Curriculum Supplement to Support Young Children's Mathematics Learning: Results of a Randomized Controlled Trial. SREE Spring 2015 Conference Abstract. https://sree.org/conferences/2015-conference/
title: Pair well-designed digital math resources with a cohesive curriculum and adequate teacher supports rather than leaving teachers to select technology resources piecemeal
description: The article argues that "the thoughtful integration of well-designed digital resources coupled with adequate teacher supports can positively influence child and teacher outcomes". It contrasts the Supplement's "sharp, cohesive curricular focus" with a common approach that leaves teachers to select resources piecemeal and on their own, and states the study results provide further evidence of the weakness of such an approach.
requirements: Teachers prepared with the content knowledge and pedagogical experience needed to mediate children's learning with technology
Adequate teacher supports including training and ongoing coaching
constraints: In the Technology & Media condition, learning gains did not appear and teachers reported spending less time on math instruction than Business as Usual teachers
target_learners: preschool children, especially those from low-income households
target_learning_goals: early mathematics learning
examples: The RCT's Technology & Media condition provided the same technology and coaching but no structured curriculum, and produced no significant math learning gains.
key_sources: Llorente, C., Pasnik, S., Moorthy, S., Hupert, N., Rosenfeld, D., & Gerard, S. (2015). Preschool Teachers Can Use a PBS KIDS Transmedia Curriculum Supplement to Support Young Children's Mathematics Learning: Results of a Randomized Controlled Trial. SREE Spring 2015 Conference Abstract. https://sree.org/conferences/2015-conference/

article_title: From a Gloss to a Learning Tool: Does Visual Aids Enhance Better Sentence Comprehension?
citation: Takeshi Sato and Akio Suzuki. (2012). From a Gloss to a Learning Tool: Does Visual Aids Enhance Better Sentence Comprehension? EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://research-publishing.net
title: Computer-mediated learning material for English spatial prepositions with image-schema visual glosses
description: The authors developed computer-mediated learning material for English prepositions covering eight spatial prepositions (above, across, along, below, in, into, on and over), presented as two kinds of dictionaries using planar still images or animated stereo images depicting conceptual schemes. Learners used the dictionaries for ten minutes between a pre-test and a randomized post-test of forty-five questions with no feedback.
requirements: Depiction of image schemas as a visual gloss to mediate the senses of polysemous prepositions
constraints: Tested with Japanese university students not majoring in English language, in a ten-minute intentional learning session
target_learners: Japanese university students from freshmen to postgraduates
target_learning_goals: Differentiating and comprehending the senses of English spatial prepositions
examples: Both participant groups answered forty-five multiple questions about the sense of eight spatial prepositions before and after ten minutes of dictionary use
key_sources: Takeshi Sato and Akio Suzuki. (2012). From a Gloss to a Learning Tool: Does Visual Aids Enhance Better Sentence Comprehension? EUROCALL Conference, Gothenburg, Sweden, Proceedings. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED574946

article_title: Joint Book Reading: How Do Blogs Foster Collaborative Comprehension?
citation: Fatemeh Behjat. (2013). Joint Book Reading: How Do Blogs Foster Collaborative Comprehension? i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 3 No. 2, April-June.
title: Orient out-of-class reading toward peer interaction and collaboration rather than individualistic self-study
description: The article argues that out-of-class reading activities should be designed for interaction and collaboration through joint work, because this, compared with individualistic self-study, leaves a profound effect on students' learning potential and lowers affective filters. In the study this was implemented by requiring blog readers to check their understanding of texts in collaboration with peers via posted comments.
requirements: A shared virtual space (such as a blog) where learners can post comments and respond to peers
Teacher structuring and incentives so students actually take part in peers' discussions
constraints: Evidence comes from one three-month quasi-experiment with 62 Iranian EFL university students
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension in a foreign language
examples: The experimental group was required to be in interaction with peers in understanding different parts of the texts, with interactions posted on the blog
key_sources: Fatemeh Behjat. (2013). Joint Book Reading: How Do Blogs Foster Collaborative Comprehension? i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 3 No. 2, April-June. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068891

article_title: The Effect of Learner Constructed, Fill in the Map Concept Map Technique, and Summarizing Strategy on Iranian Pre-University Students' Reading Comprehension
citation: Hassan Soleimani & Fatemeh Nabizadeh. (2012). The Effect of Learner Constructed, Fill in the Map Concept Map Technique, and Summarizing Strategy on Iranian Pre-university Students' Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 5(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n9p78
title: Concept map technique as a graphical tool rooted in Ausubel's assimilation theory
description: A concept map (CM) is defined as a "graphical tool for organizing and representing relationships between concepts indicated by a connecting line linking two concepts" (Novak & Canas, 2007, p. 1). The article states the technique is rooted in Ausubel's Assimilation Theory, in which learning occurs by assimilating new concepts into existing frameworks. It assigns three distinctive features to CMs: "hierarchical structure, cross links and specific examples", and lists versions including expert-constructed, learner-constructed, fill in the map, and cooperative concept maps. The study applies two of these versions to L2 reading comprehension.
requirements: Instruction in the CM drawing procedure (the study followed Novak and Gowin's 1984 step-by-step procedure)
Provision of feedback on students' maps, which the article calls an important stage
constraints: The study limited CM's extension to reading comprehension of intermediate-level L2 learners
target_learning_goals: L2 reading comprehension
examples: In the study, learner-constructed group students drew CMs of five taught passages at home and received holistic good/fair/weak scoring with feedback
key_sources: Hassan Soleimani & Fatemeh Nabizadeh. (2012). The Effect of Learner Constructed, Fill in the Map Concept Map Technique, and Summarizing Strategy on Iranian Pre-university Students' Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 5(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n9p78

article_title: The Influence of Explicit Cross-Linguistic Consciousness-Raising on the EL Writing of the Iranian English Language Learners
citation: Seyyed Yavar Hosseininik & Hamid Rahmani Sangani. (2014). The Influence of Explicit Cross-Linguistic Consciousness-Raising on the EL Writing of the Iranian English Language Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 5(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.3p.147
title: Consciousness-raising as a form-focused technique that develops explicit awareness of target-language features
description: Consciousness-raising (C-R) is defined in the article as "the drawing of the learner's attention to features of the target language" (Rutherford, 1987). It is treated as a subcomponent of form-focused instruction that helps learners notice formal properties of input and build explicit representations of target forms, distinct from practice, which the article calls "primarily behavioral" while "consciousness-raising is essentially concept-forming in orientation." In this study C-R was operationalized as explicit cross-linguistic comparison of Persian and English structures.
requirements: Learners are provided with data illustrating the target feature and use intellectual effort to understand it, per Ellis (1992) as cited in the article
constraints: The article notes C-R is more influential for developing awareness at the level of understanding than for authentic communicative use, and is necessary though not sufficient for successful acquisition
target_learning_goals: explicit knowledge of grammatical structures such as subject-verb agreement and adverb position
examples: The experimental groups' instructor explained language items by comparing and contrasting Persian and English and provided information revealing usage to help learners distinguish L1 and L2 structures
key_sources: Seyyed Yavar Hosseininik & Hamid Rahmani Sangani. (2014). The Influence of Explicit Cross-Linguistic Consciousness-Raising on the EL Writing of the Iranian English Language Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 5(3). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.3p.147

article_title: Combined Teaching Method: An Experimental Study
citation: Iryna V. Kolesnikova. (2016). Combined Teaching Method: An Experimental Study. World Journal of Education, 6(6). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v6n6p51
title: Combined teaching method: lecture plus varied active learning activities
description: The article's combined teaching method pairs traditional lecture delivery with active learning activities. In the experimental group, "participants were engaged in the lecture format plus variet y of activities, such as reading, writing, discussion, use of modern technology, presentation and seminar that promote analysis, synthesis and evaluation of content", while the control group received lecture with PowerPoint slides and no student input. The pattern was tested in a pre/post control-group experiment with future primary school teachers.
requirements: Instructor preparation to run lecture plus activities such as reading, writing, discussion, technology use, presentation and seminar within the course
constraints: The study notes "difficulty with participants’ cooperation due to alteration and adaptation from traditiona l teacher centered to the combined teaching strategy" and "A lack of proper space for having group di scussion sessions"
target_learners: 5th-year university students training as primary school teachers
target_learning_goals: Knowledge formation in education training subject matter
examples: Forty Ukrainian 5th-year students were pre-tested, randomly divided into two equal groups of 20, taught for a semester under lecture-only or combined methods, and post-tested with the same open-ended questions scored with a rubric (maximum 20)
key_sources: Iryna V. Kolesnikova. (2016). Combined Teaching Method: An Experimental Study. World Journal of Education, 6(6). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v6n6p51

article_title: Using Alice Software with 4C-ID Model: Effects in Programming Knowledge and Logical Reasoning
citation: Joana Martinho COSTA, Guilhermina Lobato MIRANDA. (2019). Using Alice Software with 4C-ID Model: Effects in Programming Knowledge and Logical Reasoning. Informatics in Education, 18(1), 1-15. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2019.01
title: Validated 13-item programming knowledge test based on Bloom's Taxonomy
description: The programming knowledge test, developed and validated by Costa and Miranda (2017b), comprises 13 items scored zero for wrong and one for correct answers, with a maximum of 13 points. "We obtained a Cronbachs' alpha value of 0.837, which is a good reliable value for internal consistency (Peterson, 1994)." The first ten items are multiple-choice questions covering the first four levels of Bloom's Taxonomy, each with one correct and three wrong answers; the last three are development questions covering the last two levels. It was previously validated by a group of specialists and a pilot group.
requirements: Administered after the experimental treatment to infer programming knowledge acquisition
target_learners: secondary education students without previous programming experience
target_learning_goals: initial programming knowledge
examples: The test was applied in the final lesson of the intervention in both groups.
key_sources: Joana Martinho COSTA, Guilhermina Lobato MIRANDA. (2019). Using Alice Software with 4C-ID Model: Effects in Programming Knowledge and Logical Reasoning. Informatics in Education, 18(1), 1-15. https://doi.org/10.15388/infedu.2019.01

article_title: Combining Instructional Activities for Sense-Making Processes and Perceptual-Induction Processes Involved in Connection-Making among Multiple Visual Representations
citation: Martina A. Rau & Sally P. W. Wu (2018). Combining Instructional Activities for Sense-Making Processes and Perceptual-Induction Processes Involved in Connection-Making Among Multiple Visual Representations. Cognition and Instruction, 36:4, 361-395. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2018.1494179
title: Combine explicit connection-making activities with implicit connection-making activities when teaching with multiple visual representations
description: The article argues that instruction combining understanding-activities, which prompt students to verbally explain mappings between representations, with perception-activities, which expose students to numerous examples for implicit categorization with immediate correctness feedback, should yield higher learning gains than either type alone. In both the chemistry experiment and the prior fractions experiment, only the combined condition outperformed the control condition. The article hypothesizes that "instruction that combines both types of activities should yield higher learning gains of domain knowledge, compared to instruction that provides only one or neither of these activities."
requirements: Instruction must include both understanding-activities and perception-activities, not only one of them
Time on task should be held constant across conditions
constraints: Understanding-only or perception-only conditions did not outperform the control condition in either experiment
target_learning_goals: chemistry content knowledge
connection-making among multiple visual representations
key_sources: Martina A. Rau & Sally P. W. Wu (2018). Combining Instructional Activities for Sense-Making Processes and Perceptual-Induction Processes Involved in Connection-Making Among Multiple Visual Representations. Cognition and Instruction, 36:4, 361-395. https://doi.org/10.1080/07370008.2018.1494179

article_title: Effect of Concept Attainment Model on Acquisition of Physics Concepts
citation: Kumar, A., & Mathur, M. (2013). Effect of Concept Attainment Model on Acquisition of Physics Concepts. Universal Journal of Educational Research, 1(3), 165-169. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2013.010304
title: Concept attainment model: teaching specific concepts by comparing and contrasting positive and negative examples
description: The concept attainment model, historically linked with Jerome S. Bruner and his associates, is "intended to teach specific concepts by comparing and contrasting examples that contain the concept and that do not contain the concept". It is built from Bruner's work on categorizing, which "helps to reduce the complexity of environment and necessity for concept learning". The model was used as the experimental treatment in this study.
requirements: Instruction must present examples that contain the concept and examples that do not, for comparison and contrast.
constraints: The article describes the model's application to specific physics concepts in class IX; effectiveness evidence comes from this single study.
target_learning_goals: Concept learning and categorizing in physics
examples: Group A was taught by concept attainment model while group B was taught by the traditional method, on alternative days for one month.
key_sources: Kumar, A., & Mathur, M. (2013). Effect of Concept Attainment Model on Acquisition of Physics Concepts. Universal Journal of Educational Research, 1(3), 165-169. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2013.010304

article_title: The Effect of Corpus-Based Activities on Verb-Noun Collocations in EFL Classes
citation: Uçar, S., & Yükselir, C. (2015). The Effect of Corpus-based Activities on Verb-Noun Collocations in EFL Classes. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology – April 2015, volume 14 issue 2
title: Use corpus-based concordance activities to teach verb-noun collocations in EFL classes
description: The article recommends that language teachers use corpus-based materials, specifically concordance lines drawn from COCA, to teach verb-noun collocations instead of relying solely on dictionary meanings and coursebook exercises. In the study, the instructor "made use of concordance lin es taken from the corpus COCA to teach collocations" and designed practice exercises from sentences in the concordance lines, delivered via printed worksheets. This approach produced significantly higher post-test collocation recognition scores than conventional instruction.
requirements: Access to a corpus such as COCA and concordancing tools to extract example sentences for the target collocations
constraints: The evidence base comes from only two two-hour treatment sessions with 30 pre-intermediate learners, so effectiveness beyond this scope is untested
target_learning_goals: Recognition of verb-noun collocations in English
examples: The experimental group was taught 15 target verb-noun collocations from the coursebook 'Speak Out Intermediate' using COCA concordance lines, cloze activities, and error-spotting exercises over two two-hour sessions
key_sources: Uçar, S., & Yükselir, C. (2015). The Effect of Corpus-based Activities on Verb-Noun Collocations in EFL Classes. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology – April 2015, volume 14 issue 2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057374

article_title: The Role of Comic Reading Materials in Enhancing the Ability to Read in EFL
citation: Roozafzai, Z. S. (2012). The Role of Comic Reading Materials in Enhancing the Ability to Read in EFL. Journal of English Language Teaching. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ
title: Use comic reading materials to build motivation and readability in EFL reading instruction
description: The article recommends that EFL teachers and curriculum designers introduce comic reading materials because they combine high motivation with high readability. As the author states, "it can be proposed to curriculum designers to introduce comic reading materials for extensive reading or outside-the-class activities and persuade students to make use of them." Comics serve as a bridge from conversational to academic language and foster pleasurable reading habits.
requirements: Comics should be matched to learners' proficiency level and contain no culturally unfamiliar points
constraints: Evidence comes from adult female pre-intermediate Iranian learners; generalizability to other ages, sexes, and proficiency levels requires further study
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
reading motivation
examples: The experimental group was treated by comic materials consisting of comic strips and illustrated stories from the book Steps to Understanding over 20 sessions
key_sources: Roozafzai, Z. S. (2012). The Role of Comic Reading Materials in Enhancing the Ability to Read in EFL. Journal of English Language Teaching. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1070200

article_title: The Role of Comic Reading Materials in Enhancing the Ability to Read in EFL
citation: Roozafzai, Z. S. (2012). The Role of Comic Reading Materials in Enhancing the Ability to Read in EFL. Journal of English Language Teaching. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ
title: Comics as multi-dimensional materials merging words, pictures, humor and reasoning
description: The article characterizes comics as multi-dimensional instructional materials that "merge words and pictures, on the one hand; and humor and reasoning, on the other hand." They work on "mind, cognition, mental imagery and psyche" to enhance EFL reading ability. Humor reduces stress and anxiety, creates a positive learning environment, and may enhance recall according to Berk and Friedman & Amoo as cited by the author.
requirements: Comics must be selected to match learners' proficiency and cultural background
constraints: The humor and affective benefits are drawn from cited literature rather than directly tested in this study
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension
reading motivation
reduced anxiety
key_sources: Roozafzai, Z. S. (2012). The Role of Comic Reading Materials in Enhancing the Ability to Read in EFL. Journal of English Language Teaching. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1070200

article_title: Language-Learner Strategy Instruction and English Achievement: Voices from Ghana
citation: John T. Agor. (2014). Language-Learner Strategy Instruction and English Achievement: Voices from Ghana. English Language Teaching, 7(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n6p175
title: Coach learners in productive strategies from primary school onward so they become autonomous language learners
description: The article concludes that one of the key ingredients separating successful language learners from less successful ones is the learner's repertoire of strategies, and recommends building an adequate stock of strategies through training. It states that learners equipped with productive strategies "will build an adequate st ock of strategies from which to draw when engaged in a language task", enabling them to eventually become autonomous language learners. The recommendation spans primary, high school and college levels.
requirements: Strategy training that supplies learners with productive strategies
Opportunities for learners to draw on their strategy stock during language tasks
constraints: The article's evidence comes from one public junior high school at Madina, Ghana, with the hypothesis holding only if all other variables remain constant
target_learners: Primary and junior high school learners of English in Ghana
target_learning_goals: Autonomous second-language learning and improved English attainment
examples: The article recommends that primary learners be coached in learner strategies, that high school students get ample opportunities to further develop acquired skills, and that teacher trainees be exposed to ways of equipping their prospective clients
key_sources: John T. Agor. (2014). Language-Learner Strategy Instruction and English Achievement: Voices from Ghana. English Language Teaching, 7(6). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n6p175

article_title: An Investigation of the Effectiveness of Concept Mapping on Turkish Students' Academic Success
citation: Yavuz Erdoğan. (2016). An Investigation of the Effectiveness of Concept Mapping on Turkish Students' Academic Success. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 4(6). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i6.1380
title: Concept map as a graphical tool of concepts and labeled connections
description: The article describes the concept map as "a graphical tool to create and show illustration the connections between ideas and concepts", comprised of concepts embedded in closed shapes such as boxes and circles, with connections displayed as lines joining the shapes. It can serve as an assessment tool, an instructional material, and a means of revealing learners' mental organization of concepts.
requirements: Concepts and their connections must be displayed graphically so hierarchical relationships become visible
constraints: The article notes effects on outcomes other than academic success (attitude, retention, anxiety) were outside the scope of this meta-analysis
target_learning_goals: reflecting knowledge about a subject
easing the burden of studying
facilitating learning of new concepts and their relationships
key_sources: Yavuz Erdoğan. (2016). An Investigation of the Effectiveness of Concept Mapping on Turkish Students' Academic Success. Journal of Education and Training Studies, 4(6). https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i6.1380

article_title: The Visual Memory-Based Memorization Techniques in Piano Education
citation: Yucetoker, I. (2016). The visual memory-based memorization techniques in piano education. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 65, 111-128. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.65.07
title: Color-coded visual scheme for Bach invention memorization
description: A visual analysis tool for Bach's two-part inventions in which themes, counter-themes, and other elements are marked with different colors and shapes on note cards given to students. Main themes are red, counter themes green, frequent themes yellow, and long voices purple, with tonalities written under the elements to facilitate memorization.
requirements: Students must be identified as having strong visual memory
constraints: Developed specifically for visual learner type
target_learning_goals: memorization of Bach inventions
structural analysis of contrapuntal music
examples: Applied to BWV 772 Do major diaphonic invention over 6 weeks
key_sources: Yucetoker, I. (2016). The visual memory-based memorization techniques in piano education. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 65, 111-128. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.65.07

article_title: The Effect of Cooperative Learning Method and Systematic Teaching on Students' Achievement and Retention of Knowledge in Social Studies Lesson
citation: Korkmaz Toklucu, S., & Tay, B. (2016). The effect of cooperative learning method and systematic teaching on students' achievement and retention of knowledge in social studies lesson. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 66, 315-334. http://dx.doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.66.18
title: Use cooperative learning and systematic teaching alongside the constructivist approach to enhance achievement and retention in social studies
description: The article recommends that social studies instruction not rely solely on teacher guide book activities aligned to the constructivist approach. Based on its experimental findings, it recommends that "the cooperative learning method and systematic teaching be used to enhance academic achievement and retention of gains in social studies lessons," supplementing constructivist instruction with these active learning methods.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of the basic philosophy and steps of the methods they implement
constraints: The recommendation rests on a single experimental study in one 4th-grade social studies unit, "The Place We Live"
target_learning_goals: Social studies achievement and retention of knowledge in the unit 'The Place We Live'
examples: Experiment group 1 was taught with five cooperative learning techniques over five weeks; experiment group 2 was taught with systematic teaching lesson plans based on Sonmez (2010)
key_sources: Korkmaz Toklucu, S., & Tay, B. (2016). The effect of cooperative learning method and systematic teaching on students' achievement and retention of knowledge in social studies lesson. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 66, 315-334. http://dx.doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.66.18

article_title: The Comparison of the Effect of Block Flute Accompanied Song Teaching with Multi-Sound Notation and Vocalization Program Accompanied Song Teaching on the Success of Students' Song Learning Behavior
citation: ŞAKTANLI, S. C., & ÖZDEMİR, G. (2011). THE COMPARISON OF THE EFFECT OF BLOCK FLUTE ACCOMPANIED SONG TEACHING WITH MULTI-SOUND NOTATION AND VOCALIZATION PROGRAM ACCOMPANIED SONG TEACHING ON THE SUCCESS OF STUDENTS’ SONG LEARNING BEHAVIOR. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(1).
title: Use computer-supported multi-sound notation and vocalization programs instead of block flute accompaniment when teaching songs in primary music education.
description: The article recommends that "Instead of using the block flute as an accompaniment instrument in teaching songs, using multi-sound accompaniment prepared in the computer is more effective" across all five evaluated singing behaviors. It argues this contributes "easy application and higher success rate" and can fill the gap of rarely available multi-sound instruments in Turkish primary schools.
requirements: A computer supported notation and vocalization program with a multi-sound arrangement of the target song, used through aural-song training method
constraints: Evidence comes from a single song ("Bir Dünya Bırakın") taught to 5th, 6th and 7th graders in Burdur primary schools over 15-minute sessions
target_learning_goals: Singing songs accurately in melody, rhythm, lay-rhythm, intonation and as a whole
examples: The experimental group worked on a multi-sound string-orchestra arrangement of the song for 15 minutes with the notation and vocalization program, while the pilot group used block flute in mono-sound; unaccompanied recordings were scored by three experts.

THE COMPARISON OF THE EFFECT OF BLOCK FLUTE ACCOMPANIED SONG TEACHING WITH MULTI-SOUND NOTATION AND VOCALIZATION PROGRAM ACCOMPANIED SONG TEACHING ON THE SUCCESS OF STUDENTS’ SONG LEARNING BEHAVIOR. article_title: The Effect of Conceptual Change Approach to Eliminate 9th Grade High School Students' Misconceptions about Air Pressure
citation: Akbaş, Y., & Gençtürk, E. (2011). The Effect of Conceptual Change Approach to Eliminate 9th Grade High School Students' Misconceptions about Air Pressure. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 11(4), 2217-2222.
title: Use conceptual change texts together with concept maps to remediate misconceptions
description: Teaching should use conceptual change texts together with concept maps when addressing known misconceptions, because this combination outperformed traditional methods in this study. Concept maps "visualize the relationship and hierarchy between concepts" while texts help students explore and correct misconceptions.
requirements: Identify students' existing misconceptions before instruction (via pretests or success tests) to prepare targeted conceptual change texts.
constraints: Some misconceptions persisted even after conceptual change instruction, attributed to students' resistance to change.
target_learning_goals: Understanding air pressure concepts
Eliminating misconceptions about atmospheric pressure
examples: Experiment group taught with conceptual change texts and concept maps; control group taught the same air pressure topic with traditional methods.

article_title: Tutoring with Alphie: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Centre for Effective Education, Queen's University Belfast. (2015). Tutoring with Alphie: Evaluation report and Executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Combine digital technology with collaborative pair or group learning rather than individual use
description: Drawing on Higgins et al.'s (2012) synthesis, the report argues the effectiveness of digital learning technologies "depends less on the technology itself, but rather on the way in which they are used", and that approaches combining digital technology with collaborative learning in groups or pairs appear more effective than individual use. Tutoring with Alphie embodies this by pairing pupils as reader and coach at one computer. The report also notes it may work best as a short (5–10 weeks) regular catch-up intervention for low attaining pupils.
requirements: Pedagogical integration of the technology (paired cooperative roles, tutor monitoring) rather than software adoption alone
constraints: The report notes relatively few rigorous evaluations of combined cooperative learning plus computer-assisted instruction exist, so further evaluation is required to establish efficacy across ages
target_learners: Low-attaining primary pupils needing literacy catch-up
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Reading fluency
examples: Tutoring with Alphie pairs pupils by attainment to alternate reader and coach roles at a computer, with software prompts for role switching and error support

article_title: Utilizing Instructional Media for Teaching Infrastructure Administration
citation: Ulfah Nur Fajriah, Madziatul Churiyah. (2016). Utilizing Instructional Media for Teaching Infrastructure Administration. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.6. https://www.iiste.org
title: Corel VideoStudio Pro X7-based multimedia learning media for infrastructure administration
description: A video-based instructional module developed with Corel VideoStudio Pro X7, assisted by Corel Draw X5, Adobe Photo Shop, and QuizCreator for post-test questions. Its main menu contains learning objectives, basic and core competences, manual instruction, material with photographs of office layout factors, and a developer profile. The article states the software "provides complete arrangement of capturing, burning and editing video from one another, and distributing the video to DVD or Blu-ray Disc, mobile devices or the web".
requirements: Supported facilities such as a laptop or computer, LCD and projector are needed to run the media
constraints: The article states the media cannot be implemented in all schools, only particular schools with such facilities
target_learners: Class XI office administration students at SMK Negeri 1 Ngawi, East Java, Indonesia
target_learning_goals: Office spatial factors material of Basic Competence 3.1 and 4.1 in infrastructure administration
examples: The module was validated by material and media experts, tried out with a limited group of six students, and field-tested with class XI AP1.

article_title: Utilizing Instructional Media for Teaching Infrastructure Administration
citation: Ulfah Nur Fajriah, Madziatul Churiyah. (2016). Utilizing Instructional Media for Teaching Infrastructure Administration. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.6. https://www.iiste.org
title: Edgar Dale's Cone of Experience: concrete learning yields more experience and knowledge
description: Edgar Dale's Cone of Experience classifies learning experiences on a level scale ordered from the most concrete to the most abstract. The article uses it to justify embedding photographs and concrete examples of office layout factors in the multimedia module, so that students who could previously only imagine the objects can see them directly. The article infers that "the more concrete way students lear n, the more experience and knowledge will be gained".
requirements: Learning experiences should be arranged from concrete toward abstract representations
target_learning_goals: Understanding concrete subject matter such as office layout factors
examples: The module inserted photographs of lighting, color, room light, and sound structuring systems to give students a real picture of office layout factors.

article_title: The Effect of Contextual and Conceptual Rewording on Mathematical Problem-Solving Performance
citation: Majid Haghverdi and Lynda R. Wiest. (2016). The Effect of Contextual and Conceptual Rewording on Mathematical Problem-Solving Performance. The Mathematics Educator, 25(1), 56–73. https://matheducator
title: Two types of word-problem rewording: contextual (situational) and conceptual
description: The article distinguishes two rewording approaches. In contextual rewording, "the context —or non -mathematical content —of a problem is altered", for example replacing unfamiliar story content with personally familiar content while maintaining problem structure. In conceptual rewording, "textual modifications make semantic relations among key problem elements (e.g., given and unknown sets) more explicit and transparent by, for example, adding or rearranging text". The study built three reworded tests (T1, T2, T3) from these types plus their combination and tested their effects on seventh-grade error rates.
requirements: Rewording must maintain the problem's mathematical structure while altering context or making semantic relations explicit
constraints: Contextual rewording is also known as situational rewording; both types were tested without accompanying instruction in problem solving
target_learning_goals: solving two-step arithmetic word problems
examples: Test T1 reworded an unfamiliar Ardabil/Tehran/Arak temperature problem into a familiar problem about Ali's scores in mathematics, literature, and geography; Test T2 reorganized the same problem to state the three-city temperature relations explicitly.
key_sources: Majid Haghverdi and Lynda R. Wiest. (2016). The Effect of Contextual and Conceptual Rewording on Mathematical Problem-Solving Performance. The Mathematics Educator, 25(1), 56–73. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1110640

article_title: Design and Effects of a Concept Focused Discussion Environment in E-Learning
citation: Yilmaz, E. O., & Yurdugul, H. (2016). Design and effects of a concept focused discussion environment in e-learning. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research, 63, 353-374. https://doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2016.63.20
title: Concept Focused Discussion Environment (CFDE)
description: CFDE is an LMS-integrated discussion environment inspired by the wiki connection metaphor: significant concepts in content texts appear as dark, underlined links, and clicking a concept opens a discussion frame that slides from the right side of the same screen rather than moving students to a separate module. The article built the LMS with Adobe Flash and the discussion infrastructure with PHP-based Vbulletin on a Linux host. It was compared against a traditional threaded discussion environment over six weeks.
requirements: Content texts must mark concepts directly related to the subject and significant to learning the content as links, and significant concepts are also listed under the content text
constraints: The study reports the environment as an independent module alternative to traditional hierarchical threaded discussions within LMSs; effectiveness evidence comes from one six-week university course
target_learning_goals: concept-focused discussion of course content in an online blended learning environment
examples: Experimental group students signed in and navigated weekly subject lists; clicking a concept opened only that concept's discussion window, and a black 'Discussion' box toggled the most recent discussion subject

article_title: Reusing Comprehensive Charts of Tense Forms to Teach EFL Students in a University of Science and Technology
citation: Tsai, Min-hsiu. (2017). Reusing Comprehensive Charts of Tense Forms to Teach EFL Students in a University of Science and Technology. World Journal of Education, 7(3). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v7n3p115
title: Comprehensive Charts of 24 Tense Forms
description: A synthesized instructional chart, created by the researcher in 1998, laying out all active and passive English tense forms together with formulas and example sentences. The article describes it as demonstrating "the whole framework of the tense forms to learners concerning how they are formed and what their similar and different patterns are". It comprises an active-tense chart and a passive-tense chart (Appendices 1 and 2), each organized by present, past, and future across simple, continuous, perfect, and perfect continuous aspects.
requirements: Learners need sufficient English competence for the instruction to be effective; the article reports it worked best for advanced achievers
constraints: The study tested only three translation items, limiting the written-context evidence
target_learners: EFL college freshmen at intermediate or upper-intermediate level
target_learning_goals: recognizing and producing English tense-aspect forms
examples: Three experimental classes were taught with the charts while three control classes received instruction without them

article_title: Effectiveness of Community of Inquiry Based Online Course: Cognitive, Social and Teaching Presence
citation: Aktı-Aslan, S. & Turgut, Y. E. (2021). Effectiveness of community of inquiry based online course: Cognitive, social and teaching presence. Journal of Pedagogical Research, 5(3), 187-197. https://doi.org/10.33902/JPR.2021371365
title: Community of inquiry model: social, cognitive and teaching presence as interacting dimensions of online learning
description: The community of inquiry (CoI) model holds that "learning takes place in a community as a result of three elements including social presence, cognitive presence, and teaching presence". Cognitive presence is the process of constructing knowledge through research and discussion, unfolding in four stages from triggering events to resolution; social presence covers open communication, group cohesion and effective expression; teaching presence covers design and organization, facilitating conversation, and direct teaching. The article uses CoI both as a design framework for online activities and as the measured outcome, noting the three dimensions "represent different aspects of education while interacting with each other".
requirements: All three dimensions must be present and interacting for an online community to function as an inquiry community
constraints: Prior studies disagree on which presence dominates: some report equal roles, others that cognitive presence dominates or that teaching presence suppresses the others
target_learning_goals: meaningful online learning experiences
critical discourse and reflection
collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The experimental course used cooperative learning, breakout-room group work, provocative open-ended questions, and prompt feedback to enact the three presences
key_sources: Aktı-Aslan, S. & Turgut, Y. E. (2021). Effectiveness of community of inquiry based online course: Cognitive, social and teaching presence. Journal of Pedagogical Research, 5(3), 187-197. https://doi.org/10.33902/JPR.2021371365

article_title: Effectiveness of Community of Inquiry Based Online Course: Cognitive, Social and Teaching Presence
citation: Aktı-Aslan, S. & Turgut, Y. E. (2021). Effectiveness of community of inquiry based online course: Cognitive, social and teaching presence. Journal of Pedagogical Research, 5(3), 187-197. https://doi.org/10.33902/JPR.2021371365
title: Presence-stratified teaching strategy set for CoI-based online courses
description: The article compiles a table of teaching strategies organised by type of presence, drawn from Fiock (2020) and the seven principles of Sorensen and Baylen (2009). Social presence strategies include "Encouraging students to share their experiences and beliefs in online discussions" and working in teams; cognitive presence strategies include provocative open-ended questions and gradual weekly activities; teaching presence strategies include facilitating rather than dominating discussion, constructive on-time feedback, and keeping resources one click away. The pattern was implemented weekly over seven weeks in a synchronous Zoom course with breakout-room group work.
requirements: Synchronous online platform with breakout rooms and communication channels
Instructor time for mentoring, prompt feedback and e-mail responses
constraints: In this study social presence did not improve significantly, possibly because students never met in person and teamwork occurred only in online lessons
target_learning_goals: cognitive presence
teaching presence
social presence
online community building
examples: Six groups of 6-7 students worked in Zoom breakout rooms; group leaders shared outputs; the instructor visited rooms and guided discussions
key_sources: Aktı-Aslan, S. & Turgut, Y. E. (2021). Effectiveness of community of inquiry based online course: Cognitive, social and teaching presence. Journal of Pedagogical Research, 5(3), 187-197. https://doi.org/10.33902/JPR.2021371365

citation: Aktı-Aslan, S. & Turgut, Y. E. (2021). Effectiveness of community of inquiry based online course: Cognitive, social and teaching presence. Journal of Pedagogical Research, 5(3), 187-197. https://doi.org/10.33902/JPR.2021371365
title: Community of inquiry scale (Arbaugh et al. 2008, Turkish adaptation by Öztürk 2012)
description: The study's outcome measure is "The five -point Likert type scale consists of 34 items with three factors": social presence (9 items), cognitive presence (12 items), and teaching presence (13 items). In the original version "the Cronbach's alpha value was calculated as .97", with sub-factor reliabilities of .88, .75 and .92. Items probe, for example, whether online discussions helped develop a sense of collaborating with others and whether the teacher kept the class focused on course work.
requirements: Administered after instruction; interpreted via skewness/kurtosis normality checks and independent samples t-tests
constraints: Sub-factor reliability of .75 for one factor is the lowest reported
target_learners: higher education students in online courses
target_learning_goals: measuring perceptions of social, cognitive and teaching presence
examples: Used as the sole post-instruction measure comparing the experimental and control groups in the Information Technologies course

article_title: The Effects of the Classroom Performance System on Student Participation, Attendance, and Achievement
citation: Termos, M. H. (2013). The Effects of the Classroom Performance System on Student Participation, Attendance, and Achievement. International Journal of Teaching and Learning in Higher Education, 25(1), 66-78. http://www.isetl.org/ijtlhe/
title: Design clicker questions that are conceptual, challenging, and assess higher Bloom's levels
description: Drawing on Wood (2009), the article states that questions developed by the instructor should be "conceptual and challenging . . . and should assess higher Bloom's levels of understanding". Bloom's taxonomy divides understanding into six levels — knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis, and evaluation — with evaluation the highest. In biology classes it is used to develop formative assessment questions at the appropriate cognitive level and to revise course design, so clicker questions pitched at higher levels promote genuine critical thinking rather than random answering.
requirements: Instructors must know the six Bloom's levels and write questions targeting the appropriate cognitive level
constraints: The article ties this recommendation to college anatomy and physiology and biology classes, where it was drawn from Wood (2009)
target_learners: college students in anatomy and physiology and biology courses
target_learning_goals: critical thinking and higher-level understanding of course concepts
examples: The study's group work-based CPS questions lasted five to 15 minutes and required critical thinking and active participation in a group with the use of available resources before reaching the answer

article_title: A Student-Centered Guest Lecturing: A Constructivism Approach to Promote Student Engagement
citation: Lei Li; Rong Guo. (2015). A student-centered guest lecturing: A constructivism approach to promote student engagement. Journal of Instructional Pedagogies, 15. http://www.aabri.com/copyright.html
title: Constructivism as the theoretical basis for converting speaker-centered guest lecturing into student-centered knowledge construction
description: The paper grounds its approach in constructivism, described as an instructional theory that "encourages experimental learning, hands-on learning and collaborative learning" and is identified as "a necessary strategy for learner-centered approach in online environment". The researchers argue that if a guest lecturing process lets students construct knowledge themselves through collaborative project work, students will learn better and be more engaged. Traditional guest lecturing is characterized as speaker-centered, leaving students passive, which the authors see as especially problematic online where lectures are often asynchronous videos.
requirements: The guest lecturing process must allow students to construct knowledge themselves through collaborative effort in a well-designed project
target_learning_goals: student engagement
deeper understanding of course content through active involvement
examples: The researchers redesign guest lecturing so students initialize the process by generating questions, the guest lecture is done in pure question-and-answer format, students reflect via discussion boards and essays, and teams work throughout
key_sources: Lei Li; Rong Guo. (2015). A student-centered guest lecturing: A constructivism approach to promote student engagement. Journal of Instructional Pedagogies, 15. http://www.aabri.com/copyright.html

article_title: Determination Instructions Efficiency of Teaching Methods in Teaching Physics in the Case of Teaching Unit "Viscosity. Newtonian and Stokes Law"
citation: Branka Radulović, Maja Stojanović. (2015). Determination Instructions Efficiency of Teaching Methods in Teaching Physics in the Case of Teaching Unit „Viscosity. Newtonian and Stokes law“. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 8, Number 2. https://adn.teaching.ro
title: Three-component cognitive load framework (intrinsic, extraneous, germane) as a criterion of teaching-method fit
description: The article applies cognitive load theory, distinguishing three load types: intrinsic load "depends only on complexity of teaching material", extraneous load "is not necessary for adoption of teaching material" and is manipulable by teaching method, and germane load "is related to classification of terms, differentiation, interpretation, giving of examples". A method is convenient when the sum of the three loads stays within working-memory capacity; if it exceeds capacity, extraneous load should first be reduced.
requirements: The sum of the three kinds of cognitive load must stay within the capacity limits of working memory for the method to suit students
constraints: Intrinsic load is not subject to manipulation by the choice of teaching method
target_learning_goals: understanding of physics content (viscosity, fluid mechanics)
examples: The framework was used to interpret why the experiment method achieved both lower load and higher achievement in the viscosity unit

article_title: Effect of Conceptual Change Texts for Overcoming Misconceptions in "People and Management" Unit
citation: Orhan Dağdelen, İlker Kösterelioğlu. (2015). Effect of Conceptual Change Texts for Overcoming Misconceptions in “People and Management” Unit. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 8(1), 99-112. https://www.iejee.com
title: Conceptual change text structure: question, dissatisfaction, refutation, and example-based reinforcement
description: Conceptual change texts, proposed by Roth (1985), are refutation-style texts designed to make students aware of their misconceptions. The article describes their operation: "Conceptual change texts start with a question and students are made aware that they lack information about the concepts in question"; dissatisfaction then creates ground for exchanging inaccurate knowledge with new knowledge, and accurate and inaccurate examples reinforce learning so misconceptions are replaced with accurate concepts. In this study researchers prepared such texts for nine social studies concepts.
requirements: Conceptual misunderstandings must be expressed in detail for activities aiming at conceptual change to be successful, according to Case & Fraser (1999) as cited.
constraints: Most prior research on CCTs is in Science; social studies use had been limited to teacher candidates at higher levels.
target_learning_goals: Accurate, meaningful concept learning and overcoming misconceptions
examples: Researchers prepared CCTs from literature on the nine concepts' misconceptions, had them reviewed by experts and teachers, and checked intelligibility with 8 4th graders.
key_sources: Orhan Dağdelen, İlker Kösterelioğlu. (2015). Effect of Conceptual Change Texts for Overcoming Misconceptions in “People and Management” Unit. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 8(1), 99-112. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1078838

citation: Nisreen Saleh Khader Khader. (2016). The Effectiveness of Blended Learning in Improving Students' Achievement in Third Grade's Science in Bani Kenana. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(35). https://www.iiste.org
title: Computerized lesson pattern: recall prior experiences, state objectives, guided activity, then independent student work with worksheets
description: The article describes a lesson structure used to build the computerized material: "The computerized lessons were built through a certain pattern and mechanism through recalling the previous experiences of the new lesson, followed by a presentation of the educational objectives and outcomes". The teacher then displays an activity and works with students, after which students work independently, accompanied by teacher and student interaction and motivation, with worksheets for answers.
requirements: Teachers who mix ordinary methods with the computerized curriculum
Worksheets and computerized activities prepared and accessible, printable if necessary
target_learning_goals: science concepts in the studied units
examples: Teachers used data shows connected with laptops to display educational means and moved with complete flexibility with the educational material.

article_title: Advancing Diagnostic Skills for Technology and Engineering Undergraduates: A Summary of the Validation Data
citation: Foster, W. T., Shahhosseini, A. M., & Maughan, G. (2016). Advancing Diagnostic Skills for Technology and Engineering Undergraduates: A Summary of the Validation Data. Journal of Technology Education, 28(1). https://scholar.lib.vt.edu/ejournals/JTE/v28n1/
title: Conceptual mapping as a treatment for developing diagnostic and problem-solving skills
description: Drawing on Novak's conceptual mapping (based on Ausubel, Piaget, and Vygotsky) and on systems thinking, the article frames forcing in-depth analysis of technical problems through map construction as a way to develop diagnostic skill. The premise tested was that mapping the student's intentions during diagnosis would increase accuracy relative to expert process maps and make students 'more agile in their thinking regarding ill-defined problems.' Concept mapping is described as a graphical representation where nodes represent concepts and links represent relationships, integral to systems thinking.
requirements: Practice with ill-defined problems within a supportive and instructional environment, and knowledge of how to process information, form and test hypotheses, and make choices based on data
constraints: The experimental data did not support the conclusion that the treatment caused an increase in diagnostic performance; qualitative analysis found the majority of students treated the experience as a trivial academic exercise, seriously limiting their efforts
target_learners: undergraduate engineering and technology students (novice troubleshooters)
target_learning_goals: diagnostic inference and root cause analysis
systems thinking about technical problems
metacognitive reasoning skills
examples: The team encouraged continued and expanded use of conceptual mapping as a tool for improving diagnostic and problem-solving skills, extending to all stages from problem identification to solution and follow-up assessment
key_sources: Foster, W. T., Shahhosseini, A. M., & Maughan, G. (2016). Advancing Diagnostic Skills for Technology and Engineering Undergraduates: A Summary of the Validation Data. Journal of Technology Education, 28(1). https://scholar.lib.vt.edu/ejournals/JTE/v28n1/

article_title: Game-Based Tasks for Foreign Language Instruction: Perspectives on Young Learners' Vocabulary Acquisition
citation: Masoumeh Mehregan. (2014). Game-Based Tasks for Foreign Language Instruction: Perspectives on Young Learners' Vocabulary Acquisition. The IAFOR Journal of Language Learning. https://iafor.org/journal
title: Concrete, game-based tasks suit young learners who cannot yet think abstractly
description: The article argues that teaching young learners should rely on concrete and tangible activities because they struggle with abstract content: "The use of game-based activities and tasks presents an effective way of teaching vocabularies concretely to the young language learners who do not have the advantage of thinking abstractly." Games also add interest, lower anxiety, and encourage shyer learners to participate, according to the authors' framing of prior literature.
requirements: Games matched to learners' proficiency level; the authors note games are not limited to beginner levels
constraints: The authors attribute the advantage partly to participants being at elementary proficiency level
target_learners: young language learners at elementary proficiency
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning in a low-anxiety, motivating environment
examples: The discussion attributes the experimental group's advantage to elementary-level learners being more at ease with the game-based approach and to the concreteness of the tasks.

article_title: Scenario-Based Case Study Method and the Functionality of the Section Called "From Production to Consumption" from the Perspective of Primary School Students
citation: Ahu TANERİ (2018). Scenario-Based Case Study Method and the Functionality of the Section Called 'from Production to Consumption' from the Perspective of Primary School Students. Asian Journal of Education and Training, 4(1): 56-61. https://doi.org/10.20448/journal.522.2018.41.56.61
title: Evaluation form and 'I am self-evaluating as a consumer' form as data collection tools
description: Two researcher-developed qualitative instruments collected the data: an evaluation form with open-ended questions about the teaching methods, liked and disliked aspects, daily-life contribution, and willingness to reuse the method; and the 'I am self-evaluating as a consumer' form comparing students' prior behaviors with the consumer behaviors learned during the study. Answers were content-analyzed with students coded S1 to S28 by class-list number.

constraints: Qualitative instrument within a single-classroom study; the article states the evaluation form "forms the basic data collection tool of this research"
target_learning_goals: evaluating teaching methods
self-assessing informed consumer behavior
examples: The evaluation form asked whether students had used the unit's teaching methods in another course and what similarities and differences they saw.

article_title: A Teacher-Friendly Method of Improving Reading and Mathematics
citation: Kidd, J. K., Gadzichowski, K. M., Gallington, D. A., Lopez, C., & Pasnak, R. (2013). A Teacher-Friendly Method of Improving Reading and Mathematics. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22A+Teacher-Friendly+Method+of+Improving+Reading+and+Mathematics%22+SREE
title: Year-long small-group instruction on increasingly complex patterns with individual mastery before progression
description: This instructional design replaces conventional simple alternation patterning with complex patterns — symmetrical patterns, progressions with increasing numbers of elements, rotations, and arbitrary repeating patterns — taught in 15-minute sessions three times weekly during centers time. Each pattern had a missing element, and "performance was scaffolded through explanation and repetition until each child was able to demonstrate mastery of each pattern" on three consecutive first attempts. Children also extended patterns with manipulatives and created patterns for others.
requirements: Individual mastery of each pattern before moving on to the next
Instruction continuing across the school year rather than a few weeks
constraints: The article states it is unlikely that a few weeks of whole class instruction on simple alternation patterns would have produced the outcomes found
target_learners: First-graders with relatively poor understanding of patterns (low scorers on a patterning screening test)
target_learning_goals: Understanding of complex repeating patterns, supporting mathematics and reading achievement
examples: Patterns were displayed on note cards, white boards, table tops, or minicomputers; children identified the correct option from four choices and used manipulatives to extend or create patterns

article_title: Air Reading: A Randomized Evaluation of a Virtual Tutoring Model in Louisiana Schools
citation: Neitzel, A.J., & Storey, N. (2025). Air Reading: A randomized evaluation of a virtual tutoring model in Louisiana schools. Center for Research and Reform in Education, Johns Hopkins University. https://education.jhu.edu/crre
title: Consistent small-group live virtual tutoring with embedded assessment
description: The Air Reading model pairs small groups of students with the same tutor over time and embeds assessment into placement and progress monitoring. "Small groups of up to four students are paired with the same highly-qualified tutor in 30-minute sessions four times each week." Diagnostics identify learning needs and inform group placement, while bi-weekly assessments track progress, and sessions are monitored on a proprietary platform to maintain consistent standards.
requirements: Highly qualified, paid tutors; ongoing training and support; a systematic reading curriculum; session tracking and monitoring
constraints: The model is designed to be scalable and replicable regardless of school geography or staffing capabilities, per the article
target_learners: Elementary students performing below grade level in reading
target_learning_goals: Foundational reading skills
examples: The Louisiana RCT implemented the model across a full school year, with treatment students attending a mean of 54.2 sessions (SD = 14.5)

article_title: Development of Learning Management Model Based on Constructivist Theory and Reasoning Strategies for Enhancing the Critical Thinking of Secondary Students
citation: Dudduan Chaipichit, Nirat Jantharajit and Sumalee Chookhampaeng. (2015). Development of learning management model based on constructivist theory and reasoning strategies for enhancing the critical thinking of secondary students. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2193
title: Learning Management Model Based on Constructivist Theory integrating reasoning strategies for critical thinking
description: The article develops a learning management model grounded in Constructivist Theory, in which students construct knowledge by associating new experience with prior knowledge, and integrates reasoning strategies for enhancing critical thinking into science instruction. It was built through a Research and Development process and structured following Joyce, Weil and Calhoun's model of teaching, including "the basic rationale, approach, and theory", objectives, implementation steps, social system, principle of response, and support system.
requirements: Developed through a Research and Development process including literature survey, situation analysis, expert focus-group examination, and a pilot try-out
constraints: Designed for science content at the secondary school level; the authors note the subject matter itself may affect results
target_learners: secondary school students (grade 9 science students in Thailand)
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills
science learning achievement
examples: The model was implemented with one class of 33 grade 9 students as the experimental group and compared with a control class of 30 students taught by the traditional approach

Development of learning management model based on constructivist theory and reasoning strategies for enhancing the critical thinking of secondary students. article_title: The Impact of Online Algorithm Visualization on ICT Students' Achievements in Introduction to Programming Course
citation: Fatih Saltan. (2017). The Impact of Online Algorithm Visualization on ICT Students' Achievements in Introduction to Programming Course. Journal of Education and Learning, 6(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v6n1p184
title: Code.org 20-hour introduction course as the online algorithm visualization environment
description: The OAV environment used in the study was provided by code.org, a non-profit organization launched in 2013 that "aims to teach computer programming and computer science through visualization" online. The researcher used its "20 hour introduction course", which students completed individually during course hours, and the environment "allows the instructor to observe his or her students' progress in real-time". It was chosen because it is online, free, and provides a user-friendly interface.
requirements: Internet access from computers or mobile devices, since the program is accessible online
constraints: The study used only the 20 hour introduction course, covering algorithms and semantics before C# coding began
target_learners: second-year ICT students with no prior programming experience
target_learning_goals: algorithmic thinking
understanding programming semantics
examples: All treatment-group students individually completed the 20 hour introduction course during the first four weeks while the researcher tracked their progress and encouraged them.

article_title: Effect of Inclusion versus Segregation on Reading Comprehension of EFL Learners with Dyslexia: Case of Lebanon
citation: Ghada M. Awada & Mar Gutiérrez-Colón. (2017). Effect of Inclusion Versus Segregation on Reading Comprehension of EFL Learners with Dyslexia: Case of Lebanon. English Language Teaching, 10(9), 49. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n9p49
title: Combined strategy instruction package of ten reading strategies
description: The treatment element is a combined strategy instruction package consisting of graphic organizers, visual displays, mnemonic illustrations, computer exercises, predicting, inference, text structure awareness, main idea identification, summarization, and questioning. It was delivered over four months at six contact hours per week by teachers who "received a 5-day training on the use of each strategy of the combined strategy instruction." Pre- and post-tests included items reflecting the strategies of the combined treatment.
requirements: Teachers trained in the use of the ten reading strategies; same supplementary and basic materials and tests employed across conditions
constraints: In public schools the treatment lacked the computer exercises due to unavailability of needed equipment
target_learners: Middle school EFL learners with and without dyslexia
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension of narrative and expository texts
examples: Private schools implemented the full package including computer exercises; public schools implemented the same package minus computer exercises

article_title: Early Integration of Tutorial Support in Beginning Algebra
citation: Copus, C., & McKinney, B. (2016). Early Integration of Tutorial Support in Beginning Algebra. Journal of Developmental Education, 40(1). https://www.nade.net
title: Coordinated integration of tutoring laboratories with classroom instruction
description: Drawing on Boylan (2002), the article characterizes integrated developmental education support by "the way in which they [classroom activities and tutoring laboratories] are coordinated with each other". The pattern treats tutoring not as a separate one-to-one service but as coordinated with course objectives, assignments, and logistics, so that support services and classroom instruction function as one system rather than parallel offerings.
requirements: Instructors consult tutoring personnel
Laboratory materials are coordinated with course objectives
Tutoring activities are required as part of course assignments or grades
Reasonably close physical proximity of the laboratory and the courses it supports
constraints: The article notes the ITS program's own physical proximity condition was disrupted when logistics required relocating tutoring services, with effects under investigation
target_learners: Developmental education students in community college courses
target_learning_goals: Integration of prerequisite skill support with credit course content
Improved course success and persistence
examples: ITS required tutoring attendance as part of program conditions, aligned ALEKS worksheets to deficit topics, and initially located tutoring near the classroom

article_title: Analyzing the Effect of Concept Cartoon Usage on Students' Cognitive Structures Developments and Science Achievements through Flow Maps
citation: Ceylan, Ö., & Yiğit, E. A. (2018). Analyzing the Effect of Concept Cartoon Usage on Students’ Cognitive Structures Developments and Science Achievements through Flow Maps. Science Education International, 29(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Analyzing+the+Effect+of+Concept+Cartoon+Usage+through+Flow+Maps
title: Researcher-developed concept cartoons for the particulate nature of matter unit
description: Concept cartoons are, in the article's words, "a poster drawn in cartoon style containing different ideas about a scientific subject," with ideas expressed as arguments by cartoon characters that students then discuss. For this study the researchers developed 20 concept cartoons covering the 7th-grade particulate nature of matter unit, using up to four characters (Oktay, Ata, Asya, Öykü), drawn by a graphic artist and validated by a subject-matter professor. The cartoons were shown in slides, usually in the elaboration phase of 5E lessons, to the experimental group over 8 weeks while the control group received traditional teaching.
requirements: A subject-matter specialist should check the cartoons' validity against the learning outcomes and students' level.
Cartoons are added to existing 5E-model content; the control content in this study was taught without them.
constraints: Some students judged the cartoons "deficient in information," and a minority (4 of 27) found them not funny.
target_learners: 7th-grade middle school science students (12–13 years old)
target_learning_goals: Learning the particulate nature of matter unit
Addressing misconceptions about atoms, elements, compounds and mixtures
examples: 20 cartoons presented in slides during the elaboration section of 8-week 5E lessons; semi-structured interviews about them followed the unit.
