article_title: Exploring the Impact of Parallel Teaching on General Language Proficiency of EFL Learners
citation: Aliakbari, M. & Bazyar, A. (2012). Exploring the Impact of Parallel Teaching on General Language Proficiency of EFL Learners. Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 16(1), 55-71. https://www.paaljapan.org
title: Typologies of co-teaching models and structures
description: The article reviews several classifications of co-teaching arrangements. Watkins and Caffarella identified four working-style variations, and Friend and Cook (2004) "introduce six approaches to co-teaching", including parallel teaching, in which co-teachers teach the same information to divided class groups simultaneously. Morocco and Mata-Aguilar's structures and Bacharach, Heck, and Dahlberg's strategies are tabulated, defining arrangements such as station teaching, alternative teaching, and team teaching.
requirements: Two or more educators working in a coordinated, collaborative relationship with shared planning, delivery, and assessment
constraints: Buckley cautions there is no universal approach to team teaching; collaboration varies along a continuum from individually taught co-planned courses to fully co-planned and co-taught courses
target_learners: heterogeneous or blended groups of students in K-12 and language classrooms
target_learning_goals: general academic and language instruction delivered through shared teaching arrangements
examples: The study implemented the parallel model: each co-teacher taught his own group the same material in the same classroom setting simultaneously, without changing roles or groups
key_sources: Aliakbari, M. & Bazyar, A. (2012). Exploring the Impact of Parallel Teaching on General Language Proficiency of EFL Learners. Journal of Pan-Pacific Association of Applied Linguistics, 16(1), 55-71. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ979922

article_title: Successful Learning of Academic Word List via MALL: Mobile Assisted Language Learning
citation: Minoo Alemi, Mohammad Reza Anani Sarab & Zahra Lari. (2012). Successful Learning of Academic Word List via MALL: Mobile Assisted Language Learning. International Education Studies, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n6p99
title: Academic Word List (Coxhead, 2000) as the source of target vocabulary
description: The Academic Word List is organised into "10 sublists based on decreasing level of frequency" and "totally contained 3000 academic words." The study chose it because it highlights words university students encounter in academic texts, accounts for 10% of tokens in the academic corpus, and compensates for the low academic-word coverage (4.63%) of the participants' general English textbook. Target words were drawn from the headwords of the last 7 sublists, deemed suitable for the students' level.
requirements: Selection of headwords appropriate to learners' proficiency level
constraints: The first 3 sublists proved too easy for the participants and were excluded
target_learners: university freshmen preparing for ESP coursework
target_learning_goals: academic vocabulary knowledge
examples: 320 headwords from the last 7 sublists were taught over 16 weeks, 10 words per delivery session
key_sources: Minoo Alemi, Mohammad Reza Anani Sarab & Zahra Lari. (2012). Successful Learning of Academic Word List via MALL: Mobile Assisted Language Learning. International Education Studies, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n6p99

article_title: Students' Proficiency and Textual Computer Gloss Use in Facilitating Vocabulary Knowledge
citation: Mohamad A. Yusuf, Tam S. Sim & Su’ad A. (2014). Students’ Proficiency and Textual Computer Gloss Use in Facilitating Vocabulary Knowledge. English Language Teaching, 7(11). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n11p99
title: Computer textual glosses embedded in a narrative text, at word and sentence levels in L1 and English
description: The element is a set of textual glosses embedded in the narrative text "A Scar y Night", uploaded to a website. Thirteen words were glossed in Bahasa Melayu and English; word glosses provided definitional meaning while sentence glosses provided "meaning in contextualised form". Students clicked colour-highlighted words to view meanings, and gloss use was operationalised as the clicking done on the glossed words.
requirements: Glossed words must be marked in a different colour from the rest of the text so learners can click them to consult meanings
constraints: The study used textual glosses only and had not incorporated multimedia glosses, which the authors note are more complex to design
target_learning_goals: Productive and receptive vocabulary knowledge of glossed words
examples: Thirteen unfamiliar words in the narrative were glossed at word and sentence levels in BM and English, selected by researchers and a pilot student group circling difficult words
key_sources: Mohamad A. Yusuf, Tam S. Sim & Su’ad A. (2014). Students’ Proficiency and Textual Computer Gloss Use in Facilitating Vocabulary Knowledge. English Language Teaching, 7(11). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n11p99

article_title: The Impact of Concept Mapping on EFL Learners' Critical Thinking Ability
citation: Khodadady, E., & Ghanizadeh, A. (2011). The Impact of Concept Mapping on EFL Learners' Critical Thinking Ability. English Language Teaching, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n4p49
title: Concept mapping as a meaningful-learning tool grounded in Ausubel's and Novak's theory
description: The article grounds concept mapping in Ausubel's meaningful learning, "based on the assumption that learning takes place in the human organization through a meaningful process of relating and anchoring new events or items to already existing cognitive concepts or propositions". Novak and Gowin's three requirements for meaningful learning are relevant prior knowledge, meaningful material, and the learner's deliberate choice to learn meaningfully. The epistemology builds on human constructivism, in which learners actively integrate thinking, feeling, and acting to construct meaning. The article uses this framework to justify concept maps as metacognitive tools for reflective thinking in EFL reading.
requirements: For meaningful learning to occur, the article lists: relevant prior knowledge, meaningful material, and the learner's conscious and deliberate choice to learn meaningfully
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
reading comprehension
examples: The experimental group constructed concept maps of each reading passage and organized post-reading activities such as discussion, exercises, and reflective practices around those maps
key_sources: Khodadady, E., & Ghanizadeh, A. (2011). The Impact of Concept Mapping on EFL Learners' Critical Thinking Ability. English Language Teaching, 4(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n4p49

article_title: Impact of Co-Operative Learning Strategies in English
citation: G. Singaravelu. (2010). Impact of Co-operative Learning Strategies in English. i-manager's Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. 4, No. 2, August-October 2010.
title: Co-operative learning as small mixed-ability teams with mutual responsibility
description: The article defines co-operative learning as "a successful teaching strategy in which small teams, each with students of different levels of ability, use a variety of learning activities to improve their understanding of a subject." Each member is responsible for learning and for helping teammates learn, creating an atmosphere of achievement in which students work until all members understand. The framework stresses mutual benefit: members gain from each other's efforts, share a common fate, and jointly celebrate success. It is used in the study as the theoretical basis for expecting grammar gains from team-based learning.
requirements: Small teams mixing ability levels, with activities structured so all members must understand and complete the assignment
constraints: The article notes less CL research has been done in second-language instruction than in other areas
target_learning_goals: English grammar and second-language content learning
examples: The study applied this framework by assigning 80 standard-X students to control and experimental groups taught grammar in teams
key_sources: G. Singaravelu. (2010). Impact of Co-operative Learning Strategies in English. i-manager's Journal of Educational Psychology, Vol. 4, No. 2, August-October 2010. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102270

article_title: Constructivist Approach Enhances the Learning: A Search of Reality
citation: Dr.(Ms.) Meenu Dev, Ph.D. (2016). Constructivist Approach Enhances the Learning: A Search of Reality. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.25. https://www.iiste.org
title: Constructivism as a learner-centered pedagogy in which the teacher acts as a facilitator and students construct meaning
description: The article frames constructivism as a pedagogy where "the emphasis will be mor e on what students do than what teachers do", contrasting it with direct instruction in which the teacher diffuses knowledge and students receive it. In the constructivist classroom students organize information, explore the learning environment, and monitor their own learning, while the teacher assumes a supporting or reflective role. In the study the teacher "acted as a facilitator of learning both inside and outside the classroom" and problem-based learning made learning an active process.
requirements: Teachers must focus on depth of understanding and assume a supporting or reflective role while students construct meaning
target_learning_goals: English language achievement
problem-solving ability
critical thinking
examples: In the study, the experimental group was taught English concepts with the researcher applying the constructivist method as per plan, and the teacher discussed with students how they had learned.
key_sources: Dr.(Ms.) Meenu Dev, Ph.D. (2016). Constructivist Approach Enhances the Learning: A Search of Reality. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.25. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1115872

article_title: Effect of Constructivist Based Training on Learning and Teaching: An Experiment in Classroom
citation: Laxmi Pandey, Devendra Ameta. (2017). Effect of Constructivist Based Training on Learning and Teaching: An Experiment in Classroom. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.13. https://www.iiste.org
title: Constructivist pedagogy as learner-centred, activity-based teaching
description: The article frames constructivism as "a new kind of pedagogy where  the emphasis is given more on what students do than what teachers do", using performance assessment rather than standardized achievement testing. In activity-based teaching, students organize information, explore the learning environment, conduct learning activities, and monitor their own learning. The study operationalized this approach through 200 hours of teacher training applied to elementary Hindi instruction.
requirements: Teachers trained in the approach (200 hours of constructive teaching training in the study)
Learning tasks planned in keeping with children's psychological development and interests
constraints: Studied at elementary level in Hindi language teaching; the article notes limited prior work in language compared with science and math
target_learning_goals: Hindi language achievement
problem-solving ability
examples: One group of 40 students was taught Hindi via the constructive approach while another 40 were taught conventionally, after their teachers completed 8 weeks of training.
key_sources: Laxmi Pandey, Devendra Ameta. (2017). Effect of Constructivist Based Training on Learning and Teaching: An Experiment in Classroom. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.8, No.13. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1143831

article_title: The Effects of Using Corpus Tools on EFL Student Teachers' Learning and Production of Verb-Noun Collocations
citation: Galip Kartal, Gonca Yangin Eksi. (2018). The Effects of Using Corpus Tools on EFL Student Teachers' Learning and Production of Verb-Noun Collocations. PASAA, Vol. 55. https://so04.tci-thaijo.org/index.php/pasaa
title: COCA and BNC corpora as free concordancing tools for collocation learning
description: The study used the Corpus of Contemporary American English (COCA) and the British National Corpus (BNC) as web-based concordancing tools. The article states COCA "is free to access, and it is a mega corpus which includes over 570 million words as well as comprehensive and representative data", covering 1990-2017 and spanning spoken, fiction, magazines, newspapers and academic genres; BNC contains more than 100 million words and uses the same interface. Participants searched verb-noun collocations and viewed KWIC-style example sentences, e.g. seeing that "run damage" or "make damage" return no results while "do damage" does.
requirements: Participants were told to work only with COCA and BNC and received a guideline about concordancing usage before the experiment
target_learning_goals: learning and producing English verb-noun collocations
examples: Figure 1 shows a COCA screenshot for the do-damage collocation used to demonstrate searching to student teachers
key_sources: Galip Kartal, Gonca Yangin Eksi. (2018). The Effects of Using Corpus Tools on EFL Student Teachers' Learning and Production of Verb-Noun Collocations. PASAA, Vol. 55. https://so04.tci-thaijo.org/index.php/pasaa

article_title: Understanding Atmospheric Carbon Budgets: Teaching Students Conservation of Mass
citation: Collin Reichert, Cinzia Cervato, Dale Niederhauser, and Michael D. Larsen. (2015). Understanding Atmospheric Carbon Budgets: Teaching Students Conservation of Mass. Journal of Geoscience Education 63, 222–232. https://doi.org/10.5408/14-055.1
title: Conceptual-change instructional design combining constructivist disequilibrium, andragogy, and cognitive flexibility principles
description: The article's intervention design rests on a conceptual change model in which inaccurate schemas must be directly confronted to prompt the cognitive effort necessary for accommodation: students are provided "an appropriate conceptual pathway" from naive understandings to scientific ones while their erroneous schemas are perturbed through activities designed to create disequilibrium. This is combined with andragogy principles (drawing on prior experience via familiar scenarios like bathtubs and bank accounts, real-life relevance, problem solving) and cognitive flexibility theory's five principles, including avoiding oversimplification, using multiple representations, teaching through cases, interconnecting cases, and having learners construct knowledge. The four Thinkspace tasks instantiate these principles in a snow-cone business scenario.
requirements: Inaccurate conceptions must be directly confronted to prompt the cognitive effort necessary for accommodation
A scientifically accurate conceptualization of the phenomenon must be provided so learners can abandon inaccurate schemas
constraints: The authors report these design principles alone were likely necessary but not sufficient, since most students still relied on the misconception after the intervention
target_learners: adult learners in large lecture courses
target_learning_goals: conceptual change about stock-flow systems and conservation of mass
generalizing budget concepts across contexts
examples: Task 3 presented bank-account records in which maximum balance occurred in October but maximum deposits occurred in July, requiring students to account for a contradictory example
key_sources: Collin Reichert, Cinzia Cervato, Dale Niederhauser, and Michael D. Larsen. (2015). Understanding Atmospheric Carbon Budgets: Teaching Students Conservation of Mass. Journal of Geoscience Education 63, 222–232. https://doi.org/10.5408/14-055.1

article_title: Comparative Effectiveness of Contextual and Structural Method of Teaching Vocabulary
citation: Malik Behlol & Mohammad Munir Kaini. (2011). Comparative Effectiveness of Contextual and Structural Method of Teaching Vocabulary. English Language Teaching, 4(1). http://www.ccsenet.org/elt
title: Contextual and structural approaches as two contrasting methods of vocabulary teaching
description: The article contrasts two vocabulary-teaching frameworks. The contextual approach teaches "the meanings of new words by having them used in different contexts surrounding the words", drawing on referent words, synonyms, antonyms, hyponyms and restatement, and distinguishes instructional from natural context. The structural approach "is based on the morphological analyses of the word", breaking words into prefixes, root and suffixes so learners generate and modify words across parts of speech. The experiment operationalized both as validated lesson plans taught by trained teachers.
requirements: Teacher training in the basic principles of each method; the study trained teachers before assigning them to groups
constraints: The article notes massive exposure of vocabulary may confuse students, and a single exposure is not enough to develop rich understanding
target_learners: secondary school students learning English vocabulary
target_learning_goals: word meaning, use in different contexts, and vocabulary building
examples: 40 lesson plans (20 per method) were developed and validated by university English language teaching experts
key_sources: Malik Behlol & Mohammad Munir Kaini. (2011). Comparative Effectiveness of Contextual and Structural Method of Teaching Vocabulary. English Language Teaching, 4(1). http://www.ccsenet.org/elt

article_title: The Effects of Explicit and Implicit Pragmatic Instruction on the Development of Compliments and Compliment Responses
citation: Saman Ebadi, Mahsa Pourzandi. (2015). The Effects of Explicit and Implicit Pragmatic Instruction on the Development of Compliments and Compliment Responses. li-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 5, No. 4, October - December. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+Effects+of+Explicit+and+Implicit+Pragmatic+Instruction+on+the+Development+of+Compliments+and+Compliment+Responses
title: Consciousness-raising account of pragmatic instruction
description: The article explains the gains of both explicit and implicit instruction through consciousness raising: pragmatic functions and contextual factors are often not salient to learners, so instruction of either type makes learners aware of what they are learning and how to use speech acts. As the abstract states, "pragmatic instruction regardless of type speeds up the process of learning through consciousness rising". The account draws on Schmidt's (1993) argument that simple exposure is not enough for developing pragmatic competence.
requirements: Instruction must direct learners' attention to the target speech acts and their contexts of use, whether through explicit explanation or guided practice with examples
constraints: The article frames this account for EFL learners in a non-English-speaking context and does not test the mechanism itself
target_learners: intermediate EFL learners in a foreign-language context
target_learning_goals: pragmatic competence in producing and responding to compliments
examples: The explicit group was taught what Cs and CRs are and how, where, why, and when to use them; the implicit group practiced making Cs and responses and generalized principles from examples and model conversations
key_sources: Saman Ebadi, Mahsa Pourzandi. (2015). The Effects of Explicit and Implicit Pragmatic Instruction on the Development of Compliments and Compliment Responses. li-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, Vol. 5, No. 4, October - December. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=The+Effects+of+Explicit+and+Implicit+Pragmatic+Instruction+on+the+Development+of+Compliments+and+Compliment+Responses

article_title: Teacher and Student Based Instructions on Probability Achievement Outcomes and Attitudes of Secondary School Students in Bungoma North, Kenya
citation: Joseph W. Pale. (2016). Teacher and Student Based Instructions on Probability Achievement Outcomes and Attitudes of Secondary School Students in Bungoma North, Kenya. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.24. https://www.iiste.org
title: Constructivist learning theory (Papert and Piaget) as the framework for student-based instruction
description: The study is framed by constructivist learning theory developed from Seymour Papert and Jean Piaget, under which learning is an active process. The article states that "Social constructivist scholars view  learning as an active process where learners shoul d learn to discover principles, concepts and facts for themselves". Social constructivists hold that collaborative elaboration — sharing individual perspectives — lets learners construct understanding together that would not be possible alone, and constructivist models stress collaboration among learners in direct contradiction to teacher-centred competitive approaches.
requirements: Instruction must actively engage students in constructing their own learning rather than positioning them as passive recipients
constraints: The article presents the theory as a framing background, not as a tested component of the experiment
target_learning_goals: probability concepts and achievement
attitudes toward mathematics
examples: The experimental group worked in small groups of two to four members exchanging information and strategies, operationalising the constructivist premise that students actively construct their own learning
key_sources: Joseph W. Pale. (2016). Teacher and Student Based Instructions on Probability Achievement Outcomes and Attitudes of Secondary School Students in Bungoma North, Kenya. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.24. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1112852

article_title: Using Voice Thread to Enhance Speaking Accuracy: A Case Study of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Ebadi, S., & Asakereh, A. (2018). Using Voice Thread to Enhance Speaking Accuracy: A Case Study of Iranian EFL Learners. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, 8(3). https://www.imanagerpublications.com
title: Comprehensive output hypothesis as the framework for asynchronous online speaking tasks
description: The study is framed by Swain's comprehensive output hypothesis, under which language production drives fluency and accuracy because learner output serves "consciousness raising, hypothesis testing, and metalingustic functions". Because EFL learners rarely produce oral language outside class, the authors treat Voice Thread as an asynchronous context supplying sufficient output opportunities, where learners can craft, alter, and practice responses before posting.
requirements: An out-of-class asynchronous context in which learners generate oral output and receive feedback on it
constraints: The authors note asynchronous contexts may not support real-life interaction or relationship building, which learners in this study valued
target_learners: EFL university freshmen in teacher-centered, input-limited contexts
target_learning_goals: Speaking accuracy in specific grammatical structures (English tenses, hypothetical conditionals)
examples: The experimental group posted one-minute voice entries on hypothetical conditional tasks across four sessions and received direct corrective feedback from the professor
key_sources: Ebadi, S., & Asakereh, A. (2018). Using Voice Thread to Enhance Speaking Accuracy: A Case Study of Iranian EFL Learners. i-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, 8(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1198886

article_title: Effects of Written Corrective Feedback: A Synthesis of 10 Quasi-Experimental Studies
citation: Albatool Abalkheel & Tara Brandenburg. (2020). Effects of Written Corrective Feedback: A Synthesis of 10 Quasi-Experimental Studies. English Language Teaching, 13(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v13n7p97
title: Cognitive-overload account: comprehensive correction addressing a range of errors prevents learners from effectively processing feedback
description: This explanatory account, attributed in the article to Sheen et al. (2009), explains why focused feedback outperforms comprehensive feedback: "when the correction addresses a range of grammatical errors, learners are unable to process the feedback effectively, and even if they attend to the corrections, they are unable to work out why they have been corrected". Comprehensive feedback may overburden students and is often unsystematic and arbitrarily selected, whereas focused CF helps learners notice errors, engage in hypothesis testing, and monitor their own writing using existing grammatical knowledge.
requirements: Feedback must be limited to selected error categories so learners can process the corrections and understand why they were corrected
constraints: The account is offered as the authors' interpretation via Sheen et al. (2009), not a result tested within this meta-analysis
target_learning_goals: grammatical accuracy in L2 writing
examples: The article cites this account to interpret why focused DCF showed a large positive effect while unfocused DCF showed a large negative effect in Sheen et al. (2009)
key_sources: Albatool Abalkheel & Tara Brandenburg. (2020). Effects of Written Corrective Feedback: A Synthesis of 10 Quasi-Experimental Studies. English Language Teaching, 13(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v13n7p97

article_title: The Effect of the 5E Instructional Model Enriched with Cooperative Learning and Animations on Seventh-Grade Students' Academic Achievement and Scientific Attitudes
citation: İkramettin Daşdemir. (2016). The Effect of the 5E Instructional Model Enriched With Cooperative Learning and Animations on Seventh-Grade Students' Academic Achievement and Scientific Attitudes. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 9(1), 21-38. https://www.iejee.com
title: Cooperative-learning-enriched 5E implementation with question-asking groups of four
description: An instructional implementation in which the 5E instructional model was enriched with cooperative learning: "the cooperative group was divided into groups of four and they were required to ask each other questions about the subject", so that "the subject matter was reinforced". It ran alongside the same 4-week, 16-hour light-unit schedule and the same science teacher as the other conditions. The study used it to address individual diversity in learning styles.
requirements: Division of the class into groups of four and mutual question-asking about the subject
constraints: In this study the cooperative group's achievement gain over the control was not statistically significant
target_learning_goals: academic achievement on the light unit
scientific attitudes toward science
examples: The cooperative group (n=27) received the 5E model enriched with cooperative learning while the control group (n=28) received the 5E model alone, all taught by the same teacher
key_sources: İkramettin Daşdemir. (2016). The Effect of the 5E Instructional Model Enriched With Cooperative Learning and Animations on Seventh-Grade Students' Academic Achievement and Scientific Attitudes. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 9(1), 21-38. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1126710

article_title: Using Supplementary Readings (Short Stories) in Increasing the Conceptual Fluency, the Case of Idioms in English
citation: Elahe Mokhtari, Mohammed Reza Talebinezhad. (2014). Using Supplementary Readings (Short Stories) in Increasing the Conceptual Fluency, the Case of Idioms in English. Advances in Language and Literary Studies. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.1p.134
title: Conceptual Fluency Theory: native-like L2 use requires operating within the target language's metaphorically structured conceptual system
description: Conceptual Fluency Theory holds that a linguistic system rests on an underlying conceptual system: "we speak, perceive, think, and interpret the world in terms of our conceptual system" (Danesi, 1992). The article uses it to explain why L2 learners may reach verbal fluency yet produce discourse lacking native-like conceptual appropriateness, because they map target forms onto L1 conceptualizations. It frames idioms and metaphorical competence as the neglected dimension of L2 teaching that supplementary contextualized readings can address.
requirements: Learners must be exposed to how the target language encodes concepts via metaphorical reasoning, not only to grammar and vocabulary
constraints: The article notes learners can gain considerable fluency without conceptual fluency, and that speakers with low conceptual fluency will never seem native-like
target_learning_goals: conceptual fluency
metaphorical competence
idiom comprehension and use
examples: The study operationalized conceptual fluency gains as performance on 30-item multiple-choice idiom tests administered before and after thirty sessions of idiom instruction
key_sources: Elahe Mokhtari, Mohammed Reza Talebinezhad. (2014). Using Supplementary Readings (Short Stories) in Increasing the Conceptual Fluency, the Case of Idioms in English. Advances in Language and Literary Studies. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.1p.134

article_title: Using Supplementary Readings (Short Stories) in Increasing the Conceptual Fluency, the Case of Idioms in English
citation: Elahe Mokhtari, Mohammed Reza Talebinezhad. (2014). Using Supplementary Readings (Short Stories) in Increasing the Conceptual Fluency, the Case of Idioms in English. Advances in Language and Literary Studies. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.1p.134
title: Teach idioms in contexts resembling real-life situations, since context plays a major role in constructing idiomatic meaning
description: The article concludes that "context plays a major role in the construction of idiomatic meaning" and that contextualized idioms in the syllabus can enhance idiomatic conceptual fluency. It further states that contexts containing idioms with more similarity to real-life situations have a better effect on developing conceptual fluency. The principle follows from the study's finding that supplementary story readings, which supply such contexts, improved post-test performance.
requirements: Idioms should be presented within contexts rather than in isolation
Contexts should resemble real-life situations and match learner proficiency
constraints: The article notes comparing L2 idioms to native-language idioms helps develop conceptual fluency only "if they are somehow the same"
target_learning_goals: idiom comprehension
conceptual fluency
idiomatic production in speech and writing
examples: The experimental treatment supplied short stories containing the taught idioms, giving learners contextualized rather than decontextualized exposure to idiomatic expressions
key_sources: Elahe Mokhtari, Mohammed Reza Talebinezhad. (2014). Using Supplementary Readings (Short Stories) in Increasing the Conceptual Fluency, the Case of Idioms in English. Advances in Language and Literary Studies. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.5n.1p.134

article_title: Improving Reading Fluency and Comprehension in Adult ESL Learners Using Bottom-Up and Top-Down Vocabulary Training
citation: Rhonda Oliver, Shahreen Young. (2016). Improving reading fluency and comprehension in adult ESL learners using bottom-up and top-down vocabulary training. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 6(1), 111-133. https://doi.org/10.14746/ssllt.2016.6.1.6
title: Prefer contextualized vocabulary training over isolated word-list training in adult ESL classrooms, at least for reading fluency
description: The article recommends that adult ESL instruction present target vocabulary in meaningful context rather than as isolated word lists, because contextualized training was linked to improved reading speed while isolated training was not. It states that "contextualized training may be more beneficial in the classroom than isolated training (i.e., having learners memorize lists of words), at least in terms of fluency". The recommendation is coupled with increased exposure to target vocabulary.
requirements: Couple contextualized training with increased exposure to the target language, since retention may require numerous encounters with a word
constraints: The benefit was observed for fluency only; comprehension showed no significant difference
Findings come from a small exploratory quasi-experiment with limited-proficiency learners and reduced contact time
target_learners: adult ESL tertiary-bound students in intact university-preparation classes
target_learning_goals: reading fluency
reading comprehension
academic vocabulary development
examples: Experiment 2 trained 32 target words highlighted in a projected class text read aloud over three days, and participants then read a novel transfer text containing those words faster than a control text
key_sources: Rhonda Oliver, Shahreen Young. (2016). Improving reading fluency and comprehension in adult ESL learners using bottom-up and top-down vocabulary training. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 6(1), 111-133. https://doi.org/10.14746/ssllt.2016.6.1.6

article_title: Improving Reading Fluency and Comprehension in Adult ESL Learners Using Bottom-Up and Top-Down Vocabulary Training
citation: Rhonda Oliver, Shahreen Young. (2016). Improving reading fluency and comprehension in adult ESL learners using bottom-up and top-down vocabulary training. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 6(1), 111-133. https://doi.org/10.14746/ssllt.2016.6.1.6
title: Context superiority hypothesis as an account of why contextual vocabulary training supports fluent word recognition
description: The article invokes the context superiority hypothesis, first proposed by Craik and Lockhart (1972) and later supported by others, to explain why top-down contextual training improved fluency. The account holds that "vocabulary recognition is long term and thus easily recalled when semantic prompts are used, whereas fast memory loss occurs when the use of orthography or phonemes are employed to recall vocabulary". The authors align their Experiment 2 fluency result with this account.
requirements: Training must present words in meaningful context so that semantic prompts and deep processing become possible
constraints: Offered as the authors' interpretation of their results, not directly tested in the study; the accompanying comprehension gain was absent
target_learners: adult ESL learners with limited English proficiency
target_learning_goals: vocabulary recognition and retention
reading fluency
examples: The authors propose that the efficacy of contextual training lies with the semantic prompts or deep processing that becomes possible through context, aligning their Experiment 2 fluency gain with this hypothesis
key_sources: Rhonda Oliver, Shahreen Young. (2016). Improving reading fluency and comprehension in adult ESL learners using bottom-up and top-down vocabulary training. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 6(1), 111-133. https://doi.org/10.14746/ssllt.2016.6.1.6

article_title: Employing Concept Mapping as a Pre-Writing Strategy to Help EFL Learners Better Generate Argumentative Compositions
citation: Al-Shaer, Ibrahim M. R. Ph.D. (2014). Employing Concept Mapping as a Pre-writing Strategy to Help EFL Learners Better Generate Argumentative Compositions. International Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning. https://doi.org/10.20429/ijsotl.2014.080210
title: Concept mapping as a visual representation of conceptual relationships rooted in Ausubel's assimilation theory
description: The article presents concept mapping as a technique derived from cognitive theory springing out of Ausubel's assimilation theory, in which learning is most productive when new information connects with prior knowledge. Novak developed concept mapping in the 1960s as techniques for visualizing the relationship among different concepts, and the article uses paper-and-pencil maps at the pre-writing stage so students generate, classify, and connect ideas before composing. The article states that "By creating essential connections in a hierarchical way prior to performing any activity, concept maps could bring about better understanding of the material."
requirements: Learners need prior knowledge to connect new information with, since the key determinant of learning is previous knowledge
constraints: The article notes there is no guarantee the strategy will benefit every student group, as the Palestinian EFL group studied had not been studied before
target_learners: EFL university students in academic writing courses
target_learning_goals: Generating and organizing ideas for argumentative essay writing
examples: Students first drew an idea map placing the main idea as a nucleus, then transformed it into a hierarchical concept map with squares connected by labeled arrows
key_sources: Al-Shaer, Ibrahim M. R. Ph.D. (2014). Employing Concept Mapping as a Pre-writing Strategy to Help EFL Learners Better Generate Argumentative Compositions. International Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning. https://doi.org/10.20429/ijsotl.2014.080210

article_title: Exploring Optimal Pronunciation Teaching: Integrating Instructional Software into Intermediate-Level EFL Classes in China
citation: Yang Gao and Barbara E. Hanna. (2016). Exploring optimal pronunciation teaching: Integrating instructional software into intermediate-level EFL classes in China. CALICO Journal. https://doi.org/10.1558/cj.v33i2.26054
title: Combine human-aided instruction with instructional software when teaching pronunciation to young lower-proficiency learners
description: The article argues that neither mode alone is optimal for young learners: software supplies self-paced practice, models and recording comparison, while teachers provide individualized feedback and behaviour management. Its evidence "align to suggest that the combination of human-aided instruction and instructional software is best for young learners of pronunciation". In the study, Group 3 received about 20 minutes of teacher instruction followed by 25 minutes of software use daily.
requirements: A competent teacher available to deliver the human-aided portion of instruction
Instructional software whose content matches what the teacher teaches
Scheduled time in which both modes can be delivered within the same lessons
constraints: The study tested one specific package (New Oriental Pronunciation) in one setting over two weeks with 45 minutes per day; time on task was controlled, excluding individual pacing and practice in learners' own time
The omnibus ANOVA effects on both performance and attitude change were non-significant; the advantage over teacher-only instruction on performance was not established
target_learners: Young adolescent EFL learners (aged 13–16) at lower-intermediate proficiency
target_learning_goals: English pronunciation (segmental and suprasegmental aspects)
Positive attitudes towards pronunciation learning
examples: Group 3 students were first instructed by the teacher for around 20 minutes, then used the instructional software individually for 25 minutes, with the same teacher as Group 1 to eliminate the variable of teacher's approach
key_sources: Yang Gao and Barbara E. Hanna. (2016). Exploring optimal pronunciation teaching: Integrating instructional software into intermediate-level EFL classes in China. CALICO Journal. https://doi.org/10.1558/cj.v33i2.26054

article_title: Developing Contextual Mathematical Thinking Learning Model to Enhance Higher-Order Thinking Ability for Middle School Students
citation: Damianus D. Samo, Darhim & Bana Kartasasmita. (2017). Developing Contextual Mathematical Thinking Learning Model to Enhance Higher-Order Thinking Ability for Middle School Students. International Education Studies, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n12p17
title: Contextual mathematical thinking learning model
description: A learning model the authors develop by combining constructivism, problem-based learning, contextual teaching and learning, and higher-order thinking strategies. Its six-phase syntax runs from presenting contextual problems through critical/analytical questioning, individual and group investigation, presentation and discussion, and reflection, to a higher-order thinking test. The article states it is "supported by generally standard theories" and shows internal consistency among its components: purposes, syntax, reaction principle and support system.
requirements: Implementation follows the six syntax phases with the allocated times (about 10, 10, 30, 20, 5 and 15 minutes)
Teacher acts as facilitator providing scaffolding to raise students' thinking to a higher-order level
constraints: Results come from one Grade VIII sample of 78 students on cone, cylinder and sphere material; the authors state results "should be validated by a larger sample size"
target_learners: Grade VIII junior high school students
target_learning_goals: higher-order thinking ability (analyzing, evaluating, creating) in mathematics
examples: In the implementation phase the model was taught to 78 Grade VIII students in experimental and control classes on cone, cylinder, and sphere material
key_sources: Damianus D. Samo, Darhim & Bana Kartasasmita. (2017). Developing Contextual Mathematical Thinking Learning Model to Enhance Higher-Order Thinking Ability for Middle School Students. International Education Studies, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n12p17

article_title: Improving the Reasoning Ability of Elementary School Student through the Indonesian Realistic Mathematics Education
citation: Saleh, M., Prahmana, R.C.I., Isa, M., & Murni. (2018). Improving the Reasoning Ability of Elementary School Student through the Indonesian Realistic Mathematics Education. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 41-54. https://jme.ejournal.unsri.ac.id
title: Cobek (mortar) broken into pieces as a contextual concrete object for fraction as part of a whole
description: The cobek, or mortar, is "a kitchen utensil made of clay which is usually used to traditionally grind chili, onion, and another spice in Aceh". One mortar was given to each group to be broken into pieces to represent the meaning of fraction, especially the concept of fraction as part of a whole. It grounds the abstract fraction concept in a familiar local object from students' daily life.
requirements: One mortar per student group
Breaking the mortar into pieces to model parts of a whole
constraints: Used specifically for the part-of-a-whole interpretation of fraction
target_learning_goals: Understanding fraction as part of a whole
examples: Each group broke a mortar into pieces to represent fraction values (Figure 4)
key_sources: Saleh, M., Prahmana, R.C.I., Isa, M., & Murni. (2018). Improving the Reasoning Ability of Elementary School Student through the Indonesian Realistic Mathematics Education. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 41-54. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1173650

article_title: Improving the Reasoning Ability of Elementary School Student through the Indonesian Realistic Mathematics Education
citation: Saleh, M., Prahmana, R.C.I., Isa, M., & Murni. (2018). Improving the Reasoning Ability of Elementary School Student through the Indonesian Realistic Mathematics Education. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 41-54. https://jme.ejournal.unsri.ac.id
title: Five-step learning sequence moving from concrete objects to fraction symbols and operations
description: The article prescribes a sequence for fraction learning with the fraction board: first reinforce the meaning of fraction "through a concrete object without symbol of fraction", then show different and equivalent fraction values via model sizes, then introduce division of continuous and discrete objects for equivalent fractions, then introduce the fraction symbol, and finally introduce operations on fraction through concrete object. This orders abstraction after concrete experience, matching students' concrete thinking stage.
requirements: Concrete objects such as the fraction board and paperboards
Teacher guidance at each step
constraints: Designed for the part-of-a-whole fraction interpretation in grade 4
target_learning_goals: Fraction concept understanding
Equivalent fractions
Fraction operations
examples: The addition of two fractions with different denominators was taught via four steps of selecting, substituting, checking, and calculating from the illustration
key_sources: Saleh, M., Prahmana, R.C.I., Isa, M., & Murni. (2018). Improving the Reasoning Ability of Elementary School Student through the Indonesian Realistic Mathematics Education. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 41-54. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1173650

article_title: Improving the Reasoning Ability of Elementary School Student through the Indonesian Realistic Mathematics Education
citation: Saleh, M., Prahmana, R.C.I., Isa, M., & Murni. (2018). Improving the Reasoning Ability of Elementary School Student through the Indonesian Realistic Mathematics Education. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 41-54. https://jme.ejournal.unsri.ac.id
title: Begin fraction learning with concrete objects before introducing fraction symbols
description: Because fourth-grade students are at the concrete thinking stage, abstract mathematical objects should be represented through concrete objects as a bridge to students' existing knowledge. The article states that learning "has to be started by understanding the concept of fraction through activities utilizing concrete object", and only once students understand the meaning of fraction is a symbol given corresponding to the representation they have seen. This creates a strong trace in students' minds because they directly observe and experience the concept.
requirements: Concrete objects, discrete or continuous, that can represent the fraction values
Symbols introduced only after the concrete representation is understood
constraints: Grounded in students at the concrete developmental stage; the study's evidence covers grade-4 fraction material
target_learning_goals: Fraction concept understanding
Mathematics reasoning
examples: The study's first learning step reinforced the meaning of fraction through a concrete object without fraction symbols before the teacher introduced the symbol and operations
key_sources: Saleh, M., Prahmana, R.C.I., Isa, M., & Murni. (2018). Improving the Reasoning Ability of Elementary School Student through the Indonesian Realistic Mathematics Education. Journal on Mathematics Education, 9(1), 41-54. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1173650

article_title: The Effects of Classic and Web-Designed Conceptual Change Texts on the Subject of Water Chemistry
citation: Taş, E., Gülen, S., Öner, Z., & Özyürek, C. (2015). The effects of classic and web-designed conceptual change texts on the subject of water chemistry. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 7(2), 263-280. http://www.iejee.com
title: Conceptual change text approach: four conditions for changing conceptual errors
description: The article describes conceptual change texts as texts that "define what the conceptual errors of students are and they try to explain these errors with examples" then "prove with explanation or examples that these errors are insufficient or wrong." Drawing on Köse, Ayaş & Uşak (2006), it states changing conceptual errors requires four strategies: awareness that existing knowledge is insufficient, perceiving new knowledge as comprehensible, believing it is reasonable, and finding it useful for later problems.
requirements: Texts must be scripted and associated with daily life for conceptual change
target_learning_goals: Replacing misconceptions with scientifically correct concepts
examples: Conceptual change texts in this study explained errors with examples then refuted them
key_sources: Taş, E., Gülen, S., Öner, Z., & Özyürek, C. (2015). The effects of classic and web-designed conceptual change texts on the subject of water chemistry. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 7(2), 263-280. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057892

article_title: The Effects of Hypertext Gloss on Comprehension and Vocabulary Retention under Incidental and Intentional Learning Conditions
citation: Zandieh, Z., & Jafarigohar, M. (2012). The Effects of Hypertext Gloss on Comprehension and Vocabulary Retention under Incidental and Intentional Learning Conditions. English Language Teaching, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n6p60
title: Combine incidental and intentional vocabulary-learning modalities in CALL environments
description: The article argues that because each modality has complementary strengths — intentional learning favoring immediate gain and incidental learning favoring retention — both should be used together. It states it would be "a more profitable option to combine both modalities to facilitate learning of new items, and for longer retention." This rests on the study's finding that neither modality dominated across immediate and delayed tests.
requirements: A virtual or computer-mediated learning environment offering hypertext glosses on target vocabulary
constraints: The delayed-retention difference favoring the incidental modality was not statistically significant
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary acquisition and retention
reading comprehension
examples: Participants read the same enhanced electronic text with permanently highlighted target vocabulary in the intentional condition and temporarily highlighted target ones in the incidental condition
key_sources: Zandieh, Z., & Jafarigohar, M. (2012). The Effects of Hypertext Gloss on Comprehension and Vocabulary Retention under Incidental and Intentional Learning Conditions. English Language Teaching, 5(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v5n6p60

article_title: The Effects of Computer-Assisted Instruction Based on Top-Level Structure Method in English Reading and Writing Abilities of Thai EFL Students
citation: Nattapong Jinajai & Saowalak Rattanavich. (2015). The Effects of Computer-Assisted Instruction Based on Top-Level Structure Method in English Reading and Writing Abilities of Thai EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 8(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n11p231
title: Computer-assisted instruction (CAI) as a delivery medium for TLS-based English instruction
description: Computer-assisted instruction refers to "instruction or remediation presented on a computer" that provides interactive activities with animation, sound, and demonstration. CAI allows students to "progress at their own pace", provides "immediate feedback", and offers "a change of pace from teacher-led or group instruction". In this study, CAI served as the delivery medium for TLS-based English reading and writing instruction over 10 weeks with 20 teaching hours.
requirements: Computers or computer access for students
Educational software or programs designed for the target instruction
target_learning_goals: English reading and writing skills
interest in learning English
key_sources: Nattapong Jinajai & Saowalak Rattanavich. (2015). The Effects of Computer-Assisted Instruction Based on Top-Level Structure Method in English Reading and Writing Abilities of Thai EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 8(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n11p231

article_title: The Effect of Using the Constructivist Learning Model in Teaching Science on the Achievement and Scientific Thinking of 8th Grade Students
citation: Qarareh, A. O. (2016). The Effect of Using the Constructivist Learning Model in Teaching Science on the Achievement and Scientific Thinking of 8th Grade Students. International Education Studies, 9(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n7p178
title: Constructivist Learning Model: four-stage teaching framework
description: The Constructivist Learning Model is a teaching framework grounded in constructivism theory in which learners actively build knowledge through collecting information, forming hypotheses, discussing solutions, and applying findings in new situations. The article describes it as four complementary stages: "Engagement or Invitation Stage", "Exploration Stage", "Explanation Stage", and "Decision Making Stage (Problem Solving)", each closely linked to the next. The researcher applied these stages in designing the light-unit lessons for the experimental group.
requirements: Lesson plans must be designed around the four stages of engagement, exploration, explanation, and decision-making
constraints: The cognitive structure of the learner is resistant to change, per the theory's bases
target_learning_goals: science achievement
scientific thinking
examples: Ten 45-minute lesson plans on light, mirrors, and lenses were prepared following the four stages and reviewed by faculty and teachers
key_sources: Qarareh, A. O. (2016). The Effect of Using the Constructivist Learning Model in Teaching Science on the Achievement and Scientific Thinking of 8th Grade Students. International Education Studies, 9(7). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n7p178

article_title: The Directed Reading-Thinking Activity (DR-TA) and the Traditional Approach Using Tales of Virtue Based on His Majesty the King's Teaching Concepts in Seventh Grade Students' Reading Comprehension
citation: Chaemsai, R. & Rattanavich, S. (2016). The Directed Reading-Thinking Activity (DR-TA) and the Traditional Approach Using Tales of Virtue based on His Majesty the King’s Teaching Concepts in Seventh Grade Students’ Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n9p18
title: Combine a thinking-focused reading method with morally rich texts to raise reading comprehension and ethical awareness together
description: The article concludes that pairing DR-TA with tales of virtue improves both English reading comprehension and ethical awareness more than a traditional approach alone. It argues that "stories with strong morals are appropriate for teaching reading skills, as well as allowing students to have fun by increasing engagement in lessons", and that the DR-TA's prediction cycle arouses curiosity and enables purposeful reading while the tales instill morality.
requirements: Texts with inherent moral themes and a student-centered reading method with the teacher as facilitator
target_learners: seventh-grade English learners in Thai secondary schools
target_learning_goals: English reading comprehension
ethical awareness
examples: The study taught the experimental group through DR-TA using tales of virtue for 10 weeks with 20 teaching hours and compared outcomes with a traditionally taught control group
key_sources: Chaemsai, R. & Rattanavich, S. (2016). The Directed Reading-Thinking Activity (DR-TA) and the Traditional Approach Using Tales of Virtue based on His Majesty the King’s Teaching Concepts in Seventh Grade Students’ Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 9(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n9p18

article_title: Enhancing Argumentative Writing Skill through Contextual Teaching and Learning
citation: Hasani, A. (2016). Enhancing argumentative writing skill through contextual teaching and learning. Educational Research and Reviews, 11(16), 1573-1578.
title: Contextual teaching and learning (CTL) with seven principles
description: The article describes contextual teaching and learning as an instructional approach that helps students "comprehend instructional subjects and develop creative ideas in the form of writing and make a link between academic subject and real world context". Context relates to existing experience, personal life, and societal problems. The article lists seven principles contained in contextual teaching: constructivism, inquiry, questioning, learning community, modeling, reflecting, and authentic assessment. In the study, CTL was operationalized as the experimental treatment for argumentative writing instruction.
requirements: Instruction must connect academic content to students' real-world context and prior experience
constraints: The article reports CTL was less effective for students with low critical thinking ability, who needed lecturer guidance
target_learning_goals: argumentative writing skill
examples: The experimental group received contextual learning instruction while the control group continued normal lessons in a quasi-experiment with 52 Indonesian university students.
key_sources: Hasani, A. (2016). Enhancing argumentative writing skill through contextual teaching and learning. Educational Research and Reviews, 11(16), 1573-1578. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1113515

article_title: Comparative Study between Drill Skill and Concept Attainment Model towards Physics Learning Achievement
citation: Izaak Hendrik Wenno, Pieter Wattimena, Luky Maspaitela. (2016). Comparative Study between Drill Skill and Concept Attainment Model towards Physics Learning Achievement. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), Vol.5, No.3. http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE
title: Concept attainment model as a learning model designed to help students learn concepts more easily
description: The concept attainment model is described as "a model of achievement of learning model that is designed to help students to be more easily learn a concept". It focuses on providing learners with a number of concepts and on how to develop the concept, helping students identify and define concepts through discovery of essential attributes. In this study it was the treatment for the second experimental group. The authors note it requires teachers to support student hypotheses, direct argumentation in testing hypotheses, and focus students on specific examples.
requirements: Teacher should have a supportive attitude toward student hypotheses
Teacher should provide direction for students to provide arguments in testing hypotheses
Teacher should establish students to focus on specific examples
Requires samples to be delivered to students with direct student involvement
constraints: It does not always work with all age groups or topics
Students may become too verbal and shout out answers
target_learning_goals: Concept understanding in physics
Identifying relevant and irrelevant information
examples: Used as the treatment for group 2 in the quasi-experiment, after which 46.7% of students remained in the fail category
key_sources: Izaak Hendrik Wenno, Pieter Wattimena, Luky Maspaitela. (2016). Comparative Study between Drill Skill and Concept Attainment Model towards Physics Learning Achievement. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), Vol.5, No.3. http://iaesjournal.com/online/index.php/IJERE

article_title: When Creative Problem Solving Strategy Meets Web-Based Cooperative Learning Environment in Accounting Education
citation: CHENG Kai Wen. (2011). When Creative Problem Solving Strategy Meets Web-Based Cooperative Learning Environment in Accounting Education. New Horizons in Education, 59(1), 106-118.
title: Cooperative learning sheets and creative problem-solving learning sheets used in web-based cooperative learning
description: The learning sheets 'contained issues for group discussions during the group learning session' and came in two types: 'cooperative learning sheets' used by both EG1 and EG2, and 'creative problem-solving learning sheets' used only by EG1. Through the use of the learning sheets in group discussion, the author states that 'students' spirit of CL and CPS could be cultivated.' Answers to the learning sheets were released after group discussion to familiarize students with the problems.
requirements: Heterogeneous groups with students of different competencies distributed across groups, logging into the web-based teaching system with a given account
target_learning_goals: cooperative learning
creative problem solving
accounting content mastery
examples: The teacher observed each group discussion in EG1 to ensure the discussion proceeded according to CPS process and gave suggestions for rectification and compliment.
key_sources: CHENG Kai Wen. (2011). When Creative Problem Solving Strategy Meets Web-Based Cooperative Learning Environment in Accounting Education. New Horizons in Education, 59(1), 106-118. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ955493

article_title: Effects of Modality and Redundancy Principles on the Learning and Attitude of a Computer-Based Music Theory Lesson among Jordanian Primary Pupils
citation: Osamah (Mohammad Ameen) Ahmad Aldalalah & Soon Fook Fong. (2010). Effects of Modality and Redundancy Principles on the Learning and Attitude of a Computer-Based Music Theory Lesson among Jordanian Primary Pupils. International Education Studies, 3(3). https://www.ccsenet.org/ies
title: Cognitive theory of multimedia learning (dual-channel, limited-capacity account) as the explanatory framework for modality and redundancy effects
description: The article grounds its design and interpretation in Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning, which proposes that "the human information processing system comprises dual channels, that is, one for visual processing and the other for auditory processing", each with limited capacity. Presenting images visually and narration auditorily balances load across channels, while redundant onscreen text overloads the visual channel and induces split-attention. The study used this theory to predict and explain the superiority of the AI mode and the null TI-AIT difference.
requirements: Instructional messages must be designed so that visual and verbal information are distributed across the two channels rather than concentrated in one
constraints: The theory's predictions were tested here only for third-grade pupils learning music theory in a computer-based setting
target_learning_goals: multimedia lesson learning outcomes and attitude
examples: The study's three courseware modes (AI, TI, AIT) were constructed to operationalize the modality and redundancy principles derived from this theory
key_sources: Osamah (Mohammad Ameen) Ahmad Aldalalah & Soon Fook Fong. (2010). Effects of Modality and Redundancy Principles on the Learning and Attitude of a Computer-Based Music Theory Lesson among Jordanian Primary Pupils. International Education Studies, 3(3). https://www.ccsenet.org/ies

article_title: Direct versus Indirect Explicit Methods of Enhancing EFL Students' English Grammatical Competence: A Concept Checking-Based Consciousness-Raising Tasks Model
citation: Đặng, T. T. Đ., & Nguyễn, H. T. (2012). Direct versus Indirect Explicit Methods of Enhancing EFL Students' English Grammatical Competence: A Concept Checking-based Consciousness-raising Tasks Model. English Language Teaching, 6(1), 112. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v6n1p112
title: Indirect explicit grammar instruction via consciousness-raising tasks (inductive rule discovery)
description: IEGI favors "induction or the learners' discovery of the grammatical rules through tasks" without grammatical explanations: students receive data illustrating a structure, analyze it, and construct the rule themselves. Indirect consciousness-raising tasks aim "to help learners construct their own explicit grammar of the target language and to encourage communication in the L2 between learners" (Ellis, 1997). The article operationalizes this through a concept checking-based task model and contrasts it with deductive DEGI, where students are supplied a rule and apply it.
requirements: Tasks must present data illustrating the target structure so learners can analyze it and arrive at a generalization
Teacher feedback and confirmation after rule search, plus a rule summary after pair/group discussion
constraints: The article notes these tasks "may not be appropriate to beginners or young learners", citing Ellis (1991) and Sheen (1992) as cited in Ellis (2003)
Effects may be delayed rather than immediate, per Thornbury (2005)
target_learners: EFL high school students at pre-intermediate level
target_learning_goals: Explicit knowledge of English tense and aspect forms, meanings, and use
Accurate productive use of tenses in oral and written discourse

title: Support content should follow the principles of continuity, continuity of significant personal qualities, and an integrated approach to methods
description: In the conclusion the article states that the content of psychological and pedagogical support for students' adaptation meets three principles: "the principle of continuity, which takes into account the student experience before entering a high school, the continuity of significant personal qualities during educational adaptation period, an integrated approach in method selection and support techniques". These principles ground the tutoring program and the two courses.
requirements: Support content must take account of students' pre-university experience and maintain significant personal qualities across the adaptation period
target_learning_goals: adaptation to educational activity in high school
development of personal qualities supporting adaptation
examples: The tutoring program and the courses "Training activities technology" and "Life science" were implemented under these principles and evaluated in the pedagogical experiment.

citation: Peerasak Kingpum, Chaiyot Ruangsuwan and Sumalee Chaicharoen. (2015). Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2350
title: Collaborative Blended Learning (CoBl) instructional model
description: The CoBl model combines traditional face-to-face learning with online instruction on a Moodle LMS, using collaborative learning activities to develop thinking ability. The article states "The proportion of online learning and face to face learning is approximately 50 percent." It has four components (principles, objectives, procedures and instructional activities, measurement and evaluation) and three instructional phases: pre-instruction, instruction with nine steps integrating collaborative and thinking-ability activities, and evaluation. Students work in small groups of 4-6 using chat room, web board, and e-mail tools.

Cooperation from stakeholders such as administrators and teachers

thinking ability (organizing, applying, analyzing, knowledge generating, integrating, evaluating)

Promoting Student Teachers' Content Related Knowledge in Teaching Systems Thinking: Measuring Effects of an Intervention through Evaluating a Videotaped Lesson. Higher Education Studies, 6(4). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v6n4p156
title: Combine technical and subject-related didactic input in roughly equal proportions when promoting student teachers' CRK for teaching systems thinking
description: Based on their finding that only the Mixed Course produced significant gains, the authors conclude that "a mixed course with equal technical and didactical input seems to be most effective in fostering student teachers' reflective Content Related Knowledge for teaching systems thinking". The principle addresses the ongoing teacher-education debate over the extent of technical versus didactic input, and the authors hope their empirical evidence will inform these discussions.

article_title: Investigating the Longitudinal Effects of a Core Mathematics Program on Evidence-Based Teaching Practices in Mathematics
citation: Doabler, C. T., Nelson, N. J., Kennedy, P. C., Stoolmiller, M., Fien, H., Clarke, B., Gearin, B., Smolkowski, K., & Baker, S. K. (2018). Investigating the Longitudinal Effects of a Core Mathematics Program on Evidence-Based Teaching Practices in Mathematics. Learning Disability Quarterly, 41(3), 144–158. https://doi.org/10.1177/0731948718756040
title: COSTI-M classroom observation instrument for evidence-based teaching practices
description: The Classroom Observations of Student–Teacher Interactions—Mathematics (COSTI-M) is "a validated, low-inference observation tool designed to document the frequency of evidence-based teaching practices." It targets four practices — teacher models, academic feedback, group responses, and individual responses — captured in real time and coded serially, with rates per minute computed as frequency divided by observation duration. It has evidence of predictive validity with a standardized mathematics achievement measure (p = .004, pseudo R2 = .08) and a battery of curriculum-based measures (p = .017, pseudo R2 = .05).
requirements: Observers required 14 hours of training across three sessions and had to pass a video reliability checkout and a real-time classroom checkout with agreement of .85 or higher before observing independently.
constraints: The article states the COSTI-M does not capture the complexity, duration, or clarity (e.g., volume and pacing) of a teacher's overt demonstrations and explanations, and within-year ICCs were modest, indicating day-to-day volatility of classroom instruction.
target_learners: Kindergarten students in core mathematics instruction
target_learning_goals: Frequency of teacher models, academic feedback, group response opportunities, and individual response opportunities during core mathematics lessons
examples: Across Year 1 and Year 2, 658 observations were completed in fall, winter, and spring rounds, with interobserver reliability ICCs ranging from .67 to .95.

article_title: Improving Students' Chinese Writing Abilities in Taiwan with the "Conditioned Writing System"
citation: Yuan-Chen Liu, Wan-Chun Lee, Tzu-Hua Huang, Hsiao-Mei Hsieh. (2012). IMPROVING STUDENTS’ CHINESE WRITING ABILITIES IN TAIWAN WITH THE “CONDITIONED WRITING SYSTEM”. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 11(3). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Conditioned writing approach for teaching Chinese essay writing
description: Conditioned writing is an approach to teaching Chinese essay writing, developed by Chen in Taiwan, that differs from guided writing by explaining questions through both directions and conditions for instruction. Chou (2005) explains that it "provides explicit instructions to the students for composing a Chinese essay" and focuses on specific writing skills requiring students to respond accordingly. By combining sample reading and writing, it aims to develop writing abilities progressively from phrases to sentences and from paragraphs to the entire essay. This study embedded it in question sets within the CWB online system, drawing on the cognitive process theory of writing (Flower & Hayes, 1981) across planning, translating, reviewing, and monitoring.
requirements: Suitable question sets are required for effective guidance, and students must be allowed to practise progressively
constraints: The article notes conditioned writing instructions are framed as more suitable and effective than traditional guided writing, per Chou (2005)
target_learners: junior high school students of limited writing abilities as well as general seventh-grade students
target_learning_goals: Chinese essay writing skills: argumentation, organization and structure, and language use
examples: The study designed conditioned-writing question sets for five writing exercises targeting the three assessment standards over ten weeks
key_sources: Yuan-Chen Liu, Wan-Chun Lee, Tzu-Hua Huang, Hsiao-Mei Hsieh. (2012). IMPROVING STUDENTS’ CHINESE WRITING ABILITIES IN TAIWAN WITH THE “CONDITIONED WRITING SYSTEM”. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 11(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ989211

article_title: Teaching Compound Nouns in ESP: Insights from Cognitive Semantics
citation: Fries, M.-H. (2017). Teaching compound nouns in ESP: insights from cognitive semantics. In C. Sarré & S. Whyte (Eds), New developments in ESP teaching and learning research (pp. 93-107). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2017.cssw2017.747
title: Cognitive-semantic framework for teaching compound nouns: encyclopedic meaning, grammar-lexicon continuum, and symbolic nature of language
description: The chapter draws on three tenets of cognitive linguistics to frame compound-noun instruction: word meaning is encyclopaedic, so students can draw on specialised domain knowledge to interpret CNs; grammar and lexicon form a continuum, so lexicalised CNs are learnt as terms; and grammar is symbolic in nature, so CN formation can be explained graphically via metonymy-style highlighting diagrams. The framework motivates the experimental condition of the case study and three research questions about implicit learning, repeated exposure, and word order.
requirements: Learners must possess specialised domain knowledge (from internships or field study) that they can mobilise to interpret compounds in their discipline
constraints: The graphic representation fails to capture a small number of figurative CNs based on metaphor or metonymy
target_learners: French lower-intermediate (A2-B1) university students of English for Specific Purposes in science and technology
target_learning_goals: understanding and correctly producing English noun+noun compound constructions in specialised domains
examples: In the experimental condition, students received the standard morphosyntactic textbook lesson complemented with encyclopedic-meaning discussion, term status of CNs, and circle-and-arrow diagrams of compounds as active zones within domains
key_sources: Fries, M.-H. (2017). Teaching compound nouns in ESP: insights from cognitive semantics. In C. Sarré & S. Whyte (Eds), New developments in ESP teaching and learning research (pp. 93-107). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2017.cssw2017.747

article_title: Teaching Compound Nouns in ESP: Insights from Cognitive Semantics
citation: Fries, M.-H. (2017). Teaching compound nouns in ESP: insights from cognitive semantics. In C. Sarré & S. Whyte (Eds), New developments in ESP teaching and learning research (pp. 93-107). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2017.cssw2017.747
title: Teach compound nouns through a cognitive-semantic approach as a complement to, not a replacement for, morphosyntactic instruction
description: The chapter recommends adding a cognitive-semantic treatment of compound nouns — emphasising encyclopedic meaning, the term status of lexicalised CNs, and graphic word-order explanation — on top of standard grammar teaching. The author concludes such an approach "could be beneficial to ESP teaching, as a complement to a morphosyntactic perspective", because it directs attention to specialised terminology, supports implicit learning, and helps students adapt writing to slide register.
requirements: One hour of explicit CN teaching including practice exercises, followed by a task-based course with note-taking and oral presentations
constraints: The cognitive perspective showed no clear added value for understanding and reusing key CNs in video summaries, so it complements rather than replaces morphosyntactic teaching
target_learners: lower-intermediate French university students in science and technology programmes
target_learning_goals: implicit learning of specialised compound nouns and appropriate stylistic use in scientific and technical writing
examples: Sixteen Master's process-engineering students split into two comparable groups by adaptive-test proficiency; the experimental group received the textbook lesson plus the cognitive-semantic complement

article_title: Effect of Cooperative Learning on Achievement of Students in General Science at Secondary Level
citation: Qaisara Parveen, Sadia Batool. (2012). Effect of Cooperative Learning on Achievement of Students in General Science at Secondary Level. International Education Studies, Vol. 5, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v5n2p154
title: Cooperative learning material package: five lesson plans, five worksheets and five quizzes with Slavin-style group scoring
description: The instructional package used to implement cooperative learning in General Science consisted, in the article's words, of "five lesson plans, five work sheets and five quizzes", prepared in light of the literature on cooperative learning. Students worked in six groups of three, helped each other complete worksheets, checked answers, and took individual 10-item quizzes whose marks were converted to group scores "strictly according to the scheme given by Slavin (1995)".
requirements: Groups of about three students, worksheets with answer sheets, individually administered quizzes, and conversion of individual marks into group scores following Slavin's scheme
constraints: Used in this study only on one school subject, General Science, with female 9th-grade students
target_learning_goals: General Science achievement
examples: After each lesson, groups completed worksheets, received answer sheets, and took a 10-item quiz the following day with individual and group marks announced
