article_title: Benefits of Teaching Interdisciplinary Subjects Collaboratively in Jordanian Pre-Vocational Education
citation: Al-Saaideh M, Nasr-allah Al-Zyoud MS. (2015). Benefits of teaching interdisciplinary subjects collaboratively in Jordanian pre-vocational education. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2461
title: Co-teaching and its delivery models as a framework for collaborative teaching
description: The article frames co-teaching as collaborative teaching in which "two or more professionals delivering substantive instructions to a diverse, or blended, group of students in a single physical space". It distinguishes co-teaching from team teaching, where teachers have equal roles using the same strategies, and reviews the delivery models made prominent by Friend and Cook (2010): one instruct/one watch, one educate/one aid, station teaching, parallel educating, option instructing, and group educating. The study applied a synthesis of team teaching models in which dual sub-teams planned each unit and both teachers attended lessons, taking different roles in the classroom or workshop.
requirements: Collaboration between more than one teacher; joint planning time; co-teacher similarity and content mastery
constraints: Effectiveness depends on teachers' subject mastery, experience, availability of joint planning time, and co-teacher similarity, per the article's review
target_learning_goals: practical vocational skills
positive attitudes towards pre-vocational education
integration of vocational and academic knowledge
examples: The dual sub-team of teachers planned each unit's activities and specified each teacher's role; the other teachers attended 58 lessons, 90% of the year's PVE lessons
key_sources: Al-Saaideh M, Nasr-allah Al-Zyoud MS. (2015). Benefits of teaching interdisciplinary subjects collaboratively in Jordanian pre-vocational education. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2461

article_title: Benefits of Teaching Interdisciplinary Subjects Collaboratively in Jordanian Pre-Vocational Education
citation: Al-Saaideh M, Nasr-allah Al-Zyoud MS. (2015). Benefits of teaching interdisciplinary subjects collaboratively in Jordanian pre-vocational education. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2015.2461
title: Teach interdisciplinary practical subjects through collaboration between the subject teacher and teachers of other school subjects
description: The article recommends delivering interdisciplinary subjects like PVE through multi-teacher collaboration rather than a single specialist, because collaboration pairs the PVE teacher with teachers whose specialties match curriculum units (science for agricultural and health units, arts for painting and engineering drawing, math for financial units). It found this "better improved students’ achievement and attitudes towards PVE in comparison to teaching only by the PVE teacher", and also yielded better skills training, subject integration, progress recording for guidance, and time utilization.
requirements: Joint planning before each unit; both teachers attending the lessons; commitment of teachers and school administration; training of the teacher team
constraints: Lengthy planning time, timetable conflicts, team-member compatibility issues, possible student reluctance toward team-implied techniques, and difficulty in schools with teacher shortages
target_learners: basic-education students studying interdisciplinary practical subjects
target_learning_goals: practical skills mastery
achievement in interdisciplinary content
positive attitudes towards the subject
examples: Five teachers (PVE, science, arts, math, physical education) co-taught the experimental class for a full school year, with the other teachers attending 58 of the year's PVE lessons

article_title: Interactional Feedback in Naturalistic Interaction between L2 English Learners
citation: Mahishi Ranaweera. (2015). Interactional Feedback in Naturalistic Interaction between L2 English Learners. English Language Teaching, 8(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n11p47
title: Conversation partner activity: an out-of-class naturalistic small-group activity with an advanced ESL conversation leader
description: The conversation partner activity is an out-of-classroom Program in Intensive English activity in which learners meet without a teacher but are "accompanied by a proficient speaker of English as a second language even if a formal t eacher is not present in the group". In this study one MA TESOL student with native-like proficiency, assigned by the PIE director, led a group of three learners of mixed L1 background. Conversations were recorded over three weeks and followed by tailor-made review tests of 3-5 questions, so the activity doubles as a natural setting for observing interactional feedback.
requirements: A conversation leader who is an advanced or near-native proficient English speaker, in this study an MA TESOL student with a high TOEFL score
constraints: As an outdoor activity, recordings were made on the move or in public places and were at times unclear or filled with background noise; visiting members dominated conversations and limited interaction time for the observed partners
target_learners: international intensive English program students of mixed L1 background
target_learning_goals: second language interaction and uptake of feedback on grammar, vocabulary and pronunciation
examples: Recordings of one hour, one and a half hours, and forty-five minutes were analyzed, and simple tests containing 3-5 questions were distributed at the start of the next meeting

citation: Irina V. Khairova & Nodira M. Egamberdieva. (2016). Communicatively Developing Technology of Speech Activation of Tatar Schools` Teachers. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 433-451.
title: Model of communicatively developing technology of teachers' speech activation
description: The article presents a model of communicatively developing technology of learning in which "the technology of communicatively developing type is assigned as the algorithm of reflexive activity of two subjects in educational process (trainer and trainee)". It rests on psychological and methodological principles such as successive formation of the communicative core, maintaining high-level difficulty, and pedagogic communication equality moving trainees from object to active subject of self-education. The model is built on activity, system-related, structural and person-centered approaches, with a controlling and a controlled cluster.
requirements: Trainer acts as facilitator of interpersonal communication, role model, group leader and partner
Positional places determining position and relation to the subject of activity must be distributed between trainees
constraints: Assigned mainly to teachers' personal self-realization and formation of individual verbal behavior

Communicative competence
Oral activity activation

article_title: Communicatively Developing Technology of Speech Activation of Tatar Schools' Teachers
citation: Irina V. Khairova & Nodira M. Egamberdieva. (2016). Communicatively Developing Technology of Speech Activation of Tatar Schools` Teachers. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 433-451.
title: Diagnostic toolkit of formulas and characteristics for assessing teachers' coherent speech
description: The article defines a set of diagnostic characteristics of coherent Russian speech — pronunciation norms, inter phrase connection, word-order (theme and rheme structure), information concentration, complex syntactic unity, syntactic complexity, notional complexity and logic connection — each operationalized in a printed formula. For example, information concentration is defined as "Тko – level of information concentration" computed from information cores and first- and second-grade developments, and logic connection between sentences is graded with strong, weak, absent and false types. Results were visualized in diagnostic maps drawn as a circle on eight radiuses.
requirements: Selection of sentences with information cores based on microtext structure (beginning, body and ending)
Analysis of utterances on the three printed levels
constraints: Developed and applied for teachers of Tatar schools in the IAT course-retraining system
target_learners: Teachers of Tatar schools attending advanced training courses
target_learning_goals: Assessment and development of coherent Russian oral speech
examples: Diagnostic maps were created from analysis of experimental and control group members' utterances

article_title: Hybrid Learning in Enhancing Communicative Skill in English
citation: G. Singaravelu. (2010). Hybrid Learning in Enhancing Communicative Skill in English. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, Vol. 7 No. 1, April - June. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Hybrid+Learning+in+Enhancing+Communicative+Skill+in+English
title: Communicative competency as three components (grammatical, socio-linguistic, strategic)
description: The article adopts a three-part account of communicative competency, citing Canale and Swain (1980): "Grammatical competence: words and rules, Socio-linguistic competence: appropriateness. Strategic competence: appropriate use of communication strategies." It frames communicative competency as a language user's grammatical knowledge of syntax, morphology and phonology plus appropriate use of utterances, and treats it as the goal of language education that teacher trainees must acquire for effective classroom transaction.

target_learners: Pre-service and in-service teachers of English
target_learning_goals: Communicative competency in English for classroom transaction
examples: The study's oral test operationalises these components through vocabulary, appropriateness, pronunciation and coherence sub-scores

article_title: Comics as a Literary-Didactic Method and Their Use for Reducing Gender Differences in Reading Literacy at the Primary Level of Education
citation: Maja Kerneža and Katja Košir. (2016). Comics as a Literary-Didactic Method and Their Use for Reducing Gender Differences in Reading Literacy at the Primary Level of Education. c e p s Journal, Vol. 6, No. 2. https://cepsj.pef.uni-lj.si

description: A structured programme embedding comics in Slovene language and art lessons for primary pupils, delivered in "eight units, at 19 Slovene and art lessons" over approximately seven weeks. It progresses from learning comics' basic characteristics and speech bubbles, through creating comics and detecting text incoherence, to active work with literary texts. Teachers received a six-hour training in three parts and a graded lesson-plan manual (one version for grades 2–3, another for grades 4–5, differing mainly in text difficulty).

ability to perceive text incoherence
interest in reading literary texts
attitude towards reading

article_title: Latinos: Higher Education and Technology
citation: Sylvia L. Flores & Luis A. Flores. (2018). Latinos: Higher Education and Technology. Journal of Learning in Higher Education, 14(1). https://www.aabri.com/copyright.html
title: Conflict theory as a framework for understanding technology, higher education, and Latino-ethnic academic success
description: The article adopts conflict theory, created by Karl Marx, as its explanatory framework. It states that "Conflict theory explains how macro groups are seen to always fight for scarce resources," casting the majority as capitalists and the Latino-ethnic group as proletariats competing for the scarce resource of academic success. The authors argue this leaves the Latino-ethnic group at a disadvantage when colleges utilizing technology benefit the majority of students, and that the theory supports the meta-analysis method for this study.
requirements: Applied alongside a meta-analysis of accessible literature on the Latino-ethnic group, technology, and academic success in higher education
target_learning_goals: Understanding dynamics of academic success in higher education
examples: The article frames colleges that utilize technology to increase learning as benefiting the majority of students, leaving the Latino-ethnic group at a disadvantage
key_sources: Sylvia L. Flores & Luis A. Flores. (2018). Latinos: Higher Education and Technology. Journal of Learning in Higher Education, 14(1). https://www.aabri.com/copyright.html

article_title: Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions
citation: Fuchs, L. S., Schumacher, R. F., Long, J., Namkung, J., Hamlett, C. L., Cirino, P. T., Jordan, N. C., Siegler, R., Gersten, R., & Changas, P. (2013). Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032446
title: Intervention should compensate for at-risk learners' domain-general limitations through chunking, segmenting, automaticity, and attentive-behavior supports
description: Because at-risk children often experience limited working memory capacity, inattentive behavior, and slow processing speed, the intervention incorporated methods to reduce demands on these systems. These included teaching efficient strategies for chunking and segmenting measurement interpretation tasks, creating automaticity with fractional values relative to marker fractions, and providing structure to encourage attentive behavior and hard work.
requirements: Instructional methods that teach chunking or segmenting strategies, build automaticity with fractional values, and structure students to exercise attentive behavior
target_learners: at-risk students with limited working memory, inattentive behavior, or slow processing speed
target_learning_goals: fraction concepts and procedures
examples: Tutors set a timer to beep at three unpredictable times during each lesson, awarding checkmarks if all students were on task.

article_title: The Impact of an Interdisciplinary Learning Community Course on Pseudoscientific Reasoning in First-Year Science Students
citation: Franz, T. M., & Green, K. H. (2013). The impact of an interdisciplinary learning community course on pseudoscientific reasoning in first-year science students. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 13(5), 90–105.
title: Cognitive acceleration stages (concrete preparation, cognitive conflict, metacognition, bridging) as the LC's structure for developing critical thinking
description: The article structures the LC's critical-thinking development after cognitive acceleration (Adey & Shayer, 1993) "through stages of concrete preparation, cognitive conflict, metacognition and bridging". Concrete preparation came from connections to real situations such as the psychic demonstration; cognitive conflict was generated through readings, discussions, and media exposing students to multiple perspectives; the writing component provided opportunities for metacognition; and parallels among situations and common ways thinking goes wrong served as a bridge throughout the course.
requirements: Writing assignments to make metacognition manifest
Readings, discussions, and media presenting multiple components and perspectives to generate cognitive conflict
constraints: The article applies this structure specifically to a first-year interdisciplinary science learning community
target_learners: first-year undergraduate science and mathematics students
target_learning_goals: critical thinking
scientific reasoning
metacognition
key_sources: Franz, T. M., & Green, K. H. (2013). The impact of an interdisciplinary learning community course on pseudoscientific reasoning in first-year science students. Journal of the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 13(5), 90–105. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1017127

article_title: The Effect of Form versus Meaning-Focused Tasks on the Development of Collocations among Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners
citation: Pishghadam, R., Khodadady, E., & Daliry Rad, N. (2011). The Effect of Form versus Meaning-Focused Tasks on the Development of Collocations among Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 4(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n2p180
title: Use collaborative output tasks such as dictogloss to promote noticing and language learning through collaborative dialogue
description: The article recommends tasks requiring learners to produce output collaboratively, arguing that 'through talk in collaborative task, learners notice their linguistic problems' and engage in making meaning clearer. Dictogloss, where small groups reconstruct a listened-to text, elicits collaborative dialogue and meta-talk that can deepen awareness of forms and their relationship to meaning.
requirements: Teacher modeling of task procedures in early sessions
Teacher availability during collaborative activities to attend to accuracy of the final product and provide feedback
constraints: A task that elicits meta-talk from one group of learners may not do so from another, depending on proficiency level and age
target_learning_goals: collocation development
grammatical accuracy
language awareness
examples: Students in small groups of three used their notes to reconstruct a text as closely as possible to the original, then compared and analyzed the versions they produced
key_sources: Pishghadam, R., Khodadady, E., & Daliry Rad, N. (2011). The Effect of Form versus Meaning-Focused Tasks on the Development of Collocations among Iranian Intermediate EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 4(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v4n2p180

article_title: The Acquisition of Phrasal Verbs through Cognitive Linguistic Approach: The Case of Iranian EFL Learners
citation: Mohammad Javad Ansari. (2016). The Acquisition of Phrasal Verbs through Cognitive Linguistic Approach: The Case of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.1p.185
title: Cognitive Linguistics as a usage-based approach linking language to general cognition
description: The article presents Cognitive Linguistics as a school of linguistics and cognitive science that "treats language and its acquisition as usage-based and as reflecting the general cognitive abilities that operate in our interaction with the world" (Boers, 2013, as cited). It rests on two key commitments — the generalization commitment and the cognitive commitment — and rejects the modular approach of formal linguistics, instead seeking explanations of linguistic phenomena in general cognitive strategies such as metaphor and prototype theory.
requirements: Explanation of linguistic phenomena in terms of general cognitive strategies rather than autonomous language modules
constraints: The article notes Cognitive Linguistics is not a single theory but a broad concept, and that prototype theory is no longer seen as an accurate view of categorization
target_learning_goals: understanding how conceptual mechanisms such as metaphor support L2 learning
examples: The study applied cognitive-linguistic ideas by teaching orientational particles through their metaphorical, embodied meanings with visual aids
key_sources: Mohammad Javad Ansari. (2016). The Acquisition of Phrasal Verbs through Cognitive Linguistic Approach: The Case of Iranian EFL Learners. Advances in Language and Literary Studies, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.1p.185

article_title: A Mindful Approach to Teaching Emotional Intelligence to Undergraduate Students Online and in Person
citation: Cotler, J. L., DiTursi, D., Goldstein, I., Yates, J., & DelBelso, D. (2017). A Mindful Approach to Teaching Emotional Intelligence to Undergraduate Students Online and in Person. Information Systems Education Journal, 15(1). http://isedj.org
title: Combine online EI workshops with mindfulness instruction for maximum impact on peer-assessed EI growth
description: The article's regression findings show that neither online EI workshops nor mindfulness training alone produced statistically significant improvement in peer-assessed EI, but their combination did. This principle recommends pairing direct EI instruction with mindfulness practice rather than delivering either in isolation. The mindfulness component follows the format of the Google Search Inside Yourself program and includes breath awareness and mindful listening exercises practiced during lecture sessions and independently.
requirements: Both online EI workshops and mindfulness instruction must be present together
Mindfulness practice includes in-class sessions and independent practice assignments
constraints: The mindfulness practices were only taught by one instructor, so the effect cannot be separated from the instructor
Low score variability and possible gamma change may account for the observed pattern
target_learning_goals: emotional intelligence growth as measured by peer assessment
examples: Students receiving online EI workshops plus mindfulness reported greater EI growth than control; the Online x Mindfulness interaction coefficient was 3.25 (p = .04)
key_sources: Cotler, J. L., DiTursi, D., Goldstein, I., Yates, J., & DelBelso, D. (2017). A Mindful Approach to Teaching Emotional Intelligence to Undergraduate Students Online and in Person. Information Systems Education Journal, 15(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1135358

article_title: Enhancing Expectations of Cooperative Learning Use through Initial Teacher Training
citation: Duran, D; Corcelles, M. & Flores, M. (2017). Enhancing Expectations of Cooperative Learning Use through Initial Teacher Training. International Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(3), 278-300. https://doi.org/10.17583/ijep.2017.2504
title: Combine conceptual training with direct experience of cooperative learning in initial teacher education
description: The article concludes that initial teacher training should pair conceptual instruction about cooperative learning with opportunities to experience it as a learner. The authors state that "the combined use of conceptual training and experience of CL is what the Teacher Training education has to offer to the future teachers". This dual approach raised expectancy of success and the Index of CL use in their quasi-experimental study.
requirements: Conceptual training in CL fundamentals (4 sessions, 6.5 hours in this study)
Structured opportunities to experience CL methods such as peer tutoring in university classrooms
constraints: The reduced sample size and specific university and cultural context make it difficult to generalize results
target_learning_goals: Expectancy of success in implementing cooperative learning
Disposition to use cooperative learning in future classrooms
examples: Group B received conceptual training plus two peer tutoring sessions where 8 tutors prepared materials and taught groups of 5 tutees
key_sources: Duran, D; Corcelles, M. & Flores, M. (2017). Enhancing Expectations of Cooperative Learning Use through Initial Teacher Training. International Journal of Educational Psychology, 6(3), 278-300. https://doi.org/10.17583/ijep.2017.2504

article_title: Efficacy of Multimedia Learning Modules as Preparation for Lecture-Based Tutorials in Electromagnetism
citation: James Christopher Moore. (2018). Efficacy of Multimedia Learning Modules as Preparation for Lecture-Based Tutorials in Electromagnetism. Educ. Sci. 2018, 8, 23. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci8010023
title: Cognitive load theory as the theoretical framework explaining why multimedia learning modules reduce cognitive load and support pre-class learning
description: The article frames MLMs within cognitive load theory and working memory limitations. By "mixing auditory and visual presentations, meaningful learning can take place by helping the learner make connections between multiple representations of the same content without taxing limited capacity memory channels". The modules used in the study were designed to reduce cognitive load and mix presentation modes, drawing on physics education and multimedia learning research. The author uses this framework to explain the larger learning gains observed with MLMs, while acknowledging the improvements "may not be completely explainable through cognitive load theory alone".
requirements: MLM content must be designed informed by cognitive load theory and multimedia learning research
constraints: The author states the cognitive achievement improvements may not be completely explainable through cognitive load theory alone
target_learners: natural science majors (biology and marine science) in calculus-based introductory physics
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of electricity and magnetism
key_sources: James Christopher Moore. (2018). Efficacy of Multimedia Learning Modules as Preparation for Lecture-Based Tutorials in Electromagnetism. Educ. Sci. 2018, 8, 23. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci8010023

article_title: On the Communicative Functions of Context in Foreign Language Education
citation: Polok, K. (2021). On the Communicative Functions of Context in Foreign Language Education. International Journal of Instruction, 14(2), 1051-1072. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2021.14260a
title: Sequence context-embedded activities before context-reduced ones in FL lessons
description: The article recommends that 'easier tasks ought to precede more demanding ones which could be modified to mean that context-embedded activities should come before any contest-reduced ones'. An exemplary lesson should begin with cognitively undemanding communication paired with easily discovered context, and only after learners master slightly reduced context should deeply reduced material be proposed. This sequencing is offered to counteract motivation-extinguishing situations.
requirements: Teachers must assess learners' current proficiency level so tasks do not surpass it (+1)
constraints: The article frames this as a 'slogan-like stance' adapted from the general easier-before-harder principle
target_learning_goals: Context discovery and comprehension
Sustained motivation in FL lessons
examples: Lessons beginning with preferred, cognitively undemanding activities with easily discovered context elements before deeply reduced-context material
key_sources: Polok, K. (2021). On the Communicative Functions of Context in Foreign Language Education. International Journal of Instruction, 14(2), 1051-1072. https://doi.org/10.29333/iji.2021.14260a

article_title: Effects of Reflective Thinking in the Process of Designing Software on Students' Learning Performances
citation: Hsieh, P.-H., & Chen, N.-S. (2012). Effects of reflective thinking in the process of designing software on students' learning performances. Computers & Education, 58(1), 419-431. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.021
title: Compeau and Higgins (1995) Computer Self-Efficacy Questionnaire measuring magnitude of self-efficacy for using packaged software.
description: This study adopts the Compeau and Higgins (1995) Computer Self-Efficacy Questionnaire, which contains ten Yes/No questions and measures the magnitude of self-efficacy, providing data of students' abilities to use packaged software. If the answer is the former, students make a personal self-assessment of strength of self-confidence on a 1 to 10 scale.
requirements: Reliability analysis, followed by a Paired-Samples T-Test, explored the presence of significant differences between pre-test and post-test average scores
constraints: the scale is sensitive to, and situation-dependent upon, students' current computer use status
target_learners: college students in a software design course
target_learning_goals: animation software design
examples: All the students completed the questionnaire twice, one before the beginning of the course and again at the course's completion
key_sources: Hsieh, P.-H., & Chen, N.-S. (2012). Effects of reflective thinking in the process of designing software on students' learning performances. Computers & Education, 58(1), 419-431. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2011.12.021

article_title: Performance in an Online Introductory Course in a Hybrid Classroom Setting
citation: Aly, I. (2013). Performance in an online introductory course in a hybrid classroom setting. Canadian Journal of Higher Education, 43(2), 85-99. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1103163
title: Constructivist learning theory as a framework for online course design
description: The article applies constructivist learning theory to online and hybrid course design, emphasizing that the learner plays an active role in acquiring knowledge through interaction and association with prior experience. The instructor acts as a coach and facilitator rather than a transmitter of knowledge. The theory is operationalized through four overlapping environments: learner-centred, knowledge-centred, assessment-centred, and community-centred, which together guide the design of effective online learning spaces.
requirements: Students must develop clear goals from the beginning, with action plans and realistic timelines
Instruction should promote collaborative learning environments encouraging student interaction with content, instructors, and classmates
constraints: The framework was applied within a single introductory accounting course context
target_learning_goals: active knowledge construction
self-regulated learning
collaborative learning
examples: Weekly online assignments provided timely, meaningful feedback and assessment, promoting an active, collaborative, and participatory form of learning
key_sources: Aly, I. (2013). Performance in an online introductory course in a hybrid classroom setting. Canadian Journal of Higher Education, 43(2), 85-99. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1013589

article_title: Comparing the Effects of Four Instructional Treatments on EFL Students' Achievement in Writing Classified Ads
citation: Khodabandeh, F. (2016). Comparing the Effects of Four Instructional Treatments on EFL Students’ Achievement in Writing Classified Ads. English Language Teaching, 9(3), 139-. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n3p139
title: Combine different instructional approaches and techniques to help learners improve their writing skills.
description: The article's conclusion recommends that teachers take advantage of different approaches and techniques and combine them to help learners improve their skills. The findings offer English teachers the chance to reconsider their practices through the advantages and disadvantages of traditional and new techniques employed in the research. By asking students to do a task, they benefit from a different approach that is more motivating and more meaningful than other traditional instruction-based approaches.
requirements: Teachers must be familiar with the advantages and disadvantages of traditional (explicit, implicit) and non-traditional (self-study, task-based) techniques.
constraints: The scope of the study both in terms of its content and the population was limited, and the participants and duration of the study were also limited.
target_learners: Iranian EFL junior students at Payame Noor University distance education system
target_learning_goals: Second language writing development of genre-based classified ads
examples: The post-test results showed that explicit and task-based instruction assisted the explicit and task-based groups to outperform the other groups on most of the categories assessed.
key_sources: Khodabandeh, F. (2016). Comparing the Effects of Four Instructional Treatments on EFL Students’ Achievement in Writing Classified Ads. English Language Teaching, 9(3), 139-. https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n3p139

article_title: Concept Maps and Informational Read-Alouds: Strengthening Both Science and Reading for Elementary Students
citation: Berry, J., Potter, J., & Hollas, V. (2014). Concept Maps and Informational Read-Alouds: Strengthening both Science and Reading for Elementary Students. Texas Journal of Literacy Education, 1(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ
title: Pair concept mapping with informational interactive read-alouds to strengthen science and literacy learning
description: The article recommends combining concept mapping with informational interactive read-alouds as an effective strategy for learning science concepts. The treatment group "scored higher on three of the four assessments" without taking more time than answering comprehension questions. Concept maps can be used as pre-reading, during reading, or post-reading activities.
requirements: A science trade book focusing on the specific concept being taught
Time for students to create, share, and discuss concept maps before and after reading
constraints: Study was moderate in scale with only five days between post-test and delayed post-test
target_learning_goals: Science knowledge organization and retention
Relational vocabulary
Written expression
examples: Third graders created concept maps before and after read-alouds on soil formation over eight days
key_sources: Berry, J., Potter, J., & Hollas, V. (2014). Concept Maps and Informational Read-Alouds: Strengthening both Science and Reading for Elementary Students. Texas Journal of Literacy Education, 1(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1110818

article_title: Concept Maps and Informational Read-Alouds: Strengthening Both Science and Reading for Elementary Students
citation: Berry, J., Potter, J., & Hollas, V. (2014). Concept Maps and Informational Read-Alouds: Strengthening both Science and Reading for Elementary Students. Texas Journal of Literacy Education, 1(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ
title: Concept map as science learning tool
description: Created by Novak (1990) as a tool to help students organize ideas and thoughts especially in science. Students "identify key concepts and then draw lines to connect and show relationships between concepts." Linking words or phrases define these connections. Cross-links highlight relationships between concepts in different domains, signaling hierarchical relationships that can be immediately perceived.
requirements: A topic to be mapped
Linking words or phrases to define connections between concepts
target_learning_goals: Organizing ideas and relationships between science concepts
Relational knowledge
examples: Students created concept maps on soil formation before and after read-alouds
key_sources: Berry, J., Potter, J., & Hollas, V. (2014). Concept Maps and Informational Read-Alouds: Strengthening both Science and Reading for Elementary Students. Texas Journal of Literacy Education, 1(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1110818

article_title: Exploring the Classroom: Teaching Science in Early Childhood
citation: Dejonckheere, P.J.N., De Wit, N.L., Van de Keere, K., & Vervaet, S. (2016). Exploring the classroom: Teaching science in early childhood. European Journal of Educational Research, 5(3), 149-164. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.5.3.149
title: Connect preschool science activities to children's interests and classroom themes
description: The article argues that preschool science activities should be connected to the themes and interests already present in the classroom to maximise engagement and immersion. Activities were "designed and coordinated closely with the pre -service teacher and with the actual teac hers of the classes" so that they were "more closely connected to the children's interest and curiosity". This grounding is presented as a key condition for the intervention's success in a real classroom setting.
requirements: Teachers must collaborate on activity design and link science materials to ongoing classroom themes and children's existing knowledge.
constraints: The article notes that not all children are equally excited about each activity, so variation in subjects over time matters.
target_learning_goals: scientific inquiry skills
engagement with science
curiosity and motivation to explore
examples: For the sinking and floating activity, the introduction phase asked what rubber ducks do (floating or sinking) and what kind of materials should sink or float, linking to children's everyday experience.
key_sources: Dejonckheere, P.J.N., De Wit, N.L., Van de Keere, K., & Vervaet, S. (2016). Exploring the classroom: Teaching science in early childhood. European Journal of Educational Research, 5(3), 149-164. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.5.3.149

article_title: The Effect of Fire Context on the Conceptual Understanding of Students: "Expansion-Contraction"
citation: Sibel Er Nas, Tülay Şenel Çoruhlu and Arzu Kirman Bilgin. (2016). The effect of fire context on the conceptual understanding of students: “expansion-contraction”. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.2958
title: Context-based learning theory as a framework for science instruction
description: The article frames its intervention within context-based learning theory, which "emphasises that it is possible to eliminate academic failure by establishing a relationship between life and science". The theory holds that teaching within a context helps students relate extrascholastic experiences to scientific concepts, facilitating learning. The REACT teaching model (Relating, Experiencing, Applying, Cooperating, Transferring) operationalises this theory.
requirements: Instruction must be designed around a context that connects scientific concepts to students' everyday experiences.
constraints: The article applies this theory specifically to 5th grade science concepts of expansion and contraction in Turkey.
target_learning_goals: Connecting scientific concepts to everyday life phenomena
examples: The study used fire alarm systems as a context for teaching expansion-contraction, following the REACT model's five steps.
key_sources: Sibel Er Nas, Tülay Şenel Çoruhlu and Arzu Kirman Bilgin. (2016). The effect of fire context on the conceptual understanding of students: “expansion-contraction”. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2016.2958

article_title: Corpus-Based Data-Driven Learning to Augment L2 Students' Vocabulary Repertoire
citation: Ira Rasikawati (2019). Corpus-Based Data-Driven Learning to Augment L2 Students’ Vocabulary Repertoire. International Dialogues on Education, 6(2), 83-98.
title: Corpus-based DDL framework for augmenting students' vocabulary repertoire in Reading EAP
description: The article proposes a framework (Figure 1) for enhancing students' vocabulary knowledge within an inquiry-based Reading EAP curriculum. It comprises "four curriculum elements – course content, instructional approach, activities, and assessment" and structures key learning variables in "a recurring cycle of activities". The cycle begins with instruction on complex syntax and multi-word sequences, moves through teacher-activated inquiries, collaborative corpus investigation and synthesis of lexico-syntactic patterns, and ends with independent query solving, sharing, and use of new knowledge in reading and writing.
requirements: Students' use of authentic materials and higher-order thinking skills, engagement in problem-solving, and scaffolded inquiries
Sufficient training in query types across the first few meetings
Ongoing assessment of vocabulary understanding and use for feedback and adjustment
constraints: Paper-based concordance activities are recommended at the early stage before transitioning to web-based corpus data
target_learners: Undergraduate EAP students in non-English speaking countries
target_learning_goals: Expanding vocabulary size and understanding of word nuances
Comprehension of academic texts
Lexico-grammatical pattern knowledge
examples: The cycle starts with instruction on complex syntax and multi-word sequences; teacher questions gradually shift to student-invented problems and hypotheses as students progress
key_sources: Ira Rasikawati (2019). Corpus-Based Data-Driven Learning to Augment L2 Students’ Vocabulary Repertoire. International Dialogues on Education, 6(2), 83-98. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1245249

article_title: Open Education Students' Perspectives on Using Virtual Museums Application in Teaching History Subjects
citation: Ulusoy, K. (2010). Open Education Students' Perspectives on Using Virtual Museums Application in Teaching History Subjects. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 11(4). https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tojde/issue/16922/176560
title: Constructivism as the learning theory underlying virtual museum design.
description: The article identifies constructivism as the learning theory that "underlies much educational practice in museums and has come to inform the design of virtual museums as well". This aligns with Turkey's 2004 curriculum reform based on constructivist teaching and learning theories, which emphasized museum visits and included virtual museums in social science curriculums.
requirements: Virtual museum projects should allow students to make choices about what they want to study and provide meaningful topics incorporating academics and culture.
target_learning_goals: student-centred learning
constructing meaning from historical objects and sources
examples: The Nah Tah Wash School virtual museum project was described as providing a student-centred, constructivist learning environment where students select topics, research them, and create web pages demonstrating their knowledge.
key_sources: Ulusoy, K. (2010). Open Education Students' Perspectives on Using Virtual Museums Application in Teaching History Subjects. Turkish Online Journal of Distance Education, 11(4). https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/tojde/issue/16922/176560

article_title: Measuring the Impact of Language-Learning Software on Test Performance of Chinese Learners of English
citation: Nicholes, J. (2016). Measuring the Impact of Language-Learning Software on Test Performance of Chinese Learners of English. TESL-EJ, 20(2). https://tesl-ej.org/pdf/ej76/a3.pdf
title: Comprehension or natural theory as the theoretical underpinning of Rosetta Stone
description: The article identifies the theoretical basis of Rosetta Stone as "the comprehension or natural theory, in which second language acquisition (SLA) starts with listening comprehension, mimicking the process of first language acquisition (FLA)." Under this account, learners view an image with English text, hear a stimulus, and are prompted to repeat or explain it into a microphone, with a speech-recognition tool measuring comprehensibility. The article situates this theory as the design rationale behind RS's immersion approach.
requirements: learners must have access to microphone-equipped computers for speech-recognition feedback
constraints: peer-reviewed evaluations cited in the article question the theory's application, citing unclear theoretical underpinnings and culturally inappropriate images
target_learners: beginning-to-intermediate second language learners using self-study software
target_learning_goals: second language listening comprehension and pronunciation through immersion
examples: RS learners view an image with English text, hear and repeat the stimulus into a microphone, and receive speech-recognition comprehensibility feedback
key_sources: Nicholes, J. (2016). Measuring the Impact of Language-Learning Software on Test Performance of Chinese Learners of English. TESL-EJ, 20(2). https://tesl-ej.org/pdf/ej76/a3.pdf

article_title: Bridging the Gap between Expert-Novice Differences: The Model-Based Feedback Approach
citation: Ifenthaler, D. (2010). Bridging the Gap between Expert-Novice Differences: The Model-Based Feedback Approach. Journal of Research on Technology in Education, 43(2), 103-117. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-009-9119-8
title: Use concept mapping rather than written text when the goal is structural alignment with expert knowledge
description: Because concept maps were found to be structurally and semantically more similar to an expert solution than written texts, learning activities that aim to align novice understanding with expert knowledge structures should prefer concept mapping as the externalization method. The article notes that concept mapping techniques and systematic text analysis cannot be used as complements, since they represent different dimensions of understanding.
requirements: Learners need an introduction to concept maps and causal diagrams before using them
constraints: Written text covers a broader area of the phenomenon in question (more vertices), so may be preferable when breadth of coverage is the goal
target_learning_goals: structuring domain knowledge
aligning with expert mental models
examples: Participants constructed concept maps and wrote texts about climate change before and after receiving model-based feedback
key_sources: Ifenthaler, D. (2010). Bridging the Gap between Expert-Novice Differences: The Model-Based Feedback Approach. Journal of Research on Technology in Education, 43(2), 103-117. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-009-9119-8

article_title: Learning Alone or Together? A Combination Can Be Best!
citation: Olsen, J. K., Rummel, N., & Aleven, V. (2017). Learning Alone or Together? A Combination Can Be Best! Proceedings of the 12th International Conference on Computer Supported Collaborative Learning. https://learning-analytics.info/journals/index.php/ijcscl/article/view/9151
title: Collaborative fractions intelligent tutoring system with embedded collaboration scripts
description: A fractions ITS covering three units (equivalent fractions, least common denominator, comparing fractions), built with CTAT and extended to support collaborative tutors. The collaborative versions embed "collaborative scripts for each tutor problem to provide social support for students," distributing responsibility to create accountability and interdependence, and supporting cognitive group awareness. Students sat at their own computer with a shared, differentiated view of the problem state.
requirements: Embedded collaboration scripts that distribute responsibility and support cognitive group awareness
constraints: Collaborative and individual ITS versions were otherwise identical
target_learning_goals: fractions: equivalent fractions, least common denominator, comparing fractions
examples: Students received only some fraction symbols and had to share with their partner to solve the problem
key_sources: Olsen, J. K., Rummel, N., & Aleven, V. (2017). Learning Alone or Together? A Combination Can Be Best! Proceedings of the 12th International Conference on Computer Supported Collaborative Learning. https://learning-analytics.info/journals/index.php/ijcscl/article/view/9151

article_title: Effects of School Counselors' Cognitive Behavioral Consultation on Irrational and Efficacy Beliefs of Elementary School Teachers
citation: Jeffrey M. Warren, Edwin R. Gerler, Jr. (2013). Effects of School Counselors' Cognitive Behavioral Consultation on Irrational and Efficacy Beliefs of Elementary School Teachers. The Professional Counselor, 3(1), 6-15. https://doi.org/10.15241/jmw.3.1.6
title: School counselors should adopt a collaborative approach when consulting with teachers
description: The article recommends that school counselors take a collaborative stance during consultation with teachers. Citing Kampwirth and Powers (2012), the authors state that "school counselors will find consultation with teachers is most effective when a collaborative approach is taken." Collaboration and teaming encourage teachers to be proactive and to invest in the goals of the consultation efforts, supporting systemic change through comprehensive school counseling services.
requirements: School counselors must demonstrate intentional leadership, advocacy and collaboration when implementing consultation as part of comprehensive school counseling programs
target_learning_goals: reduce irrational beliefs
promote positive mental health
examples: The face-to-face consultation used interactive discussions, songs, humor and participation in demonstrations, with case examples and analogies focused on teaching and classroom situations
key_sources: Jeffrey M. Warren, Edwin R. Gerler, Jr. (2013). Effects of School Counselors' Cognitive Behavioral Consultation on Irrational and Efficacy Beliefs of Elementary School Teachers. The Professional Counselor, 3(1), 6-15. https://doi.org/10.15241/jmw.3.1.6

article_title: A Case Study of a Co-Instructed Multidisciplinary Senior Capstone Project in Sustainability
citation: Rhee, J., Oyamot, C., Parent, D., Speer, L., Basu, A., & Gerston, L. (2014). A Case Study of a Co-instructed Multidisciplinary Senior Capstone Project in Sustainability. Advances in Engineering Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED
title: Schedule shared project courses in a common time slot to enable co-instruction without new courses
description: The co-instruction model schedules existing project courses at a common time slot so they can meet jointly, separately, or in subsets, allowing cross-disciplinary instruction while preserving each instructor's autonomy. The article states this design lets courses have "the capability of meeting jointly, separately, or in subsets, allowing cross-disciplinary instruction and interaction." It was tested as an alternative to resource-intensive dedicated team-taught courses.
requirements: A set of relevant project courses scheduled at a common time slot
Projects with disciplinary subprojects of sufficient scope for similar-sized student teams
constraints: Does not tackle all barriers to multidisciplinary co-taught instruction, e.g. it does not by itself resolve team conflict or reward-system misalignment
target_learners: senior undergraduate engineering, business, political science, and industrial design students
target_learning_goals: sustainability content knowledge
multidisciplinary teamwork and collaboration
examples: Five courses (EE, ME, industrial design, green entrepreneurship, public policy) ran the ZEM House joint project in 2010–11 without a dedicated course or facility.
key_sources: Rhee, J., Oyamot, C., Parent, D., Speer, L., Basu, A., & Gerston, L. (2014). A Case Study of a Co-instructed Multidisciplinary Senior Capstone Project in Sustainability. Advances in Engineering Education. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1076079

article_title: Using Concept Mapping and Paraphrasing for Reading Comprehension
citation: Marashi, H., & Bagheri, N. (2015). Using concept mapping and paraphrasing for reading comprehension. li-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, 5(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1070579
title: Concept mapping as a spatial learning strategy grounded in assimilation theory and constructivism
description: The article situates concept mapping as a spatial learning strategy with origins in David Ausubel's work, developed by Novak in the 1970s. It is grounded in "assimilation theories and the constructivist movement" which "emphasize incorporating new information into previous ones." The strategy uses visual symbols and graphic representations to show relationships among concepts, supporting comprehension by leveraging learners' strong capacity for remembering visual concepts.
requirements: Learners must activate prior knowledge and connect new information to existing mental structures
target_learners: Students in sciences and language learning
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension
Meaningful learning
Organization of knowledge
key_sources: Marashi, H., & Bagheri, N. (2015). Using concept mapping and paraphrasing for reading comprehension. li-manager's Journal of English Language Teaching, 5(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1097361

article_title: Play and Productivity: Enhancing the Creative Climate at Workplace Meetings with Play Cues
citation: West, Samuel E., Eva Hoff, and Ingegerd Carlsson. (2016). Play and Productivity: Enhancing the Creative Climate at Workplace Meetings with Play Cues. American Journal of Play, 9(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1111974
title: Use contextual play cues to signal that play is permissible in work settings
description: Organizations can implicitly convey permission to play through contextual cues such as playful props—games, toys, sweets—or playful rearrangement of furniture. These cues signal "that new, more playful rules temporarily apply." The article's field experiment placed such cues mid-meeting and found significant increases in creative climate, playfulness, and productivity.
requirements: Cues must be placed without obligation for participants to engage, preserving the voluntary aspect of play
constraints: No single cue suits all individuals or groups; some individuals may not find particular cues playful
target_learning_goals: creative climate
playfulness
productivity
examples: Researchers randomly placed colorful childish sweets, toy guns with foam darts, self-adhesive mustaches, or a silly meeting game on conference tables mid-meeting
key_sources: West, Samuel E., Eva Hoff, and Ingegerd Carlsson. (2016). Play and Productivity: Enhancing the Creative Climate at Workplace Meetings with Play Cues. American Journal of Play, 9(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1123863

article_title: The Effects of an Experimental Training Program for Teachers of Vocational English Using Concentrated Language Encounter Instructional Processes and Reciprocal Peer Teaching Strategies
citation: Saowalak Rattanavich. (2017). The Effects of an Experimental Training Program for Teachers of Vocational English Using Concentrated Language Encounter Instructional Processes and Reciprocal Peer Teaching Strategies. English Language Teaching, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n12p58
title: Concentrated language encounter (CLE) instructional process
description: CLE is a sequence of lessons focused on producing a specific target text chosen before teaching, in which "the teacher and student both take an active part in negotiating the student's learning". It rests on Vygotskian scaffolding and contextualised, activity-based learning, and is organised into three stages of literacy development from beginner to advanced learners. In this study it was implemented through five steps: sharing the structured experience, reconstructing the experience, negotiating a group text, making a big book, and language activities through games.
requirements: A learning text carefully chosen to suit the language contextual resources and the activity-based vocational context
constraints: Originally developed for literacy programs; the article applies it to vocational English classes
target_learners: literacy learners from beginner to advanced stages
target_learning_goals: English listening, speaking, reading and writing
vocational language use in real contexts
examples: In the experiment, activity-based units were used for procedural vocational genres such as answering a telephone call as a secretary
key_sources: Saowalak Rattanavich. (2017). The Effects of an Experimental Training Program for Teachers of Vocational English Using Concentrated Language Encounter Instructional Processes and Reciprocal Peer Teaching Strategies. English Language Teaching, 10(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v10n12p58

article_title: Gamify Online Courses with Tools Built into Your Learning Management System (LMS) to Enhance Self-Determined and Active Learning
citation: Chen, C.-C., Huang, C., Gribbins, M., & Swan, K. (2018). Gamify online courses with tools built into your learning management system (LMS) to enhance self-determined and active learning. Online Learning, 22(3), 41-54. https://doi.org/10.24059/olj.v22i3.1466
title: Concept Review Bingo: a wiki-based LMS review game with points, levels, and bonus rewards
description: A 16-question statistical concept review game arranged in a 4 x 4 wiki table within the LMS. "Each correctly answered question earned the student one point of extra credit" and completing a row, column, or diagonal earned a bingo for double points. The first-come, first-choice wiki editing mechanism created competition and challenge. Feedback with detailed answers and explanation videos was provided after all questions were answered.
requirements: An LMS with built-in wiki functionality allowing editable tables and single-user editing locks
constraints: Storytelling, theme, role-playing, and replayability elements were not implemented (marked N/A in Table 1)
target_learners: Graduate students in online statistics courses
target_learning_goals: Review key statistical concepts for exam preparation
examples: Played twice for three days each during a 16-week semester

article_title: Analyzing Research Tendencies of ELT Researchers and Trajectory of English Language Teaching and Learning in the Last Five Years
citation: Ayan, E., & Demirel, E. (2017). Analyzing Research Tendencies of ELT Researchers and Trajectory of English Language Teaching and Learning in the last Five Years. International Journal of Curriculum and Instruction, 9(2), 89-106. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1150914
title: Corpus-based keyword detection methodology using Zotero, AntConc, and JASP
description: The study employed a corpus-based detection methodology in which article data was collected via the citation manager Zotero, exported as RefWorks Tagged .txt files, and analyzed using the concordancer AntConc for keyword and cluster/n-gram frequency. Statistical analysis was then performed in JASP using contingency tables. The authors state the method "is composed of storing variable data in .txt files and analyzing variables over the concordancer."
requirements: Articles must provide author keywords; articles missing keywords were disregarded and deleted from the file
constraints: Limited to articles published between 2012 and 2016 in Modern Language Journal and Language Learning; special issues were excluded
target_learning_goals: Identifying research tendencies and trajectories in English language teaching and learning
examples: 374 articles were downloaded and tagged in total, purified to 287 (149 from Modern Language Journal, 138 from Language Learning)
key_sources: Ayan, E., & Demirel, E. (2017). Analyzing Research Tendencies of ELT Researchers and Trajectory of English Language Teaching and Learning in the last Five Years. International Journal of Curriculum and Instruction, 9(2), 89-106. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1207254

Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. http://ies.ed.gov/pubsearch/pubsinfo.asp?pubid=NCEE20134011
title: Control for type and severity of disability in transition program evaluations
description: The review recommends that researchers "Control for type and severity of disability in the research analysis," because these student attributes were the most consistently important in differentiating post-high school results. Although many studies described students using these attributes, analyses rarely included them, making it difficult to separate program effects from pre-existing differences between groups.
requirements: Ensure program and comparison groups are equivalent on disability type and severity before the program is provided
target_learning_goals: Employment
Postsecondary education and training
Independent living
examples: The review notes 39 percent of students with intellectual disabilities were employed at eight-year follow-up versus 67 percent of students with learning disabilities.

citation: Downer, J., Brown, J., Jimenez Herrera, M., Stuhlman, M., Bourassa, K., Gologor, B., & Wong, P. (2013). Coaching Quality and Teachers' Implementation of the 4Rs Social-Emotional and Literacy Curriculum: Testing the Link between Two Levels of Intervention Fidelity. SREE Spring 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563035
title: Coaching quality and 4Rs fidelity measurement rubrics developed for the study
description: The study develops three rubrics: an 11-item 3-point rubric scoring coaches' online prompts for specificity and detail in focusing teachers' attention on their interactions and for pushing teachers to reflect and analyze; a 17-item 3-point rubric scoring in-person conferences on balancing guidance with teacher expression, focusing on specific interactions, facilitating teacher-generated strategies, collaborating on actionable next steps, and maintaining a non-judgmental attitude; and a 5-point fidelity rubric with behavioral anchors rating read aloud, Book Talk, and Applied Learning quality.
requirements: Independent observers code videotaped lessons
Coach prompts are scored from the written record on each teacher's website; conferences are scored from audiotaped transcripts
target_learning_goals: Objectively measure quality of coaching implementation and teacher fidelity to the 4Rs curriculum
examples: Prompt quality is scored across 3 prompts in 4 coaching cycles, totaling 12 prompts per teacher
