article_title: Comprehension and Writing Strategy Training Improves Performance on Content-Specific Source-Based Writing Tasks
citation: Weston-Sementelli, J. L., Allen, L. K., & McNamara, D. S. (2016). Comprehension and Writing Strategy Training Improves Performance on Content-Specific Source-Based Writing Tasks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0127-7
title: Content-specific source-based essay task with AP synthesis prompts and modified AP rubric scoring
description: The study's outcome measure was a 40-min content-specific source-based essay task in which writers are provided the sources on which to base their essays. Two prompts from past Advanced Placement English Language and Composition synthesis sections (2011, green living and locavore movement) were counterbalanced within condition. Essays were scored holistically (0 to 9) using a modified version of the AP rubric; the only change was that "credit was given for any direct reference to the source material", since participants received no training on explicit sourcing. Essays referencing fewer than 3 sources cannot score above a 4.
requirements: Participants accessed sources via a webpage and typed essays in Microsoft Word, using a split screen function for simultaneous viewing
constraints: Participants were not explicitly instructed on and did not receive training on how to cite source material
target_learning_goals: source-based writing
synthesis of multiple sources
examples: The green living prompt supplied six sources and the locavore prompt supplied seven sources, including excerpts from news articles, books, graphs, and comics
key_sources: Weston-Sementelli, J. L., Allen, L. K., & McNamara, D. S. (2016). Comprehension and Writing Strategy Training Improves Performance on Content-Specific Source-Based Writing Tasks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0127-7

article_title: Comprehension and Writing Strategy Training Improves Performance on Content-Specific Source-Based Writing Tasks
citation: Weston-Sementelli, J. L., Allen, L. K., & McNamara, D. S. (2016). Comprehension and Writing Strategy Training Improves Performance on Content-Specific Source-Based Writing Tasks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0127-7
title: Combine reading comprehension and writing strategy instruction to improve source-based writing performance
description: Because source-based essay writing relies on proficiency in both reading and writing, the article's central design recommendation is to provide students with a combination of reading comprehension and writing strategy instruction rather than either alone. The experiment found that "participants in the blended strategy training condition produced higher quality source-based essays than participants in the reading comprehension-only, writing-only, or control condition". This principle is grounded directly in the study's headline comparison.
requirements: Instruction must cover both comprehension strategies (e.g., self-explanation) and writing strategies (e.g., planning, evidence selection, conclusion building)
constraints: The finding comes from a single randomized experiment with undergraduate psychology students using two specific intelligent tutoring systems over approximately 3 hours of training
target_learners: developing writers in content area courses
target_learning_goals: source-based writing
reading comprehension
essay composition quality
examples: Participants received blended training via abridged 1-hour versions of both iSTART and Writing Pal, with the order of presentation counterbalanced
key_sources: Weston-Sementelli, J. L., Allen, L. K., & McNamara, D. S. (2016). Comprehension and Writing Strategy Training Improves Performance on Content-Specific Source-Based Writing Tasks. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0127-7

article_title: The Impact of Different Types of Journaling Techniques on EFL Learners' Self-Efficacy (El impacto de diferentes tipos de diario en la autosuficiencia de estudiantes de inglés como lengua extranjera)
citation: Baleghizadeh, S., & Mortazavi, M. (2014). The impact of different types of journaling techniques on EFL learners’ self-efficacy. PROFILE Issues in Teachers’ Professional Development, 16(1), 77-88. https://doi.org/10.15446/profile.v16n1.37184
title: Use collaborative reflective journals with teacher or peer feedback to build EFL learners' self-efficacy
description: The article advises instructors to have learners keep reflective journals documenting strategies, goals, difficulties, and achievements, and to share them with a teacher or peer who adds written feedback every other session. Feedback providers should focus on content rather than language errors, and teacher help should be offered cautiously. The authors state instructors are "advised to make learners aware of the advantages such reflective notes can offer and to promote the use of such reflective techniques in their classes."
requirements: Learners need a briefing session on what to include in reflective notes and how to exchange journals; journals should reach at least ten entries over the term.
constraints: Peer comments should avoid focusing on target language errors and instead attend to content; unsolicited teacher advice can be perceived by students as a signal of low ability.
target_learners: upper-intermediate EFL learners in private language schools
target_learning_goals: general self-efficacy for language learning
strategy use and reflection on learning
examples: TFC learners submitted journals to the teacher every two sessions and received comments and questions; PFC learners exchanged journals with self-chosen partners every two sessions.
key_sources: Baleghizadeh, S., & Mortazavi, M. (2014). The impact of different types of journaling techniques on EFL learners’ self-efficacy. PROFILE Issues in Teachers’ Professional Development, 16(1), 77-88. https://doi.org/10.15446/profile.v16n1.37184

article_title: Linking Learning Styles and Learning on Mobile Facebook
citation: Chen, Y. (2015). Linking Learning Styles and Learning on Mobile Facebook. International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 16(2). https://www.irrodl.org/index.php/irrodl/article/view/1973
title: Provide concrete experiments and problem-solving chances for Accommodating learners and problem-solving opportunities for Converging learners when using mobile Facebook
description: Because Accommodating and Converging learners scored lower on achievement and attitudes in the mobile Facebook environment, the author recommends supplementing it with activities matching their active experimentation orientation. "More concrete experiments and chances to share should be provided for students in the Accommodating groups to improve their learning." Converging learners should also be given chances to solve problems to illustrate target knowledge, and instructors should encourage them to share resources and create multimedia content on mobile devices for upload to mobile Facebook.
requirements: Instructors must design supplementary activities beyond the Facebook discussion format, such as homework problem solving and multimedia content creation
constraints: The recommendation addresses the active experimentation dimension (Accommodating and Converging) specifically, whose learners underperformed in the discussion-based mobile Facebook format the study implemented
target_learners: university students in an Electronic Commerce course
target_learning_goals: course content knowledge, application, and analysis in electronic commerce
examples: The study implemented weekly discussions and problem solving assignments such as marketing students' graduation projects using social networking sites, with course materials uploaded as videos, graphs, and documents
key_sources: Chen, Y. (2015). Linking Learning Styles and Learning on Mobile Facebook. International Review of Research in Open and Distributed Learning, 16(2). https://www.irrodl.org/index.php/irrodl/article/view/1973

article_title: Competitive Team-Based Learning versus Group Investigation with Reference to the Language Proficiency of Iranian EFL Intermediate Students
citation: Hosseini, S. M. H. (2014). Competitive Team-Based Learning versus Group Investigation with Reference to the Language Proficiency of Iranian EFL Intermediate Students. International Journal of Instruction, 7(1).
title: Competitive Team-Based Learning (CTBL)
description: CTBL is the author's holistic, contextualized approach to teaching and learning that "reflects the real world holism" by structuring heterogeneous teams of usually four members who work in a "highly 'competitive motivational dialogic-based learning environment.'" Its evaluation system holds each member individually accountable, rewards teams for outgaining other teams, and recognizes best teams and high-achieving captains. The procedure follows two phases (teaching and assessment), each with five main components, forming a regular activity cycle.
requirements: Heterogeneous teams of usually 4 members
Individual accountability mechanisms including random selection of team representatives
A teams' recognition chart and special rewards for best teams
constraints: The evaluation system is against undifferentiated group grading for teamwork
target_learning_goals: Language proficiency (vocabulary, grammar, reading comprehension, pronunciation)
key_sources: Hosseini, S. M. H. (2014). Competitive Team-Based Learning versus Group Investigation with Reference to the Language Proficiency of Iranian EFL Intermediate Students. International Journal of Instruction, 7(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085235

article_title: Competitive Team-Based Learning versus Group Investigation with Reference to the Language Proficiency of Iranian EFL Intermediate Students
citation: Hosseini, S. M. H. (2014). Competitive Team-Based Learning versus Group Investigation with Reference to the Language Proficiency of Iranian EFL Intermediate Students. International Journal of Instruction, 7(1).
title: Structure cooperative learning around inter-group competition, individual accountability, and full participation
description: The article argues that most cooperative learning methods fail because they disregard "1) inter-group competition, 2) individual accountability, and 3) involvement of all learners in the learning process." CTBL addresses these three factors by making teams compete against each other while holding every member accountable for their own and teammates' learning. The author claims this structure motivated the majority, not just a minority, of students to engage in shared learning.
requirements: Team-based evaluation that rewards both individual improvement and outgaining other teams
Mechanisms ensuring every member has mastered the assigned material
target_learning_goals: Language proficiency
Collaboration and communication skills
examples: In the CTBL class the author would "randomly call upon a student to represent his team," requiring reasons for answers before the class.
key_sources: Hosseini, S. M. H. (2014). Competitive Team-Based Learning versus Group Investigation with Reference to the Language Proficiency of Iranian EFL Intermediate Students. International Journal of Instruction, 7(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085235

article_title: Using Anticipatory Reading Guides to Improve Elementary Students' Comprehension
citation: Ortlieb, E. (2013). Using Anticipatory Reading Guides to Improve Elementary Students' Comprehension. International Journal of Instruction, 6(2), 145-162. https://www.e-iji.net
title: Cognitivist learning theory frames reading skill acquisition as progressing through cognitive, associative, and autonomous stages.
description: The article grounds anticipatory reading guides in cognitivist learning theories influenced by Anderson, Gagne and Briggs, and Schank, holding "that information is received, processed, mapped, and constructed into mental models." Reading skill acquisition follows a progression "beginning with early stages of cognition which progress to an associative stage before finally reaching the autonomous stages of information processing" (Fitts and Peterson, 1964). This framework supports the article's argument that explicit strategy instruction moves struggling readers toward autonomous, transferable comprehension.
requirements: Explicit teaching with application and practice opportunities, since "if application and practice are missing, then comprehension will be affected"
constraints: Framework assumes learners progress through stages; the article notes metacognitive awareness develops over time and varies by student
target_learners: Elementary students, especially those experiencing reading difficulties
target_learning_goals: Development of autonomous reading comprehension and metacognitive strategy use
key_sources: Ortlieb, E. (2013). Using Anticipatory Reading Guides to Improve Elementary Students' Comprehension. International Journal of Instruction, 6(2), 145-162. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085407

article_title: Practitioner Inquiry with Early Program Teacher Candidates
citation: Michele Hollingsworth Koomen. (2016). Practitioner Inquiry with Early Program Teacher Candidates. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i11.1915
title: Cognitive Load Theory as a Framework for Novice Teacher Learning
description: The article applies cognitive load theory to explain why early program teacher candidates struggle to assimilate research-based practices during live teaching. Working memory is overwhelmed by the simultaneous demands of content instruction, student engagement, and diverse learner needs, causing cognitive overload. This overload explains why planned strategies, such as attention getters or equitable questioning, go unused in the moment. The framework links intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load to the development of teaching expertise through schema construction and automaticity.
requirements: Teacher candidates must have opportunities to study their own teaching through video review and structured reflection to identify where overload occurs.
constraints: The framework was applied retrospectively, as data were analyzed after moments of teaching rather than in real time.
target_learning_goals: assimilating theory into practice
developing knowledge of teaching practice
key_sources: Michele Hollingsworth Koomen. (2016). Practitioner Inquiry with Early Program Teacher Candidates. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i11.1915

article_title: Influences of Constructivist-Oriented Nutrition Education on Urban Middle School Students' Nutrition Knowledge, Self-Efficacy, and Behaviors
citation: McCaughtry N, Fahlman M, Martin JJ, Shen B. (2011). Influences of constructivist-oriented nutrition education on urban middle school students' nutrition knowledge, self-efficacy, and behaviors. Am J Health Educ. 2011; 42(5):276-285.
title: Constructivism as a three-component learning theory guiding nutrition education
description: The article uses constructivism as the theoretical framework for both teacher professional development and the student curriculum. It describes three components: "active learning and knowledge construction, over passive, rote memorization"; the interaction of new information with prior knowledge (via Piaget's accommodation and assimilation, Vygotsky's scaffolding, and Rumelhart and Norman's accretion, tuning and restructuring); and learning as a socio-cultural activity in which knowledge is negotiated in groups and transferred to the context where it will be used.
requirements: Lessons must position students as active learners, connect new content with prior knowledge, maximize social interaction, and connect content to students' lives inside school, at home and in the community, as the article's lesson-review criteria state.
target_learners: urban middle school students in health education classes
target_learning_goals: nutrition knowledge
dietary self-efficacy
healthy eating behaviors
examples: The intervention embedded the three components into eight hours of weekend professional development and a six-lesson curriculum including group work, role assignments, food group presentations, a school advertising campaign, home eating analyses, and parent interviews.
key_sources: McCaughtry N, Fahlman M, Martin JJ, Shen B. (2011). Influences of constructivist-oriented nutrition education on urban middle school students' nutrition knowledge, self-efficacy, and behaviors. Am J Health Educ. 2011; 42(5):276-285. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ944012

article_title: Influences of Constructivist-Oriented Nutrition Education on Urban Middle School Students' Nutrition Knowledge, Self-Efficacy, and Behaviors
citation: McCaughtry N, Fahlman M, Martin JJ, Shen B. (2011). Influences of constructivist-oriented nutrition education on urban middle school students' nutrition knowledge, self-efficacy, and behaviors. Am J Health Educ. 2011; 42(5):276-285.
title: Constructivist nutrition curriculum design: six lessons combining active learning, prior knowledge, group work and socio-cultural connections
description: The article's curriculum comprises "six one-hour lessons" covering food groups, analyzing influences on eating, food labels, health claims, body image and fast food restaurants. Lessons "position students as active learners, have them connect the new content with their prior knowledge, encourage students to work in groups and share their work, discuss, and debate with their peers, and connect new content with students' lives outside of schools." Experienced health educators reviewed each lesson against these constructivist criteria.
requirements: Lessons must be reviewed to ensure students are actively learning, that new information connects with prior knowledge, that social interaction is maximized, and that lessons involve students' lives in school, at home and in the community.
target_learners: middle school students in health education
target_learning_goals: nutrition knowledge
healthy eating behaviors
dietary self-efficacy
examples: Lesson one included reflection on eating patterns, role-based group discussion of prior knowledge about food groups, comparison with the food pyramid, class presentations, a school advertising campaign, a home eating analysis, and parent interviews.
key_sources: McCaughtry N, Fahlman M, Martin JJ, Shen B. (2011). Influences of constructivist-oriented nutrition education on urban middle school students' nutrition knowledge, self-efficacy, and behaviors. Am J Health Educ. 2011; 42(5):276-285. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ944012

article_title: Using Convergent and Divergent Tasks to Improve Writing and Language Learning Motivation
citation: Marashi, H., & Tahan-Shizari, P. (2015). Using convergent and divergent tasks to improve writing and language learning motivation. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 3(1), 99-117. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr
title: Use convergent tasks in EFL writing instruction to improve writing performance
description: The article recommends that ELT teachers use convergent tasks — tasks requiring a single agreed outcome through collaborative information exchange — when teaching writing. The authors state that "using convergent tasks is highly recommended to ELT teachers" based on their experimental finding that convergent tasks produced significantly greater writing gains than divergent tasks. They also recommend providing learners with sufficient input and opportunities for active participation alongside convergent task use.
requirements: Tasks must require learners to exchange information and collaborate toward a single agreed outcome, as in the convergent condition where groups "engaged in information exchange" toward one outcome.
constraints: Evidence comes from female intermediate EFL learners aged 18-26 in Iran; the authors caution results "may not necessarily be generalizable to males and learners of other age groups."
target_learning_goals: improve L2 writing performance
examples: In the convergent condition, groups of five learners completed pre-task, while-task, and post-task phases including information gap, decision making, reasoning, and problem solving tasks, writing collaboratively toward a single outcome.
key_sources: Marashi, H., & Tahan-Shizari, P. (2015). Using convergent and divergent tasks to improve writing and language learning motivation. Iranian Journal of Language Teaching Research, 3(1), 99-117. https://www.urmia.ac.ir/ijltr

article_title: The Relationship Between Holistic Humanistic Caring Perception, Thriving at Work and Clinical Nursing Competency Among Newly Graduated Nurses: A Mediation Study With Latent Profile Analysis.
citation: Zhang Yuping, Wang Guimei, Hou Weihua, Shi Dandan, Yin Xiaobing. (2026). The Relationship Between Holistic Humanistic Caring Perception, Thriving at Work and Clinical Nursing Competency Among Newly Graduated Nurses: A Mediation Study With Latent Profile Analysis. title: Conservation of resources theory frames caring perception as resources supporting newly graduated nurses' adaptation
description: The article uses conservation of resources theory as its explanatory framework, proposing that "individuals strive to obtain, retain, foster and protect resources they value" and that "individuals with greater resources are better positioned to acquire additional resources." Caring perceived across personal, work and nonwork contexts is conceptualised as resources available to newly graduated nurses, which may support learning, vitality and ultimately clinical nursing competency development.
requirements: Caring must be perceived across multiple contexts (personal, work-related, nonwork social) to function as a resource pool
constraints: The theory is applied as an interpretive framework for cross-sectional associations, not as a tested causal mechanism
target_learning_goals: professional adaptation and clinical competency development
examples: Self-care was conceptualised as a resource from the personal domain; caring from hospital management, the department and patients as work-related resources; and caring from family and friends as nonwork social resources.
key_sources: Zhang Yuping, Wang Guimei, Hou Weihua, Shi Dandan, Yin Xiaobing. (2026). article_title: Enhancing Obstetric Emergency Management Through Simulation-Based Training: A Focus on Shoulder Dystocia.
citation: Toumi Dhekra, Bergaoui Haifa, Ben Farhat Imen, Ghaddab Imen, Aribi Ikram, Gharbi Nedra, Hajji Ahmed, Zouari Ines, Zoukar Olfa, Faleh Raja. (2025). title: Combine high-fidelity and low-fidelity mannequins with structured three-phase debriefings in simulation training programs
description: The article's training program combined a high-fidelity SimMOM mannequin with supplementary low-fidelity mannequin practice, with each session followed by a structured debriefing in three phases: "descriptive, analytical, and synthetic, aimed at optimizing learning outcomes". Low-fidelity training reinforced essential concepts in a less complex environment. This combination is presented as the design behind the observed knowledge gains and satisfaction.
requirements: A supervisory team with specialized roles (mannequin operator, technical assistant, facilitator midwife, medical support, evaluator)
Cameras to record sessions for post-simulation debriefing
A dedicated debriefing room
constraints: The article notes obstetric simulation presents challenges such as financial costs and the need for adequate expertise among trainers
target_learning_goals: Management of shoulder dystocia
Technical obstetric maneuvers
Team communication and coordination
examples: Three monthly simulation sessions at the Cesim simulation center during the 2021-2022 academic year, with six residents in high-fidelity scenarios and the remainder practicing on low-fidelity mannequins after debriefing and theoretical review

title: Construct visibility: assessment systems privilege readily observable competencies
description: The review proposes that assessment systems do not merely measure competence but also make particular forms of competence visible within educational practice. "Assessment systems inevitably privilege those aspects of competence that can be most readily specified, observed and measured", so visibility within assessment frameworks may not correspond to educational importance. Behavioural competencies are more readily represented because they are directly observable, whereas integrative competencies involve synthesis, contextual interpretation and clinical judgement that are less immediately visible.

constraints: Interpretations are constrained by the level of detail reported by study authors; integrative competence may have been addressed but not explicitly described in publications

citation: Cary Tawnya L., Hong Seung M., Kowalkowski Anna, Harris Michelle A. (2026). title: Conclusion Assessment Rubric (CAR)
description: The CAR is a five-component rubric for evaluating undergraduate biology students' ability to generate evidence-based conclusions from experimental data. Its five key components are: (1) articulates a connection between data analysis and claims about hypothesis/predictions/research question(s) and addresses whether differences/relationships within data are biologically meaningful; (2) formulates an argument that positions findings within the proposed biological rationale model and existing literature; (3) evaluates how experimental design influences reliability of data; (4) places study findings within an appropriate scope such that broader implications are generalized to an appropriate level; and (5) proposes future studies. Each component is scored across five performance levels (0 = not addressed to 4 = excellent).
requirements: Applied to written research papers (lab reports or thesis papers) resulting from research experiences
Evaluator must have a solid understanding of the student's work before applying the CAR to the Discussion section
Assessors should be trained (calibrated/normed) using sample student papers before independent rating
constraints: Designed for written artifacts; reviewers informed that using the rubric on non-lab report artifacts (e.g., posters) required modification
Time commitment necessary to review all previous sections of the paper before applying the CAR to the conclusions section
Disciplinary expertise of the assessor and familiarity with the students' research affected inter-rater reliability
target_learning_goals: generating evidence-based conclusions from experimental data
making context-driven claims with appropriate scope
scientific argumentation

article_title: Improving emergency management of status epilepticus: a randomized high-fidelity simulator-based trial.
citation: Kliem Paulina S. C., Tisljar Kai, Baumann Sira M., Grzonka Pascale, De Marchis Gian Marco, Bassetti Stefano, Bingisser Roland, Hunziker Sabina, Marsch Stephan, Sutter Raoul. (2026). Improving emergency management of status epilepticus: a randomized high-fidelity simulator-based trial. Journal of Neurology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00415-026-14058-8
title: Condense complex clinical guidelines into single-page formats with symbols to improve adherence in time-critical emergencies
description: The article supports condensing complex treatment guidelines into a single-page format incorporating symbolic representations designed to facilitate rapid information assimilation and evaluation. In a randomized simulator-based trial, this format improved adherence to key emergency interventions compared to both full guidelines and no guidelines. Guideline usability represents a modifiable target for improving management of time-critical neurological emergencies.
requirements: Guidelines must summarize pivotal recommendations of the original full guideline
Symbolic representations should facilitate rapid information assimilation and evaluation
constraints: Improvements were limited to selected interventions (side positioning and second-line ASD administration), not all aspects of management
Results need confirmation in real-life clinical settings
target_learners: resident physicians in intensive care, emergency medicine, internal medicine, and neurology
target_learning_goals: adherence to guideline-recommended emergency interventions for status epilepticus
examples: Physicians provided with a condensed single-page guideline summarizing pivotal NCS recommendations with symbolic representations showed higher adherence to key interventions in a simulated SE scenario
key_sources: Kliem Paulina S. C., Tisljar Kai, Baumann Sira M., Grzonka Pascale, De Marchis Gian Marco, Bassetti Stefano, Bingisser Roland, Hunziker Sabina, Marsch Stephan, Sutter Raoul. (2026). Improving emergency management of status epilepticus: a randomized high-fidelity simulator-based trial. Journal of Neurology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00415-026-14058-8

article_title: Practice and application of blended teaching based on RG-UClass in a preventive medicine course.
citation: Liu Sha, Zhang Jiale, Shang Yuqi, Jiang Yufei, Zhang Xueyan, Hu Zhiyong, Chen Caiyun, Mi Wei. (2026). Practice and application of blended teaching based on RG-UClass in a preventive medicine course. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1885005
title: Match instructional delivery mode to content type: online for theoretical knowledge, offline for practical knowledge
description: The article recommends selecting online and offline teaching methods according to the characteristics of chapter content. Theoretical knowledge-based content is delivered through the platform's online live-streaming mode, while offline classroom lecture mode is used for practical knowledge-based content "that require students to understand through face-to-face interactive discussions, case studies, and demonstrations of methodological processes," facilitating more intuitive understanding and intensive learning.
requirements: A platform capable of live-streaming lectures and retaining learning results online
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of theoretical content
methodological skill acquisition through interactive demonstration
examples: Introduction, clinical preventive services, rational nutrition, and chronic disease management were taught online; cohort studies, case-control studies, and screening experiments were taught offline
key_sources: Liu Sha, Zhang Jiale, Shang Yuqi, Jiang Yufei, Zhang Xueyan, Hu Zhiyong, Chen Caiyun, Mi Wei. (2026). Practice and application of blended teaching based on RG-UClass in a preventive medicine course. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1885005

article_title: Resident autonomy in orthopedic trauma: independent femoral IMN by senior residents yields comparable outcomes to fellowship-trained surgeons.
citation: Balziano Snir, Nesher Gilad, Ben Nun Nitzan, Segev Tomer, Freidlander Alon, Prat Dan. (2026). Resident autonomy in orthopedic trauma: independent femoral IMN by senior residents yields comparable outcomes to fellowship-trained surgeons. Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00402-026-06460-8
title: Grant surgical autonomy based on demonstrated competency rather than seniority alone
description: The article advocates that operative independence should be granted when residents have demonstrated competency through structured assessments and training milestones, rather than automatically at a certain postgraduate year. The study found that "appropriately trained residents can perform IMN safely and effectively in selected cases" when autonomy is embedded in a structured framework with preoperative review, eligibility criteria, and ongoing quality feedback. This supports competency-based progression as a design principle for surgical education programs balancing training with patient safety.
requirements: Successful completion of national-level exams (PGY 1–3)
Consistent intraoperative evaluations
A dedicated surgical principles course
Preoperative case and plan review with an attending
Postoperative performance review in departmental feedback sessions
constraints: Evidence derives from a single-center retrospective cohort at a level I trauma center with a well-established residency program, which may limit generalizability to other training environments
target_learning_goals: independent performance of complex trauma procedures (femoral intramedullary nailing)
operative decision-making and technical competency in surgical training
examples: The six-year residency program allowed independent operating from PGY-4 onward under a structured autonomy protocol with attending availability on call
key_sources: Balziano Snir, Nesher Gilad, Ben Nun Nitzan, Segev Tomer, Freidlander Alon, Prat Dan. (2026). Resident autonomy in orthopedic trauma: independent femoral IMN by senior residents yields comparable outcomes to fellowship-trained surgeons. Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00402-026-06460-8

article_title: Evaluation of a peer-assisted, simulation-based clinical skills training program in Spain: a prospective single-group before-and-after study.
citation: López-Brotons Maria, Javaloy-Ballestero Sergio, Ramos-Rincón José-Manuel. (2026). Evaluation of a peer-assisted, simulation-based clinical skills training program in Spain: a prospective single-group before-and-after study. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.15
title: Combine clinical simulation with peer-assisted learning to expand practical training while optimizing educational resources
description: The article's program pairs simulation-based skills training with near-peer tutoring, in which "senior students facilitate the learning of junior students, promoting active engagement and collaborative learning." The authors state this combination "offers a valuable opportunity to expand practical training while optimizing available educational resources," especially where faculty availability is limited. Workshops used small groups of 5 students led by trained senior tutors under faculty supervision.
requirements: Tutors selected based on academic performance, prior experience, and motivation, and received structured training covering content, teaching procedures, and learning objectives
constraints: The study lacked a control group, so causal interpretation is limited; findings reflect perceived rather than actual effectiveness
target_learners: second- and third-year undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: clinical skills including physical examination and basic procedures
examples: Six workshops were delivered in 2023–2024 and 8 in 2024–2025, each approximately 60 minutes following a standardized sequence of brief introduction, demonstration, supervised practice, and feedback
key_sources: López-Brotons Maria, Javaloy-Ballestero Sergio, Ramos-Rincón José-Manuel. (2026). Evaluation of a peer-assisted, simulation-based clinical skills training program in Spain: a prospective single-group before-and-after study. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.15

article_title: Application of retrospective teaching method in stomatology undergraduate education.
citation: Gao Jie, Zhang Haolin, Qin Wen, Liu Xin. (2026). Application of retrospective teaching method in stomatology undergraduate education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09665-y
title: Constructivist learning theory as an explanation for CBL effectiveness
description: The article invokes constructivist learning theory to explain why CBL may be effective. The article states "Consistent with constructivist learning theory, embedding knowledge within clinical contexts may shift learning from passive reception toward active cognitive processing." These features may enhance the organization of knowledge structures, improve contextual understanding, and increase perceived relevance of learning materials.
requirements: Embedding knowledge within clinical contexts.
target_learning_goals: Conceptual integration
Learning motivation and self-directed learning behaviors
key_sources: Gao Jie, Zhang Haolin, Qin Wen, Liu Xin. (2026). Application of retrospective teaching method in stomatology undergraduate education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09665-y

article_title: Mind the Gap: Rethinking Procedural Skill Assessment in Medical Residency.
citation: Meliagros Pete MD, Garber Adam MD, Ambrosio Matthew MS, Kang Le PhD, Forrest Rebecca MD. (2026). Mind the Gap: Rethinking Procedural Skill Assessment in Medical Residency. Southern Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.14423/SMJ.0000000000001992
title: Combine checklists and GRSs with self-evaluation coaching and timely feedback for comprehensive procedural assessment
description: The article recommends that "the combined use of comprehensive performance checklists and GRSs, coupled with deliberate self-evaluation coaching and timely feedback, provides a more comprehensive and precise evaluation of procedural performance." Checklists capture discrete steps while GRSs capture procedural cadence and clinical judgment. This combination is positioned as superior to minimum procedure volume thresholds alone.
requirements: Faculty must be educated in proper use of assessment tools to ensure validity and reliability
constraints: Interrater variability was not formally assessed; results based solely on a 2-week MPS rotation without long-term performance effects
target_learning_goals: Procedural competence in bedside procedures
examples: Hospitalists on the MPS reviewed residents' checklists and GRS self-assessments immediately postprocedure and provided feedback using the same GRS
key_sources: Meliagros Pete MD, Garber Adam MD, Ambrosio Matthew MS, Kang Le PhD, Forrest Rebecca MD. (2026). Mind the Gap: Rethinking Procedural Skill Assessment in Medical Residency. Southern Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.14423/SMJ.0000000000001992

article_title: Registered Dietitians' Knowledge, Attitudes and Use of Simulation-Based Education in Ireland: A Mixed-Methods Study.
citation: A. Power, C. Lee, C. Corish, and A. Shaw. (2026). Registered Dietitians' Knowledge, Attitudes and Use of Simulation‐Based Education in Ireland: A Mixed‐Methods Study. Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics. https://doi.org/10.1111/jhn.70326
title: COM-B model as a framework for explaining dietitians' underuse of SBE
description: The Capability, Opportunity, Motivation–Behaviour (COM-B) model is the study's organising framework: "Capability includes knowledge and skills to design and facilitate simulation; opportunity encompasses environmental and organisational factors such as time, space, resources and institutional support; and motivation reflects beliefs, attitudes and professional identity." The article applies it as a common analytic lens for the interview schedule, thematic coding, and integration of quantitative and qualitative findings. It explains why enthusiasm for SBE does not necessarily result in widespread implementation.
requirements: Capability and opportunity must be present alongside motivation for the behaviour (SBE use) to occur
target_learning_goals: use of simulation-based education in pre-registration dietetic training
examples: The interview guide was organised around the COM-B domains of capability, opportunity and motivation, and transcripts were coded deductively to those domains
key_sources: A. Power, C. Lee, C. Corish, and A. Shaw. (2026). Registered Dietitians' Knowledge, Attitudes and Use of Simulation‐Based Education in Ireland: A Mixed‐Methods Study. Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics. https://doi.org/10.1111/jhn.70326

article_title: The Frankfurt 'whisper exam' - a case-based collaborative summative examination to assess clinical decision-making skills in hygiene, microbiology and virology- feasibility and evaluation.
citation: Vorbeck L, Ruesseler M, Steinmetzer J, Kohmer N, Kempf VAJ, Brandt C. (2026). The Frankfurt ‘whisper exam’ - a case-based collaborative summative examination to assess clinical decision-making skills in hygiene, microbiology and virology– feasibility and evaluation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10018-y
title: Constructive alignment as the design rationale linking learning objectives, case-based teaching, and collaborative assessment
description: The article applies the principle of constructive alignment to justify the whisper exam design: the curricular learning objectives, teaching methods and assessment format are aligned so that “assessments validly reflect students’ achievement of these objectives”. The assessed learning objectives covered clinical topics in medical microbiology, virology, and infection control, “all of which had been covered in the preceding laboratory course mostly in a case-based format”. The authors state instructors are expected to clearly communicate learning objectives and align teaching methods accordingly.
requirements: Clearly communicated learning objectives
Teaching methods aligned to those objectives
Assessment format that validly reflects achievement of the objectives
constraints: The alignment depends on the preceding laboratory course having covered the assessed objectives in a case-based format
target_learning_goals: Clinical reasoning and diagnostic decision-making in infectious disease topics
key_sources: Vorbeck L, Ruesseler M, Steinmetzer J, Kohmer N, Kempf VAJ, Brandt C. (2026). The Frankfurt ‘whisper exam’ - a case-based collaborative summative examination to assess clinical decision-making skills in hygiene, microbiology and virology– feasibility and evaluation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10018-y

article_title: Integrating problem-based learning with virtual simulation in trauma orthopedic education: effects on learning outcomes and student satisfaction.
citation: Xue Gang, Zhang Xin, Ji Shengyi, Qi Jin. (2026). Integrating problem-based learning with virtual simulation in trauma orthopedic education: effects on learning outcomes and student satisfaction. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09558-0
title: Complementary educational advantages framework: PBL strengthens problem awareness and clinical reasoning while virtual simulation enhances intuitiveness, interactivity, and operability
description: The article proposes that PBL and virtual simulation offer complementary educational advantages when combined. PBL "provides a problem-oriented framework that encourages students to identify learning needs, actively seek relevant information, analyze clinical scenarios, and generate potential solutions", while virtual simulation "provides a visual, interactive, and operational environment in which students can apply their judgments and rehearse procedural strategies in a safe and controllable setting". The article states that virtual simulation "appears to enhance the intuitiveness, interactivity, and operability of teaching, whereas PBL may strengthen problem awareness, self-directed learning, and collaborative engagement".
requirements: Requires both approaches to be integrated rather than used separately, as the article states a single teaching method may be insufficient to meet the dual learning needs of trauma orthopedic education
constraints: The article notes this interpretation is the authors' pedagogical perspective and that the two-arm design could not distinguish the independent effects of PBL alone, virtual simulation alone, or their potential synergistic interaction
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
spatial understanding
practical skills
self-directed learning
key_sources: Xue Gang, Zhang Xin, Ji Shengyi, Qi Jin. (2026). Integrating problem-based learning with virtual simulation in trauma orthopedic education: effects on learning outcomes and student satisfaction. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09558-0

article_title: Integrated Team-Based Learning in a UK Undergraduate Medical Programme.
citation: Drovandi Aaron, Sheader Elizabeth, Kingston Margaret. (2026). Integrated Team-Based Learning in a UK Undergraduate Medical Programme. The Clinical Teacher. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70470
title: Integrated TBL should be considered by other medical programmes where increasing student numbers may affect the quality of PBL teaching.
description: The article concludes that TBL represents a potentially effective and efficient method for teaching undergraduate medical students on a large scale and should be considered by other medical programmes where increasing student numbers may affect the quality of PBL teaching. This principle is grounded in the study's findings of positive student and staff perceptions, mixed assessment results by assessment type, and greater financial viability of TBL compared with PBL through reduced staff time requirements despite initial cost outlays.
requirements: Requires a large learning community of 8–10 teams per room, four TBL rooms active simultaneously, each facilitated by three academics and digitally interconnected by a central coordinator who manages the timing of activities.
constraints: This study was conducted at a singular UK medical school reducing confidence in the generalisability of findings outside of this setting.
Assessment analyses had mixed results, with TBL students performing worse in semester tests, though better in progress tests.
target_learning_goals: Core medical science knowledge and clinical application through weekly integrated themes
examples: The University of Manchester MBChB commenced integrated TBL for the 2023/2024 academic year, enrolling approximately 450 Year 1 students annually, with closing sessions involving students working in teams of six, in a larger learning community of 8–10 teams per room.
key_sources: Drovandi Aaron, Sheader Elizabeth, Kingston Margaret. (2026). Integrated Team-Based Learning in a UK Undergraduate Medical Programme. The Clinical Teacher. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70470

article_title: The construction and implementation of a clinical nursing experts-oriented retraining program for peritoneal dialysis specialist nurses.
citation: He Peipei, Yin Xiaohong, Xu Ying, Yang Tingjun. (2026). The construction and implementation of a clinical nursing experts-oriented retraining program for peritoneal dialysis specialist nurses. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09379-1
title: The competency iceberg model distinguishes visible components (knowledge and skills) from hidden components (personal traits, motivation, social roles, and self-concept).
description: According to the competency iceberg model, professional competencies consist of "visible" elements above the surface and "hidden" elements beneath it. The visible components include knowledge and skills, which can often be improved relatively quickly through structured training. The hidden components include personal traits, motivation, social roles, and self-concept, which are more difficult to modify but exert a substantial influence on job performance. The retraining program was designed to cultivate clinical nursing experts by emphasizing both practical competencies and intrinsic professional qualities.
requirements: Structured training can improve visible components relatively quickly, but fostering deeper hidden attributes among peritoneal dialysis SNs is particularly important.
constraints: The hidden components are more difficult to modify than the visible ones.
target_learning_goals: professional competencies including knowledge, skills, personal traits, motivation, social roles, and self-concept
key_sources: He Peipei, Yin Xiaohong, Xu Ying, Yang Tingjun. (2026). The construction and implementation of a clinical nursing experts-oriented retraining program for peritoneal dialysis specialist nurses. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09379-1

article_title: Effective Educational Programs for Disaster Preparedness and Management: A Rapid Evidence Assessment.
citation: Delbene Lara, Mezini Sara, Cacciabue Camilla, Watson Roger, Aleo Giuseppe, Di Nitto Marco, Zanini Milko, Catania Gianluca, Sasso Loredana, Bagnasco Annamaria. (2026). Effective Educational Programs for Disaster Preparedness and Management: A Rapid Evidence Assessment. International Nursing Review. https://doi.org/10.1111/inr.70193
title: Competency-based framework for disaster nursing education built on the disaster cycle
description: The review proposes a "comprehensive educational framework that promotes innovative and targeted training approaches for more effective disaster preparedness in nursing practice." It builds on the International Council of Nurses and WHO Core Competencies in Disaster Nursing (Version 2.0), which translates "the disaster cycle into a structured, competency‐based reference articulated through progressive levels of nursing practice and operational domains including communication, incident management, safety, ethical practice, and recovery." The framework organizes educational programs around the disaster cycle phases and competency domains, with progressive levels of nursing practice.
requirements: Alignment with the WHO operational framework covering prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery
Standardized key competencies at the national level
constraints: The review notes that disaster preparedness levels among nurses remain variable and often suboptimal, particularly in high-risk regions
target_learning_goals: disaster cycle competencies
communication
incident management
safety
ethical practice
recovery
examples: The Jennings Disaster Nursing Management Model organizes training around pre-disaster, during disaster, post-disaster, and recovery phases
Scott et al. built a curriculum around 9 learning objectives, 18 competencies across 5 competency domains, and 34 performance objectives
key_sources: Delbene Lara, Mezini Sara, Cacciabue Camilla, Watson Roger, Aleo Giuseppe, Di Nitto Marco, Zanini Milko, Catania Gianluca, Sasso Loredana, Bagnasco Annamaria. (2026). Effective Educational Programs for Disaster Preparedness and Management: A Rapid Evidence Assessment. International Nursing Review. https://doi.org/10.1111/inr.70193

article_title: Real-time interaction with artificial intelligence and its association with learning experience and academic performance among undergraduate nursing students in Peshawar: an analytical cross-sectional study.
citation: Zakir Husain, Ebrahimi Hamideh, Khan Abdullah, Ullah Ikram, Ullah Barkat. (2026). Real-time interaction with artificial intelligence and its association with learning experience and academic performance among undergraduate nursing students in Peshawar: an analytical cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09229-0
title: Conceptual framework linking real-time AI interaction to learning experience and academic performance, informed by constructivist and self-directed learning theory
description: The article proposes a conceptual framework in which greater engagement with AI tools enhances students' learning experiences, which subsequently contribute to improved academic performance. Learning experience is conceptualized as a mediating variable. The framework is guided by "constructivist learning theory and self-directed learning theory, both of which emphasize the active role of learners in constructing knowledge". Real-time interaction with AI represents the interactive learning environment, learning experience reflects internal learning processes including engagement, understanding, and self-regulation, and academic performance represents the resulting learning outcomes.
requirements: Students with prior exposure to AI tools
Real-time interaction capabilities with AI tools
constraints: The mediating role of learning experience was not empirically tested; future studies are encouraged to apply mediation analysis or structural equation modeling
target_learning_goals: Knowledge construction through interaction
Self-regulated learning
Academic performance

article_title: AI-powered simulated patients with automated feedback for enhancing headache history-taking skills: a convergent mixed-methods study.
citation: Kridipaka S, Ruengwattanachot K, Leksuwankun S, Pongpitakmetha T, Hiransuthikul A, Surawattanawong T, Anukoolwittaya P, Panjasriprakarn P. (2026). AI-powered simulated patients with automated feedback for enhancing headache history-taking skills: a convergent mixed-methods study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09511-1
title: Cortex: a GPT-4o-powered AI simulated patient chatbot with dual-prompt architecture and automated rubric-based feedback
description: Cortex is a custom-built, voice-enabled web application for history-taking practice powered by GPT-4o with a dual-prompt architecture: one prompt constrains patient simulation to a predefined script to reduce hallucination risk, and a second drives an automated evaluation module generating rubric-based feedback after each session. Students selected one of three headache cases (migraine, tension-type, cluster) developed per ICHD-3 and reviewed by three board-certified neurologists, interacted via voice or text, then recorded a diagnostic impression and received feedback including comparison with the reference diagnosis.
requirements: Students need access to the web application with voice or text input
Cases must be clinically validated scripts per ICHD-3
constraints: Only three simulated headache scenarios were included
The chatbot responds only to user-initiated questions constrained by the script
target_learning_goals: Headache history-taking
Clinical reasoning and differential diagnosis
examples: Students completed a median of 11 chatbot sessions (IQR 9-14) over one week, with a cohort total of 44.1 hours of use

AI-powered simulated patients with automated feedback for enhancing headache history-taking skills: a convergent mixed-methods study. article_title: Teaching persuasive essay writing online to first-year undergraduates: A phenomenological study of instructional design and learning experiences.
citation: Karim, K. A., Al Mamun, M. A., Sultana, S., & Kabilan, M. K. (2026). Teaching persuasive essay writing online to first-year undergraduates: A phenomenological study of instructional design and learning experiences. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0353171
title: Collective working memory as a CLT-based rationale for collaborative writing
description: The article draws on Kirschner et al.'s concept that "effective collaborative learning involves a collective working memory that otherwise remains inactive." Through communication and coordination, group members create a shared cognitive space where they draw on one another's knowledge, clarify uncertainties, and jointly address writing challenges. This distributes processing demands and reduces extraneous cognitive load arising from confusion or fragmented understanding.
requirements: Group members who communicate and coordinate effectively
constraints: Presented as a theoretical interpretation rather than an empirically tested mechanism in this study
target_learners: Higher education students in collaborative writing tasks
target_learning_goals: Managing cognitive load during complex writing tasks

citation: Alrashed Fahad Abdulaziz, Ahmad Tauseef, Alangari Saad M., Albabtain Mohammed A., Aldughaither Abdullah S., Alrashed Rashed, Alsabih Ahmed Othman, Abdulghani Hamza M. (2026). title: Constructivist learning theory and student engagement theory explain the relationship between engagement and perceived CBL benefits
description: The article frames the engagement–benefit relationship through constructivist learning theory, which "posits that knowledge is actively constructed through meaningful interaction with learning materials rather than passively received." Social learning theory emphasizes interaction and collaboration, while student engagement theory suggests that behaviorally, cognitively, and emotionally engaged students invest more effort and perceive greater educational benefits.
requirements: Active participation in group discussions and collaborative problem-solving
target_learning_goals: Critical thinking
Clinical reasoning
Collaborative skills
examples: CBL sessions at King Saud University require students to prepare in advance and participate in faculty-facilitated group discussions of clinical cases.

article_title: The effect of web-based learning with peer-facilitated discussion on nursing students' knowledge and practices in work-related biological exposure: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Chen Lulin, Liang Danyan, Zhu Yuhuan, Huang Weihong, Li Chenglin, Liang Xiong, Liang Yutao, Lu Yunyun, Gan Yongjiang, Zhong Yao. (2026). The effect of web-based learning with peer-facilitated discussion on nursing students’ knowledge and practices in work-related biological exposure: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09333-1
title: Combine web-based learning with peer-facilitated discussion for occupational safety training
description: The article supports combining standardized web-based learning content with peer-facilitated group discussion for training on work-related biological exposure. The web component ensures content accuracy and consistency while peer facilitators organize 15-minute sessions to share experiences, guide protection concepts, and answer questions. The authors report this combination improved knowledge, behaviors, exposure rates, and reporting compliance compared to lectures alone.
requirements: Peer facilitators selected for voluntary participation, good leadership and interpersonal communication skills, and care for group members
A web-based platform with content similar to traditional lecture material
Training limited to one hour
constraints: Cannot isolate whether observed changes are attributable to peer teaching, web-based learning, or their combination
Baseline knowledge was not collected
Groups differed by internship start year, introducing potential cohort confounds
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of work-related biological exposure prevention and control
Safe clinical behaviors around sharps and biological hazards
Compliance with exposure reporting requirements
examples: Experimental group used the 'Infection Control Workspace' platform followed by 15-minute peer-facilitated group sessions; control group received a 45-minute PowerPoint lecture with 15 minutes of teacher-centered discussion.

article_title: The impact of interactive digital tools on genetics education: a field study across large and small learning groups.
citation: Barrio Eva, Solanas Estela, Alcaine Clara, Emperador Sonia, Ayensa-Jimenez Jacobo, Mena Andrés, Ciriza Jesús. (2026). The impact of interactive digital tools on genetics education: a field study across large and small learning groups. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09168-w
title: Pair normal and pathological cases and give immediate explanatory feedback in digital diagnostic-training tools
description: The article concludes that presenting normal karyotypes alongside pathological ones, plus clear contextual explanations after incorrect anomaly identification, helps students consolidate understanding autonomously. It states these results "highlight the importance of immediate, targeted feedback in digital learning environments", calling this "a fundamental component of effective educational tool design". This suits tools teaching visual diagnostic skills where instructor time is scarce.
requirements: Inclusion of both normal and abnormal example cases
Explanatory content shown when students fail to identify an anomaly correctly
constraints: Evidence is self-reported perception from a single pre–post study without a control group
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in large-enrollment courses
target_learning_goals: identifying chromosomal abnormalities
interpreting karyograms
examples: The tool showed explanations after incorrect anomaly identification, rated very useful by 59.81% of Zaragoza students

The impact of interactive digital tools on genetics education: a field study across large and small learning groups. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09168-w

citation: Dang Hai Nguyen Ngoc, Luong Thang Viet, Vo Hoa Thi Ha, Nguyen Linh Thi Khanh, Tran Trung Nguyen, Pham Hong Thi Anh, Truong Huong Thanh, Tran Hoa, Tran Toan Thanh, Hoang Tien Anh, Doan Thang Chi, Huynh Quan, Marwick Thomas H. title: Conventional standardized patient (SP) program
description: The control condition used conventional standardized patients recruited from recovered patients or healthy volunteers. All SPs "underwent formal training and rehearsal sessions to ensure consistent performance" and were compensated for their time. Instructors reviewed and verified each SP's role before each class to maintain simulation integrity.
requirements: Each SP was thoroughly trained on the assigned clinical scenario, including the presenting symptoms, emotional tone, and expected responses.
constraints: Training SP requires significant time and manpower, and maintaining these programs incurs ongoing financial and logistical costs.
target_learning_goals: history-taking skills
examples: SPs were recruited from adults who had previously recovered from the illnesses or from healthy volunteers.

article_title: The association between adolescents' recreational screen exposure and academic performance and its mediating mechanisms.
citation: Zhao Jianping; Zhao Jianyi. (2026). The association between adolescents' recreational screen exposure and academic performance and its mediating mechanisms. Frontiers in Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1840524
title: Cognitive load and self-regulation theories as framework for screen exposure effects on learning
description: The study grounds its mediation model in cognitive load theory and self-regulation theory. Cognitive load theory posits that "excessive screen exposure introduces fragmented information input, which occupies adolescents limited cognitive resources, increases extraneous cognitive load, reduces the efficiency of deep information processing." Self-regulation theory suggests excessive screen use diminishes self-control, weakens delay of gratification, encroaches on sleep, and disrupts mental health, reducing learning engagement. Together they structure the "total recreational screen exposure → sleep/mental health/cognition → academic performance" model.
requirements: Mediating variables selected must have strong theoretical support to avoid model overloading
constraints: Framework tested only in a cross-sectional Chinese adolescent subsample; causal ordering not established
target_learners: Chinese junior high school students aged 12–15
target_learning_goals: Academic performance in Chinese, mathematics, and English

article_title: Enhancing musculoskeletal examination skills through near-peer teaching: student outcomes and perspectives.
citation: Qian Kevin, Malau-Aduli Bunmi, Sundaraj Keran. (2026). Enhancing musculoskeletal examination skills through near-peer teaching: student outcomes and perspectives. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09235-2
title: Cognitive and social congruence framework explains near-peer teaching effectiveness
description: The article uses cognitive and social congruence as theoretical frameworks to explain why near-peer teaching works. "Cognitive congruence refers to the tutor’s ability to pitch teaching at an appropriate level due to their recent experience of learning the same material". "Social congruence reflects the rapport and trust that develops between peers, reducing anxiety and encouraging honest disclosure of uncertainties". Together these create a safe, motivating environment that enhances satisfaction, confidence, and performance.
requirements: A tutor who is at least one year senior to the learner and has recent experience learning the same material
constraints: Near-peer facilitators have less depth of knowledge than faculty and may provide incomplete information without adequate preparation
target_learning_goals: clinical examination skills
musculoskeletal examination competence
examples: The authors attribute large post-test gains in palpation and range-of-motion tasks to peer tutors presenting concepts at an accessible level, likely reducing cognitive load

citation: Li, Yan, Chen, Yu, Xu, Wenji, Sun, Jie, Du, Shizheng. (2026). "More Than My Own Effort": A Qualitative Study of Factors Influencing EBP Competence Among Traditional Chinese Medicine Specialist Nurses. Journal of Nursing Management. https://doi.org/10.1155/jonm/8658721
title: COM-B model as an interpretive framework for EBP competence development and enactment
description: The Capability, Opportunity, Motivation, and Behavior (COM-B) model conceptualizes behavior as arising from the interaction of capability, opportunity, and motivation. In this study it served as a sensitizing and interpretive framework: initial coding was inductive, and themes were subsequently mapped onto capability-related factors, opportunity-related factors, motivation-related factors, and behavioral enactment of EBP competence in practice. The article states the model "allows attention to individual capability, external opportunity, and motivational influences on practice."
requirements: Used at the interpretive stage rather than as a rigid a priori coding structure, per the article's rigor procedures
constraints: The article notes implementation frameworks such as CFIR are better suited to organizational determinants, while COM-B was chosen for competence development and enactment
target_learners: registered nurses in post-registration specialist training
target_learning_goals: evidence-based practice competence
evidence-based nursing uptake
examples: The study's four thematic domains were interpreted in relation to COM-B, with behavioral enactment presented as the practical expression of competence in practice (Figure 1)

title: Design screen-based simulation videos with cognitive load theory–informed features: short single-skill videos, standardized checklists, and consistent delivery
description: The article designed its intervention "with cognitive load theory–informed considerations to minimize extraneous demands and support learning efficiency": videos were kept short (approximately 10-12 min) and focused on a single skill topic, procedural steps were standardized with checklists, and the platform was consistent across groups. The authors report these as design features rather than demonstrated mechanisms because cognitive load was not directly measured.
requirements: Videos kept short (approximately 10-12 min) and focused on a single skill topic
Step-by-step procedural checklists reinforced during instructor-guided discussion
Consistent learning environment and delivery platform across conditions
constraints: Cognitive load was not directly measured; unmeasured cognitive load, attention, or fatigue may have influenced EEG indices and learning outcomes
target_learning_goals: procedural skill learning with reduced extraneous load
examples: Both conditions used the same module structure: brief orientation, 10-12 min video viewing, and a 20-minute instructor-facilitated discussion

article_title: Structured phantom-assisted simulation for early abdominal ultrasound skill training in ultrasound medicine residents: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Wei Tianhong, Ke Mujing, Zhang Bo, He Zhiyou, Xie Xiuyun. (2026). Structured phantom-assisted simulation for early abdominal ultrasound skill training in ultrasound medicine residents: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09395-1
title: Cognitive Load Theory as an explanatory account of why phantom-based simulation supports early ultrasound skill acquisition
description: The authors interpret the observed performance gains through "the lens of Cognitive Load Theory". Learning diagnostic abdominal ultrasound requires simultaneous integration of probe manipulation, spatial orientation, and real-time image interpretation; in authentic clinical settings, extraneous load such as patient discomfort, time pressure, and case variability may exceed beginners' working memory capacity. The structured phantom-assisted training may have mitigated this by offering "a stable and reproducible setting for stepwise supervised practice" under reduced clinical distractions.
requirements: A structured, low-distraction practice environment with stepwise supervised practice
constraints: This interpretation is the authors' explanatory account, offered as educationally plausible rather than directly tested in the study
target_learning_goals: Formation of stable visual-anatomical associations and scanning routines

title: Cognitive apprenticeship model as the instructional framework for clinical preceptorship
description: The preceptorship program was grounded in the cognitive apprenticeship model, whose six instructional methods are "modeling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, exploration." Preceptors received training in these methods, and adherence was measured with a 12-item questionnaire that showed excellent internal consistency (Cronbach's α=0.935) with a mean score of 51.6±6.9 out of 60. The model emphasizes progressive support so learners gradually construct their own clinical reasoning.
requirements: Preceptor training covering all six instructional methods
Session structure aligned with cognitive apprenticeship principles
constraints: Limited session duration and frequency likely reduced opportunities to fully apply all cognitive-apprenticeship techniques
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
clinical decision-making
examples: The end-of-program questionnaire adapted from cognitive apprenticeship literature evaluated intervention fidelity

This study adopted it as the theoretical framework, combined with literature and semi-structured interviews with eight experts, to derive the incontinence-specific index system.

examples: The study used the framework to structure the preliminary index pool of 6, 21 and 83 primary, secondary and tertiary indicators before Delphi screening.

article_title: Riding toward better math: executive functions mediate the link between horseback activities and children's mathematical achievement.
citation: Almutairi Seham. (2026). Riding toward better math: executive functions mediate the link between horseback activities and children's mathematical achievement. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04596-1
title: Cognitively rich physical activity framework: complex coordinative activities support academics via executive processes
description: The article's organizing framework holds that physical activities with rich sensorimotor and cognitive demands—such as horseback-riding, which requires "continuous postural adjustments, bilateral coordination, and rapid adaptation"—stimulate executive-control networks more robustly than repetitive aerobic exercise. It proposes that such activities enhance academic outcomes "primarily by strengthening executive processes rather than through direct transfer to academic skills." The study's full-mediation SEM result is presented as supporting this theoretical model in children aged 7–9.
requirements: Activities must embed sustained cognitive demands (attentional control, postural regulation, working-memory engagement) alongside physical exertion
constraints: The article states the potential for supporting mathematics learning "remains speculative and would require confirmation through longitudinal or experimental research before informing practice"
target_learners: typically developing children aged 7–9 years in recreational (non-clinical) equestrian activities
target_learning_goals: executive function development supporting mathematics achievement
examples: Recreational horseback-riding in Riyadh clubs with standardized 60-minute sessions (groundwork, mounted riding, cool-down)

title: The Complex Instruction framework posits that status characteristics drive unequal group participation and empowers instructors to disrupt status hierarchies through group-worthy tasks, delegated authority, and status interventions.
description: The essay draws on the Complex Instruction framework (Cohen, 1994; Cohen et al., 1999; Lotan, 2003, 2006), which "posits that differences in participation stem from status characteristics (e.g., academic ability, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, gender, and popularity) that students apply to one another." It considers three key components: "group-worthy tasks, delegation of authority, and addressing status problems." The framework empowers instructors to disrupt status hierarchies and shift expectations around competence, promoting equitable participation in learning.

constraints: its benefits have rarely been assessed at the college level

description: Complete Anatomy (CA) version 10.4 by 3D4Medical from Elsevier was chosen as "an example of a professional and commercially available AR application designed for learning human anatomy." description: The authors propose that the effectiveness of XR-based training may be explained through Cognitive Load Theory: "3D visualization likely reduces extraneous cognitive load by visually and interactively organizing spatial information, thus freeing up working memory capacity for germane processing".
