article_title: The role of gamification in sustainable teacher education: Examining concept images of curriculum elements using a solomon four-group design.
citation: Uysal, F. (2026). The role of gamification in sustainable teacher education: Examining concept images of curriculum elements using a solomon four-group design. PLOS One, 21(4). https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0346892
title: Concept image theory (Tall and Vinner) as the framework for pre-service teachers' mental representations of curriculum elements
description: Concept image theory, introduced by Tall and Vinner, holds that concept image is 'a complex phenomenon that includes all cognitive structures associated with a concept in an individual's mind', encompassing mental images, properties, processes, and experiences beyond the formal definition. The article uses this theory as the framework for examining how pre-service teachers' mental structures of curriculum elements develop, and it operationalizes the theory in the study's questionnaire and rubric through conceptual understanding and exemplification dimensions.
requirements: Formation of a concept image occurs through the interaction of all formal and informal experiences related to the concept, which the article describes as a dynamic process
constraints: In this study the theory is applied to abstract curriculum elements (objectives, content, learning experiences, and evaluation) among second-year pre-service teachers in a curriculum development course
target_learners: pre-service teachers in teacher education programs
target_learning_goals: developing concept images of curriculum elements
curriculum literacy
examples: The study assessed two dimensions for each curriculum element: conceptual understanding (defining, explaining properties, articulating relationships) and exemplification ability (generating contextually appropriate examples)
key_sources: Uysal, F. (2026). The role of gamification in sustainable teacher education: Examining concept images of curriculum elements using a solomon four-group design. PLOS One, 21(4). https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0346892

article_title: The role of gamification in sustainable teacher education: Examining concept images of curriculum elements using a solomon four-group design.
citation: Uysal, F. (2026). The role of gamification in sustainable teacher education: Examining concept images of curriculum elements using a solomon four-group design. PLOS One, 21(4). https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0346892
title: Concept image questionnaire and 0–8 rubric for assessing concept images of curriculum elements
description: An open-ended questionnaire with two questions per curriculum element (what the element means and giving an example), scored with a rubric evaluating conceptual understanding and example-giving separately on 0–4 levels. Per the article, 'The total score for each element consisted of the sum of conceptual understanding and example-giving scores. That is, it ranged from 0 to 8 points,' yielding 32 points for full scores across all four elements. The instrument was expert-reviewed and piloted with 15 second-year pre-service teachers.
requirements: Criterion-referenced rubric scoring by trained raters, since traditional internal consistency coefficients were not applicable for the open-ended format
Expert review and pilot testing to establish item comprehensibility and scoring consistency
constraints: One of the two raters was the researcher, who was not blind to group membership or measurement time
target_learning_goals: assessing conceptual understanding and exemplification ability for objectives, content, learning experiences, and evaluation
examples: Rubric levels for the objective concept ranged from complete failure to understand (0 points) to comprehensive understanding with objectives written across cognitive, affective, and psychomotor domains (4 points)
key_sources: Uysal, F. (2026). The role of gamification in sustainable teacher education: Examining concept images of curriculum elements using a solomon four-group design. PLOS One, 21(4). https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0346892

article_title: The Impact of High-Fidelity Simulation and Curriculum Integration on Nursing Students' Competence and Satisfaction: A Quasiexperimental Study.
citation: Ismail Ahmad, Al-Modallal Hanan, Aldardeir Njoud, Gomma Nada, Eltohamy Nadia Abd ElHamed. (2026). The Impact of High‐Fidelity Simulation and Curriculum Integration on Nursing Students’ Competence and Satisfaction: A Quasiexperimental Study. Journal of Nursing Management. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13140285/
title: Nursing education programs should combine high-fidelity simulation with curriculum integration to enhance competence and bridge theory and practice
description: The article recommends embedding HFS within an integrated curriculum rather than using either strategy in isolation, because the combination significantly enhanced students' cognitive and psychomotor competencies. The authors state that "Nursing management should facilitate the use of HFS and curriculum integration in nursing education, as this approach significantly enhances students’ clinical competence while bridging the gap between theory and practice," and that the strategy "may be adopted as a valuable and effective teaching strategy in courses with clinical or laboratory parts."
requirements: Institutional support through investment in HFS infrastructure
Structured faculty development
Competency-based assessment frameworks
constraints: Evidence base is a small, single-setting quasiexperimental study; the authors call for multi-institutional studies with larger and more diverse samples before broader implementation
target_learning_goals: clinical competence in maternal and newborn care
bridging theory and practice
critical thinking and clinical reasoning
examples: The study embedded a five-session HFS intervention integrating women's health and child health nursing content, assessed by written examination and OSCE two weeks later
key_sources: Ismail Ahmad, Al-Modallal Hanan, Aldardeir Njoud, Gomma Nada, Eltohamy Nadia Abd ElHamed. (2026). The Impact of High‐Fidelity Simulation and Curriculum Integration on Nursing Students’ Competence and Satisfaction: A Quasiexperimental Study. Journal of Nursing Management. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13140285/

article_title: The use of coaching to enhance students' learning, self-efficacy and performance in endodontics.
citation: Fox, K., Jarad, F. & Baaij, A. (2025). The use of coaching to enhance students' learning, self‐efficacy and performance in endodontics. International Endodontic Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iej.14241
title: A coaching model for endodontic education combining coaching in the moment and coaching over time to raise student self-efficacy
description: The article proposes a model in which a coaching approach enhances endodontic education 'by increasing their self‐efficacy and empowering students to take personal responsibility for their learning'. It operates on two timescales: coaching in the moment during clinical teaching sessions, and coaching over time in periodic development reviews away from the chairside. Both are structured around the GROW model and deliberately target Bandura's four sources of self-efficacy.
requirements: A relationship of absolute trust between coach and student, with clarified roles, expectations and goals
An environment of psychological safety created for the coaching conversations
constraints: No published investigations specifically address the use of coaching in endodontics, and there are no recommended models; the model is a proposal, not a tested intervention
Coaching over time has, as yet, only been reported in medicine, not dentistry
target_learning_goals: Clinical skills acquisition and performance in endodontics
Self-efficacy and personal responsibility for learning
examples: Using the GROW model at the start and end of a clinical teaching session (Table 1a, 1b)
Reviewing an endodontic portfolio of assessment data with a student away from the clinical environment
key_sources: Fox, K., Jarad, F. & Baaij, A. (2025). The use of coaching to enhance students' learning, self‐efficacy and performance in endodontics. International Endodontic Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iej.14241

article_title: The use of coaching to enhance students' learning, self-efficacy and performance in endodontics.
citation: Fox, K., Jarad, F. & Baaij, A. (2025). The use of coaching to enhance students' learning, self‐efficacy and performance in endodontics. International Endodontic Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iej.14241
title: Separate coaching roles from supervisory and progress-decision roles to protect trust in the coaching relationship
description: Because a dual supervisor-and-coach role creates a perceived conflict of interest that can undermine trust, the article recommends that 'faculty with coaching roles should be distinctly separate from those in supervisory roles and not make progress decisions'. Where staffing is limited, a 'four‐eyed approach' with a second assessor can help reduce the perceived conflict.
requirements: Institutional capacity to assign coaching and supervisory roles to different staff, or a second assessor where this is not possible
constraints: Separation may not be easy to accommodate within an institution with a limited number of supervising staff
target_learning_goals: Honest self-disclosure of weaknesses and effective developmental coaching
examples: Developmental coaching over time delivered by a coach away from the chairside who has no direct influence on the student's progress
key_sources: Fox, K., Jarad, F. & Baaij, A. (2025). The use of coaching to enhance students' learning, self‐efficacy and performance in endodontics. International Endodontic Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iej.14241

article_title: Adverse outcomes of post-core restorations performed by undergraduate and postgraduate dental students: a retrospective comparison.
citation: Taşdemir Murat, Keskin Büşra Ekin, Aydoğan Ayaz Elif, Çelik Davut. (2026). Adverse outcomes of post-core restorations performed by undergraduate and postgraduate dental students: a retrospective comparison. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09270-z
title: Consider confounding factors and case-allocation practices when interpreting outcome comparisons between trainee levels in dental education research
description: The article argues that comparisons of clinical outcomes across trainee levels must account for confounding before drawing conclusions about competence. It emphasizes that "unadjusted comparisons may lead to misleading conclusions" because case allocation in dental education settings is experience-based, with undergraduates typically assigned simpler cases. The recommendation is to adjust for patient, tooth, and contextual variables and to interpret unadjusted differences descriptively.
requirements: Multivariable adjustment for patient demographics, tooth-related variables, and operator education level before comparing outcomes across trainee levels
constraints: Findings limited to a single university-based training setting under supervision; retrospective design restricts causal interpretation
Case allocation based on operator experience may itself confound outcome comparisons
target_learning_goals: clinical competence in post-core restorative procedures
examples: The study adjusted for age, gender, tooth region, tooth location, and operator education level in a multivariable logistic regression, after which the operator-level association was no longer significant
key_sources: Taşdemir Murat, Keskin Büşra Ekin, Aydoğan Ayaz Elif, Çelik Davut. (2026). Adverse outcomes of post-core restorations performed by undergraduate and postgraduate dental students: a retrospective comparison. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09270-z

article_title: The core competencies in hospital medicine: Procedures 2025 update.
citation: Nichani S, Brooks ME, Bryson C, Fitterman N, Issa M, Lukela M, Marzano N, Sopko K, Sweigart JR. (2025). The core competencies in hospital medicine: Procedures 2025 update. Journal of Hospital Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1002/jhm.70042
title: Procedural curricula should be built from consensus-derived, evidence-updated learning objectives spanning knowledge, skills, attitudes, and systems
description: The article recommends using its revised objective sets as the basis for procedural curriculum and CME design: the objectives "provide a framework to guide curricular development, continuing medical education, and hospital medicine practitioners in developing and maintaining procedural competence essential for high‐quality inpatient care." Objectives were revised from the 2017 framework "to reflect evolving clinical evidence, advancements, and shifts in hospital medicine practice patterns."
requirements: Periodic expert review and revision of objectives as evidence and practice patterns evolve
constraints: Objective sets are procedure-specific and consensus-based rather than empirically validated against patient outcomes
target_learning_goals: Procedural competence
Continuing medical education
examples: Methodology combined a comprehensive literature review, expert consensus panels, and feedback from practicing hospitalists across diverse clinical settings
key_sources: Nichani S, Brooks ME, Bryson C, Fitterman N, Issa M, Lukela M, Marzano N, Sopko K, Sweigart JR. (2025). The core competencies in hospital medicine: Procedures 2025 update. Journal of Hospital Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1002/jhm.70042

article_title: An Interprofessional Approach to Teaching About Postpartum Depression.
citation: Howe‐Heyman Abigail CNM, PhD; Schatz Joseph DNP, PMHNP; Siegel Marissa DeCesaris DNP, PMHNP. (2025). An Interprofessional Approach to Teaching About Postpartum Depression. Journal of Midwifery & Women's Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmwh.70056
title: Use training that improves provider confidence in postpartum depression management to address a leading barrier to PPD care
description: The article argues that a major barrier to care for patients with postpartum depression is limited access to providers who are comfortable managing the condition, and that education improving provider confidence has the potential to improve care. Interprofessional simulation is offered as one such training modality, on the reasoning that clinicians who feel prepared are more likely to diagnose and treat PPD, expanding the workforce confident in PPD management.
requirements: Training that measurably improves provider confidence in PPD assessment and management
constraints: The study did not measure the prolonged impact of the simulation on clinical practice; the authors' link to practice rests on other researchers' findings about simulation's lasting influence
target_learners: Advanced practice nursing students preparing for postpartum care
target_learning_goals: Increase comfort and confidence in diagnosing and managing postpartum depression
examples: The simulation increased professional confidence subscale scores, and students reported feeling more confident working with patients outside of their specialty
key_sources: Howe‐Heyman Abigail CNM, PhD; Schatz Joseph DNP, PMHNP; Siegel Marissa DeCesaris DNP, PMHNP. (2025). An Interprofessional Approach to Teaching About Postpartum Depression. Journal of Midwifery & Women's Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmwh.70056

article_title: Efficacy of a hybrid case-based learning and simulated clinical encounter model versus lecture-based learning in dental education.
citation: Rao Lijia, Wu Jiahua, Deng Bixia, Hong Yubing, Wu Juan, Chen Yiming, Chen Mu. (2026). Efficacy of a hybrid case-based learning and simulated clinical encounter model versus lecture-based learning in dental education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08937-x
title: Cognitive Load Theory explanation for clinical thinking gains
description: The authors interpret the clinical thinking improvement through Cognitive Load Theory, which "categorizes cognitive load into three types: intrinsic (inherent task complexity), extraneous (generated by ineffective instructional design), and germane (effort dedicated to schema construction)". They argue the hybrid model manages intrinsic load via pre-class case review, reduces extraneous load via simulator realism, and frees resources for germane load, building clinical schemas.
requirements: Pre-class preparation to manage intrinsic load before sessions
Physical realism (simulator) to align mental models with physical reality
constraints: Offered as the authors' interpretation; the study did not measure cognitive load
target_learning_goals: clinical schema construction
diagnostic reasoning in endodontics
examples: In the LBL group, students mentally visualized 3D root canal structures from 2D slides while passively listening
key_sources: Rao Lijia, Wu Jiahua, Deng Bixia, Hong Yubing, Wu Juan, Chen Yiming, Chen Mu. (2026). Efficacy of a hybrid case-based learning and simulated clinical encounter model versus lecture-based learning in dental education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08937-x

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Chatbots as Virtual Patients in Dental Education: A Constructivist Approach to Classroom Implementation.
citation: B. Jones, A. Desu, and C. D. F. Honig. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Chatbots as Virtual Patients in Dental Education: A Constructivist Approach to Classroom Implementation. European Journal of Dental Education 30(2): 447–456. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.13135
title: Constructivist design framework for AI role-play in classroom simulation
description: The article applies constructivism, rooted in Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, as the theoretical lens for designing the AI role-play. Constructivism "posits that learners actively construct their own understanding of the world through experience," emphasising social interaction, dialogical learning, and student autonomy. In the design, students actively construct knowledge by applying it in history taking, framing it through discourse with an AI supervisor designed as a 'Socratic tutor' who probes for justifications, and reflecting on leading feedback. The authors stress that the surrounding educational design, including facilitation, interaction, feedback, and reflection, situates the chatbot within a constructivist paradigm.
requirements: Surrounding educational design including facilitation, student interaction and feedback, and reflection; the chatbot acts as a prompt for exploration and discussion, not a standalone teaching tool
constraints: The article notes text-based interactions cannot convey nonverbal cues and emotional nuances essential in sensitive patient encounters
target_learners: novice clinician dental and oral health students
target_learning_goals: problem solving and critical thinking
clinical reasoning
constructing meaning through real-world application
examples: The AI patient was programmed to deliver information gradually and only in response to targeted questioning, mirroring reticent or unclear real patients
key_sources: B. Jones, A. Desu, and C. D. F. Honig. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Chatbots as Virtual Patients in Dental Education: A Constructivist Approach to Classroom Implementation. European Journal of Dental Education 30(2): 447–456. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.13135

article_title: Enhancing health professional clinical performance through supervision strategies: from 5311 facilities across eight countries in sick child healthcare.
citation: Li Mengyao, Zhou Zhongliang, Mitchell Rebecca, Wang Dan, Boyle Brendan, Wang Wenhua. (2026). Enhancing health professional clinical performance through supervision strategies: from 5311 facilities across eight countries in sick child healthcare. Journal of Global Health. https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.16.04123
title: Combine supervision with feedback or training and institutional support rather than implementing supervision alone
description: The article recommends that supervision be implemented as part of an integrated package: supervision paired with feedback or targeted training, supported by facility-level quality assurance activities and data collection systems. It states "to avoid inefficient use of supervision resources, support contexts at the institutional level were necessary to nudge supervision toward greater effectiveness." In LMICs it advises first ensuring widespread data systems, then improving data utilisation, and expanding quality assurance from auditing toward total quality management.
requirements: Facilities need data collection systems and quality assurance activities in place for supervision alone to be effective
Supervision must be paired with feedback or targeted in-service training to show significant associations with quality
constraints: Findings derive from sick child healthcare services in LMICs; the authors caution against generalising to other healthcare settings or service areas
Supervision modalities were measured as binary indicators, which fail to capture the extent of supervision implementation
target_learners: Health professionals in low- and middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: Improve adherence to clinical guidelines in sick child healthcare
Enhance health worker clinical performance and quality of care
examples: The study analysed SPA survey data from 5311 facilities across eight countries, comparing supervision alone, with feedback, and with training, and subgrouping facilities by organisational context
key_sources: Li Mengyao, Zhou Zhongliang, Mitchell Rebecca, Wang Dan, Boyle Brendan, Wang Wenhua. (2026). Enhancing health professional clinical performance through supervision strategies: from 5311 facilities across eight countries in sick child healthcare. Journal of Global Health. https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.16.04123

(2026). Moderators' Role in Fostering Health Practitioner Engagement Within an Online Active Learning Program (The Community Fracture Capture Learning Hub): Qualitative Relational Content Thematic Analysis. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/83764
title: Invest in competency-based moderator training emphasizing empathetic communication and collaborative techniques to structure effective virtual communities of practice
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that effective VCoPs should be structured by preparing moderators as a trained group. The authors state that "Future studies should consider investing in competency-based moderator training that emphasizes empathetic communication and collaborative techniques as a means of structuring effective VCoPs." This principle rests on their finding that moderators' blending of relational skills, clinical authenticity, and adaptive facilitation drove knowledge coconstruction and practice-relevant engagement in the analyzed hub.
requirements: Moderators prepared and trained as a group so they can provide more strategic approaches that increase participant engagement, as the introduction states
constraints: The recommendation is forward-looking; the article calls for future studies rather than reporting a test of moderator training itself
target_learners: Moderators of health professional virtual communities of practice
target_learning_goals: Fostering participant engagement and knowledge coconstruction in web-based professional learning
examples: CFC moderators' progression from formal instructions to informal dialogue and personalized feedback illustrates the adaptive facilitation the training would target

article_title: Agreement and reliability of global rating versus checklist scores in a high-stakes undergraduate OSCE in Rwanda.
citation: Ibrahim Olayinka Rasheed, McCall Natalie, Bekele Abebe, Zelelew Biniam Ewnte, Ojomo Oluwaseun, Belachew Anteneh Gadisa, Amare Equlinet Misganaw, Gashaw Zelalem Mengistu, Ayana Birhanu Abera, Ndayikeje Ariane Nina. (2026). Agreement and reliability of global rating versus checklist scores in a high-stakes undergraduate OSCE in Rwanda. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08809-4
title: Combine checklists and GRS in high-stakes OSCE scoring to capture both critical steps and overall competence
description: The article recommends that high-stakes OSCEs use both scoring systems together: checklists to document coverage of critical observable steps, and GRS to capture overall clinical competence and reasoning, with the final score as a weighted composite of both. The authors state that "GRS should be considered an essential component of high-stakes examinations, complementing rather than replacing checklists." This rests on their findings that the two correlate strongly yet GRS discriminates failures checklists miss.
requirements: Examiners trained and calibrated on both scoring systems before the examination
A standard-setting pass mark established for interpreting both score types
constraints: Evidence base is single-institution data from 36 students, which the authors state may limit generalizability to the sub-region
The same examiners scored both methods, which the authors note may have introduced potential bias
target_learning_goals: clinical competency assessment at exit examinations
examples: In the studied exit OSCE, each station used a 20-mark checklist plus a three-level GRS (failed, borderline, passed), and GRS identified station failures that checklists did not

article_title: Development and evaluation of a literature seminar course based on flipped classroom and team-based learning in the graduate nursing curriculum.
citation: Qi Hong, Ban Jingjing, Wang Nana, Guo Huimin, Yang Yang, Tang Shan. (2026). Development and evaluation of a literature seminar course based on flipped classroom and team-based learning in the graduate nursing curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08823-6
title: Constructivist and cooperative learning theories, informed by TPACK, as the theoretical basis for integrating flipped classroom and team-based learning
description: The authors ground their FC-TBL instructional model in constructivist and cooperative learning theories, further informed by the Technological Pedagogical and Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework. Constructivism "emphasizes that learners construct knowledge through active engagement and reflection, rather than passive reception." The TPACK lens highlights that "effective flipped learning depends on instructors' integrated understanding of content, pedagogy, and technology when designing pre-class materials and orchestrating in-class learning activities." The authors also invoke Vygotsky's zone of proximal development to explain how peer interaction and timely instructor guidance enable learners to reach higher cognitive levels, and Bandura's social cognitive theory to explain self-efficacy gains through mastery accomplishments, vicarious learning, and social persuasion.
requirements: Instructors must assume multiple roles as facilitator, supporter, and evaluator—providing resources before class, guiding academic exchange with immediate feedback during class, and implementing individualized pedagogical support after class.
constraints: Evidence for the FC model has largely concentrated on undergraduate populations; its application in graduate-level literature seminar courses remains underexplored according to the authors.
target_learning_goals: research competence
research self-efficacy
critical thinking
self-directed learning
key_sources: Qi Hong, Ban Jingjing, Wang Nana, Guo Huimin, Yang Yang, Tang Shan. (2026). Development and evaluation of a literature seminar course based on flipped classroom and team-based learning in the graduate nursing curriculum. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08823-6

article_title: Near-peer teaching of laparoscopic skills among medical students: a randomised feasibility study.
citation: Ho Martin Patrick, Heskin Leonie, Dablouk Lena, Richa Yasmina, Nolan Joshua, Brien Andrew O’, Abrar Samin, Hennessey Derek. (2026). Near-peer teaching of laparoscopic skills among medical students: a randomised feasibility study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08461-4
title: Cognitive and social congruence as the mechanism underpinning near-peer teaching
description: The article invokes the concept of cognitive and social congruence to explain why near-peer teaching improved laparoscopic performance. As printed: "The concept of cognitive and social congruence underpins near-peer teaching; It suggests that learners better understand material when taught by peers, as they share a similar knowledge foundation and feel more comfortable and supported." The article presents this as the explanatory account for the observed advantage of peer-taught over self-taught students, citing prior peer-teaching psychology literature.
requirements: Near-peer teachers who share a similar knowledge foundation with learners
constraints: Presented as the authors’ interpretation rather than a mechanism tested in this study
target_learners: Junior medical students taught by senior medical students
target_learning_goals: Understanding and acquisition of technical surgical skills

article_title: Educational benefits of pre-class videos and viewing perspectives on ultrasound-guided central venous catheterization training: a prospective randomized controlled trial.
citation: Liao Po-Hsiang, Chen Chung-Ting, Lee Yi-Tzu, Lee Cheng-Hao, How Chorng-Kuang, Huang Hsien-Hao, Hsu Teh-Fu. (2026). Educational benefits of pre-class videos and viewing perspectives on ultrasound-guided central venous catheterization training: a prospective randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08870-z
title: Cognitive Load Theory framing: pre-class videos reduce extraneous load and support early schema formation before hands-on procedural practice
description: The article applies Cognitive Load Theory to procedural video pretraining: "According to Cognitive Load Theory [8], novices benefit when instructional designs reduce extraneous load and support early schema formation." It argues that pre-class videos, particularly first-person perspectives, "may help learners construct initial cognitive frameworks before hands-on practice, thereby lowering cognitive burden during early attempts." This framework explains why video groups entered training with higher baseline performance and why the authors suggest POV visualization reduces cognitive load and improves motor sequencing.
requirements: Instructional designs must reduce extraneous load for novices to benefit, per the theory as the article invokes it
constraints: Cognitive load was not formally measured in this study; the article notes NASA Task Load Index was omitted to avoid disrupting procedural flow
target_learners: Novice postgraduate physicians acquiring complex procedural skills
target_learning_goals: Procedural skill acquisition under high intrinsic cognitive load
Early schema formation for multi-step invasive procedures

article_title: Checklist- and algorithm-based simulation training produce comparable improvements in teamwork-related shared mental models: a cluster-randomized study in trauma resuscitation teams.
citation: Beaugé Yvonne, Kusch Simon, Thorsson Lukas, Zentgraf Michael, Schauwienold Julian, Muenzberg Matthias, Verboket Rene, Lefering Rolf, Schweigkofler Uwe, Faul Philipp, Sterz Jasmina, Ruesseler Miriam. (2026). Checklist- and algorithm-based simulation training produce comparable improvements in teamwork-related shared mental models: a cluster-randomized study in trauma resuscitation teams. European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00068-026-03161-0
title: Cognitive load and collaborative learning account for how simulation training improves team shared mental models
description: The authors interpret SMM improvements through collaborative learning and cognitive load frameworks: in high-acuity trauma resuscitation, teams operate under substantial intrinsic cognitive load, and "Structured simulation training may reduce extraneous load by clarifying task sequencing, reinforcing role expectations, and promoting standardized communication strategies". Repeated scenario-based practice aligns expectations about leadership, information flow, and escalation pathways. SMMs are described as a collective cognitive resource that distributes cognitive demands across the team, supporting anticipatory coordination and reducing the need for corrective communication during time-critical phases of care.
requirements: Structured simulation training that clarifies task sequencing and reinforces role expectations
Repeated, scenario-based practice allowing team members to align expectations
constraints: The authors present this as an interpretation of observed improvements, not a tested mechanism; the observed improvements likely reflect enhanced cognitive alignment rather than format-specific mechanisms
target_learners: interprofessional trauma teams in high-acuity clinical environments
target_learning_goals: team cognitive alignment and anticipatory coordination under time pressure
examples: The authors link the pre–post SMM gains in the 29-team study to reduced extraneous cognitive load and aligned expectations from repeated scenario practice
key_sources: Beaugé Yvonne, Kusch Simon, Thorsson Lukas, Zentgraf Michael, Schauwienold Julian, Muenzberg Matthias, Verboket Rene, Lefering Rolf, Schweigkofler Uwe, Faul Philipp, Sterz Jasmina, Ruesseler Miriam. (2026). Checklist- and algorithm-based simulation training produce comparable improvements in teamwork-related shared mental models: a cluster-randomized study in trauma resuscitation teams. article_title: Evaluating a problem-based learning model integrated with 3D anatomy software and software-assisted annotation in undergraduate spinal surgery education: a randomized controlled trial.

description: Because carbonization is often related to inadequate countertraction by the non-dominant hand, and experts regard countertraction as an essential head and neck surgery skill, the article recommends emphasizing countertraction during repeated practice. The authors link this to their novice findings: novices showed higher carbonization, longer resection times, and more repeated grasps, so improving countertraction may both support safer electrosurgical handling and enhance efficiency.

title: Build learners' confidence calibration through structured feedback to improve diagnostic interpretation skills
description: The article argues that diagnostic performance depends not only on knowledge but on the alignment between perceived certainty and actual accuracy, which it calls "confidence calibration, defined as the alignment between an individual’s perceived certainty and their actual diagnostic accuracy." It recommends educational interventions designed to enhance calibration, such as structured feedback sessions, reflective practice, and simulation-based training, to strengthen diagnostic proficiency and reduce errors.
requirements: Feedback and training must reinforce confidence, since the article states self-confidence alone cannot guarantee accurate diagnosis and should be paired with critical thinking
constraints: Cross-sectional design does not allow causal conclusions between confidence and diagnostic performance
target_learners: clinical trainees in visually demanding diagnostic tasks
target_learning_goals: radiographic interpretation and diagnostic accuracy
metacognitive monitoring of diagnostic confidence
examples: In the study, students rated confidence per case on a four-point scale while diagnosing 11 confirmed lesions, and accuracy tracked confidence levels from 23.8% (Very unsure) to 74.7% (Sure).

title: Confidence calibration theory as a lens for diagnostic performance
description: The article interprets its findings through "metacognitive accuracy and confidence calibration theory, which suggest that diagnostic performance is influenced not only by knowledge but also by an individual’s ability to judge the correctness of their own decisions." Within this account, misalignment between perceived certainty and actual accuracy—whether overconfidence or underconfidence—may increase the risk of diagnostic errors, and higher confidence may indicate stronger metacognitive monitoring of one's own knowledge.
requirements: Learners must make diagnostic judgments and report their own confidence so calibration can be assessed
constraints: The article notes confidence may reflect underlying knowledge and skills rather than directly influencing diagnostic ability
target_learners: medical and health-professions trainees making diagnostic decisions
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of diagnostic certainty
diagnostic decision-making under uncertainty
examples: The study applied the framework by relating case-level confidence ratings to diagnostic accuracy across 11 radiographic lesions and testing moderation by gender and personality.

article_title: Evidence-based teaching: The examination and use of psychological theories in medical education research using the example of cognitive load theory.
citation: Paridon H. (2026). Evidence-based teaching: The examination and use of psychological theories in medical education research using the example of cognitive load theory. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://journals.publisso.de/en/journals/jme/volume43/zma001805
title: Cognitive Load Theory: learning depends on managing limited working memory capacity
description: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) by Sweller and colleagues is a pedagogical-psychological theory of knowledge acquisition that deals primarily with learning complex cognitive content. The article states that "The theory assumes that learning occurs best under conditions that are consistent with human cognitive architecture", placing working memory at the center of its consideration. It distinguishes intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load, which sum to a total load on working memory; when total load is too high, learning becomes less effective. The theory has grounded numerous empirical studies on learning with media, worked examples, and skill acquisition, and serves as the basis for instructional design recommendations.
requirements: Working memory capacity is limited, so total cognitive load should ideally not exceed this capacity during learning
constraints: CLT primarily deals with the learning of complex cognitive content, not simple serial learning
target_learning_goals: sustainable acquisition of knowledge and competencies in complex domains
examples: The article uses CLT to derive fifteen recommendations for medical education on reducing external load, controlling intrinsic load, and optimizing germane load

title: Control-value theory of achievement emotions (CVT) as a framework for simulation emotions
description: The study is guided by Pekrun's control-value theory of achievement emotions, which "characterizes emotions by pleasantness (valence; positive to negative), degree of physiological arousal (activation; activating to deactivating), the stimuli triggering the emotion (object focus; task‐related or outcome‐related) and the place in time the emotion was directed to (time frame)". CVT predicts positive activating emotions typically enhance achievement and negative deactivating emotions impair it; the article's findings on happiness/hopefulness align with this pattern, while its null individual-performance result echoes cited divergent findings that positive emotions do not universally enhance performance.
requirements: Applied to emotions classified along valence, activation, object focus and time frame dimensions
constraints: The article notes prior studies found effects diverging from CVT's general pattern, so emotion effects are context-, task- and population-dependent
target_learning_goals: understanding how achievement emotions relate to performance perceptions in team-based learning
examples: Used to frame hypotheses about leaders' negative activating emotions and the role of positive activating emotions in team-level perceptions

citation: Ehsanzadeh Seyed Jafar, Dwyer Eric, Barzegar Mohammad, Hamidi Hadi. (2025). Teaching medical terminology: comparing the effectiveness of lecture-based and corpus-assisted methods. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-025-07584-7
title: Corpus-assisted lesson plans for medical terminology using COCA Medical subcorpus data (concordancing, collocation, frequency)
description: Three 70-minute corpus-assisted lesson plans, each targeting the same eight cardiovascular terms from Chapter 10 of Medical Terminology: An Illustrated Guide, were compared against a lecture-based plan. The concordancing plan used "Handouts with 10–15 concordance lines per term from COCA Medical subcorpus" with pairs highlighting syntactic, collocational, and discourse-level patterns; the collocation plan used top-5 collocations per term (e.g., treat embolism) with sentence-writing; and the frequency plan used handouts with normalized frequencies and morphological breakdowns (e.g., fibrill- = 42.1/million). All groups shared identical learning goals, differing only in teaching method and post-teaching activities.
requirements: Access to the COCA Medical subcorpus and corpus tools such as Sketch Engine or AntConc, which the authors note are open-access
constraints: The study used only eight cardiovascular terms of 2–3 syllables, selected to control frequency, semantic, and morphological complexity
target_learners: EFL medical students at intermediate proficiency (CEFR B1–B2) in a medical terminology course
target_learning_goals: Retention and contextual understanding of specialized medical terminology in English
examples: Each group participated in a 70-minute teaching session plus 20-minute post-teaching activities targeting the eight terms; the lecture-based plan used slides and flashcards emphasizing rote memorization

description: The article applies co-design, defined as "a collaborative process of joint inquiry and imagination, where diverse stakeholders collectively explore problems and develop solutions". In this project, patients, healthcare staff and the public were engaged throughout all phases, with iterative co-design meetings generating shared values that informed context-specific QPS domains and competencies. The article presents this as an adaptive approach tailored to panel members' needs, combining a Delphi survey, scoping review evidence, and iterative workshops.

citation: Skariah Tisha Ann, Rao Udaya Kumar, Karthika Manjush. (2025). Competency gaps in respiratory therapy: evidence from a global survey. Korean Journal of Medical Education, 37(4), 437-451. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2025.355
title: Comprehensive Competency-Based Framework for respiratory therapy with gap-tiered, simulation-integrated structure
description: The article proposes a Comprehensive Competency-Based Framework for RT education that "ensures no competency is overlooked, making the framework all-inclusive and structured for progressive learning." It organizes competencies by gap severity (critical, high, medium, low from the survey's gap analysis), integrates simulation-based training strategies, and is intended to be globally adaptable and aligned with international accreditation. Fig. 2 illustrates the proposed framework linking training gaps, simulation use, and competency outcomes.

Consensus validation via an international expert Delphi process
Alignment with international RT certification and accreditation standards
constraints: High-cost technologies such as ECMO simulators may limit feasibility in low- and middle-income countries
Participation was limited in regions where RT education is still emerging, restricting generalizability
target_learning_goals: High-risk, low-frequency procedural competencies such as ECMO and lung ultrasound
Clinical, equipment-based, and procedural competencies
Non-technical competencies including communication, teamwork, and decision-making

article_title: A nursing-led pathway to safe task sharing in Japan: Interprofessional simulation and a common competency credential.
citation: Kubota, K., Nishimura, A., & Funaki, J. (2026). A nursing‐led pathway to safe task sharing in Japan: Interprofessional simulation and a common competency credential. Japan Journal of Nursing Science, 23(1), e70036. https://doi.org/10.1111/jjns.70036
title: Common competency credential (CCC) assessed via standardized simulation-based scenarios
description: The common competency credential (CCC) is a proposed credential verifying proficiency in the five shared domains through standardized, simulation-based assessment. It "would be profession‐agnostic yet context‐sensitive": nurses, clinical engineers, and laboratory technologists complete role-relevant scenarios but are judged against the same domain standards. The assessment system would use a standardized scenario library of high-fidelity ward, intensive care, and diagnostic cases embedding "explicit supervision levels, stop rules, checklists, and escalation criteria." Objective assessment would use validated teamwork and technical scales, behaviorally anchored checklists, trained raters, and interrater reliability audits, with expert-panel thresholds and re-credentialing every 3–5 years or after significant scope changes.

Trained raters and interrater reliability audits
Proficiency thresholds set by expert panels, with remediation pathways
constraints: The credential is a proposal; the article states documentation must align with institutional policies and Japanese law to delineate delegated tasks, supervision levels, and escalation triggers
target_learners: prelicensure and continuing nursing and allied health trainees
target_learning_goals: verifiable proficiency in the five shared competency domains
safe delegated task performance within defined supervision frameworks
examples: Governance would launch via a nursing-led board progressively adding allied health representation and external examiners, with a national registry of credentialed practitioners and accredited simulation centers.

article_title: Preparing Midwifery Students for the Certification Examination by Debunking Prevalent Test-Taking Myths.
citation: Faucett K. (2025). Preparing Midwifery Students for the Certification Examination by Debunking Prevalent Test‐Taking Myths. Journal of Midwifery & Women's Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmwh.70016
title: Cognitive bias and heuristic account of test-taking errors (confirmation bias, framing effect, recency heuristic, negativity bias, first instinct fallacy)
description: The article frames poor multiple-choice decisions through named cognitive biases and heuristics drawn from cognitive psychology: confirmation bias as "the tendency to stick with our preexisting beliefs"; the framing effect, where choices rest on how options are framed; the recency and availability heuristics; negativity bias, which makes painful right-to-wrong changes more memorable; and the first instinct fallacy. The author uses this framework, plus stress physiology (the amygdala hijack), to explain why common test-taking tips fail a diverse midwifery student population and to ground replacement strategies.
requirements: Educator understanding of neuropsychology, heuristics, and cognitive biases to better serve students
constraints: Applied here to the 175-question AMCB certification examination context; the bias concepts are cited from prior literature

target_learning_goals: accurate metacognitive judgment and bias-aware decision-making on multiple-choice examinations
examples: A stem with several blood-pressure data points about a routine screening colonoscopy leads test takers down the hypertension path, distracting them from the patient's age

article_title: Eight practical strategies for designing case-based flipped learning to foster clinical reasoning in preclinical medical students.
citation: Si J. (2025). Eight practical strategies for designing case-based flipped learning to foster clinical reasoning in preclinical medical students. Annals of Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1080/07853890.2025.2586874
title: Manage novice learners' cognitive load in clinical reasoning activities with just-in-time procedural information, worked examples, and collaborative worksheets, fading support as expertise grows
description: Grounded in cognitive load theory — learning is impaired when demands exceed working memory capacity — the article recommends scaffolding strategies for in-class clinical reasoning. These include just-in-time procedural information such as a clinical reasoning worksheet, instructor-completed worked examples before class to reduce extraneous load from unguided practice, and collaborative group work exploiting the collective working memory effect. Crucially, "such support should be gradually withdrawn as students gain expertise", promoting autonomous reasoning and a smooth transition to independent problem solving.
requirements: Scaffolds (worksheets, worked examples, group work) must be provided at the moment of need and then faded as students gain expertise
constraints: Support that is not faded keeps students dependent; the article states scaffolding must be gradually withdrawn to develop autonomous clinical reasoning skills
target_learners: Novice preclinical medical students who struggle to process multiple information sources simultaneously
target_learning_goals: Successful engagement with cognitively demanding clinical reasoning tasks
examples: Providing instructor-completed worksheet versions before class as worked examples, and a blank worksheet just-in-time during reasoning activities

title: Combine digital technology with case-based learning rather than relying on digital navigation alone
description: The article argues that digital tools and case-based teaching each supply what the other lacks, so implant training should integrate them. It reports that "we attempted to integrate digital technologies with traditional teaching, combining online and face-to-face instruction through a case-based learning (CBL) approach," and states that relying solely on digital navigation cannot achieve the best teaching results because practical skill acquisition requires further support. The blended model is said to reinforce theoretical understanding, enhance practical skills in a clinically relevant context, and support clinical reasoning through case discussion and real-time instructor feedback.

constraints: The article states a sufficient number of cases is needed to establish an appropriate case database, which requires clinical time to collect data, sufficient hardware to store digital data, and dedicated personnel to manage it and avoid information leakage
target_learners: oral and maxillofacial surgery specialists without prior implantology training
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning and treatment decision-making
procedural understanding of implant surgery
learner engagement and retention
examples: The department screened appropriate cases from its case database using the newly introduced implant navigation system and gradually tried the implant specialist training mode combining CBL with digitization

description: This principle holds that growth mindset promotion should be calibrated to the national and socioeconomic context rather than assumed universally beneficial. The article's cross-national analysis shows mindset–achievement links and SES moderation vary by country, so it concludes that "the importance of considering contextual and cultural factors when promoting growth mindsets" should guide stakeholders, because benefits "may differ depending on students‚Äô socioeconomic backgrounds". title: Colored model tooth with red target region for Class II cavity preparation
description: An injection-molded #19 (FDI #36) standard model tooth on which the region requiring tissue removal is marked in color. "The target area—defined as the region requiring tissue removal—was colored red, with the remaining anatomical structures rendered in white." The design was derived from 3D scans of a standard reference Class II cavity prepared by an experienced dentist. Students used it as visual-spatial guidance before practicing on standard teeth, which the authors say enhanced stereognostic perception through three-dimensional tactile-visual integration.

article_title: Effects of virtual reality-based disaster simulation education on nursing students.
citation: Kim Kyeng-Jin, Choi Moon-Ji, Kim MinJi. (2025). Effects of virtual reality-based disaster simulation education on nursing students. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0329563
title: Cognitive continuum theory with four simulation learning elements as a design framework for disaster triage training
description: The article applies cognitive continuum theory, which posits that "cognition moves along a continuum from intuition to analytical thinking", with the suitable process depending on task characteristics: intuition supports fast responses when time or information is limited, while analytical processes suit detailed decision-making. Simulation design operationalizes this through four learning elements—analytical cognition in tasks, situational awareness, cognitive control, and self-awareness—integrated into the VR disaster triage training with pre-briefing, structured simulation, and reflective debriefing.
requirements: Simulation tasks that mimic real situations with realistic and immersive tasks, enabling safe repetitive learning so learners can optimize cognitive judgments
constraints: Applied and evaluated here only in the disaster triage context with nursing students
target_learners: Nursing students as future healthcare first responders
target_learning_goals: Structured evidence-based triage decision-making
Context-sensitive clinical judgment
Self-regulation under pressure
examples: The reflection stage used a debriefing protocol with structured questions such as "What cues did you use to make your decision" and "How would you handle a similar situation differently?"

citation: Montemayor VJ, Bossart EL, Burmeister JW, Cetnar A, Deeley MA, Fagerstrom JM, Harper JM, Homann KL, James JR, Lee TK, Malhotra HK, Mamalui M, Popovic M, Stanley DN. (2025). AAPM WGTEACH Report 366: Best practices in the teaching and mentoring of medical physics. J Appl Clin Med Phys. https://doi.org/10.1002/acm2.70259
title: Design cognitively active rather than cognitively passive activities, and use metacognition to support self-directed learning
description: Drawing on the National Research Council report How People Learn, the report recommends that educators facilitate environments where students construct usable knowledge and develop metacognition—thinking about one's thinking. "Metacognition is critical to self‐directed learning, and a valuable tool in the transfer of learning to new tasks or contexts." A key ingredient is providing cognitively active versus cognitively passive activities, which lets students actively transfer factual knowledge into understanding in new contexts and externalizes the learning process for teachers and students.
requirements: Educators must engage students' initial preconceptions, since unengaged preconceptions cause learners to revert to them outside the classroom
target_learners: medical physics students and trainees at all levels
target_learning_goals: metacognition, self-directed learning, and transfer of learning to new tasks
examples: The report cites active learning techniques such as peer instruction, problem-based learning, debates, simulations, or case studies as conferring substantial benefit in overcoming initial preconceptions

citation: Levy Manon, Dopff Cécile, Audibert Gerard, Bouquet Antoine, Gurda Thomas, Sy Mohammed, Bleuze Pauline, Michelet Daphné. (2025). Effect of mental imagery using cognitive aids on the performance of novice anesthesiology residents during a simulated cardiopulmonary resuscitation. title: Mechanism account: the clear, sequential structure of a cognitive aid makes mental imagery efficient by freeing cognitive resources for the environment
description: The authors propose an explanatory account for why mental imagery based on a cognitive aid improved non-technical performance: "the clear and sequential structure of the cognitive aid, organized into distinct steps, may be a key element for mental imagery efficiency". Mentally rehearsing the precise sequence of steps is hypothesized to free cognitive resources so residents can focus on their environment, supporting better role allocation and communication and a better ability to anticipate and adapt. article_title: The Link Between Contextual Poverty and Academic Achievement: Evidence Using Panel Data From a Lower-Middle-Income Country.
citation: Hossain Mobarak. (2025). The Link Between Contextual Poverty and Academic Achievement: Evidence Using Panel Data From a Lower‐Middle‐Income Country. The British Journal of Sociology. https://doi.org/10.1111/1468-4446.13208
title: Collective socialisation (role model effect) and social capital as mechanisms linking local poverty to achievement in LMICs
description: The article adapts two sociological mechanisms to explain why subdistrict poverty relates to school achievement in Bangladesh. Under the role model effect, "Communities with higher concentrations of educated adults provide more visible role models for younger generations to be more aspirational about their education and careers", drawing on social learning theory. Under social capital, disadvantaged communities lack networks of educated individuals who provide guidance and access to resources. The author argues both mechanisms apply strongly in collectivist, religious LMIC societies like Bangladesh, and uses them to derive predictions about stream differences and urban–rural variation.
requirements: Local areas must be socially meaningful units where children socialise outside the home; the author applies neighbourhood theory to subdistricts because rural areas are spatially homogeneous
constraints: The author notes aggregated subdistrict units cannot strictly be seen as neighbourhoods, and heterogeneous large cities like Dhaka and Chittagong make neighbourhood theorising less suitable; data limitations prevented finer spatial disaggregation
target_learners: secondary school students in Bangladesh and other lower-middle-income countries
target_learning_goals: academic achievement in national exit examinations across arts/general, business and science streams
examples: The study tests the framework's predictions using subdistrict educational and economic poverty measures in four-level multilevel models of school achievement

title: Match simulator choice to the learning objective, combining modalities rather than relying on a single simulator
description: The article recommends that educators select simulators according to the specific objectives of individual learners within a structured curriculum, since no single platform covers every learning area. Participants reported that "Most participants felt that a combination of simulator modalities is beneficial, typically use of a cadaver for revision of surgical technique with human anatomy, followed by live animals for practice of haemorrhage control in a team setting." This supports the 3Rs principle of replacing animal use wherever an alternative achieves the objective.
requirements: Clear learning objectives identified before choosing a simulator
Awareness of the strengths and limits of each modality (e.g., cadaver anatomy versus live bleeding)
constraints: The article notes no single model can currently replicate all aspects of a live animal, making full replacement of LTT challenging for open surgery

Haemorrhage control practice under team conditions

Webinars were "theoretical‐based pre‐recorded lectures and promoted passive learning," and the webinar-only group did not achieve better results, which the authors attribute to limited interactivity with the educator and between colleagues. title: Constructivist-based flipped classroom design combining situational and collaborative learning for nursing skills
description: The article grounds its flipped classroom implementation in constructivism, which "emphasizes the important role of 'situation' and 'collaboration' in learning". Pre-class stages shift passive knowledge acquisition to videos, animations and presentations so learners construct meaning beforehand; classroom time is devoted to active, collaborative, problem-based activities such as case discussion, think-pair-share, and skills laboratory practice, with instructors acting as facilitators who correct misconceptions and give timely feedback.

Classroom time must be organized for collaborative, active learning activities with instructor guidance
constraints: The article notes some prior studies found no statistically significant differences in certain skills
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge of vital signs, nutrition and drug administration
psychomotor nursing skills (blood pressure measurement, blood glucose measurement, drug preparation, nasogastric tube insertion)
persistence of knowledge and skills

article_title: The effect of simulation training on the counseling skills of nutritional science students in dietetic internships.
citation: Linder Ifat, Lukach Zafit, Pergament Keren, Steckler Rafi, Tepper Sigal. (2025). The effect of simulation training on the counseling skills of nutritional science students in dietetic internships. BMC Medical Education 25:1114. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07674-x
title: Consecutive-scenario simulation pattern: progressive multi-session cases with the same simulated patient, each round running briefing-simulation-debriefing with structured multi-source feedback
description: The program's distinctive design is a "continuous storyline" in which each workshop's three counseling rounds follow one patient across an intake and follow-up visits covering adherence, missed appointments, and weight-regain challenges. Each round is "composed of three phases: briefing, counselling session simulation, and debriefing", with debriefing lasting 20–30 minutes and including self-reflection, multi-source feedback from the actor, peers, supervising dietitian, and facilitator, analytical discussion, and an application phase. Scenarios were co-developed by faculty and experienced clinical dietitians from real patient cases.
requirements: Professional actors trained in a full-day standardized protocol covering character briefing, role-play practice, emotional consistency, and feedback delivery; a simulation facilitator; scenarios aligned with learning objectives and derived from real cases.
A dedicated simulation room with audio-visual recording and an observation room for peer viewing.
constraints: The authors note resource constraints, curriculum integration difficulties, and limited faculty development as documented barriers to multi-session simulation implementation, which their approach addresses within existing structures.
target_learners: final-year nutrition students in practicum tracks
target_learning_goals: counseling skills
communication skills
self-efficacy
emotional regulation in patient interactions
examples: Workshop cases included an obese patient using a GLP-1 analog, a patient with high blood lipid (TG, LDL) levels, and a bariatric patient four years after surgery with weight regain; regulatory approval allowed simulation to substitute for 30% of field hours.

citation: Ford James S. MD, MAS, Malhotra Atul MD, Pearce Alex K. MD, Wardi Gabriel MD, MPH. (2025). CPADS-30: Mastering the first 30 seconds of adult cardiac arrest resuscitation. The American journal of emergency medicine. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajem.2025.06.056
title: Cognitive load theory design principles underlying the CPADS-30 mnemonic
description: The article grounds the mnemonic's design in cognitive load theory, applying chunking (grouping related information to improve recall), serial recall and memory chains (ordered recall where one unit primes the next), schema formation linking declarative and procedural knowledge, written semantic cues, and the primacy effect. The authors state they "incorporated our ranked list into a mnemonic using principles of cognitive load theory, including chunking, serial recall, and the primacy effect". Because research suggests individuals can hold only about five items in working memory, the mnemonic deliberately contains just five tasks.
requirements: deliberately limited to five tasks to minimize burden on working memory
the two most mortality-robust interventions (CPR and defibrillation) are placed first and second to exploit the primacy effect
constraints: applies to the first 30 seconds of adult cardiac arrest resuscitation only, complementing rather than replacing the full ACLS algorithm
target_learners: code leaders managing adult cardiac arrest resuscitations
target_learning_goals: rapid recall and prioritization of critical early resuscitation tasks under high cognitive load
examples: The first two letters C and P correspond to CPR, and the written syllable PADS corresponds to pad placement, providing hidden semantic memory triggers

title: Cognitive load theory's three load types as a framework for evaluating technology-based learning tools
description: The article applies cognitive load theory, whose "main premise ... is that the capacity of our working memory and information processing for long-term memory is limited". It distinguishes three load types: intrinsic load inherent to task complexity, extraneous load determined by how teaching is delivered, and germane load reflecting effort to build mental schema. The article uses this framework to interpret the VR simulator's load profile, arguing that technologies with smaller extraneous and greater germane load are optimal for learning.
requirements: Assessment of cognitive load when learners must learn to use a new technology in addition to the content it delivers.
constraints: The article notes intrinsic load is generally expected to be unaffected by instructional technology, and that extraneous load should be reduced through user-friendly technologies and avoidance of irrelevant elements.
target_learners: Medical students learning technical skills with new technologies
target_learning_goals: Acquisition and retention of technical skill and theoretical knowledge under managed cognitive load
examples: The study measured intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load with Leppink's scale after immersive VR chest tube insertion training.

article_title: Comparison of Practical Skills Teaching by Near-Peers and Faculty.
citation: Hari Roman MD, MME; Oppliger Sarah; Dolmans Diana H.J.M. PhD; Huwendiek Sören MD, MME, PhD; Stalmeijer Renée E. MSc, PhD. (2025). Comparison of Practical Skills Teaching by Near-Peers and Faculty. Academic Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/ACM.0000000000006003
title: Cognitive apprenticeship as a framework for describing and comparing practical-skills teaching methods
description: The article uses cognitive apprenticeship (CA) to structure the analysis of instructor methods, in which instructors make their "thinking" visible via modeling, coaching, scaffolding, articulation, reflection, and exploration. Clinical teaching is described as a 3-stage process: creating a safe learning climate and modeling, coaching with decreasing supervision, and using articulation and exploration to stimulate self-directed learning. CA teaching methods informed the deductive arm of the reflexive thematic analysis, and the three identified areas of difference were reviewed through the lens of CA.
requirements: Instructors need to make expert thinking visible through the CA methods across the three phases of clinical teaching.
constraints: The article notes near-peers and faculty use CA methods to a similar degree, but near-peers spend more time creating a safe learning experience.
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in practical skills courses
target_learning_goals: Practical clinical skills such as clinical examination, history taking, cannulation, basic life support, and ultrasonography
examples: Vignettes depicting typical instructor actions were written for each phase of CA clinical teaching and used to prompt focus-group discussion.

citation: Schwartz A, Postareff L, Parpala A, Nokelainen P, Kosenkranius M, Puhakka I, Pylväs L, Rintala H, Räisänen M, Wallin A. (2025). An Intervention to Support Higher Education Teachers' Teaching Processes and Well-Being: Protocol for an Intervention Study. JMIR Research Protocols. https://doi.org/10.2196/65428
title: Constructivist curriculum framework guiding the intervention design
description: The intervention follows the framework of "Constructivist curriculum", in which "participants’ reflective learning process is guided by using social interaction, activating previous knowledge, authentic learning experiences, and cooperative dialogue". Every group meeting includes a discussion of the previous session's topics and participants' experiences, group discussions and individual reflection, and a closing learning discussion on Moodle in which participants reflect on what was important to them. The authors use this framework to justify structuring the intervention around guided reflections and group meetings that stimulate the social aspects of higher education teachers' reflection.
requirements: Group meetings with peer discussion, Moodle-based reflective learning discussions, and authentic learning experiences drawn from teachers' own recorded teaching
target_learners: higher education teachers in professional development
target_learning_goals: pedagogical development through reflective learning
adopting learning-focused teaching methods
examples: Each group meeting ends with participants joining a Moodle learning discussion reflecting on what was important for them after the session

article_title: Latent profiles of learning engagement and anxiety in high school students: the mediating role of academic self-efficacy.
citation: Zhou Tian, Zhou Xuejun, Wang Baozhu. (2025). Latent profiles of learning engagement and anxiety in high school students: the mediating role of academic self-efficacy. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-025-03114-z
title: Control-Value Theory as the framework linking engagement, self-efficacy, and learning anxiety
description: The article adopts Pekrun et al.'s Control-Value Theory as its explanatory framework, which 'integrates Expectancy-Value Theory, Attribution Theory, and Sense of Control Theory' and defines academic emotion as experience 'directly related to school learning, classroom interaction, and academic achievement'. Within this framework, the core source of learning anxiety stems from control and value assessments, with self-efficacy as the core component of control assessment. Engagement is posited to reinforce self-efficacy beliefs, reducing threatening cognitions and alleviating anxiety, which grounds the study's mediation hypothesis.
requirements: The framework presupposes that engagement accumulates successful learning experiences that reinforce self-efficacy beliefs, linking control assessment to emotional response.
target_learning_goals: understanding and reducing learning anxiety
supporting academic self-efficacy
examples: The study operationalized the theory as a multi-category mediation model based on latent profile analysis (Fig. 1).

article_title: Investigating the role of self-assessment in enhancing self-regulated learning amongst medical students in problem-based learning.
citation: Khoiriyah Umatul, Roberts Chris. (2025). Investigating the role of self-assessment in enhancing self-regulated learning amongst medical students in problem-based learning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07359-5
title: Combine structured self-assessment with external tutor feedback and opportunities to refine performance to support SRL
description: The article finds self-assessment's benefits are maximised when paired with constructive tutor feedback and opportunities for students to refine their performance. Qualitative findings showed students "sometimes struggled to determine the best way to improve without external input", and the authors state that "integrating self-assessment with tutor feedback can expedite the development of self-regulated learning skills". The principle operationalises the article's implementation steps: applying the tool continuously, providing external feedback from tutors, and providing students with opportunities to refine their performance.
requirements: Structured self-assessment content aligned with the tutorial context; tutors trained to deliver constructive written feedback; students given opportunities to refine their performance based on self-assessment outcomes
constraints: Tutor feedback was provided personally for each student, which the authors note "might be a confounding factor affecting the research results"
target_learners: novice medical students in PBL tutorials
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning, accurate self-evaluation, and improved tutorial performance
examples: Students completed the SSACT three times during the course and tutors provided written feedback each unit based on students' self-assessment and their own tutorial observations, without prior access to students' responses

citation: Mielke, I., Breil, S. M., Hissbach, J., Ehrhardt, M., & Knorr, M. (2025). Predicting undergraduate OSCE performance using traditional and construct-driven situational judgment tests at admission. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 30(3), 777–794. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-024-10379-3
title: Use construct-driven SJTs to supplement undergraduate medical admission with a theory-based assessment of social skills
description: The article concludes that construct-driven SJTs can supplement medical admission with a theory-based social-skills assessment that scales to large applicant numbers. Because single skill scores allow differentiated selection profiles and feedback, a construct-driven SJT measuring communion predicted OSCE Interaction performance beyond cognitive criteria and gender in the high-stakes sample. The authors recommend further research on generalizability and feasibility before admission use.
requirements: Further research on generalizability and feasibility (e.g., faking or creation of parallel test versions) is recommended before construct-driven SJTs are used for admission decisions
constraints: Evidence comes from one construct-driven SJT with agentic and communal scales; the agentic scale was unrelated to OSCE performance, and low-stakes results were null

examples: In the 2020 Hamburg admission cycle the HAM-SJT contributed 20% of the largest selection quota while the CD-SJT was administered for research with feedback provided to participants

title: COLOMASTER: a non-animal-tissue laparoscopic right hemicolectomy training simulator
description: COLOMASTER is a physical training kit for laparoscopic right hemicolectomy built from dry polyester fibers laminated with bonding technology and infiltrated with a conductive hydrosol so tissues can be dissected with an electric scalpel. It reproduces named vessels (ICA, MCA, ICV, SMV, ARCV, GCT, MCV) and organs, and "surgeons can train in all surgical steps of Lap-RHC," including complete mesocolic excision, central vascular ligation, and intracorporeal anastomosis with a linear stapler. The unit measures 450 x 320 x 80 mm, weighs 2.6 kg, and costs $2000.
requirements: Requires ultrasonically activated devices and linear staplers to perform the dissection and anastomosis steps as demonstrated
constraints: The article states COLOMASTER is not reusable; CME and CVL can only be performed once, though intracorporeal anastomosis can be practiced several times because the intestine is long
target_learners: surgeons training in laparoscopic right hemicolectomy
target_learning_goals: understanding of anatomical and membrane structures
complete mesocolic excision technique
central vascular ligation
intracorporeal anastomosis
examples: The demonstration used a lateral-to-medial approach: peritoneum dissected, mesentery detached from retroperitoneum, ICA/ICV clipped and ligated, vessels along the SMV dissected, and ileocolic anastomosis performed with an overlapping method and barbed suture closure

title: Five-feature dry-lab simulator design: bonded multilayer membranes, anatomical reproducibility, electrocautery-compatible materials, color-coded layers, and uniform kits
description: The article enumerates COLOMASTER's design characteristics as a reusable template for anatomy-faithful dry-lab simulators: "(1) a multilayered membrane structure created using bonding technology, (2) high reproducibility of human anatomy, (3) materials that can be dissected using an electric scalpel, (4) visualization of differences in the structure of the anatomical layers using colored polyester fibers, and (5) uniform training kits." Peeling strength is controlled via per-layer adhesive strength so learners can dissect along the correct layer, enabling CME training. Colored fibers make layer structure visible, which the authors say makes it ideal for resident training.
requirements: Bonding technology to control adhesive strength per layer; hydrosol infiltration to make fibers conductive for electric scalpel dissection
constraints: Materials and safety were confirmed in combustion experiments as previously described for SIGMASTER; the kit is single-use for CME and CVL steps

anatomical structure recognition

article_title: Self-transitioning or other-transitioning? The positive effects of LGBTQ + college students' positive coping and perceived academic support.
citation: Ma Chenwei, Li Jiangyu. (2025). Self-transitioning or other-transitioning? The positive effects of LGBTQ + college students' positive coping and perceived academic support. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07204-9
title: Conservation of Resources (COR) theory account of stress, coping, and academic disengagement in LGBTQ+ students
description: The article applies Conservation of Resources theory, under which "when individuals perceive stress, they take measures to prevent further depletion of personal resources". For LGBTQ+ college students, stress is framed as resource loss prompting reduced academic commitment, while proactive coping and perceived academic support act as protective resources that offset depletion. Combined with the minority stress model, COR explains both the main effects of stress and the two buffering moderations the study tests.
requirements: Perceived stress must be interpretable as perceived resource loss, as the article frames it for LGBTQ+ students in the Chinese context
constraints: The article applies COR within a cross-sectional, self-report study of Chinese LGBTQ+ college students; it does not test the theory's mechanisms longitudinally
target_learners: LGBTQ+ college students in Chinese higher education
target_learning_goals: Maintaining academic performance and psychological well-being under minority stress
examples: The study used COR and the sexual minority stress model to derive four hypotheses about stress, well-being, performance, and the two moderators
