title: Compositional and institutional effects framework for differences between school types
description: The article organizes its explanation of track differences with the framework by Baumert et al. (2006), under which "compositional and institutional effects account for differences among students attending different school types". Compositional effects arise because tracks differ in student‐body SES, migration background and ability mix, while institutional effects concern differences in teacher qualifications, equipment, curricula and instruction quality between academic and non‐academic track schools.
requirements: Explaining track differences requires accounting for both the composition of the student body (SES, migration background, ability mix) and institutional factors (teacher qualifications, equipment, curricula, instruction quality).
constraints: The article's own design "does not uncover the specific school‐related factors driving these differences"; it notes that "further research is needed to fully understand how these mechanisms function".

target_learning_goals: math competence development in secondary school

article_title: The role of video and direct laryngoscopy in medical student intubation training: a comparative study on success rates and learning curves.

title: Complementary learning-curve account of VL and DL skill acquisition
description: The article explains its findings through a learning-curve account: VL is "a more user-friendly and rapidly learnable method, particularly for novice learners", attributed to superior glottic visualization that helps novices identify anatomical structures. DL has "a steeper and longer" learning curve, "allowing users to achieve significant improvements with practice", so the two methods play complementary roles in training — VL for rapid initial success, DL for long-term skill development.

title: Cognitive-load framing of robotic surgical training linking workload, proficiency and EEG spectral markers
description: The article frames surgical skill learning through cognitive load theory: cognitive load is "the amount of finite working memory resources an individual must allocate to meet the cognitive demands of a task", and overload can harm surgical training. It links subjective workload (NASA TLX), performance, and EEG spectral power (beta for cognitive load, low-gamma for attention and motor engagement), arguing trained operators perform effectively at lower cognitive load as proficiency increases.

article_title: Gaze behavior and decision-making among handball referees: exploring gender and expertise differences.
citation: Świdwa, Jacek; Klatt, Stefanie; Kantanista, Adam. (2025). Gaze behavior and decision-making among handball referees: exploring gender and expertise differences. PeerJ. https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.19401
title: Cognitive-interpretation account of refereeing expertise: decision accuracy reflects experience-based interpretation of visual information, not gaze patterns
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that expertise differences in refereeing decisions arise from cognitive processing rather than visual search. Drawing on the information-reduction hypothesis, it proposes that "higher level referees use cognitive processes that allow them to process and extract relevant visual information, perhaps by more effectively comparing what they see to their long-term memory". The study's null gaze findings alongside significant accuracy differences are presented as support for this account over gaze-based explanations.
requirements: Referees must possess accumulated experience and domain knowledge that supports interpretation and categorization of visual game information
constraints: The account is advanced for laboratory video-based decision tasks; the article notes gaze behaviors can differ between laboratory and real-world settings due to varying task constraints
target_learning_goals: accurate rule-based decision-making in fast-paced match situations
examples: Higher-level referees made more correct decisions overall and in punishment scenarios while showing no significant differences in fixation or saccade measures

article_title: Teaching Self-efficacy and Teaching Methods in the Aquatic Environment.
citation: Fonseca-Pinto R and Moreno-Murcia JA (2024). Teaching Self-efficacy and Teaching Methods in the Aquatic Environment. F1000Research 13: 1363. https://doi.org/10.12688/f1000research.150535.1
title: Comprehensive Aquatic Method (MAC) as a constructivist, student-centred approach to aquatic education
description: The MAC, introduced by Moreno and Gutiérrez in 1998, is described as "a constructivist approach that centers on student interests and needs, promoting autonomy and interaction". It employs play as a medium, encourages problem-solving and exploration in aquatic environments, and develops knowledge, skills and attitudes contributing to student autonomy and personal growth. In the study it is measured with a validated 26-item scale and tested as a predictor of, and predictor by, teaching self-efficacy. constraints: The article notes there is no infallible method; methodology choice depends on content, learner age, autonomy and expected effects

target_learning_goals: Aquatic literacy and water competence
autonomy, problem-solving and decision-making in aquatic environments
examples: The study measured MAC use among 607 aquatic educators with a 26-item scale covering way of teaching, game and interpersonal style

article_title: Learning curve analysis of 100 consecutive robotic liver resections.
citation: Rahimli M, Gumbs AA, Perrakis A, Al-Madhi S, Dölling M, Stelter F, Lorenz E, Andric M, Franz M, Arend J, Croner RS. (2025). Learning curve analysis of 100 consecutive robotic liver resections. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-025-11551-5
title: Competency-proficiency-mastery framework for surgical learning curves, extended to a four-phase model
description: The article adopts the competency-proficiency-mastery framework proposed by Kuemmerli et al. for standardizing learning curve assessment in minimally invasive liver surgery, which identifies "operative time, blood loss, conversion rates, and complications as critical endpoints for assessing learning curves". Because the single-surgeon robotic series showed an additional transition when major resections began, the authors extended the three-phase model into four phases: Competency (cases 1–20), Proficiency (21–30), Early Mastery (31–65), and Full Mastery (66–100). The framework operationalizes skill acquisition through cumulative average curves of operation time and difficulty score plus phase-wise statistical testing.
requirements: A series of consecutive procedures by one surgeon with metrics such as operation time and a difficulty score amenable to cumulative average analysis and phase-wise regression
constraints: Derived from a retrospective, single-surgeon, single-center series; the authors state this "may constrain the generalizability of the results" and call for prospective multicentric trials
target_learners: surgeons in training or early adoption of robotic liver surgery
target_learning_goals: acquisition of proficiency and mastery in robotic liver resection
examples: The framework was applied to 100 consecutive robotic liver resections, with linear regression per phase and Kruskal–Wallis comparisons across phases

article_title: Study longer or study effectively? Better study strategies can compensate for less study time and predict goal achievement and lower negative affect.
citation: Theobald, M. (2025). Study longer or study effectively? Better study strategies can compensate for less study time and predict goal achievement and lower negative affect. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95, 405–420. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12725
title: Component model of self-regulated learning: study time yields good outcomes only when used effectively via metacognitive and resource management strategies
description: The article frames its hypotheses with the component model of self-regulated learning (Schmitz & Wiese, 2006), in which learning quantity (study time) and learning quality (strategy use) interactively predict goal achievement. Strategies are organized into metacognitive strategies (planning before learning, self-monitoring during and after learning) and resource management strategies regulating internal resources such as attention and motivation and external resources such as time. goal achievement

title: Cognitive load rationale for profession-tailored preparation in interprofessional emergency training
description: The article applies cognitive load theory to interprofessional team training: working memory has limited capacity and can be overloaded by too much learning activity at once, and the theory discriminates intrinsic, extraneous and germane cognitive load. It postulates a simple-to-complex educational design that fosters germane load by reducing intrinsic and extraneous load. In this context the authors argue that reducing intrinsic cognitive load requires profession-tailored instructional approaches and individual preparation rather than mixed-group teaching only, which motivated the profession-specific virtual patient versions.

article_title: Developing clinical reasoning along the cognitive continuum: a mixed methods evaluation of a novel Clinical Diagnosis Assessment.
citation: Ainge Lucinda E., Edgar Amanda K., Kirkman Jacqueline M., Armitage James A. (2025). Developing clinical reasoning along the cognitive continuum: a mixed methods evaluation of a novel Clinical Diagnosis Assessment. BMC Medical Education, Volume 25, Article 31. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06613-6
title: Cognitive continuum theory framing of clinical reasoning with task features shifting Type 1 and Type 2 processing
description: The article frames clinical reasoning using dual process theory together with cognitive continuum theory (CCT), which "describes intuitive and analytical thinking on opposite ends of a continuum". Most decisions are quasirational, with the balance depending on case ambiguity and diagnostic certainty. The article proposes that assessment task features — number of cues, duration of display, level of redundancy, and sequential versus simultaneous delivery — can be manipulated to induce processes at different loci on the continuum, making distinct thinking processes visible to students. The CDA operationalises this by restricting image display time to induce Type 1 thinking and requiring decision justification to prompt Type 2 thinking.
requirements: Assessment task features (type, amount, and display of clinical data) must be manipulated to shift the task's location on the continuum
constraints: The article notes a more in-depth analysis is required to understand when students utilize different strategies and what task features prompt different approaches
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
metacognitive awareness of Type 1 and Type 2 reasoning strategies
examples: Part 1 restricted display of ocular condition images to thirty seconds per image to evaluate Type 1 thinking, while Part 2 required decision justification within 40-minute simulated cases to prompt analytical Type 2 thinking.

article_title: "No pain, no gain": Simulation-based learning in teacher education: The mediating role of simulation hindrances.
citation: Levin, O., Frei-Landau, R., & Goldberg, C. (2025). "No pain, no gain": Simulation-based learning in teacher education: The mediating role of simulation hindrances. PLoS ONE, 20(1), e0317255. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0317255
title: Comfort-zone model applied to simulation-based learning: stretch, danger, and panic zones
description: The article applies the comfort-zone model to SBL in teacher education: leaving one's comfort zone produces stress whose extent is tied to learning efficacy. In this account, a controlled departure into a "stretch zone" promotes effective learning, but an uncontrolled departure in an insecure environment turns the stretch zone into a danger zone or panic zone "where no learning is possible". The study treats hindrances such as stress, embarrassment, and anxiety as the measurable expression of this departure, operationalized via the SLOTE hindrance factor.
requirements: Departure from the comfort zone must be controlled and occur in a secure simulation environment for the stretch zone to promote learning
constraints: If the departure is uncontrolled or the environment insecure, the stretch zone can become a danger or panic zone where no learning is possible
target_learning_goals: communication skills
collaborative learning insights
professional handling of conflictual situations
examples: The study measured hindrance experience via the SLOTE scale's simulation-related hindrances factor (α = .74) in clinical simulation workshops with professional actors

title: Control-Value Theory (Pekrun, 2006) as the review's overarching framework for emotions and achievement
description: Control-Value Theory is a conceptual framework illustrating the relationship between emotions and academic achievement through two appraisals: control and value. The review states "Control pertains to the perceived ability of a learner to exert influence over their learning activities and the results they achieve", while value relates to a student's perceived significance of these actions and results. Students with strong control and value appraisals experience positive emotions such as satisfaction and pride; those perceiving low control or worth experience adverse emotions such as fear and embarrassment, which then affect motivation, learning strategies and achievement. The review uses it to interpret its four finding categories and to guide intervention design.
requirements: Applicable in settings with high-stakes assessment where students' control and value appraisals can be identified and addressed
constraints: The review applies it as an interpretive lens for narrative synthesis, not as a directly tested model in the included studies
target_learning_goals: understanding how emotional appraisals influence motivation, learning strategies and academic achievement
key_sources: Alshareef N, Fletcher I, Giga S. (2024). The role of emotions in academic performance of undergraduate medical students: a narrative review. BMC Medical Education 24:907. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05894-1

article_title: Development of the Competency Evaluation Scale for Clinical Nutritionists in China: A Delphi Study.
citation: Zhou Ailin, Li Zhourong, Wang Tiankun, Wu Rongxin, Yang Shuang, Shi Zumin, Zeng Huan, Zhao Yong. (2024). Development of the Competency Evaluation Scale for Clinical Nutritionists in China: A Delphi Study. Nutrients. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162593
title: Competency Evaluation Scale for Clinical Nutritionists in China
description: A five-dimension competency evaluation instrument for clinical nutritionists developed via literature review, semi-structured interviews with ten experts, a two-round Delphi consultation, and AHP weighting. It comprises "five primary indicators, twelve secondary indicators, and sixty-six tertiary indicators" with printed weights for every indicator (Table 3). The authors state it "provides assessment criteria for the training and assessment of clinical nutritionists" and report high reliability and validity from a 30-respondent questionnaire survey.
requirements: Administration as a self-designed questionnaire taking approximately ten minutes, with respondents being practicing clinical nutritionists in secondary or higher level hospitals
constraints: Developed and validated only in the Sichuan and Chongqing regions; the article states it lacks real-world clinical application and warrants future surveys
target_learners: clinical nutritionists in secondary or higher level hospitals in China
target_learning_goals: assessment of professional theoretical knowledge, practical skills, humanistic practice, interpersonal communication, and professional development competencies
examples: Used in a cross-sectional questionnaire survey of clinical nutritionists in Sichuan and Chongqing distributed via the Questionnaire Star platform in October 2022
key_sources: Zhou Ailin, Li Zhourong, Wang Tiankun, Wu Rongxin, Yang Shuang, Shi Zumin, Zeng Huan, Zhao Yong. (2024). Development of the Competency Evaluation Scale for Clinical Nutritionists in China: A Delphi Study. Nutrients. https://doi.org/10.3390/nu16162593

article_title: [Agency: occupational therapists' perspectives on their sense of competence and their skills following training].
citation: Carrier Annie, Éthier Alexandra, Beaudoin Michaël, Hudon Anne, Bédard Denis, Jasmin Emmanuelle, Lavoie-Trudeau Étienne, Verville France. (2024). Agency: occupational therapists’ perspectives on their sense of competence and their skills following training. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.78346
title: Seven-hour co-development-based change-agent training for practising occupational therapists
description: A continuing-education workshop of seven hours built on a co-development pedagogical approach leveraging participants' prior experience. Its theoretical content covered four themes: "l’analyse du contexte de réalisation du projet de changement, le développement de partenariat, les stratégies de communication et la planification des actions". It was offered on seven days between January 19 and October 19, 2019, to occupational therapists recruited via professional association member lists, and evaluated with a pre-post questionnaire and group interviews.
requirements: Participants needed sufficient French comprehension, the training's language; there were no exclusion criteria
constraints: The training was not specifically focused on systemic injustices, though it addressed elements relevant to meso- and macro-system action
target_learning_goals: exercising agency as a change agent
effective communication
intentional collaboration
observation and analysis
action planning
examples: 103 occupational therapists completed the training and the pre-post questionnaire; 24 participated in five follow-up group interviews

article_title: An exploration of the relationship between active learning and student motivation in STEM: a mixed methods study.
citation: Stieha Vicki, Earl Brittnee, Hagens Harrisen, Haynes Meagan, Ulappa Amy, Bond Laura, Oxford Julia Thom. (2024). An exploration of the relationship between active learning and student motivation in STEM: a mixed methods study. Advances in Physiology Education. https://doi.org/10.1152/advan.00247.2022
title: COPUS teaching profiles: didactic, interactive lecture, and student-centered
description: The Classroom Observation Protocol for Undergraduate STEM (COPUS) codes instructor and student activity per 2-min period, and the COPUS Analyzer generates three teaching profiles. "Didactic classes were characterized by lecturing 80% or more of the time with minimal question and answer." Interactive lecture classes are mainly lecture with some group activities or clicker questions, and student-centered profiles use learner-centered strategies for most instructional time. In this study 31 observations across seven instructors were profiled, with most instructors falling into one profile across all observations.
requirements: Observations conducted by a trained observer using the COPUS protocol and COPUS Analyzer
constraints: Observations across all three profiles is atypical; the article notes 9% of COPUS observations vary that widely
target_learning_goals: characterizing active teaching practice in undergraduate courses
examples: INSTs E and F were recorded as didactic across all observations, INST B as interactive lecture, and INST G as student-centered
key_sources: Stieha Vicki, Earl Brittnee, Hagens Harrisen, Haynes Meagan, Ulappa Amy, Bond Laura, Oxford Julia Thom. (2024). An exploration of the relationship between active learning and student motivation in STEM: a mixed methods study. Advances in Physiology Education. https://doi.org/10.1152/advan.00247.2022

article_title: Optional Exam Retakes Reduce Anxiety but may Exacerbate Score Disparities Between Students with Different Social Identities.
citation: Supriya K., Bang Christofer, Ebie Jessica, Pagliarulo Christopher, Tucker Derek, Villegas Kaela, Wright Christian, Brownell Sara. (2024). Optional Exam Retakes Reduce Anxiety but may Exacerbate Score Disparities Between Students with Different Social Identities. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11440740/
title: Control value theory of achievement emotions as a framework for how exam retakes change anxiety and performance
description: Control value theory holds that two appraisals shape achievement emotions: students' perceived control over activities and outcomes, and the value they place on achievement activities and outcomes. The article applies it to hypothesize that "Having the opportunity to retake an exam may help a student feel more control over their exam performance and may also reduce the value associated with their performance on the first attempt", thereby reducing anxiety and improving scores. It also links stereotype threat to increased value and decreased control appraisals.
requirements: Applicable to instructional practices that change students' control and value appraisals, such as performance goal structures and assessment design
constraints: The theory posits negative activating emotions such as anxiety have an ambivalent effect on performance, though they often impact exam performance negatively
target_learners: undergraduate students in academic settings with high-stakes assessments
target_learning_goals: understanding and reducing test anxiety
improving exam performance through appraisal change
examples: The authors hypothesized retakes would increase perceived control and decrease the value of a single exam attempt, maximizing performance
Competitive norm-referenced grading is described as reducing perceived control compared with mastery goal structures
key_sources: Supriya K., Bang Christofer, Ebie Jessica, Pagliarulo Christopher, Tucker Derek, Villegas Kaela, Wright Christian, Brownell Sara. (2024). Optional Exam Retakes Reduce Anxiety but may Exacerbate Score Disparities Between Students with Different Social Identities. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11440740/

article_title: Increase in Newborns Ventilated Within the First Minute of Life and Reduced Mortality After Clinical Data-Guided Simulation Training.
citation: Vadla MS, Mduma ER, Kvaløy JT, Mdoe P, Hhoki BH, Sarangu S, Michael P, Oftedal B, Ersdal H. (2023). Increase in Newborns Ventilated Within the First Minute of Life and Reduced Mortality After Clinical Data-Guided Simulation Training. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000740
title: Sustain simulation-based training and QI efforts continuously, because clinical performance gains partially reverse once organized training stops
description: The article's 2-year postintervention follow-up showed that when monthly QI meetings stopped and simulation training decreased, the proportion of newborns ventilated within the Golden Minute fell and time to ventilation rose again. The authors conclude that "Improvements are partially reversed after intervention, highlighting the need for continuous simulation-based training and research into QI efforts essential for sustainable changes." The principle recommends maintaining organized, data-guided simulation training and QI structures rather than treating training campaigns as one-off events.
requirements: Ongoing local champions or facilitators to maintain frequent training
Continued clinical data feedback to keep performance gaps visible
constraints: The article notes the optimal frequency and structure of efforts to prevent skill loss may vary across clinical settings and requires further research
target_learners: Midwives and clinical teams in low-resource maternity settings
target_learning_goals: Retention of time-critical resuscitation skills and guideline adherence over time
examples: During the postintervention period there were no monthly QI meetings and less focus on frequent simulation-based training, and performance declined toward baseline levels
key_sources: Vadla MS, Mduma ER, Kvaløy JT, Mdoe P, Hhoki BH, Sarangu S, Michael P, Oftedal B, Ersdal H. (2023). Increase in Newborns Ventilated Within the First Minute of Life and Reduced Mortality After Clinical Data-Guided Simulation Training. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000740

article_title: Optimal Duration of High-Fidelity Simulator Training for Bronchoscope-Guided Intubation: A Noninferiority Randomized Trial.
citation: Jiang Luyang, Yang Qingyue, Li Qingyue, Jiang Bailin, Laba Ciren, Feng Yi. (2023). Optimal Duration of High-Fidelity Simulator Training for Bronchoscope-Guided Intubation: A Noninferiority Randomized Trial. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000739
title: Base simulator training duration on individual skill acquisition (competency) rather than fixed time
description: The article argues that simulation-based technical training should be based on skill acquisition rather than elapsed time: "simulation-based technical training does not need to be time-based; rather, it should be based on skill acquisition." Because trainees acquire skills at variable pace and further training contributes little once the learning curve asymptote is reached, individualized end points avoid unnecessarily lengthened training while providing adequate preparation. The trial supports this with noninferior clinical performance at roughly half the training time.
requirements: A way to measure individual performance repeatedly (e.g., automated simulator scoring) to determine when the individual learning goal is achieved
constraints: Whether the modality maintains skills as long as fixed training, and whether it works during retraining, was not established; learning decay and difficult airway management were not studied
target_learners: Novice trainees learning technical procedures via simulation, e.g., anesthesiology residents and interns
target_learning_goals: Technical procedural skill acquisition (FOB intubation) with efficient use of training time
examples: Group New trainees stopped simulator training once their individualized learning curve end point was achieved, averaging 28.4 minutes versus the fixed 60 minutes, and then performed clinical intubation noninferiorly
key_sources: Jiang Luyang, Yang Qingyue, Li Qingyue, Jiang Bailin, Laba Ciren, Feng Yi. (2023). Optimal Duration of High-Fidelity Simulator Training for Bronchoscope-Guided Intubation: A Noninferiority Randomized Trial. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000739

article_title: Prevalence of Dunning-Kruger effect in first semester medical students: a correlational study of self-assessment and actual academic performance.
citation: Knof Harald, Berndt Markus, Shiozawa Thomas. (2024). Prevalence of Dunning-Kruger effect in first semester medical students: a correlational study of self-assessment and actual academic performance. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11515314/
title: Provide opportunities for collaborative learning and social comparison so students can develop a social reference standard for calibrating their self-assessments
description: The article argues that "When collaborative learning occurs, students can compare with other group members, the knowledge levels of other learners can be related to one’s own, and thus students are able to develop a (social) reference standard" which "helps them to assess themselves adequately". It links the pandemic-era absence of such opportunities to unrealistic self-assessment and notes that realistic self-assessments increased as collaborative learning opportunities were increasingly created again. This principle is offered as an interpretation of the observed data rather than a tested intervention.
requirements: Collaborative learning formats must actually allow students to compare knowledge levels with group members
constraints: The article states this account is a discussion of possible influences under COVID-19 conditions, not a manipulated or tested variable in this study; the data must be seen in the light of the then present COVID-19 conditions
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment
realistic calibration of performance expectations
examples: In summer semester 2021 teaching was fully digital and collaborative learning significantly restricted; in winter 2021/22 and summer 2022 collaborative opportunities returned and realistic self-assessments, especially among male students, increased
key_sources: Knof Harald, Berndt Markus, Shiozawa Thomas. (2024). Prevalence of Dunning-Kruger effect in first semester medical students: a correlational study of self-assessment and actual academic performance. BMC Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11515314/

article_title: Research on the application of CBL combined with BOPPPS teaching mode in oral and maxillofacial surgery teaching: a randomized controlled study.
citation: Gao Ning, Fu Kun, Li Na, He Wei. (2024). Research on the application of CBL combined with BOPPPS teaching mode in oral and maxillofacial surgery teaching: a randomized controlled study. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-77432-4
title: Combine case-based learning with a structured session framework such as BOPPPS to strengthen clinical thinking in case-rich medical specialties
description: The article recommends combining CBL with the BOPPPS model because the pairing is "clinical cases-based and student-oriented, which can fully cultivate students' peculative thinking, strengthen the combination of teaching and clinical practice, improve teaching quality". CBL embeds core issues in a clinical case situation while BOPPPS supplies the session structure that makes objectives, pre-assessment, participatory case work, post-assessment, and summary explicit. The randomized comparison in this article supports higher theoretical and most clinical-thinking scores for the combined mode over lecture-based learning.
requirements: Clinical cases that can carry the core issues of the topic
A session structure with explicit objectives and assessment phases
Teachers willing to shift from lecture delivery to case facilitation
constraints: Evidence comes from one single-center randomized study of 38 master's students in one specialty over 12 months; the authors call for larger multicenter studies
target_learners: Medical and dental postgraduate students in clinical specialties
target_learning_goals: Clinical critical and speculative thinking
Basic theoretical knowledge and clinical case analysis
Adaptation to the clinical rhythm
examples: The experimental group followed the six BOPPPS phases with real cases at the core; the control group received traditional lecture-based teaching over the same 12-month course
key_sources: Gao Ning, Fu Kun, Li Na, He Wei. (2024). Research on the application of CBL combined with BOPPPS teaching mode in oral and maxillofacial surgery teaching: a randomized controlled study. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-77432-4

article_title: The links between experiential learning and 4E cognition.
citation: Lebert, A., & Vilarroya, Ó. (2024). The links between experiential learning and 4E cognition. Ann NY Acad Sci, 1541, 37–52. https://doi.org/10.1111/nyas.15238
title: Concrete experience as a bridging notion: an embodied, embedded, extended, and enactive engagement of an individual with their environment
description: The article proposes concrete experience, introduced by Kolb as a cornerstone of EL, as the concept bridging EL and 4E cognition. It offers a tentative definition: "A concrete experience refers to an embodied, embedded, extended, and enactive engagement of an individual with their environment." Engagement is understood as ongoing action in which the individual actively manages the stakes of the situation rather than passively receiving information; embodied engagement grounds experience in bodily sensorimotor features, embedded engagement focuses on the physical, social, and cultural context, extended engagement concerns how external resources and tools contribute, and enactive engagement identifies the meaningful aspects of the engagement.
requirements: Learning models must ground learning in concrete active engagements of learners with their environment for the bridging notion to apply
constraints: The article notes it is still unclear what a concrete experience amounts to in the Kolb model, calling this a key unresolved interpretive issue
target_learners: learners in experiential and active learning contexts across domains
target_learning_goals: integrating experiential, embodied, situated, extended, and enactive aspects of learning into a unified account of concrete experience
examples: The article aligns this definition with Kiefer and Trump's argument that reinstatements of sensory–motor memory traces are essential for memory performance.
key_sources: Lebert, A., & Vilarroya, Ó. (2024). The links between experiential learning and 4E cognition. Ann NY Acad Sci, 1541, 37–52. https://doi.org/10.1111/nyas.15238

article_title: Innovation and Competency Development in Occupational Therapy Fieldwork During the COVID-19 Pandemic.
citation: Gill Monique, Hunt Anne, Duncan Andrea. (2024). Innovation and Competency Development in Occupational Therapy Fieldwork During the COVID-19 Pandemic. Canadian Journal of Occupational Therapy. https://doi.org/10.1177/00084174231190768
title: Six-domain competency codebook drawn from the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada (2021) used to analyze fieldwork learning
description: The study deductively coded interview transcripts using the domains, competencies, and indicators of the Competencies for Occupational Therapists in Canada, operationalized in a codebook of six domains: OT expertise, excellence in practice, communication and collaboration, engagement with the profession, culture, equity and justice, and professional responsibility. For example, excellence in practice "Views OTs as lifelong learners, regularly self-evaluating and cognizant of external modifiers." Two researchers coded and resolved discrepancies to consensus.
requirements: Coding by two researchers with team discussion of discrepancies until consensus
constraints: The COTC document was introduced in 2021, in the midst of the study, and preceptors and students may not have been familiar with its newer language, domains, and indicators
target_learning_goals: clinical competency development across professional practice domains
examples: The codebook defined communication and collaboration as including explaining the role of OTs to other professions and learning workplace social culture, while explicitly excluding independence and initiative
key_sources: Gill Monique, Hunt Anne, Duncan Andrea. (2024). Innovation and Competency Development in Occupational Therapy Fieldwork During the COVID-19 Pandemic. Canadian Journal of Occupational Therapy. https://doi.org/10.1177/00084174231190768

article_title: Do the teaching, practice and assessment of clinical communication skills align?
citation: Dewi Sari Puspa, Amanda Wilson, Robbert Duvivier, Brian Kelly, Conor Gilligan. (2024). Do the teaching, practice and assessment of clinical communication skills align? BMC Medical Education 24:609. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05596-8
title: Constructive alignment as the evaluative lens for communication skills curricula
description: The article frames communication skills curricula through constructive alignment, defined as "aligning teaching methods, as well as assessment, to the intended learning outcomes". In medical education this alignment is meant to ensure students achieve communication outcomes needed for patient-centred care in diverse contexts. The study uses this framework to evaluate whether classroom teaching, clinical practice and OSCE assessment demand and reward the same communication skills, finding that alignment remains an elusive goal in many medical schools.
requirements: Intended learning outcomes must be specified so teaching methods and assessment can be aligned to them
constraints: The article notes achievement of constructive alignment remains elusive in many medical schools, with challenges aligning skills learnt, modelled and applied across environments
target_learning_goals: patient-centred clinical communication across diverse contexts
examples: The study evaluated alignment by observing the same students' communication in classroom workshops, real patient encounters and an OSCE station using the CCOG
key_sources: Dewi Sari Puspa, Amanda Wilson, Robbert Duvivier, Brian Kelly, Conor Gilligan. (2024). Do the teaching, practice and assessment of clinical communication skills align? BMC Medical Education 24:609. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05596-8

article_title: Exploring the responses of preclinical medical students and professors to flipped learning for the development of clinical reasoning.
citation: Si Jihyun. (2024). Exploring the responses of preclinical medical students and professors to flipped learning for the development of clinical reasoning. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2024.297
title: Cognitive load theory as rationale for scaffolding preclinical clinical reasoning with worksheets and collaboration
description: The article applies cognitive load theory to justify its design: because "a human has a limited-capacity information processing system," high intrinsic load from complex authentic cases can prevent learning in novices. The theory suggests instructional strategies including process worksheets, which "alleviate task difficulty by providing procedural information," and collaborative learning, which distributes intrinsic load across group members. The authors use this account to explain why illness script worksheets and group work within flipped learning appeared to ease the cognitive burden of novice students.
requirements: Novice learners facing complex tasks with high intrinsic cognitive load
constraints: The theory's capacity limitation applies only to novel information, per the article
target_learners: preclinical medical students as novice learners
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
managing intrinsic cognitive load in complex learning
examples: The authors state that illness script worksheets and collaborative learning in flipped learning appeared to alleviate the cognitive burden of novice students
key_sources: Si Jihyun. (2024). Exploring the responses of preclinical medical students and professors to flipped learning for the development of clinical reasoning. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2024.297

article_title: Evaluation of a 12-hole clock model for improving bronchoscopic skills in simulated normal and difficult airways among anesthesia residents: A randomized controlled study.
citation: Zhou Z, Zhang K, Zhao X, Hu Y, He Y, Wan L, Yao W. (2024). Evaluation of a 12-hole clock model for improving bronchoscopic skills in simulated normal and difficult airways among anesthesia residents: A randomized controlled study. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000038510
title: Cognitive load rationale for the clock model: increasing germane load via a familiar concept
description: The authors ground the model in cognitive load theory, which holds that working memory "can process only a limited number of informational elements at any given time" and classifies load as extraneous, intrinsic, and germane. The 12-hole clock model "increases intrinsic cognitive load by allowing for adjustment of the FOB in different directions," while the familiar 12-hour clock face may promote retention in long-term memory; the authors state this manages working memory load by increasing germane load to stimulate interest and improve performance.
requirements: A familiar anchoring concept (the standard 12-hour clock face) to support retention in long-term memory
constraints: Simple manikin tasks can produce a short-term learning plateau with insufficient intrinsic cognitive load for novices
target_learners: novice anesthesia residents learning bronchoscopic manipulation
target_learning_goals: FOB tip control in three-dimensional space
retention of manipulation skills in long-term memory
examples: Sequential manipulation from the 1st to 12th hole trains adjustments of the FOB in all directions, and the transparent box lets trainees observe FOB dynamics from outside the visual field
key_sources: Zhou Z, Zhang K, Zhao X, Hu Y, He Y, Wan L, Yao W. (2024). Evaluation of a 12-hole clock model for improving bronchoscopic skills in simulated normal and difficult airways among anesthesia residents: A randomized controlled study. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000038510

article_title: Does an instructional video as a stand-alone tool promote the acquisition of practical clinical skills? A randomised simulation research trial of skills acquisition and short-term retention.
citation: Ott Thomas, Demare Tim, Möhrke Julia, Silber Saskia, Schwab Johannes, Reuter Lukas, Westhphal Ruben, Schmidtmann Irene, Dietz Sven-Oliver, Pirlich Nina, Ziebart Alexander, Engelhard Kristin. (2024). Does an instructional video as a stand-alone tool promote the acquisition of practical clinical skills? A randomised simulation research trial of skills acquisition and short-term retention. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05714-6
title: Combine an instructional video with immediate hands-on self-study to optimise practical skill acquisition, irrespective of sequence
description: The article recommends pairing a stand-alone instructional video with unsupervised hands-on practice: "To optimise learning success, a combination of an instructional video with self-study is recommended, independent of the sequence of both teaching methods." In Study 2, both sequences produced mean scores of 16.5 of a possible 20, the highest scores in either study, against 14.8 for video alone and 7.7 for self-study alone at first exposure. The principle rests on a single simulation-based pair of trials in one procedural skill.
requirements: Access to a produced instructional video of the target procedure
Access to the device and a skill trainer for unsupervised hands-on exercise
Both methods performed in immediate succession before testing
constraints: Evidence comes from a simulation centre with last-year medical students learning humeral intraosseous access; generalizability is limited to laboratory conditions per the authors
The score used to measure performance was adapted from a validated tibial IOA checklist and not statistically validated
target_learners: undergraduate clinical trainees learning procedural skills
target_learning_goals: acquisition and short-term retention of practical clinical procedures (humeral intraosseous access)
examples: In Study 2, participants watched the ten-minute instructional video and then did ten minutes of unsupervised self-study (or the reverse order) immediately before testing, and both groups scored 16.5 points

article_title: The core competencies of a health education teacher.
citation: Paakkari, O., Kulmala, M., Lyyra, N., Saaranen, T., Lindfors, P., Tyrväinen, H. (2024). The core competencies of a health education teacher. Health Promotion International. https://doi.org/10.1093/heapro/daae078
title: Use defined health education teacher competencies to build competence-based curricula and support teacher self-evaluation
description: The article proposes that clearly defined competence domains and competencies serve as practical tools for programme development and teacher reflection. According to the authors, "The core competencies can be used to evaluate the content, emphasis, prioritization needs and future directions of HE teacher education programmes", and defined competencies can serve as a development and assessment tool for self-evaluation and reflection among pre- and in-service teachers. They argue clearly defined domains increase conceptual coherence and reduce the risk of fragmented teacher education programmes.
requirements: Identification of core health education competencies as a basis for competence-based curricula
constraints: The authors caution that defining individual competencies and domains can give a simplistic picture of the expertise required
target_learners: pre-service and in-service health education teachers
target_learning_goals: professional self-evaluation and reflection
teacher education programme development
examples: The study's 52-competency list and eight domains are offered for use in teacher education programmes, teaching development and self-evaluation

article_title: Perceived competence and related factors affecting the development of the clinical competence of nursing students at two university sites in Namibia: a cross-sectional study.
citation: Munangatire Takaedza, Jacob Victoria, Tomas Nestor. (2024). Perceived competence and related factors affecting the development of the clinical competence of nursing students at two university sites in Namibia: a cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education, 24, 743. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05729-z
title: Nursing students' self-reported competence improves as they progress through years of study, with fourth-year students reporting the highest competence.
description: This pattern describes the accumulation of knowledge, skills, and experience as students move from one year of study to the next, ultimately increasing their competence. Fourth-year students were more likely to report being competent than students in their first, second, or third years. The discussion notes it is not just the passing of the years but actual teaching and learning experiences that result in increased competence.
requirements: ongoing monitoring of nursing students' competence on an ongoing basis
constraints: the cross-tabulations show fourth-year students more likely to report competence, but the discussion cautions that actual teaching and learning experiences, not just passing years, drive the increase
target_learning_goals: clinical competence development across years of training
examples: the cited studies by Kang, Amsalu, and Sahin all reported that nursing students' competence improved as they progressed through their years of study

Perceived competence and related factors affecting the development of the clinical competence of nursing students at two university sites in Namibia: a cross-sectional study. article_title: Effect of Tronclass combined with team-based learning on nursing students' self-directed learning and academic performance: a pretest-posttest study.
citation: Hu Longyi, Li Siqi, Zhou Leshan. (2024). Effect of Tronclass combined with team-based learning on nursing students’ self-directed learning and academic performance: a pretest-posttest study. BMC Medical Education, Volume 24, Article 752. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05741-3
title: Combine an online learning platform with team-based learning so each method offsets the other's drawbacks
description: The article recommends combining the two methods because their weaknesses are complementary: platform learning upgrades self-management but “reduced communication between students to the detriment of teamwork”, while team-based learning “suffers from an uncontrollable division of labor among team members”. The proposed mechanism is anonymous platform scoring, which “can encourage nursing students to take the initiative to learn and reduce the possibility of an unbalanced division of labor”.
requirements: An online platform with anonymous peer-rating and automatic scoring and analysis functions, so teachers can give specific solutions depending on scoring details and devote more time to instruction.
constraints: The article states independent online learning “may weaken cooperation and communication abilities” and that team division of labor is uncontrollable without an anonymity mechanism; the supporting evidence comes from one course at one university without a parallel control group.
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning ability
academic performance
examples: The pediatric nursing course combined TC-delivered chapter videos, reflection questions and time-limited tests with team health-education and role-playing assignments graded by teachers and anonymous peer scoring.

article_title: Cost of simulation-based mastery learning for abdominal ultrasound.
citation: Post JH, Teslak KE, Tolsgaard MG, Rasmussen S, Friis ML. (2023). Cost of simulation-based mastery learning for abdominal ultrasound. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04919-5

description: The article sets the mastery level by the "contrasting groups method": radiologist experts completed the test once and their "median sum score... constituted the mastery learning level to be 85% of the maximum score". Trainees trained until the benchmark was reached "twice in a row", a criterion introduced "to reduce the chance of passing by coincidence and because expertise is characterized by consistency in performance". constraints: The mastery benchmark derived from one expert group completing the test once; the study was single-centre.

article_title: Variable practice is superior to self-directed training for laparoscopic simulator training: a randomized trial.
citation: Anishan V, Konge L, Bjerrum F. (2024). Variable practice is superior to self-directed training for laparoscopic simulator training: a randomized trial. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-10688-z
title: Contextual interference and desirable difficulties as the explanatory account of variable practice benefits
description: The article explains variable practice benefits through the contextual interference effect first hypothesized by Battig: variability causes an initial impairment of performance but stronger long-term retention and increased adaptability. It connects this to cognitive load theory, in which "learning is most effective when learners have enough mental capacity to reflect on the task they are learning (germane load)", and to the idea that "intentionally creating difficulties during training leads to an enhanced learning experience". The trial's SIM-TLX and feedback-timing findings are interpreted through this account.
requirements: Tasks must be practiced in random order rather than a pre-specified order
trainees must adapt to randomly assigned tasks, raising intrinsic load
constraints: Prior surgical studies with time- or repetition-limited training found mixed results and failed to demonstrate superiority of variable practice
the article states no clinical-setting transfer was examined
target_learners: novices without laparoscopic experience, e.g., medical students and junior doctors
target_learning_goals: psychomotor laparoscopic skills acquisition, transfer, and retention
examples: The intervention presented a unique string of tasks evenly distributed between four basic skills in random order, with each task removed once proficiency was reached twice within five consecutive attempts

title: Connectivism as a framework for explaining learning transfer from immersive VR simulation
description: The authors invoke Connectivism, which "proposes that people process information by forming connections and that people do not stop learning after completing their formal lessons", to explain why VR-trained students transferred skills to the real OSCE. They argue that in VR simulation "immersion, presence and interactivity combine to offer users an engaging learning environment free from distractions", that the HMD closes the user's senses from the real world so the brain believes the virtual world is real, and that the resulting conditions are ideal for learning and learning transfer.

constraints: The authors present this as an interpretive framework rather than a tested mechanism in this study

citation: Jee Marcus, Murphy Ella, Umana Etimbuk, O'Connor Paul, Khamoudes Daniel, McNicholl Brian, O'Donnell John J, James Binchy, Irish Trainee Emergency Research Network (ITERN). (2023). citation: Premo, J., Wyatt, B. N., Horn, M., & Wilson-Ashworth, H. (2022). Which Group Dynamics Matter: Social Predictors of Student Achievement in Team-Based Undergraduate Science Classrooms. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 21(3). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.21-06-0164
title: Conditional cooperation: students invest in peers when they perceive a return to their own learning
description: Conditional cooperation (drawing on interdependency theory and behavioral economics) holds that "individuals invest energy and resources into helping others in situations where they will receive a return." In this study, students were more willing to work with peers who directly contributed to the group's knowledge construction, supporting the idea that perceived learning benefit drives cooperative investment. The article frames this as a key mechanism for understanding which group dynamics sustain effective collaboration in GI classrooms.

constraints: The exact mechanism of the type of benefit students perceive was not directly measured in this study

target_learning_goals: willingness to collaborate effectively in group work
examples: Regression models showed contributions (B = 0.59 biology, B = 0.48 chemistry) and personal connection (B = 0.51 biology, B = 0.43 chemistry) predicted continued willingness to work with a student.

title: Definitions of cognitive training, near transfer, and far transfer
description: The article defines cognitive training as "interventions using cognitive tasks or intellectually demanding activities, the goal of which is to enhance general cognitive ability," deliberately covering brain-training tasks plus music learning and video-game playing. It defines near transfer as generalization across closely related domains (e.g., algebra to geometry) and far transfer as generalization across loosely related domains (e.g., algebra to Chinese), with graded variants such as "nearest transfer." These definitions frame the empirical question of whether cognitive-training methods, taken as a group, yield far-transfer benefits.
requirements: Definitions must be applied consistently across studies for meta-analytic integration
constraints: The transfer classification is qualitative and admits some ambiguous cases

academic achievement

Simulation is positioned as an important and effective supplement that addresses the shortage of clinical practice opportunities, not a wholesale replacement for real-patient experience.

application of theoretical knowledge in clinical practice

article_title: A 'compensatory selection' effect with standardized tests: Lack of correlation between test scores and success is evidence that test scores are predictive of success.
citation: Huber David E., Cohen Andrew L., Staub Adrian. (2022). Compensatory selection with standardized tests. PLoS ONE 17(5): e0265459. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0265459
title: Compensatory selection: a collider-bias effect in multi-predictor selective admissions
description: The article introduces compensatory selection: when a selective admissions process lets strong values on some application components offset weak values on others, selection "introduces a negative correlation between test scores and other predictors among those admitted (a 'collider bias' or 'Berkson's paradox' effect)". This negative covariance among predictors distorts the observed correlation between any single predictor, such as a standardized test, and later academic success, eliminating positive correlations for valid predictors and creating spurious negative correlations for invalid ones.
requirements: "that the standardized test is not perfectly correlated with other measures"
"that admissions committees use multiple predictors in a compensatory manner"
constraints: "these simulations assumed that all degree programs adopt the same procedures and provide the same level of support"
"The present simulations are an existence proof regarding a 'compensatory selection' effect when evaluating standardized scores"
target_learning_goals: correctly interpreting correlations between standardized test scores and subsequent academic success in selectively admitted samples
examples: Simulations of a 10,000,000-applicant pool under four ground truths and three admissions policies, with degree completion as the binary outcome
key_sources: Huber David E., Cohen Andrew L., Staub Adrian. (2022). Compensatory selection with standardized tests. PLoS ONE 17(5): e0265459. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0265459

title: CompensatorySelection simulation code (commented Matlab, GitHub)
description: The article's released artifact is the commented Matlab code implementing the applicant-pool simulations, including latent characteristics, four observed predictors, measurement noise, and alternative admissions policies. The article states "The computer code for these simulations can be found on the first author's GitHub account", allowing readers to reproduce or extend the reported ground-truth conditions and selectivity sweeps.
requirements: Commented Matlab code, available at the first author's GitHub account, to run the applicant-pool simulations
constraints: "This study only involves computer simulations"; no human applicant data were analyzed
target_learning_goals: reproducing and extending simulations of how compensatory selection distorts predictive-validity correlations
examples: Simulations varying number of latent characteristics, factor loadings, admissions policies, selectivity levels, measurement noise, and functional forms

citation: Lin Zi-mei, Hong Yu-rong, Liu Chun-mei, Luo Zhi-yan, Zhang Ying, Xie Xiao-jie, Huang Pin-tong. (2022). PBL teaching in ultrasonography resident standardization training in the COVID-19 pandemic. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03555-9
title: Combine PBL with LBL rather than using PBL alone when online training must cover basic theory
description: The article recommends pairing problem-based learning with lecture-based learning so that basic theory coverage is not lost when teaching moves online. The authors state "That is why we applied the combination of the PBL and LBL methods in the observation group rather than use the PBL method alone", because insufficient time in PBL to cover basic US feature interpretation carries "the risks of ignoring theory." The combination significantly improved theoretical and practical performance and satisfaction in their resident cohort.
requirements: Identical standardized teaching content across methods
Online delivery infrastructure (e.g., teleconferencing and video archives) for lectures and demonstrations
constraints: Evidence comes from a small, single-center study of years 2–3 US residents; the authors caution that residents of other majors should be included in future research
target_learners: US residents in standardization training during disrupted face-to-face teaching
target_learning_goals: theoretical knowledge of liver, gallbladder, pancreatic and spleen sonography
practical ultrasound examination skills
examples: The observation group received LBL lectures plus PBL discussions in a 30-day online program; the control group received LBL alone

article_title: Resuscitation simulation among people who are likely to witness opioid overdose: Experiences from the SOONER Trial.

(2022). Resuscitation simulation among people who are likely to witness opioid overdose: Experiences from the SOONER Trial. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0270829
title: Communities of practice among people who use drugs in the context of overdose response
description: The article invokes Etienne Wenger's communities of practice, "a group that shares a concern or passion for something they do and learn how to do it better as they interact regularly", and proposes such communities may exist among people who use drugs around overdose response. Participants reported primarily acquiring resuscitation skills by responding to real overdoses and learning from others' experiences, suggesting simulation-based education could support these existing community efforts.
requirements: Regular interaction around a shared concern; participants reported learning from the experiences of others in their communities
constraints: The term is most used in academic settings; the article presents the application as a notion supported by participants' accounts, not a tested result
target_learners: People who use opioids and their communities
target_learning_goals: Acquisition and maintenance of overdose resuscitation skills
examples: Participants described shelters where overdoses occur daily as settings where response experience circulates

article_title: Putting self-regulated learning in context: Integrating self-, co-, and socially shared regulation of learning.
citation: Bransen D, Govaerts MJB, Panadero E, Sluijsmans DMA, Driessen EW. (2022). Putting self‐regulated learning in context: Integrating self‐, co‐, and socially shared regulation of learning. Med Educ. 2022;56(1):29–36. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.14566
title: Co-regulated learning as unevenly distributed social regulation mediated through interaction
description: The article defines co-regulated learning (CRL) as capturing social and contextual influences on regulation, coined in the late 1990s from sociocultural learning theories. CRL 'refers to non‐reciprocal engagement in regulatory processes and activities, with the co‐regulator guiding the regulation of the co‐regulated', making it an unevenly distributed form of social regulation. Learners can trigger CRL by summarising, requesting information, giving explanations, paraphrasing, or giving prompts for thinking and reflection; the unit of analysis is always the interaction between individual and context.
requirements: Social interactions between learners or professionals through which regulatory processes are mediated
constraints: Power dynamics in hierarchical relationships or perceived expertise differences may influence the nature and potentially effectiveness of CRL; peer co-regulation may differ substantially from supervisors' CRL
target_learning_goals: mediation of metacognitive and cognitive activities
development of self-regulatory learning skills
examples: Box 1 describes a supervising surgeon co-regulating a student's wound-closure learning across strategic planning, monitoring, and reflection

article_title: A novel retraining strategy of chest compression skills for infant CPR results in high skill retention for longer.
citation: Gugelmin-Almeida Debora, Jones Michael, Clark Carol, Rolfe Ursula, Williams Jonathan. (2022). A novel retraining strategy of chest compression skills for infant CPR results in high skill retention for longer. European Journal of Pediatrics 181(12):4101-4109. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00431-022-04625-2
title: Base CPR retraining schedules on individual performance (competence-based) rather than pre-set intervals for everyone
description: The article argues that retraining at predefined intervals ignores the degree of learning already achieved, and that a competence-based design grounded in the 'mastery learning strategy' individualizes retraining: learners practice, receive feedback and repeat assessments until a predefined competence level is reached. The authors state that 'a more nuanced approach to iCPR retraining, based on an individuals' performance is recommended' to maximize retention and reduce costs. In the study, monthly assessments continued only until two consecutive passes were achieved.
requirements: A quantitative, criterion-referenced assessment of performance (here, four instrumented chest-compression quality metrics on a mannequin) to determine when competence is reached
constraints: Assessments were individually performed in a simulated environment for two minutes only; participants were not exposed to the stress, distractions or fatigue of real-life CPR, limiting transferability of the results to real-life performance
target_learners: university healthcare students with no previous pediatric CPR training
target_learning_goals: psychomotor skill competence in infant chest compression (depth, rate, recoil, duty cycle)
examples: Participants returned for monthly two-minute mannequin assessments until passing twice consecutively; each 'FAIL' earned up to six minutes of practice with real-time feedback

The authors argue this matters because human resources are the main limitation to implementing full-scale simulation. Omitting confederates could ease implementation without measurable performance cost.

article_title: Determining the effects of blended learning using the community of inquiry on nursing students' learning gains in sudden patient deterioration module.
citation: Liu Weichu, Wang Jun, Zhang Han, Yu Changfeng, Liu Shuai, Zhang Cen, Yu Jingya, Liu Qiao, Yang Bing. (2021). Determining the effects of blended learning using the community of inquiry on nursing students' learning gains in sudden patient deterioration module. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.914
title: Community of Inquiry framework with social, cognitive and teaching presence
description: The community of inquiry (CoI) framework is a student-centred teaching model for online and blended education. The article states that "The CoI framework is a student‐centred teaching model that assumes learning occurs within the community through the interaction of these three core elements (Stenbom, 2018)." The three presences interact: social presence supports trusting communication, cognitive presence supports constructing and confirming meaning through reflection and discourse, and teaching presence designs and directs the other two. The authors use CoI to structure their blended SPD module and interpret their outcome differences through it.
requirements: Learning must occur within a community through interaction of the three presence elements, with learning groups, online forums and teacher-student interaction in place.
constraints: The framework is described as mainly implemented in online environments, and the article notes concern that the distancing and virtual nature of a programme may hinder development of advanced communication skills needed in nursing programmes.
target_learners: Undergraduate nursing students in a sudden patient deterioration module
target_learning_goals: Integration of knowledge, skills, clinical reasoning and teamwork for recognising and responding to deteriorating patients
examples: The experimental group's SPD module was structured in four steps: learning groups with online forums, self-directed online and virtual skills learning, group discussion, and team skill practice in a simulation laboratory.

article_title: The Effect of Educational Intervention on the Improvement of Nontechnical Skills in Circulating Nurses.
citation: Kalantari Reza, Zamanian Zahra, Hasanshahi Mehdi, Faghihi Seyed Aliakbar, Jamali Jamshid, Niakan Hadi. (2021). The Effect of Educational Intervention on the Improvement of Nontechnical Skills in Circulating Nurses. BioMed Research International. https://doi.org/10.1155/2021/5856730
title: Complement nontechnical skills education with policymaking and hierarchy correction when training alone does not suffice
description: Because some behaviors (e.g., not using mobile phones, avoiding unnecessary exits, warning surgeons) did not improve or stayed below average after training, the article argues education alone may be insufficient. It states that "educational intervention may not be sufficient for improvement of all nontechnical skills, and policymaking can be considered another way for enhancing these behaviors" and that correcting existing operating room hierarchies can let circulating nurses show their skills. Undergraduate education about nontechnical skills in early training is also recommended.
requirements: Organizational willingness to enact policies and correct operating room hierarchies alongside training
constraints: Grounded in a context where operating room hierarchies in Iranian hospitals prevent nurses from warning surgeons
target_learning_goals: sustained improvement of nontechnical skill behaviors such as maintaining standards and assertiveness
examples: The article recommends policymaking, retraining programs, and sufficient educational materials in the early years of circulating nurse training

article_title: A rollercoaster of emotions: An integrative review of emotions and its impact on health professional students' learning in simulation-based education.
citation: Madsgaard, A., Smith‐Strøm, H., Hunskår, I., & Røykenes, K. (2022). A rollercoaster of emotions: An integrative review of emotions and its impact on health professional students' learning in simulation‐based education. Nursing Open, 9, 108–121. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.1100
title: Educators should consider the full range of students' emotions, including curiosity, interest and confusion, when planning and performing simulation-based education
description: The review recommends that educators move beyond the usual recommendation of simply reducing stress in SBE. Because simulation "can trigger multiple and changing emotions", educators "should consider the full range of students' emotions when planning and performing SBE", and should also "consider using SBE to trigger comprehensive emotions that can benefit students' learning such as curiosity, interest and confusion". The black-and-white perspective that stress and anxiety only harm learning may be misleading.
requirements: Educators must plan and perform SBE with awareness that a wider spectrum of emotions than stress and anxiety occurs in simulation
constraints: The review found no unilateral empirical proof for promoting positively or negatively loaded emotions to limit or enhance learning; the role of arousal needs further clarification
target_learners: Health professional students (nursing, medicine, pharmacy and allied professions)
target_learning_goals: Clinical skills, clinical reasoning, critical thinking and professional learning outcomes in simulation
examples: The review's synthesis showed simulation can trigger curiosity, frustration, confusion and surprise, and recommends future research on how to scaffold scenarios to trigger such academic emotions.

article_title: The Effect of a Paired Lab on Course Completion and Grades in Nonmajors Introductory Biology.
citation: DeFeo, D. J., Bibler, A., & Gerken, S. (2020). The Effect of a Paired Lab on Course Completion and Grades in Nonmajors Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(3). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.20-03-0041
title: Studies of lab effects on content outcomes should condition on selection, since self-selection inflates apparent lab benefits
description: Because labs are almost always paired with lecture and students self-select into them, prior small studies comparing pedagogies within labs confound the lab treatment itself. The authors apply a bounding strategy comparing unconditional and conditional correlations across increasingly restrictive regressions with lecture-section fixed effects and student covariates, arguing that if the correlation shrinks as controls are added, "selection bias is inflating the correlation." This design moves observational studies toward more credible causal interpretation.
requirements: Institutional data with student demographics, academic records, and lecture-section identifiers; a setting where lab enrollment is optional or nonconcurrent
constraints: Still cannot rule out bias from unobserved characteristics such as motivation; falls short of randomized assignment
target_learners: Undergraduate students in introductory science courses
target_learning_goals: Course completion and final grades in the lecture component
examples: The authors replicated Matz et al.'s (2012) correlational approach but included more variables in the regression, and applied Altonji et al.'s (2005) coefficient-stability logic across 291 lecture sections
key_sources: DeFeo, D. J., Bibler, A., & Gerken, S. (2020). The Effect of a Paired Lab on Course Completion and Grades in Nonmajors Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education, 19(3). https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.20-03-0041

citation: Jaber Mohamed, Al-Samarrai Basim, Salah Afraa, Varma Sudhir Rama, Karobari Mohmed Isaqali, Marya Anand. (2022). Does General and Specific Traits of Personality Predict Students' Academic Performance? BioMed Research International. https://doi.org/10.1155/2022/9422299
title: Use conscientiousness profiling, including its narrow facets, to inform dental student selection decisions
description: The article recommends that administrators consider basing selection decisions on conscientiousness measures: "With accumulating knowledge about facets and their correlates, administrators may base their selection decisions on facets of conscientiousness." It grounds this in the finding that conscientiousness and its dutifulness, competence and achievement facets predicted GPA and clinical marks, and that narrow traits added incremental validity. The authors present this as promising but not yet definitive.
requirements: A psychometrically sound, valid personality measure must be used, as prior authors recommended, and robust facet measures with high convergent and discriminant validity
constraints: The authors state a prospective study with a larger, multicenter sample would be required for a definite answer on selection use
This study was confined to one cohort of one dental college in one country, limiting generalizability, and face-to-face personality measurement may have introduced response bias
target_learners: Fifth-year dental students in undergraduate dental programs
target_learning_goals: Predicting and supporting students' academic and clinical performance in dental education
examples: The study used the BFI 44-item inventory and NEO-PI-R conscientiousness facet scales with fifth-year dental students, correlating scores with weighted GPA and clinical dentistry course grades

article_title: Youth well-being predicts later academic success.
citation: Cárdenas, D., Lattimore, F., Steinberg, D., & Reynolds, K. J. (2022). Youth well-being predicts later academic success. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-022-05780-0
title: Composite subjective well-being index combining positive affect and reversed negative affect
description: The article constructs a composite subjective well-being score meant to match the theoretical definition of subjective well-being as the presence of positive affect and the absence of negative affect. It standardises the three measured dimensions (depression, anxiety, positive affect) and combines them: "we standardised the subjective well-being dimensions and created a composite score (using the first principal component of a principal component analysis of these constructs)". Because positive and negative affect are also distinct, the article additionally tests each component separately.
requirements: Requires standardised measures of positive affect and negative affect (depression and anxiety) that can be combined via principal component analysis
constraints: Life satisfaction, part of the theoretical construct of subjective well-being, is not measured in this study
target_learning_goals: quantifying the relationship between student well-being and later academic achievement
examples: Grade-8 students completed the SCARED anxiety subscale, the CES-D 10-item short form, and the MHI Australian Adolescent positive-affect subscale in an annual school climate survey

article_title: A constructivist-based proposal for bioinformatics teaching practices during lockdown.
citation: Gallardo-Alba Cristóbal, Grüning Björn, Serrano-Solano Beatriz. (2021). A constructivist-based proposal for bioinformatics teaching practices during lockdown. PLoS Computational Biology. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008922
title: Constructivism and social constructivism as the philosophy of learning for distance bioinformatics education
description: The article adopts constructivism as the philosophy of learning for distance bioinformatics education: knowledge acquisition is 'a dynamic process which must be led by the learner through experience, discussion, and reflection'. Social constructivism adds that construction 'takes place more efficiently in a social context, where ideas can be shared and challenged', grounding recommendations on technology, teaching practices, learning communities, and motivation.
requirements: Teachers must identify common misconceptions and guide students in building the conceptual foundation that helps them 'develop their learning process autonomously'.
constraints: The article notes that although constructivism has profoundly influenced science and mathematics teaching, 'its applicability to computer science–related fields has received much less attention'.
target_learning_goals: autonomous thinking
construction of conceptual foundations for solving biological problems
examples: The article points to publications analysing computer science educational practices from a constructivist point of view, 'includ[ing] Ben-Ari (2001), Chesnevar and colleagues (2004), Connolly (2006), and Feliciano (2015)'.
