article_title: A constructivist-based proposal for bioinformatics teaching practices during lockdown.
citation: Gallardo-Alba Cristóbal, Grüning Björn, Serrano-Solano Beatriz. (2021). A constructivist-based proposal for bioinformatics teaching practices during lockdown. PLoS Computational Biology. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008922
title: Practical tips for constructivist online bioinformatics teaching: active learning, motivation, clarity, flexibility, bidirectional channels, and community building
description: Box 1 condenses the article's practical recommendations for bioinformatics instructors: 'Make the learning process active and dynamic', 'Keep the motivation up' with real-life problems and students' personal learning goals, 'Be clear', 'Be flexible' by letting students control the pace, avoid hierarchical media because 'Bidirectional communication promotes critical thinking', match synchronous and asynchronous channels to their purposes, and build a cooperative community.
requirements: Instructors should act 'as a facilitator rather than as an authority on the subject', establishing a cooperative environment in which students can self-organize the learning process from given guidelines.
constraints: Web-based environments require 'deep cultural shifts, such as sharing control of the learning process, which can result in a loss of teacher's professional identity', usually linked to higher stress.
target_learning_goals: student engagement and motivation in online courses
autonomous thinking
examples: Box 1 advises instructors to 'Make the learning process active and dynamic' by boosting discussion and reflection, and to 'Build a community' that encourages constructive discussion and sharing of ideas.
key_sources: Gallardo-Alba Cristóbal, Grüning Björn, Serrano-Solano Beatriz. (2021). A constructivist-based proposal for bioinformatics teaching practices during lockdown. PLoS Computational Biology. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008922

article_title: Long experience with a web-based, interactive, conversational virtual patient case simulation for medical students' evaluation: comparison with oral examination.
citation: Oliven Arie, Nave Rachel, Baruch Adam. (2021). Long experience with a web-based, interactive, conversational virtual patient case simulation for medical students' evaluation: comparison with oral examination. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2021.1946896
title: Conversational web-based virtual patient level-II system for complete patient management training and assessment
description: A web-based, OSCE-like virtual patient system in which students "conduct a free dialog with the VP, based on natural language processing, with a lexicon of keywords", writing medically relevant questions in free wording rather than choosing from question lists. Level-II covers complete patient management from history and physical through laboratory, imaging, other diagnostic procedures and treatment, with feedback lists of asked/ordered and missing items, a practice grade per case, and automatic production of item difficulty, point biserial correlation and Cronbach's alpha. More than 200 VP cases were compiled.
requirements: Requires preparation of cases with a keyword lexicon enabling the VP to understand questions in various formulations, which the authors call the most complex part of creating a new case
Requires exam security measures such as a lock-down browser and identity verification when used for assessment
constraints: Does not enable practicing or evaluating true physical examination or interpersonal communication skills
Students need practice with the system before using it for an exam
target_learners: fourth-year medical students during the internal medicine clerkship
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning and patient management
history taking and physical examination decision-making
diagnostic and therapeutic decision-making
patient safety
examples: Used regularly during the internal medicine clerkship for both practice cases and the final level-II exam, with five cases presented sequentially per exam and 25–45 minutes per case
key_sources: Oliven Arie, Nave Rachel, Baruch Adam. (2021). Long experience with a web-based, interactive, conversational virtual patient case simulation for medical students' evaluation: comparison with oral examination. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2021.1946896

article_title: Competences in the training of nurses to assist the airway of adult patients in urgency and emergency situations.
citation: Miranda Fernanda Berchelli Girão; Alves Gerson Pereira-Junior; Mazzo Alessandra. (2021). Competences in the training of nurses to assist the airway of adult patients in urgency and emergency situations. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.3380.3434
title: Competence frameworks and EPAs as a competence-based model for training and assessment
description: The article grounds its material in two complementary constructs. "Competence frameworks are descriptions of the knowledge, skills and attitudes for each of the competences expected during student training", demonstrated repeatedly across clinical environments of different complexity. "The EPAs are characterized as an evolution of the educational concept based on competences, in which the concept of competences of an apprentice is applied in specific contexts in the workplace", operationally defining a profession through specific tasks in a plannable period. The study applies this model by mapping frameworks and EPAs onto essential competence domains for nurse airway care.
requirements: Competences must be demonstrated repeatedly throughout training in clinical environments of different complexity levels
constraints: The authors note competency-based education is "on a new path to education that has not yet fully developed"
target_learners: nursing students and novice nurses in urgency and emergency training
target_learning_goals: integration of knowledge, skills and attitudes in airway management competence
examples: The study's Figures 1 and 2 associate the competence frameworks with essential competence domains and EPAs 1-6
key_sources: Miranda Fernanda Berchelli Girão; Alves Gerson Pereira-Junior; Mazzo Alessandra. (2021). Competences in the training of nurses to assist the airway of adult patients in urgency and emergency situations. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.3380.3434

article_title: Effects of using a cognitive aid on content and feasibility of debriefings of simulated emergencies.
citation: Freytag J, Stroben F, Hautz WE, Penders D, Kämmer JE. (2021). Effects of using a cognitive aid on content and feasibility of debriefings of simulated emergencies. GMS J Med Educ 38(5):Doc95. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2021-38/zma001491.shtml
title: Use a structuring cognitive aid such as TeamTAG to predefine thematic focus and support time management when specific learning objectives or inexperienced instructors are involved
description: The article concludes that "Cognitive aids such as TeamTAG can be used to predefine thematic focuses and the structure of debriefings and thus help to adapt them to the different levels of learners", and that "the use of a guideline supports time management during debriefings". It recommends this approach when certain learning objectives are to be achieved, for example when teaching the basics of teamwork, and as a further argument for inexperienced instructors or debriefings with little time available.
requirements: A trained facilitator who has received an introduction to the guideline and the CRM concept
constraints: A difference in learning outcomes (quality of teamwork) could not be identified; debriefing effects remain highly dependent on the instructor; guideline-free debriefing may be more learner-focused and suit more experienced participants and facilitators
target_learners: Medical students in simulation-based emergency training
target_learning_goals: Consistent coverage of selected teamwork (CRM) learning objectives in debriefings
examples: Facilitators in the intervention condition discussed a median of 5 of the six TeamTAG principles versus a median of 3 in control, and reported the guideline helped them conduct and time the debriefing
key_sources: Freytag J, Stroben F, Hautz WE, Penders D, Kämmer JE. (2021). Effects of using a cognitive aid on content and feasibility of debriefings of simulated emergencies. GMS J Med Educ 38(5):Doc95. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2021-38/zma001491.shtml

article_title: Comparing the effectiveness of augmented reality-based and conventional instructions during single ECMO cannulation training.
citation: Wolf Julian, Wolfer Viviane, Halbe Maximilian, Maisano Francesco, Lohmeyer Quentin, Meboldt Mirko. (2021). Comparing the effectiveness of augmented reality-based and conventional instructions during single ECMO cannulation training. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-021-02408-y
title: Provide step-by-step instructions contextually and in close proximity to the point of execution during procedural skills training
description: The article argues that AR step-by-step instructions offer two chief advantages during task execution: "contextual information, which reduces complexity to manageable increments", and "the proximity of information", which lets learners continuously check their execution against the tutorial in real time and adjust behavior. The error results, concentrated in knowledge errors, agree with this assumption, and the authors expect fewer errors to lead to fewer necessary training iterations and less supervision.
requirements: Instructions must be consultable during execution without leaving the task, e.g., via an OST-HMD; the article also recommends integrating video-skip functionality and currently missing steps like ultrasound verification or guidance
constraints: Benefits emerged for the more complex procedure; for the first, low-complexity procedure no large differences were found, and findings rest on a single training iteration with only 21 medical students, with long-term effects not explored
target_learners: medical students and physicians training for surgical procedures such as ECMO cannulation
target_learning_goals: accurate execution of multi-step surgical procedures; fewer knowledge-related errors during training
examples: Participants using AR switched regularly between the displayed information and the point of execution, while conventional-instruction users consulted instructions less frequently but spent more time per consultation
key_sources: Wolf Julian, Wolfer Viviane, Halbe Maximilian, Maisano Francesco, Lohmeyer Quentin, Meboldt Mirko. (2021). Comparing the effectiveness of augmented reality-based and conventional instructions during single ECMO cannulation training. International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-021-02408-y

article_title: Effectiveness of a standard clinical training program in new graduate nurses' competencies in Vietnam: A quasi-experimental longitudinal study with a difference-in-differences design.
citation: Horii Satoko, Nguyen Chinh Thi Minh, Pham Huong Thi Thu, Amaike Naomi, Ho Hien Thi, Aiga Hirotsugu. (2021). Effectiveness of a standard clinical training program in new graduate nurses’ competencies in Vietnam: A quasi-experimental longitudinal study with a difference-in-differences design. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0254238
title: Competency questionnaire based on the Basic Competency Standard for Vietnamese Nurses (110 indicators, 25 competencies)
description: A web-based self-administered questionnaire developed for this study because no competency assessment tool was readily available for Vietnamese nurses. "To assess the levels of 25 competencies, the scores for the 110 competency indicators were self-determined by new graduate nurses" on a three-point scale (0 = cannot do, 1 = can do with assistance, 2 = can do independently). Competency scores are means of their indicators (0–2 points) and the total score sums the 25 competencies (0–6 points). Internal consistency was high: total scale Cronbach's α = 0.98, with domain subscales 0.97, 0.96, and 0.87.
requirements: Content validity was ensured by assessing and confirming the 110 competency indicators through discussion and consensus among national and international nursing educators
Back translation into Vietnamese was completed by a Vietnamese professional not engaged in questionnaire development
constraints: The Competency Standard "had not been developed for this specific use" of self-reported assessment, which the authors list as a limitation
Self-reported competency assessments tend to result in greater increases in competencies related to technical knowledge and skill
target_learning_goals: Self-assessment of clinical competencies across the three domains of the Basic Competency Standard for Vietnamese Nurses
examples: Administered at baseline (April–September 2019) and follow-up (December 2019–May 2020) via a web-based questionnaire accessed with unique IDs and QR codes on participants' mobile phones
key_sources: Horii Satoko, Nguyen Chinh Thi Minh, Pham Huong Thi Thu, Amaike Naomi, Ho Hien Thi, Aiga Hirotsugu. (2021). Effectiveness of a standard clinical training program in new graduate nurses’ competencies in Vietnam: A quasi-experimental longitudinal study with a difference-in-differences design. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0254238

article_title: A novel system for teaching the in-plane vascular access technique: A simulation study.
citation: Kikuchi M, Asao T, Tokumine J, Lefor AK, Matsushima H, Andoh H, Tanaka K, Kanamoto M, Ideno Y. (2021). A novel system for teaching the in-plane vascular access technique: a simulation study. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000027201
title: Competency-based modular teaching system for the long-axis in-plane technique
description: The article introduces a competency-based modular teaching system structured in three steps: training minimum required component skills (needle and probe handling, for both hands), integrating those skills with coordinated two-hand motion, and advanced training on simulated vessels varying in depth, size, and direction. Trainees "could repeatedly practice each component skill until it is mastered, and then integrate them as a complete skill set". Evaluation follows integration, and trainees who fail enter feedback-loop training. "Progression is based on acquiring competency in each component and not on time pent practicing the skill", distinguishing it from time-based training.
requirements: Component skills must be mastered and pass evaluation before progression; trainees who fail enter feedback-loop training to acquire the necessary skill
constraints: Real-time feedback from an instructor cannot be obtained when the system is used for self-learning; difficulty maintaining motivation is an inherent drawback of self-learning systems, per the authors
target_learners: nurses novices to the in-plane technique
target_learning_goals: performing the long-axis in-plane approach for ultrasound-guided vascular access with needle tip visualization and puncture accuracy
examples: Six hands-on seminars used the system: a 2-hour lecture with component-based learning on a box-type simulator with a 6 mm inner diameter vessel at 5 mm depth, between pre-test and post-test on a torso simulator
key_sources: Kikuchi M, Asao T, Tokumine J, Lefor AK, Matsushima H, Andoh H, Tanaka K, Kanamoto M, Ideno Y. (2021). A novel system for teaching the in-plane vascular access technique: a simulation study. Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000027201

article_title: Randomized controlled trial comparing the effectiveness of mass and spaced learning in microsurgical procedures using computer aided assessment.
citation: Teo Wendy Z. W., Dong Xiaoke, Yusoff Siti Khadijah Bte Mohd, Das De Soumen, Chong Alphonsus K. S. (2021). Randomized controlled trial comparing the effectiveness of mass and spaced learning in microsurgical procedures using computer aided assessment. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-82419-6
title: Digital Surgicals computer-aided assessment of suture placement (MicroTrainer Platform)
description: A computer program from Digital Surgicals scored the elastic practice strips, with an "algorithm is based on uniform and optimal suture density as well as alignment of the sutures with a maximum total score of 35 points". Participants sutured 4 mm-wide elastic strips under the microscope using the MicroTrainer Platform, completing five strips total. The article states the assessment method "has previously been validated and eliminates the possibility of bias arising from a non-blinded assessor".
requirements: Participants produce physical suture strips that can be scanned or captured for algorithmic scoring
constraints: Assessment focused on suture placement precision (deviation from wound edge and spacing) rather than speed or global subjective ratings
target_learning_goals: precision of microsurgical suture placement
examples: Used as the objective outcome measure for all five strips in the mass-vs-spaced randomized trial
key_sources: Teo Wendy Z. W., Dong Xiaoke, Yusoff Siti Khadijah Bte Mohd, Das De Soumen, Chong Alphonsus K. S. (2021). article_title: Application and practice of a step-by-step method combined with case-based learning in Chinese otoendoscopy education.
citation: Wei Fanqin, Sun Qiyang, Qin Zili, Zhuang Huiwen, Jiang Guangli, Wu Xuan. (2021). Application and practice of a step-by-step method combined with case-based learning in Chinese otoendoscopy education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02513-1
title: Combine case-based learning with hands-on surgical training, because CBL alone cannot build operative ability
description: The article recommends that CBL be paired with practical operative training rather than used alone for surgical specialties. Because "the CBL method lacks experience in otoendoscopic surgery", students cannot match CT and MR images to operative findings, remain unfamiliar with anatomical signs and surgical details, and get few chances to operate while teachers perform surgery. The authors therefore state: "in otoendoscopy teaching, we need to combine the CBL method with other methods and increase surgical training based on discussions and explanations to effectively improve the teaching effect." The SBS & CBL arm operationalised this by adding graduated hands-on training to shared CBL.
requirements: Access to hands-on surgical training opportunities (outpatient procedures, temporal bone specimens, guided operative practice) alongside case discussions
constraints: Stated for otoendoscopy teaching, where qualified physicians require repeated and intensive surgical training; the recommendation rests on the study's comparison, not on an isolated test of CBL alone
target_learners: physicians training in otoendoscopic and other endoscopic surgery
target_learning_goals: surgical ability
clinical thinking
reduction of surgical complications
examples: The study's Group A combined CBL case discussion with the three-step SBS hands-on sequence, while Group B received CBL with lectures and teaching ward rounds; Group A rated surgical ability significantly better
key_sources: Wei Fanqin, Sun Qiyang, Qin Zili, Zhuang Huiwen, Jiang Guangli, Wu Xuan. (2021). Application and practice of a step-by-step method combined with case-based learning in Chinese otoendoscopy education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-021-02513-1

article_title: Understanding teaching and learning conceptions among clinical faculty as a means to improve postgraduate training.
citation: Pacifico JL, Donkers J, Jacobs J, van der Vleuten C, Heeneman S. (2020). Understanding teaching and learning conceptions among clinical faculty as a means to improve postgraduate training. International Journal of Medical Education, 11, 175-185. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.5f2a.76eb
title: Measuring teaching conceptions can stimulate reflective thinking and serve as a stepping stone for faculty development programs
description: The article proposes that measuring teachers' conceptions of teaching serves as a tool to promote reflection and faculty development. It states that "A tool to measure conceptions can stimulate reflective thinking on the perspectives of teachers" and that reflecting on these perspectives "can convert a tacit pedagogic knowledge to explicit, which can improve the teaching effectiveness of a medical teacher." The authors recommend discussing measurement outcomes within the teaching staff to improve training quality.
requirements: Faculty must be willing to complete a conception measurement instrument and engage in discussion of the results with colleagues
constraints: The article notes that some participants may have strong opinions about postgraduate training, which could bias participation
target_learning_goals: reflective teaching practice
faculty development
improved postgraduate training
examples: The study used the COLT questionnaire with 172 clinical teachers and vignette-based interviews with 12 faculty to initiate discussion on teaching perspectives
key_sources: Pacifico JL, Donkers J, Jacobs J, van der Vleuten C, Heeneman S. (2020). Understanding teaching and learning conceptions among clinical faculty as a means to improve postgraduate training. International Journal of Medical Education, 11, 175-185. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.5f2a.76eb

article_title: Development and pilot test of ComCare - a questionnaire for quick assessment of communicative and social competences in medical students after interviews with simulated patients.
citation: Gärtner Julia, Prediger Sarah, Harendza Sigrid. (2021). Development and pilot test of ComCare – a questionnaire for quick assessment of communicative and social competences in medical students after interviews with simulated patients. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7994874/
title: ComCare questionnaire: an eight-item instrument for rapid post-consultation assessment of communication and interpersonal skills
description: ComCare is a newly developed short questionnaire combining three communication items with four interpersonal (CARE-derived) items plus one general satisfaction item, each rated on a five-point Likert scale. It exists in a simulated-patient version (ComCareP) and a physician-perspective self-assessment version (ComCareD). Its design purpose was "the need for quick evaluation by the simulated patients directly after the consultations" so formative feedback could be given between patient interviews.
requirements: Simulated patients received a training with ComCareP before the assessment to standardize their answers
Items were not shown to participants beforehand to avoid item-specific behavior
constraints: No validation study preceded the assessment
Items were not anchored by examples to keep reading time short
target_learning_goals: Communication skills
Interpersonal skills
Social competence
examples: Used by simulated patients after each of four consultations and by students as self-assessment after the fourth consultation in a simulated first day of residency
key_sources: Gärtner Julia, Prediger Sarah, Harendza Sigrid. (2021). Development and pilot test of ComCare – a questionnaire for quick assessment of communicative and social competences in medical students after interviews with simulated patients. article_title: Development and pilot test of ComCare - a questionnaire for quick assessment of communicative and social competences in medical students after interviews with simulated patients.
citation: Gärtner Julia, Prediger Sarah, Harendza Sigrid. (2021). title: Communication and interpersonal skills as inseparably connected components of interactional competence
description: The article builds ComCare on the framework that "Communication and interpersonal skills have been proposed in a framework to be inseparably connected". The single-factor factor-analysis result is presented as empirical support for this view, and the authors note the term "interactional skills" is being used in the field for this combined construct, with recommendations for future research already given.
requirements: Assessment instruments must measure communication and interpersonal skills together rather than as separate scales
constraints: The article notes the field has only recently begun using the combined term interactional skills and has issued recommendations for future research
target_learning_goals: Communication skills
Interpersonal skills
examples: ComCare operationalizes the framework by combining communication items and CARE-derived interpersonal items into one eight-item scale

article_title: Cognitive training for the prevention of skill decay in temporarily non-performing orthopedic surgeons.
citation: Kelc Robi, Vogrin Matjaz, Kelc Janja. (2020). Cognitive training for the prevention of skill decay in temporarily non-performing orthopedic surgeons. Acta Orthopaedica 91(5). https://doi.org/10.1080/17453674.2020.1771520
title: Cognitive task analysis (CTA) training for novice surgeons
description: Cognitive task analysis is described as "a method by which experts are used to construct a teaching program for novices through intuitive knowledge and thought processes." The article calls CTA "the most effective" cognitive training technique at a novice level and cites a randomized controlled trial in hip arthroplasty showing "shorter procedure time, decrease in the number of errors, and increase in accuracy of acetabular cup orientation." Its main practical drawback is that it "requires a mentor to be present."
requirements: A mentor (expert) must be present to construct the teaching program, which the article notes may be inaccessible in some situations
constraints: Requires a mentor, an option that may be inaccessible in some specific situations such as during an epidemic or a surgeon's illness
target_learning_goals: acquisition of new surgical techniques and procedures
examples: The article cites its use in anterior approach total hip arthroplasty training

article_title: How Can We Make Active Learning Work in K-12 Education? Considering Prerequisites for a Successful Construction of Understanding.
citation: Garvin Brod. (2021). How Can We Make Active Learning Work in K–12 Education? Considering Prerequisites for a Successful Construction of Understanding. Psychological Science in the Public Interest. https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100621997376
title: Construction-of-understanding ecosystem modified to include four prerequisite nodes: agency beliefs, prior knowledge, cognitive capacities, and metacognitive capacities
description: The construction-of-understanding ecosystem, proposed by Lombardi and colleagues, assumes active-learning practices afford students agency over their learning, requiring them to "make sense of data and observations themselves" by integrating data and observations "with prior knowledge and scientific models." The author modified the framework (Figure 1b) by adding four prerequisite nodes—agency beliefs, prior knowledge, cognitive capacities, and metacognitive capacities—with arrows to "Student," reflecting that these constructs "determine how strongly students can benefit from active learning and are thus targets for providing support."
requirements: The framework assumes active-learning practices are beneficial for student achievement in STEM; the prerequisites must be considered for that benefit to occur.
constraints: The commentary states the author's evidence-based answers are "preliminary and subject to future research."
target_learning_goals: constructing understanding in STEM subjects
scientific literacy
examples: Figure 1b adds the four prerequisite nodes with arrows to "Student" in the original ecosystem of Lombardi and colleagues.
key_sources: Garvin Brod. (2021). How Can We Make Active Learning Work in K–12 Education? Considering Prerequisites for a Successful Construction of Understanding. Psychological Science in the Public Interest. https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100621997376

article_title: A Cocurricular Program That Encourages Specific Study Skills and Habits Improves Academic Performance and Retention of First-Year Undergraduates in Introductory Biology.
citation: Hawkins Whitney, W.; Goddard, K.; Favero, C. (2021). A Cocurricular Program That Encourages Specific Study Skills and Habits Improves Academic Performance and Retention of First-Year Undergraduates in Introductory Biology. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.20-06-0117
title: 8-week Co-Curricular (CoC) study-skills program for first-year introductory biology
description: An 8-week voluntary program meeting once weekly for 80 minutes on Fridays, led by a biology faculty member assisted by undergraduate peer leaders, focused on time management and active-learning strategies without content review. The article states it "met once a week on Fridays, for 80 minutes each session, for eight consecutive weeks." Students applied to join, received extra credit for attending seven or eight sessions, and could attend drop-in sessions staffed by peer leaders as makeup or study-group time.
requirements: Students must complete an application and attend all eight sessions (or make up via drop-in) to count as full participants and receive extra credit
Sessions led by a faculty member not teaching the course, assisted by peer leaders who earned at least a B in Bio101
constraints: Participation was voluntary and self-selected, so student motivation may be a factor in findings
Only 17% of enrolled students participated; attendance was inversely related to preparedness
target_learners: First-year undergraduates in introductory biology, particularly those with low and medium predicted preparedness
target_learning_goals: Time management
Active-learning study strategies
Metacognition and course retention in a STEM gateway course
examples: Weekly topics included a detailed "Plan of Study" schedule for the 7 days before each exam, exam post-mortem sessions ("Exam BIOpsy"), and end-of-meeting intention setting
key_sources: Hawkins Whitney, W.; Goddard, K.; Favero, C. (2021). article_title: Blended learning: ten tips on how to implement it into a curriculum in healthcare education.
citation: Hege I, Tolks D, Adler M, Härtl A. (2020). Blended learning: ten tips on how to implement it into a curriculum in healthcare education. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(5): Doc45. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001338.shtml
title: Combine and align varied teaching and assessment methods across online and face-to-face phases, consistent with constructive alignment
description: The article describes three possible combinations of online and face-to-face phases: online learning as preparation for face-to-face courses (flipped or inverted classroom), online learning as follow-up after a face-to-face course, and online elements during a face-to-face session such as simulated environments or part-task trainers. It recommends combining a variety of teaching methods to meet learning objectives, and states that "learning objectives, teaching methods and formative and summative assessment should be aligned with each other, consistent with the model of constructive alignment". A variation of teaching methods can also lead to a more satisfactory learning experience, and online phases should address higher-level learning objectives, not only knowledge.
requirements: Learning objectives, teaching methods and formative and summative assessment aligned with each other
Selection of formats depending on the learning objectives defined in the needs-assessment step
target_learning_goals: Clinical skills and higher-level learning objectives across delivery modes
examples: Videos and interactive online tasks prepare for a face-to-face course training a clinical skill with simulated patients or part-task trainers; virtual patients then place the skill in a wider clinical context before bedside teaching rounds
key_sources: Hege I, Tolks D, Adler M, Härtl A. (2020). Blended learning: ten tips on how to implement it into a curriculum in healthcare education. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(5): Doc45. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001338.shtml

article_title: Development and Usability of a Novel Interactive Tablet App (PediAppRREST) to Support the Management of Pediatric Cardiac Arrest: Pilot High-Fidelity Simulation-Based Study.
citation: Corazza F, Snijders D, Arpone M, Stritoni V, Martinolli F, Daverio M, Losi MG, Soldi L, Tesauri F, Da Dalt L, Bressan S. (2020). Development and Usability of a Novel Interactive Tablet App (PediAppRREST) to Support the Management of Pediatric Cardiac Arrest: Pilot High-Fidelity Simulation-Based Study. JMIR mHealth and uHealth. https://doi.org/10.2196/19070
title: Interactive cognitive aid screen design pattern: timely information, timer-triggered priority, and sequential-versus-alternative button layout
description: The article articulates three user-experience design criteria applied when building the app's screens. First, "timely information": each screen gathers only the information necessary for the current phase of the PALS algorithm, communicated both visually and acoustically, aiming to reduce load on the team leader's working memory through multichannel communication. Second, "priority": actions triggered by timers, such as epinephrine administration, take precedence over other on-screen actions. Third, "sequential versus alternative choices": sequential actions are displayed as vertically aligned rectangular buttons, while alternative choices are organized as horizontally aligned square buttons. This pattern makes a complex, time-critical guideline algorithm navigable under high cognitive load.
requirements: Content must be decomposed into screens matched to phases of the target algorithm
Timer-triggered critical actions must be given display priority
constraints: Developed and evaluated specifically for pediatric cardiac arrest management by team leaders in high-fidelity simulation
target_learners: clinicians leading resuscitation teams (pilot participants were pediatric residents)
target_learning_goals: guideline-adherent execution of resuscitation actions in sequence and timing
examples: The app's epinephrine screens prompt correct doses automatically calculated on patients' weight and time intervals of administration

article_title: '10% of your medical students will cause 90% of your problems': a prospective correlational study.
citation: Sawdon Marina, McLachlan JC. (2020). '10% of your medical students will cause 90% of your problems': a prospective correlational study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2020-038472
title: Conscientiousness Index (CI): an objective scalar measure of medical students' conscientiousness in routine tasks
description: The CI is a point-based measure of conscientiousness in routine tasks calculated for first- and second-year medical students. "The Index included: having brought required 'induction' information (photographs, criminal records information and immunisation status), attendance at compulsory sessions (unless a good reason had been notified), submission of assignments on time, fulfilling essential administrative requirements... and completion of course evaluations." One point is awarded per positive activity, well over 100 points per year, recorded as percentages. Students were aware of the data collection.
requirements: Multiple routine-task observations across the academic year (typically well over 100 point opportunities per year) to compute a percentage score
constraints: The measure is most valid as a predictor of professional outcomes at the lower end of the scale
Data were collected at a single UK medical school
target_learners: first- and second-year undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: professionalism
conscientiousness in routine academic and administrative tasks
examples: Students knew CI data were being collected; the authors report no evidence that students changed their behaviour in response

article_title: '10% of your medical students will cause 90% of your problems': a prospective correlational study.
citation: Sawdon Marina, McLachlan JC. (2020). '10% of your medical students will cause 90% of your problems': a prospective correlational study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2020-038472
title: Conscientiousness as a common underlying factor explaining both examination success and later professional behaviour
description: The article proposes that a single trait, conscientiousness (one of the Big 5 personality factors), underlies both examination success and the probability of professional problems in later practice. The authors hypothesise "there is a common factor underlying both examination success and the probability of fitness to practice sanctions in later practice, namely, the trait of conscientiousness", noting the work psychology literature identifies conscientiousness as the biggest single predictor of workplace performance. They postulate the mechanism operates "through behaviour patterns such as good note and record keeping, good hand overs, following up patients, keeping up to date with developments".
requirements: An objective, multi-observation measure of conscientiousness in routine tasks to operationalise the trait
constraints: The mechanism account is the authors' postulate; the study's results are described as tentative and further research is required to establish the nature of the relationships
target_learning_goals: professional behaviour in clinical practice
academic performance
examples: The article contrasts this account with Papadakis et al's summary 'It's good to be good, and it's good to be smart', arguing virtue is not directly related to intelligence
key_sources: Sawdon Marina, McLachlan JC. (2020). '10% of your medical students will cause 90% of your problems': a prospective correlational study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2020-038472

article_title: How can communicative competence instruction in medical studies be improved through digitalization?
citation: Schick K, Reiser S, Mosene K, Schacht L, Janssen L, Thomm E, Dinkel A, Fleischmann A, Berberat P O, Bauer J, Gartmeier M. (2020). How can communicative competence instruction in medical studies be improved through digitalization? GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(6): Doc57. https://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2020-37/zma001350.shtml
title: Combine video modeling with video reflection in e-learning for communicative competence, following 4C/ID
description: The voLeA learning environment pairs video modeling (presenting very good and very detrimental communicative behaviour patterns, linked with targeted explanations to promote action schemata) with video reflection (work assignments such as identifying key points, justifying selections, or analyzing scenes against criteria). The article grounds this combination in the 4C/ID model: "The authors recommend, among other things, the combination of deductive instructional procedures (as they are to be carried out within the framework of the theory-based VM modules) with inductive elements (such as reflection via video examples in the VR modules)". Fictional video cases are used because they allow realistic presentation and narrative extension beyond what is shown.
requirements: Video examples combined with reflective instructional items and guiding questions; text-based instructional stages continuously linked with video sequences
constraints: The planned effectiveness research will examine which design principle is most effective: video reflection, video modeling, or a combination of the two
target_learning_goals: professional perception of communicative situations and communicative competence
examples: Students watch positive and negative examples of clinical communication and reflect on them via guiding questions before attending role plays

article_title: Adaptation of an international virtual patient collection to the COVID-19 pandemic.
citation: Hege I, Sudacka M, Kononowicz AA, Nonnenmann J, Banholzer J, Schelling J, Adler M, Espinoza B, Garrido MA, Radon K. (2020). Adaptation of an international virtual patient collection to the COVID-19 pandemic. GMS Journal for Medical Education 37(7): Doc92. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7740015/
title: Context influences the clinical reasoning process, and changed contexts require adaptation of the learning environment
description: Drawing on the perspective that context shapes clinical reasoning, the authors argue that the pandemic's rapid global change of the teaching context "requires manifold and quick adaptations of the teaching environment", while offering "a great opportunity for students to experience how context influences the clinical reasoning process". The VP adaptations were designed to demonstrate this: pre-assessing possible COVID-19 infection, considering COVID-19 as a new differential diagnosis, and weighing regional probability of diagnosis.
requirements: Teaching cases must reflect the contextual factors (e.g. pandemic status, regional disease probability) under which learners will reason
constraints: VPs were originally designed for a non-pandemic environment and do not automatically reflect new contextual factors
target_learning_goals: Understanding how context influences the clinical reasoning process
examples: The authors added an introduction explaining that the VPs were designed for a non-pandemic context, so learners experience the contrast.

article_title: Perceptions of managers regarding prerequisites for the development of professional competence of newly graduated nurses: A qualitative study.
citation: Södersved Källestedt M-L, Asp M, Letterstål A, Widarsson M. (2020). Perceptions of managers regarding prerequisites for the development of professional competence of newly graduated nurses: A qualitative study. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 29, 4784–4794. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.15522
title: Competence-in-use as a dynamic learning process mediating between the nurse's capacity and the profession's requirements
description: The article adopts Eilström and Kock's definition of professional competence as the capacity to handle situations or complete tasks, and frames development through competence-in-use: "Competence‐in‐use is considered a dynamic process of learning mediating between the capacity of the nurse and the requirements of the profession". Individual factors (self-understanding, self-confidence) and profession-related factors (workplace organisation, participation, feedback) facilitate or limit the extent to which competence is used and developed; only competence that is used develops further. The study's three themes are related back to this definition in the discussion.
requirements: Supportive environment and institutional practice, including workplace organisation for participation and feedback
constraints: Only competence-in-use is developed; factors on both the individual and profession side may limit the extent to which competence can be used
target_learners: newly graduated nurses in a 1-year residency programme
target_learning_goals: development of professional competence in practical skills, leadership and clinical practice
examples: The article relates its three manager-perceived themes (relationships, skills expectations, conditions for continued learning) to this competence-development definition in the discussion

article_title: Hybrid simulation of pediatric gynecologic examination: a mix-methods study of learners' attitudes and factors affecting learning.
citation: Torres Anna, Horodeńska Magdalena, Witkowski Grzegorz, Torres Kamil. (2020). Hybrid simulation of pediatric gynecologic examination: a mix-methods study of learners' attitudes and factors affecting learning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02076-7
title: Conceptual model of six attitude-connected factors influencing learning in hybrid-model HFS
description: The article proposes a conceptual model (Fig. 2) in which six factors connected to attitude components influence learning of PAG examination in high-fidelity simulation with the hybrid model. Thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with nine participants "revealed six themes important to learners and informing learning of PAG examination in HFS". The factors are task difficulty, attention, emotional realism of the simulation, patient's emotions, physical realism of the simulation, and technical issues. The model rests on the Tripartie Model of attitude as theoretical framework.
requirements: Learning of PAG examination in a high-fidelity simulation environment using a hybrid model combining a simulated patient with a task trainer
constraints: Developed from interviews with nine participants in a single institution; the authors note validity is limited by a relatively small number of participants
target_learning_goals: pediatric and adolescent gynecological examination skills
communication and interpersonal skills
examples: Themes included that physical realism positively influenced learning while making the task more challenging, and that participants perceived the trainer-SP-voice scenario as low fidelity despite the identical HFS environment

citation: Chick Robert Connor, Clifton Guy Travis, Peace Kaitlin M., Propper Brandon W., Hale Diane F., Alseidi Adnan A., Vreeland Timothy J. (2020). Using Technology to Maintain the Education of Residents During the COVID-19 Pandemic. Journal of Surgical Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsurg.2020.03.018
title: A bundled set of five technology-based solutions for maintaining surgical resident education during restrictions on in-person activities
description: The article organizes its response to pandemic restrictions on gatherings, elective operations, and rotations into a bundle of five solutions, listed in Table 2: flipped virtual classroom model, online practice questions, academic conferences via teleconference, telehealth clinics with resident involvement, and facilitated use of surgical videos. The authors state that "although there is no substitute for hands-on learning through operative experience and direct patient care, these may be ways to mitigate the loss of learning exposure during this time."
requirements: Institutional commitment to adapting existing technology-based education strategies
Cooperation between institutions, particularly regionalization of educational teleconferences and shared access to nearby institutions
constraints: These solutions mitigate but do not replace hands-on operative experience and direct patient care
There were not yet nationwide or multi-institutional recommendations at the time of writing
target_learning_goals: maintaining rigorous surgical education during restrictions on in-person gatherings and elective operations
examples: The program paired its pre-existing Monday 3-hour academic block and daily 30-minute conferences with flipped classroom sessions and the ABSITE Daily social media group

article_title: Differentiated need support by teachers: Student-specific provision of autonomy and structure and relations with student motivation.
citation: Domen, J., Hornstra, L., Weijers, D., van der Veen, I., & Peetsma, T. (2020). Differentiated need support by teachers: Student‐specific provision of autonomy and structure and relations with student motivation. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 90(2), 403–423. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12302
title: Teacher training and interventions should focus on combining autonomy support with structure for different students
description: The article recommends that teacher training programmes and interventions target the combination of autonomy support and structure at the level of individual students, because teachers in this study found it hard to provide both to the same student. As the authors state, "Interventions as well as teacher training programmes may be even more effective by focusing especially on how teachers can combine autonomy support with structure for different students." This builds on meta‐analytic evidence that autonomy‐support training can improve teaching and student motivation.
requirements: Teacher training programmes aimed at autonomy support, of the kind the article says several studies have shown can positively affect teaching and student motivation
constraints: The article states more research is needed to understand why teachers offer some students more or less need support than others
target_learning_goals: Supporting students' autonomous motivation through need‐supportive teaching
examples: In the study, teachers rated each student individually on shortened TASC autonomy support and structure scales, and the within‐level association between the two was negative (b = −.25, p < .001)

article_title: Effects of a Cognitive-Functional Intervention Method on Improving Executive Function and Self-Directed Learning in School-Aged Children with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Single-Subject Design Study.
citation: Kim Mi Ji, Park Hae Yean, Yoo Eun-Young, Kim Jung-Ran. (2020). Effects of a Cognitive-Functional Intervention Method on Improving Executive Function and Self-Directed Learning in School-Aged Children with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder: A Single-Subject Design Study. Occupational Therapy International. https://doi.org/10.1155/2020/1250801
title: Cog-Fun intervention program for executive function and self-directed learning in children with ADHD
description: Cog-Fun is an occupational therapy intervention, designed based on the Person-Environment-Occupation Model and the Model of Human Occupation, to enhance executive function and self-efficacy in children with ADHD. Its main properties include "setting child-centered goals, providing training in the three execution strategies of \"stop, plan, and review,\"" and aiding children to set their own strategies. In this study it ran as ten 60-minute sessions with parent consultation after each session.
requirements: Delivery by a therapist across ten 60-minute sessions, twice weekly, with parent consultation after each session
A Daily Occupational Goal Planner provided so children continue practicing acquired strategies in daily life
constraints: The authors note "the Hawthorne effect could not be neglected as most studies used parent report assessment tools for measuring dependent variables"
The authors state that "not enough measures were taken to ensure objective analysis of participant performance"
target_learners: School-aged children (9-10 years) diagnosed with ADHD
target_learning_goals: Executive function, including inhibition, working memory, and planning and organization
Self-directed learning and homework performance
examples: Three boys aged 9-10 with ADHD completed the program in an A-B-A single-subject study; "The results of TEI-SF showed that all three parents perceived the Cog-Fun program positively"

article_title: The academic outcomes of working memory and metacognitive strategy training in children: A double-blind randomized controlled trial.
citation: Jones JS, Milton F, Mostazir M, Adlam ALR. (2020). The academic outcomes of working memory and metacognitive strategy training in children: A double‐blind randomized controlled trial. Developmental Science. https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.12870
title: Combine working memory training with metacognitive strategy instruction (planning, monitoring, evaluating) to broaden and consolidate transfer
description: The article pairs an adaptive working memory training programme with a workbook teaching children to "plan, monitor and evaluate" while completing training tasks, reading exercises and maths problems, prompting strategy generation rather than teaching fixed task-specific strategies. This combination produced greater working memory gains at 3 months and transfer to the least similar task than working memory training alone.
requirements: Children require specific instruction and guidance on how to apply newly acquired capacity in other situations, as the article states children may be unable to intuitively apply increased capacity
constraints: Metacognitive strategy training provided no additional benefit to maths or reading comprehension compared to Cogmed alone
The combination's advantage appeared on working memory measures, not academic far-transfer
target_learning_goals: working memory performance
mathematical reasoning
reading comprehension
examples: The MetaCogmed group completed the standard Cogmed protocol plus a 25-section metacognitive workbook with reflection exercises, prompts to plan before, monitor during and evaluate after tasks, and a Personal Strategy Guide, while comparison groups received placebo workbooks

article_title: Conference Didactic Planning and Structure: An Evidence-based Guide to Best Practices from the Council of Emergency Medicine Residency Directors.
citation: Wood D. Brian, Jordan Jaime, Cooney Rob, Goldflam Katja, Bright Leah, Gottlieb Michael. (2020). Conference Didactic Planning and Structure: An Evidence-based Guide to Best Practices from the Council of Emergency Medicine Residency Directors. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2020.5.46762
title: Cognitive load theory: intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load in creating long-term memories
description: The review presents cognitive load theory as an account of how instructors should design conference talks: "Cognitive load theory states that there are three main components involved in the creation of long-term memories: intrinsic load; extraneous load; and germane load." Intrinsic and germane load are described as generally fixed, while extraneous load is highly modifiable and shaped by how material is presented. Because working memory is fixed at a given time, increases in extraneous load detract from learning and retention, so instructors should focus talks on delivery of information and limit unnecessary or overly complex presentation.
requirements: Instructors must limit unnecessary information and overly complex presentations so extraneous load does not consume fixed working memory
constraints: The review states intrinsic load and germane load are generally fixed, leaving extraneous load as the main modifiable lever
target_learning_goals: long-term retention of didactic content
examples: The review recommends lecturers ensure presentations comply with cognitive load theory, multimedia learning theory, and active learning principles (Level 1a; Grade B)

article_title: Do cognitive aids reduce error rates in resuscitation team performance? Trial of emergency medicine protocols in simulation training (TEMPIST) in Australia.
citation: Hall Charlotte, Robertson Dean, Rolfe Margaret, Pascoe Sharene, Passey Megan E., Pit Sabrina Winona. (2020). Do cognitive aids reduce error rates in resuscitation team performance? Trial of emergency medicine protocols in simulation training (TEMPIST) in Australia. Human Resources for Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12960-019-0441-x
title: Cognitive overload and stress during crises degrade clinician performance, which cognitive aids offset by externalising the recommended sequence
description: The article's explanatory account is that resuscitation of time-critical patients imposes cognitive demands that degrade performance: human factors research shows that "during a crisis, memory worsens, cognition is overloaded, performance degrades, and distractions interrupt planned actions". Cognitive aids such as checklists are prompts designed to assist workers in completing tasks, borrowed from aviation Crew Resource Management, and a structured, easy-to-follow approach is argued to reduce error rates and standardise care by removing unwanted variation.
requirements: Cognitive aids depend on the right content and design and are supported by appropriate training to enable task execution (usability)
constraints: Adoption of checklists in critical care medicine has overall been slow despite numerous recommendations
target_learning_goals: maintaining guideline-adherent performance under stress
completing key life-preserving steps in correct sequence
examples: The TEMPIST trial operationalised this account by observing team error rates with and without a bedside cognitive aid across four simulated crises

article_title: Training by visual identification and writing leads to different visual word expertise N170 effects in preliterate Chinese children.
citation: Zhao Pei, Li Su, Zhao Jing, Gaspar Carl M., Weng Xuchu. (2015). Training by visual identification and writing leads to different visual word expertise N170 effects in preliterate Chinese children. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2015.09.002
title: Competition hypothesis of visual word expertise development
description: The article invokes the competition hypothesis of visual word expertise development (Dehaene and Cohen, 2007), which "proposes that there is competition between culturally or environmentally shaped visual processing and perhaps the more hard-wired visual processes like face perception". Explicitly teaching children to read may induce them to devote more neural resources to word processing at the expense of neural resources for face processing. The article presents its finding of decreased left-hemisphere face N170 after visual identification training as further and direct evidence supporting this hypothesis.
requirements: Explicit literacy training that shifts neural resources toward word processing
constraints: The article notes the underlying mechanism of experience–brain interactions still needs investigation due to the limitation of the sample size
target_learners: Preliterate children aged 4–5 years learning to read
target_learning_goals: Visual word expertise processing for written characters
examples: In the visual identification group, face N170 amplitude in the left hemisphere decreased significantly after training while tool N170 did not change
key_sources: Zhao Pei, Li Su, Zhao Jing, Gaspar Carl M., Weng Xuchu. (2015). Training by visual identification and writing leads to different visual word expertise N170 effects in preliterate Chinese children. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2015.09.002

article_title: How to assess communication skills? Development of the rating scale ComOn Check.
citation: Radziej K, Loechner J, Engerer C, Niglio de Figueiredo M, Freund J, Sattel H, Bachmann C, Berberat PO, Dinkel A, Wuensch A. (2017). How to assess communication skills? Development of the rating scale ComOn Check. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2017.1392823
title: ComOn check: a six-domain rating scale with 13 items on a five-point Likert scale for assessing medical students' general communication skills
description: The ComOn check is a rating scale for evaluating general communication skills of medical students in doctor-patient encounters, developed over ten steps from prior oncology-specific checklists plus literature-derived items. As the authors state, "our checklist consists of a global rating and 12 specific items" covering initiating conversation, patient's perception, conversation structure, patient's emotions, end of conversation, and general communication skills, each rated 0 (poor) to 4 (excellent). It was designed for on-the-spot ratings within 5-10 minutes and for use in research and OSCE evaluation.
requirements: Ratings only by trained expert raters, with an informative instruction manual for rater training
constraints: The scale focuses only on general communication skills and does not combine content (medical subject matter) variables with process variables
target_learners: medical students in their first clinical year
target_learning_goals: physician-patient communication skills
examples: Two trained psychologist raters applied the final version to 135 videotaped consultations of 66 students with standardized patients, rating individually and then settling divergences by consensus agreement
key_sources: Radziej K, Loechner J, Engerer C, Niglio de Figueiredo M, Freund J, Sattel H, Bachmann C, Berberat PO, Dinkel A, Wuensch A. (2017). How to assess communication skills? Development of the rating scale ComOn Check. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2017.1392823

article_title: How to assess communication skills? Development of the rating scale ComOn Check.
citation: Radziej K, Loechner J, Engerer C, Niglio de Figueiredo M, Freund J, Sattel H, Bachmann C, Berberat PO, Dinkel A, Wuensch A. (2017). How to assess communication skills? Development of the rating scale ComOn Check. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2017.1392823
title: ComOn check's design rationale: operationalizing observable general communication skills while balancing efficiency, detail, and psychometric quality
description: The article articulates a framework of seven design requirements for communication assessment instruments: general application, efficiency, detailed evaluation, rated behavior, specific setting, psychometric properties, and qualified raters. The authors state the aim "to integrate the issues of general application, efficiency, purpose, detailed evaluation, setting, good psychometric properties, and qualified raters." The framework responds to shortcomings of existing interaction analysis systems, which are resource-intensive and often transcript-only, and to extensive checklists that lack a balance between efficacy and informative value. It operationalizes good communication through observable behaviors anchored to literature-derived models such as SPIKES, the Langewitz book metaphor, and the NURSE model.
requirements: An informative instruction manual for the training of raters; ratings only by trained experts because patient and student ratings are considered highly subjective
constraints: The instrument focuses on general communication skills only, not medical content expertise; it is difficult for one single instrument to meet all requirements simultaneously
target_learning_goals: general physician-patient communication skills
examples: Development proceeded in ten steps: integrating items from the COM-ON-Checklist, literature review, item phrasing on a five-point Likert scale, rater feedback, iterative rating of videotaped consultations, and final anchor-point definition

article_title: Evaluation of an online training tool for scoring programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) diagnostic tests for lung cancer.

title: Provide continued post-training access to scoring training materials, because continual retraining or recalibration maintains inter-reader consistency
description: The article recommends that trainees retain access to the online training materials after the initial course. It states that "The facility to revisit training materials subsequent to the initial training is important, as continual retraining or recalibration is key to maintaining good levels of inter-reader and inter-laboratory consistency and in minimising any intra-reader 'drift'." The freely available e-trainer tool makes this feasible, and the authors note that infrequent scorers are less likely to be internally consistent.

target_learners: practising pathologists who score PD-L1 slides, especially those who score infrequently
target_learning_goals: maintaining inter-reader and inter-laboratory scoring consistency over time
examples: The article points readers to the open access trial version of the tool on the IDPDL1 website for continued use

article_title: Codebook for rating clinical communication skills based on the Calgary-Cambridge Guide.
citation: Iversen Else Dalsgaard, Wolderslund Maiken Overbeck, Kofoed Poul-Erik, Gulbrandsen Pål, Poulsen Helle, Cold Søren, Ammentorp Jette. (2020). Codebook for rating clinical communication skills based on the Calgary-Cambridge Guide. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02050-3
title: Codebook pattern: operationalizing a crude 5-point rating scale into described micro-skills with point-allocation criteria per item
description: The pattern is to convert each global item of an observation scheme into enumerated micro-skills and explicit criteria for allocating points. The article reports that "Each item has 0 to 5 described micro-skills" and "the codebook described the criteria for delivering a rating from 0 to 4 depending on how successful the different micro-skills... was accomplished." Micro-skills were grouped into four point levels, with conventions such as merging connected micro-skills and rating jargon by the number of medical words used.
requirements: Raters must first understand the micro-skills as described in the Calgary-Cambridge Guide, since the coding procedure is based on identifying them.
constraints: Item 3 contains no micro-skills, so points were allocated by counting medical words, and difficult words required judgement of whether the patient understood them; non-verbal items are challenging in audio-only recordings.
target_learners: Health care providers being assessed on clinical communication skills
target_learning_goals: Objective, reliable rating of clinical communication skills
examples: The codebook was developed by rating 23 audio recordings from seven HCPs; items 3, 4, 7 and 9 received extra coding detail because they were troublesome for the coders.

title: Long MCQ option lists require the cover test and a consistent logical option order
description: The article states that long option lists are not a problem "as long as the question meets the cover test (the correct answer can be determined without seeing the options), and the options are presented in a consistent logical order (e.g. alphabetical)". Questions not meeting these standards are likely flawed irrespective of option number.

Options are presented in a consistent logical order such as alphabetical
constraints: Questions not meeting these standards are most likely flawed irrespective of the number of options

article_title: Peer-supported faculty development and workplace teaching: an integrative review.
citation: Campbell N, Wozniak H, Philip RL, Damarell RA. (2019). Peer‐supported faculty development and workplace teaching: an integrative review. Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/medu.13896
title: Prefer a collaborative peer support model with trusted peer contributors over outside experts
description: The review concludes that initiatives employing a collaborative model of peer support and/or selecting peers based on trusted and respected relationships, rather than relying on outside expertise, were most acceptable and effective. "By choosing a collaborative model for peer support, the emphasis becomes one of encouraging democratic relationships between equals, facilitation of mutual learning." Trusted peer contributors become valid feedback providers, and reciprocity promotes personal accountability for professional development.
requirements: Participants must take responsibility for their own learning rather than assuming only education experts provide feedback
Voluntary participation with trusted colleagues
constraints: The evaluative and developmental models, by comparison, focus on identifying underperformance and demonstrating competency, so this principle applies to development-oriented goals rather than judgement-oriented ones
target_learners: Clinician teachers in health care workplaces
target_learning_goals: Improving clinical teaching practice through reciprocal peer feedback and reflection
examples: The review reports clinician peers are more readily available in the workplace than external education experts, making availability an enabler of participation

article_title: Measuring the impact of an interdisciplinary learning project on nursing, architecture and landscape design students' empathy.
citation: Donnelly S, Dean S, Razavy S, Levett-Jones T. (2019). Measuring the impact of an interdisciplinary learning project on nursing, architecture and landscape design students’ empathy. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0215795
title: Cognitive and affective empathy as distinct components of state empathy
description: The article organises empathy around two components and a trait-state distinction. "Cognitive empathy refers to the accurate perception of another person’s perspective or mental state (feeling into), whereas affective empathy involves an ability to experience actual feelings or emotions that are consistent with another person". It also distinguishes trait empathy, a psychological disposition, from state empathy, an empathetic response at a specific point in time, and argues trait scales are unsuitable for short pre-test post-test studies. The Comprehensive State Empathy Scale operationalises this framework, measuring cognitive, affective and state empathy, and is used as the study’s outcome measure.
requirements: A validated state empathy measurement tool such as the CSES, prefaced with a written scenario depicting the target group
constraints: Trait empathy scales are stated to be inappropriate for pre-test post-test studies over a short time frame
target_learners: undergraduate nursing, architecture and landscape design students
target_learning_goals: empathy towards women and children accessing refuge services
examples: The CSES prefaced pre and post-tests with a written scenario depicting authentic experiences of women requiring refuge accommodation, with a relevant image

article_title: Institutional differences in USMLE Step 1 and 2 CK performance: Cross-sectional study of 89 US allopathic medical schools.
citation: Burk-Rafel J, Pulido RW, Elfanagely Y, Kolars JC. (2019). Institutional differences in USMLE Step 1 and 2 CK performance: Cross-sectional study of 89 US allopathic medical schools. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0224675
title: Control for students' prior academic performance (GPA and MCAT) when comparing institutions' knowledge-exam outcomes
description: The article's central methodological recommendation is that institutional comparisons on high-stakes knowledge exams must account for incoming students' prior academic performance. Its regression showed "the strongest predictor of institutional USMLE scores was prior student academic performance," and factors such as private status or NIH funding appeared significant only before this control. The authors extend this to data consumers, arguing score data should be contextualized so pre-medical students interpret institutional means correctly.
requirements: Institutional mean GPA and MCAT data for the entering cohorts matched to the exam years must be available
constraints: The analysis is ecological: no inference can be made that institution-level findings translate to individual students
Self-reported institutional data via third-party publications may involve misreporting
target_learning_goals: interpreting institutional performance data on high-stakes licensing examinations
examples: The study regressed institutional mean USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 CK scores on institutional mean GPA and MCAT across 89 schools, identifying outliers outside the 95% prediction interval

article_title: Computerized Speechreading Training for Deaf Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Pimperton, H., Kyle, F., Hulme, C., Harris, M., Beedie, I., Ralph-Lewis, A., Worster, E., Rees, R., Donlan, C., & MacSweeney, M. (2019). Computerized Speechreading Training for Deaf Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Speech, Language, and Hearing Research. https://doi.org/10.1044/2019_JSLHR-H-19-0073
title: Adaptive computerized speechreading training program for deaf children (seven space-themed games, 48 ten-minute sessions)
description: A computerized intervention delivered within "a suite of seven space-themed computer games", designed to run across forty-eight 10-min sessions with adaptive algorithms that varied trial difficulty "based on the child's performance". The first 16 sessions trained video-to-picture matching of 103 trained words; sessions 17–48 added trials with orthographic stimuli focusing on mappings between visual speech patterns and letters and words. Sessions carried a narrative structure with a virtual reward collected in an online trophy cabinet, and built-in speechreading assessments occurred every eight sessions.
requirements: Children must be able to meet the physical and attentional demands of playing a computer game for 10 min a day
Delivery requires school logistical and technological support, including help logging on to the program
constraints: The complete program provided only 8 hours of speechreading training over approximately 3 months
Adherence in the trial was variable, with less than two thirds of children in each group completing the planned number of sessions
target_learners: Deaf children aged 5–7 years with severe or profound bilateral hearing loss
target_learning_goals: Speechreading of visual speech
Mappings between visual speech patterns and letters and words
examples: In the trial, 66 deaf children were randomized to complete this program or an active maths control, with assessments before training, immediately after, and 3 and 11 months later

article_title: Effects of virtual reality-based cognitive training in older adults living without and with mild dementia: a pretest-posttest design pilot study.
citation: Zając-Lamparska Ludmiła, Wiłkość-Dębczyńska Monika, Wojciechowski Adam, Podhorecka Marta, Polak-Szabela Anna, Warchoł Łukasz, Kędziora-Kornatowska Kornelia, Araszkiewicz Aleksander, Izdebski Paweł. (2019). Effects of virtual reality-based cognitive training in older adults living without and with mild dementia: a pretest–posttest design pilot study. BMC Research Notes. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13104-019-4810-2
title: Excessive cognitive burden of game control as a mechanism reducing VR training efficacy and increasing withdrawal in older adults with mild dementia
description: The authors propose that the interface of the VR game imposed an excessive cognitive burden on participants with mild dementia: to operate the interface they "had to memorize and coordinate the functions of several buttons on the pad under the right and left thumbs as well as several ways of controlling the game with the Oculus", while the Oculus prevented visual verification of button choices, requiring maintenance of functional and spatial mapping in working memory. This burden, they argue, led to low learnability, decreased training efficacy, and withdrawal from training in this group. Interface control remained difficult even with practice tutorials.
requirements: Game control that does not overload working memory, e.g. allowing visual verification of button choices
constraints: The authors frame this as an interpretation of their observed dropout and weak effects, not a directly tested mechanism
target_learning_goals: sustained engagement with cognitive training tasks
examples: Interface control was difficult to achieve in participants with mild dementia even when they were provided with a practice tutorials

The model rests on a set of fundamental competencies common to all US use plus application-specific competencies for RUSI, diagnostic, interventional or research US, and is intended as a foundation for developing or evaluating US courses for physical therapists.

article_title: How theory and design-based research can mature PBL practice and research.
citation: Dolmans, D. H. J. M. (2019). How theory and design-based research can mature PBL practice and research. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 24(5), 879–891. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09940-2
title: Contextual learning principle: center learning on whole, professionally relevant, ill-defined tasks to stimulate transfer
description: The paper presents contextual learning as a principle holding that learning should start by engaging students in tasks drawn from a professionally relevant context. It advocates task-centered instruction built on "whole, complex, ill-defined tasks", with tasks ordered from simple to complex and scaffolds that diminish, so learners notice critical features by comparing contrasting tasks and transfer knowledge to new situations.
requirements: Learning tasks must be meaningful, authentic or professionally relevant and presented as problems, cases or projects
constraints: The paper states this is a principle for preparing learners for future learning, not a tested intervention in this article
target_learners: higher education students, especially health professions students
target_learning_goals: transfer of learning to new situations
integration of knowledge, skills and attitudes
examples: In PBL, students' learning starts from discussing problems relevant for the students' future profession; the paper also describes inter-professional education around an elderly patient with chronic illness

article_title: How theory and design-based research can mature PBL practice and research.
citation: Dolmans, D. H. J. M. (2019). How theory and design-based research can mature PBL practice and research. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 24(5), 879–891. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09940-2
title: Constructive learning principle: students actively construct knowledge networks via prior knowledge activation and elaboration
description: The paper describes constructive learning as students acquiring new knowledge "in an active process in which they construct and reconstruct their knowledge networks". It grounds this in prior knowledge activation theory and elaboration theory, noting that stimulating meaningful new relations between prior and new knowledge positively affects long-term memory, and that PBL group discussions are designed to prompt elaboration, critical questions and reasoning.
requirements: Students must be encouraged to activate prior knowledge, elaborate, and relate new ideas to prior knowledge
constraints: The paper notes concept-map effectiveness might be dependent on the context, e.g. the degree to which students are stimulated to actively reconstruct and retrieve knowledge
target_learners: higher education students in PBL programs
target_learning_goals: deep approach to studying
long-term recall
meaningful learning
examples: Initial and final small-group discussions in PBL are aimed at stimulating students to construct and reconstruct their knowledge network
