article_title: How theory and design-based research can mature PBL practice and research.
citation: Dolmans, D. H. J. M. (2019). How theory and design-based research can mature PBL practice and research. Advances in Health Sciences Education, 24(5), 879–891. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-019-09940-2
title: Collaborative learning principle: collaboration enhances learning on complex tasks when learners are interdependent, psychologically safe and co-construct ideas
description: The paper presents collaborative learning as beneficial when learners work on ill-defined or complex tasks, share a common goal and depend on each other's contributions (interdependence theory). It adds that successful groups require sharing of knowledge, co-construction and open dialogue about cognitive disagreements, supported by psychological safety and social cohesion, and connects this to communities of practice theory in which learning is participation in a community with mutual goals.
requirements: The learning task should be ill-defined or complex
Students should share a common goal and depend on each other's contributions
Psychological safety is an important condition for a group to enhance learning
constraints: The paper notes social cohesion might have both positive and negative effects on learning, since too strong a social connection could lead members to avoid discussing cognitive disagreements
target_learners: students in small-group learning, e.g. PBL tutorial groups of 6–10 students
target_learning_goals: collaborative knowledge construction
learning from and with each other
examples: In PBL, students discuss complex problems in small groups in which they are expected to build upon each others' contributions

article_title: What Patients Want in a Smartphone App That Supports Colonoscopy Preparation: Qualitative Study to Inform a User-Centered Smartphone App.
citation: Sewitch MJ, Fallone CA, Ghali P, Lee GE. (2019). What Patients Want in a Smartphone App That Supports Colonoscopy Preparation: Qualitative Study to Inform a User-Centered Smartphone App. JMIR Mhealth Uhealth. https://doi.org/10.2196/12242
title: colonAPPscopy smartphone app for colonoscopy preparation
description: colonAPPscopy is a smartphone app developed from the focus group findings to support patients preparing for colonoscopy. Its content areas cover colonoscopy description and purpose, food, liquid, and medication restrictions, preparation logistics, clear liquid diet and laxative instructions, and "what to expect postcolonoscopy including when to seek medical help". Features include check boxes or drop-down menus for simple data input, daily tailored reminders and alerts beginning 7 days before colonoscopy, disability considerations (resizable content, color contrast, bell notification images), and safety considerations such as red alerts on medications needing cessation. Users must secure their smartphones with passwords for privacy of notifications
constraints: Videos were not included owing to budgetary constraints
Communication with endoscopy unit staff was not included owing to firewalls, though direct phone numbers are provided
target_learners: Patients aged 50-75 preparing for screening colonoscopy
target_learning_goals: Following multi-step colonoscopy preparation instructions correctly and on time
examples: The title screen includes the name of the sponsoring institution to signal a trusted source
Daily tailored reminders cover stopping medications, foods, and liquids, beginning the laxative, checking hospital cards, and finding an escort

article_title: Does academic interest play a more important role in medical sciences than in other disciplines? A nationwide cross-sectional study in China.
citation: Wu Hongbin, Zheng Juan, Li Shan, Guo Jianru. (2019). Does academic interest play a more important role in medical sciences than in other disciplines? A nationwide cross-sectional study in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1737-1
title: Consider academic interest in student recruitment and foster domain-specific interest to enhance academic performance
description: The article recommends that higher-education institutions treat academic interest as a selection and intervention lever. It states it "would therefore be beneficial for universities or colleges to consider academic interest as an important criterion when recruiting students" and that institutions "could foster domain-specific interest as an effective intervention strategy to enhance students' academic performance". The recommendation rests on the study's PSM-estimated positive effect of interest on grades across disciplines.

constraints: The article cautions that unmeasured variables such as personalities, learning styles and motivational preferences cannot be accounted for using PSM
The direction of the interest-performance relationship is unclear, so fostering interest may not be the operative causal lever
Interest was measured with a single item, which the authors say could undermine the validity of the measurement

target_learning_goals: Academic achievement (cumulative grades) across disciplines
examples: The study estimated ATTs of academic interest on cumulative grades for 54,398 undergraduates across five disciplines using propensity score matching

article_title: Does 'online confidence' predict application success and later academic performance in medical school? A UK-based national cohort study.
citation: Tiffin Paul A, Paton Lewis W. (2019). Does 'online confidence' predict application success and later academic performance in medical school? A UK-based national cohort study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-034437
title: Confidence judgement: an IRT-based metacognitive metric of the accuracy of self-appraisal of test performance
description: The article introduces 'confidence judgement', a novel measure defined as "the accuracy of one's own judgement in relation to one's ability at an online or written test", conceptualised as an aspect of metacognition. It is computed as the within-candidate correlation between the log odds of answering each item correctly, predicted by a two-parameter logistic IRT model, and the candidate's own confidence ratings rescaled as within-person z-scores to separate ability from trait confidence. A score of 1 represents perfect judgement, 0 no relationship, and −1 perfect inverse correlation.
requirements: Requires item-level confidence ratings and item responses suitable for a two-parameter logistic IRT model; candidates with no variation in confidence responses (about 10%) provide invalid data and must be excluded.
constraints: Traditional reliability metrics are not applicable because the measure is itself a within-person correlation coefficient; the article notes lower correlations in some analyses may reflect lower reliability.
target_learning_goals: metacognitive accuracy in self-assessment of test performance
examples: Applied to 56,785 UKCAT candidates who completed a pilot confidence rating within the decision analysis subtest between 2013 and 2016.
key_sources: Tiffin Paul A, Paton Lewis W. (2019). Does 'online confidence' predict application success and later academic performance in medical school? A UK-based national cohort study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-034437

article_title: Competencies required for general practitioners/family physicians in urban areas versus non-urban areas: a preliminary study.
citation: Mitsuyama Toshichika, Son Daisuke, Eto Masato. (2018). Competencies required for general practitioners/family physicians in urban areas versus non-urban areas: a preliminary study. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-018-0869-4
title: Contextual care framework: primary care physicians should provide the most appropriate care taking into account the context surrounding patients and medical personnel
description: The article connects its findings to "the theoretical framework called contextual care in primary care," in which "primary care physicians should provide the most appropriate care for patients taking into account the context surrounding the various backgrounds of patients and medical personnel." The study applies this framework to urban settings, concluding that a competency necessary for urban general practitioners is "to understand the urban context and provide contextual care suitable for urban areas." It serves as the explanatory account unifying the ten extracted urban competencies.
requirements: Understanding the characteristics of the surrounding context, including patient backgrounds and available medical resources, before selecting care approaches
constraints: The article presents the framework as an interpretive lens for its qualitative findings rather than a tested model
target_learners: Primary care physicians practicing in urban areas
target_learning_goals: Providing primary care appropriate to the urban context
Understanding how regional context shapes required clinical competencies
examples: The study's ten urban competency themes were interpreted as inseparable competencies grounded in the urban context of diverse socioeconomic conditions and segmented healthcare services.
key_sources: Mitsuyama Toshichika, Son Daisuke, Eto Masato. (2018). Competencies required for general practitioners/family physicians in urban areas versus non-urban areas: a preliminary study. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-018-0869-4

article_title: The virtual patient as a learning tool: a mixed quantitative qualitative study.
citation: Isaza-Restrepo Andrés, Gómez María Teresa, Cifuentes Gary, Argüello Arturo. (2018). The virtual patient as a learning tool: a mixed quantitative qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1395-8
title: Constructivist course design pattern: repeated varied cases, learning by doing, safe error, and permanent feedback around a VP
description: The course was structured around five stated constructivist principles: "Learning is a process of individual construction" through activity and interaction with others; meaningful learning anchored on prior experiences; "To confront repeatedly the same problem with different variations"; learning by doing in situations similar to the real professional environment; and the chance of making mistakes and getting proper permanent feedback. Each weekly two-hour session centered on a VP abdominal-pain case targeting a specific aspect of history taking and clinical reasoning, followed by small group question-guided discussions.
requirements: A VP tool with modifiable cases, small-group collaborative work, and professor guidance connecting prior and new knowledge
constraints: The authors state the VP as the sole methodology becomes somewhat monotonous and complementary methodologies must be used
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning
history taking
examples: 16 weeks of two-hour sessions, each around a VP case of abdominal pain of different etiology, with pre/post standardized-patient assessment
key_sources: Isaza-Restrepo Andrés, Gómez María Teresa, Cifuentes Gary, Argüello Arturo. (2018). The virtual patient as a learning tool: a mixed quantitative qualitative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1395-8

article_title: An evidence-based approach to understanding the competency development needs of the health service management workforce in Australia.
citation: Liang Zhanming, Blackstock Felicity C., Howard Peter F, Briggs David S, Leggat Sandra G, Wollersheim Dennis, Edvardsson David, Rahman Aziz. (2018). An evidence-based approach to understanding the competency development needs of the health service management workforce in Australia. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3760-z
title: Professional development for health service managers should be context-sensitive rather than one-size-fits-all
description: The article's findings that managerial strengths and weaknesses varied across sectors and organisations lead to the principle that management education and development should be designed for context. The authors state that "the design of ongoing management education and development should be context sensitive" and that "a 'one size fits all' approach to training is not likely to be effective". Separate consideration should be given to different management levels and groups from different sectors and organisations, with workforce development strategies formulated collaboratively between policy-makers and managers at system, organisational and team levels.
requirements: Competency assessment data that can reveal variation between management levels, sectors and organisations
Collaboration between policy-makers and managers at system, organisational and team levels
constraints: Demonstrated in the Victorian health service setting; the authors note further evaluation beyond Victoria is needed to understand competency levels nationally
target_learners: Middle-level health service managers in hospitals and community health services
target_learning_goals: Managerial competency development matched to sector-, organisation- and level-specific needs
examples: The study found competency scores varied between hospital and community health sector managers in both self- and combined-colleague assessments despite similar competency requirements
key_sources: Liang Zhanming, Blackstock Felicity C., Howard Peter F, Briggs David S, Leggat Sandra G, Wollersheim Dennis, Edvardsson David, Rahman Aziz. (2018). An evidence-based approach to understanding the competency development needs of the health service management workforce in Australia. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-018-3760-z

article_title: Materials count: Linear-spatial materials improve young children's addition strategies and accuracy, irregular arrays don't.
citation: Schiffman J, Laski EV. (2018). Linear-spatial materials improve young children's addition strategies and accuracy, irregular arrays don't. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0208832
title: Cognitive Alignment Framework for instructional design
description: The Cognitive Alignment Framework is a theoretical view of instructional design holding that "the more precisely physical materials and learning activities align with the desired mental representation, the more likely students are to acquire that representation." Key features of the target mental representation must be instantiated in the physical materials for learning to occur. The article extends the framework to cases with an indirect mapping, where materials instantiate an intermediary representation (the mental number line) underlying a desired procedural outcome (arithmetic strategies), rather than mapping directly onto the outcome itself.
requirements: Instructional materials must instantiate the key features of the underlying mental representation targeted for learning.
constraints: The framework was developed and tested with young children learning numerical magnitude and arithmetic; the article notes benefits depend on learners possessing relevant prior knowledge to activate.
target_learning_goals: arithmetic accuracy
use of advanced addition strategies
numerical magnitude knowledge
examples: Linear-spatial materials (discrete squares organized linearly on sticks of varying length) instantiated the linear and spatial features of the mental number line, whereas random star arrays did not.
key_sources: Schiffman J, Laski EV. (2018). Linear-spatial materials improve young children's addition strategies and accuracy, irregular arrays don't. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0208832

article_title: Virtual reality simulation in endoscopy training: Current evidence and future directions.
citation: Mahmood T, Scaffidi Michael Anthony, Khan Rishad, Grover Samir Chandra. (2018). Virtual reality simulation in endoscopy training: Current evidence and future directions. World Journal of Gastroenterology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6319131/
title: Cognitive load theory as a framework for feedback delivery in endoscopic simulation training
description: The review applies cognitive load theory to feedback in simulation-based endoscopy training. It defines cognitive load as "the effort used in working memory" with three types: intrinsic load tied to essential task components, extraneous load from non-essential distractions, and germane load involved in forming schemas. Feedback during procedures should be minimal and directive, while post-session facilitative feedback elicits trainee reflection.
requirements: Feedback delivery must be calibrated to the trainee's cognitive load
constraints: The framework is presented in the context of endoscopic simulation training
target_learning_goals: endoscopic technical skills
reflective learning and problem solving
key_sources: Mahmood T, Scaffidi Michael Anthony, Khan Rishad, Grover Samir Chandra. (2018). Virtual reality simulation in endoscopy training: Current evidence and future directions. World Journal of Gastroenterology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6319131/

article_title: Trauma simulation training: a randomized controlled trial -evaluating the effectiveness of the Imperial Femoral Intramedullary Nailing Cognitive Task Analysis (IFINCTA) tool.
citation: Bhattacharyya R, Sugand K, Al-Obaidi B, Sinha I, Bhattacharya R, Gupte CM. (2018). Trauma simulation training: a randomized controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of the Imperial Femoral Intramedullary Nailing Cognitive Task Analysis (IFINCTA) tool. Acta Orthopaedica. https://doi.org/10.1080/17453674.2018.1517442
title: Cognitive task analysis as expert-devised multimedia instruction making procedural steps easier to visualize and digest
description: The article frames cognitive task analysis (CTA) as a process in which "experts provide complex information to trainees in a logical and simplified manner", making procedural steps easier to visualize and digest. CTA packages technical steps, cognitive decision points, and potential errors and solutions, delivered here through simultaneous written and audiovisual modalities. It has been used to train pilots and in other surgical specialties, and the authors position it as relatively new to orthopedic training.
requirements: Expert elicitation (e.g., modified Delphi with consensus) to extract steps, decision points, and errors
Multimedia presentation combining written, video and audio modalities
constraints: The authors state the use of CTA within orthopedics is in its infancy; evidence cited is from other specialties and one prior orthopedic tool
target_learning_goals: cognitive understanding of procedural steps and intraoperative decision-making
examples: The IFINCTA tool operationalizes CTA for femoral intramedullary nailing; a prior tool (IKACTA) applied it to diagnostic knee arthroscopy
key_sources: Bhattacharyya R, Sugand K, Al-Obaidi B, Sinha I, Bhattacharya R, Gupte CM. (2018). Trauma simulation training: a randomized controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of the Imperial Femoral Intramedullary Nailing Cognitive Task Analysis (IFINCTA) tool. Acta Orthopaedica. https://doi.org/10.1080/17453674.2018.1517442

article_title: Animation and interactivity facilitate acquisition of pediatric life support skills: a randomized controlled trial using virtual patients versus video instruction.
citation: Lehmann Ronny, Lutz Thomas, Helling-Bakki Astrid, Kummer Sebastian, Huwendiek Sören, Bosse Hans Martin. (2019). Animation and interactivity facilitate acquisition of pediatric life support skills: a randomized controlled trial using virtual patients versus video instruction. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1442-5
title: Combine animation with interactivity in self-instruction materials for complex procedural skills
description: The article concludes that neither animation nor interactivity alone is optimal: "the combination of animations and interactive learning by detailed VP facilitates optimal reflective skill acquisition". Video alone led to suboptimal performance quality, and interactive VP with only static media produced the poorest competency ratings. Designers of self-instruction for procedural skills should therefore embed animated media (video clips) inside interactive, case-based environments rather than delivering either component separately.
requirements: Animated media depicting the procedural steps
Interactive elements (questions, feedback) within a case-based format
constraints: Transferability to clinical practice and sustained retention of skills over time were not addressed in the study
Findings are from fifth-year medical students with prior adult CPR training, not beginners
target_learners: Medical students learning pediatric basic life support
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor procedural skills and overall competency in resuscitation
examples: In the trial, video sequences were removed from VP for the static group as a quasi-control for animation effects, and a video-only group served as quasi-control for VP interactivity
key_sources: Lehmann Ronny, Lutz Thomas, Helling-Bakki Astrid, Kummer Sebastian, Huwendiek Sören, Bosse Hans Martin. (2019). Animation and interactivity facilitate acquisition of pediatric life support skills: a randomized controlled trial using virtual patients versus video instruction. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1442-5

article_title: Improving the Learning Experience through Evidence-based Education.
citation: Love, J. N., Messman, A. M., & Merritt, C. (2019). Improving the Learning Experience through Evidence-based Education. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2018.10.41320
title: Conceptual frameworks (theories, best practices, models) as the basis for educational design decisions and outcome selection
description: Central to success in any educational initiative, the article argues, is selecting a conceptual framework: theories, best practices, or models. The chosen framework highlights the designers' theory most likely to accomplish the intended goal, and "Once selected, this framework becomes the basis for decision-making regarding the design of the education experience and outcomes to be measured". Additional relevant theories may supplement one dominant framework.
requirements: An early determination of the conceptual framework appropriate to the educational goal, selected from among candidate theories and best practices
constraints: From an academic perspective, the lack of a conceptual framework is a common reason for journals to reject scholarly submissions
target_learners: physician educators designing curricula, rotations, workshops, and presentations
target_learning_goals: designing and evaluating educational initiatives in medical education
examples: Example 2 redesigned an ophthalmologic trauma presentation using non-analytical reasoning and Kolb's experiential learning theory; Example 3 framed a pediatrics curriculum redesign in situated learning
key_sources: Love, J. N., Messman, A. M., & Merritt, C. (2019). Improving the Learning Experience through Evidence-based Education. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2018.10.41320

article_title: When to Introduce Three-Dimensional Visualization Technology into Surgical Residency: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Lin Chen, Gao Junyi, Zheng Hua, Zhao Jun, Yang Hua, Zheng Yue, Cao Yihan, Chen Yufei, Wu Guoliang, Lin Guole, Yu Jianchun, Li Hanzhong, Pan Hui, Liao Quan, Zhao Yupei. (2019). When to Introduce Three-Dimensional Visualization Technology into Surgical Residency: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Systems. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10916-019-1157-0
title: Combined 2D+3D imaging learning model: "2D + 3D → 3D → 2D"
description: The article contrasts a classical learning model, "2D → 3D → 2D", in which trainees must imagine 3D structures from 2D cross-sectional images, a "long and difficult" process that often yields inaccurate 3D structures, with a new model, "2D + 3D → 3D → 2D". In the new model, combined 2D and 3D images allow structures to be corrected "in both a timely and repeated manner", producing accurate 3D structures that are then applied in clinical practice. The authors speculate that introducing this model at PGY1 may improve the anatomy-imaging-surgery learning curve.
requirements: Requires 3D reconstructed images generated from the same CT cases as the 2D images, as provided by the multi-touch visualization touchscreen table used in the study
constraints: The model's benefit was observed for junior (PGY1) residents; senior residents showed no significant differences between modalities
The authors state the hypothesis needs further confirmation with novel standard training courses combining 2D and 3D technology
target_learning_goals: anatomy learning
imaging reasoning
establishing accurate 3D anatomical structures from 2D images
examples: The trial provided the 3D group with 3D reconstructed images and the CT group with original CT images from the same nine built-in cases on the MVT table
key_sources: Lin Chen, Gao Junyi, Zheng Hua, Zhao Jun, Yang Hua, Zheng Yue, Cao Yihan, Chen Yufei, Wu Guoliang, Lin Guole, Yu Jianchun, Li Hanzhong, Pan Hui, Liao Quan, Zhao Yupei. (2019). When to Introduce Three-Dimensional Visualization Technology into Surgical Residency: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Systems. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10916-019-1157-0

article_title: Evaluation of the role of near-peer teaching in critical appraisal skills learning: a randomized crossover trial.
citation: Widyahening Indah S., Findyartini Ardi, Ranakusuma Respati W., Dewiasty Esthika, Harimurti Kuntjoro. (2019). Evaluation of the role of near-peer teaching in critical appraisal skills learning: a randomized crossover trial. International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.5c39.b55b
title: Cognitive congruence theory as an explanation for near-peer tutors' acceptance and effectiveness
description: Cognitive congruence theory holds that a teacher whose knowledge base is "similar (i.e., congruent) to the learner's is likely to be more effective than an expert in the field who has a dissimilar knowledge base". The authors invoke it to explain why students rated near-peer tutorials more highly, and add that peer tutors "provide a more comfortable and safe learning environment for students, as they come from a similar social environment". In this study the near-peer tutors were recently graduated doctors selected for proximity in age to fourth-year students.
requirements: Tutors selected on the basis of proximity in level and age to the learners
constraints: Offered as the authors' interpretation of the acceptance results, not tested directly in this trial
target_learning_goals: Critical appraisal skills within evidence-based medicine
examples: Near-peer tutors were newly graduated doctors aged 23-26 (median 24) teaching fourth-year students aged 22.1 years on average, after a three-day training of teachers on tutoring skills and group dynamics.
key_sources: Widyahening Indah S., Findyartini Ardi, Ranakusuma Respati W., Dewiasty Esthika, Harimurti Kuntjoro. (2019). Evaluation of the role of near-peer teaching in critical appraisal skills learning: a randomized crossover trial. International Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5116/ijme.5c39.b55b

article_title: The Influence of Physical Fitness on Reasons for Academy Separation in Law Enforcement Recruits.
citation: Lockie R.G., Balfany K., Bloodgood A.M., Moreno M.R., Cesario K.A., Dulla J.M., Dawes J.J., Orr R.M. (2019). The Influence of Physical Fitness on Reasons for Academy Separation in Law Enforcement Recruits. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16030372
title: Law enforcement academy training staff should consider the total training load imposed during academy so it does not exceed some recruits' physical capabilities
description: The article recommends that agencies monitor the physical training load recruits experience, because a paramilitary 'one-size-fits-all' model may apply inappropriate training loads to less fit recruits and contribute to injury, separation, or reduced motivation. The authors state LEA training staff "should consider the total training load they impose during academy to ensure it is not beyond the physical capabilities of some recruits". They also suggest moderating running volume, citing evidence that lower running mileage reduced injury without harming physical readiness.
requirements: Awareness of each recruit's current fitness level relative to the imposed training load
constraints: Recommendation is grounded in retrospective data from one agency whose PT emphasized high volumes of running; the authors note results could have been influenced by the PT practices adopted by the LEA staff
target_learning_goals: completing academy physical training requirements
graduating from academy
examples: The study's LEA used a paramilitary one-size-fits-all model with circuit-style callisthenics and formation runs; recruits who separated for personal reasons had completed fewer MSFT shuttles than graduates
key_sources: Lockie R.G., Balfany K., Bloodgood A.M., Moreno M.R., Cesario K.A., Dulla J.M., Dawes J.J., Orr R.M. (2019). The Influence of Physical Fitness on Reasons for Academy Separation in Law Enforcement Recruits. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16030372

article_title: Boost your brain, while having a break! The effects of long-term cognitively engaging physical activity breaks on children's executive functions and academic achievement.
citation: Egger Fabienne, Benzing Valentin, Conzelmann Achim, Schmidt Mirko. (2019). Boost your brain, while having a break! The effects of long-term cognitively engaging physical activity breaks on children's executive functions and academic achievement. PLoS ONE 14(3): e0212482. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0212482
title: Cognitive stimulation hypothesis: cognitively demanding exercise activates brain regions underlying higher-order cognition, producing domain-specific EF benefits
description: The article invokes the "cognitive stimulation hypothesis" (Tomporowski et al.) to explain why cognitively engaging PA benefits executive functions. Its assumption is that "cognitively demanding exercises activate similar brain regions used to control higher-order cognitive processes", so repeated activation through demanding exercise yields benefits "in the circumscribed domains of executive functioning". The study tests it by systematically varying cognitive engagement across three PA break conditions.
requirements: PA exercises must carry genuine cognitive demands (e.g., rule changes, keyword-movement remapping) to induce cognitive engagement
constraints: The article notes the mechanism is only indirectly supported: the cognition group improved mathematics without improving shifting, so CE is not the only crucial characteristic responsible for EF gains
target_learning_goals: executive functions (updating, inhibition, shifting)
academic achievement in mathematics
examples: The combo condition's "Horserace" game required children to update new keywords, inhibit previous movements, and shift between word-movement pairings as difficulty incremented
key_sources: Egger Fabienne, Benzing Valentin, Conzelmann Achim, Schmidt Mirko. (2019). Boost your brain, while having a break! The effects of long-term cognitively engaging physical activity breaks on children's executive functions and academic achievement. PLoS ONE 14(3): e0212482. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0212482

article_title: Boost your brain, while having a break! The effects of long-term cognitively engaging physical activity breaks on children's executive functions and academic achievement.
citation: Egger Fabienne, Benzing Valentin, Conzelmann Achim, Schmidt Mirko. (2019). Boost your brain, while having a break! The effects of long-term cognitively engaging physical activity breaks on children's executive functions and academic achievement. PLoS ONE 14(3): e0212482. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0212482
title: Design classroom PA breaks to combine physical exertion with high cognitive engagement rather than relying on pure aerobic activity
description: The article concludes that cognitively engaging PA breaks are the most effective classroom-based format for cognitive outcomes: "only a combination of long-term PA breaks with high cognitive engagement leads to a stronger improvement in EFs". Pure aerobic breaks with little cognitive effort failed to enhance EFs or academic achievement, while breaks embedding rule changes and task switching benefited shifting and mathematics.
requirements: Breaks must include cognitively demanding elements such as changing rules, additional keywords, and altered corresponding movements
Teachers need training in the program's principles and materials before implementation
constraints: Classroom space and time limit achievable intensity; the suggested 70%–85% heart-rate range was hard to reach
Implementation fidelity declined over time (77% of breaks implemented in the first 10 weeks, decreasing by 7% in the second half)
target_learning_goals: executive functions, particularly shifting
mathematics performance
examples: Teachers delivered two 10-minute breaks daily over 20 weeks; combo-group games like "Horserace" paired running on the spot with keyword-triggered movement changes at increasing difficulty
key_sources: Egger Fabienne, Benzing Valentin, Conzelmann Achim, Schmidt Mirko. (2019). Boost your brain, while having a break! The effects of long-term cognitively engaging physical activity breaks on children's executive functions and academic achievement. PLoS ONE 14(3): e0212482. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0212482

article_title: Simulation of Urgent Airway Management in a Postthyroidectomy Hematoma.
citation: Wu Kitty, Kim Stephanie, Rajasingham Shihan J., Bruni Ida, Fung Kevin, Roth Kathryn E. (2019). Simulation of Urgent Airway Management in a Postthyroidectomy Hematoma. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10802
title: Cognitive load theory applied to simulation scenario design (intrinsic, extraneous, and germane loads)
description: The article invokes cognitive load theory to explain why distractor removal improved performance: "there is limited working memory within the human cognitive architecture," and excess cognitive load harms learning. It maps three components onto the simulation: intrinsic load is the task complexity of assimilating patient information to identify the complication; extraneous load encompasses superfluous distractors such as family member questions and consultant phone calls; germane load is the learning process converting working memory into long-term memory.
requirements: Scenario designers must distinguish task-essential complexity (intrinsic) from removable interruptions (extraneous) when building scenarios for a given learner level
constraints: The article applies the framework specifically to simulation scenario design in health professions education
target_learners: Junior residents in surgical and acute-care specialties
target_learning_goals: Managing rare emergency complications without overwhelming working memory
examples: The authors state the distractors in previous iterations negatively impacted learning, citing cognitive load literature
key_sources: Wu Kitty, Kim Stephanie, Rajasingham Shihan J., Bruni Ida, Fung Kevin, Roth Kathryn E. (2019). Simulation of Urgent Airway Management in a Postthyroidectomy Hematoma. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10802

article_title: Non-guided self-learning program for high-proficiency optical diagnosis of diminutive and small colorectal lesions: A single-endoscopist pilot study.
citation: Bustamante-Balén M, Satorres C, Puchades L, Navarro B, García-Morales N, Alonso N, Ponce M, Argüello L, Pons-Beltrán V. (2019). Non-guided self-learning program for high-proficiency optical diagnosis of diminutive and small colorectal lesions: A single-endoscopist pilot study. World Journal of Gastroenterology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6421233/
title: Require continuous practice with a refresher course after any long non-practice period to maintain optical diagnosis performance
description: The article concludes that self-learning can reach expert-level optical diagnosis but that the skill decays without use: "continuous practice is needed to maintain performance and a refresher course is needed if a long non-practice period occurs." Performance parameters behave differently after a stopping period, which the authors say should be considered when planning a monitoring program.
requirements: A monitoring program that tracks performance parameters, since the article states performance values behave differently after a stopping period
constraints: Observed in a single-endoscopist pilot with a highly motivated trainee in a FIT-positive screening population; the article notes this may enhance the learning process
target_learners: endoscopists learning optical diagnosis of colorectal lesions
target_learning_goals: accurate optical diagnosis of diminutive colorectal lesions
maintenance of diagnostic competency over time
examples: The study embedded a predefined 6-month stopping period with no OD and no refresher course, after which almost all performance parameters dropped significantly
key_sources: Bustamante-Balén M, Satorres C, Puchades L, Navarro B, García-Morales N, Alonso N, Ponce M, Argüello L, Pons-Beltrán V. (2019). Non-guided self-learning program for high-proficiency optical diagnosis of diminutive and small colorectal lesions: A single-endoscopist pilot study. World Journal of Gastroenterology. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6421233/

article_title: Relationship among school socioeconomic status, teacher-student relationship, and middle school students' academic achievement in China: Using the multilevel mediation model.
citation: Xuan Xin, Xue Ye, Zhang Cai, Luo Yuhan, Jiang Wen, Qi Mengdi, Wang Yun. (2019). Relationship among school socioeconomic status, teacher-student relationship, and middle school students’ academic achievement in China: Using the multilevel mediation model. PLoS ONE 14(3): e0213783. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0213783
title: Context-process-outcomes model of school effects
description: The article organizes its inquiry with the "context-process-outcomes" model developed by Roeser et al., in which "school context may influence students’ developmental outcomes through multiple process factors" such as school-level, classroom-level and student-level characteristics. School SES is treated as a context input, teacher-student relationship as a process factor, and academic achievement as the outcome. The study’s multilevel mediation results are presented as empirical verification of this model in Chinese middle schools.
requirements: Testing the model requires measuring context, process and outcome variables simultaneously in nested student-within-school data, as the study did with HLM.
constraints: The article notes many process factors in the model have not been tested empirically and their effectiveness remains uncertain given school context and student outcomes.
target_learners: middle school students in grades 7–9 in mainland China
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement
Chinese (language) achievement
examples: The study operationalized context as school SES, process as students’ perceived math and Chinese teacher-student relationships, and outcomes as standardized math and Chinese test scores.
key_sources: Xuan Xin, Xue Ye, Zhang Cai, Luo Yuhan, Jiang Wen, Qi Mengdi, Wang Yun. (2019). Relationship among school socioeconomic status, teacher-student relationship, and middle school students’ academic achievement in China: Using the multilevel mediation model. PLoS ONE 14(3): e0213783. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0213783

article_title: Practice makes perfect! Patient safety starts in medical school: Do instructional videos improve clinical skills and hygiene procedures in undergraduate medical students?
citation: Bäwert Andjela, Holzinger Anita. (2019). Practice makes perfect! Patient safety starts in medical school: Do instructional videos improve clinical skills and hygiene procedures in undergraduate medical students? GMS J Med Educ. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001224.shtml
title: Combine online instructional videos with written course materials to increase effectiveness and retention of practical clinical skills
description: The article recommends supplementing written learning scripts with three-dimensional video demonstrations of clinical and hygiene procedures, made permanently available online so students can review them before practical placements. It states that "the combination of e-learning formats, such as online videos, with conventional formats, such as textbooks or lecture notes, is well suited to increase effectiveness and sustainability when learning practical skills". The videos were shown shortly before the OSCE as preparation for the first clinical clerkship.
requirements: Videos must demonstrate precise sequences of manual steps that two-dimensional written material cannot fully convey, and be permanently available online for repeated viewing.
constraints: The study could not show significant OSCE improvement from the videos; randomized, case-control studies are needed to gather supporting evidence for this method.
target_learners: undergraduate medical students preparing for their first clinical clerkship
target_learning_goals: clinical skills such as urinary catheter insertion and sterile technique
hygiene standards including hand disinfection
patient safety
examples: Five videos were produced for the Basic Medical Skills course, covering sterile gloves, hand disinfection, surgical hand disinfection, and urinary catheter insertion in men and women; 647 students viewed the catheter videos in computer learning studios before the OSCE.
key_sources: Bäwert Andjela, Holzinger Anita. (2019). Practice makes perfect! Patient safety starts in medical school: Do instructional videos improve clinical skills and hygiene procedures in undergraduate medical students? GMS J Med Educ. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2019-36/zma001224.shtml

article_title: Development and evaluation of a training model for paracentetic suprapubic cystostomy and catheterization.
citation: Gao Wei, Ou Tongwen, Jia Jianguo, Fan Jie, Xu Jianjun, Li Jin, Cui Xin, He Xinzhou, Li Xueli. (2019). Development and evaluation of a training model for paracentetic suprapubic cystostomy and catheterization. Clinics. https://doi.org/10.6061/clinics/2019/e435
title: Comprehensive simulation training combining literature review, instructor video, model preparation, and hands-on practice
description: The experimental training protocol layered four components: reading related English literature over approximately 50 days, watching an instructor's video of suprapubic catheter insertion, personally preparing the simulation model, and practicing puncture and catheter insertion with it. The control group received the same protocol "except without hands-on practice using the model". This layered design produced significantly higher performance scores than video and literature alone.
requirements: Access to a reusable, low-cost simulation model so every trainee can practice hands-on
An instructor-recorded video of the procedure and related literature for pre-study
constraints: Evaluated only with pre-clinical fourth-year medical students who had no prior patient contact or procedural experience
target_learning_goals: surgical procedure skills for suprapubic catheter insertion
procedural understanding and confidence
examples: Experimental-group students read literature during the winter break, watched the instructor video, prepared the model, and practiced the puncture before being video-recorded for expert scoring
key_sources: Gao Wei, Ou Tongwen, Jia Jianguo, Fan Jie, Xu Jianjun, Li Jin, Cui Xin, He Xinzhou, Li Xueli. (2019). Development and evaluation of a training model for paracentetic suprapubic cystostomy and catheterization. Clinics. https://doi.org/10.6061/clinics/2019/e435

article_title: Pairing pedagogical and genomic advances to prepare advanced practice nurses for the era of precision health.
citation: Flowers Elena, Martin Margaret, Abid Hamza, Binford Sasha, Mackin Lynda. (2019). Pairing pedagogical and genomic advances to prepare advanced practice nurses for the era of precision health. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1542-x
title: Community of Inquiry framework as the conceptual basis for hybrid online/in-person curricular design
description: The article grounds its hybrid course redesign in the Community of Inquiry conceptual framework, which it says "focuses on process and iteration of curricular design". Under this framework, students first obtained rote knowledge through online modules, reinforced knowledge through online discussion boards, and then engaged collaboratively with faculty during in-person meetings. Student feedback gathered informally and formally was applied to each iteration of the curriculum during and after each term.
requirements: Availability of content anytime, anywhere (asynchronous); moderation and facilitation of open online forums; and faculty collaboration, as the article lists as key components of knowledge management for online learning
constraints: Applied in a graduate nursing program where the majority of coursework is in-person and online courses are primarily limited to electives
target_learners: Graduate-level Advanced Practice Nursing students in a Master's of Science program
target_learning_goals: Applying genomic knowledge and competencies in clinical practice
examples: The three-course 2016–2017 genomics series used asynchronous online modules with self-paced graded quizzes, online discussion boards, and in-person sessions; the first and second courses met in-person four times over 10 weeks and the final course was entirely online
key_sources: Flowers Elena, Martin Margaret, Abid Hamza, Binford Sasha, Mackin Lynda. (2019). Pairing pedagogical and genomic advances to prepare advanced practice nurses for the era of precision health. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1542-x

article_title: Learning end-of-life care within a constructivist model: Undergraduate nursing students' experiences.
citation: Van der Wath, A.E. & Du Toit, P.H., 2015, 'Learning end-of-life care within a constructivist model: Undergraduate nursing students' experiences', Curationis 38(2), Art. #1537. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v38i2.1537
title: Constructivist model of experiential learning for end-of-life care nursing education
description: The article frames end-of-life care learning within a constructivist model of experiential learning in which "students are believed to interpret their worlds actively and construct knowledge through processes of reflection". Learning proceeds through Kolb's cycle of concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation. The model was operationalised in a second-year nursing module through co-operative group presentations and written reflections.
requirements: Learning opportunities must provide concrete experiences followed by reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation and active experimentation, supported by structured reflection such as written narratives
constraints: Studied within one second-year psychiatric nursing module at a single higher education institution; the study collected only qualitative data and did not illuminate real-life clinical experiences
target_learning_goals: end-of-life care competence including self-competence, emotional awareness and value clarification about death and dying
key_sources: Van der Wath, A.E. & Du Toit, P.H., 2015, 'Learning end-of-life care within a constructivist model: Undergraduate nursing students' experiences', Curationis 38(2), Art. #1537. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v38i2.1537

article_title: A model of collaboration for the implementation of problem-based learning in nursing education in South Africa.
citation: Rakhudu, M.A., Davhana-Maselesele, M. & Useh, U. (2017). A model of collaboration for the implementation of problem-based learning in nursing education in South Africa. Curationis 40(1), a1765. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v40i1.1765
title: A six-element model of collaboration for implementing problem-based learning in nursing education
description: The article presents a theory of collaboration for effective PBL implementation in nursing education, developed through concept analysis, relationship construction, description and evaluation. As printed, "The model for collaboration in implementation of PBL has six main elements: higher education, nursing education and health care services (context), institutions initiating PBL, clinical services, colleges affiliated to PBL universities, students and healthcare users (recipients), centres of excellence in PBL (agents), effective implementation of PBL (terminus) collaboration, (process) and commitment, communication, cooperation, trust and respect (dynamics)." The model is intended as a frame of reference for designing collaboration interventions.
requirements: Collaborators share a common goal, vision and mission, and organisational climate and culture of the PBL institutions can influence collaboration activities
constraints: The model has not yet been tested
The empirical data from nurse managers were from one province, and therefore, the findings can only be transferable within the province
target_learners: undergraduate nursing students in PBL programmes in South African nursing education institutions
target_learning_goals: effective implementation of problem-based learning
integration of theory into clinical practice
examples: The model was developed from opinions of nurse educators at three South African universities offering PBL and nurse managers at all three North West Province hospitals placing PBL students
key_sources: Rakhudu, M.A., Davhana-Maselesele, M. & Useh, U. (2017). A model of collaboration for the implementation of problem-based learning in nursing education in South Africa. Curationis 40(1), a1765. https://doi.org/10.4102/curationis.v40i1.1765

article_title: Just watching is not enough: Fostering simulation-based learning with collaboration scripts.
citation: Zottmann Jan M., Dieckmann Peter, Taraszow Tatjana, Rall Marcus, Fischer Frank. (2018). Just watching is not enough: Fostering simulation-based learning with collaboration scripts. GMS Journal for Medical Education 35(3), Doc35. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2018-35/zma001181.shtml
title: Collaboration scripts as scaffolds distributing roles and activities among learners
description: Collaboration scripts are instructional supports for group learning: "sets of scaffolds that distribute roles and activities among learners in group learning situations" that structure learning by "introducing a sequence for collaborative activities". The article applies them to observational phases of simulation-based training, where they direct attention to specific CRM heuristics and prompt elicitation, externalisation, and consensus building, drawing on script theory of guidance in computer-supported collaborative learning.
requirements: Scripts must induce specific activities, assign an order to them, and assign roles to learners, as the study's script did
constraints: Only few empirical studies have investigated collaboration scripts in medical education and simulation-based learning, per the article
target_learning_goals: acquisition of heuristics (CRM principles) for coping with critical incidents
collaborative knowledge-building activities
examples: In the study, dyads observed one CRM principle each, with an analyst for positive and an analyst for negative situations, switching roles after each scenario
key_sources: Zottmann Jan M., Dieckmann Peter, Taraszow Tatjana, Rall Marcus, Fischer Frank. (2018). Just watching is not enough: Fostering simulation-based learning with collaboration scripts. GMS Journal for Medical Education 35(3), Doc35. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2018-35/zma001181.shtml

article_title: Does narrative medicine education improve nursing students' empathic abilities and academic achievement? A randomised controlled trial.
citation: Yang Ningxi, Xiao Han, Cao Yingnan, Li Shiyue, Yan Hong, Wang Yifang. (2018). Does narrative medicine education improve nursing students’ empathic abilities and academic achievement? A randomised controlled trial. The Journal of International Medical Research. https://doi.org/10.1177/0300060518781476
title: Combine narrative medicine theory with clinical practice rather than theory alone when teaching empathy to nursing students
description: The article concludes that narrative medicine education works best when theoretical study is paired with supervised clinical practice: "Narrative medicine education that combines theory with practice is an effective strategy for improving nursing students’ empathic ability and academic achievement." Theory-only instruction produced smaller, largely non-significant gains, while the practice component (parallel charts, diary exchange, reflective writing) drove the differences from controls. The authors also state that "narrative medicine interventions alone have limited effects."
requirements: Trained narrative medicine teachers and nurse mentors
opportunities for students to interact with patients and write about their narratives
constraints: The trial was conducted with predominantly female Grade 3 nursing students in China; the authors note the impact on male nursing students was difficult to assess and hypotheses must be tested in a larger sample
target_learners: young nurses in their first years of practice
target_learning_goals: empathic ability
academic achievement
humanistic care
nurse–patient communication
examples: Group 3 received the same 12-session theoretical course as Group 2 plus an autumn-term clinical practice component with mentor-led groups of 10 students, and outperformed the control group on empathy and internship scores
key_sources: Yang Ningxi, Xiao Han, Cao Yingnan, Li Shiyue, Yan Hong, Wang Yifang. (2018). Does narrative medicine education improve nursing students’ empathic abilities and academic achievement? A randomised controlled trial. The Journal of International Medical Research. https://doi.org/10.1177/0300060518781476

article_title: Enhancement of student perceptions of learner-centeredness and community of inquiry in flipped classrooms.
citation: Lee Young Hwan, Kim Kyong-Jee. (2018). Enhancement of student perceptions of learner-centeredness and community of inquiry in flipped classrooms. BMC Medical Education, 18, 242. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1347-3
title: Community of Inquiry framework: teaching, social, and cognitive presence as elements of a successful learning environment
description: The community of inquiry framework "represents elements of a successful learning environment by creating a collaborative-constructivist learning experience". It comprises three elements: teaching presence (design and facilitation of learning experiences by the instructor), social presence (level of interaction and cohesiveness of participants), and cognitive presence (extent to which students construct meaning through sustained communication). The article operationalizes it with the 34-item Revised Community of Inquiry instrument, drawn from 10 sub-scales across the three presences, and uses it to measure change in perceptions in a flipped medical course.
requirements: Measurement requires a validated instrument; the study used a Korean version translated and validated by Yu and Richardson with Cronbach's α of 0.91 or higher for all three presences
target_learning_goals: constructing meaning through sustained communication
collaborative-constructivist learning experience
examples: Pre- and post-course administration of the 34-item instrument (13 teaching, 9 social, 12 cognitive presence items) during the first and last week of the semester
key_sources: Lee Young Hwan, Kim Kyong-Jee. (2018). Enhancement of student perceptions of learner-centeredness and community of inquiry in flipped classrooms. BMC Medical Education, 18, 242. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1347-3

article_title: Construction and validation of competency frameworks for the training of nurses in emergencies.
citation: Miranda Fernanda Berchelli Girão, Mazzo Alessandra, Alves Gerson Pereira-Junior. (2018). Construction and validation of competency frameworks for the training of nurses in emergencies. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.2631-3061
title: Competency frameworks as descriptions of knowledge, skills and attitudes organized to show progressive development across training
description: The article defines competency frameworks as "descriptions of the knowledge, skills, and attitudes pertaining to each competency expected during the students’ training", organized so that they show "the results of the progressive development of students based on competencies" from university entry to post-graduate training. They describe competencies to be repeatedly demonstrated in clinical environments of different complexity, and in this study they structure the ABC emergency-care competencies expected of nursing students at each level of progression.
requirements: Frameworks must be organized to show progressive development of students based on competencies, and competencies must be repeatedly demonstrated during curricular schedules in clinical environments with different levels of complexity.
target_learners: nursing trainees in supervised curricular internship
target_learning_goals: airway, breathing and circulation (ABC) emergency care competencies: knowledge, skills and attitudes
examples: The study's frameworks classify expected competencies into three levels: level 1 (student before immersion in the supervised curricular internship), level 2 (student immersed in the supervised curricular internship) and level 3 (nurse).
key_sources: Miranda Fernanda Berchelli Girão, Mazzo Alessandra, Alves Gerson Pereira-Junior. (2018). Construction and validation of competency frameworks for the training of nurses in emergencies. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.2631-3061

article_title: Effectiveness of the Malnutrition eLearning Course for Global Capacity Building in the Management of Malnutrition: Cross-Country Interrupted Time-Series Study.
citation: Choi S, Yuen HM, Annan R, Pickup T, Pulman A, Monroy-Valle M, Aduku NEL, Kyei-Boateng S, Velásquez Monzón CI, Portillo Sermeño CE, Penn A, Ashworth A, Jackson AA. (2018). Effectiveness of the Malnutrition eLearning Course for Global Capacity Building in the Management of Malnutrition: Cross-Country Interrupted Time-Series Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/10396
title: Constructivist scenario-based eLearning design with authentic tasks and embedded reflective questions
description: The course is designed on a constructivist view of learning as "an active process of constructing knowledge," using two key design strategies: (1) scenario- and task-based learning activities using authentic cases to support acquiring, linking, integration, and application of knowledge and skills, and (2) activities embedded within content, including revisable reflective questions and conversational style to promote active reflection and cognitive dialogue. The course incorporates aspects of problem-based learning and situated learning with authentic tasks, delivered through 3 interactive modules using rich media that runs on low-specification computers with limited internet speed.
requirements: Interactive, scenario-based design with authentic cases
Content conforming to WHO case-management guidelines
Accessibility on low-specification computers with limited internet speed, with a CD version for areas without internet access
constraints: No support or assistance was given to participants while taking the course
Course was originally implemented in Adobe Flash (being reimplemented in html5)
target_learners: In-service health professionals working with undernourished children
Educators and trainers in medical, nursing, and health science schools
target_learning_goals: Identification and classification of malnutrition
Assessment and screening of children for malnutrition
Management of malnourished children using WHO Ten Steps
Differentiating chronic and acute malnutrition
Supporting mothers and caregivers to prevent recurrence
examples: The course uses virtual patients and branching scenarios for clinical reasoning, with modules on definition/classification, identification, and management of malnutrition, each taking 2-3 hours asynchronously
key_sources: Choi S, Yuen HM, Annan R, Pickup T, Pulman A, Monroy-Valle M, Aduku NEL, Kyei-Boateng S, Velásquez Monzón CI, Portillo Sermeño CE, Penn A, Ashworth A, Jackson AA. (2018). Effectiveness of the Malnutrition eLearning Course for Global Capacity Building in the Management of Malnutrition: Cross-Country Interrupted Time-Series Study. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/10396
